en: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
I pay homage to the Teacher of Reality, who has extinguished all darkness in every respect and has pulled sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death;
I shall now expound the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra.
The Commentary says:

Now, desiring to compose this treatise, I wish to manifest that my own teacher’s essential nature is most venerable and transcends all the assembly of noble ones; therefore, I first praise his virtues before proffering my respectful salutation.
The term "all" (sarva) refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One; because he is able to destroy darkness, he is called the "Extinction of Darkness" (tamo-nirghāta).
Regarding the phrase "the extinction of all kinds of darkness," this means the extinction of all categories of darkness concerning all objects.
Because various forms of ignorance can obscure the true meaning and obstruct true vision, they are called "darkness" (*tamas*).

Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained the eternal antidote; because he has realized the state of non-arising regarding all objects and in all aspects of darkness, it is termed "extinction" (*nirodha*).
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have extinguished all darkness, because they have not utterly severed defiled ignorance, this is not in every respect.
Why is this? Because regarding the Buddha’s teachings—encompassing extremely distant times and places as well as infinite varieties of meanings—their non-defiled ignorance has not yet been severed.
Having already praised the Blessed One’s perfection of virtues for his own benefit, one should next praise the Buddha’s perfection of virtues for the benefit of others.

Regarding the phrase "one who pulls sentient beings out from the mire of birth and death": because this cycle of birth and death is the place where all sentient beings sink and drown, and because it is so difficult to escape, it is likened to mud.

Sentient beings are submerged within it without rescue; out of compassion, the World-Honored One bestows upon them what is appropriate for each, using the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma to pull them out and deliver them.
Having praised the Buddha’s virtues, I next prostrate in reverence.
"Prostration to such a teacher of reality as he is" means that one pays homage by bowing the head to his feet; thus it is called "prostration.
Because he possesses all the aforementioned qualities of benefit for both self and others, he is described as "such."
One who provides instruction and admonition that is according to reality and without error is called a "Teacher of Reason.

The term "Teacher of Reason" manifests the virtue of benefiting others; it refers to one who is able to skillfully expound the correct teaching according to reason and pull sentient beings out from the mire of saṃsāra, not by means of power, vows, or supernormal powers.
"Having paid homage to the Teacher of Reality, what is it that I intend to do?
I shall explain the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra"—it is called a "treatise" (śāstra) because it instructs students.
What is this treatise?
This refers to the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
What is meant by "Abhidharma"?
The verse says:
The Abhidharma is defined as pure wisdom along with its attendants, as well as the various wisdoms and treatises that can attain this.
The commentary states:
"Wisdom" refers to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); "pure" refers to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*); and the retinue of pure wisdom is termed "attendants."
Thus, the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) taken as a whole are called Abhidharma; this is the ultimate (*paramārtha*) Abhidharma.
If one speaks of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) Abhidharma, it refers to the wisdoms and treatises by which this [ultimate Abhidharma] is attained.

"Insight" (*prajñā*) refers to this contaminated wisdom acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), as well as the wisdoms arising from reflection (*cintāmayī*), hearing (*śrutamayī*), and innate acquisition (*upapattilābhika*), along with their attendants.
"Treatise" (*śāstra*) refers to the teachings that give rise to uncontaminated wisdom.
Since these various forms of wisdom and the treatises are the provisions for that [uncontaminated wisdom], they are also designated as *abhidharma*.
To explain this name: it is called "dharma" because it can maintain its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If one speaks of ultimate dharma (*paramārtha-dharma*), it refers exclusively to nirvāṇa; if one speaks of dharmas as phenomena (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*), it refers to all four noble truths. Because this [treatise] can direct toward or correctly contemplate these [dharmas], it is termed "Abhidharma" (the Dharma that faces toward).
The Abhidharma has already been explained.
For what reason is this treatise called the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma)?
The verse says:
Because it encompasses that ultimate reality and relies upon it, this work is established with the name *Abhidharmakośa*.
The commentary states:
Because the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) within that treatise on Abhidharma is subsumed herein, this work receives the name "Treasury" (*kośa*).
Alternatively, because this [treatise] relies upon that [Abhidharma], is derived from it, and is its treasury, it is also called a "Treasury" (Piṭaka).
Therefore, this treatise is named the Abhidharmakośa (The Treasury of Abhidharma).
For what reason is it called Abhidharma?
Who was it that first taught the Abhidharma, such that one now composes this treatise to reverently explain it?
The verse says:
“If one were to exclude the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya), there would truly be no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions.”
"Because of delusion, the world drifts in the ocean of existence; for this reason, the Buddha transmitted the Abhidharma.
The treatise says:
Apart from the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), there is no superior means capable of extinguishing all delusions.

The various afflictions cause the world to drift and wander in the great ocean of birth and death; for this reason, it is traditionally said that the Buddha taught the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*) so that the world might attain the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
Apart from the teaching of the Abhidharma, disciples would be unable to discern the characteristics of phenomena correctly.

However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the Abhidharma in fragments throughout various places, which the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and other great śrāvakas subsequently compiled and established.
It is as the Vaibhāṣika masters have traditionally taught: that the Udānavarga verses, such as the Chapter on Impermanence (*Anityavarga*) compiled by the Venerable Dharmatrāta, are like this.
What dharma is it that is discerned by those [verses], because of which the Buddha is said to have taught the Abhidharma?
The verse says:
Contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena— excluding the Path,
all remaining conditioned phenomena are called "contaminated" because contaminants increase therein.
The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—namely, space and the two types of cessation. Among these, space is characterized by non-obstruction.
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is defined as disjunction; it is distinct for each specific object of bondage.
When that which is destined to arise is ultimately obstructed, one separately attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The treatise says:
It is taught that all phenomena are, in brief, of two kinds, namely, contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
What are the phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) except for the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). Why is this so?
Because the various outflows (āsrava) increase in accordance with [the truths of suffering and origination] within them;

whereas although the various outflows arise when taking the truths of cessation and the path as objects, they do not increase in accordance with them, and thus these are not "outflow-tainted" (sāsrava).
The meaning of "not increasing in accordance" will be explained in detail within the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* (Chapter on Latent Dispositions).
Having already explained that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
what is that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
It refers to the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*) and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the three?
They are space and the two types of cessation.
What are the two types of cessation?
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

These three types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), beginning with space (*ākāśa*), together with the noble truth of the path (*mārga-āryasatya*), are called untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). Why is this so?
Because the various outflows (āsrava) do not increase therein.
Among the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) briefly described, space has non-obstruction as its intrinsic nature; because it is without hindrance, matter moves within it.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has the nature of dissociation (*visamyoga*). When all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are distanced from their fetters and liberation is attained, it is termed cessation through deliberation.
"Deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to discernment (*vicaya*), which is a specific type of wisdom (*prajñā*), because it involves the individual discernment of each of the Four Noble Truths.

Cessation obtained through the power of discernment is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is like calling a cart driven by oxen an "ox-cart," where the intermediate words have been omitted; thus it is so described.
Is there a single cessation through discernment for all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)?
Not so. Why? Because it varies according to the specific objects to which one is bound.
That is to say, the measure of the entities of dissociation is equal to the measure of the entities of bondage.

If it were otherwise, then at the time of realizing the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, one would have to realize the cessation of all afflictions to be abandoned.
If this were the case, the cultivation of other remedies would be useless.
Based on what meaning is it said that cessation has no "homogeneous" (sabhāga) [cause]?
It is said so because, by its very nature, cessation lacks a homogeneous cause and likewise does not bestow one upon others; it is not that it simply lacks a homogeneous [result].
The cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has already been explained.

That which permanently obstructs future arising is the attainment of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); that is to say, it can permanently obstruct the arising of future dharmas.
Because its attainment of cessation differs from the former, it is named "cessation not through deliberation."
This is obtained not through analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), but solely due to the deficiency of conditions.
For example, when the eye and the mind are focused on a single form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass away.

The five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) that would have taken those objects as their spheres remain in the future and never arise at all; because they cannot take past objects as their spheres and because their conditions are incomplete, they obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Regarding the attainment of cessation in relation to phenomena (*dharma*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Either there is the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) alone with respect to certain phenomena— namely, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that have arisen in the past or present—

or there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) alone with respect to certain phenomena— namely, unarisen phenomena that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
In some cases, one attains both types of cessation regarding certain phenomena, namely those tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena that are not to arise.
In other cases, one does not attain either type of cessation regarding certain phenomena, namely all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena that have already arisen in the past or present.
Thus, the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena have been explained.
Previously, it was stated that with the exception of the Path, all other conditioned phenomena are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).
What, then, are conditioned phenomena?
The verse says:
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena— namely, the five aggregates such as form—
are also called "paths of time," "bases of speech," "possessing disjunction," "possessing objects," and so forth.
The treatise states:
The five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and ending with the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), comprise all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
This is because these five factors are produced through the collective operation of a multitude of conditions.
There is not even a single dharma produced by a single condition, because it belongs to that class [of phenomena].
There is no contradiction regarding the future, just as there is with milk or firewood.

These conditioned dharmas are also called "paths of time" (*adhvan*), because they possess the nature of having already gone, currently going, or yet to go; or because they are swallowed up by impermanence.
Alternatively, it is called the "basis of speech" (*nāma-adhiṣṭhāna*). "Speech" refers to verbal expression; that which serves as its basis consists of the meaning associated with names.
Thus, this basis of speech fully encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
If it were not so, it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
That treatise states that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are subsumed under the category of "possessing separation" (*saviyoga*).
Here, "separation" (*viyoga*) refers to permanent separation, which is precisely nirvāṇa; for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) possess that separation.
Alternatively, it is called "possessing an object" (*savastuka*) because it has a cause; here, "object" (*vastu*) signifies "cause.
This is the traditional teaching of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Such categories as these are various designations for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) among those conditioned phenomena that have been discussed.
The verse says:
That which is contaminated is called the "aggregates of clinging" (upādānaskandha);
it is also described as "with conflict" (saraṇa), as well as suffering, origin, the world, the locus of views, and the three realms of existence, and so forth.
The treatise says:
What is established here?
It is established that the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) are also called simply "aggregates" (*skandha*).
There are some aggregates that are not "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha), namely, untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*).
Defilements are called "grasping"; because aggregates arise from grasping, they are termed "aggregates of grasping," like a fire of straw and chaff.
Alternatively, the aggregates are called "appropriation-aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*) because they belong to appropriation, just as one speaks of a king’s ministers.
Or, they are called "appropriation-aggregates" because the aggregates give rise to appropriation, just as one speaks of fruit-bearing or flower-bearing trees.

These contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also called "contending" (*saraṇa*); "conflict" (*raṇa*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), so they are called "contending" because they disturb the wholesome side, harm oneself and others, and because conflict increases in accordance with them.
Just as that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is also called "suffering" (*duḥkha*) because it contradicts the noble mind,
and is also called "origination" (*samudaya*) because it can summon suffering,
and is also called "the world" (*loka*) because it is subject to destruction and has an antidote.
They are also called "abodes of views" (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*), because views abide within them and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase accordingly.
They are also called the "three realms of existence" (*trai-dhātuka*), because they are subsumed within the three realms as the cause of existence and the basis of existence.
Such categories of phenomena are *sāsrava* (with outflows).
The specific names according to their meanings are as stated above.
The five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are called conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
What is the aggregate of form?
The verse says:
Form consists only of the five sense organs, the five objects, and the unmanifest.
The commentary says:
The five faculties refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
The five objects refer to the spheres of the five faculties, namely: form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible.
Regarding "and the unmanifest," this refers to unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
It is solely based on this measure that the name "aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*) is established.
Within this context, the characteristics of the five sense faculties (*indriya*) should first be explained.
The verse says:
That consciousness relies upon pure matter; these are called the five faculties, beginning with the eye.
The commentary says:
He refers to the five objective spheres previously mentioned—form and so forth—and the consciousnesses that take them as objects, namely the consciousnesses of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch.
One should understand that the five kinds of translucent matter which serve as the bases for those consciousnesses are, respectively, the five faculties beginning with the eye.
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the eye is an internal sense base (āyatana), having as its nature translucent matter derived from the four great elements.
Thus it is explained at length.
Alternatively, "those" refers to the five faculties previously mentioned, such as the eye and so forth; "consciousness" refers to the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The five kinds of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serve as the bases for those consciousnesses are called the "eye and other faculties," in the sense that they are the supports for the eye-consciousness and the others.
In this way, it accords with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
As that treatise states:
"What is the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?"
The nature of the eye-faculty is pure matter that serves as the basis for visual consciousness;
thus it is explained in detail.
Thus, the five faculties have been described.
Next, the five objects are explained.
The verse says:
Visible form is of two kinds, or twenty; Sound has only eight types.
Taste has six types; odor has four; and touch has eleven as its nature.
The treatise says:
regarding the two kinds of form, the first is color (varṇa) and the second is shape (saṃsthāna).
There are four primary colors:
blue, yellow, red, and white; all other manifest colors are variations of these four.
There are eight types of shape, beginning with long and ending with the irregular.

Alternatively, there are twenty; that is, this same sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is further said to be twentyfold, namely: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Other masters state that there is a twenty-first [type of] visible form, namely "uniform color" (*ekarūpa*).

Herein, "even" refers to even shape; uneven shape is called "uneven. The rising vapor of earth and water is termed "mist" (*mahikā*). The radiance of the sun is called "light" (*āloka*). The radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, jewels, and lightning is called "luminosity" (*ābhā*). When light is obstructed and other colors become visible within that space, it is called "shadow" (*chāyā*); the opposite of this is "darkness" (*andhakāra*).
The remaining types of form are easy to understand and are therefore not explained here.
Alternatively, there are sense-bases of form that possess color-appearance (varṇa) but lack shape (saṃsthāna), namely: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
There are some instances of the sense-sphere of form that possess shape but lack color,
namely, a portion of [qualities] such as length and so forth, which have the nature of bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*).
There are also some instances of the sense-sphere of form that possess both color and shape, namely, all other forms.
Other masters say:
"Only the color of light possesses manifest color (varṇa) but lacks shape (saṃsthāna), for we observe in the world that places of color such as blue possess length and so forth.
How can a single entity possess both manifest color and shape?"
Because both [the agent and the action] can be known therein,
the term "existence" (*bhava*) here carries the sense of "cognition of existence," not the sense of "an existing object. If that were so,
then there should also be a cognition of manifestation (*varṇa*) within bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
The sense-sphere of visible form has already been explained; now the sense-sphere of sound shall be explained. Sound is of only eight types:

it is caused by primary elements that are either appropriated or non-appropriated; and there is a fourfold distinction based on whether they belong to sentient beings or non-sentient things. These, further divided into the agreeable and the disagreeable, constitute the eight types.
Sound caused by appropriated primary elements refers to sounds produced by speech, the hands, and so forth.
Sounds produced by wind, forests, rivers, and the like are termed those caused by non-appropriated primary elements.
Sounds that designate sentient beings refer to vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*); other sounds are those that do not designate sentient beings. Some say:

there are sounds that have as their cause both appropriated (*upātta*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*), such as the sound produced by the conjunction of a hand and a drum.
Just as it is not admitted that a single atom of visible form (*varṇa-paramāṇu*) is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the same should apply to sound.
Having explained the sphere of sound, the sphere of taste shall now be explained.
There are six kinds of taste, distinguished by their differences as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland.
The sense-field of taste has already been explained; now the sense-field of odor shall be explained.
There are four kinds of odors:
pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and those that are both equal and unequal, owing to their distinctions.
In this treatise, it is stated that there are three kinds of odors:
pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and neutral odor.
Having explained the sphere of odor, the sphere of tangibles shall now be explained.
There are eleven types of tangibles: namely, the four great elements, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Among these, the great elements will be explained in detail later.
Softness is called smoothness;
coarseness and rigidity constitute roughness;
that which can be weighed is called heaviness.
The opposite of this is lightness.
Heat is called cold;
desire for food is called hunger.
Craving for sensory desires is called "thirst.
These three are spoken of in this way because the name of the effect is applied to the cause.
As a verse says:
The appearance of the Buddhas is joy; the proclamation of the True Dharma is joy;
the harmony of the Saṅgha is joy; and practicing together with diligence is joy.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no contact of hunger or thirst, though other contacts do exist.
The garments in that realm cannot be weighed individually, but they can be weighed when gathered together.
Although cold and heat do not cause harm there, they do provide benefit;
such is the traditional teaching.
Among these, many types of visible objects (*rūpāyatana*) have already been explained.
Sometimes visual consciousness arises in dependence upon a single object, which means that at such times it discerns them individually.

Sometimes visual consciousness arises in dependence upon multiple objects, which means that at such times it does not discern them individually; this is as when one observes from a distance an army, a mountain forest, or a vast collection of various colors, shapes, and jewels.
It should be understood that the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth are likewise.
Other masters say:
the body-consciousness most frequently arises in dependence upon five types of tangibles, namely, the four great elements and any one of the [secondary qualities] such as smoothness.
Some say: "At most, all eleven types of tangibles arise by taking everything collectively as their object.

If this were so, then because the five consciousnesses take objects collectively, the five bodies of consciousness would necessarily apprehend common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) rather than specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of their respective bases, it is accepted that the five groups of consciousness apprehend objects characterized by their own specific characteristics, rather than the specific characteristics of the individual entities themselves; what fault is there in this?
Now, one should investigate: when the two bases of the body and the tongue both reach their respective objects simultaneously, which consciousness arises first?
Whichever object is more intense, its corresponding consciousness arises first;
if the objects are equal in strength, the gustatory consciousness arises first, because food and drink sustain the body and cause it to continue.
Having already explained the sense faculties, their objects, and the manner in which they apprehend objects, the characteristics of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"Whether the mind is distracted or non-existent, Flowing along as pure or impure,
And having the nature of being derived from the great elements— For these reasons, it is called 'unmanifest' (avijñapti)."
The Treatise says:
"A distracted mind" refers to any other state of mind besides those [two].
"A mindless state" refers to entering the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The term "and so forth" indicates a state of mind that is not distracted.
A similar continuity is called "flowing along.
The wholesome and the unwholesome are termed "pure" and "impure," respectively.
To distinguish these from other similar successions of acquisitions (*prāpti*), it further states that they are "derived from the primary elements" (*bhautika*).
The *Vibhāṣā* explains:
"Derived" (*kṛta*) has the sense of "cause," meaning that they act as the five kinds of causes, such as the cause of production (*janana-hetu*), and so forth.
To clarify the reason for establishing its name, it is said "by this":

although non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) has the nature of form-action (*rūpa-karman*) just like informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), it does not manifest itself so as to make it known to others; therefore, it is called "non-informative."

The term "it is said" indicates that this is the statement of the Master's school; "briefly explained" refers to the virtuous and non-virtuous matter produced by manifest action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is termed "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*).
Since it is stated that the non-manifest is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), what are these primary elements?
The verse says:
The primary elements (mahābhūta) are the four realms— namely earth, water, fire, and wind—
which perform the functions of supporting and so forth, and possess the natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
The treatise says:

Earth, water, fire, and wind can maintain their own characteristics as well as derived matter; therefore, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*). These four elements are also called "great primaries" (*mahābhūta*), because they serve as the basis for all other forms of matter and because their substance is vast and extensive.
Alternatively, because their form and appearance are vast within the dense aggregations of earth and so forth, or because they initiate various great functional activities.
What karmic functions are these four great elements capable of accomplishing?

Respectively, they are able to accomplish the four functions of supporting, cohesion, maturation, and growth: the earth element supports, the water element coheres, the fire element matures, and the wind element grows.
"Long" (dīrgha) means increasing or flowing forth.
Since their functional activity is thus, what are their intrinsic natures?

In their respective order, they have solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion as their intrinsic natures: the earth element has the nature of solidity, the water element the nature of moisture, the fire element the nature of warmth, and the wind element the nature of motion.

Because it can induce the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) to arise in succession and reach another location—just as a lamp’s flame is blown by the wind—it is called "motion.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* and the sūtras state:
"What is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*)?"
This refers to the nature of lightness and mobility.

Furthermore, since lightness is said to be a derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) must have motion as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is called "light" as well because its substance is manifested by means of its activity.
What are the elements such as earth?
They are the distinct categories of the elements, such as earth.
The verse says:
"Earth refers to color and shape, Names are established according to worldly convention;
The same applies to water and fire, And for wind, it is likewise both an element and such.
The Commentary says:
"Earth" refers to color and shape; its substance is the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). This name is conventionally established in accordance with worldly designations.
This is because when people in the world point out earth to one another, they do so by means of its color and shape.
Water and fire are likewise so.
Wind is the wind-element, for the world establishes the name "wind" based on motion.
Alternatively, just as earth and the others follow worldly conceptual designations, wind also manifests form; therefore, it is said to be the same.
As it is said in the world regarding "black winds" or "whirlwinds," these are used to represent wind by means of its manifested form.
For what reason is this aggregate, even including non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) as its final member, designated as "matter" (*rūpa*)?
Because it is subject to transformation and decay.
As the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that it is called the aggregate of appropriation of form (rūpôpādānaskandha) because it is subject to transformation and decay."
Who is it that undergoes transformation and decay?
It is through contact with the hand that it immediately undergoes transformation and decay;
and so on, as explained at length.
"Transformation and decay" (vipariṇāma) carries the sense of being subject to affliction and destruction; therefore, it is said in the *Arthavargīya*:
"For those who pursue various desires, Constantly giving rise to longing, If those desires are not fulfilled, The affliction and destruction are like being struck by an arrow."
Furthermore, what is form (*rūpa*)?
It is that which is afflicted and ruined by desire, because it arises as something disturbed, tormented, and subject to transformation. Some say:
It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it is subject to transformation and resistance.
If that were so, then atoms (*paramāṇu*) should not be called form, as they lack transformation and resistance.
This objection is not valid.
Not a single atom exists in isolation; it is only through the aggregation of many atoms that the meaning of "changeable resistance" (rūpaṇā) is established.

If this were so, then past and future [atoms] should not be called "matter" (rūpa), because they too have had, or will have, changeable resistance, and because they belong to the same category—just as firewood is so called even when not currently burning.
Furthermore, all unmanifest matter (avijñapti-rūpa) would likewise not be called "matter."
One interpretation states:
Because informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) possesses the quality of change and resistance (*rūpaṇa*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) also receives the designation "matter" by following it,
just as when a tree moves, its shadow also moves accordingly.
This explanation is incorrect, because [unmanifest form] lacks the quality of resistance (*sapratigha*).
Furthermore, when the manifest (*vijñapti*) ceases, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) should also cease, just as when a tree perishes, its shadow necessarily follows in perishing.
Another explanation states:

Because its basis—the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—is subject to transformation and resistance (*pratigha*), non-informative action (*avijñapti-karman*) also receives the designation "matter" (*rūpa*).
If that were so, since their bases are also subject to transformation and resistance, the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, should likewise be called "matter."
This objection is not equivalent.
When the unmanifest (avijñapti) arises in dependence upon the primary elements (mahābhūta), it is like a shadow depending on a tree or light depending on a jewel;
the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, do not depend on the eye and so forth in this same manner, because they merely serve as auxiliary conditions for their arising.
The statement that "this shadow depends on the tree and the light depends on the jewel" does not, for now, accord with the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*.
According to that school, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of manifest color (*varṇa*), such as shadows and so forth, each individually depend upon their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Even if it were granted that shadows and light depend upon trees and jewels, the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) differs from those cases; for they maintain that although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as its basis may perish, the unmanifest form does not perish along with them.
Therefore, what has been said does not yet resolve the objection. Furthermore, there is another explanation for that objection:

the supports of the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, are not fixed; they may be characterized by resistance, as in the case of the sense organs like the eye, or they may lack resistance, as in the case of the immediately preceding mind (*manas*). The support of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), however, is not like this. Thus, the previous objection is certainly inconsistent; the principle that "that which is characterized by resistance is called matter" (*rūpa*) is thereby established.
The verse says:
Herein, the faculties and their objects are accepted as being the ten bases and elements.
The commentary says:

Regarding the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) previously described, it is accepted that the sense faculties and their objects constitute ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Specifically, within the framework of the bases (*āyatana-mukha*), they are established as ten bases:
the eye base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the form base (*rūpa-āyatana*), and so on, up to the body base (*kāya-āyatana*) and the tangible base (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).

If established according to the classification of elements (*dhātu*), they constitute the ten elements: the eye element, the form element, and so forth, up to the body element and the tangible element.

Having already explained the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) along with its corresponding bases (*āyatana*) and elements, we shall now explain the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), as well as their corresponding bases and elements.
The verse says:
Feeling has the nature of experiencing; perception has the taking of images as its essence;
the four remaining [aggregates] are called the aggregate of formations. Thus, these three—feeling and the others—[are explained].
Together with the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these are called the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
The treatise says:
The aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) consists of three types; it is the experience that accords with contact, namely: pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
This, further analyzed, constitutes the six groups of feeling (*ṣaḍ-vedanā-kāya*), namely: feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has the nature of grasping images; that is, it is able to apprehend such characteristics as blue, yellow, long, short, male, female, enemy, friend, suffering, and pleasure.
This, further analyzed, constitutes the six groups of perception (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*), which should be explained in the same manner as sensation (*vedanā*).

With the exception of the aforementioned [form] and the subsequent [aggregates of] form, sensation, perception, and consciousness, all remaining conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
However, when the Bhagavat stated in the sūtras that the six types of volition constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it was because of their preeminence. Why is this so?
"Formations" means "constructing";
since volition is of the nature of karma, its sense of constructing is particularly strong, and thus it is preeminent.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that if one can produce that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-upādānaskandha*).

If this were not the case, other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) would not be included within the aggregates; consequently, they would not be suffering or its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), and thus could not be objects to be known or abandoned (*parijñeya-prahātavya*).
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one has not attained and does not know even a single dharma, I say that one cannot bring an end to suffering.
The same applies to what has not been abandoned and what has not been extinguished.

Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that, with the exception of the four aggregates, all other conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

These aforementioned factors—the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) and the three kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—these seven dharmas are established as the "dharma-base" (*dharmāyatana*) in the system of bases, and as the "dharma-element" (*dharmadhātu*) in the system of elements.

Having already explained the three aggregates, bases, and elements beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) shall now be explained, along with its establishment as a base and an element.
The verse says:
"Consciousness is the individual discernment [of objects]; this is itself called the mind-base (*manāyatana*)."
And one should know that the seven elements [are also included]; the six consciousnesses, when they transform, become the mind-element (*manas*).
The commentary states:
Because each [consciousness] individually cognizes its respective object and grasps the general characteristics of that object, it is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, this is differentiated into six groups of consciousness, namely, from the group of visual consciousness up to the group of mental consciousness.
It should be understood that the aggregate of consciousness thus described is established as the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) within the classification of bases.

Within the classification of elements (*dhātu*), they are established as seven elements, namely the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element; these same six consciousnesses, when transformed, constitute the mind-element (*manodhātu*).

Thus, the five aggregates (*skandha*) explained herein are identical to the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); that is to say, with the exception of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), all remaining forms within the aggregate of form are termed the ten bases and are also termed the ten elements.

The aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, along with unmanifest form and the unconditioned, are collectively termed the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and are also called the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

One should know that the aggregate of consciousness is itself termed the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and is also called seven spheres: namely, the six consciousness-spheres and the mind-sphere (*manodhātu*).
Do you not recognize that the aggregates consist of nothing but the six groups of consciousness? Apart from these, what else could be called the "mind-element" (manodhātu)?
There is no distinct dharma whatsoever.
Regarding this very point, the verse says:
"By means of the six consciousness-bodies themselves, that which has ceased without interval constitutes the mind.
The treatise says:

Because the six consciousness-bodies, having ceased without interval, are able to produce the subsequent consciousness, they are called the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*). This is like how the same person is called a son in one context and a father in another, or like how the same thing is called a fruit in one context and a seed in another.

If that were so, the actual elements (dhātus) would be only seventeen or only twelve, because the six consciousnesses and the mind (manas) mutually subsume one another; for what reason, then, can eighteen elements be established?
The verse says:
Because they constitute the basis for the sixth [consciousness], the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) should be known.
The commentary says:

Just as the five consciousness-elements have the five distinct elements of the eye and so forth as their supports, the sixth mental consciousness has no separate support; therefore, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is taught in order to establish this support.
Thus, these bases, the faculties based upon them, and their objects should each be understood as consisting of six elements, forming eighteen [dhātus] in total.

If this were so, the final moment of mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) would not be the mental element (manodhātu), because no subsequent consciousness arises immediately after its cessation, and thus it would not be the mental element.
It is not so; because this [consciousness] has already abided in the nature of mind and lacks other conditions, subsequent consciousness does not arise.

Among these, the aggregates (*skandha*) encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) encompass only all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); and the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) collectively encompass all phenomena without exception.
The individual classifications are thus; how is the collective classification?
The verse says:
All phenomena are collectively subsumed by one aggregate, one base, and one element.
It subsumes its own nature and nothing else, because it is devoid of other-nature.
The treatise says:

By means of the single aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the sense-base of mind (*mano-āyatana*), and the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), one should know that all phenomena are exhaustively subsumed.

This means that regarding all bases (*āyatana*), from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), only their own-nature (*svabhāva*) is subsumed, not the nature of others (*parabhāva*). Why is this so?
Because a phenomenon (*dharma*) is eternally dissociated from the nature of others.
The principle that something is included while being distinct from another is not tenable.

For instance, the eye-faculty includes only the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*), the element of the eye (*cakṣurdhātu*), and the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkhasatya* and *samudayasatya*), because these are of its own nature; it does not include the other aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and so forth, because they are not of its nature.

If one speaks according to conventional truth regarding the various bases (*āyatana*), it should be understood that other dharmas are likewise subsumed by others—just as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) subsume a retinue and so forth.
Since the three bases of eye, ear, and nose each have two [physical locations], for what reason does the nature of the elements (*dhātu*) not consist of twenty-one?
This objection is unreasonable. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Because their type, object, and consciousness are identical, although they are two, their substance is one.
The treatise says:
"Identity of type" means that both locations share the same intrinsic nature of the eye.
Regarding "identical object": this means that both locations take visible form (*rūpa*) as their common object.
Regarding "identical consciousness": this means that both locations serve as the common support for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
For these reasons, although the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is twofold, it is considered one.
The ears and nose should also be established in this same manner.
If that is so, for what reason do they arise based on two locations?
The verse says:
However, in order to make [the body] dignified and beautiful, each [sense organ], such as the eye, arises in two locations.
The Commentary says:
Because the physical form of the supporting body must be dignified and beautiful, although the essence of the element (*dhātu*) is one, it arises in two places.
If the locations of the eye and ear faculties were to arise as only one, and the nose had no two nostrils, the body would not be dignified.
This explanation is incorrect;
if it were originally thus, who would say it was ugly?
Furthermore, although cats, owls, and the like are born in two locations, what dignity or beauty do they possess?
If that is so, for what reason do the three faculties arise in two places?
It is for the sake of making the consciousness they produce clear and distinct.
It is observed in the world that when one closes one eye and so forth, the discernment of forms and other objects becomes indistinct; therefore, each of the three faculties arises in two locations.
Having already explained the inclusion of the aggregates, bases, and elements, their meaning shall now be discussed.
What are the specific meanings of these aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)?
The verse says:
"Accumulation, doors of arising, and lineage— these are the meanings of aggregate, base, and element."
The treatise says:
The meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a collection or assemblage of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). As the Sūtra states:

"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all such things, when briefly condensed into a single collection, are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)."
By virtue of this meaning of "collection," the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is established.

In this sutra, that which has ceased and is impermanent is called "past"; that which has not yet arisen is called "future"; and that which has arisen but not yet passed away is called "present. That which belongs to one's own continuum is called "internal," while all else is called "external."
Alternatively, they may be distinguished according to their locus: that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*) is called coarse, and that which lacks resistance (*apratigha*) is called subtle.
Alternatively, they are established in mutual dependence.
If one says they are established through mutual dependence, then the categories of coarse and subtle cannot be established.
This objection is not valid, because the relata differ.

That which is coarse in relation to one thing has never been subtle in relation to it, and that which is subtle in relation to one thing has never been coarse in relation to it. This is just like the case of father and son, or the truths of suffering and its origin; likewise, what is defiled is called inferior, while what is non-defiled is called superior; what is past or future is called distant, while what is present is called near. One should know that this applies even to the aggregate of consciousness.
There is, however, a distinction: that which relies on the five physical faculties is called "coarse," while that which relies solely on the mental faculty (*manas*) is called "subtle.
Alternatively, this is distinguished according to the levels (*bhūmi*); such is the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta further states:
That which is grasped by the five sense-faculties is called coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*); the remainder is called subtle matter (*sūkṣma-rūpa*).
That which is not agreeable to the mind is called inferior matter (*hīna-rūpa*); the remainder is called superior matter (*praṇīta-rūpa*).
Forms that are not within the range of vision are called "distant forms," while those within the range of vision are called "near forms.

Past and other such forms are evident from their respective names; the same applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates. It should be understood that their distance, proximity, coarseness, and subtlety follow the power of their bases, as previously explained.
The meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is the sense of being a gateway for the arising and growth of mind and mental factors.
Regarding the etymological derivation: it is called a "base" because it can cause the arising and growth of mind and mental factors; this signifies its functional capacity to produce them.

The meaning of "dhātu" (element) is the sense of a "seed-lineage" (*gotra*). Just as a single mountain containing many lineages of copper, iron, gold, silver, and so forth is called a "multitude of elements," likewise, within a single body or a single continuum, there are eighteen classes of dharma-seed-lineages, which are termed the "eighteen *dhātus*."
In this context, "lineage" (*gotra*) has the sense of being the basis for arising.
Thus, what is the basis for the arising of the eye and so forth?
It is their own kind, because they are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If that were so, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should not be called a "constituent" (*dhātu*), because it is the basis for the arising of mind and mental factors. Some say:

the term "constituent" (*dhātu*) expresses the sense of "category"; thus, because the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of these eighteen phenomena are each distinct and different in their categories, they are called the "eighteen constituents."

If it is argued that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a "collection," then an aggregate would have to be a conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*), because it is established by the collective accumulation of many real entities, like a heap or like a self (*ātman*).
This objection is not valid, because even a single, real atom (*paramāṇu*) is designated as an aggregate.
If that were so, one should not say that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the meaning of "collection," because a single real entity cannot possess the meaning of a collection. Some say:
the meaning of "aggregate" is the sense of being able to bear a heavy burden; for this reason, the world speaks of the shoulder as an "aggregate," since it is where things are gathered.
Some say that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is "that which can be divided into parts"; thus, there is a worldly saying:
"If you return my three aggregates, I shall give them to you."
This explanation deviates from the Sūtra, because the Sūtra states that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a "collection," as the Sūtra says:
"Whatever form there may be, whether past...
and so forth, as explained in detail previously.

If it is argued that this sūtra reveals that each individual past form (*rūpa*) and so forth is separately called a "skandha," and therefore every single real entity of past form and so forth is individually termed a skandha.
This position is irrational; therefore, that sūtra states:

"Because all these [factors] are briefly gathered into a single collection, they are called 'aggregates' (skandha). Thus, like a collection, an aggregate must necessarily be a conventional existence (prajñaptisat).

If that were so, one would have to admit that the various material bases (*rūpāyatana*) are also conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye and so forth must accumulate to a great extent to constitute a gateway for the arising [of consciousness].
This objection is irrational, because within a great accumulation, each individual atom possesses causal efficacy.

If it were not so, then since the sense faculties and their objects assist one another to produce consciousness and so forth, they would not be distinct locations; consequently, there would be no distinction between the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
However, the *Vibhāṣā* states as follows:
If the masters of the Abhidharma consider the aggregates to be conventional designations, they say that an atom is a portion of one element, one base, and one aggregate;
if they do not so consider them, they say that an atom is itself one element, one base, and one aggregate.
This should be designated as "having parts" (*sāvayava*) by way of its constituent parts, just as one speaks of "burning the cloth" even when only a small portion of it is burned.
For what reason did the Blessed One provide these three types of explanations regarding the objects of knowledge through the categories of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth?
The verse says:
Because of the three [types of] delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the three—aggregates, bases, and elements—are taught.
The commentary says:
Because the sentient beings to be converted fall into three categories, the Blessed One taught the three gateways of the aggregates (skandha) and so forth.

It is traditionally said that there are three kinds of delusion among sentient beings: some are deluded regarding mental factors (caitta), grasping them collectively as a self; some are deluded regarding form (rūpa) alone; and some are deluded regarding both form and mind.
The faculties are also of three kinds: sharp, medium, and dull.
Interest is likewise of three kinds: those who prefer what is concise, those who prefer what is intermediate, and those who prefer extensive texts.
Accordingly, the Blessed One taught the three categories of aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

For what reason did the Blessed One state that other mental factors are collectively placed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), while feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are separately established as two distinct aggregates?
The verse says:
Because they are the roots of contention, the causes of birth and death, and for the sake of the sequential order.
Among all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
The treatise says:
There are two roots of contention (*raṇa-mūla*): namely, attachment to various desires (*kāma*) and attachment to various views (*dṛṣṭi*).

These two—feeling and perception—are, respectively, the most predominant causes: through the power of the relishing of feeling, one becomes attached to various sensual desires; through the power of distorted perception, one becomes attached to various views.
Furthermore, among the phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are the most predominant causes;

because one revolves in *saṃsāra* by giving rise to inverted perceptions through attachment to feelings, these two causes, along with the sequential causes to be explained later, show that feeling and perception should be established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
The sequential causes for this will be explained immediately following.
For what reason are the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) said to be included within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), but not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*)?
The verse says:
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), because their meanings are incompatible.
The treatise states:
The three unconditioned phenomena cannot be said to exist within the aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because they are incompatible with the meaning of form and the other aggregates.

This means that its essence is neither form (*rūpa*) nor, up to, consciousness (*vijñāna*); furthermore, it cannot be designated as a sixth aggregate (*skandha*), because it does not correspond to the meaning of "aggregate.
As previously explained in detail, the meaning of "aggregate" is that of a collection.

This refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); unlike form (*rūpa*) and so forth, they do not possess distinctions of categories such as the past and so on, whereby they could be briefly grouped together and termed an "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛta-skandha*).
Furthermore, the term "appropriation aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*) is used to indicate the basis of defilement; the term "aggregates" (*skandha*) signifies both the bases of defilement and purity.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lacks both of these two meanings; because its meaning is incompatible [with the definition of an aggregate], it is not established as an aggregate (*skandha*). Some say:

"Just as when a jar is broken it is no longer a jar, so too when the aggregates cease, they should no longer be aggregates. This argument would lead to a fallacy by analogy regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
Having thus explained the establishment and exclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*), their sequential order shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"In accordance with coarseness, defilement, vessel, and so forth, The sequence is established according to the distinctions of the realms (*dhātu*)."
The Treatise says:

Because form (rūpa) is characterized by resistance (sapratigha), it is the coarsest among the aggregates. Among the formless [aggregates], sensation (vedanā) alone has a coarse aspect; therefore, in common worldly parlance, one speaks of "pain in my hand" and so forth.
The two types of perception (*saṃjñā*) are coarse because perceptions such as male and female are easily discerned.
Mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are coarser than consciousness (*vijñāna*), because formations such as greed and hatred are easily discerned.
Consciousness is the most subtle, because it grasps the general characteristics of objects and is difficult to differentiate.
Based on this, the order of the aggregates is established according to their relative coarseness.

Alternatively, from beginningless saṃsāra, men and women have mutually delighted in form; this is due to their attachment to the flavor of pleasant feeling. This attachment to feeling arises from perverted perception, and this perverted perception arises from the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, these afflictions arise dependent upon consciousness (*vijñāna*).
These [two] and the preceding three are all defiled consciousnesses; it is on this basis that the order of the aggregates is established according to their defilement.

Alternatively, form is like a vessel, feeling resembles food and drink, perception is similar to condiments, formations are like a cook, and consciousness is compared to the eater; thus, the order of the aggregates is established according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth.

Alternatively, the order of the aggregates is established according to the distinction of the realms: in the desire realm, there are various exquisite sensual desires, and thus the characteristic of form is prominent;
in the meditative absorptions of the form realm, there is superior joy and so forth, and thus the characteristic of feeling is prominent.
Within the three formless realms, the characteristics of perception (*saṃjñā*) are clearly manifest as one grasps the signs of space and so forth.
Within the realm of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (the Peak of Existence), volition (*cetanā*) is most predominant, and its modes of activity (*ākāra*) are clearly manifest.
These constitute the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); consciousness abiding therein is like the sequence of seeds and fields in the world.
Therefore, the sequence of the aggregates is as follows.

By this, the five aggregates are free from the fault of increase or decrease. Precisely because of these reasons for the sequence, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as two separate aggregates apart from the formations (*saṃskāra*); that is to say, among all formations, feeling and perception are coarse, give rise to defilement, share the same category of nutriment, and assist in the same way; because they are powerful within the two realms, they are established as separate aggregates.

Within the section on the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), one should first explain the sequence of the six faculties; from this, the sequence of their objects and consciousnesses can be understood.
The verse says:
The five [faculties] have only present objects; Four [of those objects] consist only of derived matter.
The others are used according to their distance, speed, and clarity, or according to their spatial order.
The treatise says:
Among the six sense faculties, the first five—beginning with the eye—perceive only present objects; therefore, they are mentioned first.
The objective spheres (ālambana) are not fixed; they are the conditioned phenomena of the three times and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). One may apprehend only one, or two, three, or four of them.
As for the statement that the four spheres consist solely of derived matter (upādāyarūpa), this follows from what was previously discussed.
Among the five [objects], the first four have as their objects only derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*); therefore, they are mentioned first.
The object of the body faculty is indeterminate: it may apprehend primary elements (*mahābhūta*), or derived matter, or both. "The rest" refers to the aforementioned four.
They are taught first because their functions are applied to distant objects with speed and clarity.
That is to say, because the faculties of the eye and the ear apprehend distant objects, they are mentioned before the other two.
Between these two, the eye is mentioned first because its function reaches further; one can see mountains and rivers from afar without hearing their sounds.
Furthermore, the function of the eye is rapid, because one first sees a person striking a bell or drum from a distance and only afterwards hears the sound.
The functions of both the nose and the tongue do not reach distant objects.
The nose is mentioned first because its function is more rapid and clear.
Just as when facing various fragrant and delicious foods, the nose first smells the aroma and the tongue subsequently tastes the flavor;

or as the sequence of the faculties is explained according to their respective locations within the body from top to bottom—namely, the support of the eye is situated highest, followed by the ear, nose, tongue, and body which mostly occupy lower positions, while the mind has no fixed location.
Since there are [bases] that arise depending immediately upon the sense faculties (*indriya*), they are mentioned last.
For what reason, when all ten bases (*āyatana*) are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), is the name "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*) established for only one of them?
Furthermore, since the essence of all twelve bases (*āyatana*) is *dharma*, why is the name "base of *dharmas*" (*dharmāyatana*) applied to only one of them?
The verse says:
To distinguish it as most excellent, Because it encompasses many and is predominant.
Therefore, one portion of form is designated as the sense-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
The treatise says:

To establish distinctions—that is, to enable the clear understanding of the various differences between the nature of objects and the nature of subjects—the ten sense-fields are established based on the differentiated characteristics within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), rather than being combined into a single unit.

If there were no distinct designations such as "eye" and so forth, yet its substance is matter (*rūpa*), it would be established by the name "form-base" (*rūpāyatana*); this is distinguished from names such as "eye," and although it expresses a general term, it is itself a specific name.
Furthermore, among all forms (*rūpa*), the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is the most preeminent; therefore, it is established as the general designation.
Because it is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), it undergoes transformation and decay when touched by hands and the like.
Moreover, because it is visible (*sanidarśana*), its distinctions—such as being "here" or "there"—can be demonstrated.
Furthermore, in the world, it is only in this case that people collectively refer to something as "form" (*rūpa*), and not in the case of the eye and so forth.

Moreover, a single "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) is established for the sake of differentiation, rather than for all [dharmas] indiscriminately; this should be understood in the same way as with form.
Furthermore, because it encompasses numerous phenomena such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth within this context, a general designation should be established.
Moreover, since the supreme phenomenon—namely, *nirvāṇa*—is included herein, it is established independently as a "phenomenon" (*dharma*).
Other masters say:

Among the bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), twenty kinds of form are most coarse and manifest; furthermore, because they are the objects of the three eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom-eye—they alone are designated by the name "form."
Because within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) there are the names of all phenomena and the cognition of all phenomena, it alone is designated by the name "phenomena.
In various sūtras, other kinds of aggregates (skandha), spheres (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) are found under different names and concepts.
Are these included within this [category],
or are they excluded from it?
One should understand that they are all included herein, as is appropriate.
Furthermore, to distinguish and subsume the names and concepts of the remaining aggregates,
the verse says:
The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma;
That essence is either speech or names; it is subsumed within the aggregates of form and formations (*rūpa-skandha* and *saṃskāra-skandha*).
The treatise says:
For those who assert that the Buddha’s teaching has speech as its essence, they maintain that all such aggregates of dharma (*dharma-skandha*) are subsumed within the aggregate of form.

Regarding those who state that the teaching of the Buddha is the essence [of this treatise], they maintain that these aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandha) are all subsumed within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
What is the magnitude of these aggregates of Dharma?
The verse says:
Some say that the measure of the aggregates of dharmas is as stated in that treatise;
others say it follows the words "aggregates" and so forth, acting as an antidote according to actual practice.
The treatise says:
Some masters say:

"Each of the eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* is equal in extent to the *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra*; that is, each one consists of six thousand stanzas, as explained in the *Dharmaskandha* within the *Abhidharma*."
Some say:

The *dharmaskandhas* (aggregates of dharma) number eighty thousand according to the individual distinctions of the categories such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; that is to say, each teaching door—such as the aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), absence of strife (*araṇā*), knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), and analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—is called one *dharmaskandha*.

To speak according to reality: because the sentient beings to be converted possess eighty thousand distinct behavioral patterns, such as desire and hatred, the Blessed One proclaimed eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) as an antidote to those eighty thousand behaviors.

As it is said that all those eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma are subsumed within two of these five [aggregates], so too should it be understood for other categories of aggregates, bases, and elements elsewhere.
The verse says:
Likewise, the remaining aggregates and so forth, each according to its respective application, are subsumed within what has been previously explained;
one should carefully examine their specific characteristics.
The Treatise says:

The aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) mentioned in other sūtras are, as appropriate, subsumed within those previously explained. One should carefully examine the individual specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) of each of these aggregates and so forth as they are described in this treatise.

Furthermore, within the various sūtras, other five aggregates are taught—namely, the five aggregates of ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). Among these, the aggregate of ethical discipline is subsumed under this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), while the remaining four aggregates are subsumed under this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Furthermore, various sūtras speak of the ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth. Because the first eight spheres of totality have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If they are taken together with their associated factors (*sahabhū*), which consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they are then subsumed under both the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
It should be understood that the inclusion of the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) is likewise.

As for the two spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*)—space and consciousness—and the four formless spheres beginning with infinite space, because they consist of the nature of the four aggregates (*skandha*), they are subsumed under these very sense-sphere bases (*āyatana*): the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).
The five bases of liberation (pañca-vimukti-sthānāni), having wisdom as their intrinsic nature, are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharma-āyatana);
if accompanied by their associated factors, they are subsumed under the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects.

Furthermore, there are two other bases: the abode of the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñi-sattva-deva) and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). The former is subsumed under these ten spheres, as it lacks odor and taste.
The subsequent bases are subsumed under these very mind-base (*manāyatana*) and mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*), as they consist of the nature of the four aggregates (*skandha*).

Furthermore, the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* states that there are sixty-two distinctions of elements (*dhātu*); it should be understood that, according to their respective natures, all of them are subsumed within these eighteen elements.

Furthermore, regarding the six elements taught in that sutra, while the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind have already been explained, the characteristics of the two elements—space and consciousness—have not yet been stated.
Is it the case that space itself is called the space element, and is it all consciousness that is called the consciousness element?
It is not so; how then? The verse says:
The space element refers to apertures and cavities; Tradition explains it as light and darkness.
The consciousness element is contaminated consciousness, the basis for the arising of sentient beings.
The commentary states:
all internal and external cavities and apertures, such as doors, windows, mouths, and nostrils, are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
How should these apertures be understood?

It is traditionally taught that the aperture is itself light and darkness; since no aperture can be perceived apart from light and darkness, it is said that the space-element has light and darkness as its essence.
One should know that this substance is not separate from day and night; it is precisely this that is called "color adjacent to ākāśa" (*āgāntaka-rūpa*).
According to tradition:
*ākāśa* refers to accumulated matter (*saṃcita-rūpa*), and because it is extremely capable of acting as an obstruction, it is therefore called *ākāśa*.
This matter of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is adjacent to that [matter of the great elements]; therefore, it is called "matter adjacent to the non-obstructive" (*āgāsannarūpa*). Some say:
*āga* is precisely the matter of the space-element; because there is no obstruction within it, it is called *āga*.
That is to say, *āgha*-color (obstructive color) is that which is adjacent to other obstructive forms; therefore, it is called "color adjacent to *āgha*.

All contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) are termed the "consciousness element" (*vijñānadhātu*); why then are all uncontaminated consciousnesses (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) not called the consciousness element?

Because it is accepted that the six elements are the basis for the birth of all sentient beings, these elements constantly sustain life from the mind at the moment of rebirth until the mind at the end of life.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not like this.

Among those six elements (*dhātu*), the first four are subsumed within this element of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*); the fifth is subsumed within this element of visible form (*rūpa-dhātu*); and the sixth is subsumed within these seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*).
The remaining elements (*dhātu*) in those other sūtras are all subsumed within these eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) as appropriate.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 1; *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle 2.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter One: Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga), Part Two. Furthermore, among the eighteen elements previously mentioned, how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and how many are invisible (*anidarśana*)?
How many are with resistance (*sapratigha*), and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
How many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:
One is visible, namely form; ten are material and possess resistance.
Excluding form and sound, eight of these are neutral; the remaining three types [of dharmas] are of all three natures.
The treatise says:
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the form element (*rūpa-dhātu*) is visible (*sanidarśana*), because it can be demonstrated through the distinction of "this" and "that.
By this same principle, it is implied that the others are invisible (*anidarśana*).
Thus has been explained what is visible and what is invisible.
Only the ten elements subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) possess resistance (sapratigha); "resistance" here has the meaning of obstruction.
This, moreover, is of three kinds, due to the distinction between obstructive resistance, objective-field resistance, and object-of-cognition resistance.
Obstruction by resistance (*pratighāta*) refers to the ten material spheres (*rūpadhātu*).
It is the state of being obstructed from arising in another location; for example, a hand obstructing a hand, a stone obstructing a stone, or the mutual obstruction of two [objects].

Obstruction by way of objective sphere (*viṣayapratighāta*) refers to those twelve elements and a portion of the dharma-element that possess cognitive capacity (*saviṣaya*) with respect to objects such as visible form; thus, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"There is an eye that has obstruction in water but not on land, such as the eyes of fish and the like."
There are eyes that are obstructed on land but not in water; this is spoken of in terms of the majority, such as the eyes of humans and others.
There are eyes that are obstructed by both, such as the eyes of piśācas, śūkaras, fishermen, frogs, and so forth.
There is that which is obstructed by neither, namely, excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
There is an eye that is obstructed at night but not during the day, such as the eyes of bats, owls, and the like.
There is an eye that is obstructed during the day but not at night; this is said from the perspective of the majority, such as the eyes of human beings and others.
There are eyes that are both obstructed, such as the eyes of dogs, jackals, horses, leopards, wild dogs, wolves, cats, and weasels.
There are those that are neither obstructed, namely excluding the aforementioned cases.
These are called "obstruction by way of object" (*viṣayapratighāta*).
Resistance with respect to the object (*ālambana-pratighāta*) refers to the mind and mental factors with regard to their own objects.
What is the difference between "sphere" (*viṣaya*) and "object" (*ālambana*)?
If a certain factor has efficacy toward a particular phenomenon, that phenomenon is said to be the sphere of that factor.
