The mind and mental factors arise by grasping that [object]; therefore, for the mind and so forth, that is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).
Why, then, is it said that the eye and other faculties are "obstructed" (*sapratigha*) when they operate upon their own respective objects and conditions?
Because it does not function with respect to other objects beyond those [specific ones].
Alternatively, "obstructing" (āvaraṇa) has the sense of "conjoining," meaning that phenomena such as the eye function by conjoining with their own respective domains and their own respective objects.

It should be understood that this is stated here solely with reference to obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*); therefore, it is said that only the ten material phenomena are resistant, because they mutually obstruct one another.
By this principle, the remaining [phenomena] are described as non-resistant.
If a dharma is an object-obstruction (*viṣayapratighāta*), is it also an obstruction by way of resistance (*āvaraṇapratighāta*)?
One should formulate this as four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That is to say: the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and that portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) consisting of associated dharmas (*saṃprayuktadharma*) constitute the first alternative.
The five objects, such as visible form and so forth, constitute the second phrase.
The five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, constitute the third phrase.
A portion of the dharma-dhātu that is non-associated with mind constitutes the fourth phrase.
If a dharma is resistant with respect to its objective field (*viṣaya-pratighāta*), is it also resistant with respect to its object (*ālambana-pratighāta*)?
One should answer by following the latter clause: that is to say, if it is resistant with respect to its object, it is necessarily resistant with respect to its objective field.

There are those that possess resistance regarding their objective field (*viṣayapratighāta*) but do not possess resistance regarding their focal object (*ālambanapratighāta*), namely, the five sense faculties beginning with the eye.
Regarding this, the Venerable Kumāralāta stated:
"In a place where the mind intends to arise, another obstructs it so that it does not occur."
One should know that "with resistance" (sapratigha) is the opposite of "without resistance" (apratigha);
this is what is accepted.
Thus has been explained "with resistance" and "without resistance."

Among these ten types of resistance (*sapratigha*) that have been explained, with the exception of visible form and sound, the remaining eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). That is to say, the five material sense faculties and the objects of odor, taste, and tangibility cannot be designated as being of a wholesome or unwholesome nature; therefore, they are called "indeterminate."
Some say: it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) because its ripened fruit (vipāka-phala) cannot be specified.
If that were so, then the untainted (anāsrava) would be exclusively indeterminate.

The remaining ten elements pertain to all three categories, beginning with the wholesome. That is to say, the seven mental elements are called wholesome when associated with non-greed and so forth; they are called unwholesome when associated with greed and so forth; and the rest are called indeterminate.

If the dharma-realm is of the nature of non-attachment and so forth, associated with them, or arising from them, it is designated as wholesome; if it is of the nature of attachment and so forth, associated with them, or arising from them, it is designated as unwholesome; otherwise, it is designated as indeterminate.

The visible-form element and the sound element, when comprised by bodily and vocal intimation produced by the power of wholesome or unwholesome minds, are wholesome or unwholesome; the remainder are indeterminate.
The wholesome and so forth have thus been explained.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The verse says:
Eighteen are bound to the desire realm; Fourteen are bound to the form realm.
Excluding odor, taste, and the two consciousnesses, the final three belong to the formless realm.
The commentary states:
"Tied" (繫) means being bound, which carries the sense of being fettered.

Those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are complete with all eighteen; those bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu) consist of only fourteen types, excluding the objects of odor and taste as well as the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses.
The reason for excluding odor and taste is that they are of the nature of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra); one must be free from the desire for such food in order to be born there.
This is because, with the exception of nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness, there is no object of perception [for them].

If that were so, the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) should likewise be absent there; however, just as the objects of smell and taste are of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), the tangibles possessed there are not of the nature of edible food.

If that were so, the same would apply to odors and tastes; for apart from food, there is no other enjoyment of odor or taste, whereas touch has distinct functions such as supporting the sense organs, clothing, and so forth. Since those who are free from the desire for food find no use for odor or taste, yet possess sense organs, clothing, and the like, it follows that touch is not absent [for them].
Other masters say:

While abiding here, one sees forms and hears sounds by means of those meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and attainments (*samāpatti*); because the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) that arises together with them includes a sublime tactile sensation that benefits the body, these three [sights, sounds, and touches] follow one another even when one is born into those meditative absorptions. Odors and tastes are not like this; therefore, they do not exist there.
If that were so, the nose and tongue would not exist there, as they would have no function regarding their objects, smell and taste.
This is not the case; these two faculties do have a function there, namely, for the purpose of verbal expression and the adornment of the body.
If [the organs] are for the purpose of adorning the body or for the function of speaking, they need only have a physical basis; what need is there for two organs?
For instance, if the male organ were absent, its basis would also not exist; likewise, if the two organs were absent, their bases would also not exist.
In those [heavens], there may be no physical basis for the male organ, as it serves no purpose there.
Since the bases for the nose and tongue serve a purpose there, they should exist even apart from their respective faculties.
There are cases where the faculty arises despite being useless, such as in the case of one who dies while still in the womb.
Although these [faculties] may be useless, they are not without a cause; from what cause, then, does the arising of the faculties occur?
It is through craving for the faculties that extraordinary karma is produced.
If one were to be free from craving for objects while remaining fixed in craving for the faculties, then those who are free from greed for objects would necessarily lack the nose and tongue.

Alternatively, one must admit that the male organ (*puruṣendriya*) also arises [in such beings]. If you argue that it does not arise because it is ugly, how could it be considered ugly when it is concealed within a sheath?
Furthermore, the arising of the sense organs is not due to their utility; if the power of causes exists, they arise even if they serve no purpose.

Although the male organ may be considered unsightly there, if one were to grant that it has a cause, it should arise there; yet since the male organ does not exist [there], the nose and tongue should likewise be absent.
If this were so, it would contradict what is stated in the Sūtra:
"They have no missing limbs, nor are they deficient in any faculties."
Regarding those sense faculties that ought to be present according to their respective [beings], they are said to be non-deficient.
What contradiction is there?
If this were not admitted, then the male faculty would have to exist [in all].

According to this explanation, the two faculties of nose and tongue do exist there; it is simply that odors and tastes are absent. This is because craving for the six faculties arises based on the internal body, rather than arising in dependence upon external objects.

The craving for the male organ arises dependent upon sexual contact; since that [contact] does not exist there, the male organ is absent. Therefore, among the eighteen elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is established by principle that only fourteen exist.

In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are only the last three [elements], namely the mind-element (manodhātu), the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu). Since birth in that realm requires the transcendence of desire for form, the ten material elements do not exist within the formless realm.

Because the five consciousnesses lack their objective conditions (*ālambana*), they also do not exist [in the formless realm]; therefore, only the latter three [consciousnesses] are bound to the formless realm.
Having explained the realm-bound nature (*dhātu-saṃyoga*), among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
The mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness are common to both [the outflowing and the non-outflowing]; the remainder are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The commentary says:
The mind (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), when subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), are called untainted (*anāsrava*); the rest are called tainted (*sāsrava*).
As for the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), if it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the Truth of the Path, it is called untainted; the rest are called tainted.
The remaining fifteen elements are exclusively termed "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Thus, having already explained what is with outflows and what is without outflows, [one may ask]:

among the eighteen elements, how many have both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), how many have no applied thought and only sustained thought, and how many have neither applied nor sustained thought?
The verse says:
The five consciousnesses possess only vitarka and vicāra; the last three possess all three; the remainder possess none.
The commentary says:

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, possess both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), because they are always associated with vitarka and vicāra; since their modes of activity are coarse and operate toward external objects, and because their apprehension of meaning is determinate, the word "only" is used [to indicate this].

The latter three refer to the mind-element (*manas*), the mental-object-element (*dharma*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñāna*), as each occupies the final position within their respective categories of faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.

These latter three elements all comprise three types: the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the associated mental-object-element, excluding *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).

If one is in the desire realm or the first dhyāna, there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); in the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka and only vicāra; and from the second dhyāna and above, up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
The non-associated factors subsumed within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are likewise [without vitarka]. In the intermediate dhyāna, vicāra is also thus:
at all times it is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra, because there is no second vitarka and it is associated only with vicāra.
Since *vicāra* (sustained thought) within the desire realm and the first dhyāna is not included among the three categories [of vitarka, vicāra, and avitarkāvicāra], what should it be named?
It should be called "without *vicāra* and with *vitarka* only," because there is no second *vicāra* and it is associated solely with *vitarka*.
For this reason, it is said that the stage with vitarka and vicāra (savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ) consists of four categories of phenomena:
first, those with both vitarka and vicāra, which refers to all associated mental factors other than vitarka and vicāra themselves;
second, those without vitarka and with vicāra only, which refers to vitarka itself.
Third, those without vitarka and without vicāra refer to all non-associated dharmas (*viprayukta-dharma*).
Fourth, those without vicāra and with only vitarka refer to vicāra itself.
The remaining ten material realms (*rūpa-dhātu*) are devoid of both vitarka and vicāra, because they are eternally dissociated from vitarka and vicāra.
If the five groups of consciousness possess vitarka and vicāra, how can they be said to be non-conceptual?
The verse states:
The five are said to be non-conceptual Because [they lack] discursive and recollective conceptualization.
With the scattered wisdom of the mental stage, it takes the various mental attentions as its essence.
The treatise says:
It is traditionally taught that there are three kinds of discrimination:

There are three types of conceptualization: first, innate conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*); second, discursive conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*); and third, recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).

Although the five groups of sensory consciousness possess innate conceptualization, they lack the other two; therefore, they are said to be "without conceptualization," just as a horse with only one leg is called "legless."
The essence of intrinsic discrimination (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is exclusively vitarka; this will be explained in its proper place among the mental factors (*caitta*) later on.

The other two types of discrimination, in their respective order, have as their essence the wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) that are distracted (*asamāhita*) within the stage of the mind (*manobhūmi*). "Distracted" means not being in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Discursive wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is called "discrimination by calculation" (abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa).
All mindfulness associated with the mental consciousness, whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, is called "recollection discrimination" (anusmaraṇa-vikalpa).
Having thus explained that which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (dhātus), how many have an object (sālambana) and how many are without an object?
How many are appropriated (upātta) and how many are unappropriated?
The verse says:
Seven consciousnesses and half of the dharma-element possess objects; the rest do not.
The first eight elements and sound are non-appropriated; the rest are of both kinds.
The Treatise says:

The six consciousnesses, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are called "having an object" (*sālambana*), because they are able to apprehend objects.

The remaining ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) subsumed within the dharma-element are called "without an object" (*anālambana*), as this is established by logical implication.
Thus, having already explained those with objects of perception and so forth:

among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), nine are non-appropriated (*anupāttaka*). These are the first seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and the entire dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*); these eight, along with sound (*śabda*), are all non-appropriated.
The remaining nine elements each pertain to two categories, namely, being appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
The five sense organs, such as the eye, when abiding in the present, are called appropriated; those of the past and future are called non-appropriated.

Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility that exist in the present and are not separated from the five sense organs are termed "appropriated" (upātta); those that exist in the present but are not separated from the organs, or those belonging to the past and future, are termed "non-appropriated" (anupātta).

For example, within the body—excluding those things conjoined with the sense faculties—such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, feces, urine, mucus, saliva, blood, and so forth, as well as color, odor, taste, and tangibility found in external earth, water, and other elements: although these exist in the present, they are not appropriated.
Regarding the term "appropriated" (*upātta*): what is its meaning?

It is called "appropriated" because it is collectively grasped and maintained by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as their basis; for they mutually follow one another in terms of benefit and harm.
That is to say, it is because worldly people speak of there being a "conscious contact," since one experiences pleasure and so forth when touched by various conditions.
That which is the opposite of this is called "non-appropriated.
Thus, the appropriated and so forth have been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are of the nature of primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and how many are of the nature of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
How many are accumulative, and how many are non-accumulative?
The verse says:
Within the element of tangibility there are two [types]; the remaining nine are derived from matter.
The same applies to one portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Ten material elements are accumulative.
The treatise says:
The element of tangibility (spraṣṭavyadhātu) comprises two categories: the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived elements (upādāyarūpa).
There are four primary elements, namely solidity and so forth.
There are seven derived elements, namely smoothness and so forth; they are called "derived" because they arise in dependence upon the primary elements.
The remaining nine material elements (*rūpadhātu*) are exclusively derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); that is to say, the five sense organs and the four objects such as visible form.
A portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), namely unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-rūpa*), is likewise exclusively derived matter.

The remaining seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), excluding non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*), are neither of the two types [of derived matter].
The Venerable Buddhadeva asserts that the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) consist exclusively of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
That argument is incorrect, because the sūtras state that only the four characteristics—solidity and so forth—are the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Since these four great elements are subsumed solely under the category of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), solidity, moisture, and the rest are not apprehended by the eye and other [faculties], nor are color, sound, and the rest perceived by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Therefore, that argument is certainly illogical.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the eye is an internal sense base (āyatana), consisting of translucent matter derived from the four great elements; it is material, invisible, and resistant. This is explained in detail for the other bases up to the body base as well."
"Monks, you should know that 'form' refers to the external sense base (bāhyāyatana) produced by the four great elements; it possesses form, is visible, and is resistant.
'Sound' refers to the external sense base produced by the four great elements; it possesses form, is invisible, and is resistant."
The two bases of odor and taste are explained at length in the same manner.

Tangible objects refer to the external base; they consist of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements, and are characterized by being material, invisible, and resistant.

In this way, the sūtra states that only the sense-base of the tangible (spraṣṭavyāyatana) subsumes the four great elements (mahābhūta), clearly demonstrating that all other sense-bases possessing form (rūpāyatana) are not great elements.
If this is so, why does the sūtra say: "That which, within the physical mass of the eye, is internal, individual, solid, and of a solid nature," and so forth, at length?
That explanation—that the nature of solidity and so forth is not separate from the physical mass of the eye-faculty—is free from the fault of contradiction.

As for the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra* stating that the six elements alone constitute the person (*pudgala*), this is intended to reveal the fundamental material basis that constitutes a person; it does not mean that the person consists of nothing more than those, for that same sutra further mentions the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

Furthermore, because mental factors would otherwise not exist, one should not maintain that mental factors are identical to the mind; for a sūtra states that mental factors such as perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) depend upon the mind.
Furthermore, because it is also said that there are minds characterized by attachment and so forth,
the distinctions among the various elements (*dhātu*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), as previously described, are thereby established.
Thus has the nature of the primary elements been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the ten material elements—the five faculties and the five objects—are accumulative because they are aggregates of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
By implication, the remaining eight are not accumulative, as they are not composed of atoms.
Having thus explained that which is accumulative and so forth,
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are capable of cutting and how many are objects to be cut?
How many are capable of burning and how many are objects to be burned?
How many are capable of cutting, and how many are that which is cut?
The verse says:
Only the four external elements are both capable of cutting and that which is cut.
It is also that which is burned and that which weighs; it is the burner and the weighed, the subject of dispute.
The treatise says:
Form, odor, taste, and tangibility constitute the axe, the firewood, and so forth; these are precisely what are termed "the cutter" and "the cut."
What dharma is called "cutting"?

When a mass of matter, such as firewood, arises in continuous succession in close proximity, and an axe or similar instrument separates it so that each part continues to arise individually—this dharma is called "cutting.
The material sense-faculties, such as the body, are not called "that which is cut," because they cannot be entirely severed to become two distinct parts.
The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth cannot be divided into two parts, because when a limb is separated from the body, it no longer possesses the faculty.
Furthermore, the body-faculty and the others are not capable of cutting, because they are pure and subtle, like the luster of a precious gem.

Just as the entities that cut and that are cut consist solely of the four external elements, so too do the entities that are burned and that are weighed; that is to say, only the four external elements are designated as "that which is burned" and "that which weighs."
The material sense-faculties, such as the body, are likewise not two distinct entities, because they are pure and subtle, like the light of a precious gem.
The sound-element is entirely excluded [from being a cause of burning or weighing], because it does not persist in a continuous stream.
Regarding that which burns and that which is weighed, there is a dispute; for some say:
The nature of that which can burn and that which is weighed is also as previously stated: they consist solely of the four external elements.
Alternatively, some say:
only the fire element may be called "that which can burn," while that which is weighed is solely weight.
Having thus explained the agent and object of cutting and so forth,

among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), how many are nurtured (*aupacayika*), how many are of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), how many possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*), and how many are momentary (*ekakṣaṇika*)?
The verse says:
The five internal [bases] possess the nature of being born of maturation and of nourishment; sound lacks that which is born of maturation;
eight [types of dharmas], including the unimpeded, are of the nature of outflow, and also possess the nature of being born of maturation.
The remaining three are real entities that are exclusively *dharmas*; the last three are exclusively momentary.
The treatise says:
The five internal [bases] are precisely the five elements beginning with the eye.

There are those produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) and those nurtured (*aupacayika*) that are not of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), because there is no distinct nature apart from what is produced by maturation and what is nurtured.

That which is produced by a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is called "produced by maturation," just as a cart drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart"; this is stated thus by omitting the intermediate term.
Alternatively, because the karma that has been performed transforms and reaches maturation at the time the fruit is obtained, it is called *vipāka* (maturation).
Because the fruit arises from that [karma], it is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Because the fruit obtained is of a different category from its cause and yet is that which has matured, it is called *vipāka*.
Alternatively, one may metaphorically designate the name of the effect upon the cause, just as one metaphorically designates the name of the cause upon the effect.
As a sūtra states:
"One should know that these present six bases of contact are precisely the karma created in the past."
That which is benefited by superior conditions such as food and drink, physical support, sleep, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called "nourished" (*aupacayika*).
Some say that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) can also provide nourishment.
This merely prevents harm; it does not provide any additional benefit.
It nurtures the continuity [of the life-stream] and is constantly able to protect the continuity of maturation (vipāka), just as an outer wall defends and assists an inner city.
Sound has both outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and nurtured (*aupacayika*) types, but no retribution-born (*vipākaja*) type. Why is this?
Because it functions according to one's will.
If that were so, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* should not state that by well-cultivating the avoidance of harsh speech, one obtains the mark of a Great Being’s Brahma-like voice. Some say:
because the sound belongs to the third transmission, although it arises from that [avoidance], it is not a maturation (*vipāka*).
This means that from those karmas the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise, and from the primary elements, sound is produced through the impact of conditions.
Some say: because sound belongs to the fifth stage of transmission, although it arises from those [karmas], it is not a maturation (*vipāka*).

That is to say, the maturation primary elements (*vipāka-mahābhūta*) arise from that karma; from these, the nourishment primary elements (*aupacayika-mahābhūta*) are successively produced; and from these, the homogeneous primary elements (*naiṣyandika-mahābhūta*) are successively produced, which then give rise to sound.
If that were so, since bodily sensation arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by karma, it would not be a maturation (*vipāka*).
If sensation were like sound, it would contradict correct reasoning.
Regarding the eight unobstructed [realms], the seven mental and mental-object realms possess the nature of being both outflows (*niṣyanda*) and born of maturation.

That which is produced by the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). That which is induced and produced by the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*). Since all unobstructed phenomena lack accumulation, they are not "nourished" (*aupacayika*).

The "remainder" refers to the other four—visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—all of which pertain to all three types: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*), and those of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
Regarding "only the real is dharmas": "real" refers to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it is firm and substantial.
Since this is subsumed within the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*), only the dharma-sphere alone is said to possess reality.
The mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness are called the "last three," as they are spoken of last among the triads of the six [bases].

Only within these three realms is there that which is "a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇika*), namely the category of the first untainted *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*. It is called a single moment because it is not a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
This statement refers to that which is ultimately not a result of outflow; for among all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there is none that is not a result of outflow.

The mind associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the other factors arising simultaneously are called the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
Thus, the [categories] such as those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) have been explained.

Now one should reflect upon this: if the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) was previously unaccomplished and is now accomplished, is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) also [accomplished]?
And if the eye-consciousness-element was previously unaccomplished and is now accomplished, is the eye-element also [accomplished]?
Regarding such questions as these, they shall now be answered briefly.
The verse says:
The eye and the eye-consciousness element Are acquired either independently or simultaneously; they are not equal.
The Commentary states:

Regarding "attaining alone," this refers to cases where the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is first achieved but the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not. This occurs when one born in the desire realm gradually attains the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), or when one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages.

There may be cases where visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is not previously established but is now established, while the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is not; this refers to when visual consciousness arises in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages, as well as at the time of passing away from those stages to be reborn in a lower stage.

Regarding "attaining both": this refers to cases where one who previously did not possess [the faculties] of two realms now attains their possession—namely, when one dies in the formless realm and is born into the desire realm or the Brahma-world.
"Neither" refers to the negation of both, meaning the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
"Etc. refers to the following: if one possesses the eye-element, does one also possess the eye-consciousness?
This should be analyzed in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
The first phrase refers to those born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages whose eye-consciousness does not arise.
The second phrase refers to those born in the desire realm who have not yet obtained the eye-faculty, or who have obtained it but subsequently lost it.

The third case refers to those born in the desire realm who have obtained the eye faculty and do not lose it, as well as those born in the Brahma-world or in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages when they are actually perceiving forms.
The fourth alternative refers to cases other than those previously described.

In this manner, the acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*) and the form-faculty (*rūpa-dhātu*), as well as of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the form-faculty, should be considered according to reason. To include such meanings not yet explicitly stated, the verse again uses the term "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Thus, the attainment of accomplishment and so forth have already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are internal and how many are external?
The verse says:
The twelve internal [bases], such as the eye, etc., and the six external [objects], such as form, etc.
The treatise says:
The six faculties and the six consciousnesses are termed the twelve internal; "external" refers to the remaining six objects, such as form, etc.
That which depends on the "self" is called internal; everything else is called external.
Since the substance of the self does not exist, how could there be internal or external?
Because it is the basis for the grasping of a self, the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self."
Therefore, a sutra says:
"By well-taming the self, the wise attain birth in heaven.
Elsewhere, the Blessed One spoke of taming the mind, as stated in a sutra:
One should skillfully subdue the mind; when the mind is subdued, it can lead to happiness.
Therefore, the "self" is merely a conventional designation for the mind.
Because the eyes and other faculties are its immediate supports, they are called "internal."
Since form and so forth are remote from this [consciousness] as its objects, they are called "external.
If that were the case, the six consciousnesses would not be called "internal," because they have not yet reached the state of the mind (manas) and thus do not serve as the support for the mind.

When [a consciousness] reaches the state of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), it does not lose its nature as one of the six consciousness-elements; nor does it, while not yet having reached the state of the mind-element, transcend the characteristic of being the mind.

If this were otherwise, the mind-element would exist only in the past, and the six consciousnesses would exist only in the present and future, which would contradict your own school’s tenet that all eighteen elements (*dhātus*) pervade all three periods of time.

Furthermore, if the six consciousnesses of the future and present lacked the characteristic of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), then the past mind-element could not be established either, because characteristics do not undergo alteration across the three periods of time.
The internal and external [bases] have already been explained.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and how many are "counter-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*)?
The verse says:
The dharma-element is of one type; the remaining two are of both types, depending on whether they perform their own function or not.
The commentary states:
"The dharma-element is of one type" means that the single dharma-element is exclusively of the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) type.

If an object is definitely the focal condition (*ālambana*) for a consciousness, and that consciousness has already arisen, is arising, or is destined to arise with respect to it, this focal object is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).

There is no single element of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) with respect to which an infinite number of mental consciousnesses have not already arisen, are currently arising, or will arise; for all noble ones (*ārya*) necessarily give rise to the thought that observes all phenomena as being without self (*anātman*).
Excluding its own substance and its co-existent dharmas, all other dharmas serve as its objects of perception (*ālambana*).

These excluded factors likewise serve as the objects of perception for the mind of the second moment; thus, these two moments of mind encompass all objects without exception. For this reason, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is always termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
Regarding "the remaining two": this refers to the fact that the remaining seventeen elements all possess both the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and the "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
What are these termed "homogeneous" and "non-homogeneous"?
They are defined as those that perform their own function and those that do not perform their own function.
If it performs its own function, it is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga); if it does not perform its own function, it is called "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).

In this context, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-dhātu*) that has seen, is seeing, or will see visible forms is called the "homogeneous eye. This should be explained in detail for each [faculty], up to the mental faculty (*mano-dhātu*), according to their respective objects and functions.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr state that the "similar-to-that" (sabhāga) eye has only four types:
namely, those that have not seen form and are already past, currently perishing, or destined not to arise.
The masters of the West maintain that there are five types:

namely, the category of non-arising phenomena is further divided into two—first, those associated with consciousness, and second, those dissociated from consciousness—and it should be understood that this applies likewise up to the element of the body (*kāyadhātu*).
The *tatsabhāga* (homogeneous) is exclusively that which is of a non-arising nature (*anutpattidharman*).

Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), when it is seen by the eye—whether already seen, currently being seen, or yet to be seen—it is termed "form that is *sabhāga*" (functioning). There are likewise four types of *tatsabhāga* form: namely, that which is not seen by the eye, whether already ceased, currently ceasing, or yet to arise. This is explained in detail up to the tactile element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), which is also the same.
Each should be explained according to its own faculty and its respective function; one should understand the "homogeneous" (sabhāga) and the "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
If the eye is homogeneous with respect to one [object], it is likewise homogeneous with respect to all others.
The same applies to the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) [eye], and so on in detail up to the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Form (*rūpa*), however, is not like this: for one who sees it, it is *sabhāga*; for one who does not see it, it is *tatsabhāga* (of that same class).

Why is this so? Because with respect to visible form (*rūpa*), such a thing occurs: that which is seen by one person may also be seen by many, as in the case of observing the moon, a dance, or a wrestling match.

With respect to the eye, however, such a thing does not occur: it is not the case that two eye-faculties (*cakṣur-indriya*) can see visible form simultaneously. Since the eye is not shared [between individuals], the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) states are established based upon a single continuum.
Because form is common [to many], the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*) are established based on multiple continuities (*saṃtati*).
As it is said regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), so it should be understood for sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects as well.
Sound may be like visible form;

however, the three—odor, flavor, and tangible objects—are apprehended only when they reach the sense faculties. Because these are not shared [with other senses], one is apprehended by one alone and not by others.
By logic, this should be like the eye and other faculties, and should not be explained in the same manner as visible form.
Although this principle holds, there may still be commonality.
Why is this? For the three elements—odor and so forth—possess the capacity to give rise to nose-consciousness and the other cognitions, both in relation to a single object and in relation to others.
The eye and the other [faculties] are not like that; therefore, they are explained as in the case of visible form.

Because the six consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and the rest—are dharmas that arise or do not arise according to their being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga), they are explained as in the case of the element of mind (manodhātu).
What is the meaning of *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (its counterpart)?

Because the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness mutually interact, it is called a "share" (*bhāga*). Alternatively, "share" refers to its own activity; or again, "share" refers to the contact (*sparśa*) produced [thereby]. Because they equally possess this share, they are called *sabhāga*.
That which is contrary to this is called "sabhāga" (homogeneous). Because it is not "asabhāga" (non-homogeneous) but shares the same category as that [sabhāga], it is named "sabhāga.
Thus have "sabhāga" and "tatsabhāga" been explained.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
The verse says:
Fifteen are abandoned only by cultivation; The final three elements pertain to all three.
They are not defiled, nor are they born of the six [consciousnesses]; form is certainly not abandoned by insight.
The commentary says:
"The fifteen elements" refers to the ten material elements and the five consciousness elements.
"Only abandoned by cultivation" means that these fifteen elements are abandoned solely through the path of cultivation.
"The last three elements" refers to the mind element (manodhātu), the phenomena element (dharmadhātu), and the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu).
"Pervading all three" means that each of these last three elements pertains to all three types [of abandonment].

The eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), along with their concomitant factors and their associated acquisitions (*prāpti*), are all abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). All other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), while all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

Is it not the case that there are further factors abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), namely the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the bodily and vocal actions that bring about rebirth in the evil destinies, because these are utterly incompatible with the Noble Path?

Nevertheless, this dharma is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). To briefly state its characteristics: non-defiled dharmas that are not produced from the six [consciousnesses] and are not form (*rūpa*) are certainly not abandoned by insight.

This is because the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is non-defiled and subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); it continues to be possessed even by those who have already abandoned desire and by those who have severed their roots of virtue.

If this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), then one would still be an ordinary person at the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

"Six" refers to the sense base of the mind (*manāyatana*); that which arises differently from this is called "not born from the six" (*a-ṣad-aja*), meaning it arises from the five faculties such as the eye, namely the five consciousnesses and so forth.
"Matter" refers to all bodily and vocal actions, etc., as well as the aforementioned [unmanifest] matter. Neither of these is definitely abandoned by insight. Why is this so?
Because it does not arise directly from delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*).
Having thus explained what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and so forth, [one may ask]:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are not?
The verse says:
The eye and a portion of the dharma-dhātu are said to be the eight kinds of seeing;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not seeing, because it does not deliberate.
The eye sees visible forms when it is of the same class (*sabhāga*); it is not the consciousness that depends upon it which sees them.
It is traditionally taught that [the eye] cannot perceive [forms] because it is obstructed by other material forms.
The treatise says:
The eye faculty is entirely seeing (*darśana*). A portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)—consisting of eight types—is also seeing; all others are not seeing.
What are these eight?

They are the five defiled views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), along with mundane right view, the right view of those in training (*śaikṣa*), and the right view of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), these eight are views (*dṛṣṭi*); the remainder are not views.
The five [views] beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) will be explained when the time comes in the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (*anuśaya-nirdeśa*).
Mundane right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) refers to wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Right view of those in training refers to all untainted views within the continuum of one in training.
Right view of those beyond training refers to all untainted views within the continuum of one beyond training.

Just as during the night or the day, the perception of various forms and images differs in clarity depending on whether there are clouds or no clouds, so too do the various views of the world differ according to whether they are defiled or undefiled.

Regarding the views of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are differences in the clarity or obscurity with which they observe the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Why is this?

Because mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*) is associated only with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); for the wisdom (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five sensory consciousnesses is incapable of deliberative judgment (*pariccheda*). It is defined as "view" because it involves judgment preceded by investigative reflection (*nirūpaṇa*).
The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses lacks such capacity because it is devoid of conceptual discrimination; therefore, it is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
By this same principle, it should be understood that all other forms of wisdom—whether defiled or non-defiled—as well as all other dharmas, are not "view."
If that is so, since the eye-faculty cannot perform deliberation, how can it be called "seeing"?
It is also called "seeing" because it can clearly and acutely observe various forms.
If it were the eye that sees, then it should also be called "seeing" whenever other consciousnesses are active.
Not all eyes are capable of direct perception.
Which ones are capable of direct perception?
It is said that it is the eyes of the same class (*sabhāga*) in conjunction with consciousness that can see, and nothing else.
If that were so, then it would follow that the consciousness which depends upon it sees the form, and not the eye.
This is not the case; visual consciousness certainly cannot see. Why is this?
It is traditionally said that because one cannot perceive forms obstructed by a barrier, when one sees various forms obstructed by walls and the like, they cannot be perceived.
If it were consciousness that sees, then since consciousness is non-obstructive (*apratigha*), walls and such would not hinder it, and one should therefore perceive the obstructed forms.
Visual consciousness does not arise with respect to obstructed forms; since consciousness does not arise, how could one see them?
Why does visual consciousness not arise in that case?
For those who maintain that the eye sees, because the eye is possessed of resistance (*sapratigha*), it lacks the functional capacity to see such obstructed forms.
Since consciousness and its support (the eye) operate upon the same object, one might say that visual consciousness does not arise with respect to that [distant object].
If you admit that consciousness sees, for what reason would it fail to arise?
Is the eye like the body-faculty, which only apprehends when in contact with its object, such that it fails to see that [distant object] because it is "resistant" (sapratigha)?
Furthermore, how is it that one can see objects obstructed by crystal, lapis lazuli, mica, water, and so forth?
Therefore, it is not because the eye is resistant (*sapratigha*) that it lacks the capacity to see those obscured forms.
If that is so, what of the visual consciousness you maintain?
Visual consciousness arises with respect to an obstructed form where there is no obstruction to light;
it does not arise with respect to an obstructed form where there is an obstruction to light.
Since consciousness does not arise, it cannot see.
However, when the sūtras state that the eye can see forms, they mean it is the basis for seeing; therefore, it is said to be able to see.
As that sūtra says:
It is the mind that cognizes phenomena;
it is not the [past] mind that cognizes, because that has already passed away.
What, then, is able to cognize?
This refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Since the mind (*manas*) is the support (*āśraya*) for consciousness, it is said to "cognize.

Alternatively, the function of the supported is expressed by means of its support, just as in common worldly usage one speaks of the "sound of the bed" when referring to the sound of the person sitting upon it.
Furthermore, as a sutra states:
"Forms cognized by the eye are lovely and desirable.
However, in reality, it is not these lovely and desirable forms that are actually cognized by the eye.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
"O Brahmin, you should know that the eye serves as a gate solely for the purpose of seeing forms.
Thus, we know that visual consciousness relies upon the eye-gate to see.
Nor should it be said that the gate (the eye-organ) is itself the seeing; for how could a sutra state that the eye constitutes seeing solely for the purpose of seeing visible forms?
If consciousness were able to see, what else would there be to perform the function of discerning?
What is the difference between the two functions of "seeing" (*darśana*) and "discerning" (*vijñapti*)?
Since the very act of seeing form is called discerning form—just as a certain portion of wisdom (*prajñā*) is called both "capable of seeing" and "capable of discerning."
Thus, a portion of consciousness is called both "that which sees" and "that which discerns.
Others raise this objection:
"If the eye can see, and the eye is the seer, then what is the function of seeing?"
This statement is not difficult to refute; for example, it is commonly accepted that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which cognizes, yet there is no cognizer.
Just as the function of cognition differs [from the agent], so too should it be with seeing (*darśana*).
Others further say:
Visual consciousness is that which sees; because the eye is the basis for this seeing, the eye is also said to "see.
Just as a bell is said to "ring" because it is the basis for the sound, so too is the eye described as seeing.
If that were the case, then since the visual faculty is the basis for consciousness, it should also be called "that which cognizes."
There is no such fault.
The world collectively agrees that visual consciousness is "seeing"; when it arises, one says it "sees forms," not that it "cognizes forms.
The *Vibhāṣā* also states this:
That which is apprehended by the eye and experienced by visual consciousness is called "the seen.
Therefore, it is said that only the eye is "able to see," and not "able to cognize.
It is only when consciousness manifests before one that it is said to be "able to cognize form," just as the sun is called "that which makes the day."
The masters of the Sautrāntika school have made this statement:
"How can they gather together to grasp at empty space? From the conditions of the eye, forms, and so forth, visual consciousness arises;
among these, which is the seer, and which is the seen?"

In reality, dharmas as cause and effect possess no functional activity; however, to conform to worldly convention, we employ provisional expressions, such as calling the eye "that which sees" and consciousness "that which cognizes. The wise should not harbor dogmatic attachment to these designations.
As the Blessed One has said:
"One should not be dogmatically attached to regional dialects, nor should one insistently seek after conventional designations.
Nevertheless, the Vaibhāṣika school of Kaśmīra maintains that the eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body feels, and the mind cognizes.
When seeing a form, is it seen by one eye or by both eyes?
There is no fixed rule on this matter.
The verse says:
Or [it is] because when both eyes are used simultaneously, the perception of forms is distinct.
The treatise says:
All the great masters of the Abhidharma unanimously state:
At times, both eyes see together; for when both eyes are open, the perception of forms is clear, whereas when one eye is open, it is not so.

Furthermore, when one eye is open and the other is touched, one sees two moons before oneself; this does not occur when one eye is closed and the other is touched. Therefore, at times both eyes see together.
It is not the case that consciousness, as the supported [subject], becomes two parts; for it abides without spatial location and thus differs from obstructive matter.

If this school asserts that the eye sees, the ear hears, and so forth up to the mind cognizing, then when those respective sense organs correctly apprehend their objects of perception, are they in contact with them or not?
The verse says:
The faculties of eye, ear, and mind, and their objects, are mutually contradictory regarding whether they reach [their objects] or not.
The commentary says:

The faculties of the eye, ear, and mind apprehend objects that are not in direct contact with them. This means that while the eye can see forms at a great distance, it cannot perceive things such as medicinal ointments applied to the eye itself.
Likewise, the ear can hear sounds from afar, yet it cannot hear those sounds that are in immediate proximity to the auditory faculty.

If the eye and ear faculties apprehend only objects that come into contact with them, then those who practice meditative concentration should not cultivate the production of the divine eye and ear faculties, just as they do not cultivate the nose faculty and so forth.
If the eye can see forms that do not come into contact with it, why is it unable to see all distant, obstructed, and other non-contacting forms universally?
Why does a magnet attract iron that is not in contact with it, yet does not attract all such non-contacted iron?
The objection regarding the view that the visual faculty perceives objects through direct contact faces the same difficulty.
Why is it that the eye cannot universally perceive all visible forms in contact with it, such as eye-salve or the applicator stick?

Furthermore, just as the nose and other [senses] can apprehend objects that reach them, yet cannot apprehend all odors and so forth that coexist with the sense organ itself, so too the eye faculty, though it perceives what does not reach it, does not perceive everything; the ear faculty is likewise.
Because the mind is formless, it cannot possess the quality of reaching [its object].
Some maintain that the auditory faculty perceives both objects that are reached and those that are not reached, because one can hear sounds within one's own ears.
The remaining three material faculties, such as the nose and so forth, are the opposite of the aforementioned; they apprehend only objects that come into contact with them.
How is it known that the nose apprehends only odors that reach it?
Because one does not smell odors when breathing is suspended.
What is meant by "reaching" (*prāpti*)?
It refers to arising without interval.
Furthermore, do atoms (*paramāṇu*) touch one another?
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra maintain that atoms do not touch one another. Why is this?
If the entire substance of atoms were to touch, there would be the logical error of the substantial bodies of things intermingling.
If they were to touch even a single part, they would incur the fault of being composite; yet atoms have no further subdivisions.
If this is so, why do they produce sound when striking one another?
It is simply because atoms arise in immediate succession.
If it were admitted that they touch one another, then when striking a stone or clapping hands, their substances would become intermingled.
If they do not touch, how is it that an aggregate of matter does not disperse when struck?
It is because it is held together by the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) that it does not disperse.
There are wind elements capable of disintegration and dispersion, such as at the time of the kalpa’s destruction;
there are wind elements capable of formation and cohesion, such as at the time of the kalpa’s formation.
How is it that the three faculties, by arising without interval, are said to grasp their objects through contact?
It is precisely by virtue of being "immediate" that it is said to grasp the object; this means that there is absolutely no intervening substance whatsoever.
Furthermore, since it is admitted that composite matter possesses parts, there is no fault in their mutual contact.
Since this principle is accepted, the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā* is well established.
Thus it asks:
"Do all things that possess tangibility arise because they have tangibility as their cause?"
"Does it arise with non-contact as its cause?
The same question applies to all things that are non-contact.

To this principle, he provides an indeterminate answer: sometimes contact serves as the cause for the arising of non-contact, namely at the moment when conjoined objects are in the process of separating.
Sometimes non-contact serves as the cause for the arising of contact, namely when separated objects are in the process of coming together.
Sometimes contact serves as the cause for the arising of contact, namely when conjoined objects further come together.
Sometimes that which is non-contact arises with non-contact as its cause; this refers to the homogeneous continuity of motile dust particles.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"If atoms were to touch one another, they would necessarily persist into the subsequent moment."
However, the Venerable [Vasumitra] says:
"All atoms do not actually touch one another; it is merely by virtue of their being without interval that the conventional designation 'contact' is established.
This intention of the Venerable should be accepted with delight.
If it were otherwise, these atoms would necessarily have intervals between them.
Since the space between them would be empty, what would obstruct their movement such that they could be considered "possessing resistance" (sapratigha)?
Furthermore, there is no composite matter apart from the atoms; thus, when composites touch, it is the atoms themselves that touch.
Just as that which is subject to transformation and obstruction [is so], this too should be the same.
Furthermore, if you admit that atoms possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga), then whether they touch or do not touch, they must both have parts.
If they lack spatial dimensions, then even if one admits they touch, this fault does not arise.

Furthermore, regarding the sense organs such as the eye: do they perceive their respective objects only when the object is equal in size to the organ, appearing as a great mountain and so forth due to rapid movement—like a whirling firebrand—or do they perceive objects both equal and unequal in size?
The verse says:
One should know that the three beginning with the nose perceive objects of equal magnitude.
The commentary says:
Regarding the three faculties previously mentioned that reach their objects—the nose and so forth—it should be understood that they can only apprehend objects of equal magnitude.
Just as the atoms of the faculty are minute, the atoms of the object are likewise; for the consciousnesses of the nose and so forth arise from the meeting of these two in mutual correspondence.

The visual and auditory faculties are indeterminate; that is to say, the eye perceives forms at times as small, such as when seeing the tip of a hair; at times as large, such as when momentarily opening one's eyes and seeing a great mountain; and at times as equal in size, such as when seeing a grape.

In this way, the auditory faculty hears various sounds, whether small or large, such as those produced by mosquitoes or thunder; it perceives them according to their respective magnitudes, whether small or large.
Since the mental faculty lacks material obstruction, its distinctions of shape and magnitude cannot be determined.
How are the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the various faculties, such as the eye, arranged?
The atoms of the eye-faculty are situated upon the pupil, spread out horizontally; they are like a cumin flower, being covered by a clear, translucent membrane so that they do not scatter.
Some say that they abide in a manner like a mass of spheres piled one upon another; because their substance is transparent, they do not obstruct one another, like crystal (*sphaṭika*).
The atoms of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) reside within the cavity of the ear, arranged in a spiral, like the rolled-up bark of a birch tree.
The atoms of the olfactory faculty reside within the nasal bridge, facing backward and downward like a pair of fingernails.
These first three faculties are arranged horizontally; their distribution is level, without elevation or depression, like a floral crown upon a head.
The atoms of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed across the tongue, shaped like a half-moon.
It is traditionally taught that an area in the center of the tongue, the size of a hair-tip, is not pervaded by the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
The atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya-paramāṇu) are distributed throughout the entire body, corresponding to its physical dimensions.
The atoms of the female faculty (strīndriya-paramāṇu) are shaped like a drumhead, and the atoms of the male faculty (puruṣendriya-paramāṇu) are shaped like a thumb.

The atoms of the eye faculty are sometimes all of the same class (sabhāga), sometimes all of the corresponding class (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are of the corresponding class while the rest are of the same class.
The same applies even to the atoms of the tongue-faculty.

Regarding the atoms of the body-faculty, it is certain that they do not all constitute the "homogeneous" (sabhāga); even in the most intensely heated hells where the body is enveloped in fierce flames, there still exist infinite atoms of the body-faculty that are "of the same class" (tat-sabhāga).

It is traditionally taught that if the body-faculty were to produce consciousness throughout its entire extent, the body would disintegrate; for it is impossible for a single atom of the faculty and a single atom of the object to serve respectively as the support and the objective condition for the production of body-consciousness.
Because the five consciousnesses necessarily require the accumulation of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) before they can constitute the nature of a support (*āśraya*) or an object (*ālambana*),
it is for this very reason that the atom is also described as having the nature of being "invisible" (*anidarśana*), since it cannot be seen.

As previously stated, there are six kinds of consciousness, namely the visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element. Just as the five [sensory] consciousnesses take only the present as their object while the mental consciousness takes all three times and the non-temporal (unconditioned) as its objects, is it the case that the bases (*āśraya*) of these various consciousnesses are likewise?
Not so; how then? The verse says:
The subsequent supports are exclusively past; the supports of the five consciousnesses are either simultaneous or [past].
The treatise states:

Mental consciousness relies solely upon the immediately preceding ceased mind; the supports of the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, are either simultaneous or—by the use of the term "or"—are also indicated to rely upon the past.
The eye is the co-nascent support for visual consciousness; likewise, up to the body being the co-nascent support for tactile consciousness, because they exist simultaneously in the present.
The mind that has ceased without interval is the past support.

The supports for each of these five groups of consciousness are twofold: the five [faculties] such as the eye are their specific supports, while the mind-faculty (*manas*) serves as the common support-nature for all five; therefore, it is stated thus.
If it is the nature of the support for visual consciousness, is it also the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for visual consciousness?
And if it is the equal-and-immediate condition for visual consciousness, is it also the nature of the support for visual consciousness?
Four propositions should be formulated.
The first proposition refers to the co-nascent eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The second proposition refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) that have ceased in the immediately preceding moment.
The third phrase refers to the past mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The fourth phrase refers to all factors other than those mentioned.
This applies likewise up to body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), for each of which one should state its own respective faculty.

The response regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should follow the preceding formulation: that which is the nature of the support (*āśraya*) for mental consciousness is necessarily its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

However, there are cases where something is the immediately preceding condition for mental consciousness without being its supporting nature; this refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that have ceased in the immediate past.
For what reason do consciousnesses arise by depending upon two conditions alike, yet only the sense organs—and not their objects—are designated as their "support" (*āśraya*)?
The verse states:
Because consciousness varies according to the transformation of the organ, The eye and so forth are called the supports.
The treatise says:
The eye and so forth are precisely the six elements of the eye and so forth, because the sense organs such as the eye undergo transformation.
As the various consciousnesses evolve differently, they follow the increase or decrease of the organs, such that the clarity or dullness of the consciousness corresponds to them.
It is not that the transformation of form and so forth causes consciousness to differ, because consciousness follows the sense faculty and does not follow the object.
The designation "based on" applies only to the eye and so forth, and not to others.

For what reason, when form and so forth are precisely what is cognized, is it called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," rather than being called "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness"?
The verse says:
Because of those [factors] and their unique causes, consciousness is designated according to its sense organ.
The commentary says:

He says that what was previously described as the "basis" refers to the sense faculties (*indriya*); because the faculty is the basis, consciousness is designated according to it. Furthermore, regarding the "unshared" factor:

the eye is the exclusive basis for its own visual consciousness, whereas visible form is also taken as an object by the visual consciousnesses of other bodies and by the mental consciousnesses of both oneself and others. This should be understood to apply likewise up to the body and tangibles. Consciousness receives its name based on the superiority of its basis and the cause of its exclusivity.
It follows the faculty, not the object, as in the cases of the name "drum-sound" or "barley-sprout.
When the eye sees a form while residing in a particular body, are the levels (bhūmi) of the body, the eye, the form, and the visual consciousness the same?

One should say that these four are either different or the same. That is to say, if one born in the desire realm sees forms of their own level with an eye of their own level, all four belong to their own level.
If one sees forms of the desire realm with an eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to the desire realm, while the eye and the visual consciousness belong to the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm and three [factors—eye, consciousness, and contact] belong to the first dhyāna.

If one sees the forms of the desire realm with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to the desire realm, the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm, the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness of form belongs to the first dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the second dhyāna, the body belongs to the desire realm, both the eye and the forms belong to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
In this way, one should reflect accordingly on how, with the eye of the third or fourth dhyāna stage, one sees forms of a lower stage or forms of one's own stage.

When born in the first dhyāna, if one sees forms of one's own stage with the eye of that same stage, all four [factors] belong to the same stage; when seeing forms of the desire realm, three [factors—the eye, consciousness, and the mental faculty] belong to the first dhyāna, while the form belongs to the desire realm.
If one sees the forms of the first dhyāna with the eye of the second dhyāna, three factors belong to the first dhyāna while the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.
When seeing the forms of the desire realm, the body and consciousness belong to the first dhyāna, the forms belong to the desire realm, and the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.
When seeing forms of the second dhyāna, the body-consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna, while the eye and the forms belong to the second dhyāna.
In this same manner, one should reflect accordingly on cases where the eye of the third or fourth dhyāna levels sees forms of its own level, or of lower or higher levels.
In this same way, one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna should be considered according to principle as seeing forms of their own or other levels with the eye of their own or other levels.
The other realms should also be distinguished in this manner.
Now, the definitive characteristics of these shall be briefly explained.
The verse says:
The eye is not inferior to the body; form and consciousness are not superior to the eye.
Visible forms relate to consciousness in all [stages]; the same applies to the other two [objects] regarding the body.
As it is for the eye, so it is for the ear; the next three [senses] belong to their own stage.
Body-consciousness belongs to its own stage or a lower one; it should be known that the mental faculty is not fixed.
The treatise says:

The body, the eye, and visible forms—these three all pertain to five stages, namely, the desire realm and the four dhyānas; however, visual consciousness exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
In this context, with respect to the stage of birth, the eye-faculty is either equal to or superior to the body, but never inferior to it.

Visible forms and visual consciousness are either equal to or inferior to the eye, but never superior to it; for an eye of a lower stage cannot see visible forms of a higher stage, and a consciousness of a higher stage does not depend upon an eye of a lower stage.

Regarding the relationship between visible form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they may be equal, superior, or inferior; the relationship between visible form and consciousness is the same as that between visible form and the body.

It should be understood that the detailed explanation for the ear-element (*śrotra-dhātu*) is analogous to that of the eye: namely, the ear is not inferior to the body, sound-consciousness is not superior to the ear, and sound is [related to] consciousness in all three ways (equal, superior, or inferior).
The same applies to the body; as appropriate, this should be understood in detail according to the explanation of the eye.

Regarding the triad of nose, tongue, and body, all are generally of their own level (*svabhūmika*). Among these, there is a distinction: the body and its corresponding tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) must necessarily belong to the same level.

In relation to contact (*sparśa*), the body, and consciousness (*vijñāna*), [the latter] may be of its own level or a lower level; "its own level" refers to when one is born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna, while "lower level" refers to when one is born in the three higher dhyānas.

It should be understood that the four factors regarding the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are not fixed: that is, at times the mind, the body, consciousness, and phenomena (*dharma*) all belong to the same level, while at other times they belong to different levels (upper or lower).
The body belongs exclusively to the five stages, while three [of the supernormal knowledges] pervade all [stages].

Regarding their occurrence during the attainment of meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and at the time of rebirth, they may be either identical to or different from one another according to what is appropriate, as will be analyzed in detail later in the "Chapter on Meditative Concentrations" (*Samādhivarga*).
To avoid excessive elaboration, this will not be analyzed here; to discuss it again later would require little effort for much gain.
Having concluded this digression, we should now analyze the primary subject.
We shall now investigate: among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many within each of the six consciousnesses are cognized by which consciousness?
How many are permanent? How many are impermanent?
How many are faculties (*indriya*)? How many are non-faculties?
The verse says:
The five external [objects] are cognized by two; the eternal dharmadhātu is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
one portion of the dharma[-dhātu] is a faculty (*indriya*), as are the twelve internal elements.
The Treatise says:

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the five elements beginning with form (*rūpa*) are, respectively, the objects of the five consciousnesses beginning with visual consciousness; furthermore, they are all collectively the objects of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Thus, each of these five elements is cognized by two of the six consciousnesses.

By this analogy, it should be understood that the remaining thirteen elements are all cognized solely by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because they are not the objective spheres of the five groups of sensory consciousness.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), there is not a single element that is entirely permanent; only a portion of the dharma-element—the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is permanent. By implication, all other dharmas and all other elements are impermanent.

Furthermore, the Sūtras speak of twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), namely: the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, faculty of pleasure, faculty of pain, faculty of joy, faculty of grief, faculty of equanimity, faculty of faith, faculty of vigor, faculty of mindfulness, faculty of concentration, faculty of wisdom, faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," faculty of "knowing," and faculty of "one who has known."

The great masters of the Abhidharma all deviate from the sequence of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) found in the Sūtras, placing the mental faculty (*manas*) after the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it possesses an object of cognition (*sālambana*).

The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) thus described are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*): specifically, the twelve internal elements and a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

This "portion of the element of phenomena" consists of the eleven [faculties] beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and a portion of the final three [faculties], because they are included within the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the twelve internal [bases]: the five faculties, such as the eye, are subsumed under their respective names; the mind faculty is generally subsumed within the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*); the final three [faculties] are partially subsumed within the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*); and the female and male faculties are subsumed as portions of the body element (*kāyadhātu*).
As will be explained later,
by extension of this principle, the remaining [elements]— the five elements of form and so forth, and a portion of the dharma-element—
all have as their essence that which is not a faculty (*indriya*). *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Two.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

2. Chapter on the Analysis of Faculties (Indriya-vibhāga). Part One of the Second Chapter: Analysis of Faculties. Having thus enumerated the faculties based on the elements (*dhātu*), what is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) in this context?
The term "faculty" (*indriya*) is derived from the sense of supreme sovereignty (*ādhipatya*). By means of this, the general meaning of "predominance" as a faculty is established.
With respect to what does this predominance apply?
The verse says:
It is said that the five [faculties] have predominance over four [faculties], and the four faculties have predominance over two kinds;
within the categories of defilement and purification, the five and eight [faculties] each act as predominant factors individually.
The treatise says:
Each of the five faculties, such as the eye, exercises sovereignty over four matters:
first, the adornment of the body; second, the guidance and nourishment of the body; third, the generation of consciousness and so forth; and fourth, their unique function.
