Furthermore, as for the faculties of the eye and ear adorning the body, this refers to the fact that if one were blind or deaf, the body would be unsightly.
As for their guiding and nourishing the body, this refers to avoiding dangers and difficulties by means of seeing and hearing.
"Producing consciousness and so forth" means that they give rise to the two types of consciousness along with their associated mental factors.
"Unique function" means that they are distinct in their respective abilities to see forms and hear sounds.
Regarding the nose, tongue, and body faculties adorning the body, it is as explained for the eyes and ears.
That which guides and nourishes the body refers to its ability to experience edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
That which generates consciousness and so forth refers to its arousal of the three consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors.
Its unique function refers to its smelling, tasting, and sensing of odors, flavors, and tangibles.
The female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, and the mind faculty each serve as predominant conditions for two matters.
First, regarding the female and male faculties, their two predominant functions are: first, the differentiation of sentient beings; and second, the differentiation of their specific characteristics.
Regarding the distinction of sentient beings: it is by means of these two faculties that sentient beings are categorized as female or male.
Regarding the distinction of differentiation: it is by means of these two faculties that there are differences in physical form, voice, breasts, and so forth.
Some say: Because it exercises sovereignty over both defilement and purification, it is said to "pertain to both. Why is this so?
Their fundamental nature is impaired.

For those who are *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, or hermaphrodites, there are no impure dharmas such as non-restraint, the immediate transgressions, or the severance of the roots of goodness; nor are there pure dharmas such as restraint, the attainment of the fruits [of the path], or the detachment from defilements.
The life-faculty has two functions: it can continue and sustain the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
The mind-faculty has two functions: it can continue subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) and it acts with sovereign control in accordance with its course.
Regarding that which can continue existence in a future life, as the Sūtra says:
"At that time, the gandharva manifests one of two states of mind, namely, either that accompanied by craving or that accompanied by aversion, and so forth."
Regarding "acting with mastery," as a sutra states:
"The mind can lead the world; The mind can universally encompass it.
Thus, this single dharma that is the mind Acts with mastery over all."
The five feelings, beginning with pleasure, and the eight faculties, beginning with faith, are predominant, respectively, within the realms of defilement and purification.

Regarding the predominance of the five feelings, beginning with pleasure, within defilement: this is because they are accompanied by and increased through the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) such as greed.
Regarding the predominance of the eight faculties, such as faith, for purification: it is because all pure phenomena arise and develop in accordance with them.
Other masters state that pleasure and the others also exercise predominance with respect to purification.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Because of pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated"; "suffering is the basis for faith"; and also, "renunciation is based on joy, sorrow, and equanimity."
The Vaibhāṣika masters transmit it thus.
Other teachers say:

"It is not the function of the eyes and so forth that guides and nourishes the body; rather, this is due to the predominance of consciousness. It is only through the discernment of consciousness that one can avoid dangers and difficulties and partake of solid food."

Since the functions of seeing forms and so forth are not distinct from consciousness, these non-common activities cannot be established as the specific predominant functions of the eye and other faculties; therefore, the eye and others do not constitute faculties on this basis.
If that is so, how is it? The verse says:
Because they exercise sovereignty over the cognition of their respective objects, The six faculties are established as a whole.
Based on the body, two faculties are established:
female and male, because they exercise predominance over the physical form, its maintenance, its defilement, and its purification.
It should be known that the life-faculty and the five sensations, as well as faith and the others, are established as faculties.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) are likewise so;
in the attainment of each successive path, they exercise sovereignty over [the attainment of] nirvāṇa and the like.
The commentary says:
That which cognizes its own object refers to the six groups of consciousness.

The five faculties, such as the eye, possess predominant power over the consciousnesses that can discern their respective individual objects; the sixth faculty, the mind, possesses predominant power over the consciousness that can discern all objects. Therefore, each of these six—the eye and so forth—is established as a faculty (*indriya*).
Is it not the case that visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth should also be established as faculties (*indriya*), since they likewise exercise sovereignty over the cognizing consciousness? [Response:
Objects do not exercise sovereign power over consciousness.

Sovereign power refers to preeminent mastery. Because the eye possesses the most preeminent mastery over the consciousness that arises to cognize visible forms, it is called "sovereign. It serves as the common cause for the cognition of various forms, and because consciousness varies in clarity or dullness according to the faculty of the eye.
Form is not so, because it is contradictory to both [the male and female characteristics].
This applies likewise to the mental faculty (manas) regarding phenomena (dharma).
Furthermore, the female and male faculties are established separately from the body faculty because they possess predominance over the states of femininity and masculinity.
The essential substance of the female and male faculties is not separate from the body faculty, as these names are established based on a specific portion of the body.

In their respective capacities for femininity and masculinity, these female and male faculties possess a predominant function; because this location differs slightly from other parts of the body faculty, they are established separately from it as two distinct faculties.
The distinctions in physical form, voice, activities, and inclinations of the female body are termed "femininity.
The differences in physical form, voice, activities, and inclinations of the male body are termed "masculinity."

The distinction between the two genders is due to the female and male faculties; therefore, it is said that the female and male faculties have predominance over the two genders. Among the maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the life-faculty has predominant function; among the defilements (*saṃkleśa*), the five feelings such as pleasure have predominant function.
Why is this so? Because the sūtra states:
"Greed increases in accordance with pleasant feeling; hatred increases in accordance with painful feeling; and ignorance increases in accordance with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
The five faculties, beginning with faith, exercise a predominant influence regarding purification. Why is this?
Because by their power, they subdue the various afflictions and induce the Noble Path.

Regarding the phrase "should be known," it is intended to encourage the understanding that each [of the three] can individually function as a faculty; the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) possess a predominant efficacy in attaining the successive paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

The statement "the same applies to the others" indicates that each one can individually function as a faculty (*indriya*). That is to say, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has a predominant efficacy regarding the attainment of the path of the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); the faculty of "knowing" has a predominant efficacy regarding the attainment of the path of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*); and the faculty of "one who has known" has a predominant efficacy regarding the attainment of *nirvāṇa*, because one cannot attain *parinirvāṇa* so long as the mind is not liberated.
The word "etcetera" (ādi) is used to indicate that there are further alternative formulations (*paryāya*). What are these alternative formulations? They are as follows:

the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has predominant efficacy regarding the cessation of afflictions abandoned through seeing; the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*) has predominant efficacy regarding the cessation of afflictions abandoned through cultivation; and the faculty of "one who possesses perfect knowledge" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) has predominant efficacy regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life, because by means of this, one is able to experience the joy and bliss of liberation.

If something is established as a faculty (indriya) on account of its predominance, then ignorance and the like should also be established as faculties, because the causes such as ignorance each possess a distinct predominant function with respect to their respective effects such as volitional formations (saṃskāra).

Furthermore, the vocal apparatus and so forth should also be established as faculties, because the vocal apparatus, the hands, the feet, and the organs of excretion and reproduction possess predominance respectively over the acts of speaking, grasping, walking, and the discharge of pleasure.

Such matters as these should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), because the characteristics of what is accepted as a faculty are as follows. The verse says: The basis of the mind, its differentiation, its maintenance, and its defilement; The commentary explains: These five characteristics constitute the definition of a faculty. First, the basis of the mind: the eye-faculty and so forth serve as the support for the mental consciousness. Second, the differentiation of the mind: the male and female faculties differentiate the continuum of the mind into male and female. Third, the maintenance of the mind: the life-faculty maintains the continuity of the mind throughout successive births. Fourth, the defilement of the mind: the faculties of sensation (feeling) defile the mind by causing attachment to pleasure and aversion to pain. Fifth, the purification of the mind: the faculties of faith and so forth purify the mind by counteracting those afflictions. Since the phenomena such as the vital organ (*jīvitendriya*) do not possess these characteristics, they are not established as faculties. This is the equipment and this is the purification; by means of these measures, the faculties are established.
The treatise says:
that which is the support of the mind consists of the six faculties, beginning with the eye.

These six internal bases are the foundation of sentient beings; their differentiation as female or male is due to the female and male faculties; furthermore, they persist for the duration of a single lifetime by means of the life faculty. Their defilement is brought about by the five feeling faculties;

the accumulation of the requisites for purification is brought about by the five beginning with faith; and their attainment of purification is brought about by the final three faculties. It is on account of these that the establishment of the faculties is complete.

Therefore, it should not be admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, or the vocal apparatus and so forth, are also established as faculties (*indriya*), because they lack this predominant function within this context.
Furthermore, other masters provide a different definition of the characteristic of a faculty.
The verse says:
Either as the basis for saṃsāra, And for birth, abiding, and experience, The first fourteen [bases] are established;
The latter [fourteen], likewise, pertain to cessation.
The Commentary states:
The phrase "or" indicates that this is the opinion of other masters, who establish the twenty-two faculties based on the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*).
The basis for transmigration refers to the six [faculties] beginning with the eye; birth arises from the female and male [faculties], as it is produced from them.
Abiding depends on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), for it relies upon that for its persistence.
Enjoyment depends on the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*), for they experience [objects].
It is with reference to these that the preceding fourteen faculties are established.
Within the stage of cessation (*nirodha*), the latter eight faculties are established by classifying them according to these four meanings.

The basis for cessation consists of the five faculties beginning with faith; regarding the three untainted [faculties], it is through the first that they arise, through the next that they abide, and through the last that they are experienced. Thus, the number of faculties neither decreases nor increases.

It is precisely for this reason that the sequence is established in the Sūtra: the vocal apparatus should not be considered the faculty for speech, because speech is only accomplished by depending on specific learned distinctions.

Likewise, the hands and feet should not each be established as faculties for the acts of grasping and walking, because there is no difference in their nature; for it is simply when the hands and feet arise with distinct locations and distinct characteristics that they are termed "grasping" and "walking."
Furthermore, there is also the act of moving and grasping apart from the hands and feet, as seen in the case of those that crawl on their bellies;
therefore, the hands and feet cannot be established as faculties (*indriya*) in that regard.

The organ through which excrement is expelled should not be established as a faculty for the function of evacuation, because heavy objects would fall through space due to gravity, and because [the expulsion] is actually induced by the power of the wind (*vāyu*).
The urinary and excretory organs should not be established as faculties (*indriya*), for they give rise to pleasure only when one is standing.
Furthermore, the throat, teeth, eyelids, and joints should also be established as faculties, because they possess the functional power to swallow, chew, open and close, and bend and extend.

Alternatively, since all causes possess causal efficacy (*samarthya*) with respect to their own effects, they would all have to be established as faculties (*indriya*). However, although those [causes] possess efficacy, they are not predominant (*adhipati*);

therefore, they are not established as faculties. If that were the case, then even things such as the vocal organs (*vāk-karaṇa*) would not be predominant and thus should not be established as faculties.
Among these, the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the male faculty have already been explained as before.
Since the substance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is dissociated from mind, it shall be discussed in detail within the section on dissociated factors.
Since faith and the others are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) by nature, they shall also be extensively analyzed among the mental factors.
As for the five sensations, such as pleasure, and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), there is no other place where they are analyzed; therefore, they should be explained here.
The verse says:
Displeasure of the body is called suffering; that same [displeasure] when it is pleasure is called happiness.
Furthermore, the mental pleasure of the three dhyānas is called joy in other stages.
Displeasure of mind is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*); neutral equanimity (*upekṣā*) is undifferentiated in both [the pleasant and unpleasant].
The three faculties are established based on the nine [stages] of the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
The treatise says:
"Body" refers to bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*), so called because it arises in dependence upon the body; that is, the sensation associated with the five consciousnesses.
"Displeasure" has the meaning of affliction or harm; within bodily sensations, those that are capable of afflicting or harming are termed the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).

What is called "pleasurable" (sukha) has the meaning of "beneficial inclusion. Specifically, within bodily sensation (kāyikī vedanā), that which is capable of providing benefit is termed the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).

Furthermore, the mental sensation associated with the third dhyāna that is capable of providing benefit is also termed the faculty of pleasure. Since there is no bodily sensation in the third dhyāna—because the five sensory consciousnesses are absent—the mental joy therein is designated as pleasure.
This very mental pleasure (cittasāta), with the exception of the third dhyāna, is termed the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) in the three lower stages.
Because the mental pleasure in the third dhyāna is tranquil and free from craving for joy, it is termed only the faculty of bliss (sukhendriya).
In the three lower stages, because there is coarse mental agitation accompanied by joy and craving, it is designated solely as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
The sensation associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is capable of causing affliction is a lack of mental pleasure, which is termed the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

The "intermediate" refers to that which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; this is precisely the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant. This intermediate sensation is termed the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Is this faculty of equanimity a bodily sensation or a mental sensation?
It should be said that it pertains to both.
For what reason are these two established collectively as a single faculty?
Because this sensation, whether residing in the body or the mind, is equally non-conceptual.

Mental suffering and pleasure arise from much conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), whereas this is not the case for bodily [sensation], as it occurs according to the power of the objective field (*viṣaya*).

The same applies to Arhats and others; therefore, these are established as faculties with body and mind being distinct. Equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises spontaneously without discrimination; therefore, it is established as a faculty where body and mind are unified.

Furthermore, the sensations of suffering and pleasure—whether residing in the body or the mind—are distinct in their characteristics, as one is detrimental and the other is beneficial; therefore, they are established as separate faculties (*indriya*).

In contrast, equanimity (*upekṣā*), whether in the body or the mind, is identical in its lack of discrimination; since it is neither detrimental nor beneficial and its characteristic is thus undifferentiated, it is established as a faculty collectively.

The five faculties of intention, joy, equanimity, faith, and so forth—these nine faculties, when present within the three paths, are established respectively as the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). That is to say:

in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), based on these nine [faculties] beginning with the mental faculty, one establishes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*); if one is in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one establishes the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) based on these same nine; and in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), one also establishes the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) based on these same nine.
On what basis are these three names established?

It is because, while on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there occurs the cognitive activity of "that which is to be known as previously unknown" (*ājñātavyam ajñātam*); therefore, that [path] is called "the knowledge of the as-yet-unknown" (*ājñātāvya*).

If one is on the path of cultivation, there is nothing previously unknown; rather, for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), one repeatedly and fully cognizes those very same objects. Therefore, that [knowledge] is called "already known" (*ājñāta*).

In the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), because one knows for oneself that [the truths] have been known, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); one who possesses this knowledge is called "one endowed with knowledge" (*ājñātāvī*).

Alternatively, one who has cultivated this knowledge until it becomes their very nature is called "one endowed with knowledge," meaning that by attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they know for themselves as it truly is:
"I have fully understood suffering; there is nothing further to be fully understood."
...and so forth, as explained at length.

Those faculties are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so on. Having thus already explained that the essential natures of the faculties differ, one should now analyze their distinctions according to various categories and meanings.
Among these twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
Only the last three are without outflows; The material faculties, life, sorrow, and suffering [are with outflows].
One should know that [the last three] are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*); the remaining nine faculties pertain to both.
The treatise says:
Regarding the final three faculties mentioned immediately prior, their essence is exclusively non-outflow (*anāsrava*), which carries the meaning of being "stainless" (*vimala*).
The terms "impurity" (*mala*) and "outflow" (*āsrava*) differ in name but are identical in substance.
The seven material faculties, as well as the life-faculty, the faculty of sorrow, and the faculty of suffering, are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Regarding the seven material [faculties]: these are the five faculties beginning with the eye, along with the female and male faculties, because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The five faculties of desire, resolve, joy, equanimity, and faith—these nine are all common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Other masters state that the five faculties beginning with faith are exclusively uncontaminated; therefore, the Blessed One said:
If one completely lacks these five faculties, such as faith, I say that such a person abides in the category of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjanapakṣa*).
This is not a valid proof, for this statement was made with reference to the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).
How is this known to be so?
Because it was previously stated, after establishing the distinctions among the various noble stages based on the five untainted faculties such as faith, that these words were spoken.
Alternatively, there are briefly two kinds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
There are two types: internal and external.
"Internal" refers to those who have not severed their roots of goodness; "external" refers to those whose roots of goodness have already been severed.
It is with reference to external ordinary beings that this statement is made:
If one is entirely devoid of these five faculties, such as faith, I declare that person to abide among the class of external worldlings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"There are sentient beings dwelling in the world who, whether born or growing, possess distinctions among superior, middling, and inferior faculties."
Since this was before the Buddha had yet turned the wheel of Dharma, we know that faith and the other faculties also pertain to the out-flowing (sāsrava) realm.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"If I have not yet known these five faculties of faith and so forth, as they truly are, in terms of their origin, their disappearance, their gratification, their peril, and the escape from them, I am unable to transcend this world of gods, humans, Māras, and Brahmās, and so on, until I have realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
...and so on, as explained at length.
Because uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas cannot be analyzed in such categories, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) pertain to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
Thus, the contaminated and the uncontaminated have been explained.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are maturation (*vipāka*) and how many are not?
The verse says:
Life is exclusively maturation; Sorrow and the last eight are not.
The [five] faculties of form and the four other sensations are each associated with both [types of retribution].
The treatise says:
Only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is invariably a retribution (*vipāka*).
If this is so, when the Arhats retain their life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*), which is the very faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*), of what is this life-faculty the maturation (*vipāka*)?
As stated in the *Śāstra*:
"How does a Bhikṣu retain his life-force?"
This refers to an Arhat who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over the mind.

Whether toward the monastic community or an individual, he distributes various requisites for life, such as robes and alms bowls, as offerings. Having made the offering, he forms a vow and enters the fourth meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*). Upon arising from that concentration, he thinks and speaks aloud:
"May all my karma that is destined to produce the maturation of wealth be transformed to instead produce the fruit of the maturation of longevity."
At that time, those karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth are all transformed so as to bring about the maturation of longevity instead.
Furthermore, there are those who wish to draw forth and take up the remaining maturations of past karma.

He explains that there is residual maturation (*vipāka*) from karma previously experienced in former lives, which is drawn forth and experienced through the power of the meditative concentration on the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*) cultivated in the present life.
How does a bhikṣu relinquish his long life-span?

That is to say, an Arhat who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over the mind makes a gift to the Saṃgha and others as previously described. Having made the gift, he forms a vow and immediately enters the fourth *prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*. Upon arising from that meditative absorption, he reflects and speaks these words:
"May all my karma that is destined to produce the maturation of longevity instead bring about the maturation of wealth."
At that time, those karmas capable of producing the maturation of longevity are all transformed so as to produce the maturation of wealth instead.
The Venerable Ghosaka stated:

"He gives rise to the power of the fourth limit-concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), drawing forth the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm to manifest within his body. Those primary elements either accord with the formations of longevity or oppose them; by this causal condition, he either retains the formations of longevity or relinquishes them."

It should be stated thus: by the power of this sovereign samādhi, that Arhat transforms the momentum of the abiding of the sense-faculties and primary elements produced by previously acquired past karma, and draws forth the momentum of the abiding of the sense-faculties and primary elements produced by unprecedented concentration. Therefore, this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*); all other [faculties] are entirely results of maturation.
From this discussion, another question arises: for what causes and conditions does that Arhat retain his life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) for a long duration?

It is said to be for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to others, or for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Noble Teaching in the world; having perceived that his own life-force was about to be exhausted, yet perceiving that others lacked these two kinds of capability.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does he relinquish his long life-span?
That Arhat observes for himself that remaining in the world brings little benefit or happiness to others, or that his own person is oppressed by the suffering of illness and the like.
As it is said in a verse:
"The holy life has been well-established, The noble path has been thoroughly cultivated;
At the end of life, one rejoices, Just as when casting off many diseases."
In this regard, it should be understood: in what location and by whom can the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*) be thus retained or relinquished?

It is said to be by those in the human realms of the three continents, whether male or female, who are *arhats* possessing the concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*) and who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*). This is because within their bodies they possess mastery over concentration and are free from afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Sūtra says:
"The Blessed One retained many *jīvitasaṃskāras* and relinquished many *āyuḥsaṃskāras*.
What is the distinction between *jīvita* and *āyus*?
Some say there is no distinction,
as the root treatise states:
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It refers to the lifespan (*āyus*) within the three realms.
Other masters say:
The karmic results of past lives are called the formations of longevity (*āyusaṃskāra*); the karmic results of the present life are called the formations of life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*). Some say:
that by which this homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) persists is called the formations of longevity; that by which it abides for a time is called the formations of life-force.

The extensive explanation is intended to clarify that the maintenance and relinquishing of many moments of the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and longevity-force (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) do not occur within a single moment, because there is both maintenance and relinquishing of these forces.
Some say: this statement is intended to refute the existence of a single, substantial entity of life or longevity that persists for a long duration.

Some say: These words are intended to show that there is no single, substantial entity of life-force (*jīvita*) or lifespan (*āyus*); rather, these two names, "life-force" and "lifespan," are merely designated metaphorically upon a plurality of formations (*saṃskāra*).
If this were not the case, one should not speak of "formations."
For what reason, Blessed One, did you relinquish many life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and retain many vitality-formations (*jīvita-saṃskāra*)?
You relinquished many life-formations to demonstrate mastery over death, and you retained many vitality-formations to demonstrate mastery over life.

The reason he remained for exactly three months, neither more nor less, is that beyond this time there were no further beings to be converted, and if he had departed before this, his work for the benefit of sentient beings would not have been complete.
Furthermore, it was to establish the claim he previously made for himself:
"Because I have well cultivated the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), should I wish to remain for a kalpa or even longer than a kalpa, I am able to remain as long as my mind intends."
The Vaibhāṣika masters explain it thus:
this demonstrates that he is now able to subdue the two māras— the māra of the aggregates and the māra of death—
since the Blessed One had already subdued the māra of devas and the māra of afflictions beneath the Bodhi tree.
The digression is concluded; the main argument should now be analyzed.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the subsequent eight faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), are all not maturation (*avipāka*), because they are determinate (*vyākṛta*); all others are common to both [determinate and indeterminate].
The meaning is established by implication:
namely, the seven material faculties and the mental faculty—excluding the faculty of grief among the four remaining sensations—each of these twelve belongs to both categories.
As for the seven material faculties, if they are nurtured (aupacayika), they are not maturation (vipāka); otherwise, they are all maturation.
The mind and the four feelings, when they are wholesome or defiled;

as well as those belonging to the modes of deportment, the arts and crafts, and the power of transformation—these, according to their respective natures, are also not maturation. All others are maturation.
If it is said that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), how then should one interpret what is stated in this sutra? As the sūtra says:
There are three kinds of karma:

karma conducive to the experience of joy (*sukha-vedanīya-karma*), karma conducive to the experience of sorrow (*duḥkha-vedanīya-karma*), and karma conducive to the experience of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanīya-karma*).

There is no fault in using the term "conducive" (*anu-*) in reference to association with feeling; that is to say, because karma is associated with sorrow, it is called "karma conducive to the experience of sorrow," just as contact associated with pleasure is called "contact conducive to the experience of pleasure."
If that is so, then karma conducive to joy and karma conducive to equanimity should likewise be treated in this manner, for it is stated thus in a sutra.
Whatever you may desire, there is no contradiction for me; the principle of association with maturation (*vipāka*) remains entirely unimpaired, and there is no way to evade this refutation.
What is the underlying principle and actual cause for establishing this?
Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), because it arises from the differentiation of conceptual discrimination, and its cessation is likewise so;
maturation is not like this.
If that were so, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) would not be a result of maturation (*vipāka*), because it likewise arises from conceptual discrimination and ceases through the same.

Furthermore, if you admit that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is a result of maturation, then immediately after committing an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*), grief would arise; at that moment, this karma should be called "having already ripened into its fruit."

One should likewise challenge and question the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) in this manner: if it is admitted that the faculty of joy is a maturation (*vipāka*), then when one has performed a superior meritorious deed and joy arises immediately as a result, that karma at that moment should be called "having already ripened into its fruit."
The Vaibhāṣika masters all maintain this position:

because those who have already abandoned desire lack the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), and since maturation (*vipāka*) is not otherwise [subject to such absence], it is therefore not a result of maturation.
If that were so, one should say that for sentient beings who have abandoned desire, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is also a result of maturation.
By what mark is their existence known?

Following the existence of those marks, these marks likewise exist; that is to say, while the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) may be present in this state when it is wholesome, it should be understood by analogy that it is not absent when it is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or a maturation (*vipāka*).

In this state, because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) cannot possibly exist in any form, it is certainly not a maturation (*vipāka*). As for the eight faculties beginning with the eye: if they are in a happy destiny (*sugati*), they are a virtuous maturation; if they are in an unhappy destiny (*durgati*), they are a non-virtuous maturation. The mental faculty (*manas*), regardless of whether one is in a happy or unhappy destiny, is a maturation of both. The faculties of joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), regardless of which destiny one is in, are virtuous maturations. The faculty of pain (*duḥkha*), regardless of whether one is in a happy or unhappy destiny, is a non-virtuous maturation.

Regarding those with both sexual organs in the happy realms (*sugati*), these exist merely as the locations of the sense faculties (*indriya-sthāna*), because while unwholesome karma brings about the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) of the happy realms, it is wholesome karma that projects them.
Thus has the exposition of maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth been completed.
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have maturation (*vipāka*) and how many are without maturation?
The verse says:
Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) definitely has maturation; The first eight and the last three are without it.
The mind, the others, faith, and so forth, each and every one, pertain to both.
The Commentary says:

As was debated previously, it should be known that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) definitely possesses maturation (*vipāka*). The word "definitely" (*niyata*) is stated in the verse based on the sense of exclusion; that is to say, it is stated out of order to show that the faculty of sorrow exclusively possesses maturation while simultaneously possessing both [the qualities of being unwholesome and having maturation].
Regarding the possession of these two meanings: sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not neutral (*avyākṛta*), because it arises from forceful volition;
nor is it untainted (*anāsrava*), because it belongs exclusively to the level of distraction (*vyagracara-bhūmi*).
For this reason, it is mentioned out of sequence first: the faculty of sorrow definitely possesses karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

The first eight faculties, beginning with the eye, and the final three are definitely without maturation (*vipāka*); this is because the eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the three are untainted (*anāsrava*). All others are common to both [categories].

This meaning is established by implication: namely, the mind-faculty (*manas*), the remaining four [feeling faculties], faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth—the term "and so forth" including the four faculties beginning with vigor (*vīrya*)—these eleven each pertain to both categories.
The faculties of mental volition, joy, and equanimity are, when unwholesome or wholesome with outflows, subject to maturation; when neutral or without outflows, they are not subject to maturation.
The faculty of pain is, when wholesome or unwholesome, subject to maturation; when neutral, it is not subject to maturation.
If the five faculties beginning with faith are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they possess maturation (*savipāka*); if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they lack maturation (*avipāka*).
Thus, the possession of maturation and so forth have already been explained.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:
Only the last eight faculties are exclusively wholesome; the faculty of grief pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
the mental faculty and the remaining [four] feelings pertain to all three types; the first eight are exclusively indeterminate.
The Treatise says:
The eight faculties beginning with faith are exclusively wholesome; although their numerical order follows later, they are mentioned first here because they rely on what precedes them.

The faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) pertains only to the nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome; the mental faculty (*manas*) and the other sensations (*vedanā*) each pertain to all three natures; and the eight faculties beginning with the eye are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Having thus explained the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, [one may ask]:

among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The verse says: In the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, respectively, one excludes the last three [faculties],
as well as the female and male faculties, sorrow and suffering, and additionally excludes the [faculties of] joy and pleasure in the realm of form.
The treatise says:

In the desire realm, the last three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are excluded, because those three faculties are exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃbaddha*). By this principle, it should be understood that there are only nineteen faculties bound to the desire realm.

As with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) previously described, excluding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and additionally excluding the four faculties of male, female, sorrow, and suffering; by this analogy, it should be understood that fifteen faculties also pertain to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

Regarding the exclusion of females and males: this is because those in the form realm have already abandoned the dharma of sexual desire, and because the bodies of females and males are physically unattractive.
If that is so, why is it said that they are males?
Where is this taught?
It is taught in the sūtras. As the sūtra says:
There is no possibility and no occasion for a female body to be a Brahmā; there is the possibility and the occasion for a male body to be a Brahmā.
There exists a distinct male characteristic, namely that which belongs to a male body within the desire realm.
They lack the faculty of suffering because their bodies are pure and sublime, and because they possess no unwholesome states.
They lack the faculty of grief because their mental continuums are moistened by *śamatha*, and because they certainly have no causes for affliction or harm.

The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is as previously described, with the exception of the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), the female and male faculties, the faculties of grief (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), and furthermore, the five faculties of form along with the faculties of joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*). By this principle, it should be understood that the remaining eight faculties are associated with the formless realm; namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
Having thus explained the factors bound to the desire realm and so forth,

among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
The verse says:

The mental [faculty] and the three feelings pertain to all three; sorrow is abandoned through insight and cultivation; nine are abandoned only through cultivation; five are abandoned through cultivation, while three are neither. The treatise says: The mental faculty (*manas*) and the three feelings (*vedanā*)—namely, pleasure, pain, and equanimity—pertain to all three categories: those abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aheya*). Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is abandoned both through insight and through cultivation.

Nine faculties—namely, the five sense-faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body), the female and male faculties, and the life-faculty—are abandoned only through cultivation. Five faculties—the faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom faculties—are abandoned through cultivation; the three [faculties of] "I shall come to know the unknown," "knowing," and "one who has known" are neither abandoned through insight nor through cultivation. Thus it is said.

The faculties of mind (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) each pertain to all three categories, as they all pertain to what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and what is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*) pertains only to what is abandoned by seeing and by cultivation, as it is not untainted (*anāsrava*).

The seven faculties, the life faculty, and the faculty of suffering are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they are not afflicted (*akliṣṭa*), because they are not produced by the six [consciousnesses], and because they are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).

The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are either abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned at all, because they are not afflicted and because they pertain to both the with-outflows and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The final three faculties are exclusively non-abandonable, because they are all untainted (*anāsrava*) and because that which is without fault is not something to be abandoned.
Thus has been explained the differentiation of the categories and types of these various doors.
In which realm are how many ripening faculties (*vipākendriya*) first acquired?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, for those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture, two ripening faculties are first acquired.
The miraculously born possess six, seven, or eight; in the realm of form, six; above that, only the life-faculty.
The commentary states:

At the initial stage of receiving birth through the womb, egg, or moisture in the desire realm, one acquires only two matured faculties (vipāka-indriya), namely the body and the life-faculty, because the other faculties arise gradually in these three modes of birth.
Why does that [being] not obtain the mental faculty (*manas*) or the two faculties of renunciation (*upekṣendriya*)?
Because at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), it is necessarily defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

At the initial stage of apparitional birth (*upapāduka*), one obtains six, seven, or eight faculties; that is to say, those without gender initially obtain six faculties, as was the case at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*).
What are the six?
They are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life-faculty.
If one possesses only one gender organ, they initially obtain seven faculties, such as the devas and others.
If one who possesses both sexual organs initially acquires eight faculties,
could there be one with both sexual organs who undergoes miraculous birth (*upapāduka*)?
It is possible for those in the evil realms to be born miraculously with both sexual organs.
Having already explained the faculties first acquired within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), we shall now explain those of the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
Because desire predominates in the desire realm, it is simply called "desire"; because form predominates in the form realm, it is simply called "form."
The Sūtra also states:
"Tranquil liberation transcends the realms of form and formlessness.

In the realm of form, one initially acquires six matured faculties (*vipākendriya*), as explained in the case of those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) who are without physical form in the desire realm.
"Superior only to life" means that because the meditative absorption of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhyāna*) is superior and its rebirth is superior, it is called "superior.
Among those in the formless realm, the first matured faculty (*vipākendriya*) obtained is exclusively the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and no other.
Having explained the initial acquisition of the maturation faculties (*vipāka-indriya*), [it is now asked:
in which realm do how many faculties cease last at the moment of death?
The verse says:

At the moment of death, the faculties cease: in the formless realm, three; in the form realm, eight; in the desire realm, nineteen, eighteen, or eight, depending on whether death is sudden or gradual; for those of good rebirth, four [or] five are added. The Commentary says: [The faculties that cease at the time of death are as follows: In the formless realm, three faculties cease: the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*), and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*). In the form realm, eight faculties cease: the aforementioned three, plus the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*)—namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties. In the desire realm, nineteen faculties may cease simultaneously:

the aforementioned eight, plus the ten faculties of the female (*strīndriya*), male (*puruṣendriya*), faith (*śraddhā*), vigor (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), joy (*sukha*), and pleasure (*saumanasya*). However, if death is sudden, eighteen faculties cease: the same nineteen minus the two sexual faculties. If death is gradual, eight faculties cease: the aforementioned eight. For those of good rebirth, four additional faculties are added: the five faculties of faith and so forth (faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom), making nine in total. If one is born into a state of meditative absorption, five faculties are added: the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*), making ten in total.]
When one is about to die in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the three faculties of life (*jīvitendriya*), mind (*manas*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) cease last.
If one is about to die in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), these same three faculties along with the five beginning with the eye—thus eight types in total—cease last.
Because all those born by transformation necessarily possess the full set of faculties at the time of birth and death.

If one dies instantaneously in the desire realm, nineteen, eighteen, or eight faculties cease at the very end; that is, for those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), ten faculties cease last—namely, the female and male organs along with the eight previously mentioned.
If one possesses sexual organs, nine faculties are subsequently extinguished; from among the female and male faculties, either one is excluded.
If one is without sexual organs, eight faculties are subsequently extinguished; that is to say, there are no female or male faculties, and only the preceding eight remain.
Thus, what has been explained refers to death occurring instantaneously.

If death occurs gradually, only four [faculties] are finally relinquished; that is to say, when one dies gradually in the desire realm, the faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity perish last. These four necessarily do not have the sense of perishing sequentially.
It should be understood that what has been stated above applies only to those who die with a defiled or neutral mind.

If one dies with a wholesome mind within the three realms, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are necessarily all present; therefore, in all the states previously mentioned, their number should be increased by these five. That is to say, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the count increases to eight faculties, and so on up to nine in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the intermediate variations should be understood accordingly.
Among all the dharmas of the faculties (*indriya*) analyzed herein, one should investigate which of the twenty-two faculties can realize which fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The verse says:
Nine [faculties] attain the two extreme fruits; Seven, eight, and nine attain the two middle fruits.
"Eleven [types of] Arhats exist based on one [classification]; this is what some say.
The commentary states:
"The 'extremes' refer to the fruit of Stream-entry and the fruit of Arhatship, because they occupy the first and last positions among the fruits of śramaṇaship."
The middle refers to the fruits of once-returner and non-returner, as these are situated between the first and the last fruits.

The first fruit, that of stream-entry, is attained by means of nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty, the faculty of equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and the faculty of "knowing."

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) resides in the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), while the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) resides in the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga). These two support one another so that the first fruit may be attained.
In their respective order, they serve as the projecting cause (ākṣepaka-hetu) for the acquisition of disjunction (visamyoga-prāpti), by virtue of their nature as supporting causes (niśraya-hetu).

The fruit of arhatship is also attained by means of nine faculties: namely, the mental faculty, the five beginning with faith, the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya), and one from among the faculties of joy, pleasure, or equanimity—these constitute the nine.

The faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) resides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), while the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) resides in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); these two support one another to attain the final fruit.
Respectively, they act as the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*) for the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyogaprāpti*), by virtue of their nature as supporting causes (*niśrayahetu*).
The two intermediate fruits are each obtained by seven, eight, or nine faculties, as appropriate. Why is this so?

First, regarding the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) attained through the gradual path: when realized via the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), it is obtained by means of seven faculties—namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
It is attained by means of eight faculties through the supramundane path—namely, the aforementioned seven faculties with the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) as the eighth.
For one who attains it by leaping over while being doubly detached from sensual desire, it is attained by nine faculties, just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

If the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*) is attained sequentially, it is attained by seven faculties when relying on the mundane path, and by eight faculties when relying on the supramundane path.
As previously described in sequence,

one who attains the fruit of a once-returner by completely transcending desire through leaping over stages does so by means of nine faculties, just as one who attains the fruit of a once-returner by leaping over stages as previously explained.

Although this is said in general, there are distinctions; namely, because these depend on different stages (*bhūmi*), one may take any one from among pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the case of the aforementioned fruit of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*), there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Furthermore, regarding one who realizes the fruit of non-returner through the gradual path (*anupūrva-sākṣātkriyā*): if they enter the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), they attain it by means of eight faculties (*indriya*) based on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).

That path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is associated with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), while within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) there is also the sensation of joy (*prīti-vedanā*); these two assist one another to attain the third fruit.

Regarding the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*), there are two causes as previously stated: it is attained by means of nine faculties when following the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*). Eight faculties are as before, with the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) as the ninth, because both the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation coexist therein.
Is it not asked in the *Mūla-abhidharma*:
"By how many faculties (*indriya*) does one attain arhatship?
The answer is:
There are eleven faculties.
Why, then, do you say that one attains [the fruit] by means of nine faculties?
In reality, one attains the fourth [fruit] solely by means of nine faculties.
As for the statement in the *Mūla-śāstra* regarding eleven faculties, it is spoken on the basis that they may potentially exist within a single body.

That is to say, there may be a certain *pudgala* who, having repeatedly fallen back from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), attains the fruit of Arhatship again and again through the manifestation of any one of the [three] feelings: pleasure, joy, or equanimity.

Based on this, the root treatise speaks of eleven faculties; however, since the three feelings do not arise simultaneously, it is therefore stated here that [the attainment of the fruit of non-returner] is necessarily by means of nine faculties.
Why is it not stated in the same way regarding the fruit of non-returning?
One who realizes the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) by means of the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) may subsequently undergo falling away;

yet, having fallen away, one does not regain it through that same pleasure. It is not the case that one who previously abandoned desire and directly realized the third fruit could subsequently fall away from it.
This fruit of the separation from desire is obtained through two paths and is therefore extremely firm.
One should now investigate: which faculties are accomplished [in this state], and among those various faculties, how many are necessarily accomplished?
The verse says:
One who possesses life, mind, or equanimity necessarily possesses three;
one who possesses pleasure or the body necessarily possesses four.
One who achieves the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the faculty of joy, necessarily achieves five faculties.
If one achieves the faculty of suffering, they necessarily achieve seven.
If one achieves the female or male faculties, or the faculty of grief, or the faculties of faith and so forth, each necessarily achieves eight.
Two are untainted and eleven; the first untainted has thirteen.
The treatise says:

Among life, mind, and equanimity, whichever one is accomplished, those three faculties are necessarily accomplished; it is not possible for them to be accomplished while any one of these three is missing.
Regarding the remaining faculties, excluding these three, all others are indeterminate, meaning they may be either possessed or not possessed.

Among these, the four faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue are definitely not possessed by those born in the formless realm; furthermore, they are also not possessed by those born in the desire realm who have not yet acquired them or have already lost them.
The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is not possessed only by those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The female and male faculties (*strī- and puruṣendriya*) are not possessed by those born in the two higher realms; furthermore, they are also not possessed by those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who have not yet acquired them or have already lost them.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not established for ordinary beings born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is not established for ordinary beings born in the third or fourth dhyānas or the formless realms.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is certainly not accomplished by those born in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) or formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is certainly not accomplished by anyone who has detached from sensual desire (*kāmarāga-vītarāga*).
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*) are certainly not accomplished by one whose roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have been severed.
The first untainted faculty (anāsrava-indriya) is definitely not possessed by any ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) or those who have already abided in the fruits [of the path].
The second untainted faculty is definitely not possessed by any ordinary beings, those on the path of vision (darśana-mārga), or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Regarding the subsequent untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), it is certain that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) do not possess them.
In cases where they are not excluded, one should understand that all the faculties previously mentioned are definitely possessed.

If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four: namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and this faculty of pleasure itself.
If one possesses the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one likewise necessarily possesses four: namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, and this body-faculty itself.
If one possesses the eye faculty, one necessarily possesses five: namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, the body-faculty, and the eye-faculty itself.
It should be understood that the ear, nose, and tongue faculties likewise each consist of five; the first four are as with the eye, and the fifth is the faculty itself.

If one accomplishes the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily accomplishes five: namely, the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*), and the joy-faculty.

For one born in the stage of the second dhyāna who has not yet attained the third dhyāna—having abandoned the lower [stage] but not yet acquired the higher—what kind of pleasure-faculty does this person possess?
One should say that they possess the defiled faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of the third dhyāna, because the others have not yet been attained.
If one possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven: namely, the body, life, mind, and the four faculties of sensation, excluding sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
If one possesses the female faculty, one necessarily possesses eight: seven as explained in the case of the faculty of suffering, and the eighth being the female faculty.
If one possesses the male faculty, one likewise necessarily possesses eight: seven as explained in the case of the faculty of suffering, and the eighth being the male faculty.

If one possesses the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses eight: the seven as explained for the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and the eighth being the faculty of sorrow itself.

If one possesses the faculties of faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, one likewise possesses eight each: namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manas*), the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣā*), and the five faculties beginning with faith.

If one possesses the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya), one necessarily possesses eleven faculties: namely, the life-faculty, the mental faculty, the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculty of one who has already known.
If one possesses the faculty of "already known" (*ājñātendriya*), one necessarily possesses eleven faculties: the ten faculties mentioned above plus the faculty of "already known.

If one possesses the faculty of "not yet known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), one necessarily possesses thirteen faculties: namely, the body, life, mind, suffering, pleasure, joy, equanimity, the five faculties beginning with faith, and the faculty of "not yet known."
How many faculties do those with the very minimum possess?
The verse says:
The very minimum is eight, lacking the wholesome; They possess the faculties of feeling, body, life, and mind.
The fool born in the formless realm possesses wholesome life, mind, and equanimity.
The commentary states:
one who has already severed the roots of goodness is said to be "without goodness."
If one possesses the minimum number of faculties, one achieves eight: namely, the five feeling faculties, as well as the body, life, and mind faculties.
"Feeling" (vedanā) refers to that which feels, because it is capable of experiencing [objects].
Alternatively, it is called "feeling" (vedanā) because its nature is to feel, just as one establishes the name "complete" based on the nature of being complete.
For example, when the roots of virtue are severed, the minimum number of faculties possessed is eight; likewise, when a fool is born into the formless realm, they also possess eight faculties.
The "fool" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) because they have not yet seen the Truths.
What are these eight?
They are the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), along with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manas*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*).
Because the five faculties beginning with faith are exclusively wholesome, they are collectively termed "wholesome.
If that were so, the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) should also be included.
This is not the case, because this context relies upon eight faculties, and furthermore, it speaks of a fool being born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
How many faculties (*indriya*) do those who possess the maximum number achieve?
The verse says:
The maximum is nineteen; for those of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), three pure faculties are excluded.
The Noble One who has not yet abandoned desire possesses [the faculties], excluding two purities and one form.
The commentary states:
Those who possess both sexual organs (dviliṅga) are endowed with the eye and other faculties; excluding the three untainted (anāsrava) faculties, they possess the remaining nineteen.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "pure" (*śuddha*) because it is free from the two bonds.
Those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) are necessarily ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), for they have not yet abandoned sensual craving;
thus, they possess nineteen [faculties]. Do only these possess nineteen, or are there others?

A noble one who has not yet abandoned desire also possesses nineteen; that is to say, when a noble learner (śaikṣa) who has not yet abandoned sensual desire achieves the maximum number, they likewise possess nineteen, excluding two untainted faculties and excluding one gender faculty.
If one abides in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the faculty of "already known" (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are excluded.
If one abides in the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the faculty of "not yet known" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "one who has fully known" are excluded.
Furthermore, either the female or male faculty is excluded from the two, because no noble being (*ārya*) possesses both sexual organs.
Having analyzed the distinctions between the elements (*dhātu*) and the faculties (*indriya*) as well as the non-faculties, this extensive discussion of the twenty-two faculties is hereby concluded.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Three.
*Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.

Chapter Two: Analysis of the Faculties (II). Now it should be investigated: while all conditioned phenomena differ in their characteristics and their arising is likewise distinct, are there any dharmas that necessarily arise together, or is there a fixed rule for simultaneous arising?
That is to say, all phenomena (dharmas) briefly comprise five categories:
first, matter (rūpa); second, mind (citta); third, mental factors (caitta); fourth, formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra); and fifth, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The unconditioned and the unarisen are not discussed herein.
Now, first, the simultaneous arising of matter (*rūpa*) is established.
The verse says:
The subtle aggregate of desire is without sound;
it consists of eight entities when lacking the sense-faculties, nine entities when possessing the body-faculty, and ten entities when possessing the remaining faculties.
The commentary says:
The most subtle aggregate of matter is designated as a "subtle cluster" (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*) to indicate that there is nothing subtler than this.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when it is devoid of sound and sense-faculties, these eight substances arise together, with none of them being absent.
What are the eight things?
They are the four great elements and the four derived forms: visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible.
In an aggregate of atoms that contains no sound but possesses sense faculties, these co-arising things are either nine or ten.
In the aggregate of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), nine things arise together: eight as previously described, with the body as the ninth.
In other aggregates of faculties, ten things arise together: nine as previously described, plus one such as the eye-faculty.
The eye, ear, nose, and tongue are necessarily not separate from the body, because they occupy distinct locations relative to one another.

If sound arises within any of the aforementioned aggregates, the respective counts increase by nine, ten, eleven, and twelve respectively; this is because the location of sound does not arise apart from the sense faculties, being produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are appropriated (upātta).
If the four great elements arise inseparably, why is it that within various aggregates only one—such as solidity, moisture, heat, or motion—is perceived while the others are not?
It is because that which possesses a predominant efficacy within a given aggregate is clearly perceived, yet the other substances are not non-existent therein.
It is like perceiving the sensation of a needle-point meeting with a tally, or like tasting the flavor of salt mixed with flour.
How is it known that there is something further [to these elements]?
Because they possess the functions of collecting, maturing, growing, and maintaining.
Some say:

because solidity and so forth possess the characteristics of fluidity and so forth when they encounter conditions—just as within a mass of water, the characteristic of heat arises due to extreme cold—and although these are not mutually exclusive, the function of cold predominates, just as the functions of sensation (*vedanā*) and sound (*śabda*) have degrees of superiority and inferiority.
Other masters say:
Within this aggregate, there exist other seeds whose substantial characteristics have not yet manifested; therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Within a mass of wood, there are various elements (*dhātu*)."
The "element" (dhātu) refers to the seed.
How can one know that visible form exists within the wind?
This meaning is to be accepted through faith; it cannot be known through inference.

Alternatively, because the fragrance that is combined [with other elements] is perceptible in the present, and because fragrance is never dissociated from visible color (rūpa), it was previously stated that neither fragrance nor taste exists in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Therefore, in that realm, when there is no sound, six, seven, or eight [elements] arise together; when there is sound, seven, eight, or nine arise together.
This can be understood by analogy, and therefore it is not explained separately.
In this context, when the term "entity" (*vastu*) is used, does it refer to the substantial essence (*svabhāva*) or to the locus (*āyatana*)?
If so, what fault would there be?
Both positions are flawed.

If it were explained according to substance, then [stating] eight, nine, or ten would be too few, because every aggregate of atoms necessarily possesses shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), as it is formed by the collective accumulation of many atoms.
Either heaviness or lightness must necessarily be present; the same applies to either smoothness or roughness.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that some places possess cold, hunger, or thirst, this entails the fault of being too restrictive in what is stated.

If one were to speak in terms of bases (*āyatana*), then enumerating eight, nine, ten, and so forth would be excessive; since the four great elements are subsumed within the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), one should instead speak of four and so on. Thus, the aforementioned [enumerations] suffer from the fault of being too many.
There is no fault in either case.

It should be understood that what is referred to here as "the thing" (*vastu*) is explained in two parts: one part is explained in terms of its substance, namely the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis;
the other part is explained in terms of its location, namely the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) which depends upon them.

If that were so, the substantial entities of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would become manifold, because each derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) would depend on its own distinct set of four primary elements.
One should understand, however, that here the statement is made in terms of their generic class (*jāti*), for there is no difference among the various classes of the four primary elements.
What is the use of such analytical discussion regarding words?
Words arise according to one's intention; it is their meaning that should be investigated.
Thus has it been established that matter necessarily arises simultaneously [with its primary elements].
The co-arising of other meditative absorptions will now be discussed.
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; So too do the characteristics of conditioned phenomena, or acquisitions.
The treatise says:
Mind and mental factors necessarily arise together; if even one of them is absent, the others do not arise.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are these very things: namely, form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).

The previous discussion regarding "necessarily concomitant" extends to this point: it means that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) arise, they necessarily arise together with the four characteristics of the conditioned (*samskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
As for the phrase "or acquisition" (*prāpti*), it means that among all conditioned phenomena, only those pertaining to sentient beings arise together with acquisition;
other phenomena are not so, which is why the word "or" is used.
Regarding what was previously mentioned as "mental factors" (*caitta*), which ones are they?
The verse says:
Mental factors are, for now, of five kinds, distinguished by the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) and other categories.
The treatise says:
There are, for now, five categories of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*). What are these five?
1. Universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma);
2. Universally wholesome mental factors (kuśalamahābhūmikadharma);
3. Universally afflicted mental factors (kleśamahābhūmikadharma).
4. The great unwholesome mental factors (akuśala-mahābhūmika);
5. The minor afflictive mental factors (parītta-kleśa-bhūmika).
"Ground" (bhūmi) refers to the sphere of activity; if this is the sphere of activity for those [factors], it is said that this is the ground of those factors.

Because it is the ground of the great dharmas, it is called the "great ground" (*mahābhūmi*); those dharmas which belong to this great ground are called "dharmas of the great ground," meaning those dharmas that are always present in all minds.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
Sensation, perception, volition, contact, desire, wisdom, mindfulness, and attention.
The samādhi of resolute conviction pervades all states of mind.
The treatise says:
It is traditionally taught that...
These ten dharmas listed above are present in every combination within each moment of consciousness.
Among them, "feeling" (*vedanā*) refers to three types of experience:
painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant, as there are distinctions between them.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to the grasping of specific characteristics within an object.
Volition (*cetanā*) refers to that which enables the mind to engage in purposeful activity.
Contact (*sparśa*) arises from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness; it has the capacity for sensory confrontation.
Desire (chanda) refers to the aspiration for the undertaking of an activity.
Wisdom (prajñā) refers to the capacity for discernment regarding phenomena.
Mindfulness (smṛti) refers to clear recollection of an object without forgetting.
Mental attention (*manasikāra*) means that which causes the mind to be alert.
Resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) means that which confirms the object.
Meditative concentration (*samādhi*) means one-pointedness of mind.

The distinct characteristics of the various minds and mental factors are subtle; it is already difficult to discern them one by one in their continuity, let alone when they exist simultaneously in a single moment.

Even the distinctions in taste among material medicinal herbs, which are perceived by the physical sense organs, are difficult to discern; how much more so for formless phenomena, which are apprehended solely by the faculty of wisdom?
Thus, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*) have been explained.

The "great wholesome ground" refers to the category of great wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*); those factors that belong to this great wholesome ground are called the "great wholesome ground factors," which are the factors that are always present in all wholesome minds.
What are those dharmas?
The verse says:
Faith and heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, shame, and dread.
The two faculties and non-harming, along with diligence, are found only throughout the wholesome mind.
The commentary states:
These dharmas are found exclusively throughout the wholesome mind.
In this context, "faith" (śraddhā) causes the mind to become clear and pure.
Some say it is called faith because one directly endures and accepts the truths and the reality of karma and its results.
Heedfulness consists in cultivating all wholesome phenomena and abandoning all unwholesome phenomena.
Furthermore, what is meant by "cultivation"?
It refers to having the nature of focused attention upon the wholesome.
In the sūtras of other schools, there is an explanation such as this:
"That which can guard the mind is called heedfulness (*apramāda*);
pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) refers to the mind's fitness for action."
