Is it not the case that the Sūtras also speak of physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*)?

Although it is not that such a teaching does not exist, this should be understood as being analogous to the case of physical sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*); how, then, can this be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
It should be understood that herein, physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) refers to the body’s serviceability (*karmanyatā*).
Furthermore, how can this be called a limb of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)?
There is no fault, for it is conducive to the limbs of enlightenment.
Because physical pliancy can induce the mental pliancy that is a factor of enlightenment, is there also such a statement regarding other factors?
Yes; as it is said in a sutra:
Joy and the factors conducive to joy are called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Hatred and its causal conditions are called the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).
Right view, right thought, and right effort are called the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*).

Although reflection and diligence are not of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are nonetheless designated by the name "wisdom" because they accord with it; therefore, there is no error in designating physical pliancy as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) because it accords with the factors of enlightenment.
The equanimity of the mind and the absence of mental alertness are termed *upekṣā*.
How can it be said that within a single moment of consciousness there is both mental alertness and the absence of mental alertness?
How can it be that attention (*manasikāra*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) arise in conjunction?
Was it not previously stated that the characteristics of the various minds and mental factors are subtle and difficult to discern?
Although they are difficult to discern, they can still be known through careful investigation and reasoning.
This is most difficult to understand: that they are mutually contradictory yet not in opposition.
Herein, there is alertness in one case but none in the other; since these two are so vastly different, how can there be any contradiction?
If that were so, they would not share a common object, or else all [mental factors] would be mutually associated.
Other dharmas of this same category should be investigated herein; according to that principle, it should be understood that the same applies here as well.
The two types, shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*), will be explained later.

As for the two roots, they refer to non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Since non-delusion (*amoha*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its nature, it was already mentioned previously among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*); therefore, it is not repeated here as a great wholesome ground factor (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).
"Non-harming" refers to the absence of injury or affliction.
"Diligence" has the nature of making the mind courageous and resolute.
Thus have the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) been explained.

The stage of great afflictive factors (*mahākleśabhūmi*) is called the "great afflictive ground. Any factor that belongs to this great afflictive ground is termed a "great afflictive ground factor" (*mahākleśabhūmikadharma*), meaning those factors that are always present in a defiled mind.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
Delusion, negligence, indolence, lack of faith, lethargy, and restlessness are always exclusively defiled.
The Treatise says:
Herein, "delusion" (*moha*) refers to ignorance; it is the absence of knowledge, the absence of wisdom, and the absence of illumination.
"Heedlessness" (*pramāda*) means negligence; it is the failure to cultivate various virtues and is the state opposed to the cultivation of those virtues.
Laziness refers to indolence; it is the lack of mental vigor and is the direct opposite of the diligence previously described.
Lack of faith refers to the mind's failure to attain clarity and purity; it is the direct opposite of the faith previously described.
"Lethargy" (styāna) refers to torpor (middha).
In the Abhidharma it is asked:
"What is torpor?"
It refers to heaviness of body and heaviness of mind, unserviceability of body and unserviceability of mind, and lethargy of body and lethargy of mind; this is called *styāna* (torpor).
This is a mental factor (*caitta*).
How can it be called a "body" (*kāya*)?
It is no different from the expression "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*); thus, there is no fault.
*Auddhatya* refers to restlessness (*auddhatya*), which prevents the mind from being tranquil.
There are only these six types that are called the *mahābhūmika-dharmas* (universal mental factors of great defilement).
Is it not the case that the *Mūla-abhidharma* states there are ten types of *mahābhūmika-dharmas*, and furthermore, that *styāna* (sloth) is not mentioned in that treatise?
What are the ten? They are:
lack of faith, laziness, loss of mindfulness, mental distraction, ignorance, lack of correct discernment, improper attention, wrong resolve, restlessness, and negligence, O Beloved of the Gods.
You now merely know the words, but you are not yet proficient in their intended meaning.
What is this intended meaning?

It refers to forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛtitā), mental distraction (cittavikṣepa), lack of clear comprehension (asaṃprajanya), improper attention (ayoniśomanasikāra), and wrong resolve (mithyādhimokṣa). Since these have already been stated to be among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmikadharma), they should not be established again as universal defiled mental factors (kleśamahābhūmikadharma).

Just as the wholesome root of non-delusion has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence and thus is not among the universal wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), so too should that [non-forgetfulness] be understood.

That is to say: defiled mindfulness is termed "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛtitā*); defiled meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is termed "mental distraction" (*vikṣepa*); all defiled wisdom is termed "lack of clear comprehension" (*asaṃprajanya*); and defiled attention (*manasikāra*) and resolve (*adhimokṣa*) are termed "inappropriate attention" (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and "wrong resolve" (*mithyādhimokṣa*), respectively. Thus it is said.
If something is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), is it also a universal defiled mental factor (*kleśamahābhūmika*)?
This should be analyzed in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation consists of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and desire (*chanda*).
The second phrase refers to lack of faith, laziness, ignorance, restlessness, and heedlessness.
The third phrase refers to the five factors previously mentioned, such as mindfulness and so forth.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
There are those who maintain that incorrect concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*) is not itself mental distraction (*citta-vikṣepa*); their formulation of the four phrases differs from this [position].

Furthermore, they assert that lethargy (*styāna*) is associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they do not include it among the universal mental factors of affliction (*mahā-kleśa-bhūmika-dharma*).
Whose fault is it?
Some say: It should have been stated here, but it was not stated because it conforms to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It is said that those whose temperament is characterized by lethargy (styāna-carita) quickly develop meditative concentration (samādhi), whereas those whose temperament is characterized by restlessness (auddhatya-carita) do not.
Who is characterized by lethargy and not by restlessness?
Who is characterized by restlessness and not by lethargy?
Because these two have never failed to function together.
Nevertheless, one should understand that they are described as "functioning" (*carita*) according to their predominant activity.

Although it is known that the description of their functioning follows their relative increase in activity, the mental factors (*bhūmika-dharma*) are established based on their actual existence; therefore, these mental factors are established as being only six in number. This is because they arise exclusively in association with defiled minds, and not otherwise.
Thus, the universal mental factors of great affliction have been explained.

The "universal ground of great unwholesomeness" refers to the ground of great unwholesome dharmas; herein, those dharmas that belong to the universal ground of great unwholesomeness are called the "universal dharmas of great unwholesomeness," meaning those dharmas that are always present in an unwholesome mind.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
They exist exclusively throughout all unwholesome minds: Lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
The treatise states:

Only two mental factors accompany all unwholesome minds—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). Therefore, only these two types are designated as the dharmas of this stage.
The characteristics of these two dharmas will be explained later as appropriate.
Thus, the great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) have been explained.

The ground of the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) is called the "minor affliction ground" (*upakleśabhūmi*); those dharmas that belong to this minor affliction ground are called "minor affliction ground dharmas" (*upakleśabhūmikadharma*), meaning those dharmas that accompany a limited degree of defiled mind.
What are those factors?
The verse says:
Anger, concealment, stinginess, envy, vexation, Harmfulness, resentment, guile, deceit, and pride.
Those of this kind are called the *parīttakleśabhūmikadharma* (minor defilement-ground dharmas).
The treatise says:

Dharmas of this kind are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), arise on the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), are associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃprayukta*), and manifest individually; therefore, they are called the minor defilement-ground dharmas.
This dharma will be analyzed in detail later, within the section on secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Thus, the five categories of mental factors have been explained.

Furthermore, there are other indeterminate mental factors—dharmas such as regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*)—which should now be discussed here.
In which category of mind do how many mental factors necessarily arise together?
The verse says:
Because desire possesses vitarka and vicāra, within the category of wholesome minds,
Twenty-two mental factors, with *kaukṛtya* (remorse) sometimes added;
in the case of unwholesome [minds] not shared [with other afflictions], there are only twenty when associated with views;
with the four afflictions, anger, and so forth, or with *kaukṛtya*, there are twenty-one.
In the obscured [unwholesome] state, eighteen [factors] are present; in the unobscured [neutral] state, twelve are admitted.
Sleep is universally compatible and does not contradict [any]; if it is present, one [factor] is added to all.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, within the desire realm, there are five categories of mental states (*citta-pakṣa*): first, the wholesome, which is of only one type;
second, the unwholesome, which is of two types, namely that associated with non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī-avidyā*) and that associated with other afflictions (*kleśa*).
The indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) has two types: obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, because the mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) necessarily possesses vitarka and vicāra, a wholesome mental state (*kuśalacitta*) must arise accompanied by twenty-two mental factors (*caitasika*). These consist of the ten universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*), the ten great wholesome ground-factors (*mahākuśalabhūmikadharma*), and two indeterminate factors, namely vitarka and vicāra.
Not all virtuous minds are accompanied by regret (*kaukṛtya*); at times, the number of mental factors increases to twenty-three.
What is regret? The essence of that which has been poorly done is called regret.

It should be understood that herein, "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) refers to that which takes remorseful action as its object; that is, it is the nature of the mind’s regret directed toward a remorseful act. This is just as the door of liberation taking emptiness as its object is called "emptiness," or non-attachment taking the unattractive as its object is called "the unattractive."
Furthermore, one observes that in the world, the locus of dependence is used to designate the dependent entity, as when it is said, "All the villages, towns, and kingdoms have gathered together.
Since remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is the locus of subsequent regret, it is designated as "remorse" by way of its locus.
Furthermore, the name of the cause is metaphorically applied to the essence of the effect; for example, it is said that "these six bases of contact should be known as past karma.
If one takes as an object something not yet done, how can it be called *kaukṛtya* (remorse)?
The designation "done" is also applied to an action not yet performed; for example, one says in regret: "I previously did not perform such a task;
this is my *kaukṛtya* (remorse). What kind of *kaukṛtya* is said to be wholesome?
This refers to the nature of subsequent regret regarding what was done or not done in relation to the wholesome or the unwholesome.
That which is contrary to this is called the unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Each of these two arises based on two types of mental states. In the case of an unwholesome mind that is not shared with other classes (*asādhāraṇa-citta*), there are necessarily twenty mental factors (*caitasika*) arising simultaneously: namely, the ten universal ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), the six universal affliction factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the two universal unwholesome factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and two indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), namely *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
What is called the "unshared mental complex" (*asādhāraṇa-cittapakṣa*)?
It refers to a mental complex in which there is only ignorance (*avidyā*), and no other afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*).

Within the unwholesome mental complex associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-samprayukta-akuśala-cittapakṣa*), there are likewise twenty mental factors that arise together; their names are exactly as explained in the aforementioned "unshared category."

It is not because views increase that there are twenty-one [mental factors], for "view" is merely a specific function of wisdom (*prajñā*) among the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

Regarding the phrase "a mind associated with unwholesome view," this refers to a mind in which there may be false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), or grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), or grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

In the four unwholesome mental states associated with the afflictions of greed, hatred, pride, and doubt, twenty-one mental factors arise together; these are the same twenty as in the "unshared" (āveṇika) category, with the addition of one of the [four] primary afflictions, such as greed and so forth.

In the category of secondary afflictions associated with anger and so forth as previously described, twenty-one mental factors also arise together; these are the same twenty as in the case of the non-common [afflictions], with the addition of any one of the secondary afflictions such as anger.
The category of mind associated with unwholesome *kaukṛtya* (remorse) also arises together with twenty-one mental factors; that is, *kaukṛtya* itself as the twenty-first.

Briefly stated, within the categories of unwholesome *āveṇika* (unshared) and those associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are only twenty; however, within the categories associated with the remaining four afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there are twenty-one.

If, within the category of neutral (avyākṛta) and obscured (nivṛta) minds, there are only eighteen mental factors arising together—namely, the ten universal (mahābhūmika) factors, the six universal afflictive (kleśa-mahābhūmika) factors, and two indeterminate factors, namely vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding the indeterminate obscured minds of the desire realm, these refer to those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); it should be understood that the reason why views do not increase in this context is as explained previously.

In other neutral (avyākṛta) and non-obscured (anivṛta) mental states, it is maintained that only twelve mental factors arise together: namely, the ten universal (mahābhūmika) factors along with the two indeterminate (aniyata) factors, vitarka and vicāra.
Teachers from outside [the tradition] maintain that regret (kaukṛtya) can also be neutral; according to them, this associated category would then have twelve mental factors arising together.
It should be understood that sleep is not incompatible with any of the mental categories previously mentioned, as it can be associated with the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the neutral.
Whichever category it occurs in, it is said to increase that category by one: that is, from twenty-two to twenty-three, or from twenty-three to twenty-four.
The unwholesome and the indeterminate [mental factors] should be understood according to the same principle.
Having already explained the fixed number of categories of mental factors arising together in the desire realm, we shall now explain those of the higher realms.
The verse says:
The first dhyāna eliminates the unwholesome, as well as remorse and torpor;
the middle dhyāna further eliminates vitarka; the higher [dhyānas] additionally eliminate vicāra and so forth.
The treatise says:

Within the first dhyāna, among the mental factors previously mentioned, all are present except for those that are exclusively unwholesome— namely, remorse (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), and the affliction of hatred (*dveṣa*),

as well as the remaining [secondary afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, excluding guile (*śāṭhya*), deceit (*māyā*), and pride (*mada*), along with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
As for those that possess all [factors], it is as explained regarding the desire realm.
In the intermediate dhyāna, one excludes what was previously excluded and further excludes vitarka; all others are fully present.
From the second dhyāna upward, up to the formless realm, one excludes what was previously excluded and further excludes vicāra and so forth.
The term "and so forth" indicates that, with the exception of *śāṭhya* (hypocrisy) and *māyā* (deceit), all other [defilements] are present as previously described.
The Sūtra states:
"Hypocrisy and deceit extend as far as the Brahma-heaven; because they depend upon mutual reliance, they do not exist in the higher stages."
While the Great Brahmā King was dwelling among his own assembly of Brahmās, he was suddenly questioned by the bhikṣu Aśvajit:
"In what state do these four great elements cease without remainder?"
Not knowing the state of cessation without remainder, the Brahmā King gave a prevaricating answer:
"Among this assembly of Brahmās, I am the Great Brahmā; I am the sovereign, the creator, the transformer, the progenitor, the nourisher, and the father of all."
Having spoken these words, he led the assembly outside and, with flattering words and expressions of regret, sent them back to question the Buddha.

Thus, having already explained the number and categories of mental factors (*caitasika*) within the various classes of consciousness across all realms and stages, we shall now discuss some of the specific distinctions among those mental factors previously analyzed.
What is the distinction between lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and between affection (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*)?
The verse says:
Lack of shame and lack of dread consist in a lack of reverence, And a failure to perceive fear regarding transgressions.
Affection and respect consist of faith and a sense of shame; they exist only in the realms of desire and form.
The treatise states:

Regarding the distinction between lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) herein: toward all virtues and those who possess virtue, having no reverence, no esteem, no sense of restraint, and no sense of subordination is called lack of shame; this is the state directly opposed to respect (*gaurava*).
Dharmas that are censured and loathed by all noble beings (satpuruṣa) are called "offenses" (āpatti). To see no fear in these offenses is called "lack of shame" (anapatrāpya).
Here, the word "fear" indicates that which produces dread because it is an undesirable result (aniṣṭaphala).
What meaning does the expression “not seeing fear” intend to reveal?
Does it mean that one sees [the object] but is not afraid, or does it mean that one does not see that fear?
If this were so, what would be the fault?
Both positions entail faults.
If one sees [the object] yet does not fear it, this should manifest wisdom; if one does not see it yet fears it, this should manifest ignorance.
Since these words do not manifest either seeing or not seeing, what then is being manifested?

This demonstrates that there is a distinct dharma which is a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) and serves as the cause for those two [non-shame and non-embarrassment]; it is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of embarrassment).
Other masters say:

the absence of shame when observing oneself regarding committed transgressions is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame), while the absence of shame when observing others is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of embarrassment).
If that is so, since these two have different objects of observation, how can they arise simultaneously?
It is not said that these two arise at one time while separately observing self and others.
Rather, when there is a lack of shame, that which is predominant during the observation of oneself is designated as "lack of moral dread" (*āhrīkya*).
Furthermore, there is shamelessness (*ahrīkya*); when this is observed in others, its increase is termed lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

One should understand that the distinction between shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*) is the reverse of this: that is to say, reversing the first explanation, having respect, having veneration, having a sense of restraint, and having a sense of subordination is called shame; seeing fear in transgression is called dread.

Reversing the second explanation: observing one's own shame regarding the transgressions one has committed is called *hrī* (shame), while observing the shame of others is called *apatrāpya* (embarrassment).
Thus, the distinction between the absence of shame (*āhrīkya*) and the absence of embarrassment (*anapatrāpya*) has been explained.
Regarding the distinction between affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*): affection refers to fondness, and its essence is faith (*śraddhā*).
However, there are two types of affection:
first, that which is defiled (*kliṣṭa*); second, that which is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*).
That which is defiled refers to craving, such as the affection for one's wife and children;
that which is undefiled refers to faith, such as the affection for teachers and elders.
There is faith that is not affection, namely, faith directed toward suffering and its origin.
There is craving that is not faith, namely, all defiled craving.
There is both faith and craving, namely, faith that takes cessation and the path as its objects.
There is craving that is not faith, namely, excluding the three aforementioned cases.
Some say: faith (*śraddhā*) is the patient acceptance of virtue; because it precedes [it], affection (*preman*) subsequently arises. Therefore, affection is not faith.
Respect (*gaurava*) means reverence; its essence is precisely shame (*hrī*), as was explained previously regarding shame—that it consists of respect and so forth.
There is shame that is not respect, namely shame conditioned by suffering and its origin.
There is shame that encompasses both shame and respect, namely shame conditioned by cessation and the path. Some say:

Reverence (*gaurava*) consists in that which is held in high esteem; it is only by taking this as a prerequisite that shame (*hrī*) subsequently arises. Therefore, reverence is not identical to shame.
With respect to the objective referent—the *pudgala*—one should formulate four permutations regarding the presence or absence of affection (*preman*) and reverence (*gaurava*).
There is affection without respect, as toward one's wife, children, co-residents, and disciples;
there is respect without affection, as toward the teachers of others, virtuous persons, and those of noble status.
There is both affection (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*), as in the case of one's own teacher, parents, paternal uncles, and so forth.
There is neither affection nor respect, which refers to cases other than the three aforementioned types.
Such affection and respect exist in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), but not in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Is it not the case that faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*), which are among the great wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), also exist in the formless realm?

Regarding love (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*), there are two types: those directed toward phenomena (*dharma*) and those directed toward persons (*pudgala*). Love and respect directed toward phenomena exist throughout all three realms.
The intention here is to state that because they take the *pudgala* as their object, [love and respect] exist in the desire and form realms, but not in the formless realm.
Thus has the distinction between love (*preman*) and respect (*gaurava*) been explained.
What is the distinction between vitarka, vicāra, māna, and mada?
The verse says:
Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind; māna is the elevation of the mind in relation to others.
Pride (*māna*) arises from being stained by one's own qualities; it is a loftiness of mind that disregards all else.
The commentary states:

The distinction between investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) refers to the coarseness and subtlety of the mind. The coarse nature of the mind is called investigation, while the subtle nature of the mind is called analysis.
How do these two correspond within a single mind?
Some offer this explanation:
it is like placing clarified butter upon cold water while being struck by the intense rays of the sun; because of the water and the sun, the butter is neither melted nor solidified.

In this way, within a single moment of mind there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). Because the mind is neither pervasive nor subtle due to vitarka and vicāra, they function simultaneously within that single moment of mind.

If this is so, then vitarka and vicāra are the causes of coarseness and subtlety, rather than being the essence of coarseness and subtlety themselves; they are like the freezing and melting caused by water and sunlight, whereas the essence of the sun itself is not the freezing or the melting.

Furthermore, the nature of coarseness and subtlety is established through mutual dependence; as the realms, stages, and categories differ, they are defined by their relative superiority or inferiority, such that even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there ought to be applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Moreover, since the natures of coarseness and subtlety do not possess distinct ontological entities, one cannot rely upon them to differentiate between applied and sustained thought.
Furthermore, there is another explanation:
the two factors of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are the formations of speech;
therefore, the Sūtra states that speech exists only when vitarka and vicāra are present, and that these formations of speech do not exist in the absence of vitarka and vicāra.

The coarse is called *vitarka* (applied thought) and the subtle is called *vicāra* (sustained thought). Within a single moment of mind, how is it not contradictory in principle for one distinct factor to be coarse and another distinct factor to be subtle?
If they possessed distinct ontological natures (*bhāva-jāti*), there would indeed be no contradiction in principle;

however, since they lack distinct ontological natures, it contradicts reason, because within a single ontological nature it is impossible for both the superior and the inferior to arise simultaneously.
If it is argued that there is also a distinction in their essential natures (*svabhāva*), one should explain what the distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of these essential natures are.

These distinct characteristics of the two essential natures are difficult to describe; they are manifested merely by means of "superior" and "inferior," yet it is not by means of superiority and inferiority that the distinct characteristics can be manifested, for within each individual category there exists both the superior and the inferior.
From this, it should be understood that the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra can certainly not be maintained as being associated with a single moment of mind.
If this is so, why does the sūtra state:
"In the first dhyāna, five factors are fully present"?
The statement that [the dhyānas] possess five factors refers to a single stage (*bhūmi*), not to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); therefore, there is no fault.
Thus has the distinction between vitarka and vicāra been explained.

As for the distinction between pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*): pride is the nature of the mind’s self-elevation in relation to others; by weighing the differences in the qualities and types of oneself and others, the mind elevates itself and relies upon that, looking down upon others—hence it is called pride.
*Stambha* (pride) refers to a state of mind characterized by arrogance and lack of regard for others, preceded by an attachment to one's own qualities.
Other masters say:
just as the specific state of exhilaration arising from alcohol is called intoxication (*mada*), so too the specific state of exhilaration arising from greed is called *stambha*.
This is called the distinction between pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*).
Thus far, the different categories of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as their distinct characteristics of arising together, have been explained.

However, within the sūtras, various names and designations are established for these minds and mental factors according to their specific meanings; we shall now analyze these distinctions in name and meaning.
The verse says:
Mind, thought, and consciousness are one in essence;
Minds and mental factors have a basis, an object, and an aspect; There are five meanings of association.
The treatise states:

It is called "mind" (*citta*) because it accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena]; it is called "intellect" (*manas*) because it cogitates; it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it discerns.
Furthermore, there is another explanation which says:

It is called "mind" (*citta*) because it differentiates the various distinctions between the pure and impure realms; that same entity is called "intellect" (*manas*) because it serves as the basis for others; and it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it acts as the dependent upon that basis.
Therefore, although the meanings conveyed by the three terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* differ, their essence is one.

Just as the three terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have different meanings but a single essence, so it is with all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*): they are termed "having a support" (*sāśraya*), "having an object" (*sālambana*), "having an aspect" (*sākāra*), and "associated" (*samprayukta*). Although the names and their meanings are distinct, their essence is one.
This means that both mind and mental factors are called "having a support" (*sāśraya*) because they rely upon the sense organs as their support.
Alternatively, they are called "having an object" (*sālambana*) because they apprehend an objective sphere.
Or, they are called "having an aspect" (*sākāra*), because they give rise to aspects according to the specific categories and distinctions within that objective sphere.
Alternatively, it is called "conjunction" (*samprayoga*) because of their equal integration.
Based on what meaning is it called "equal integration"?

It is because there are five meanings; that is to say, the mind and mental factors are said to be conjoined because they are equal in five respects: their basis, their object, their aspect, their time, and their substance are all equal.
Regarding the equality of function: within a single moment of association, just as the essence of the mind is one, so too is each of the mental factors (caitta-dharma) likewise.
Thus has been explained the extensive analytical meaning of the mind and its mental factors.
What are the formations dissociated from mind?
The verse says:
Formations dissociated from mind are acquisition, non-acquisition, and homogeneity;
Non-conception, the two attainments, life-force, characteristics, names, phrases, and so forth.
The treatise says:

These various phenomena are dissociated from the mind, are not of the nature of matter (*rūpa*), and are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); therefore, they are called "formations dissociated from the mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Within this context, let us first examine the characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The verse says:
Acquisition refers to obtaining and accomplishment; Non-acquisition is the opposite of this.
"Acquisition and non-acquisition exist only with respect to one's own continuum and the two types of cessation.
The treatise says:

There are two kinds of acquisition (*prāpti*): first, the obtaining of what was not previously attained or had been lost; second, the possession of what has been attained and not lost. It should be understood that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is the opposite of this.
In which phenomena are there possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*)?
They exist within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtati*) and with respect to the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).

That is to say, regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), possession and non-possession exist if they fall within one's own continuum, but not in the continuum of another; for there is no such thing as being endowed with the factors belonging to another's body.
It is not the case that there is no continuity, for there is no accomplishment of dharmas belonging to non-sentient things.

Furthermore, while conditioned dharmas are definitely of this nature, among unconditioned dharmas, acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exist only with respect to the two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
There are no sentient beings who do not possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); therefore, it is traditionally taught in the Abhidharma:
"Who possesses the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)?

It refers to all sentient beings, with the exception of noble ones who are bound by all fetters at the first moment and all other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) bound by all fetters; all remaining sentient beings possess analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
Since it is certain that no one can achieve space, one does not speak of "attainment" with respect to space; because attainment does not exist, non-attainment likewise does not exist.
This is because our school’s doctrine establishes attainment and non-attainment as mutually exclusive opposites.
For all those who possess [a dharma], there is also non-possession (*aprāpti*); this can be understood by inference from the principle, and thus it is not explained separately.
On what basis is it known that there exists a distinct entity called "possession"?
Because it is stated in the *Sūtra*.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Because the Noble One has brought about, acquired, and accomplished those ten qualities of one beyond training, he has already severed five factors," and so forth, as explained at length.
If that were so, then non-sentient things and the mental continuums of others would also necessarily possess [this quality]. Why?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a wheel-turning king who possesses the seven jewels," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Here, "possessing" (samanvāgata) refers to mastery; that is, the wheel-turning king has the power of mastery over those seven jewels because he can employ them according to his pleasure.
Since this [attainment] is already designated as "accomplishment" (siddhi) in its own right, for what other reason should one know that there exists a distinct entity?
What irrationality is there in admitting a distinct entity?

Such irrationality would consist in this: that the "attainment" you postulate has no perceivable essence, unlike [perceptible entities] such as form and sound, or [mental factors] such as greed and hatred.
Its lack of utility can be known by analogy with the eyes, ears, and so forth; therefore, there is no room for the existence of a distinct entity called "acquisition" (*prāpti*).
To maintain that such a distinct entity exists is irrational.

If it is argued that this acquisition also has a function—namely, acting as the cause for the arising of the various dharmas to be acquired—then unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena would necessarily lack acquisition.
Furthermore, regarding dharmas that have been acquired but then lost— either because of a transition between realms or stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) or through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*)—
since there is currently no acquisition (*prāpti*) for them, how could they arise?
If it is the co-arising acquisition (*sahaja-prāpti*) that serves as the cause for arising, then what function do "arising" (*jāti*) and "the arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) perform?
Furthermore, non-sentient phenomena would necessarily never arise;
moreover, for those bound by all fetters, there would be no distinction in the manifestation of afflictions as inferior, middling, or superior, because their acquisitions would lack differentiation.
If there were distinctions [in the arising of phenomena] due to other causes, then those phenomena would simply arise from them; what, then, would be the use of *prāpti*?
Therefore, the claim that *prāpti* has a function—namely, that it acts as the cause for the arising of the phenomena it acquires—is logically untenable.
Who says that this "acquisition" (*prāpti*) acts as a cause for the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)? If that were so, what function would this acquisition have?
It serves as the cause for establishing distinctions [among dharmas].

Why is this so? If there were no attainment, then when ordinary beings and noble ones give rise to conventional minds, there would be no established distinction between ordinary beings and the various noble ones.
Is it not the case that there must be a distinction [between them] because there is a difference between afflictions already abandoned and those not yet abandoned?
If one maintains that there is no "acquisition" (prāpti), how can it be said that afflictions are either abandoned or not abandoned?

The distinction between what has been abandoned and what has not yet been abandoned is established by the existence of acquisition (*prāpti*); this is because of whether or not one is separated from the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This distinction between the afflictions being already abandoned or not yet abandoned is established through the differentiation of the basis (*āśraya*).

This means that through the power of the paths of seeing and meditation, the noble ones cause their physical basis to undergo a transformation distinct from its original state, such that among the afflictions abandoned by those two paths, it no longer possesses the capacity to cause them to manifest.
Just as a seed that has been scorched by fire undergoes a transformation such that it lacks the capacity to produce [a sprout], so too,
when the basis of an noble one (ārya) is such that it no longer possesses the capacity to give rise to afflictions, this is called the abandonment of the afflictions.

Alternatively, when the seeds of afflictions within the basis (*āśraya*) are diminished by the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), this is also termed "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*); that which is contrary to this is termed "unabandoned" (*aprahīṇa*).

Those that are unabandoned are said to be "possessed" (*samanvāgata*), while those that have been abandoned are termed "not possessed" (*asamanvāgata*). These two types are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and not real entities.
Wholesome dharmas are of two kinds:

first, those acquired without effort; second, those that must be acquired through effort. These are termed "attained by birth" (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) and "attained through application" (*prāyogika*).

Regarding those acquired through cultivation rather than by effort: if the seeds within the basis have not been impaired, it is called "attainment"; if the seeds within the basis have already been impaired, it is called "non-attainment."

It should be understood that "severance" refers to the fact that for one who has severed the roots of goodness, the seeds of the roots of goodness within their basis are damaged by the power of false views; it does not mean that the seeds of the roots of goodness within the basis are utterly destroyed, which is what is called "severance."

Regarding those [dharmas] that must be acquired through effort: if, within the basis (*āśraya*), those dharmas have already arisen such that the power to produce them is present and unimpaired, it is called "attainment" (*samanvāgama*); the opposite of this is called "non-attainment" (*asamanvāgama*).
These two types [of attainment] are likewise provisional and not real.
Therefore, within the basis, there exists only the seed—unextracted, undamaged, and capable of growth—which, at such a stage, is designated by the name "attainment"; there is no separate entity.
In this context, what dharma is called the "seed"?
It refers to the successive and immediate functional capacity of name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) to produce its own effects; this arises from the specific transformation within the continuum.
What is meant by transformation?
It refers to the difference between preceding and succeeding states within a continuum.
What is meant by continuum?
This refers to the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the three times, characterized by causality.
What is meant by their "differentiation"?
It is the presence of a functional capacity (*śakti*) to produce an effect immediately [following its own arising].
However, there are passages stating that if one is "accomplished" in greed, one cannot cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
Those [passages] explain:
one who is attached to and indulges in the affliction of greed is unable to feel revulsion for it or abandon it; therefore, they are said to be "accomplished" [in it].
Because one is attached to and indulges in the time of craving, one will certainly be unable to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
Thus, that which is accomplished in every respect is merely conventional and not real.
The mere negation of these is called "non-accomplishment" (*asiddhi*); it is also conventional (*prajñapti*) and not substantial (*dravya*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
both of these two types exist as distinct entities that are substantial rather than conventional.
Thus, both of these approaches are well-explained.
Why is this so? Because they do not contradict reason and because they are what we ourselves maintain as our own tenet.
The intrinsic nature has already been explained; what, then, are its distinctions?
First, the acquisitions (prāpti) shall be explained.
The verse says:
The dharmas of the three time periods each have three [types of acquisition]; those that are wholesome and so forth are only wholesome and so forth;
those with a bond have acquisitions of their own realm, while those without a bond have acquisitions that pertain to all four realms;
those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have three [types of acquisition], and those not to be abandoned have two kinds.
The treatise states:

The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the three time periods each have three types. That is to say, past dharmas have past acquisitions, future acquisitions, and present acquisitions; likewise, future and present dharmas each have three types of acquisitions.

Furthermore, wholesome and other types of dharmas possess acquisitions that are exclusively wholesome and so forth; that is to say, for wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas, there are respectively three types of acquisition: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Furthermore, there are bound phenomena whose acquisitions belong exclusively to their own realm; that is, for phenomena of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, there are respectively only the three acquisitions belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms.

If it concerns non-bound dharmas, their acquisition (prāpti) encompasses all four types; that is to say, summarizing the acquisitions of untainted (anāsrava) dharmas, there are four types: namely, the acquisitions belonging to the three realms as well as the untainted acquisition.
Regarding the specific distinctions: the acquisition (*prāpti*) of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) pertains to all three realms (*dhātu*).
If it is the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it pertains to the form and formless realms as well as being untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is because the acquisition of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is exclusively untainted.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the non-bound dharmas (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) is of four kinds.

Furthermore, the acquisition of dharmas belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) is exclusively of the training stage; the acquisition of dharmas belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is exclusively of the stage beyond training. Regarding the acquisition of dharmas that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), there are distinctions: generally speaking, this acquisition is of three types. To distinguish them specifically, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas and the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are termed dharmas that are neither in training nor beyond training.
Furthermore, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*);

the same applies to the acquisitions of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), as well as the acquisitions of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) induced by what is not the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). However, if it is the acquisition of cessation through deliberation induced by the learner’s path (*śaikṣamārga*), it is a learner’s [acquisition]; if it is the acquisition of cessation through deliberation induced by the non-learner’s path (*aśaikṣamārga*), it is a non-learner’s [acquisition].
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas abandoned through seeing and cultivation, there are acquisitions (prāpti) abandoned through seeing and cultivation respectively.

There is no such differentiation for the acquisitions of dharmas that are not to be abandoned. To state it generally, the acquisitions of these dharmas are of two kinds; to distinguish them specifically: all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are termed "not to be abandoned," whereas the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is abandoned solely through cultivation.
The acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that is not induced by the Noble Path is also like this.
Both the acquisition of cessation through deliberation induced by the Noble Path and the acquisition of the Truth of the Path are not to be abandoned.
Although it was previously stated in general that the dharmas of the three time periods each have three [types], we should now distinguish their specific characteristics.
The verse says:
The *anivṛtāvyākṛta* (non-obscured indeterminate) arises together with [the mind], excluding the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the transformation power (*nirmāṇa*).
Obscured matter also arises simultaneously; in the desire and form realms, it does not arise beforehand.
The treatise says:
Unobscured-neutral acquisition arises only simultaneously; it does not arise before or after [the dharma], because its power is weak.
If a dharma is past, its acquisition (prāpti) is also past; if a dharma is future, its acquisition is also future; if a dharma is present, its acquisition is also present.
Is this the case for all unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) dharmas?
It is not so. Why? Because it excludes the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, as well as the power of transformation.

This refers to the supernormal knowledges of the eye and ear, as well as the mind capable of transformation; because their power is strong and they are accomplished through specific preparatory applications (*prayoga*), although they are subsumed under the category of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature, they possess acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with them.

If one has practiced the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) to an extreme degree, it is likewise permitted that their acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs in the same manner.
Is it only for unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas that their acquisition arises simultaneously with them?
It is not so. Why? The acquisition of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) matter is also like this.
That is to say, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of all obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest form (*vijñaptirūpa*) is also as previously described; it exists only as co-arising (*sahaja*).

Although there may be superior grades [of such form], they cannot produce non-manifest form (*avijñapti*), and thus their power is weak and inferior. Consequently, there is certainly no acquisition that precedes or follows [the manifest form].

Just as there are distinctions in the acquisition (*prāpti*) of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, are there also distinctions in the acquisition of wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) [dharmas]? There are indeed. How so?

That is to say, for wholesome and unwholesome matter bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises prior [to the dharma itself]; there is only acquisition that arises simultaneously with it or subsequently.
Is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) like acquisition, such that it also possesses the aforementioned categories of types?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
Non-acquisition (aprāpti) is undefiled-neutral; it exists in three ways for each of the past and future [times];
it is of the three realms or unconditioned (anāsrava).

It is accepted that the non-acquisition of the Noble Path is designated as the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva); it is abandoned by the acquisition of that dharma or by changing levels (bhūmi).
The treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), all non-attainments (*aprāpti*) are comprised exclusively within the category of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the distinction of time (*adhvan-viśeṣa*), there are three types each for the past and the future; that is to say, present dharmas definitely lack a present non-attainment, possessing only past and future non-attainments; and for each of the past and future [dharmas], there are non-attainments belonging to each of the three times.

Regarding the distinction of realms (*dhātu-vibhāga*): for the factors bound to the three realms as well as those not bound to any realm, there are three types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) each. That is to say, for factors bound to the desire realm, there are non-acquisitions belonging to all three realms; the same applies to factors bound to the form and formless realms, as well as those that are unbound.
It is certainly not the case that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) can be untainted (*anāsrava*). Why is this?
Because it is admitted that the non-acquisition of the noble path (*āryamārga*) is designated as the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
As the treatise states:
"What is the nature of an ordinary person?
It is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas."
Non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is merely another name for non-possession (*asamanvāgama*); it is not reasonable to say that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Of which noble dharmas is this non-attainment called the nature of an ordinary person?
This means that because [the sūtra] does not specifically mention the non-attainment of all [noble dharmas],
this term "non-attainment" indicates being devoid of attainment.

Were it otherwise, even the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would not have accomplished the noble dharmas of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha lineages, and they should therefore be called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If that were so, that treatise need not have used the word "pure" (kevala), for this single phrase already contains the sense of "pure," just as one says, "those who eat water" or "those who eat wind."

Some say: "The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) consists in the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the dharmas co-arising with it.

One cannot object that, because this state is abandoned at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñāna*), one would consequently become a non-noble (*anārya*); for its non-possession (*aprāpti*) has already been permanently destroyed prior to that.
If that is so, since this nature applies to all three vehicles, what is it that one has not attained that constitutes the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
To this, one should also say: "one has not attained anything at all.
If that is so, then the same objection as before would apply.
This objection should again be resolved as previously explained.
If that were so, then repeating it would be a futile exertion.
Thus, the explanation given by the Sautrāntika masters is the superior one.
What is the meaning of what the Sautrāntikas say?
It means that the specific state of the continuity of the factors of a noble one (*āryadharma*) which has not yet arisen is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*).
When, in this way, is this non-possession (*aprāpti*) abandoned?
This non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of a dharma is abandoned at the time of acquiring that dharma or upon changing planes of existence (*bhūmi*).
For example, the non-acquisition of the Noble Path is termed "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*); it is abandoned upon acquiring that Noble Path or by changing planes of existence.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of other dharmas should be considered in the same manner.
When the acquisition of a non-acquisition is severed and the non-acquisition of that non-acquisition arises, this is termed "abandoning the non-acquisition."
Regarding acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), could there be further acquisitions and non-acquisitions for these two?
One should say that each of these two has its own further acquisition and non-acquisition.
If this were so, would it not entail the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*)?
There is no fault of infinite regress, because it is accepted that they mutually establish one another through a successive series.

When a dharma arises, three dharmas arise together with its own essence: first, the primary dharma; second, the acquisition (prāpti) of the dharma; and third, the acquisition of the acquisition (prāptiprāpti).

This means that because the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma arises within the continuum, one achieves both the primary dharma and the "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāptiprāpti*); and because the acquisition of acquisition arises, one achieves the acquisition of the dharma. Therefore, there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in this case.

Thus, when any dharma—whether wholesome or defiled—first arises, three dharmas arise together with its own self-nature; at the second moment, six dharmas arise together, namely the three primary dharmas and their three acquisitions (*prāpti*); at the third moment, eighteen dharmas arise together, namely the nine acquisitions of the dharmas produced in the first and second moments and the nine acquisitions of those acquisitions (*prāpti-prāpti*).
In this way, these various acquisitions (*prāpti*) increase progressively in subsequent moments.

All past and future afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as well as innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), are associated with and co-existent (*sahabhū*) in every single moment throughout the beginningless and endless cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus, there are infinite acquisitions; for instance, within the life-stream of a single sentient being, infinite acquisitions arise in each and every moment. Since the life-streams of all sentient beings are each distinct, in every single moment, immeasurable and boundless acquisitions arise simultaneously for each one.
In this way, these various acquisitions form extremely vast assemblies; because they are without obstruction, they mutually accommodate one another.
Were it otherwise, the acquisition of a single sentient being would not find room in space, let alone those of a second and so forth.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Volume Four (Part Three);
Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Volume Five.
