Part Three of Chapter Two: Analysis of the Faculties (Indriya-viniścaya). Having thus explained the characteristics of acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), what is "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*)?
The verse says:
"Sabhāgatā is the equality among sentient beings.
The commentary says:

There exists a distinct, substantial entity called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*), which refers to the mutual similarity among sentient beings; the *Mūla-śāstra* designates this as "group homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāgatā*).
This, moreover, is of two kinds:
first, undifferentiated; second, differentiated.
Non-differentiation refers to the "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāgatā*), which exists equally in all sentient beings.

Differentiation refers to the various distinct homogeneities of sentient beings—such as those belonging to different realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), destinies (*gati*), births (*yoni*), castes (*jāti*), genders (*puruṣa-strī*), lay followers (*upāsaka*), monks (*bhikṣu*), and those who are learners (*śaikṣa*) or non-learners (*aśaikṣa*)—which exist equally within each respective class of beings.
Furthermore, there is the dharma of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā), which refers to [the similarity] following the aggregates, bases, and elements.

If this homogeneity were not a real entity characterized by non-differentiation, then among sentient beings who are mutually distinct, there could not possibly exist the undifferentiated cognition and conventional designation that "sentient being is equal to sentient being."
In this way, one should understand the cognition and designation of the aggregates and so forth as being without distinction.
Is there any case where death and birth occur without relinquishing or acquiring the commonality (nikāyasabhāga) of sentient beings?
One should formulate four propositions.
The first proposition refers to dying in a certain place and being reborn in that very same place.

The second proposition refers to when one enters the stage of the certainty of correctness (samyaktva-niyāma), relinquishing the homogeneous character of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā) and acquiring the homogeneous character of a noble one (ārya-sabhāgatā).
The third phrase refers to those who are proceeding toward death and being born into another realm of existence, and so forth.
The fourth phrase refers to those who are excluded from the aforementioned characteristics.

If there were a distinct, substantial entity called "the homogeneity of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanasabhāgatā*), what would be the purpose of separately establishing "the nature of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is not a distinct entity because it shares the same generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*) as other persons;
nor is it a separate human nature. Furthermore, it is not perceived by worldly direct observation because it is non-material (*arūpin*).
Nor can it be discerned by cognitive wisdom, as it lacks any distinct function.

Although the world does not clearly understand the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) of sentient beings, it nonetheless regards them as being without distinction; therefore, even if its substantial existence were granted, what would be its use?
Furthermore, for what reason do you not allow for the existence of a *sabhāgatā* for non-sentient things?
Furthermore, since various grains, wheat, beans, gold, iron, mangoes (*āmra*), jackfruit (*panasa*), and so forth, also possess mutual similarity within their own respective classes;

and since the various *sabhāgatās* (homogeneities) differ from one another, how could there not be further *sabhāgatās* for those [differences], such that one could give rise to a cognition of non-difference and apply a conventional designation?

Furthermore, this would also manifest and establish the tenets held by the Vaiśeṣika school; for that school maintains the existence of a "universal category" (sāmānya-padārtha), from which the verbal cognition and conceptual knowledge of a commonality regarding all phenomena arise.

They further maintain that there exists a category (padārtha) called "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*), by virtue of which the verbal cognition and conceptual knowledge of "sameness" or "difference" arise with respect to distinct classes of things. The Vaibhāṣikas state:
Their position is inconsistent with this [system], because they claim that a single entity occurs (applies) across many [individuals].

Furthermore, regardless of whether it is explicitly stated or not in that context, this *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) must necessarily exist as a real entity (*dravya*), because it is taught in the Sūtra.
As the Blessed One said:
"If one returns here and attains human homogeneity," and so forth, at length.
Although this has been said, it is not stated that there exists a separate real entity (dravya) called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
If that is so, what is this "homogeneity" that has been mentioned?

It is simply the designation (prajñapti) applied to such conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as they arise, such as the "human homogeneity" and so forth, just like the homogeneity of various grains, wheat, beans, and so on.
This is not a well-stated position, as it contradicts our own school’s tenets.
Having already analyzed *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity),
what is *asaṃjñin* (the state of non-perception)?
The verse says:
In the state of non-conception, within non-conception, the mind and mental factors cease;
it is a matured fruit residing in the Vast Fruit [heaven].
The treatise says:

If one is born among the sentient beings of the Heaven of Non-conception, there is a dharma capable of causing the cessation of the mind and mental factors; this is called "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*).
It is a substantially existent entity that can obstruct future mind and mental factors so that they do not temporarily arise, just as a dam blocks a river.
This dharma is exclusively a fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Of what is it the maturation?
It is the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Where do the sentient beings of non-conception reside?

They reside in the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) realm; that is to say, within the Vast Fruit Heaven there is a lofty and superior abode, similar to the intermediate dhyāna, which is called the Heaven of Non-conception (Asaṃjñisattva).
Is that state permanently without perception, or is there also perception?
During the stages of birth and death, perception exists for most of the time.
It is called "without perception" because those sentient beings do not give rise to perception for a long period during that interval.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Those sentient beings pass away from that place because their perception arises; yet, just as one who has been asleep for a long time awakens and gives rise to perception again, those beings, having passed away from there, are necessarily reborn in the desire realm and nowhere else. This is because the force of their prior cultivation of meditative practice has been exhausted, and they are unable to cultivate meditation further in that state, just as an arrow shot into the air falls when its momentum is spent."
If sentient beings are to be born in that place, they must necessarily possess karma of the desire realm to be experienced in a subsequent life;
just as those who are to be born in Uttarakuru must necessarily possess the karma for rebirth in the heavens.
The state of non-perception has already been explained.
What are the two meditative attainments?
They are the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
What are the characteristics of the first, the attainment of non-conception?
The verse says:
Such is the attainment of non-conception; it belongs to the final dhyāna and is sought for liberation.
Wholesome, it is experienced only in the next life; non-Aryans attain it for one lifetime.
The commentary says:

As previously stated, there is a distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors, which is termed "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*); likewise, there is another distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors, which is termed the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Regarding "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*): it is called the "attainment of non-conception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) because it is a meditative attainment characterized by the absence of conception, or because there is no conception within this attainment;
thus, the term is used to indicate that this attainment is identical to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) in its cessation of both mind and mental factors.
In which stage does this exist?
It is said to be in the final dhyāna; that is, in the fourth dhyāna and no other.
For what purpose is the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) cultivated?

This refers to those seeking liberation who cling to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) as true liberation; they cultivate the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in order to realize it.

Since it was previously stated that non-perception is a result-of-maturation (*vipāka*), it is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); this is established implicitly and need not be restated.
Now, the attainment of non-conception is exclusively wholesome; because it is wholesome, it can induce the maturation of the five aggregates within the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings.
Since it is of a wholesome nature, to what type of feeling does it correspond?
It is experienced only in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), not in the present life, the subsequent life, or as indeterminate (*aniyata*).

It is traditionally taught that even if one falls away from this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) after having arisen from it, one will necessarily be able to re-attain it in the present life and will be reborn among the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) in heaven; therefore, one who attains this meditative attainment can never enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Furthermore, it is maintained that this meditative attainment is acquired only by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and not by noble ones (*ārya*), because noble ones—viewing the state of non-ideation as if it were a deep pit—take no pleasure in entering it.
One must grasp the state of non-perception as true liberation and cultivate this meditative absorption by giving rise to the notion of renunciation;
since no noble being (ārya) grasps that which is tainted (sāsrava) as true liberation or true renunciation, they certainly do not practice this absorption.
When noble ones cultivate and attain the fourth dhyāna concentration, do they likewise attain the past and future states of the attainment of non-ideation?
They do not attain the others either.

Why is this so? Although they have practiced it in the past, because they lacked the [appropriate] mental state, it must be attained through great application and skillful means; therefore, at the time of its initial attainment, only one period is acquired—namely, the present—just as when one first receives the prātimokṣa vows.

Once this meditative absorption has been attained, from the second moment onwards until it is relinquished, it also becomes past; because it is a mindless state, there is no cultivation of future [moments].
Next, what are the characteristics of the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?
The verse says:
The attainment of cessation is likewise; it is for the sake of peaceful dwelling and belongs to the Peak of Existence.
It is wholesome, associated with two feelings, and is indeterminate [in its timing]. It is attained by noble ones through application.
One does not attain Buddhahood prior [to enlightenment], because it occurs through thirty-four moments of thought.
The Commentary says:
Just as with the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), so it is with the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
What is the meaning of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) used here?
It serves as an analogy for the cessation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

Just as it is said that there is a distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors called the attainment of non-ideation, so too there is a distinct dharma capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors called the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding the distinguishing characteristics of these two attainments: the former, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), is for the sake of seeking liberation, preceded by the mental application of the perception of renunciation;
this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is for the sake of seeking peaceful abiding, preceded by the mental application of the perception of cessation.
The previously mentioned attainment of non-ideation occurs in the final dhyāna;
this attainment of cessation, however, exists only at the Peak of Existence, which is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Like the former attainment, its nature is exclusively wholesome—never neutral or defiled—because it arises from a wholesome motivation.
The previously mentioned attainment of non-conception is experienced only in the next life;

this attainment of cessation, however, is experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives, or is indeterminate—meaning that, in terms of its maturation (*vipāka*), it may be experienced in the next life, in subsequent lives, or at an indefinite time, or it may not be experienced at all.
That is to say, if one attains parinirvāṇa in a lower realm, what stage and how many aggregates are produced by this meditative absorption?
It produces only the maturation of the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The aforementioned attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is attained only by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); [the attainment of cessation is not].

This attainment of cessation is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*); it cannot be produced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because the latter fear total annihilation, because it can only be produced through the power of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), and because it is entered through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that it is nirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmā-nirvāṇa*).
This is also as before: it is not obtained through the abandonment of defilements.
By what means is it obtained?
It is obtained through application (*prayoga*), because it must be realized precisely by means of application.

Furthermore, at the moment of first attainment, one attains only the present; one does not attain the past, nor does one cultivate the future, because cultivation can only occur through the power of the mind.
From the second moment onward, until it is relinquished, [the dharma] also becomes part of the past.
Does the Blessed One also attain it through preparatory effort? No. How so?

They are attained at the time of becoming a Buddha; that is to say, they are attained by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, at the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). There is not a single quality of a Buddha that is attained through preparatory effort (*prayoga*); rather, when a mere aspiration arises and manifests before him, all perfect qualities arise in accordance with that aspiration. Therefore, all the virtues of a Buddha are attained through the removal of defilements (*vairāgya-prāpti*).

The Blessed One had never previously arisen from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); at the moment he attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), how did he become one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
Because he had attained mastery over the attainment of cessation, he became one liberated both ways just as if he had already arisen from it.
The masters of the West (the Westerners) say that during the stage of training,
a bodhisattva first gives rise to this meditative absorption and subsequently attains awakening.
Why is their position not accepted here?
If one accepts that statement, it accords with the *Nyāyānusāra* of the Venerable Upagupta.
As that treatise states:
"It should be said that the Tathāgata first enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and subsequently gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)."
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
It is not the case that one first gives rise to the attainment of cessation and only afterwards produces the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Why is this?
It is traditionally taught that a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment through thirty-four moments of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

Within the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there are sixteen such moments; when one is free from the craving of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are eighteen moments—namely, the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) required to sever the nine grades of afflictions of the Peak of Existence. Thus, these eighteen added to the preceding sixteen constitute the thirty-four.

All Bodhisattvas must first become free from attachment to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) before entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); they no longer need to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages. Since it is impossible for a dissimilar state of mind to arise during this interval, Bodhisattvas in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) should not give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
The masters of foreign lands say:
"If one were to give rise to a mind of a different category in the interim, what fault would there be?
If that were so, it would entail the fault of transgressing the formal resolve (*samādāna*)."
However, bodhisattvas do not overstep their aspirational resolve (*cittāśaya*).
In principle, it is true that bodhisattvas do not overstep their aspirational resolve; yet, this does not mean they do not overstep the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*).
If that is so, how is it that they do not overstep their aspirational resolve?
This means: "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained the eternal exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
I am determined not to transgress such a resolve, for I shall bring all matters to completion during this single sitting alone."
What was stated previously is correct, for it is our own tenet.
Although we have already explained that the two meditative attainments possess many common and differing characteristics, there are further similarities and differences among them.
The verse says:
The two meditative attainments depend on the Desire and Form Realms; the attainment of cessation first occurs among humans.
The commentary says:
Regarding the "two attainments," these refer to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Both of these arise based upon both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
If one does not admit that the attainment of non-perception can also arise based on the form realm, one contradicts this text.
That is to say, the *Mūlaśāstra* states:
"There may be that which is the existence of form (*rūpabhava*), yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates (*skandha*).

This refers to sentient beings bound by the fetters of form (*rūparāga*) who are born in the heavens of those possessing perception (*saṃjñin*), and who abide in a mind of a different category—either having entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or having entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)."

Or, having been born in the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva), one has already attained entry into non-conception; this is called "form-existence" (rūpabhava), yet this existence does not consist of the five aggregates.
From this it is proven that these two meditative attainments both arise based upon the realms of desire and form; this is termed their common characteristic.

Regarding the distinct characteristics: it is said that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) can first arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whereas the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) first arises only among humans.

Once this [attainment of cessation] has been first cultivated and arisen among humans, one is born in the form realm only after first undergoing a regression; there, relying on a body in the form realm, one cultivates and gives rise to it once again.
Is there also regression from this attainment of cessation?
One should say that there is.
If it were not so, it would contradict the *Udāyi-sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"Venerable One!

It is possible that there are bhikṣus who, having previously in this place been endowed with pure śīla, endowed with samādhi, and endowed with prajñā, are able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."

One should know this as it truly is: in this present life or at the point of death, he is unable to apply himself diligently so that his liberation may reach fulfillment; consequently, upon the breakup of this body, he transcends the heavens of those who subsist on physical food and, according to his merit, receives a mind-made body in one of the [higher] heavens.
Once born there, it is also possible for them to repeatedly enter and emerge from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

One should know this as it truly is: the body of these mind-made gods (*manomayakāya*) is said by the Buddha to belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), whereas the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling exists only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
If one who has attained this concentration necessarily never regresses, how could they go to be reborn in the realm of form?
Other schools maintain that the concentration of cessation also exists within the fourth dhyāna.
Based on what they maintain, the fact that there is no falling back from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is established;
however, the claim that the fourth dhyāna possesses the attainment of cessation is necessarily untenable. Why is this so?
The nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) are taught in the sūtras.
If this were necessarily the case, how could there be the attainment of "leaping" (*vyutkrāntaka*)?
This sequence of attainments is taught for beginners; when mastery is attained, one may enter them in any order according to one's inclination.
These two meditative attainments differ in several respects:
first, they differ in terms of their level (*bhūmi*), as one belongs to the fourth dhyāna while the other belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);

second, they differ in terms of their preparatory application (*prayoga*), as the former is preceded by the mental attention to the perception of renunciation, whereas the latter is preceded by the mental attention to the perception of cessation.
There is a difference in their continuity, because they arise within the continuities of ordinary beings and noble ones respectively;
there is a difference in their maturation, because they are the maturational fruits of the state of non-perception and the Peak of Existence respectively;
and there is a difference in their susceptibility to feeling, because they lead to two types of feeling: those that are certain and those that are uncertain to arise.
There is a difference in their initial arising, as they first arise among humans in the two realms.

Since both meditative attainments have the cessation of mind and mental factors as their essential nature, for what reason are they specifically designated as "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*) and "cessation of sensation and conception" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) respectively?

Within the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), because one only feels aversion toward this [mind], it is called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*) even though one also knows [their] feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Now, since the mind has been interrupted for a long duration during these two attainments, how can the subsequent mind arise again?
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that past mind exists as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya) for subsequent minds.
Other teachers, however, say:
"If one is born in the formless realm, where form has been interrupted for a long time, how can form arise again later?"

That arising must necessarily be due to the mind and not to form; likewise, the mind emerging from meditative absorption should be understood in the same way, as it arises from the body endowed with sense faculties and not from the mind.
Therefore, the former masters of our tradition all maintain that these two phenomena serve as seeds for one another.
The two factors refer to the mind and the body endowed with sense faculties.
In the *Sāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, the Venerable Vasumitra states:
"If one maintains that the attainment of cessation is entirely devoid of mind, this fault would indeed follow."
I maintain that even in the meditative absorption of cessation there remains a subtle mind;
therefore, this fault does not apply. The Venerable Ghoṣaka says this is unreasonable. Why is that?

If there were still consciousness within this meditative absorption, then because of the conjunction of the three, there would necessarily be contact; and with contact as a condition, there would necessarily be feeling and perception.
As the Blessed One said:
"With the mind and mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact occurs, and together with it arise feeling, perception, and volition."
In that case, the factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) within this meditative absorption should likewise not cease.

If you argue that, as the Sūtra says "feeling conditions craving" (*vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā*), yet an Arhat does not give rise to craving despite possessing various feelings, so too must it be with contact (*sparśa*); not all contacts serve as conditions for feeling and the rest.
This analogy does not apply, because there is a distinction.
The Sūtra itself specifies:
"If the various feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance serve as conditions, craving arises."
Since there has never been a case where contact arises separately from feeling, there is a distinction between them.
By this principle, the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that all mental states are extinguished within the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
If there were no mind at all, how could it be called concentration (*samādhi*)?
It is called concentration because it causes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to function in equilibrium, or because the power of the mind reaches this state of equilibrium.
Are these two attainments substantially existent (*dravyasat*) or nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*)?
One should say they are substantially existent, because they can obstruct the mind and prevent it from arising. Some say:
This proof is logically untenable, because the preceding state of meditative concentration (samādhi-citta) acts as an obstruction.
That is to say, the preceding state of meditative concentration arises in opposition to all other states of mind; by its arising, it merely causes other states of mind not to function for a time.

Because this induces a continuity that opposes the basis of the mind, it is only conventionally designated as "concentration" (*samādhi*) during its state of non-functioning; it has no separate substantial entity.

Since this concentration is merely a provisional designation for the stage of non-functioning, it is absent both before one enters it and after one emerges from it; therefore, it is said to be included within the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Alternatively, it is the very basis that, being induced by a concentrated mind, arises in such a manner; this is conventionally designated as "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*).

One should know that the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) is likewise: it arises through a preceding mind that is incompatible with other minds. Because it arises, it causes other minds to temporarily not function; it is only during this state of non-functioning that "non-conception" is conventionally designated. Other explanations are as before.
This is not a well-stated position, as it contradicts our own school’s tenets.
Having already analyzed the two meditative attainments,
what is the life-faculty?
The verse says:
The essence of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is precisely longevity (āyus); it is able to sustain warmth and consciousness.
The commentary says:
The essence of life is itself longevity; therefore, the Abhidharma states:
"What is the life-faculty?
It is the longevity of the three realms."
Furthermore, it remains to be understood what dharma is called "life-force" (āyus).
It is said that there is a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is designated as life-force.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
When life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three factors—abandon the body, the abandoned body lies prostrate, like a piece of wood devoid of thought or awareness.
Therefore, there exists a distinct factor that serves as the cause for maintaining the continuity of warmth and consciousness; this is designated as "life-force" (*āyus*).
If that is so, by what dharma is this life-span sustained?
It is precisely warmth and consciousness that sustain this life-span.
If that is so, since these three dharmas sustain one another as they continue in succession, which dharma perishes first?
Because this ceases, the other two also cease accordingly.
In that case, these three would have to be eternal and never perish; if that were so, this life-span would have to be maintained by karma, since it proceeds as a continuum projected by karma.
If that is so, for what reason do you not admit that karma alone can sustain heat and consciousness, rather than requiring life-force (*āyus*)?
Such reasoning is incorrect, lest all consciousness from beginning to end be considered exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*).
If that is so, one should say that karma sustains heat, and heat in turn sustains consciousness; what need is there for this life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
In that case, consciousness existing within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would have nothing to sustain it, because heat is absent there.
One should say that karma is what sustains that consciousness; how can one follow mere sentiment to repeatedly formulate such shifting calculations?
Some say this consciousness is sustained by warmth alone, while others say it is sustained by karma alone.
Furthermore, it was previously stated.
What was stated previously?

It was said that not all consciousnesses from beginning to end are maturation (*vipāka*); therefore, one must necessarily admit the existence of a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is called "life-force" (*āyus*).
Now, we do not say that there is no substantial entity of life-force (*āyus*) at all; rather, we say that the life-force is not a separate, real substance.
If this is so, what dharma is designated as the life-force?
It is the momentum of the duration of the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) projected by karma in the three realms that is called the life-force.

Because the continuity of the momentum of the duration of the homogeneous state (*nikāyasabhāga*), projected by karma of the three realms, is determined to abide for a specific length of time according to its respective conditions, this momentum is designated as the essence of life-force (*āyus*).
It is like the momentum induced by a grain seed and so forth until the time of ripening, or like the momentum induced by a released arrow until the time it comes to rest.
Some say that "possession" (*prāpti*) is a specific quality (*guṇa-viśeṣa*) produced in dependence upon things such as arrows, and that it exists by virtue of its power.
Furthermore, as long as it has not fallen and continues to function without ceasing, because its substance is one and it is unobstructed,
there should be no distinction in the temporal stages of its movement toward other directions— whether rapid or slow— and moreover, there should never be a time of falling.

If it is argued that [the life-force does not fall immediately] because it is obstructed by wind, then it should either fall at the very beginning or never fall at all, since the obstructing winds are indistinguishable.
It is therefore well said that there exists a distinct, real entity capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is termed the essence of life-force (*āyus*).
Is death caused solely by the exhaustion of the life-span, or are there other causes as well?
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"There is death due to the exhaustion of the life-span, but not death due to the exhaustion of merit."
This is explained in detail through four propositions.
The first proposition refers to the exhaustion of the karmic force that brings about the maturation of lifespan.
The second proposition refers to the exhaustion of the karmic force that brings about the fruits of wealth and enjoyment.
The third phrase refers to the exhaustion of both types of karma that bring about rebirth.
The fourth phrase refers to the inability to avoid or escape from untimely and adverse conditions;
it should also be stated as the relinquishing of the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*).

In the stage when the life-span is exhausted, the exhaustion of merit has no further efficacy regarding death; therefore, when both are exhausted, death occurs, which is described as "death due to the exhaustion of both.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* asks:
Should this life-span be said to proceed in accordance with the continuity [of the aggregates], or should it be said to remain fixed once it has first arisen?

Sentient beings bound by desire do not enter the attainment of non-perception nor the attainment of cessation; it should be said that their life-span proceeds in accordance with the continuity [of the aggregates].

If they enter the attainment of non-perception, or the attainment of cessation, or if they are sentient beings bound by the realms of form or formlessness, it should be said that this life-span remains once it has arisen.
What is the meaning of those statements?
If the supporting body is subject to impairment, and thus the life-force is impaired accordingly, this is called the first type: that which proceeds in accordance with the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
If the supporting body is not subject to impairment and remains as it arose, this is called the second type: that which remains once arisen (*sakṛdutpanna*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
"The former [verse] demonstrates the presence of obstacles, while the latter demonstrates the absence of obstacles; by this, it is established that untimely death exists."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There are four ways of acquiring a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). That is to say, there is the acquisition of a personal existence that can only be destroyed by oneself and not by another.
This is elaborated in full as a tetralemma (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Those who can only be harmed by themselves and not by others refer to those born in the Desire Realm among the gods of *krīḍā-pramoṣaka* (those who lose mindfulness through play) and the gods of *manyanā-prahāṇa* (those who abandon through resentment). Because they give rise to excessive joy or anger, they perish there and not otherwise.
Furthermore, it should be stated that because the Buddhas attain parinirvāṇa by themselves,
those who can only be killed by others and not by themselves are sentient beings dwelling in the womb or egg;
those who can be killed by both are most other sentient beings of the desire realm.

Those who are neither [killing] nor harmed are all sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), as well as a portion of sentient beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), such as those in the hells (*naraka*), those in Uttarakuru, those correctly abiding in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), those in the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); royal seers (*rāja-ṛṣi*); those sent by the Buddha; Dāmilas and Udras prophesied by the Buddha; Yaśas, the son of the householder Kṛkī; Kumāra Jīvaka; the Bodhisattva in his final birth; and the mother of this Bodhisattva while she is carrying him in her womb; all universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and their mothers while they are carrying a universal monarch in their wombs.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"Venerable Sir,
what kind of sentient beings possess a self-body that can neither be harmed by themselves nor harmed by others?"
Śāriputra! This refers to sentient beings born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

It is traditionally taught that the self-bodies obtained through the remaining formless meditative attainments (*ārūpya-dhyāna*) can be destroyed by the noble path (*āryamārga*) of their own level, and can also be destroyed by the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of higher levels.
In the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), both types of harm are absent from above; therefore, it is said to be "neither of the two kinds of harm.
But is it not the case that the Peak of Existence is also harmed by the noble path (*āryamārga*) of other stages, and thus should be called "harmable by another"?

Thus, it should be explained that by mentioning the latter, the former is revealed; for in some instances, the former is mentioned to reveal the latter, while in others, the latter is mentioned to reveal the former.
How is it that in some instances the former is mentioned to reveal the latter?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Brahmakāyika devas are called the first among the heavens where bliss is born.
How is it that in this instance, the latter is mentioned to reveal the former?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Heaven of Utmost Purity of Radiance (Ābhāsvara) is called the second heaven of rebirth in bliss.

In that sūtra, the word "like" (yathā) indicates the sense of an analogy; thus one may say that by citing one case, the others are revealed, because when illustrating a dharma through an analogy, citing one instance reveals its entire class.
This "like" (yathā) does not function as a term of comparison (*dṛṣṭānta*), so it cannot be treated as equivalent to that [usage].
If the meaning of a simile were required for the term "like" to exist, then this "like" would indeed be a term of comparison; in that case, such a term should not appear in other sūtras.
As stated in other sūtras:
"There are sentient beings with form who have diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans and some gods; this is the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Therefore, one knows that even what is not a formal analogy may possess the quality of being like [the subject].
Let this digression cease for now.
Having already explained the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), what are the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*)?
The verse says:
The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), namely the natures of arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
The commentary states:
Because these four are the characteristics of the conditioned, if a dharma possesses them, it must be conditioned; that which is contrary to these is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).

Regarding these [characteristics], that which can cause dharmas to arise is called "arising" (*jāti*); that which can establish them is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); that which can cause them to decay is called "alteration" (*anyathātva*); and that which can destroy them is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
"Nature" (*svabhāva*) has the meaning of "essence" (*tattva*).
Is it not stated in the Sūtra that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned?
In this sūtra, it should have been stated that there are four [characteristics]; why is it not stated?
It is because the characteristic of "abiding" (sthiti-lakṣaṇa) is omitted.
However, when the sūtra speaks of "abiding and change" (sthity-anyathātva), this is simply another name for this very "change" (anyathātva).
Just as arising is called "origination" and cessation is called "extinction," so too should it be understood that change is called "alteration of duration.

This sutra teaches these as the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) in order to cause sentient beings to develop weariness toward and fear of the conditioned. These factors cause phenomena to undergo the transition through the three periods of time.
That is to say, those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), being driven by the power of arising, are caused to flow from the future into the present;

and being driven and pressed by the power of the characteristics of change and cessation, they are caused to flow from the present into the past, thereby undergoing decay, alteration, and destruction.
It is said that if there were a person in a dense forest and three enemies wished to cause him harm—one to drag him out of the forest, one to weaken his strength, and one to destroy his life-force.
The three characteristics should be understood to apply to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the same way.

Because abiding (*sthiti*) maintains and establishes those phenomena, and because it constantly delights in never being separated from them, it is not established as one of the characteristics of the conditioned.

Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possess their own abiding characteristic (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); however, because the characteristic of abiding would be confused with that [unconditioned abiding], the Sūtra does not mention it. Some say:
this Sūtra speaks of "abiding" and "change" combined as a single entity, naming them collectively the "characteristic of abiding-and-change" (*sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the purpose of explaining them in such a collective manner?

Because "abiding" is a state to which sentient beings are attached, it is explained in conjunction with the others to induce weariness and renunciation, just as showing Kālī together with Śrī; therefore, there are definitely four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
Since these characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) are themselves conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they must each have their own distinct four characteristics of arising and so forth.
If there were further characteristics for them, it would lead to an infinite regress, because those [secondary characteristics] would likewise possess other characteristics of arising and so on.
One should say that there is more, yet it is not infinite. Why is this?
The verse says:
These [characteristics] have "arising-of-arising" and so forth, which possess efficacy with respect to eight and one.
The commentary says:
This refers to the four primary characteristics previously mentioned.

Regarding "arising of arising" and so forth, these refer to the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*): arising-of-arising, abiding-of-abiding, alteration-of-alteration, and cessation-of-cessation.

Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are conditioned by the four primary characteristics (*mūlalakṣaṇa*), and the primary characteristics themselves are conditioned by the four secondary characteristics, would it not follow that each primary characteristic—just like the phenomena they characterize—must likewise have four secondary characteristics, and those in turn four more, resulting in an infinite regress?
There is no such fault, for the four primary and four secondary [causes] have distinct functions with respect to the eight [results] and the one [result].
What is meant by "function"?
It refers to the activity of a dharma, or what is called "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
Each of the four primary characteristics has utility with respect to eight factors, and each of the four secondary characteristics has utility with respect to one factor.
What is the meaning of this?

This means that when a dharma arises, nine dharmas arise simultaneously, including its own self-nature: the self-nature constitutes one, and the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) constitute eight.

Among these, the primary characteristic of "arising" (jāti-lakṣaṇa), excluding its own nature, gives rise to the other eight dharmas; the secondary characteristic of "arising of arising" (jāti-jāti) gives rise only to the primary characteristic of "arising" within the group of nine.

This means that just as a hen may produce many offspring or produce only one, so too do the characteristics of arising (*jāti*) and the characteristic of arising-of-arising (*jāti-jāti*): the former produces eight, while the latter produces only one.

Among the primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*), duration (*sthiti*)—excluding its own nature—abides in the other eight dharmas; the secondary characteristic of duration (*sthiti-sthiti*) abides only within the nine dharmas, specifically abiding in the primary duration itself.
The characteristics of difference (*anyathātva*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are likewise accordingly.

Therefore, although the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) have further secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because these secondary characteristics are only four.
Why does the Sautrāntika master analyze empty space (*ākāśa*) in this manner?
The characteristics such as arising do not possess a real ontological essence as they are conceptually discriminated.
Why is this so? Because there is no valid means of cognition [to establish them].

That is to say, these characteristics do not have a substantially existent essence that can be established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), as is the case with form (*rūpa*) and other such phenomena.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"The arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) can be known; their cessation (*vyaya*) and their alteration while abiding (*sthityanyathātva*) can also be known"?
O Beloved of the Gods!
You cling to the letter while being deluded regarding the meaning; the Blessed One has taught that the meaning is what should be relied upon.
What, then, is the true meaning spoken of in this sutra?

This refers to those of a foolish nature who, blinded by ignorance, grasp at the continuity of formations (*saṃskāra*) as "I" and "mine," developing deep attachment toward them throughout the long night.

To sever such grasping, the Blessed One revealed that the substance of the continuity of formations is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and of the nature of dependent origination; thus he spoke of "the three characteristics of the conditioned. This was not intended to show that all formations possess these three characteristics simultaneously within a single moment, for the three characteristics—arising and so forth—cannot be discerned within a single moment.
That which is unknowable should not be established as a characteristic; therefore, that sūtra further states:
"The arising of the conditioned can be known, and its cessation as well as its duration and alteration can also be known."

However, the reason the Sūtra repeats the term "conditioned" is to make it known that these characteristics signify what is conditioned; one must not think that these characteristics signify the existence of the conditioned, just as the presence of white egrets signifies the existence of water rather than its non-existence.
Nor should it be said that manifestation indicates good or evil, as in the case where the marks of a young girl indicate auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.

The initial arising of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is called "birth" (*jāti*); the state of its final exhaustion is called "cessation" (*nirodha*); the continuous progression in the interim is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); and the distinction between its prior and subsequent states is called "alteration while abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
Based on this, the Blessed One spoke concerning Nanda, saying:
"This son of good family well understands the arising of feeling, well understands the abiding of feeling, and well understands the fading away, change, and destruction of feeling."
Therefore, it is said in verse:
The beginning of the continuum is called "arising"; Cessation refers to the stage of final exhaustion;
That which continues through the middle is called "abiding"; The difference between earlier and later states within abiding is "alteration."
Furthermore, there is a verse that says:
"Arising occurs where there was previously nothing; continuity proceeds and abides;
the distinction between prior and subsequent states is change; and the severance of continuity is called cessation."
Furthermore, there is a verse that says:
"Because all phenomena are momentary, They perish without abiding;
since they perish spontaneously, To cling to their abiding is irrational."
Therefore, "abiding" (sthiti) is spoken of only with respect to the continuum; by this, the principle explained in the Abhidharma is established.
Thus, that treatise asks:
"What is called abiding?"

This refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that have already arisen but have not yet ceased; it is not the case that what has arisen and not yet ceased is called the momentary nature of phenomena (*kṣaṇika-dharmatā*).
Although the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
"In a single moment of mind, what arises? It is birth (*jāti*)."
Who is it that is said to die?
Who is it that abides differently and is said to age?
That treatise explains this based on the mind within the continuity of the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class), not in reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, in each and every moment, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—even when devoid of the grasping at them as substantially existent entities—still manifest the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
How are these established?

It is said that the arising of what was previously non-existent in each and every thought-moment is called "birth" (*jāti*); its passing away once it has existed is called "cessation" (*nirodha*); the succession of subsequent moments following preceding ones is called "duration" (*sthiti*); and the fact that there is a distinction between those preceding and succeeding moments is called "alteration during duration" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
When similar moments arise in succession, there is no lack of distinction between the preceding and succeeding ones.
How should that distinct characteristic be understood?

It is known by the differences in the time of falling—whether sooner or later—caused by such factors as whether a vajra or other object has been thrown or not, and whether it was thrown with great force or with weak force.
The meaning of the transformation and differentiation of the great elements is established.
When conditioned phenomena arise in a similar succession, there is not much difference between the preceding and succeeding moments; therefore, although there is change, they appear similar.

If that were so, then in the case of the final moment of sound or light, as well as at the time of nirvāṇa, the final six sense bases would lack a subsequent moment; consequently, they would be devoid of duration and change. This would mean that the definition you have established for conditioned phenomena is not universally applicable.
This does not state that "abiding" (sthiti) is a characteristic of the conditioned.
What is its meaning? It refers to the "alteration of abiding" (sthity-anyathātva).

Therefore, wherever there is duration (*sthiti*), there must also be change (*anyathātva*); by this, the definition of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is established without the fault of being non-pervasive.

Now, as for the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) briefly indicated by the Blessed One in this sūtra, they are: that conditioned phenomena, having previously been non-existent, now exist; having existed, they return to non-existence; and they abide in continuity (*prabandha*).
Since these [states] are already distinct when viewed in their temporal sequence, what need is there for separate entities such as "arising" and so forth within this context?
How can that which is characterized (lakṣya) be established as the characteristic itself (lakṣaṇa)?
And how is it that the marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa) are not distinct from the Great Being himself?

The characteristics of horns, humps, dewlaps, hooves, and tails are not distinct from the cow; likewise, the characteristics of solidity and so forth are not distinct from earth and so forth; and when one sees something rising in the distance and knows it to have the characteristic of smoke, that characteristic is not distinct from the substance of smoke itself.
This principle regarding the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) should likewise be understood as follows:

although one may comprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of conditioned phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), as long as one has not yet comprehended the distinctions of their prior non-existence, subsequent non-existence, and continuity, one still does not know that their essence is conditioned. Therefore, that intrinsic nature itself is not the characteristic of being conditioned.
However, there is no real entity such as "arising" that exists apart from that nature [of conditioned phenomena].
If there were an entity such as arising that existed apart from the intrinsic nature of conditioned things like form and so forth, what would be illogical about that?
"One phenomenon (dharma) at one time should simultaneously undergo arising, abiding, decay, change, destruction, and cessation, since you admit they are co-existent.
This objection is not valid, because their functional times differ; that is to say, the activity of "arising" occurs in the future, for what has already arisen in the present does not arise again.

When all phenomena have arisen and are currently present, the functions of the three characteristics—abiding and so forth—only then arise; they do not exist at the time of the function of arising. Therefore, although they coexist, they are not mutually contradictory.

Furthermore, one should first investigate whether the essence of future phenomena exists or does not exist; only then can it be established whether arising has utility or lack of utility in that state.
Even if one were to grant that arising possesses an activity within the future, how could it still be considered "future"?
One should explain the characteristics of the future.
When a phenomenon is in the present, its activity of arising has already ceased; how, then, can it be established as being present?
One should explain the characteristics of the present.

Furthermore, since the three functions—abiding and so forth—are simultaneous and present, a single dharma-essence within a single moment would simultaneously possess stability, decay, and destruction.

If at the very time the characteristic of abiding causes this dharma to abide, the characteristics of change and destruction simultaneously cause it to decay and perish, then at that moment, should this dharma be called "abiding," "changing," or "perishing"?
Those who claim that the functions of abiding and so forth occur at different times contradict the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).
If one were to say: "I define a single moment as the point when all the characteristics and functions of a single dharma reach their ultimate completion."

You should now explain: for what reason do the characteristic of duration and the other two arise simultaneously, yet duration alone is able to abide in the dharma it sustains without itself being different from or subject to cessation?
If the power of duration is so strong that it acts first, why does it later become weak and, together with the primary dharma, undergo decay and destruction through change and cessation?

If it is argued that the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), having already performed its function, should not perform it again—just as with the characteristic of arising (*jāti*)—then this would be acceptable for arising.
For the function of arising consists in drawing that which is to arise into the present; once it has entered the present, it should not be drawn in again.
Abiding should not be thus.
As for the function of abiding, it means to stabilize that which abides so that it does not decay or perish, because once something has abided, it can be made to abide eternally.
Therefore, the function of the characteristic of abiding should arise constantly; one cannot analogize it to arising and claim it has no further utility.
Furthermore, what obstacle hinders the function of abiding such that it exists for a moment and then ceases?
If you claim that "alteration" (*anyathātva*) and "destruction" (*vināśa*) act as obstacles, then the power of alteration and destruction must be stronger; why, then, do they not act first?

Furthermore, if [the dharma] abides through the function of duration (*sthiti*), then since the dharma itself would naturally not abide due to the distinct characteristics of change (*jarā*) and cessation (*anityatā*), where and in what manner could these two characteristics of change and cessation exercise their functions?
Moreover, what purpose would there be for these two functions?
Due to the sustaining power of duration (*sthiti*), phenomena, once arisen, do not perish for a brief interval.

Once the function of duration has ceased, the phenomenon necessarily fails to persist and perishes spontaneously; therefore, the functions of change (*jarā*) and cessation (*anityatā*) have no further role to play.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the state of a single dharma having arisen but not yet perished is called "abiding," and its state of having abided and then perishing is called "cessation.
While this may be logically plausible for a single dharma,
it is logically untenable to apply such distinctions of progression and regression to [the concept of] difference within that same single dharma.
Why is this so? "Difference" refers to the transformation of intrinsic nature and characteristics over time; it cannot be said that this very same phenomenon is different from itself.
Therefore, a verse is spoken:
If it were identical to the preceding [moment], difference would not be established; if it were different from the preceding, it would not be a single dharma.
Therefore, to posit difference within a single dharma ultimately fails to be established.

Although other schools claim that the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) can only cause a dharma subject to cessation to cease when it encounters the conditions for cessation, [this is not tenable].
Furthermore, what he has said should be like this statement:
"When taking a purgative, a deity comes to cause one to purge.

Thus, when the causes and conditions for cessation are extinguished, that which is to be extinguished is extinguished; why then must one separately maintain the existence of a "characteristic of cessation"?

Furthermore, since it is accepted that mind and mental factors perish moment by moment, they do not require any further causes or conditions for their destruction; thus, the functions of perishing and abiding must be simultaneous.

It would therefore be contrary to reason for a single phenomenon at one time to both abide and perish. Consequently, the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are explained in terms of the continuum (*saṃtāna*); this does not contradict correct reasoning and is well in accord with the sūtras.
If birth arises in the future to produce the dharmas that are to be produced, why do all future dharmas not arise simultaneously?
The verse says:
Birth can produce that which is to be produced, But not apart from the convergence of causes and conditions.
The treatise says:

It is not that the power of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) alone can produce what is to be produced apart from the conjunction of other causes and conditions; therefore, all future phenomena do not arise simultaneously.
If that is so, we see only that causes and conditions possess the capacity for production, and there is no separate characteristic of production.
When causes and conditions conjoin, all phenomena arise; when they do not, they do not arise. What need is there for a characteristic of production?
Therefore, one knows that [phenomena] arise solely through the power of causes and conditions.
How could you possibly know all existing phenomena?
Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profound and subtle, it is extremely difficult to know; thus, although they possess substantiality, it cannot be known.

If the characteristic of arising did not exist, there would be no cognition of "arising"; furthermore, the use of the genitive case (the sixth turning) would be untenable, as in "the arising of form" or "the arising of sensation," just as one should not say "the form of form."
Just as one refutes [the existence of] arising, so too should one refute everything up to cessation, according to what is appropriate for each case.
If that were so, then in order to establish the cognition of emptiness and selflessness, one would have to postulate a nature of emptiness and selflessness external to phenomena.

In order to produce cognitions of oneness, duality, largeness, smallness, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, this, that, existence, and so forth, one would have to maintain—just as the non-Buddhists do—that there exist external entities with distinct natures such as number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, thisness, thatness, and existence.
Furthermore, in order to establish the use of the sixth case (genitive), one must maintain that there exists a distinct nature of a collection of matter (*rūpa-samudāya*).
Likewise, as when it is said "the intrinsic nature of matter" (*rūpasya svabhāvaḥ*), how could this use of the sixth case be established?

Therefore, birth and so forth are merely conventional designations; they possess no separate, substantial reality. "Birth" is a provisional designation established to indicate that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which previously did not exist, now come into being.

Since such characteristics of birth—which were previously non-existent but now exist—occur in numerous varieties across phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, the sixth case (the genitive) is employed—such as saying "the birth of form" or "the birth of sensation"—to distinguish them from others. This is intended to make it known to others that this particular birth pertains only to form and not to sensation or anything else.
Other examples are likewise so.
Just as it is said in the world that there is the fragrance of sandalwood or the substance of a pebble, this case should also be understood in the same way.
One should know that the same applies accordingly to abiding and the other [characteristics].
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were to arise while being devoid of the characteristic of arising, why would unconditioned space (*ākāśa*) and so forth not also arise?

The designation "arising" for conditioned phenomena is based on their existence after having previously been non-existent; since the essence of the unconditioned is eternally present, how can it be said to arise?
Furthermore, just as it is not said that everything exists by its very nature (*dharmatā*), so too one must admit that not all phenomena (*dharma*) are capable of arising.

Moreover, although conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) equally possess the characteristic of arising, it is admitted that causes and conditions may either have efficacy or lack efficacy with respect to those conditioned phenomena.

Thus, one must admit that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are alike in their characteristic of non-arising; yet, with respect to those two types of phenomena, causal conditions possess a generative function in relation to the former, while they lack a generative function in relation to the latter.
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the characteristics such as arising (jāti) exist as distinct, substantial entities;
this principle should be established.
Why is this so? For how can one abandon one's own tenet simply because there are many who raise objections?
One does not refrain from sowing barley for fear of deer, nor does one abstain from eating fine dumplings because of the fear that flies will swarm them.
Therefore, regarding objections and difficulties, one should diligently provide thorough explanations; regarding the tenets of one's own school, one should practice in accordance with them.
Having thus explained the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*),
what is the meaning of the categories such as "name-groups" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth?
The verse says:
"Name-bodies and so forth" refers to the collective designations for concepts, phrases, and syllables.
The commentary states:
"And so forth" includes the inclusion of phrase-bodies and word-bodies.
It should be understood that herein, "name" (nāma) refers to the formation of a conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), such as the conceptualizations of form, sound, odor, taste, and so forth.
"Phrase" (pada) refers to a sentence (*vākya*), which brings a meaning to completion, such as the sentences beginning with "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
That which can distinguish the differences in the application of function, qualities, time, and association is called a *pada* (phrase).
A *vyañjana* (syllable) refers to a letter, such as the letters *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth.
Is it not the case that these syllables are also names for the components of writing?

It is not for the purpose of manifesting the components of writing that the various syllables were created; rather, it is for the purpose of manifesting the various syllables that the components of writing were created.

How else could understanding be attained even without hearing them explained? Therefore, the components of writing were created [for this purpose], and thus the various syllables are not names for the components of writing.
What is meant by "the body of names and so forth"? It refers to the collective designation of perception and the other [aggregates].
The term "collective designation" (saṃketa) carries the sense of a composite whole, because the element of *ucchada* (covering/concealment) is taught within the context of this composite meaning.
In this context, "name-body" (nāmakāya) refers to such things as visible form, sound, and fragrance.
"Phrase-body" (padakāya) refers to such [teachings] as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," "all dharmas are without self," and "nirvana is tranquility."
Regarding "phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*), these refer to [consonants] such as *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*.
Since these three are verbal by nature and have sound as their substance, they are subsumed under the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*).
How, then, can they be said to be formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?
These three do not have speech as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Speech is sound; yet sound alone does not cause the meaning to be understood.
How, then, does it cause understanding?
It is said that speech gives rise to names (*nāman*), and names are able to manifest the meaning; thus, they are able to cause understanding.
Not every sound is designated as "speech"; rather, it is only those sounds by means of which meaning can be understood that are designated as speech.
What kind of sound allows meaning to be understood?

This refers to that which speakers have collectively established as a definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*) among various meanings; for example, in ancient times, the single sound "go" was collectively established as a definitive means of expression for nine different meanings.
Therefore, a verse says:
Direction, animal, earth, light, speech, Vajra, eye, water, and heaven—
Regarding these nine meanings, The wise establish the sound "go."

Those who maintain that names are able to manifest meanings must also necessarily admit such a meaning as "name," namely, that which is collectively established as the definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*).

If the meaning of this sentence is manifested by a name, then the function of manifestation is already accomplished by the sound alone; why then needlessly postulate the existence of a separate, substantial name?
Furthermore, it is not yet understood how this name is produced by speech: is it manifested by speech, or is it generated by speech?
If it were generated by speech, then since the nature of speech is sound, all sounds should be able to generate names.
If it is argued that there is a distinction between the name (*nāman*) and the sound (*śabda*), this alone is sufficient to clarify the meaning; why then wait for a separate name?
If [the name] is manifested by speech, then because speech is of the nature of sound, all sounds should be able to manifest names.
If it is argued that the sound itself possesses distinctions that manifest the name, and that this alone is sufficient to manifest the meaning, why then wait for a separate name?
Furthermore, since successive moments of sound cannot coalesce, and no single entity arises part by part, how could the production of a name be brought about by speech?
How does it depend upon the past moments of informative action (*vijñapti*) for the final moment of informative action to be able to produce the non-informative (*avijñapti*)? If that were so,
then since a name (*nāman*) is produced by sound at the final stage, one should be able to understand the meaning merely by hearing the final sound.
If one holds this position—
that speech produces phonemes (*vyañjana*), phonemes in turn produce names (*nāman*), and names then manifest the meaning (*artha*)—
the fault and difficulty in this case should be stated as before, because multiple moments of phonemes cannot be accumulated.
If it is argued that speech reveals the name, this should be treated as an analogy to [the case of] production.
Furthermore, apart from the phonemes, no wise person, even when applying their mind to investigate, can discern its specific characteristic.
Moreover, whether speech reveals or produces the phonemes, by analogy with the case of names, both positions are illogical.

Furthermore, if one holds the view that names arise simultaneously with their referents— just as birth and so forth do— then it would be impossible for a name existing in the present to denote an object belonging to the past or the future.

Moreover, since parents and others establish names for their children and so on according to their own wishes, how can it be said that names arise simultaneously with their referents, like birth and other such phenomena?
Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would lack names, because they lack the sense of arising; yet this is not acceptable.
However, when the Blessed One spoke in verse regarding that which arises based on names (*nāman*) and phonemes (*vyañjana*), he was establishing a conventional measure for all meanings.
Sound is itself the name (*nāman*); the particular arrangement of these names constitutes a verse (*gāthā*).
For this reason, it is said that a verse depends upon names.

This verse is merely a specific arrangement of names; to maintain that it exists as a substantial entity (*dravya*) is contrary to correct reasoning, just as in the case of a forest, a procession, or the succession of moments of mind.
Alternatively, one should maintain that there exists a distinct textual substance (*vyañjana-rūpa*), which, when collected as a whole, constitutes the "bodies" of names and so forth;
to further maintain that there are other such entities would be useless.

The Vaibhāṣikas, however, assert that there are distinct entities constituting the bodies of names and so forth, which are subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is real and not provisional. Why is this?
Because it is not the case that all phenomena can be fully comprehended through conceptual investigation.
To what realm are these name-bodies and so forth bound?
Are they included within the category of sentient beings or not?
Are they born of maturation (*vipākaja*), nurtured by food (*aupacayika*), or of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*)?
Are they wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
All of these should be analyzed.
The verse says:
They are comprised within sentient beings of the desire and form realms, and are of the nature of outflow and neutral.
The commentary states:
These "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are exclusively bound to the two realms of desire and form.
Some say that [the *nāmakāya* and so forth] also pertain to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet they cannot be so designated.
Furthermore, since the *nāmakāya* and so forth are comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), they constitute the speaker rather than the meaning expressed.
Furthermore, the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are exclusively outflows (*niṣyanda*), and they are comprised solely within the category of the non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
As has been stated above, the remaining meanings concerning the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that have not yet been explained shall now be briefly elucidated.
The verse says:
Sabhāgatā is likewise, as well as the formless realms and maturation;
acquisition and the characteristics apply to all three types, while non-acquisition and meditative absorption are exclusively outflowing.
The Commentary states:

The phrase "likewise" is used to show that *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity), like the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, pertains to the desire and form realms, to sentient beings, and is of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), non-obscured, and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The inclusion of the term "and formless" (ārūpya) indicates that it is not limited to the desire and form realms alone.
The inclusion of the term "and maturation" (vipāka) indicates that it is not limited to being merely a result of outflow (niṣyanda).
Thus, as for its realm, it pervades all three; as for its category, it pervades two meanings.

Acquisition (*prāpti*) and its various categories are all common to the three types [of cause], namely: momentary (*kṣaṇika*), outflowing (*naiṣyandika*), and maturation (*vipākaja*). Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are exclusively outflowing.
The word "exclusively" is used to clarify that they are not of the nature of maturation and so forth.
Thus have been explained these meanings not previously stated.
As for the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they have already been analyzed as before.
For what reason are acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth not said to be comprised exclusively within the category of sentient beings?
Since it has already been stated that [characteristics] are constituted by sentient beings and so forth,
for what reason are they not said to pervade both the category of sentient beings and the category of non-sentient beings?
Because it has already been stated that they accompany all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Other matters not yet explained should be understood accordingly.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Five.

Chapter Two on the Analysis of the Faculties, Part Four. Thus has the treatment of the dissociated formations been explained.

Preface: When a producing characteristic (janaka-lakṣaṇa) produces that which is produced (janya), it does not do so apart from the conjunction of other causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī). Among these, what phenomena are designated as causes and conditions?
Briefly, there are six kinds of causes; what are the six?
The verse says:
The efficient cause, the co-existent, the homogeneous, the associated, the pervasive,
and the ripening— these six alone are accepted as causes.

The treatise states: There are six kinds of causes: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); second, the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); third, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); fourth, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*); fifth, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*); and sixth, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*). The masters of the Abhidharma maintain that there are only these six kinds of causes.
Furthermore, what is the definition of the first cause, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The verse says:
"With the exception of itself, all else is the efficient cause."
The treatise says:

All conditioned phenomena, with the exception of their own self-nature, serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for all other phenomena, because they abide without obstruction at the time of those phenomena's arising.

Although other types of causes can also function as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the efficient cause has no further distinct name, just as the term "form-sphere" (*rūpāyatana*) serves as both a general and a specific designation.
Is it not the case that when one does not yet know that the outflows (*āsrava*) are about to arise, those outflows do not arise once they are known?
Thus, knowledge acts as an obstacle to the arising of the outflows, just as sunlight can obstruct the sight of the stars.
How is it that conditioned phenomena, excluding their own self-nature, take all dharmas as their efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
It should be understood that when this [dharma] arises, they all abide without obstruction; therefore, they are its efficient causes.
If, in this life, that which is capable of acting as an obstacle does not so act, it may be established as a cause.
For example, when the people of a country find that their sovereign does not inflict harm upon them, they all say:
"It is because of our sovereign that we have attained peace and happiness."
If something has no obstructive function regarding the arising of that [result] in this [cause], even if it does not act as an obstruction, how could it be considered a cause?
For example, nirvāṇa and non-arising dharmas have no capacity to obstruct the arising of any conditioned phenomena whatsoever;

likewise, the personal continuum of beings in the hells and so forth has no capacity to obstruct the arising of the aggregates in the formless realm. Although they lack an obstructive function, they nevertheless serve as causes, just as a powerless king may still be described in the same manner as previously stated.
