This is a general explanation of all *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes); it is stated in terms of their predominant function, yet they are not devoid of the power to produce.

For example, the eye and visible forms [act as causes] for visual consciousness and so forth; food and drink [act as causes] for the body; and seeds and so forth [act as causes] for sprouts and so forth.
Someone raises this objection:
"If all phenomena are capable of acting as causes because they abide without obstruction, for what reason do all phenomena not arise simultaneously?
And when one person commits an act of killing, for what reason do all beings not likewise incur the karma of killing, just like the killer?"
This objection is not valid.
It is simply because there is no obstruction that all phenomena are admitted to be acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), not because they possess a direct productive power over arising.
Other masters say:
All efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) possess the power of efficacy toward the arising of their effects.
Now, in the case of nirvāṇa and so forth with respect to the arising of visual consciousness, how can they be said to possess the power of efficacy?

The mental consciousness arises taking that as its object, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome; because of this mental consciousness, the visual consciousness subsequently arises in succession, due to their being successive causes.

Just as that nirvana possesses the capacity to act as a productive cause for the arising of visual consciousness, so too should it be understood, by this same principle, that other phenomena possess the power to produce [their effects] through successive stages.
Thus, the characteristics of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) have been explained.
What are the characteristics of the second [cause], the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)?
The verse says:
Coexistent factors are mutual fruits, as in the case of the primary elements and their characteristics,
or as the mind and its concomitants follow one another.
The treatise says:
If phenomena are mutually the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) of one another, those phenomena are also mutually the *sahabhū-hetu* (co-existent cause) of one another.
What is their characteristic?

Just as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually co-existent causes for one another, so too are the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya*), as well as the mind (*citta*) and its concomitants (*cittānuparivartin*), mutually causes for one another.
Thus, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), by virtue of mutual causality, universally encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as appropriate.

A primary phenomenon (*dharma*) and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) do not stand in a relationship of mutual fruit; nevertheless, the phenomenon and the secondary characteristics act as co-existent causes for one another, whereas the secondary characteristics do not [act as such] for the phenomenon.
In this regard, it should be analyzed:
what are called the "dharmas that follow the mind"?
The verse says:
The two types of discipline associated with mental factors, as well as their characteristics and those of the mind itself—
these are the dharmas that follow the mind.
The commentary says:

All factors associated with the mind (*cittasamprayuktadharma*), the two types of restraint—meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—as well as the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) of those factors and the mind itself: all these are called factors that follow the mind (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*).
How is it that these dharmas are said to "conform to the mind"?
The verse says:
By reason of time, fruit, wholesomeness, and so forth.
The Treatise says:
Briefly stated, because they share the same time, fruit, and so forth, as well as being wholesome and so on, these dharmas are said to be "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).
First, regarding the point of "time": this means that these [dharmas] arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind, and belong to the same temporal period (*adhvan*).
Regarding "by way of fruit and so forth," this means that it shares with the mind a single fruit, a single maturation (*vipāka*), and a single outflow (*niṣyanda*).
One should understand that within this context, the first "single" in each pair indicates simultaneity, while the second "single" indicates commonality; thus, their meanings differ.
Regarding "by virtue of being wholesome and so forth," this means that these [mental factors] share the same nature as the mind—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
For these ten reasons, they are called "concomitants of the mind" (*cittānuvartin*).

Among these, even the very minimum of the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) acts as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for fifty-eight factors. These fifty-eight factors consist of: the ten universal ground-factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), their forty primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*), and the eight primary and secondary characteristics (*mūla-anulakṣaṇa*) of the mind itself. Thus, they are termed the fifty-eight factors.
Among the fifty-eight [factors], excluding the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of mind, the remaining fifty-four serve as the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) for the mind.

Some say: there are only fourteen factors that serve as causes for the mind, namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*) together with the primary characteristics (*mūlalakṣaṇa*) of the mind itself.
This explanation is not correct. Why is that?
Because it contradicts what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
As that treatise states:

"There may be a *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering) that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not itself the cause of the view of a self-identity; this refers to all other defiled *duḥkhasatya*, excluding the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors, as well as their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence."

There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause and also serves as the cause for the view of a self-identity; this refers to the aforementioned excluded factors.
Other masters do not recite the phrase "and those associated factors."
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:

That text must necessarily be recited in this way, or one should understand that the statement is incomplete according to its underlying meaning; for those things which function as causes by virtue of being simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) are necessarily co-existent.

There are cases where things coexist but do not function as causes by virtue of being "coexistent causes" (*sahabhū-hetu*); that is, the various secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) each [function] with respect to their primary dharmas, and these secondary characteristics themselves function mutually with respect to one another.
The secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) that follow the mind are related to the mind; these secondary characteristics are mutually related to one another.
All co-arisen obstructive derived matter (upādāyarūpa) is mutually related, as is a small portion of co-arisen non-obstructive derived matter.

All simultaneously arising derived matter and primary elements are mutually related to one another; all simultaneously arising acquisitions (*prāpti*) and their acquired objects (*prāpya*) are likewise mutually related.

Although such dharmas are termed "coexistent" (*sahabhū*), they do not constitute causes by virtue of being coexistent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), because they do not share a single fruit, a single maturation (*vipāka*), or a single outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The acquisition (*prāpti*) and that which is acquired (*prāpya*) do not necessarily function simultaneously, for they may arise before, after, or together.

While all such principles may be plausible, in the world-renowned processes of cause and effect—such as seeds and sprouts—it is never observed that cause and effect are simultaneous; therefore, this must now be explained.
How can there be the principle of cause and effect within a collection of phenomena that arise simultaneously?
Is it not clearly observed that the flame of a lamp and its light, or a sprout and its shadow, are simultaneous yet function as cause and effect?
This should be analyzed in detail:
Is it that the lamp-flame itself is the cause of the light?
Or is it that the flame and the light arise simultaneously through the convergence of prior causes and conditions, while other objects obstruct the light so that shadows appear?
How can it be said that this reflection has the sprout as its cause?
Such reasoning is untenable, because [the reflection] exists or does not exist in accordance with [the sprout].

Those skilled in the science of logic (hetuvidyā) explain the characteristics of cause and effect as follows: if the existence or non-existence of one thing follows the existence or non-existence of another, then the former is definitively the cause and the latter is definitively the effect.
Among co-existent dharmas, if one exists, all exist; if one is absent, all are absent. Thus, the principle of cause and effect is established.
While the principle of simultaneous arising as cause and effect may indeed be acceptable, how can it be said that they are mutually cause and effect?
This is not contradictory, precisely because of what was stated previously. If that is so,
then just as it was previously stated that derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) is mutually inseparable and thus should be mutual causes for one another,

so too derived matter and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), as well as mental concomitants such as the mental factors of attention (*manasikāra*) and the like, which are inseparable from the mind, should all be mutual causes for one another.
If it is argued that the causal relationship between simultaneously existing phenomena is established in the same way that three staffs stand by supporting one another, this must be examined:
do these three staffs stand through the power of mutual dependence arising simultaneously?
Is it because the combined force of causes and conditions from previous lives causes those three sticks to arise and remain together?

Furthermore, within that [system], are there other things such as ropes, hooks, or the earth that connect and sustain them so they remain? In this case as well, there are other similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth; therefore, the meaning of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established.
Thus has the characteristic of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) been explained.
What is the characteristic of the third [cause], the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
The verse says:
The similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) is that which is similar [to its effect], belonging to its own category (nikāya) and level (bhūmi), and produced prior [to it].
The Path (mārga) functions as a mutual cause across the nine levels, serving only as an equal or superior fruit.
The same applies to those produced through application (prayoga), such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (śruta-mayī and cintā-mayī).
The treatise says:

As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it means that similar dharmas serve as homogeneous causes for similar dharmas. That is to say, the five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) serve as homogeneous causes for one another; one should know that the same applies to defiled and defiled [aggregates], and neutral and neutral [aggregates].
Other masters say:
"The five pure-neutral aggregates are the results of form, while four are not the causes of form.
Other masters say:
The five [aggregates] are the four fruits, while form is not the cause of the four.
Other masters say:
form and the four aggregates, when viewed in relation to one another, do not serve as causes for each other.
Furthermore, within a single continuum, the *kalala* stage can serve as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all ten stages.

Each of the nine subsequent stages, such as the *arbuda*, serves as a cause for the remaining stages, excluding its own preceding stage. However, when considered in relation to the ten homogeneous stages of other continua, each of these stages serves as a cause for all ten stages.
Following this same principle, external things such as wheat and rice should be extensively analyzed within their own respective categories.
If one does not admit that matter (*rūpa*) serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for matter, that position would contradict what is stated in the original treatise.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"Past primary elements (mahābhūta) and future primary elements serve as causes through [the relations of] predominance (adhipati), etc.
Are all similar factors to be considered capable of being called homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) with respect to similar factors?

Not so. Why? Because [a dharma] of its own category and its own stage acts as a cause only for that which belongs to its own category and its own stage; therefore, it is said to be "of its own category and its own stage."
"Category" (*pakṣa*) refers to the five categories, namely: those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through cultivation.
"Level" (*bhūmi*) refers to the nine levels, namely: the desire realm as one, and the eight consisting of the dhyānas and the formless attainments.

Among these, phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) serve as homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) only for those abandoned through the vision of suffering, and not for others; likewise, up to and including those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), they serve as homogeneous causes only for phenomena abandoned through cultivation, and not for others.

Among these, each individual level acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for its own corresponding realm: the levels of the desire realm act as homogeneous causes for the desire realm; the first dhyāna level acts as a homogeneous cause for the first dhyāna; and so on, up to the Peak of Existence acting as a homogeneous cause for the Peak of Existence.
When compared across different levels, there is in all cases no causal relationship.
Furthermore, this does not apply to all cases.

Why? It means that among previously arisen dharmas, only those previously arisen dharmas that are similar to subsequent dharmas—whether those subsequent dharmas have already arisen or have not yet arisen—act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
How is this known to be so?
Because it is stated in the *Mūla-śāstra*.
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:
What is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
It refers to previously arisen wholesome roots that serve as the homogeneous cause for subsequently arisen wholesome roots of their own realm, as well as for the factors associated with them.

In this manner, the past [should be explained] in relation to the other two time periods, and the past and present in relation to the future, and so forth; all such cases should be explained in detail.
However, that very treatise poses this question:
"If a dharma is a cause for another dharma, is there ever a time when this dharma is not a cause for that one?
It then answers:
Regarding the statement "there is no time when it is not a cause," this is spoken cryptically based on the three causes—simultaneous, associated, and retributive—and therefore there is no fault.

Some maintain that a dharma in the state of "presently arising" in the future is necessarily able to serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for that [dharma]; thus, that text cryptically provides the answer "there is no time when it is not a cause" by relying on this final stage.
That [explanation] offered in response to the objection is not a sound one,
because a future dharma is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) prior to its stage of actual arising, but only becomes so afterwards.
Furthermore, if that were the case, he would further ask:
"If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for another phenomenon, is there ever a time when this phenomenon is not the equal-and-immediate condition for that one?
He replied: "When this phenomenon has not yet reached the state of having already arisen."

If it were as that [other] explanation suggests, one should likewise have answered, "There is no time when it is not a condition. Why, then, did he answer, "When this dharma has not yet arrived or has already perished"?
Yet he further explains that this is for the purpose of demonstrating two perspectives: as stated in that case, so it should be here;
as stated here, so it should be there.
What merit is gained by composing in such a manner?
It serves only to reveal that the author of the treatise is not skilled in composition.
Therefore, one should know that the previous explanation is the correct one.
If that is so, why does the *Prakaraṇapāda* state:

"There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not the cause of the view of a self-identity—namely, all other defiled truths of suffering, excluding the future view of a self-identity and the truths of suffering associated with it"?

There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause and also serves as the cause for the view of a self-identity; this refers to the aforementioned excluded factors.
That text should have stated: "excluding the truth of suffering associated with the future view of a self-identity."
Even if it were as that [other school] says, one should know by the meaning that it is not so.
Furthermore, how does this accord with the *Prajñaptipāda-śāstra*?
That treatise states that all phenomena are determined by four factors: namely, cause, fruit, support (*āśraya*), and object (*ālambana*).

One should understand that in that text, "causes" refer to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
"Fruits" refer to the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*).
The basis refers to the six faculties, such as the eye;
the objects refer to the six spheres, such as form.
If this is so, then homogeneous causes would arise where none previously existed; however, since this is accepted, there is no fault.
The state [of the cause] is not its substance; because it is a fruit of the state resulting from the combined activity [of causes], it is not a fruit of the substance.
If the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) exists in the future, just as the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) does, what fault would there be?
If they existed in the future, the *Mūla-śāstra* should have stated so.
Since the *Mūla-śāstra* speaks only of similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) that can take up and yield results, there is no error.

Such a principle does not exist; for it is logically impossible for a similar cause to project a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) while existing in the future, because there would be no sequence of before and after.
A dharma that has already arisen cannot be the outflow (niṣyanda) of one that has not yet arisen, just as past dharmas are not the fruit of present ones;
for there would otherwise be the fallacy that the effect precedes the cause. Therefore, in the future, there is no similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu).
If that were so, the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) would not exist in the future, because the fruit of maturation cannot precede or be simultaneous with its cause.
Since dharmas in the future lack temporal priority and posteriority, there is no such fault, for they are not analogous [to present or past dharmas].

This means that the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is similar to its effect; if there were no temporal sequence, they would have to be mutual causes for one another. Since they would then be mutual causes, they would also have to be mutual effects, which contradicts logical principle.

The non-heterogeneous cause (avipāka-hetu) does not resemble its fruit; thus, although it is devoid of temporal sequence, there is no such fault. Therefore, while the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) is established by way of its state (*avasthā*) and is non-existent in the future, the heterogeneous cause is established by way of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and is not non-existent in the future.
Regarding the statement that "homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) belong only to their own level," on what basis is this definitively stated?
It is definitively based on the contaminated (sāsrava).

If uncontaminated paths (anāsrava-mārga) were considered, each would mutually serve as a cause for all nine levels—namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the four fundamental dhyānas, and the three fundamental formless attainments; that is, the path-truths (mārga-satya) of these nine levels would all be mutual causes for one another.

Why is this so? Because these [paths] dwell in all stages as mere guests and do not fall within the inclusion of those stages; they do not grasp the stages through craving as their own property. Therefore, although the paths of the nine stages differ in their levels, they serve as causes for one another because they are of the same kind.
However, these can only serve as causes for that which is equal or superior, and not for that which is inferior, because they arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*).

For example, once the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) has arisen, it serves as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the future patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering; this is what is meant by "equal."

Furthermore, this very patience (*kṣānti*) can also serve as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for subsequent states, from the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*);

thus it is called "superior. To speak more extensively: even the already-arisen knowledge of non-arising serves only as a homogeneous cause for its own equal class, as there is nothing superior to it.

Furthermore, the various paths that have already arisen—the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)—act as similar causes (*sabhāgahetu*) for three, two, and one [subsequent paths] respectively, according to their order.
Moreover, within this context, the paths of those with dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*) act as similar causes for both those with dull and those with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

If a path of sharp faculties is the cause only for paths of sharp faculties—such as the paths of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), and those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*)—then they serve as similar causes (*sabhāgahetu*) for six, four, and two [subsequent paths] respectively.

The paths of those who practice according to the Dharma (dharmānusārin), those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and those liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) serve as homogeneous causes for three, two, and one [subsequent stages] respectively, according to their sequence.
Furthermore, the paths of all higher stages serve as causes for those of lower stages.
What is meant by "equal or superior"?
It is due to the increase of causes and due to the faculties (*indriya*).
That is to say, in the stages of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, from the lowest-of-the-low grade onwards, the causes progressively increase in each subsequent stage.

Although within a single continuum it is impossible for the two paths—those of "following by faith" (śraddhānusārin) and "following by dharma" (dharmānusārin)—to arise simultaneously, that which has already arisen serves as the cause for what is yet to come.
Is it the case that only the noble path (āryamārga) acts as a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) solely for that which is equal or superior?
Not so. Why is this? Other worldly dharmas produced through preparatory effort (*prayoga*) likewise serve as causes for those that are equal or superior, but not for those that are inferior.
What is the nature of the dharmas produced through application (*prayoga*)?
It refers to those produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*), those produced by reflection (*cintāmaya*), and so forth.
The phrase "and so forth" includes [those produced by cultivation].

Regarding "accomplished through cultivation" and so forth: the merits produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation are termed "accomplished by those. Because they arise from preparatory application (*prayoga*), they serve as causes only for that which is equal or superior, and not for that which is inferior.

Just as with those factors bound to the desire realm, dharmas produced through hearing can serve as homogeneous causes for those produced through hearing and reflection within their own realm, but they cannot serve as causes for those produced through cultivation, because such dharmas do not exist in the desire realm.

Dharmas produced through reflection (*cintā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those produced through reflection, but not for those produced through hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

If dharmas produced through hearing belonging to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) can serve as homogeneous causes for those produced through hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) within their own realm, they do not serve as causes for those produced through reflection, because such [dharmas] do not exist in the form realm.

Dharmas produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior.

Dharmas produced by cultivation belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) serve as homogeneous causes only for dharmas produced by cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced by hearing or reflection (*cintā-maya*), because those do not exist [in the formless realm] and because they are inferior.

These dharmas further comprise nine grades. If the lowest-of-the-low grade serves as the cause for all nine grades, the middle-of-the-low serves as the cause for eight, and so on, until the highest-of-the-high serves only as the cause for the highest-of-the-high, because the preceding inferior grades are excluded.
The nine grades of wholesome dharmas acquired at birth serve as mutual causes for one another; the defiled dharmas are likewise.

There are four types of non-obscured neutral dharmas: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those of deportment (*airyāpathika*), those of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and those associated with the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika*). According to their respective order, they can serve as causes for four, three, two, and one [subsequent category] respectively.

Furthermore, the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the desire realm has the four dhyānas as its fruits; it is not the case that a fruit of a higher dhyāna can have a fruit of a lower dhyāna as its cause. Nor is a lower, inferior fruit obtained through the cause of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), just as one must exert great labor to plant rice, wheat, and the like.
Do not exert effort only to find no gain.
For this reason, it is asked:
Is there any case where already-arisen untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not serve as the cause for untainted dharmas that have not yet arisen?

Yes. For example, the category of the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma of suffering) that has already arisen [is not the cause] for the category of the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma of suffering) that has not yet arisen; furthermore, all superior [factors] are not the causes for all inferior ones.
Is there perhaps any instance where various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, previously determined to be acquired within a single continuum, are not the causes for those arising later?

There is [such a case]: namely, when the category of the subsequent *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering) has already arisen after the category of the future *duḥkhe-dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma regarding suffering). This is because an effect can never exist prior to its cause, or because homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) do not exist in the future.
Is there any case where previously arisen uncontaminated dharmas are not the cause of subsequently arisen uncontaminated dharmas? Yes;

for example, when a superior previously arisen uncontaminated dharma is not the cause of an inferior subsequently arisen uncontaminated dharma, such as when one regresses from a higher fruit to a lower fruit that manifests before one.

Furthermore, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the previously arisen knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the subsequent acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmakṣānti*), because the latter is inferior.
Thus has the characteristic of the homogeneous cause been explained.
What is the characteristic of the fourth, the associated cause?
The verse says:
The associated cause is determined by Mind and mental factors sharing the same basis.
The treatise says:
Only mind and mental factors are associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
If that were so, then those with distinct objects (*ālambana*) and aspects (*ākāra*) would also have to be mutual associated causes for one another.
This is not so; for it can only be said that they are associated when they share the same object (*ālambana*) and mode of activity (*ākāra*).
If that were the case, then those things that share the same object and mode of activity at different times would also have to be called associated causes (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*).
It is not so; for they must necessarily share the same object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), and time (*kāla*) in order to be associated (*saṃprayukta*).

If that were the case, one would have to say that those belonging to different bodies could also be associated when their objects, aspects, and times coincide—as in the instance where a multitude of people collectively observe the new moon and so forth. To preclude such numerous objections with a single statement, it is therefore said that they must have a "common basis" (*samāśraya*).
This means that mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) must necessarily share the same basis (*āśraya*) in order to function as mutual *saṃprayuktaka-hetu* (associated causes).

Here, the term "same" indicates that the support is one and the same. That is to say, if a visual consciousness takes this particular momentary eye-faculty as its support, the associated sensations (*vedanā*) and so forth likewise take this very eye-faculty as their support; it should be understood that the same applies up to the mental consciousness and its associated factors sharing the same support in the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The essence of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) is identical to that of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). What, then, is the distinction between the meanings of these two causes?
The co-existent cause is established by virtue of being mutual fruits of one another, like traveling companions who rely on each other while traversing a perilous path together.

The associated cause (*samyuktahetu*) is established on the basis of the meaning of mutual correspondence through five kinds of equality; it is just as when traveling companions together undergo and perform activities such as eating, wherein if even one among them is missing, they are no longer in correspondence. Therefore, the sense of being mutual causes is fully established.
Thus, the characteristics of the associated cause have been explained.
What are the characteristics of the fifth, the pervasive cause?
The verse says:
"Universal [causes] refer to those previously arisen universals, Which serve as the cause for defiled states of the same stage.
The Treatise says:
As for the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it refers to previously arisen universal dharmas that act as the universal cause for subsequently arising defiled dharmas of the same stage.
Regarding the universal dharmas (*sarvatraga*), their meaning as universals will be analyzed in detail in the section on latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Because these serve as the common cause for all defiled phenomena, they are established as a distinct category apart from the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Furthermore, because it is also the cause for the defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) of other categories, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of other categories and their attendants (*pārṣada*) also grow and arise through its power.
One might ask: do the various defiled phenomena within the bodies of noble ones (*ārya*) also take this as their universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)?
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr state:
"All defiled dharmas have those abandoned through seeing as their cause.
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* speaks as follows:
What are the factors that have as their cause those things abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
They are all defiled factors (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) and the maturation (*vipāka*) produced by those factors abandoned by insight.
What are the factors that have as their cause the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
This refers to all neutral (*avyākṛta*) conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) phenomena.

There are cases where the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but does not itself serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity. This is explained in detail up to: excluding the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors, as well as their arising, aging, duration, and impermanence; all other defiled truths of suffering [are such cases].
If that is so, how do you reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*? As that treatise asks:
"Is there any phenomenon that is unwholesome and has only unwholesome phenomena as its cause?"

There is; that is to say, when a noble one (ārya) falls back from the state of freedom from desire, the first defiled volition (kliṣṭa-cetanā) that has already arisen is spoken of in this way based on causes that have not yet been abandoned.
Although factors to be abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-dharma) are also such causes, they are omitted from the statement because they have already been abandoned.
Thus has the characteristic of the omnipresent cause been explained.
What is the characteristic of the sixth, the retributive cause?
The verse says:
The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome that is exclusively outflowing (*sāsrava*).
The commentary states:
Only those factors that are unwholesome and those wholesome factors that are outflowing constitute the ripening cause, because they are ripening phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*).
For what reason do neutral states not bring about maturation?
Because they are weak in power, like rotten seeds.
For what reason do untainted states not bring about maturation?
Because they lack the moisture of craving, they are like genuine seeds that have not been watered and nourished.
Furthermore, since they are not bound to the realms of existence, how could they bring about retribution bound to those realms?
Other dharmas possess both [conditions], and therefore they can bring about such retribution, just like genuine seeds that have been moistened by water.
How can the meaning of "maturation cause" (vipāka-hetu) be understood?
Is it called a maturation cause because it is the cause of maturation,
or is it called a maturation cause because the maturation itself is the cause?
If the meaning encompasses both interpretations, what fault is there?
If the cause of maturation were called the "maturation cause," the Holy Teaching should not have stated that the eye is "born of maturation."
If the maturation itself were called the "maturation cause" (vipāka-hetu), then the sacred teachings would not speak of "the maturation of karma.
Both interpretations are valid, as has already been explained previously.
What is the meaning of "vipāka" (ripening)?
The Vaibhāṣika masters explain it as follows:
"Ripening in a different category is the meaning of vipāka," meaning that the ripening cause matures only in a different category.

The co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and others ripen only as similar-type results (*sabhāga-vipāka*), whereas the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) alone encompasses both similar and dissimilar ripening; therefore, it is this [cause] alone that is termed the "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*).
A ripened result cannot be obtained from any other cause, for a result receives the name "ripened" only when it possesses two characteristics:

first, its substance arises through a specific transformation within the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*); second, it has a temporal limit determined by the superior or inferior power of the cause.

The substantial entity that is the fruit produced by the two causes—simultaneous (sahabhū) and associated (samprayukta)—does not arise through the specific transformation of a continuum; for [the fruit] is given at the very moment it is grasped.

Furthermore, it is not the fruit of the three causes—efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—because it arises repeatedly throughout the limits of saṃsāra due to the power of wholesome and unwholesome [karma], and because its timing is without limit, depending on the relative strength or weakness of those causal forces.
Therefore, one should provide the following explanation alone:
"To ripen through transformation" is the meaning of *vipāka* (maturation); it should not be understood merely as "differentiation" to distinguish it from other causes.

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are times when a single aggregate (*skandha*) acts as a maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; that is to say, the acquisition of a dharma (*prāpti*), its subsequent non-disappearance (*anuccheda*), and their arising (*jāti*), etc.

Sometimes two aggregates act as ripening causes (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; that is to say, wholesome or unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, along with their [concomitant] origination and so forth.

Sometimes four aggregates act as ripening causes to collectively produce a single fruit; that is to say, wholesome or unwholesome mental states and mental factors, along with their [concomitant] origination and so forth.

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are times when a single aggregate (*skandha*) acts as a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to the acquisition of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and their arising (*jāti*) and so forth.

Sometimes two aggregates act as retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to wholesome informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) and its arising, etc., in the first dhyāna.

Sometimes four aggregates act as retributive causes to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers to wholesome minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita*), along with their arising, etc.

Sometimes the five aggregates function as a single maturation cause to produce one common fruit; that is to say, the states of mind and mental factors in meditative equipoise, together with their concomitant matter and their [characteristics] such as arising.

In the formless realm, there are times when a single aggregate serves as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to collectively produce a single fruit; this refers, for example, to the acquisition of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and their respective births and so forth.

Sometimes four aggregates function as a collective ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) to produce a single fruit; this refers to all wholesome minds and mental factors, along with their [characteristics] such as arising.

There are also karmas that produce maturation in only one sense-base (*āyatana*); this refers to the production of the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.
If one experiences the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), one necessarily experiences two bases, namely mind and phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
One should know that it is likewise if one experiences the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
If one experiences the sense-base of body (*kāyāyatana*), one necessarily experiences three bases, namely body, contact, and phenomena.
One should know that the same applies to the maturation of form, odor, and taste.
If one matures the sense-base of the eye, one necessarily matures four bases—namely, the eye base, as well as the body, touch, and mental-object bases.
One should know that the same applies to the maturation of the ear, nose, and tongue.
There are karmas capable of producing five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven bases (*āyatana*), because karma may have either few or many fruits.

Just as external seeds produce fruits that are either few or many—those with few fruits being such as rice and wheat, and those with many fruits being such as the lotus, the pomegranate, and the *nyagrodha* tree.

There is karma belonging to one lifetime that has maturation (*vipāka*) across three lifetimes, but there is no karma across three lifetimes that has maturation in a single lifetime; this is because the fruit must not be less than the effort exerted for its cause.

There is karma of a single moment that has maturation over many moments, but there is no karma of many moments that has maturation in a single moment; the reason for this should be understood as explained above.
However, the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) does not coexist with the karma, because the fruit is not experienced at the very moment the karma is performed.
Nor is it immediate, as it is induced by the power of the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) in the subsequent moment.
Furthermore, because a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) must depend upon a continuity (*saṃtati*) in order to produce a fruit of a different category,
these six causes are established as residing in specific time periods. Thus,
the time period in which the causes reside is fixed.
Although the meaning has already been explained, it has not yet been summarized in verse; therefore, it should be further elucidated.
The verse says:
The universal [causes] and the similar-type [causes] belong to two time periods; the other three belong to all three time periods.
The treatise states:
The pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes exist only in the past and present; they do not exist in the future, for the reasoning is as previously explained.
The three causes—associated (*samprayukta*), co-existent (*sahabhū*), and maturation (*vipāka*)—are entirely present throughout all three time periods.

Since the verse does not specify the temporal locus of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it should be understood by implication that it extends across the three time periods as well as the non-temporal (the unconditioned).
Having explained the distinctions between the characteristics of the six causes and their temporal determination,
what are the fruits that correspond to these causes?
The verse says:
"Fruits are conditioned and disjunction; the unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit.
The commentary says:
As stated in the treatise:
"What are resultant phenomena?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as well as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
If that were so, since you admit that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a fruit, it would necessarily have a cause, for it can only be designated as a fruit in relation to its cause.
Furthermore, since you admit that this unconditioned is a cause, it would also necessarily have a fruit, for it can only be designated as a cause in relation to its fruit.
Only conditioned phenomena possess causes and effects;
unconditioned phenomena do not.
Why is this? Because they lack the six causes and lack the five fruits.
For what reason is it not admitted that the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) serve as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*)?
Since an efficient cause is established as that which does not obstruct arising, what function could the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is without arising, possibly perform?
If that is so, what is the fruit?
What is the meaning of "fruit"?
It refers to the fruit of the Path, because it is obtained through the power of the Path.

If that were so, the fruit of the path would consist solely of acquisition (*prāpti*), because the path has efficacy with respect to acquisition, but not with respect to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
This is not the case, because the function of the path differs with respect to acquisition and with respect to analytical cessation.
In what way does it have efficacy regarding the path of attainment?
It means that it is able to produce [the fruit].
In what way does it have efficacy regarding the path of cessation?

This is because it is that which realizes [the cessation]. For this reason, although the Path is not the cause of cessation, one may still say that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is the fruit of the Path.
Since all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) lack a dominant fruit (adhipati-phala), how can they be said to be acting causes (kāraṇa-hetu)?
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are established as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) because they do not act as obstructions to the arising of other phenomena;
however, they possess no fruit, because apart from conditioned phenomena, they lack the functional capacity to either grasp or bestow a fruit.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a cause, because no sūtra states that a cause is unconditioned, whereas there are sūtras stating that causes are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
In which sūtra is this stated?
As it is said in a sutra:
"All causes and conditions that can produce form are impermanent.
How could the various forms produced by impermanent causes and conditions be permanent?"
The detailed explanation continues up to consciousness, which is likewise.
If that were so, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) should also not serve as the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the cognizing consciousness and so forth.

[We reply: It is only because they are said to be able to produce [consciousness] that they can serve as an object-condition. That is to say, the Sūtra states only that those causes and conditions which are able to produce consciousness are all impermanent; it does not state that everything which serves as a condition for consciousness is impermanent. Therefore, the objection is not established.

Is it not also taught that only that which is capable of producing [an effect] is impermanent? Therefore, one does not deny that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes) merely because they do not obstruct [the arising of effects].
For while there are sūtras that state unconditioned phenomena are *ālambana-pratyaya* (object conditions), there is no sūtra that states unconditioned phenomena are *kāraṇa-hetu*.

It should not be established as having the nature of a cause solely by way of non-obstruction; for although there is no sūtra that explicitly states this, nor is there any place where it is prohibited.
Furthermore, since immeasurable sūtras have now been lost, how can one definitively judge that there is no scriptural statement on the matter?
If that is so, what dharma is designated as "disjunction" (visamyoga)?
It is precisely the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) mentioned in the original treatise.
But was it not previously asked:
What is called "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha)?
The answer is: it is dissociation (visamyoga).
Now, we ask: what dharma is designated as dissociation?
The answer is "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Since these two answers thus rely upon one another, they ultimately fail to manifest its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, its intrinsic nature should be revealed by means of a different method.

The intrinsic nature of this dharma is truly existent and beyond words; it is personally realized within by the noble ones alone. It can only be described through conventional means in general terms as being "wholesome" and "permanent," and there exists a distinct substantial entity called cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), also known as disjunction (*visamyoga*).
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"All unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are not substantially real (dravyasat), because they lack the existence of distinct substantial entities like form (rūpa) or feeling (vedanā).
If that is so, for what reason are they called 'space' (ākāśa) and so forth?"
That which is merely characterized by the absence of contact is called space (*ākāśa*); that is to say, when there is no resistance to touch within darkness, one says, "This is space.

When the seeds of the arising of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been produced and are extinguished through the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), such that they do not arise again, this is called cessation through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When, apart from the power of analytical discernment, other [phenomena] do not arise again due to the absence of necessary conditions, this is called "cessation not through discernment" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), such as the remaining aggregates of one who dies prematurely within their own homogeneous life-span (nikāya-sabhāga).
The masters of other schools say:
When the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not arise due to the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When subsequent suffering does not arise because the conditions for the latent dispositions are lacking, rather than through the power of wisdom, it is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This cessation would not be established apart from the power of discernment; therefore, this non-arising is subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Some say:
because phenomena, once arisen, subsequently cease spontaneously, it is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If this is the case, the essence of the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as you conceive it should be impermanent, because it does not exist prior to its cessation.

Would it not follow that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also impermanent, since it exists only after being preceded by analysis and did not exist before? It is not the case that analytical cessation exists only after being preceded by analysis.
How can analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) also be impermanent? Why is this so?
It is not the case that analytical cessation exists first, and only thereafter do unarisen phenomena come to possess non-arising.
What is it that does not arise?
It has existed inherently from the beginning. If there were no discernment (*pravicaya*), phenomena would arise; yet when discernment arises, phenomena never arise again.

This non-arising is due to the efficacy of discernment; that is, while previously there was no obstruction to arising, now [discernment] acts as an obstruction to arising, rather than creating a state of non-arising.
If nirvana were merely non-arising, how would one interpret this scriptural passage?
The sutra states:
"If the five faculties are cultivated, practiced, and frequently cultivated, they can bring about the eternal cessation of all suffering in the past, future, and present."
This essence of permanent abandonment is itself nirvāṇa; it possesses the sense of non-arising only with respect to the future, not the past or present. Is this not contradictory?
Although there is such a textual passage, it does not contradict the underlying meaning.
The intention of this sutra is to state that because the afflictions (*kleśa*) conditioned by past and present suffering are abandoned, it is called the "abandonment of all suffering.
As the Blessed One said:

"You should abandon craving for form; when craving is abandoned, it is then called the abandonment of form and the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of form," and so on at length until "consciousness" is treated in the same way.
The same principle should apply to the meaning of severing past and present suffering.

Even if other sūtras state that one severs all afflictions of the past, future, and present, they may be explained according to the preceding reasoning, and their meaning will likewise not be contradictory.

Alternatively, there may be a specific underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) within this sūtra: "past afflictions" refers to afflictions arising in past lives, while "present afflictions" refers to afflictions arising in the present life.

Just as among the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*), those that arise in the past are explained in terms of past births; it should be understood that the same applies to the future and the present.

Thus, the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising in these two periods, for the sake of producing future afflictions, induce seeds within the present continuum. When these seeds are severed, those [afflictions] are also said to be severed.

Just as when the maturation (vipāka) is exhausted, it is also said that the karma is exhausted; so too, because future suffering and all afflictions lack seeds, they will never arise again, and this is called "abandonment" (prahāṇa).
If it were otherwise, for what reason would it be necessary to abandon the past and the present?
For one does not need to exert effort to cause that which has already ceased or is currently ceasing to cease.
If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) were entirely non-existent in essence, why does the Sūtra state:
"Of all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, freedom from passion (*vairāgya*) is the foremost"?
How can it be that among non-existents (*abhāva*), a "non-existent dharma" is established as being primary?
I do not say that the essence of all unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) is entirely non-existent; rather, they exist in the manner that I have described.

As it is said that this sound exists previously but did not exist, and exists later but will not exist, since that which does not exist cannot be described as existing, the meaning of "existence" is established.
One should know that the same applies to the statement that unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) exist.
There exists that which, though not a "being," is worthy of praise; thus, the absolute non-existence of all calamities and misfortunes is termed "freedom from defilement" (*virāga*).
Since this is the most excellent among all things that are both existent and non-existent, in order to inspire deep aspiration in those to be trained, it should be praised as the foremost.
If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) were merely non-existent, then because they do not exist, they should not be called the Noble Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the term "Noble Truth"?
Surely this word belongs to the sense of being non-erroneous (*aviparīta*).

The noble ones perceive both existence and non-existence without error; that is to say, regarding suffering, the noble ones see it only as suffering, and regarding what does not exist within suffering, they see it only as non-existent. How could this contradict the meaning of the Noble Truths?
How can that which is non-existent be established as the third Noble Truth?
Because it is seen and taught by the Noble Ones immediately following the second [truth], it constitutes the third.

If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) were merely non-existent in essence, then consciousnesses such as emptiness and nirvāṇa would have to take a non-existent object as their cognitive domain.
There is no fault in this [position] that the object of cognition does not exist; this should be investigated when discussing the past and the future.
If one were to admit that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) possess a distinct substantial entity, what fault would there be?
Furthermore, what merit is there?
To claim that one protects the Vaibhāṣika school is itself called a merit; if there were anything worthy of protection, the celestial deities would certainly know it and protect it themselves.
However, to assert that it exists substantially while claiming that its false conceptualization is what is designated as such is a fallacy. Why is this so?
Because its substantial entity cannot be apprehended like that of form or sensation, nor can its functional utility be apprehended like that of the eye or the ear.
Furthermore, if cessation were something distinct [from the entity], how could one establish the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) for the expression "the cessation of that entity"?
This is because cessation and the entity do not stand in a relationship of mutual dependence, as they are neither cause nor effect with respect to one another.
The sixth [category] can be established merely by negating that entity, because the non-existence of that entity is designated as "cessation.
Although cessation exists separately, it is only when that entity is attained or severed that this cessation is attained; thus, one may say that this cessation belongs to that entity.
For what reason is this cessation necessarily associated with this attainment?
As the Sūtra says:
"A bhikṣu attains nirvāṇa in the present life."
How can that which does not exist be said to be "attained"?
Because one attains the antidote, one achieves permanent opposition to the afflictions; subsequently, because there is a basis for existence, it is called "attaining nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, there is sacred teaching that can demonstrate that nirvāṇa has only non-existence as its intrinsic nature; as a sūtra states:
"All suffering is abandoned without remainder, individually relinquished, exhausted, detached from defilement, ceased, stilled, and forever vanished."

When further suffering does not continue, is not grasped, and does not arise—this is utter tranquility, this is utter excellence; namely, the relinquishing of all bases, the exhaustion of all craving, dispassion, and cessation, which is called Nirvana.
Why do you not allow that when one says "unborn," it is because of this non-arising that one says "unborn"?
We observe that this seventh-case (locative) construction has no power whatsoever to prove the existence of cessation.
For what reason is it said that [suffering] does not arise based on this?
If the phrase "based on this" (*niśritya*) has the sense of "already existing," then [suffering] would never have arisen in the first place, because *nirvāṇa* is eternal.

If the phrase "based on this" has the sense of "already attained," then one must admit that it is based on the attainment of the Path; thus, it is only by relying on the Path, or by the attainment of the Path, that suffering is prevented from arising.
You should accept this with faith.
By means of this, the metaphorical statement in the Sūtra is well explained: "Just as a lamp-flame, so too is the liberation of the mind through Nirvāṇa.
The intended meaning of this Sūtra is that when a lamp goes out, it is merely the cessation of the flame; there is no other distinct entity.
In this way, the World-Honored One’s mind has attained liberation; there is only the cessation of the aggregates, and nothing else exists.
The Abhidharma also states: "What are phenomena that lack a real entity (*avastuka*)?"
This refers to all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
To say they are "without an object" (*anarthaka*) means they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this interpretation.
If that is so, what is the meaning of the term *vastu* (thing) as explained therein?
It is said that there are briefly five kinds of things (*vastu*):
first, the thing as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vastu*), as it is stated in a certain passage:
If one has already attained this matter, one accomplishes that matter.
Regarding the two types of objects of focus, as it is said in a certain passage:
"All phenomena are known by wisdom according to their respective matters."
Third, the matter of the three fetters, as stated in a certain passage:
"If one is bound to this object by the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), is one also bound to that same object by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Fourth, the matter of the four causes, as stated in a certain passage:
What are the phenomena that possess a basis?
They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding the five bases included therein, as it is said in a certain passage:
Regarding matters of fields, matters of dwellings, matters of wives and children, and so forth—in this context, the term "matter" (*vastu*) refers to a cause;

this indicates that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely devoid of causes. Therefore, although unconditioned phenomena exist as real entities, because they are eternally without function, they possess neither cause nor fruit.
The general discussion is concluded.
Among the various fruits, it should now be explained which fruit is obtained by which cause.
The verse says:
The subsequent result is the ripening fruit; the preceding cause is the dominant fruit;
the similar and pervasive causes are the outflowing fruits; and the simultaneous and associated causes are the fruit of human effort.
The treatise says:

Regarding the "subsequent cause," this refers to the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); because it is taught last among the six causes, the first ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is obtained from this cause.

Regarding the "prior cause," this refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); because it is taught first among the six causes, the subsequent dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is obtained from this cause.
The fruit of predominance is called the "predominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*).
Since it consists merely in abiding without obstruction, what predominance is there?
It receives the name "predominant" precisely because of this absence of obstruction.

Alternatively, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) may also possess superior power, as for example, the ten bases and elements (*āyatana-dhātu*) do for the five groups of consciousness; the karma of sentient beings does for the receptacle world; and the ear and so forth do for the arising of visual consciousness and the rest, because after hearing [the sound], one immediately gives rise to the desire to see. Thus, there is also a successive power of dominant production.
These [other] predominances (*adhipati*) should be understood accordingly.
The homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) [causes] obtain the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), because both of these causes and their effects resemble their respective causes.

The co-existent (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayukta*) [causes] obtain the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); there is no separate "human effort" apart from the entity of the person itself, and that which is obtained by this very [effort] is termed the fruit of human effort.
To what phenomena does this term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) refer?

It refers to the functional activity of all phenomena; because it is like human effort, it receives the name "human effort. This is as worldly convention speaks of the *kāyasthā* herb or General Mattinga.
Are these two alone possessed of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), or is it the same for the others? Some say:

the other causes also possess this fruit, with the exception of the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). This is because the fruit of human effort arises either simultaneously with its cause or immediately after it, whereas the ripening fruit does not.
Other masters say:
This ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) also possesses a remote, separated result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), just like the fruit harvested by a farmer.
What are the characteristics of the ripening results and so forth?
The verse says:
Retribution is neutral; it belongs to sentient beings and arises from the determinate.
The outflowing resembles its own cause; disjunction results from the exhaustion [of defilements] through wisdom.
If it arises through the power of that [cause], this fruit is called the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
excluding the preceding conditioned phenomena, it is the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*) of conditioned things.
The commentary says:
Only among unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas is there a fruition result (*vipākaphala*).
Does this also extend to non-sentient entities, or is it restricted solely to sentient beings?
Does it also include results of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) and results of development (*aupacayikaphala*)?

It should be understood that [this] arises solely from the "determinate" (*vijñapti*). All unwholesome states and all wholesome *sāsrava* states are termed "determinate" because they can determine a maturation (*vipāka*).
Since the maturation arises at a later time from those [states], rather than simultaneously or immediately thereafter, it is called "arising from the determinate."
This is what is called the characteristic of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Even that which is not included among sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*) arises from karma; why then is it not a maturation fruit?
Because it is common to all.
This means that others might also be able to enjoy it in such a way.

However, regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), there is necessarily no sense of shared enjoyment; it is not the case that when one person performs an action, another may consequently experience its maturation fruit.
Its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is likewise produced by karma; how can it be experienced collectively?
Because it is produced by collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*).

A phenomenon that resembles its own cause is called a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), meaning it resembles [the results of] the two causes: the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
If the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also yields a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), why do you not admit that it is simply called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)?

This fruit is similar to its cause only by virtue of being defiled in terms of its level (*bhūmi*) and so forth, rather than by virtue of its category (*jāti*); if the fruit were also similar to the cause by virtue of its category, then the cause of such a fruit would indeed be called a homogeneous cause.
Therefore, this question is asked:
"If it is a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), is it also a pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu)?
One should formulate four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
The first phrase refers to non-universal dharmas acting as similar-type causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The second phrase refers to universal dharmas of other categories acting as pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
The third phrase refers to universal dharmas of their own category acting as pervasive causes.
Regarding the fourth phrase: excluding the aforementioned characteristics, the exhaustion of phenomena through wisdom is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).

It is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) because it is cessation; it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*) because it is discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*). Thus, it is stated that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is named the fruit of dissociation.
If a phenomenon is produced by the power of another, that phenomenon is called a "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

For example, when a contaminated or uncontaminated meditative absorption of a higher stage arises due to the power of the preparatory effort (*prayoga-citta*) of a lower stage, or when a transformation mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) arises due to the power of a pure dhyāna mind; in such cases, it should be said that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is obtained through the power of the Path.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), excluding those already arisen, are the dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*) of other conditioned phenomena.
What is the difference between the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit?
The term "fruit of human effort" applies exclusively to the agent, whereas the designation "dominant fruit" applies generally to both [the agent] and others.

Just as that which is produced by a craftsman receives the names of both the "human effort fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*) when considered in relation to the craftsman who produced it;
whereas, when considered in relation to others who are not craftsmen, it receives only the name of the dominant fruit.
Among the six types of causes explained above, at which stage and by which cause is the fruit grasped, and at which stage is it given?
The verse says:
Five grasp the fruit only in the present; Two give the fruit likewise.
Two causes [operate] in the past and present; one [cause] operates only in the past.
The commentary states:
The five causes grasp their fruit only in the present and certainly not in the past, because they have already grasped it.
Nor do they exist in the future, because they would have no function there.
It should also be stated that the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) does not necessarily possess a fruit; therefore, it is not mentioned here.

The same applies to the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) regarding the giving of a fruit, as these two causes take up and give their fruits only in the present, since the taking up and giving of the fruit must occur at the same time.
The two causes—the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—give rise to their fruits across both the past and the present.
While it is understandable that they do so in the past, how can they give rise to an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) in the present?
This is because such an outflowing fruit arises immediately [following the cause].
If a fruit has already arisen, the cause has already passed away; being termed "already having given its fruit," it should not give it again.
A similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) sometimes takes a fruit but does not give one; regarding this, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.
The first phrase refers to the possession that is last relinquished at the moment one severs the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
The second phrase refers to the possession first acquired at the moment one reconnects the roots of goodness; it should be stated that what is reconnected at that time is the possession from before.
The third phrase refers to those who have not severed their roots of goodness during all other remaining stages.
The fourth phrase refers to cases excluding the aforementioned characteristics.
Furthermore, regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of unwholesome states, there are likewise four phrases.
The first phrase refers to the acquisition that is last relinquished at the time one becomes free from desire and greed.

The second phrase refers to the acquisition that is first obtained at the time one falls away from desire and greed; it should be stated that at that time, the one who falls away [obtains] the previous acquisition.
The third phrase refers to all other states for one who has not yet abandoned desire and greed.
The fourth phrase refers to cases excluding those previously mentioned.

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena, there are likewise four phrases; these should be explained according to reason with respect to the time of attaining Arhatship, the time of falling away from it, the time of not yet attaining it, and other instances.

Among the homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) that are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), there is a "consequent" category: namely, at the time of giving a fruit, it necessarily also takes a fruit.

Or, there are cases where it takes a fruit but does not give one; this refers to the final aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat, in terms of the distinction between moments that possess an object (*sālambana*).
The wholesome similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) also has four permutations.
The first permutation refers to when a defiled or neutral mind arises immediately after a wholesome mind.
The second permutation refers to the opposite of the above.
The third phrase refers to when a wholesome mind arises immediately after another wholesome mind.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those previously mentioned.
Unwholesome minds and so forth also have four phrases as appropriate; they should be explained by analogy with this example.
What is the meaning of "taking the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*) and "giving the fruit" (*phaladāna*)?
It is called "taking the fruit" because it is capable of acting as the seed for that [fruit]; it is called "giving the fruit" because it actually bestows its power upon it.
Retribution (*vipāka*) gives its fruit only in the past, because a retributive fruit neither co-exists with its cause nor arises immediately after it.
Furthermore, there are other masters who, in addition to the five aforementioned fruits, separately explain four fruits:
first, the fruit of establishment (*vyavasthāna-phala*), such as the water-circle being the fruit of the wind-circle, up to grass and so forth being the fruit of the great earth.

Second is the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*), which refers to how, for example, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) serves as the remote fruit of [the practice of] impurity (*aśubhā*) and so forth.

Third is the fruit of conjunction (*sāmagrī-phala*), which refers to how, for example, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth serve as the fruits of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and so forth.
Fourth is the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*), which refers to things such as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) being the fruit of the various dhyānas.
These four fruits are all subsumed under the fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and sovereign dominance (*adhipati-phala*).
Having explained cause and effect, one should further investigate: among these, which phenomena are produced by how many causes?
Briefly, there are four types of phenomena: defiled phenomena, phenomena born of maturation, the first untainted phenomenon, and the remaining three types of phenomena.
What are the remaining dharmas?

They refer to all other indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas, excluding those that are maturation-born (vipāka), and all other wholesome (kuśala) dharmas, excluding the first moment of the untainted (anāsrava).
Regarding these four types of dharmas, the verse says:

Defiled and born-of-maturation [dharmas] arise from all; the others, and the first noble [dharma], arise respectively from two, excluding maturation and the pervasive; and from the similar, excluding the rest.
This refers to mind and mental factors; for the others, the associated [cause] is excluded.
The treatise states:
All defiled phenomena arise from five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Phenomena born of ripening arise from five causes, excluding the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Regarding the remaining three types of dharmas, they arise from four causes, excluding both the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Regarding the first type of untainted dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*), it arises from three causes, excluding the aforementioned two as well as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
What are these four phenomena for which this is taught?
They are the mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and matter—these four phenomena.
Furthermore, by how many causes are they produced?
Just as with the mind and mental factors, excluding their specific causes and excluding their associated cause, one should know that other phenomena arise from four, three, or two remaining causes.
Among these, defiled phenomena and those born of maturation arise from the remaining four causes.
The remaining three types of phenomena arise from the other three causes.
Initial untainted phenomena arise from the other two causes.
There is no phenomenon whatsoever that arises from only a single cause.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Volume Six (Continued) / Volume Seven,
composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.
The Tripitaka Master Xuanzang, by Imperial Decree, translated this.
Chapter Two, Part Five: "Analysis of the Faculties. Having extensively explained the causes, what then are the conditions?
The verse says:
It is taught that there are four kinds of conditions; the causal condition consists of the nature of the five causes;
the equal-and-immediate condition is not subsequent; it refers to those minds and mental factors already arisen.
"All phenomena are the object-condition; the predominant [condition] is the efficient cause.
The treatise asks:
Where is this stated?

That is to say, as stated in the sūtras regarding the nature of the four conditions: namely, the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the nature of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
This "neuter" [category] refers to the types of conditions (*pratyaya*).
Among the six causes, with the exception of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

With the exception of the final mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of an Arhat at the moment of entering *nirvāṇa*, all other previously arisen minds and mental factors constitute the nature of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Because these factors of dependent origination arise equally and without interval, the term "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) is established based on this meaning.
For this reason, form and other such phenomena cannot be established as equal and immediate conditions, because they do not arise in an equal manner.
