That is to say, from a form of the desire realm, there may immediately arise two types of non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa)—those of the desire realm and the form realm—or it may immediately arise as two types of non-informative matter, those of the desire realm and the untainted (anāsrava).

Because various material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) manifest in a state of confusion, whereas the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) gives rise to that which is not confused, matter is not established as having an equal-and-immediate condition.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:

Within a single body, one stream of nourished matter (*aupacayika-rūpa*) continues without interruption; yet another second stream of nourished matter may arise without mutual contradiction or harm. Therefore, it cannot be established as an equal-and-immediate condition.
The Venerable One spoke again:

"Because various material phenomena arise in immediate succession, whether in small or large quantities; that is to say, there are times when a large quantity gives rise to a small one, such as when a great heap of rice straw is burned to become ash."

Furthermore, there are times when the many arise from the few, such as when a tiny seed produces a *nyagrodha* tree; its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves gradually flourish and grow, until its towering trunk and drooping boughs provide vast shade.
Is it not the case that when mental factors (*caitta*) arise in immediate succession, there are also instances where their categories—whether few or many—are unequal?

That is to say, within minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, or within states such as *samādhi* with vitarka and vicāra, there are indeed instances of inequality across different classes. However, within their own class, there is no sense of inequality; for instance, it is never the case that a small number of sensations (*vedanā*) arise immediately after a large number, nor that a small number arises immediately after a large number. The same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other mental factors; thus, there is no fault of inequality.
Is it only those of the same category that can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for what follows? It is not so. Why is this?
The dharmas of a preceding category collectively serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for those of a subsequent category, not merely for their own kind.

Furthermore, within the category of the self-nature of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, there is no case of a small number giving rise to a large number; it is on this basis that the meaning of "equal" (*sama*) is explained.

This is the assertion of those who maintain that there is a homogeneous continuity; they claim that only things of the same kind possess the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*), such that mind produces only mind and sensation produces only sensation, and so forth, as explained at length.

If a defiled state arises immediately after an undefiled one, then the afflictions present within that defiled mind take the previously ceased afflictions as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

This is just as when emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mind arises by taking the previously ceased mind that had entered the attainment of cessation as its condition.
That explanation is not correct, because the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) would then arise lacking this condition.

Furthermore, since non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) also appear in a disordered manner just like various material forms (*rūpa*), they cannot be the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Since the three realms and that which is unconditioned can all manifest simultaneously, for what reason do you not admit that there is an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the future?
This is because future phenomena abide in a state of confusion, lacking the sequence of before and after.
How does the Blessed One know that in the future this dharma will be immediately followed by this dharma, and that this dharma should arise?
It is because he perceives it directly by analogy with past and present dharmas.
According to tradition, the Blessed One sees that from such a type of karma in the past, such a type of fruit arises; he sees that immediately after this dharma, such a dharma is produced.
Furthermore, observing that from such a type of karma in the present, such a type of fruit arises, and that this phenomenon arises immediately after that phenomenon;
having seen this, one is then able to correctly comprehend that regarding all phenomena abiding in disorder in the future, this phenomenon must arise immediately after that phenomenon.
Although one knows in this way, it is not inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).

Because the Buddha, by means of analogy, discerns the sequential order of causes and effects from the past and present, he is able to directly and clearly comprehend all phenomena abiding in disorder within the future. That is to say, he knows that in the future world, such sentient beings will perform such karma and bring forth such results; because this is subsumed under the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), it is not inferential knowledge.
If that were so, the Blessed One, not having seen the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), would be unable to know the phenomena of the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
Others further say:

within the bodies of sentient beings there exist precursors of the causes and effects of future lives, which are a specific category of the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
The Buddha knows the future simply by observing this; it is not necessary for him to presently engage in meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
If that were so, then Buddhas would know the future through divination of signs rather than through direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Therefore, as the masters of the Sautrāntika school maintain, it is well said that when the Blessed One directs his intention, he knows all phenomena through direct perception, neither by inference nor by divination.
As the Blessed One has said:
The virtuous functions and the spheres of all Buddhas are inconceivable.

If there is no fixed sequence of before and after established for the future, why is it said that immediately following the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma), only the "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) arises, and no other dharmas?

Thus it is explained in detail, up to the point that immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) arises and no other dharma arises.
If the arising of this dharma is contingent upon that dharma, it can only arise immediately following it, just as the arising of a sprout and so forth requires a seed and so forth.
However, these do not constitute equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).
For what reason is it said that the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat are not equal-and-immediate conditions?
Because no other minds or mental factors arise in succession from them.
Is it not the case that the mind which has just ceased without interval is also called the "mental faculty" (manas)?

If the subsequent mind does not arise immediately after [the preceding one], it should not be called the mental faculty; yet the mental faculty is defined by its status as a support (āśraya), not by its functional activity (kāritra).

This final consciousness possesses the sense of having a support; however, because other conditions are lacking, subsequent consciousness does not arise. This is manifested by the functioning of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Once a phenomenon has been taken as a fruit by this condition, no phenomena or sentient beings whatsoever can create an obstruction to prevent it from arising. Therefore, although the final consciousness may be designated as "mind" (*manas*), it cannot be called an equal-and-immediate condition.
If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind, is that phenomenon also immediately preceded by the mind?
This should be analyzed in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

The first permutation refers to the mind and mental factors emerging from the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), as well as the moments of the second and subsequent moments of the two attainments.

The second phrase refers to the first moment of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) during states of consciousness.
The third phrase refers to the first moments of the two meditative attainments, as well as the minds and mental factors during states of consciousness.

The fourth phrase refers to the second and subsequent moments of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as the arising, abiding, change, and cessation of the mind and mental factors upon emerging from a mindless attainment (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
If a phenomenon serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the mind, does it also serve as the immediate condition for the mindless attainment?
One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

That is to say, the former third and fourth propositions become the present first and second propositions, while the former first and second propositions become the present third and fourth propositions.

When the various minds and mental factors emerge from the second dhyāna, they are separated by a long interval from the mind that had entered that meditative absorption; how, then, can they be considered immediate (*anantara*) with respect to it?
Because there is no intervening mind or mental factor between them.
Thus, the equal-and-immediate condition has been explained.
As for the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it consists of all phenomena in relation to the mind and mental factors, as appropriate.
That is to say, for example, visual consciousness and its associated mental factors take all visible forms as their object-condition.
In this way, the ear-consciousness and its associated mental factors take all sounds as their object;
the nose-consciousness and its associated factors take all odors;
and the tongue-consciousness and its associated factors take all tastes.
The body-consciousness is associated with all tangibles as its objects;
the mental consciousness is associated with all phenomena (*dharmas*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If a phenomenon serves as an object for another phenomenon, there is no time when it does not serve as such an object; even in a state where it is not being attended to, it is still subsumed under the category of an object, because its characteristic remains the same whether it is being attended to or not.
For example, fuel and the like are called "that which is burned" even when they are not being burned, because their characteristics do not differ.

Just as the mind and mental factors are determined in three respects—regarding their object (*ālambana*), their substance (*vastu*), and their moment (*kṣaṇa*)—are they likewise determined with respect to their support (*āśraya*)?

One should say that there is likewise such a certainty; however, in the present, [the mind] is closely attached to its own support (*āśraya*), whereas in the past and future, it is separated from its support. Some say:
even in the past, it remains closely attached to its support.
Thus, the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) has been explained.
The nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is precisely the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because the efficient cause itself constitutes the dominant condition.
This condition is called the "dominant condition" because its substance is vast; for everything is a dominant condition.
Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are also objects-of-support conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), why is it that this dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) alone has such a vast essence?
While co-existent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*) have never served as objects-of-support, they do function as dominant conditions; therefore, only this [dominant condition] possesses a vast essence.

Alternatively, that which performs a broad function is called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), because all phenomena—each excluding its own nature—serve as the dominant condition for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Is there any phenomenon that is entirely not one of the four conditions for another phenomenon?
There is [existence], namely, a nature existing in relation to itself, and it also exists in relation to other natures;
that is, the conditioned in relation to the unconditioned, and the unconditioned in relation to the unconditioned.
In what state of phenomena do these various conditions exercise their activity?
The verse says:
Two causes exert their activity upon that which is ceasing; three causes, upon that which is arising;
the remaining two conditions act in opposition to these.
The Treatise says:
The five causes previously mentioned function as the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Two of these causes exert their activity at the moment of "presently perishing.
The phrase "at the moment of presently perishing" indicates that the dharma is in the present; because its cessation is manifesting, it is called the "moment of presently perishing."

The co-existent and associated causes exercise their activity precisely at the moment a dharma ceases; it is by virtue of these two causes that the simultaneously produced fruit comes to possess activity.

As for the statement that the three causes [exercise their activity] during the "moment of arising," this refers to future dharmas which, at the stage of arising, manifest themselves; therefore, it is called the "time of arising."
The three types of causes—homogeneous, pervasive, and retributive—exert their activity precisely at the moment when the dharma arises.
Having explained that the activity of these two [types of] causal conditions occurs at two times, the activity of the other two conditions is the opposite of this.

The immediately antecedent condition (samanantara-pratyaya) exerts its function at the stage when a dharma arises, because when that [dharma] arises, the preceding mind and mental factors yield their place to it.
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exerts its function at the stage when the perceiving subject ceases, because the mind and mental factors must be present in order to apprehend an object.
Only the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) remains unobstructed throughout all stages; therefore, its activity is never hindered in any stage where there is no obstruction.
Thus have the various conditions and their activities been explained.
One should state: by how many conditions do which phenomena arise?
The verse says:
Mind and mental factors arise from four; The two meditative attainments arise from only three.
The others arise from two conditions, because they are not produced by a creator god (*īśvara*) nor sequentially, and so forth.
The treatise says:
Mental states and mental factors arise from four conditions; among these, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to the nature of the five causes.
The equal-and-immediate condition refers to those mental states and mental factors that have already arisen immediately prior, excluding subsequent ones.
The object-condition refers, as appropriate, either to the five objects such as form or to all phenomena.
Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it refers to all other dharmas, excluding its own self-nature, as appropriate for each case.

The two meditative attainments—cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—arise from three conditions, excluding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because they are not cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*).
Regarding "by way of causes and conditions," this refers to two types of causes:
first, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), which refers to the characteristics such as arising (*jāti*);
second, the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which refers to previously arisen wholesome dharmas of the same stage (*bhūmi*).
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the mind entering meditative absorption and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as previously described.

Thus, these two types of absorbed minds obstruct the arising of other minds; because they arise simultaneously with the mind, they are "equal" to the mind, yet they function merely as immediately preceding [moments] and do not constitute an immediately preceding condition.
The remaining non-associated formations and all material phenomena arise from two conditions: the causal condition and the dominant condition.
All worldly phenomena arise solely from the causes and conditions described above; they do not arise from a single cause such as Īśvara, the Self (ātman), or Pradhāna. What is the reason for this?
If you admit that all things are produced by causes, would you not then be abandoning the worldly doctrine that everything arises from a single cause such as Īśvara?
Furthermore, the various worlds are not produced by a single cause such as Īśvara, because they arise sequentially and so forth.
This means that if all things in the world were produced by a single cause, such as Īśvara, then they would all arise simultaneously rather than sequentially;
yet we observe that all phenomena arise in succession, and thus we know they are certainly not produced by a single cause.

If it is maintained that [the world] arises according to the will of Īśvara—namely, that he desires this dharma to arise now, this dharma to cease now, and this [dharma] at a later time—then it would follow that things arise from multiple causes, since they are produced by the differentiation of his desires.
Alternatively, distinct desires would have to arise simultaneously, because their cause—Īśvara—is without differentiation.
If these distinct desires do not arise together because they further depend on other causes, then it is not the case that everything has Īśvara as its sole cause.

Alternatively, the causes upon which [the effect] depends would themselves have to depend on further distinct causes before arising in succession; thus, the causes upon which they depend would be infinite.

If, on the other hand, they did not depend on further distinct causes, these causes would lack the property of arising in succession, and consequently, the distinct desires would not arise in succession either.

If one grants that causes are mutually differentiated without end, then because one must believe in beginninglessness, the mere insistence that Īśvara is the cause of all phenomena does not transcend the correct principle of dependent origination within the Śākya school.

If it is argued that although the will of the Lord arises instantaneously, the various worlds do not arise simultaneously because they arise in accordance with his will, this reasoning is also incorrect.
That [alleged] sovereign will is indistinguishable from its preceding state;
furthermore, what benefit or purpose is gained by that sovereign exerting great effort to produce the various worlds?

If [the Lord] produces joy for the sake of generating the various worlds, and this joy does not arise without other means, then since the Lord must necessarily depend on others in the production of joy, he would not be sovereign.
Since this is the case regarding joy, it should likewise apply to the others, as no distinct causes or conditions can be found [to differentiate them].
Alternatively, if Īśvara creates the hells and other immeasurable instruments of suffering to torment sentient beings, he does so because he takes pleasure in seeing such things occur.
Alas! Of what use is this sovereignty?
As that verse says, it is indeed well-spoken.
Because he is fierce and sharp, capable of burning, terrifying, and constantly inflicting harm, and because he delights in consuming blood,
flesh, and marrow, he is named Rudra. Furthermore,

if one were to believe and accept that all the world arises solely from the single cause of Īśvara, one would then be repudiating the other causes and conditions of the world that are directly perceived, such as human effort and so forth.

If one claims that Īśvara becomes a cause only when his capacity is activated by depending on other auxiliary causes and conditions, this is merely a statement out of partiality toward the god Īśvara; for apart from those other causes and conditions, no distinct function [of Īśvara] is observed.
Alternatively, if that Īśvara requires the assistance of other causes and conditions in order to produce [effects], he would not be truly autonomous (an-īśvara).

If you maintain that while Īśvara is the cause for the initial arising, subsequent arisings depend on other causes, then that which first arose—being independent of other causes—would have to be beginninglessly established, just like Īśvara himself.

Regarding my own superiority and so forth, they should be extensively refuted as appropriate, just as the case of Īśvara has been; therefore, there is no phenomenon that arises from a single cause alone.
Alas! How lamentable it is that people in this world do not cultivate superior wisdom, being like ignorant birds and beasts.

In each respective birth, one creates distinct karmas and personally experiences their ripened results (*vipākaphala*) as well as their results of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), yet one falsely imagines that there exists a cause such as an *īśvara* (Lord).
Let us now cease this refutation of the heterodox and proceed to explain the correct meaning.
Introduction: Other phenomena arise from two conditions. Among these, how do the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) function as causes for one another?
The verse states:
The primary elements are two causes for the primary elements, And five kinds of causes for the derived matter.
The derived [elements] act as three kinds of causes; for the primary [elements], there is only one cause.
The commentary states:

Regarding the initial statement that the primary elements act as two causes for the primary elements, this means that when these primary elements are viewed in relation to one another, they function solely as simultaneous and homogeneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu* and *sabhāga-hetu*).
The great elements act as five causes for that which is derived from them.
What are these five? They are distinguished as:
the cause of production, the cause of reliance, the cause of establishment, the cause of support, and the cause of nourishment.
These five causes are merely distinctions of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
They are called "productive causes" because [the derived matter] arises from them; once produced, it continues to evolve in accordance with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Just as a teacher and so forth are said to be the cause of reliance because they provide support;
just as a wall supporting a painting is said to be the cause of establishment;
and because it prevents interruption, it is called the cause of maintenance.
Because it is the cause of growth, it is called the cause of nourishment (*puṣṭi-hetu*).
In this way, it is revealed that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the causes for the arising, transformation, maintenance, persistence, and growth of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
All derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), when considered in relation to one another, can have three types of causes: namely, co-existent (*sahabhū*), homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and retributive (*vipāka*).
Because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) functions without distinction, it is not always enumerated [among these specific causes].
The co-existent cause refers to the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—that follow the mind, and not other derived matter.
The similar-type cause refers to all preceding moments that are of the same type as those that follow.
As for the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it refers to bodily and vocal karma that can bring about results such as the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth as its ripening.
Derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) acts as only one cause toward the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), namely, the ripening cause.
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are capable of producing maturation (*vipāka*), as they have the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their fruit.

Previously, it was stated in general that all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) can serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for subsequent ones; however, it has not yet been determined which mind is followed by how many minds arising, nor from how many minds does which mind arise.
Now I shall provide a definitive explanation; briefly stated, there are twelve types of mind.
What are these twelve?
The verse says:
In the desire realm there are four types of mind: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral;
in the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded; and in the untainted realm, there are two types of mind.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, within the desire realm there are four types of mind: namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, the obscured-neutral, and the unobscured-neutral.
In both the form and formless realms there are three types of mind each; that is, with the exception of the unwholesome, the rest are as described above.
Thus, these ten types are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If one considers the mind without outflows (*anāsrava*), there are only two kinds: namely, that of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and that of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Together, they constitute twelve.
Regarding the mutual arising of these twelve minds, the verse says:
In the desire realm, the wholesome gives rise to nine; these, in turn, arise from eight.
The defiled arises from ten and gives rise to four; the remainder arise from five and give rise to seven.
Wholesome form produces eleven; it, in turn, arises from nine.
Obscured [neutral] arises from eight; it, in turn, produces six.
Unobscured [neutral] arises from three; it, in turn, can produce six.
The wholesome mind of the formless realm gives rise to nine; this, in turn, arises from six.
The obscured-unspecified arises from seven; the unobscured-unspecified is distinguished as in the case of the form realm.
The learner’s mind arises from four and gives rise to five; the remaining minds arise from five and give rise to four.
The treatise says:
A wholesome mind of the desire realm gives rise to nine minds in immediate succession—namely, four of its own realm;
and two minds of the form realm, which are wholesome and defiled minds respectively, arising at the time of entering meditative absorption and at the stage of rebirth.
In the formless realm, there is one [moment] at the stage of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).
A defiled mind of that realm arises immediately after a wholesome mind of the desire realm, but a wholesome mind of that realm does not arise [after it], because it is extremely distant.
The formless realm is distant from the desire realm due to four kinds of distance: [distance of place, object, time, and nature].
There are four types of distance: first, distance of basis; second, distance of aspect; third, distance of object; and fourth, distance of antidote.
Furthermore, there is the distinction between those in training and those beyond training, which refers to the time of entering meditative observation.

This [state] in turn arises immediately after eight [minds]: namely, the four [minds] of its own realm, and two minds from the form realm—the wholesome mind arising at the time of emerging from meditative absorption, and the defiled mind when one is oppressed by a defiled concentration;
from that defiled mind, a wholesome mind of the lower realm arises, for the purpose of relying on the lower wholesome mind to prevent such retrogression.
Regarding the states of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), these refer to the time when one has emerged from meditative absorption.

"Defiled" refers to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); each of these two arises immediately after ten [minds], namely, from among the twelve [minds] excluding those of training and beyond training.
At the stage of rebirth, because any mind of the three realms can arise immediately prior to a defiled mind of the desire realm, this [defiled mind] can immediately give rise to four types of minds:
namely, the four of its own realm; there is no possibility for others to arise.

The remainder refers to the unobscured-neutral states bound to the desire realm; these minds arise immediately after five [types of mind], namely the four of their own realm and the wholesome mind of the form realm, because the transformative mind of the desire realm arises from those.

Immediately following this, it can produce seven types of mind: namely, the four of its own realm, two from the form realm—both the wholesome and the defiled—and the transformation-mind of the desire realm that produces its own wholesome mind, as well as the defiled mind of that realm produced at the moment of rebirth-linking.
Together with the one [type] of the formless realm, this unobscured-neutral mind at the stage of rebirth-linking can produce those defiled minds.
Immediately following a wholesome mind of the form realm, eleven [minds] arise; that is to say, excluding the unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm.
Furthermore, this [state] arises immediately after nine types of minds: namely, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm, and excluding the non-obscured-neutral mind of the formless realm.

The obscured-neutral mind arises immediately after eight types of minds, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately following this, it can give rise to six types of minds: namely, the three of its own realm—wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-neutral—and the wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-neutral minds of the desire realm.
The non-obscured-neutral mind arises immediately after three types of minds, namely only those of its own realm; there is no possibility for it to arise from any others.
Immediately following this [neutral mind], six minds can arise: namely, three of its own realm, and the defiled minds of the desire and formless realms.

Immediately following a wholesome mind of the formless realm, nine minds can arise: namely, excluding the wholesome mind of the desire realm and the unobscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms.
That very [state] arises immediately after six: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the wholesome of the form realm, and those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).

The obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) can give rise to seven minds immediately after it: namely, the three of its own realm, the wholesome of the form realm, and the defiled minds of the desire and form realms.

This same [unobscured-neutral mind] also arises immediately after seven [minds], namely, excluding those defiled minds of the desire and form realms, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the unobscured-neutral [mind], it is as explained for the [neutral] form realm: it arises immediately after three [minds], namely, the three of its own realm; all others are illogical.
Immediately following this, six minds can arise: namely, the three of its own realm, as well as the defiled minds of the desire and form realms.
A mind of training (*śaikṣa*) arises immediately after four: namely, that very mind of training and the wholesome minds of the three realms.
Immediately following this, five minds can arise: namely, the aforementioned four minds and the one mind of an adept (aśaikṣa).

As for the remainder—that is, the minds of an adept—they arise immediately after five minds: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the two minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Immediately following this, four types of mind can arise: namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the one mind of the Aśaikṣa.
Having explained how these twelve minds mutually produce one another, how are they divided into twenty minds?
The verse says:
The twelve become twenty; that is, the wholesome minds of the three realms are divided into those acquired through application and those acquired by birth.
In the desire realm, the non-obscured [unwholesome] is divided into four: the ripening-born, the deportment, the craftsmanship, and the fruition-attainment.
In the form realm, excluding the craftsmanship, the remaining numbers are as previously stated.
The treatise states:

The wholesome minds of the three realms are each divided into two types, namely, those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*), due to their distinction.
Within the desire realm, the non-obscured [neutral] mind is divided into four types:

There are four types of non-obscured neutral minds: first, those born of maturation; second, those of deportment; third, those of the sphere of craftsmanship; and fourth, those resulting from supernormal powers.

The non-obscured neutral minds of the form realm are divided into three types, excluding those of the sphere of craftsmanship, because in the higher realms there is no performance of various types of craftsmanship at all.

Thus, these twelve become twenty minds; that is to say, the wholesome are divided into six, and the unobscured-neutral are divided into eight. Since there are no *airyāpathika* (postures) and so forth in the formless realm, and the remaining counts are as stated above, they constitute twenty.

The three types of non-obscured minds, such as those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), take visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as their objective spheres; those pertaining to craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) also take sound as an object. These three types of mind belong exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the spheres of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) also pertain to all four consciousnesses and the five sensory consciousnesses.
Other masters state:
there exists a mental consciousness induced by the modes of deportment and the spheres of craftsmanship that is capable of fully apprehending the objects of the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

Regarding these twenty [minds] that arise from one another: first, within the eight types of minds of the desire realm, the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) immediately gives rise to ten. These consist of seven minds of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*)—one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This, in turn, arises immediately after eight [minds]: namely, four from its own realm—two wholesome and two defiled—as well as two from the form realm—the preparatory wholesome mind and the obscured-unspecified mind—and finally, the learner’s and the non-learner’s minds.

The wholesome mind acquired at birth arises immediately after nine minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition—as well as the obscured-unspecified minds of the form and formless realms.

This same mind, in turn, arises from eleven minds: namely, seven of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition—two of the form realm—the preparatory wholesome mind and the obscured-unspecified mind—along with the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The two defiled minds arise immediately after seven minds; that is, the seven of their own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

These, in turn, arise from fourteen minds: namely, the seven of their own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition; the four of the form realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal fruition; and the three of the formless realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome.

The *vipāka* and *airyāpathika* minds give rise to eight immediately thereafter: namely, the six of their own realm—excluding the *prāyogika-kuśala* and the *abhijñā-phala* minds—as well as the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the form and formless realms.
This [mind] in turn arises immediately after seven [minds], namely the seven of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

The mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*) gives rise to six minds immediately after it, namely the six of its own realm, excluding the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala*) and the mind of supernormal fruition.
This [resultant mind] in turn arises immediately after seven minds, namely the seven of its own realm, excluding the fruition-of-communication mind.

Immediately after the fruition-of-communication mind, two minds arise: one of its own realm, which is the fruition-of-communication mind itself, and one of the form realm, which is the wholesome mind of application.
This [state] likewise arises immediately after two [states]: namely, the two minds previously mentioned that pertain to its own form realm.

Next, regarding the six types of minds in the form realm, twelve arise immediately after the wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala*): namely, the six of its own realm; three from the desire realm—the wholesome mind of application, the innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-labdha*), and the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala*); as well as the one wholesome mind of application from the formless realm; and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This [mind] in turn arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, four from its own realm—excluding those of deportment and those born of maturation; two from the desire realm—the preparatory and the supernormal; and two from the formless realm—the preparatory and the obscured; as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training.

Immediately after a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*), eight minds arise: namely, five of its own realm—excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala*)—and two from the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)—as well as one obscured-unspecified mind from the formless realm.
This [state] in turn arises immediately after five [minds], namely the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).

The obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind gives rise to nine minds immediately after it: the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition; and four from the desire realm—two wholesome and two defiled.

This [mind] in turn arises from eleven minds: namely, the five of its own realm—excluding the mind of fruition—and three of the desire realm—the innate wholesome mind, the mind of deportment, and the resultant mind—along with three of the formless realm—excluding the wholesome mind of application.

The *vipāka* (maturation), *airyāpathika* (postural), and *anantarya* (immediate) minds each give rise to seven [minds] in succession: namely, four of their own realm—excluding the *prāyogika-kuśala* (preparatory wholesome) and the *abhijñā-phala* (result of supernormal power) minds—and two of the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral—as well as one from the formless realm, the obscured-unneutral.
This [resultant mind] in turn arises immediately after five minds, namely the five of its own realm, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
Immediately after the mind of supernormal fruition, two minds arise: the two of its own realm, namely the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the supernormal fruition minds.
This [neutral mind] also arises immediately after two types of minds, namely, the two previously mentioned minds of its own realm.

Next, regarding the four kinds of minds in the formless realm, seven arise immediately after the preparatory wholesome mind: namely, the four of its own realm, one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This, in turn, arises immediately after six [minds]: namely, three from its own realm—excluding only the maturation mind—one preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Immediately after a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), seven minds arise: namely, the four of its own realm, one obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm, and two minds of the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified.
This [state] in turn arises immediately after four states, namely the four of its own realm.

Immediately after the obscured-unspecified state, eight states arise: the four of its own realm, the two of the form realm—the preparatory and the obscured—and the two of the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured.

This, in turn, arises immediately after ten [minds]: namely, the four of its own realm; the three of the form realm—namely, those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*), the resultant (*vipāka*), and the deportment (*airyāpathika*)—and the three of the desire realm, which are as previously described for the form realm.

Six minds arise immediately after a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*): namely, three from its own realm—excluding the wholesome produced by application (*prayoga-kuśala*)—one obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm, and two from the desire realm—the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified.
This [uncontaminated mind] in turn arises immediately after four [minds], namely the four of its own realm.

Next, regarding the two types of uncontaminated minds, six arise immediately after the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*): namely, the preparatory wholesome minds of all three realms, the innate wholesome mind of the desire realm, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This [uncontaminated mind] in turn arises immediately after four [minds]: namely, the three preparatory minds and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

Five [minds] arise immediately after the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): namely, the six previously mentioned that arise from the mind of one in training, excluding the single mind of one in training itself.

This [wholesome mind] in turn arises immediately after five types of minds: namely, the three types of preparatory wholesome minds, as well as the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For what reason is this so?

A preparatory wholesome mind can arise immediately after maturation-born, artisanal, or deportment-born minds, but those [latter] cannot arise immediately after a preparatory wholesome mind because their power is inferior and they are not produced through the exertion of effort.

Because the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) arise through the exertion of effort, they cannot give rise to a wholesome mind of application (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) in accordance with them; whereas because the emerging mind (*vyutthāna-citta*) proceeds without the need for effort, it can arise immediately after the mind of application.
If that were so, wholesome states resulting from application (*prayoga-kuśala*) should not arise immediately after a defiled state, because they are not mutually compatible.

Nevertheless, when one is weary of the manifestation of afflictions and desires to understand them, it is possible for wholesome states resulting from application to arise; this is because the innate wholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-upapatti-labdha*) are sharp and clear.

There may be minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), that arise immediately after [a mind of the desire realm]; however, because they are not produced through the exertion of effort (*abhisamskāra*), those [higher] minds cannot be induced from this [desire-realm mind].

Furthermore, because the *prāpti* (acquisition) of birth in the desire realm is clear and sharp, it can arise immediately after the defilements (*kleśa*) of the form realm; however, because the *prāpti* of birth in the form realm is not clear and sharp, it does not arise immediately after the defilements of the formless realm.
There are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*):

first, mental attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), which refers to mental attention associated with such contemplations as observing that matter has the characteristic of being subject to transformation and obstruction, up to observing that consciousness has the characteristic of discernment, and so forth.
Second is the mental attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), which refers to the mental attention associated with the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*).

Third is the mental attention of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*), which refers to the mental attention associated with such contemplations as the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the form-sphere liberations (*rūpī-vimokṣāḥ*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatanāni*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatanāni*).

In this way, the noble path manifests immediately after these three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and immediately after the noble path, one is likewise able to fully give rise to the three types of mental attention.
If one explains it thus, it accords with this statement: "One cultivates the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness, in conjunction with the contemplation of impurity."
Other masters say:

Only from the attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) does the Noble Path manifest immediately thereafter; and only after the Noble Path has manifested and one has cultivated the three types of meditation on the foul (*aśubhabhāvanā*) to subdue the mind, can one subsequently give rise to the attention to general characteristics, from which the Noble Path manifests immediately thereafter.
Based on this successive transmission of the underlying intent, it is said that one cultivates the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness, in conjunction with the meditation on impurity.
Others further state:

"The noble path manifests immediately after mental attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*), and immediately after the noble path, one can likewise only give rise to mental attention to common characteristics."

If that is so, for one who enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the three stages beginning with the *anāgamya* concentration, the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*) belonging to the desire realm may arise immediately after the noble path.

If one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, what kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises immediately after the noble path?
It is not the mental attention to the universal characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the desire realm, because it is too remote.
It is not that in those stages there already exists a previously attained general mental attention (*sāmānyamanasikāra*) distinct from the previously attained aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
For the aids to penetration of the noble ones cannot manifest again, since once the fruit has been attained, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) cannot arise anew.

If it is argued that there exists a distinct attention to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*) which has already been cultivated simultaneously with the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), because it is connected to them and belongs to their category—

just as when one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as impermanent, or contemplates all phenomena (*dharma*) as non-self and nirvāṇa as peaceful— the noble path immediately induces that [attention] to manifest.
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this position, as it contradicts correct reasoning.

If one attains the fruit of arhatship based on the *anāgamya* concentration, the mind that emerges from meditative absorption is either of that same stage or belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The mind that emerges from meditative observation after attaining the fruit of Arhatship based on the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) belongs either to that same level or to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
If one attains the fruit of Arhatship based on any other level, the mind that emerges from meditative observation belongs only to that [level] itself and not to any other.
Within the desire realm, there are three types of attention:
first, that produced by hearing; second, that produced by reflection; and third, that acquired through birth.
Within the form realm, there are likewise three types of attention:
First, that which is produced by hearing; second, that which is produced by cultivation; and third, that which is obtained through birth.
There is no [mental application] produced by reflection, because as soon as one directs the mind toward thought, one immediately enters meditative concentration.
In the formless realm, there are only two types of mental application:
First, that produced through cultivation; second, that obtained by birth.

Among these, five types of attention are immediately followed by the manifestation of the Noble Path, with the exception of the path obtained by birth, because the latter is connected to the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).
The Path of the Noble Ones (āryamārga) can also arise immediately [after these states], because the acquisition of birth in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is characterized by clarity and sharpness.
Among the twelve mental states previously mentioned, when which state is manifest, how many states can be acquired?
The verse says:
Within the defiled minds of the three realms, one obtains six, six, and two kinds [of acquisitions];
in the wholesome mind of the form realm, three; in the [wholesome] minds of the three trainings, four; for all others, they are obtained by themselves.
The treatise states:

At the stage when a defiled mind of the desire realm is currently manifest, one acquires six of the twelve minds contained therein, because those were previously unestablished and are now established.
Due to the restoration of the roots of goodness through doubt or the regression from a higher realm, the wholesome mind of the desire realm is said to be "attained" at that time.

Due to the arising of afflictions through regression or the regression from a higher realm, one attains two minds of the desire realm—the unwholesome and the obscured—and the single obscured mind of the form realm.
Due to falling away from meditative attainment through the arousal of afflictions, one acquires one obscured-unwholesome mind of the formless realm as well as a mind of one in training (śaikṣa);
thus, six minds are acquired.
In the state where a defiled mind of the form realm is actually present, six minds are also acquired among the twelve minds.
Through falling back from a realm, one acquires one type of non-obscured-neutral mind of the desire realm and three types of the form realm.

Furthermore, through falling back due to the arising of afflictions, one who has a defiled mind of the form realm also acquires one type of obscured mind of the formless realm and the mind of a learner (śaikṣa).
Therefore, it is said that six [minds] are acquired.

In the state where a defiled mind of the formless realm is actually present, only two minds among the twelve are acquired: because one acquires that defiled mind through the arising of afflictions and regression, and because one acquires the mind of a learner (śaikṣa), it is said that two are acquired.

In the state where a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is currently manifest, twelve minds can obtain three minds as their acquisitions (*prāpti*): namely, that wholesome mind itself, as well as the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms, due to the process of spiritual advancement (*abhyudgama*).

When a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is present before one, among the twelve types of minds, four are acquired: namely, the mind of one in training, the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms, and the wholesome mind of the formless realm.

This occurs by virtue of first entering the state of rightness and separation from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti*), as well as by virtue of becoming free from the defilements of the desire and form realms through the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).

"The rest" refers to the minds other than those previously mentioned, such as the defiled and so forth; it does not refer to attaining a distinction of mind at the moment when those [defiled] minds are actually manifest.
It should be understood that when that mind is manifesting before one, it can be apprehended only by itself.
Regarding this, others have stated the following in summary verse:
The wise say that when a defiled mind arises, nine [minds] are acquired;
in a wholesome mind, six are acquired; and in an indeterminate mind, only the indeterminate is acquired.

Regarding the wholesome mind, one should say that seven are acquired; this means that at the stage when the roots of goodness are reconnected through right view, the arising of a desire-realm wholesome mind is termed "acquisition."
In the final stage of being completely free from the defilements of the desire realm, one simultaneously attains the non-obscured, neutral [minds] of the desire and form realms.
When one attains the samādhis of the form and formless realms, those two wholesome minds are said to be "attained."

When first entering the stage of being free from birth (*vairāgya-bhūmi*) and realizing arhatship, the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are said to be "attained.
The characteristics of other cases should be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation.
To summarize the foregoing meaning, another verse is spoken:
Because they are acquired at the moments of conception, entering meditative absorption, becoming free from defilement, and falling away from it—
specifically during the state of restoring the roots of goodness— they are not states already previously established.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Seven, Sarvāstivāda School.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

3. Chapter on the Analysis of the World (Lokanirdeśa), Part One. Having already analyzed the mind and other factors according to the three realms, it should now be explained: what are these three realms?
How many distinct locations are there within each of these?
The verse says:
Hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, Humans, and the six heavens of the desire realm.
The Desire Realm is said to consist of twenty places, distinguished by the differences among the hells and continents.
Above this, seventeen locations constitute the Form Realm;
therein, each of the first three dhyānas has three levels, while the fourth dhyāna has eight.
In the formless realm there is no location; it is by way of birth that there are four types [of existence].
Relying upon the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita*), they cause the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession.
The treatise says:
The four [realms] beginning with the hells, together with the six heavens of the desire realm and the receptacle world, are called the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the six heavens of the desire realm: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*);
second, the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).
3. The Yāma Heaven; 4. the Tuṣita Heaven;
5. the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
Sixth, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Thus, how many distinct locations are there in the Desire Realm?
Due to the differences among the hells and continents, there are twenty-eight great hells, which are termed the distinctions of the hells.

1. The Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva), 2. the Black Rope Hell (Kālasūtra), 3. the Crushing Hell (Saṃghāta), 4. the Howling Hell (Raurava), 5. the Great Howling Hell (Mahāraurava), 6. the Heating Hell (Tapana), 7. the Great Heating Hell (Pratāpana), and 8. the Uninterrupted Hell (Avīci).
Regarding the distinction of the continents, they are the four great continents:
first, Jambudvīpa; second, Pūrvavideha; third, Aparagoyānī; and fourth, Uttarakuru.
Thus, these twelve realms, together with the six heavens of the desire realm, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts, constitute twenty.

Whether it be the realm of sentient beings, from the Heaven of Great Power (*Īśvara*) down to the Avīci Hell, or the receptacle world, down to the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), all are subsumed within the desire realm.

Above this Desire Realm, there are seventeen locations; that is, each of the three dhyāna levels has three, while the fourth dhyāna level alone has eight. These environments and sentient beings are collectively termed the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
The first dhyāna stage consists of three [levels]: first, the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapārṣadya); second, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (Brahmapurohita);

and third, the Great Brahma Heaven (Mahābrahmā). The second dhyāna stage consists of three [levels]: first, the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha); second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha); and third, the Heaven of Utmost Purity of Light (Ābhāsvara).

The third dhyāna stage consists of three [levels]: first, the Heaven of Limited Purity; second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity; and third, the Heaven of Universal Purity. The fourth dhyāna stage consists of eight [levels]:

first, the Cloudless Heaven; second, the Heaven of Merit-Born; third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit; fourth, the Heaven Free from Affliction; fifth, the Heaven Free from Heat; sixth, the Heaven of Excellent Manifestation; seventh, the Heaven of Excellent Vision; and eighth, the Heaven of the Ultimate Form.
The great masters of Kaśmīra all say that there are only sixteen locations in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
They maintain:

Within the realm of the Brahmā-purohita devas, there is a lofty terrace named Mahābrahmā, the dwelling place of the sole sovereign; it does not constitute a separate location, just as when a venerable one sits upon a throne surrounded by the fourfold assembly.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no locations whatsoever; for formless phenomena have no spatial dimension. It is a settled principle that past and future phenomena, as well as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and formless phenomena, do not abide in any spatial location.
However, there are four distinctions among those born of maturation (*vipākaja*):

first, the sphere of infinite space; second, the sphere of infinite consciousness; third, the sphere of nothingness; and fourth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These four types are called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These four [meditative attainments] do not differ in terms of superiority or inferiority due to their spatial location; rather, such distinctions arise solely from the nature of their rebirth.
Furthermore, how is it known that they lack spatial location?
It is because one who attains these meditative absorptions in a particular place is reborn in that very same place immediately upon the end of life.
Furthermore, when one passes away from that realm and is born into the desire or form realms, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises precisely at that location.
This is because, just as all sentient beings in the form realm must rely upon a physical body for the continuity of the mind and other factors.
Regarding sentient beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), upon what do their mental states and so forth depend for their continuity?
The masters of the Abhidharma state that those mental states and so forth depend upon the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) for their continuity.
If that is so, why do the minds and other mental factors of sentient beings with form not simply depend on this [vitality] and [mind] alone for their continuity?
Because these two are inferior in the realm of form.
For what reason are these two stronger in the formless realm?
Since those two realms arise from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are able to suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) by means of those attainments (*samāpatti*).
If that is so, since the continuum of mind and so forth in those realms depends solely on superior concentration, what need is there for a separate basis?

Furthermore, it should now be explained: just as for sentient beings born in the form realm, their homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) function in dependence upon form, what do these two depend upon in the formless realm?
These two revolve in mutual dependence upon one another.
Why do these two not depend [on each other] when form exists?
Because these two are inferior when born within the realm of form.
Why are these two [factors] so powerful in the formless realm?
Because those two types [of factors] in that realm arise from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As previously stated, that concentration is able to suppress the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*); thus, this returns to the same difficulty regarding the continuity of mental states.

Alternatively, since the mind and mental factors depend solely upon one another, the Sautrāntika masters maintain that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the continuity of the mind and its associates has no separate basis.

That is to say, if a cause that has not yet abandoned craving for form (*rūparāga*) gives rise to the mind and its associates, the induced mind and its associates arise simultaneously with form and function in dependence upon form.

If, having become detached from form (*rūpa*) due to causes, one turns away from form with revulsion, then the mind and its concomitants (*citta-caitta*) that are thus induced do not arise simultaneously with form nor do they depend upon form for their operation.
Why, then, are they called the three realms, such as the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)?
It is called a *dhātu* (element) because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or because it signifies a lineage (*gotra*), as has already been explained previously.

The realm to which desire belongs is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); the realm to which form belongs is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is stated by omitting the intermediate term, just as one says "pepper drink" or "diamond ring."
Because form (*rūpa*) does not exist within that realm, it is called "formless" (*ārūpya*).
What is termed "form" has the meaning of "changeable and obstructive" (*rūpaṇā*), or the meaning of "manifestation.
Since its essence is not form, it is designated by the name "formless"; it is not the case that its essence consists merely in the absence of form.
The realm to which the formless belongs is called the "formless realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*); this is an abbreviation of the middle term, as previously explained by analogy.
Furthermore, the realm of desire is named the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*), because the power of this realm is able to sustain desire.
It should be understood that the same applies to the form and formless realms.
In this context, what is meant by the term "desire"?
Briefly stated, it refers to craving induced by edible food and sexual intercourse.
As a verse in the Sūtra says:
"The various exquisite objects of the world are not true desire; True desire refers to the greed of human conceptualization.
Exquisite objects remain as they are in the world, But the wise have already eliminated desire for them."
The Ājīvika heretic then rebuked the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"If sublime worldly objects are not true desire, And you say that desire is the greed of human conceptualization,
Then a bhikṣu should be called one who experiences desire, Because he gives rise to evil conceptualizations and discursive thoughts."
Then Śāriputra countered him with these words:
"If the sublime objects of the world were true desire, And you claim that desire is not the craving resulting from human conceptualization,
Then your teacher should be called one who indulges in desire, Because he constantly contemplates pleasing and sublime forms."
If a phenomenon manifests within those three realms, is that phenomenon said to be bound to the three realms?
Not so. How is it that among them, that which increases the craving for the three realms is what is bound to the three realms?
Among these, what dharma is called "craving for the three realms"?
It refers to that which increases in accordance with each [of the realms] within the three realms. What is now being stated is like the answer to the question of who it is that binds the horse.
It is just as if someone were asked, "Who is it that binds the horse? and the reply were given accordingly.
He replied, "The owner of the horse.
He then asked again, "Who is the owner of the horse?
He replied, "The one who bound it."
Thus, both of these answers fail to provide understanding.

What is now stated differs from those answers: regarding those previously mentioned who have not yet abandoned craving for the various realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), that craving is termed "desire-craving" (*kāmarāga*); that which increases in accordance with this [craving] is called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyukta*).
Regarding the previously mentioned form and formless realms, it should be understood that the same applies accordingly.

Alternatively, craving belonging to the non-concentrated states is called "craving for sense-desires" (*kāmarāga*); that which increases in accordance with this is termed "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
The craving for the various dhyāna stages is called craving for the form realm; that which is increased by this [craving] is termed "bound to the form realm.
The craving for the various formless stages is called craving for the formless realm; that which is increased by this [craving] is termed "bound to the formless realm."
How does desire-attachment arise toward a mind that has been transformed by desire?
It arises because one hears of it from others, or because one generates a relish for it through the occurrence of one's own retrogression;
or else, it arises because one observes the sovereign power of the transformer and consequently conceives craving and attachment for that transformed mind.

If a mind can transform the two dharmas of fragrance and taste, this transforming mind belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), because a mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) cannot produce fragrance or taste.
Are there thus only one [type of] mind in each of the three realms?

The three realms are as boundless as the measure of space; therefore, although there are no sentient beings who first arise, immeasurable and infinite Buddhas appear in the world, each transforming and delivering countless sentient beings, causing them to realize the realm of nirvana without remainder, yet they are never exhausted, remaining just like space.
How should one say that the world abides?
It should be said that it abides horizontally; thus the Sūtra says:
"For example, when the heavens rain, the drops are like the axles of chariots, falling from the sky without interval and without interruption."

In this way, in the eastern direction, there are immeasurable worlds, without interval or interruption, either undergoing destruction or undergoing formation; as it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, and north—though the zenith and nadir are not mentioned.
Some say there are also the two directions of above and below, because the sūtras of other schools speak of the ten directions.
Thus, there is a desire realm (kāmadhātu) above the Akaniṣṭha heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha heaven is below the desire realm.
If one becomes detached from the craving of even a single realm within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all cravings of the desire realm are thereby extinguished and abandoned.
It should be understood that the same applies to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*).

When supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) is produced based on the first dhyāna, the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) it emits can only reach the Brahma-world of the realm in which one was born, and not others; it should be understood that the same applies to the remaining types of supernormal knowledge.
The three realms have already been explained.
What are the five destinies?
The verse says:
Among these, the hells and so forth are designated by their own names as the five destinies (*gati*).
They are exclusively non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), pertaining to sentient beings, and do not include the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The treatise says:

Within the three realms, it is said that there are five destinies (*gati*), which are as they are named: namely, those previously mentioned—hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods—are called the five destinies.
Only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are the four destinies (*gati*) complete; each of the three realms contains a portion of the heavenly destiny (*devagati*).
Are there portions of the three realms not subsumed under the destinies, such that one speaks of five destinies within the realms?

There are [states] that exist—namely, the wholesome, the defiled, the external receptacle world, and the intermediate state—which, although being of the nature of realms (*dhātu*), are not included within the destinies (*gati*).

The essential nature of the five destinies is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); for if it were otherwise, the destinies would become intermingled, since the karma and afflictions of all five destinies would be present within a single destiny.
The five destinies (gati) are comprised exclusively of sentient beings and do not, in their essence, include the intermediate state (antarābhava).
The *Prajñaptipāda-śāstra* states:
"The four modes of birth (yoni) encompass the five destinies, but the five destinies do not encompass the four modes of birth."
What is not included?
It is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The *Dharmaskandhapāda-śāstra* also states this:
What is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
It refers to the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) derived from the four great elements, which is the eye, the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*), and the eye-element.
It exists in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods, as well as in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) produced through cultivation.
The sūtras also distinguish the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from other destinies.
Which sūtra is this? It is the *Saptabhavasūtra*.

He speaks of seven types of existence: namely, existence as a hell-being, existence as an animal, existence as a hungry ghost, existence as a deity, existence as a human, karmic existence, and intermediate existence.

In that sūtra, the five destinies (*gati*), their causes, and the means for reaching those destinies are explained; therefore, it is established as a fundamental principle that the destinies themselves are exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This is because they are distinguished from karma and its causes, which are distinct from the destinies.
The Sūtra is recited in this manner in the kingdom of Kaśmīra:
the Venerable Śāriputra spoke these words:
"O Āyuṣmat!"

If, due to the manifestation of various outflows (*āsrava*) pertaining to hell, one performs and increases karma conducive to retribution in hell, then because of the crookedness, filth, and turbidity of that body, speech, and mind, one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) within the *naraka*. Once this maturation has arisen, it is designated as "hell" (*naraka*); apart from these phenomena consisting of the five aggregates, that hell is entirely non-existent.
Therefore, the destinies (*gati*) are exclusively non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
If this is so, how is one to reconcile this with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*,
which states that all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with all five destinies?

That [author] states that within the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the five destinies (*gati*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five categories and the mind of entry may be present;
to speak of them collectively as "destinies" involves no contradiction or error.
For example, both a village and its outskirts are collectively called a "village.
Some say that the substance of the "path" (gati) also includes both the wholesome and the defiled.
However, as for the *Saptabhava-sūtra*’s exclusion of *karmabhava*, it is because it is mentioned separately; therefore, it certainly is not included therein.

This is just as, among the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are mentioned separately as distinct corruptions; because they are mentioned separately, those views certainly are not included within the category of afflictions.
Although such karma and existence (*bhava*) are also types of destinies (*gati*), they are mentioned separately in order to clarify the causes of those destinies.
If that were so, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would also have to be a destiny;
however, it is not, because it does not correspond to the definition of a destiny.
A "destination" (gati) refers to that which is gone toward; one cannot say that the intermediate state (antarābhava) is a destination, because it arises at the very place where death occurs.
If that were so, then the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) would also not be destinations, since birth is experienced right at the place of death.
Since this is so, that which is called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava) should not be called a "destination" (gati).

It is named "intermediate existence" because it exists between two destinations; if it were included within a destination rather than being intermediate, then it should not be called "intermediate existence."

However, when that Venerable Śāriputra said, "Once the maturation has arisen, it is called hell," he was stating that only when the maturation arises is it designated as hell; he was not saying that hell consists exclusively of maturation.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "apart from the phenomena of the five aggregates, that hell-being (nāraka) cannot be found," this was said in order to refute the notion of a substantially existent *pudgala* who transmigrates through the various realms of existence; it was not said to refute the other aggregates.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state:
"The destinies (gati) are exclusively non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta). Some say:
It is exclusively born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Other masters state that it also includes that which is nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Within the three realms and five destinies, there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) respectively.
What are these seven?
The verse says:
Different bodies and different perceptions; different bodies and the same perception;
the reverse of these, with the same body and same perception; and the three lower formless realms—thus there are seven stations of consciousness.
The others are not, because they involve affliction and destruction.
The Treatise says:

The Sūtras state that there are sentient beings with form who possess diversity of body and diversity of perception, such as humans and a portion of the gods; this is the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
"A portion of the gods" refers to the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those of the first dhyāna, excluding those who arose at the beginning of the kalpa.
Regarding the term "diversity of body" (*nānātva-kāya*): it refers to the various colors, forms, and physical features of their material bodies (*rūpa-kāya*).
Because they possess such diversity of body, or because some have different bodies, those sentient beings are said to be "of diverse bodies."
Regarding "diversity of perception" (*saṃjñā-nānātva*): it refers to the differentiation of perceptions of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Because they possess such diversity of perception, or because they have various distinct perceptions, those sentient beings are said to be "of diverse perception."
There are sentient beings with form who differ in body but are uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-group at the beginning of a kalpa;
this is the second station of consciousness.
Why is this so? Because at the beginning of the kalpa, those gods of the Brahma-group give rise to this perception: [“We are the creators of these worlds”].
"We were all born from Mahābrahmā.
At that time, Mahābrahmā also gave rise to this thought:
'This entire assembly of Brahmās was born from me.'"
They are called "uniform in perception" because they share a single cause for their perception.

As for the Great Brahmā King, his body is vast in height and breadth, and his features, majesty, speech, radiance, clothing, and ornaments are each distinct from those of the Brahma assembly; therefore, he is called "different in body."
The Sūtra says:
The Brahmakāyika deities had this thought:
"We have previously seen such sentient beings who were long-lived and remained for a long time," and so on, until they gave rise to this aspiration: [I wish to be born here].
"How might we cause other sentient beings to be born into our own class?
As they correctly give rise to this aspiration, we are then born within that same class.
Where did the Brahmakāyika gods previously see the Brahmā King?
Other masters say:
