they resided in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; having passed away from that heaven, they were reborn here.
How is it that at this time, without having attained the second dhyāna, one is able to recollect the past lives of that realm?
And if he had already attained the second dhyāna, how could he still give rise to the grasping of rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) directed toward Mahābrahmā?
Other masters say:
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no sense of remaining there for a long duration, because there are no obstacles to taking rebirth.
How could the Brahmakāyika gods form the thought:
"We have previously seen such sentient beings living for a long time"?

Therefore, while dwelling in their own heaven, the Brahmakāyikas recollect the events experienced in this previous life; that is to say, having first seen them living for a long time, they later see them again and give rise to this thought.
There are beings with form who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is the third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Here, by mentioning the latter [category], the former is also included; it should be understood that this fully encompasses the second dhyāna.
If it were not so, under which consciousness-dwelling (*vijñānasthiti*) would those gods of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) and Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*) be subsumed?
Since those gods do not differ in their manifested forms, shapes, and appearances, they are said to have "a single body" (*ekakāya*).
Because the two perceptions of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure alternate and intermingle, it is called "diversity of perception.

According to tradition, those gods, having become weary of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) of the fundamental stage, give rise to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) which manifests before them;
and having become weary of the faculty of equanimity of the preparatory stage, they give rise to the faculty of joy of the fundamental stage which manifests before them.
Just as a wealthy person, having become weary of sensual pleasures, experiences the joy of the Dharma, and having become weary of the joy of the Dharma, returns to sensual pleasures—
would it not be the case that the perception of universal purity should likewise be so?
The Śubhakṛtsna gods have never experienced weariness with pleasure, for they have never known a time of weariness with the tranquility of bliss;
this is not the case with joy (*prīti*), because it agitates the mind.
The Sautrāntika masters say:

Another sutra explains the meaning of "diversity of perception" among those gods as follows: there are newly born gods in the Ābhāsvara Heaven who have not yet fully understood the formation and destruction of the world.
He saw the flames of the lower realms blazing intensely; having seen this, he was struck with terror and revulsion, thinking:
"Lest those flames consume the Brahma palace until it is utterly empty and then invade my own abode."
Among those gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven who had been born there previously, some who were already well-versed in the formation and destruction of the world consoled those terrified gods, saying:
"O Pure Sages! O Pure Sages!"
"Do not fear, do not fear!
Formerly, when those flames burned away the Brahma-palace until it was entirely empty, they were extinguished right there.

They are called 'diversity of perception' (saṃjñā-nānātva) because they have the perception of the flames coming or not coming, and the perception of fearing them or not fearing them; it is not because of the presence of perceptions of pleasure or neither-pleasure-nor-pain that they receive the name 'diversity of perception' through their mutual intermingling."

There are beings with form who possess a single body and a single perception, such as the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; this is the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Because they possess only the perception of pleasure, they are said to have a single perception (*ekasaṃjñin*).

In the first dhyāna, they are said to have a single perception because of the defiled perception; in the second dhyāna, they are said to have diverse perceptions because of the two wholesome perceptions; and in the third dhyāna, they are said to have a single perception because of the ripened (*vipāka*) perception. The names of the three lower formless realms are distinct [from these]; thus, including those three stations of consciousness mentioned in the Sūtra, there are seven.
Among these, what dharma is called a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)?
It refers to the five aggregates or four aggregates associated with those [stations], as appropriate; these are called stations of consciousness.
For what reason are the remaining ones not stations of consciousness?
Because in other places there are factors that impair consciousness.
What are these other places?
They are the various evil realms, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
Why is this so? Because those places contain factors that impair consciousness, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
What are the factors that impair consciousness?

This means that in the various evil realms there are intense painful sensations capable of impairing consciousness; in the fourth dhyāna there is the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*); and in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) there is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which can destroy consciousness and cause its continuity to be severed. Therefore, these are not abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
It is further stated:

"If there is a place where sentient beings from other locations take pleasure in coming to dwell, and once they have arrived there, do not seek to depart, it is called a 'station of consciousness' (*vijñānasthiti*).
In the various evil realms (*apāya*), neither of these two conditions exists."

The mind of the fourth dhyāna constantly seeks an exit: ordinary beings seek to enter the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); noble ones (*ārya*) delight in entering the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) or the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*); and the gods of the Pure Abodes delight in realizing cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is dull and inferior, it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Having thus analyzed the seven stations of consciousness,
there are further explained on this basis the nine abodes of sentient beings.
What are these nine?
The verse says:
One should know that together with the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), these are the nine abodes of sentient beings;
the others are not so, because they are not places where one dwells with pleasure.
The treatise states:

The seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the first formless realm (*bhavāgra*), and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*)—these nine are called the abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*), because all classes of sentient beings find delight in dwelling only within these nine.
Other places are not [such], because beings do not delight in dwelling there.

By "other places" is meant the various evil realms; these are not locations where sentient beings choose to reside of their own accord, for they are forced to dwell there by the rākṣasas of their own evil karma.
Like a prison, that [level] does not establish a dwelling for sentient beings.

With the exception of the Heaven of Non-conception, the remaining levels of the fourth dhyāna are not dwellings for sentient beings, as explained in the section on the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The sūtra cited previously speaks of the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Furthermore, another sūtra speaks of four stations of consciousness.
What are these four?
The verse says:
The four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*) should be known as being only the four aggregates (*skandha*) of their own respective levels;
consciousness alone is said not to be a station. They are comprised within the four categories of the outflowing (*sāsrava*).
The treatise says:
As stated in the Sūtra:

"Consciousness dwells in dependence upon form; consciousness dwells in dependence upon feeling; consciousness dwells in dependence upon perception; consciousness dwells in dependence upon formations—these are called the four kinds."
What is the nature of these four?
They consist, respectively, of the four contaminated aggregates (*skandha*).

Furthermore, these exist only within their own respective levels and not elsewhere, because they are called "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñāna-sthiti*) as they are that upon which consciousness relies and clings.
It is not the case that consciousness adheres to the aggregates of form and so forth belonging to other stages through the power of craving;
why then is consciousness not said to be a station of consciousness?
Because a "station" is established only by way of excluding that which is the "dweller."
The consciousness that is the agent of abiding cannot itself be called the "abode," just as a king cannot be called the "king's throne.
Alternatively, if there is a phenomenon upon which consciousness rides or controls, it is designated as a "station of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti) according to the analogy of a person in a boat.
Consciousness itself cannot ride upon or control its own substance; therefore, consciousness is not said to be a station of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*).
Such is the teaching of the Vaibhāṣika masters.
If that is so, why does another sūtra state:
Within the nutriment of consciousness (vijñānāhāra), there is delight and attachment; because there is delight and attachment, consciousness dwells therein and is carried by it.
Furthermore, how can it be said that the first seven stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) have the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as their essence?
Although this is said, it does not analyze the aggregates included within the place of birth separately, because joy and defilement arise collectively therein.
When consciousness evolves, it is also called a "station of consciousness" (vijñānasthiti), and it is not consciousness alone that is so described.

However, each of the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*) can individually give rise to various forms of delight and defilement, causing consciousness (*vijñāna*) to rely upon and adhere to them; consciousness alone does not do so, and is therefore said not to "abide.
Thus, within these four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness does not abide in consciousness itself, though it may be so described in relation to the others.

Furthermore, the Buddha’s intention was to state that these four stations of consciousness are like fertile fields, while all consciousnesses accompanied by grasping are collectively described as being like seeds; it is not possible for seeds themselves to be established as fertile fields.
I respectfully infer that the Blessed One’s intended meaning of the teaching is as follows:

Furthermore, while mental factors (*dharma*) and consciousness can arise simultaneously, they serve as the fertile field for consciousness and may thus be established as "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), however, is not so; therefore, it is not an abode of consciousness.
Regarding these seven kinds and four kinds of stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) thus described, although they differ, all are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Do the seven subsume the four, or do the four subsume the seven?
They do not subsume one another exhaustively.
This can be formulated as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

That is to say, by carefully examining the two gateways of the essential natures (*svabhāva*), one should know that their mutual breadth and narrowness allow for the formation of four propositions; there may also be cases where something is subsumed by the seven categories but not by the four, and so forth.
The first phrase refers to consciousness among the seven [elements].
The second phrase refers to the remaining aggregates—excluding consciousness—within the various evil realms, the fourth dhyāna, and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The third phrase refers to the four aggregates among the seven [factors].
The fourth phrase refers to that which excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
Within the realms and destinies previously described, one should know that birth is, in brief, of four kinds.
What are the four?
In what location is what present?
The verse says:
Within this, there are four modes of birth; sentient beings are categorized as egg-born and so forth.
Humans and animals possess all four; hell-beings, the various devas, and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are born only by transformation (*upapāduka*);
hungry ghosts admit of both womb-birth and transformation-birth.
The treatise says:
It refers to the classes of sentient beings—those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation; these are called the four.
"Birth" (jāti) refers to the category of birth.
Although there are various other types among sentient beings, they are equal in their birth-class.
What is birth from an egg?
It refers to those classes of sentient beings who are born from an eggshell; this is called birth from an egg, such as geese, peacocks, parrots, wild geese, and so forth.
What is birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*)?
It refers to those classes of sentient beings who are born from a fetal sac; these are called womb-born, such as elephants, horses, oxen, pigs, sheep, donkeys, and so forth.
What is moisture-born (*saṃsveda-ja*)?
That is to say, those classes of sentient beings who are born from moisture are called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*), such as insects, moths, mosquitoes, and centipedes.
What is birth by transformation (*upapāduka*)?

It refers to those classes of sentient beings whose birth has no physical support; they are called transformation-born, such as those in the hells, the gods, and intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*). Their sense faculties are complete and their limbs are produced instantaneously; because they arise suddenly where there was nothing before, it is called "transformation."
The human and animal realms each possess four modes of birth.

Regarding humans born from eggs: these refer to those such as Śaila and Upaśaila, who were born from crane eggs; the thirty-two sons born of Mṛgāramātā; and the five hundred sons of King Pañcāla, and others like them.
Those born from human wombs are like the people of the present day.
Those born from moisture are like Māndhātṛ, Cāru, Upacāru, Kapotamālinī, Āmrapālī, and others.
Those born by transformation are exclusively the humans at the beginning of a kalpa.
Animals are of three kinds, as commonly observed in the world.
Those born by transformation include beings such as nāgas and garuḍas.
All beings in the various hells, the heavens, and the intermediate state (antarābhava) are born exclusively by transformation (upapāduka).
The realm of hungry ghosts (preta) admits of both birth from a womb and transformation.
Regarding those born from a womb, as the female hungry ghost said to Maudgalyāyana:
At night I give birth to five sons, and as soon as they are born, I eat them myself;
likewise by day I give birth to five, and though they are all consumed, I am never satiated.
Among all forms of birth, which is the most excellent?
It should be said that the most excellent [beings] are born solely by transformation.
If this is so, for what reason does a Bodhisattva in his final birth, who has attained mastery over birth, undergo birth from a womb?
It is because there is great benefit in manifestly undergoing womb-birth; specifically, it is to lead the great Śākya clan and their relatives into the True Dharma by means of mutual affinity.

Furthermore, by citing other examples, he causes those of similar class to recognize that the Bodhisattva is born of the lineage of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), thereby engendering a heart of reverence and admiration; through this, they are able to abandon what is erroneous and proceed toward the True Dharma.
Moreover, it causes those being converted to give rise to a superior resolve:
"Since he was merely a human being, he was able to accomplish such great purpose."
We are just like this; why can we not arouse right diligence and single-mindedly cultivate the True Dharma?
Furthermore, if it were otherwise, our noble lineage would be difficult to discern, and one might fear suspecting us to be illusory transformations, whether gods or ghosts.
As the treatises of the non-Buddhists falsely contrive slanderous claims, saying:
"After more than a hundred kalpas, a great illusionist shall appear in the world to devour the world," he therefore undergoes birth from a womb to quell such doubts and slanders.
Other masters say:

He takes birth from a womb in order to leave behind his physical remains (śarīra-dhātu), so that immeasurable humans and various other species, by making offerings to them even once, may be reborn in the heavens a thousand times and attain liberation.
If one undergoes miraculous birth (upapāduka), there is no external seed; thus, as soon as the body perishes, nothing remains, just as when a lamp is extinguished, nothing more is seen.

If one believes that the Buddha possesses the supernormal power of sustaining vows (*dhṛti-praṇidhijñāna*) and can therefore long preserve his body, this does not constitute a valid explanation, as it leads from one argument to another.

If the body of a being born by transformation perishes without leaving a trace, like the extinguishing of a lamp’s light at death, why does the Sūtra state that a being born by transformation who is a *garuḍa* seizes a being born by transformation who is a *nāga* to serve as its food?
Because they do not know [the truth], they seize dragons for food, yet they do not say it is to satisfy hunger.
What fault is there in this?
Perhaps the dragon may temporarily satisfy their hunger before it dies, but once it has died, they become hungry again.
What fault is there in eating for a time!
Among the four modes of birth, which is the most numerous?
Only the transformation-born (upapāduka).
Why is this? Because a small portion of three destinies (*gati*), the entirety of two destinies, and all intermediate states of existence (*antarābhava*) are born by transformation (*upapāduka*).
In this context, what phenomenon is designated as the "intermediate state of existence"?
For what reason is the intermediate state (antarābhava) not itself called "birth" (jāti)?
The verse says:
Within the two states of death and birth, the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are termed the intermediate state.
"Because it has not yet reached the place it ought to reach, the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not [considered] birth.
The treatise says:

Following the existence at death (maraṇabhava) and prior to the existence at birth (upapattibhava), a self-body arises in the interval between them. This body arises in order to reach the place of birth; because it exists in the interval between two destinies (gati), it is called the intermediate state.
This body has already arisen; why then is it not called "birth"?
"Birth" refers to the place that ought to be reached in the future; the name "birth" is established based on the sense of reaching that destination.
Although the substance of this intermediate state (antarābhava) body has arisen, it has not yet reached that destination, and therefore it is not called "birth."
What is meant by "the place to which one shall go in the future"?
That for which the projected maturation (*vipāka*) has reached its ultimate and distinct completion is called "the place to which one shall go in the future.
Other schools say:

If it were the case that there is an interval or a severance between death and the place of rebirth, then there would be no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This should not be admitted. Why is that?
This is based on both reasoning and scripture.
What are the reasoning and scripture?
The verse says:

Just as with the continuity of grains and the like, which arise in uninterrupted succession at a location, the existence of a reflection as a real entity is not established; because it is not equivalent, it is not a valid analogy.
Two things cannot coexist in one place, nor can two things arise from a non-continuous [cause].
Because it is taught that there is the *gandharva*, and because of the five and seven sūtras.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, according to the correct principle (*nyāya*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not non-existent.
It is observed in the world that phenomena which proceed as a continuum must arise in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment.

For instance, just as with the continuum of grains and so forth in the world, the same principle applies to the continuum of sentient beings: they must arise in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment.
Is it not evident that there are phenomena which continue to arise even when there is an interval between them?
For example, an image arises from a substance by depending on a mirror or similar medium.
In this way, for sentient beings, there is the existence at death and the existence at birth; although there is an interval between these states, what prevents their continuity?
Because it is logically untenable that reflected images exist as real entities, and because they are not equivalent [to the subject], they fail as valid examples.
That is to say, the claim that a distinct form arises and is called an "image" is logically untenable in its substantial reality.
Since [the reflection] is established as being non-identical [to the original], it does not constitute a valid analogy.
As for the claim that the reflection is not an analogy because it is not established [as a real entity], this is because two things cannot coexist in a single location.

That is to say, although both the color of the mirror and its reflection are seen appearing together in one place, two material forms (*rūpa*) should not exist simultaneously in the same location, because they depend upon different primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, when the colors and shapes on both banks of a narrow body of water appear as two images simultaneously in the same location, those standing on opposite banks see them clearly and distinctly;
yet, at no single point are two colors seen together. Therefore, one should not claim that these two colors arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, shadow and light have never coexisted; yet we have seen a mirror suspended within a shadow, with the image of light clearly appearing upon its surface. One should not, on this basis, claim that both arise simultaneously.

Some may say that two things cannot coexist in one place; yet the moon and its reflection on the surface of a mirror are called "two," even though they are seen at different distances, like looking into a well. If they were indeed produced simultaneously, how could they be seen separately?
Therefore, one should know that these images do not exist in reality according to principle;

nevertheless, the power of the conjunction of various causes and conditions causes them to be seen in this way, for the functional capacities and distinctions of all phenomena are difficult to conceive.
Having already demonstrated that [the example] is not established and thus cannot serve as an analogy, it is further stated that it is also not an analogy because they are not equivalent.
This is because the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) do not constitute a single continuum.

That is to say, the original object and its reflection do not belong to one and the same continuum, because the reflection appears only in dependence upon a mirror or similar surface, and because the reflection and the original object exist simultaneously.

Just as death and birth constitute a single continuum that proceeds without interruption from one point to another and continues in a subsequent location, the relationship between a substance and its reflected image lacks such a continuum; because they are not similar, it does not constitute a valid analogy.
Furthermore, because a manifested image arises from two [causes], that is to say, images arise due to two conditions:
first, the original object (*bimba*); second, the mirror and so forth.

Between these two, the superior one is that upon which the image depends for its arising. While it is possible for an existence (*bhava*) to arise from two conditions, the existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*) has no such distinct superior basis. Therefore, the analogy cited is not equivalent to the phenomenon it illustrates.

Nor can it be said that external, insentient conditions such as semen and blood constitute the primary basis of existence; for since those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) appear suddenly in mid-air, what could be reckoned therein as the primary basis of existence?

Having already refuted that school’s position through correct reasoning—that there could be an interval between death and birth—it is therefore certain that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not non-existent.
Next, we shall establish the existence of the intermediate state by means of authoritative scripture (*āgama*). As a sutra states:
"There are seven types of existence (*bhava*): namely, the existences of the five destinies (*gati*), karmic existence (*karmabhava*), and intermediate existence."
If that school does not recite this sūtra, would they also not recite the *Gandharva Sūtra*?
As the sūtra says:

"For one to enter the mother’s womb, three conditions must be simultaneously present: first, the mother’s body must be in a state of seasonal fitness; second, the father and mother must be united in sexual union; and third, a gandharva must be present."
Excluding the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*), what kind of *gandharva* could there be?
Since the previous aggregates have already perished, how could anything manifest [in the present]?
If you do not recite this sutra, how then will you explain the *Aśvalāyanasūtra*?
As that sūtra says:
"Do you know now?
Is this gandharva appearing before you a brahmin, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra?"
Does it come from the east, or from the south, west, or north?
Since the preceding aggregates have already perished, one cannot say they "come"; thus, what is here called "coming" must necessarily refer to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, if one does not recite such sūtras, how would one explain the *Pañcānāgāmi-sūtra*?

As stated in the Sūtra: there are five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*): first, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*); second, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); third, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*); fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*); and fifth, those who stream upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
If the intermediate state did not exist, how could it be called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarā-parinirvāyin*)?
Other masters maintain:
there is a heaven named "Intermediate" (*antara*), and one who attains parinirvāṇa while dwelling there is therefore called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."
If that were so, one would have to admit the existence of gods such as those born with effort (*sābhisaṃskāropapadya*);
since this is not admitted, such a position is untenable.

Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of seven destinations for superior persons (*satpuruṣagati*), which are formed by dividing the first five [intermediate states] into three types of *antarāparinirvāyin*, based on the proximity, mediocrity, or distance of their location and time.
For example, when a small spark from a firebrand flies up, it is extinguished as soon as it has just arisen; such is the first type of virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*).
For example, when a small spark from heated iron flies up, it is extinguished after reaching the middle [of its flight]; such is the second type of virtuous person.
For example, when a great iron star breaks away from a fire, it is extinguished before it has fallen far; the three types of noble beings are likewise.

It is not that there exists a separate "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) as they maintain, characterized by distinctions of time, place, and the three categories [of beings]. Therefore, what they maintain is certainly not reasonable.
Others further state:

one who, either during the intermediate period of their lifespan or near the intermediate stage of heaven, severs the remaining afflictions and becomes an Arhat is called an "intermediate parinirvāyin."
Because one attains parinirvāṇa upon reaching the stage of the realm through either perception (*saṃjñā*) or vitarka, there are three grades:
first, one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately after taking up the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) of the form realm; this is called the first.
After that, having experienced celestial bliss, one then enters parinirvāṇa; this is called the second.
Furthermore, after this, one enters an assembly of celestial dharmas and then enters parinirvāṇa; this is called the third.
Having entered the assembly of the Dharma, one attains parinirvāṇa only after a long period has passed; this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).
Alternatively, because one attains parinirvāṇa after reducing much of one's lifespan rather than at the very moment of birth, it is therefore called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth."
What has been stated here is inconsistent with the analogy of the firebrand. Why is this?
Because there is no distinction in the movement within that place.

Furthermore, it should also be said that there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāṇa*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because there too one may attain parinirvāṇa during the interval of one’s lifespan.
However, it is not stated that there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state there, as it is said in the *Uddāna* verse:
“In total, all the noble sages are gathered; In each of the four dhyānas, there are ten.”
The three formless realms each have seven [levels], while there are only six for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, what they maintain is entirely false and illusory.

Furthermore, if one does not recite such sūtras as these, the Unsurpassed Dharma King has long since entered parinirvāṇa, and the great generals of the Dharma have also passed into parinirvāṇa. The holy teachings have become fragmented into many schools; divergent attachments to the literal text and its meaning race about, and the practice of accepting or rejecting according to one's own whims has grown increasingly prevalent today.
How lamentable it is that you stubbornly cling to ignorance and delusion, defying reason and rejecting the teachings; this is truly pitiable.
For those who rely upon the aforementioned principles and teachings as their authority, the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established as a reality.
If that is so, how is it that the Sūtra states that the Māra Dūṣī, having committed an extremely evil deed, fell into the Avīci Hell in his very own body?

The intention of this Sūtra is to say that even before he had relinquished his life-force, the fierce flames of hell had already scorched his body; because of this, at the end of his life, he took up an intermediate state (antarābhava), and by means of that, he fell into the Avīci Hell.

Because the power of those evil karmas is so intensified, the signs of suffering arrive even before the end of life; thus, one first undergoes the *pratyutpanna-vedanīya* (presently experienced) karma, and subsequently the *upapadya-vedanīya* (rebirth-experienced) karma.
Why, then, does the Sūtra state:
"A certain class of sentient beings, having committed and accumulated the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), will certainly be reborn in hell immediately thereafter"?
The intention of this sutra is to exclude those who would otherwise go to other realms and to demonstrate that their karma is certain to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).

If one were to adhere strictly to the literal wording, it would follow that one must possess all five factors to be born in hell; otherwise, there would be the great error of suggesting that the absence of even one factor or the presence of other karmic causes would prevent such birth.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who is born in the Avīci hell must be born immediately upon performing the act, without waiting for the disintegration of the body.
Or rather, who does not admit that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is a birth?

The term *naraka* (hell) also applies to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); when the intermediate state arises immediately after death (*cyuti-bhava*), it may also be called "birth" because it is the means for birth.
Thus, the Sūtra says that one is "born in hell without interval," but it does not mean that at that moment there is already the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*).
If that is so, how are the following scriptural verses to be reconciled? As the verse says:
"O Reborn One, you have now passed the peak of your vigor; having reached decline, you draw near to King Yama."
Desiring to proceed on the path ahead, one lacks the provisions; seeking to remain in the interim, there is nowhere to rest.
If an intermediate state (antarābhava) exists, why did the Blessed One say that in that interval there is nowhere to rest?
The meaning of this verse is to show that among humans, they quickly return to destruction without even a moment's pause.
Alternatively, it means that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) also does not remain stationary even while proceeding toward its place of rebirth, because its movement is unimpeded.
How do you know that the intent of the sutra is thus and not otherwise?
Furthermore, how do you know that it is otherwise and not thus?
Since both criticisms are equal, why do you single out one for interrogation?
Both interpretations are without contradiction regarding the sūtra; how then can one exclusively use it to prove that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not exist?
Generally, when a passage is cited as proof, its meaning must be consistent; since this passage has a different meaning, it cannot serve as valid proof.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Eight [continued] / Fascicle Nine,
composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: The Analysis of the World, Part Two. To which realm shall one go, and what is the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that arises?
The verse says:
Because this single karma projects [the existence], it has the form of the *pūrvakālabhava* (prior-time existence) as it will be;
"prior-time existence" refers to that which precedes death and follows the moment of birth.
The treatise says:
If a karma is capable of projecting one toward a future realm of rebirth (*gati*), that very karma also brings about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that travels there.
Therefore, when this intermediate state proceeds toward that realm, it takes on a form corresponding to the original form of the being destined for that realm.
If that were so, five types of intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) of the five destinies could arise simultaneously within the belly of a single dog or similar creature.
Since an intermediate being of the hell realm is already present there, why does it not burn the mother’s womb?
Does he not remain in his original existence without being constantly burned?
It is like briefly strolling in a garden; how much more so while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Even if one were to grant that it can burn, since the body of the intermediate state is extremely subtle, it is neither visible nor tangible; therefore, the objection is unreasonable.
Although the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of various destinies reside within a single womb, they do not touch or burn one another because they are shielded by karma.
While the size of an intermediate state in the desire realm is like that of a child five or six years old, its sense faculties are clear and sharp;

the intermediate state of a Bodhisattva, however, has the physical proportions and fullness of a person in the prime of life, endowed with all the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Therefore, when dwelling in the intermediate state and about to enter the womb, it illuminates hundreds of millions (*koṭi*) of the four great continents and so forth.
If that is so, why did the Bodhisattva’s mother see in a dream a white elephant calf entering her right side?
This auspicious omen does not pertain to the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Because the Bodhisattva has long since abandoned the realm of animals, he is like King Kṛkin who saw ten things in a dream:
namely, a great elephant, a well, flour, a sandalwood grove,
a small elephant, two monkeys, a broad and sturdy garment, and a quarrel.
Such dreams merely indicate omens of future events; they do not correspond exactly to what was seen.

Furthermore, all intermediate beings (*antarābhava*) enter through the birth canal rather than by breaking open the mother’s abdomen to enter the womb; therefore, among twins, the one born first is smaller and the one born later is larger.
How, furthermore, is the teaching of the Venerable Subhūti to be reconciled?
With the marks of a white elephant, dignified and majestic, Possessing six tusks and four feet,
he entered his mother’s womb with full awareness, Reclining like a sage hidden in a forest.
It is not necessary to provide an explanation, as these are not part of the Tripiṭaka.
Furthermore, some of these verses may exaggerate the facts.
If an explanation were strictly required—as in the case of the dream-omens seen by the Bodhisattva’s mother—there would be no fault in composing verses.
The intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) has a definite measure and is complete, just like the existence of the previous life.
It is born together with clothing; because shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*) are predominant there, the intermediate existence of a Bodhisattva is likewise accompanied by clothing.

Due to the power of her original vow, the Bhikṣuṇī Śvetā possessed natural garments in every lifetime that never left her body, changing according to the occasion; even at the time of her final parinirvāṇa, she wrapped her corpse in these very garments for cremation and burial.
The remaining intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are without clothing, because they all increase in a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
What is the nature of that which corresponds to the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*)?

It refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) prior to death-existence (*maraṇabhava*) and subsequent to birth-existence (*upapattibhava*); in brief, the nature of existence consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Within this, the states are analyzed into four distinct categories:
first, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the meaning of which is as previously explained;
second, the state of birth (*upapattibhava*), which refers to the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) within the various realms of existence.
Third is the existence of the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*), which refers to all positions other than the moment of birth and the period prior to death.
Fourth is the existence of death (*cyutibhava*), referring to the final moment preceding the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Sentient beings with form possess all four existences; if they are among those without form (*ārūpya*), they lack one and possess three.
The dimensions have already been explained; the remaining points shall now be analyzed.
The verse says:
Those of equal purity see with the divine eye; They possess supernormal power, speed, and complete faculties.
Without resistance and unchangeable, they feed on fragrance and do not remain long.
With inverted minds, they seek the realm of desire; those born from moisture or by transformation are stained by their respective fragrances.
The gods have their heads upward, the three [classes of humans] are horizontal, and the denizens of hell have their heads turned downward.
The treatise says:

Within this state, those with an intermediate body (antarābhava) see one another who belong to the same class; furthermore, those who have cultivated and attained the extremely pure divine eye (divyacakṣus) are also able to see them, whereas the eyes acquired through birth cannot perceive them, because they are exceedingly subtle.
Other masters say:
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the gods possesses eyes that are fully capable of seeing.

The intermediate states of the five destinies—humans, hungry ghosts (*preta*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), and hell-beings—see four, three, two, and one [respectively]; that is, they see from their own level downward, excluding those above.

Among all the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the power of action (*karmarddhi*) is the swiftest. To traverse space with mastery is the meaning of "power" (*ṛddhi*); because this power is derived from action, it is called the "power of action. Because the force and function of this power are rapid, it is termed "swift."

Among these, there are those who possess the most rapid karmic supernormal power (*karmarddhi*), such that even the World-Honored One cannot obstruct or suppress them, because the force of their karma is most powerful.

All intermediate states of existence (*antarābhava*) are endowed with the five sense faculties; "impingement" (*pratigha*) refers to physical resistance, and since these beings cannot be obstructed by things such as diamond, they are called "unimpeded" (*apratigha*).

It has been heard that when a glowing red iron mass is broken apart, worms are seen arising within it; therefore, once the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) has already arisen for a destination, no power of any kind can alter it—meaning one cannot cause the intermediate state of one being to vanish and the intermediate state of another to arise in its place—and the same applies to other categories as well.
Once the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for that destination has already arisen, one must go only to that place and certainly not to any other.
Does the body of the intermediate state of the desire realm subsist on solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)?
Although it does subsist on solid food, it is subtle and not coarse.
What is its subtle aspect?
It refers solely to the fragrance; it is for this reason that they receive the name *gandharva*.
Since the meanings within the verbal roots (*dhātu*) are not uniform, there is no fault in using a short vowel—as in the cases of *śakandhu* and *karkandhu*—as it is a matter of abbreviation.
Those with little merit consume only foul odors, while those with great merit take pleasant fragrances as their food.
How long does such an intermediate state (antarābhava) persist?
The Venerable One says:
This has no fixed limit.

As long as the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, the intermediate state (antarābhava) persists; this is because its life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is not projected by a separate karma, as it shares the same homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) with the beings of the destination where it is headed.

If it were otherwise, then at the moment when the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) finally ceases, one would have to establish it as the existence of death (*mṛtyubhava*).
Furthermore, even if there were a mass of flesh as vast as Mount Sumeru, during the summer rains it would turn into a swarm of worms.
One should ask: do all intermediate states (*antarābhava*) wait for this moment, or is it said that they come suddenly from some direction to this place?
Although there is no explicit textual judgment or explanation in the sūtras or treatises, according to correct reasoning, one should say this:

There are various classes of beings, infinite in number, who are attached to odors and flavors and possess short lifespans. Because those sentient beings smell this fragrance and crave its scent and flavor, they all die at once; due to their craving and the karma previously acquired for the body of an insect, they simultaneously receive the bodies of minute insects here.

Or, many sentient beings may be destined to be born here simultaneously; yet, because the necessary conditions have not converged, they remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and only now, encountering the convergence of many conditions, are they born here all at once.

Those who are destined to be born together certainly do not arise at different times; for example, there is karma capable of summoning a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) that only yields its fruit all at once when human life expectancy reaches eighty thousand years or exceeds it, and not at any other stage.
This should also be understood in the same way.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The differentiation of the karmic fruits of sentient beings is inconceivable."
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"This lasts for at most seven days; if the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged, one dies and is reborn repeatedly.
Other masters say:
At most, it lasts for seven weeks.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:

This dwelling is brief because, within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one seeks birth in existence with pleasure; therefore, one does not remain long, but quickly proceeds to link with rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*).

If the conditions for birth have arisen but have not yet converged, and if it is certain that one should be born in a particular place as a particular class of being, the power of karma will cause those conditions to converge.

If it is not certain that one must rely on these specific converging conditions, then one will instead take birth in another place as another class of being; some say that one may then receive a birth similar to the original one.
For instance, domestic cattle, dogs, bears, and horses increase in sequence during the summer, autumn, winter, and spring; whereas wild oxen, jackals, brown bears, and donkeys have no fixed season.
If those belonging to the first four groups do not encounter their proper time, they are successively reborn as members of the latter four corresponding species.
Is it not the case that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) necessarily lacks a commonality with the being to be born, since both are projected by a single karma?
How, then, can one say they undergo a "similar" rebirth?

Thus, for the sake of reaching its place of birth, the intermediate state first gives rise to perverted thoughts and rushes toward the objects of desire. By the power of karma, although its visual faculty remains at a distance, it is able to see the parents united at the place of birth and give rise to perverted thoughts: if male, it conceives male desire toward the mother; if female, it conceives female desire toward the father. Conversely, if it is neither, it conceives hatred toward both.
Therefore, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states as follows:
"At that time, the gandharva manifests one of two mental states, namely, either craving or aversion.
Due to the arising of these two inverted states of mind, he imagines that his own self is united with the object of his desire."

When the impurity that was loathed reaches the stage of the embryo, [the consciousness] thinks, "This is mine," and thus gives rise to joy and consolation; from this point on, the aggregates become thickened, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases, and once the state of birth (*upapattibhava*) has arisen, it is called "rebirth" (*pratisaṃdhi*).

If it is a male, it dwells in the mother’s womb resting against her right flank, facing her back, and crouching; if it is a female, it dwells in the mother’s womb resting against her left flank, facing her belly.
If it is neither male nor female, it dwells in the mother’s womb according to its inclination, abiding as it desires.
There is certainly no intermediate existence (antarābhava) that is neither female nor male, because the body of the intermediate existence necessarily possesses all the sense faculties.

Depending on whether one is female or male while in the intermediate existence, one enters the mother’s womb and dwells therein accordingly; subsequently, as the fetus develops, one may become a non-male (napuṃsaka).
Regarding this point, one should further investigate: does the physical basis of the sense faculties arise directly from the primary elements of the semen and blood through the power of karma?
Or do the primary elements that constitute a distinct basis for the sense faculties arise separately from karma and then abide supported by the semen and blood?

Some say: semen and blood themselves constitute the basis for the sense faculties; that is to say, the preceding intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which lacks sense faculties, ceases together with them, and that which subsequently possesses sense faculties arises in immediate succession, according to the principle of the cessation of a seed and the arising of a sprout.
For this reason, the first stage is called the *kalala*; it also perfectly accords with the phrasing of this sutra passage:
"The *kalala* is produced from the impurities of the father and mother.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] told the bhikṣus:
"For a long night, you have grasped and maintained drops of blood that increase into *kaṭasīs*.
Other masters say:
[these] arise from distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*)."
Just as worms arise separately from leaves or dung, the kalala is produced within a mass of impurities; therefore, it is said that the kalala is born from the impurities of the parents.
Thus, there is no contradiction with that sutra.
Thus far, the two modes of birth—womb-born and egg-born—have been explained; the others shall now be discussed in due order as appropriate.

As for moisture-born beings, they are born through attachment to odors; that is to say, by smelling from afar the fragrance of their place of birth, they immediately conceive a craving and go there to take birth. According to the requirements of their karma, these odors may be pure or foul.

If one is born by transformation (*upapāduka*), one is born because of being stained by attachment to a place; that is to say, having observed from afar and known the place where one is to be born, one immediately gives rise to craving and attachment and goes there to undergo birth. The purity or impurity of the place corresponds to what is required by one's karma.
Could it be that one also gives rise to attachment toward the hells?
There is no fault in the arising of such attachment due to the inversion of the mind.

That is to say, when in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one may see oneself being tormented by cold rain and freezing winds; seeing the blazing flames of a hot hell, one takes pleasure in the sensation of warmth and throws oneself into it.
Or one may see oneself being oppressed by hot winds and fierce fires, and seeing a cold hell, with a desire for coolness, one throws oneself into it.
The former masters have explained it thus:
because of seeing one's own previous actions, at the time when that karma ripens, one's own companions from that same class of beings rush toward that place together.

Furthermore, the intermediate state being of the gods rises upward with its head first, as if rising from a seat; those of humans, ghosts, and animals have modes of movement similar to those of humans and so forth;
while those of hell fall into it head-first with their feet upward.
Thus a gāthā says:
Falling headlong into hell, With feet above and head below,
Is the result of slandering the sages Who delight in tranquility and practice asceticism.
It was previously stated that one enters the mother’s womb with a perverted mind; is this necessarily the case for all intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*)? It is not so.
As the Sūtra says:
There are four ways of entering the womb. What are these four?
The verse says:
One is fully conscious upon entering; two and three are both [conscious] during staying and exiting;
the fourth is [conscious] in all stages; and those born from eggs are always without consciousness.
These first three types of entry into the womb refer to the Wheel-turning Kings and the two kinds of Buddhas.
Because both karma and wisdom are preeminent, four [types] and the remaining [types] arise in succession.
The treatise says:

There are sentient beings who have accumulated much meritorious karma and diligently cultivated mindfulness and wisdom; therefore, at the time of death and rebirth, they are sustained by the power of mindfulness and possess correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*) without confusion. Among them, some enter the womb with correct awareness, some remain in the womb with correct awareness while also entering, and some exit with correct awareness while also knowing the entry and the stay.
The use of the term "both" (or "simultaneously") is intended to show that what follows must necessarily include what precedes it.

There are sentient beings whose merit and wisdom are both meager; they lack correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*) during all three stages—entering, abiding, and emerging. If one lacks correct awareness upon entering, one will certainly do so while abiding and emerging. These four are stated in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the rules of metrical verse.
Those born from eggs are always devoid of consciousness during all stages, such as entering the womb;
how then can they be said to be "born from eggs" [if they emerge from them while unconscious]?
Regarding the statement "entering the womb," those born from eggs must necessarily enter the womb first.
Alternatively, this may refer to those who will be born from eggs in the future, as the Sūtra says:
"One performs conditioned [actions]."
The world also says:
"Cooking rice" or "grinding flour.
Therefore, it is said that there is no fault in [the statement that] those born from eggs enter the womb.
What constitutes correct or incorrect awareness during the three stages?

Briefly, when sentient beings possess meager merit, they give rise to perverted perceptions and conceptions upon entering the mother’s womb. They perceive great winds, rain, scorching heat, or bitter cold; or they perceive the clamor and intimidation of a vast army. Consequently, they see themselves entering thick grass, dense forests, leaf-huts, or straw-thatched huts, or taking refuge beneath trees or walls. While dwelling there, they perceive themselves as already staying within these places; and upon emerging, they perceive their bodies exiting from those locations.

If one's merit is great, upon entering the mother’s womb, one gives rise to inverted perceptions and conceptions, seeing oneself entering a magnificent garden, ascending a flowered terrace or palace, and dwelling upon an excellent couch; the process of remaining and emerging is as described before.
This is called being "unaware" during the three periods.

If one is able to maintain correct awareness throughout these three stages, one possesses non-erroneous perception and understanding at the times of entry and so forth; that is, at the stage of entering the womb, one knows one is entering the womb, and at the times of abiding and exiting the womb, one knows oneself abiding and exiting.

Furthermore, there is another classification that specifically displays four types of entry into the womb; for now, the first three types refer to the Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), the Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*), and the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*), respectively.

Regarding the first type of entry into the womb, this refers to the Wheel-turning King, who enters the womb with full awareness, but lacks such awareness while remaining in the womb or when departing from it.

Regarding the two types of entry into the womb: the first refers to the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), who possesses correct awareness during the stages of entering and abiding, but not during the stage of emerging.

The third type of entry into the womb refers to the Unsurpassed Enlightened One (Anuttarasamyaksambuddha), who is able to maintain correct awareness throughout the stages of entering, abiding, and emerging.
These first three are designated by their respective names.
For what reason are these three grades distinct?
It is because they are progressively superior in terms of karma, wisdom, and both combined, respectively.
First is the excellence of karma, meaning that because a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) has cultivated vast merit in past lives;
second is the excellence of wisdom, meaning that a Solitary Realizer (pratyekabuddha) has long practiced extensive learning and superior analytical discernment.
The third is superior in both [merit and wisdom], meaning that because the Unsurpassed Awakening (anuttara-bodhi) has cultivated superior merit and wisdom throughout vast eons.
Excluding these three types, the remaining beings born from wombs or eggs are inferior in both merit and wisdom, which together constitute the fourth category.
In this context, those non-Buddhists who cling to a self say:
"If you grant that sentient beings transmigrate to other worlds, then the existence of a self as we conceive it is established.
Now, to refute them, the verse says:
There is no self, only the aggregates, produced by afflictions and karma;
through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one enters the womb like a flame.
Like a drawn-out line, it gradually increases; this continuity proceeds by means of delusion and karma.
Proceeding further toward other worlds, there is thus a cycle that has no beginning.
The treatise says:
What are the characteristics of the "self" (ātman) as you conceive it?

The internal agent (*puruṣa*) who is able to relinquish these aggregates and continue others certainly does not exist, because it cannot be apprehended, just as [an agent distinct from] form, the eye, and so forth cannot be found.
The Blessed One has also said:
"There is karma and there is its maturation, but an agent cannot be found."
This refers to that which is able to relinquish these aggregates and is able to continue into other aggregates, setting aside the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*).
What is this conventional designation of phenomena?
It is the dependent origination explained at length: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises."
If that is so, what "self" is not being negated?
It is only the aggregates (skandhas); that is to say, it is only upon the aggregates that the designation "self" is conventionally established, and this is not what is being refuted.
If that is the case, you must then admit that the aggregates themselves pass from this world to another world.

The aggregates (*skandha*) perish moment by moment and lack the power to transmigrate; however, due to the habitual cultivation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, they cause the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to continue in succession and enter the womb.
This is like a lamp flame, which, although perishing moment by moment, is able to continue its transition to another location through succession.

The same applies to the aggregates (*skandha*): their transformation is designated without loss of identity. Thus, although there is no self (*anātman*), the principle that the aggregates continue in succession into the womb by means of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma is established.

Just as the succession of aggregates, drawn forth by karma, increases sequentially, they further proceed to another life through the power of afflictions and karma; for it is not the case that the duration of the growth and succession of all such drawn-forth aggregates is uniform, since there are differences in the causes of karma that project the lifespan (*āyuṣka-karman*).
It increases sequentially for as long as the force of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) remains predominant.
What is this sequence?
As the Noble One has said:
First is the kalala; next arises the arbuda;
from this is born the peśī, and from the peśī the ghana;
next is the praśākhā, followed by the hair, body hair, nails, and so forth.
As well as the physical faculties and their forms, they gradually increase.
Within the mother’s womb, there are five stages:
first, the *kalala* stage; second, the *arbuda* stage; third, the *peśī* stage; fourth, the *ghana* stage; and fifth, the *praśākhā* stage.

This arrow within the womb gradually increases until the stage where the physical sense organs and their forms are fully developed; then, by the power of the karmically produced winds of maturation (*vipākavāyu*), it turns the arrow within the womb toward the birth canal.
Just as when a hard mass of excrement is excessively compressed and obstructed, it then falls away with an agonizing pain that is unbearable;
so too, if the mother’s posture, diet, or activities become excessive, or due to the power of the child’s own past karmic deeds, the fetus may die within the womb.

At that time, there was a woman or perhaps a physician who was highly proficient in the methods of childbirth and skilled in nurturing infants; she warmed her hand with ghee and *śyāmāka* juice and applied it, then took up a small, sharp blade.

Internally, it is like a cesspool—most utterly base and filled with various impurities; it is a dwelling place of darkness, a refuge for immeasurable thousands of worms; foul fluids constantly flow, requiring perpetual counteraction; semen, blood, grime, and grease are putrid, rotted, stinking, and slippery; impurities overflow, so vile and loathsome as to be unbearable to behold, covered only by a thin, leaking skin upon its surface.
Drawn forth by the force of past karma, the limbs and joints are dismembered within the openings of the bodily sores and pulled out.
Yet, because this embryo is driven by the karma performed in previous lives that is to be experienced in subsequent existences, its destination is difficult to discern.
Alternatively, if he is born without difficulty and in safety, his body is like a fresh wound—delicate and soft, sensitive to touch.

Then, whether it be the mother out of love for her child or other women, they take him with both hands—which are as coarse and abrasive as knives or ashes—and wash and wipe him, placing him in a secure spot.

Next, having been nourished with clarified butter and breast milk, one is gradually led to habituate to fine and coarse foods; through successive increments until the faculties reach maturity, afflictions arise once more and various karmas are accumulated.
Due to this, upon the dissolution of the body, there is again a continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as before, leading further toward another world.

Thus, birth arises with afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma (*karman*) as its causes; birth, in turn, serves as the cause for the arising of afflictions and karma. From these afflictions and karma, there is yet again birth. Therefore, one knows that the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) revolves in a cycle without beginning.
If one maintains that there is a beginning, then that beginning must be without a cause;
if the beginning is without a cause, then all other things should arise spontaneously.
However, we observe that sprouts and the like arise from seeds and the like, because both their location and their timing are invariably determined.
Furthermore, since phenomena such as fire arise through processes like maturation and transformation, it is certain that no phenomenon arises without a cause.
Theories positing eternal causes have already been refuted as before.
Therefore, saṃsāra is definitely without a beginning, yet it has an end because its causes are exhausted.
Because birth depends upon its cause, when the cause perishes, the fruit that arises must necessarily cease; this principle is certain.
Just as a sprout will certainly not arise once the seed has perished, so too, regarding the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*), three lifetimes are designated as the stages.
The verse says:
Such dependent origination consists of twelve links across three time periods;
with two links each for the prior and posterior limits, eight are established for the middle based on completeness.
The treatise says:
As for the twelve links, the first is ignorance;
the second is volitional formations.
3. Consciousness;
4. Name-and-form;
5. The six sense bases;
6. Contact; 7. Feeling; 8. Craving;
9. Grasping; 10. Existence; 11. Birth;
Twelfth, old age and death.
Regarding the "three time periods," they are: first, the past limit; second, the future limit; and third, the middle limit—namely, the three lifetimes of the past, future, and present.
How are the twelve links established across the three time periods?
It means that two links are established for each of the prior and posterior limits, and eight links for the middle limit; thus, they constitute twelve.
Ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past limit; birth and old age and death belong to the future limit; the remaining eight factors belong to the middle limit.
Do all sentient beings possess these eight factors of the middle limit throughout this single lifetime?
Not all possess them in their entirety.
If that is so, why is it said that there are eight branches?
This is stated with reference to those who are complete.

The intention here is to say that a *pudgala* who passes through all stages is called "perfected" (*paripūrṇa*); this does not refer to those who die prematurely, nor to those in the form or formless realms, but refers only to *pudgalas* within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because it is stated in the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*.
Therein it is said that the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If consciousness were not to enter the womb, would it attain growth and expansion?"
"No, World-Honored One! ...
[and so on] as extensively explained."

Sometimes dependent origination is explained as having only two divisions: first, that which is subsumed under the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), and second, that which is subsumed under the posterior limit (*aparānta*).
The first seven members are subsumed under the prior limit, namely from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to sensation (*vedanā*);

the latter five members are subsumed under the posterior limit, namely from craving (*tṛṣṇā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). This is because they are subsumed into these two divisions of cause and effect belonging respectively to the prior and posterior limits.
What dharmas constitute the essential nature of the members beginning with ignorance?
The verse says:
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; the various past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*).
Consciousness is the aggregate at the moment of rebirth-linking; prior to the six sense bases is name-and-form.
From the arising of the eye and other faculties, the three [aggregates] precede the six sense bases.
Due to the difference in the causes of the three types of feeling, that which has not yet been discerned is called contact.
Prior to sensual craving, one experiences [feeling]; craving for the requisites of life is sensual craving.
To obtain various objects, one runs everywhere in pursuit; this is called "clinging.
"Existence" refers to that which truly creates karma that draws forth the fruits of future existence.
"Karmic formations shall have 'existence' as their name; reaching [the present], they shall undergo 'old age and death.
The commentary states:

Within the state of various afflictions during a previous birth, up until the ripening of the fruit in the present, this is collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because those [formations] function simultaneously with ignorance.
Because they manifest through the power of ignorance;
just as when it is said that "the king travels," this does not mean he has no attendants, but because the king is preeminent, he is generally referred to as "the king traveling.
Likewise, the states of karma such as merit in previous lives, up until the ripening of their fruit in the present, are collectively given the name "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
The phrase "the stage of the first link" flows through to old age and death.
At the very moment of linking rebirth within the mother’s womb and so forth, the five aggregates in that single kṣaṇa are called consciousness (vijñāna).
The various stages between the moment after the linking consciousness and before the arising of the six sense bases are collectively termed name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

In this context, it should be stated that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) exist prior to their full manifestation; however, the term "six" is used because it is established based on their completion.
Once the eyes and so forth have arisen, they receive the name "six sense bases" during the stage when the faculty, the object, and consciousness have not yet converged.

Having reached the convergence of the three [sense bases], yet not having yet discerned the distinctions among the causes of the three types of sensation, this stage is collectively termed *sparśa* (contact).
Having discerned the distinct characteristics of the causes of the three types of sensation, yet not having yet given rise to sensual desire, this stage is termed *vedanā* (feeling).
When one experiences the manifestation of sensual desire for exquisite requisites but has not yet extensively sought them, this stage is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
When one roams everywhere in pursuit of various superior and exquisite objects in order to obtain them, this stage is called *upādāna* (clinging).
Due to this pursuit, one accumulates karma that is capable of drawing forth the fruit of future existence; this stage is called "existence" (*bhava*).
By the power of this karma, when one passes away from this life and is about to link with future existence, this stage is called "birth" (*jāti*).

When the branch of birth occurs, it refers to the gradual increase following the moment of the present consciousness's arising, continuing until the stage of future feeling; this is collectively termed "aging and death.
Such aging and death correspond to the four branches of the present life: name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
The differentiation of the essential natures of the twelve links has been explained in this way.
Furthermore, there are four distinct types of dependent origination taught:
first, momentary (*kṣaṇika*); second, continuous (*sāmbandhika*); third, situational (*āvasthika*); and fourth, remote succession (*prākarṣika*).

What is a *kṣaṇa*? It refers to the moment when one commits killing out of desire, wherein twelve factors (*dvādaśāṅga*) are complete: ignorance is delusion; volition is formative action (*saṃskāra*); the discernment of various objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*); the three aggregates co-arising with consciousness are collectively called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the sense bases residing within name-and-form are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the conjunction of the six sense bases with their respective objects is contact (*sparśa*); the experiencing of contact is feeling (*vedanā*); desire is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the various entanglements associated with this are grasping (*upādāna*); the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising therefrom are becoming (*bhava*); the arising of these phenomena is birth (*jāti*); their maturation and transformation is aging (*jarā*); and their disintegration is death (*maraṇa*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that the "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and "continuous" (*sāmbandhika*) [types of dependent origination] are both universally applicable to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
All five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) present within the stages of the twelve links are subsumed under the category of "stages of existence" (*avasthika*).
This very state of being suspended at a great distance and continuing from beginningless time is termed "distant continuity" (*dūrasaṃtati*).
What is the intended meaning of the Blessed One’s statement regarding this?
The verse says:
The tradition maintains that the Blessed One spoke of the twelve links of dependent origination solely in terms of their sequential stages (*avasthā*).
The treatise states:
"The tradition maintains that the Blessed One spoke of the twelve links of dependent origination solely in terms of their sequential stages."
If each member [of the dependent origination] contains all five aggregates, for what reason are they designated by names such as "ignorance" (avidyā) alone?
It is because ignorance and the others are predominant within their respective stages.

These names, such as "ignorance," are established based on predominance; that is to say, if ignorance is most predominant in a particular stage, the five aggregates of that stage are collectively termed "ignorance."
Up to the stage [of the final existence], old age and death are most predominant; therefore, the five aggregates of this stage are collectively termed "old age and death.
Thus, although the substance is collective, there is no fault in the designation being distinct.
For what reason does the Sūtra’s exposition of these twelve links differ from that set forth in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As that treatise states:
"What is dependent origination?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena," and so forth, as explained at length.
The Sūtras speak with specific underlying intentions, whereas the Abhidharma explains according to the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) as follows:
the states of duration, the momentary, the remote continuity, and the connected bondage apply exclusively to the category of sentient beings.
The distinction lies in the fact that [the aggregates] include both sentient and insentient things.
Why, then, does the Sūtra speak only of sentient beings?
The verse says:
Regarding the past, future, and middle limits, [this is] for the purpose of dispelling the delusions of others.
The commentary says:
Is it for the sake of dispelling the delusions of others regarding these three limits?
The distinctions among the three time periods apply only to sentient beings.
How, then, are sentient beings deluded regarding the prior limit?
That is to say, they give rise to such doubts concerning the prior limit:
Did I exist in past lives, or did I not exist?
What was I in those past lives?
How was I in those past lives?
What is the delusion regarding the future limit of sentient beings?
It refers to the arising of such doubts concerning the future limit:
"Will I exist or not exist in future lives?"
"What shall I become? How shall I become?
In what way are sentient beings deluded regarding the intermediate state?"
That is to say, regarding the middle period [of existence], one gives rise to such doubts:
"What am I? How is this self?"
"What do I possess? Who will I have?"—

in order to eliminate such delusions regarding the three time periods, the Sūtra speaks only of the dependent origination of sentient beings, teaching in their proper sequence ignorance and formations, as well as birth and old age and death, along with consciousness through to existence.
Why is this so? Because a sutra states:
"Bhikṣus, listen attentively!"

If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the phenomena of dependent origination and dependently arisen dharmas, is able to perceive them with correct wisdom as they truly are, he will certainly not be deluded regarding the three periods of time, such as wondering whether "I existed or did not exist in the past," and so forth.
Other masters say:

The three [links] of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are also taught in order to eliminate delusion regarding the future (*aparānta*), because these three are all causes for the future.

Furthermore, it should be understood that although this exposition of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) consists of twelve members, its nature is comprised of three and two; the "three" refer to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and the basis (*vastu*), while the "two" refer to result (*phala*) and cause (*hetu*).
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
Three are afflictions, two are karmas; Seven things are also called fruits.
The results are abbreviated and the causes are abbreviated; by means of the middle [links], the two [extremes] can be inferred.
The treatise says:

Ignorance, craving, and grasping have the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*); the links of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) have the nature of karma; the remaining seven, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), have the nature of the basis (*vastu*), because they are the bases upon which afflictions and karma depend.
These seven matters are themselves called "fruits," and by extension, the remaining five are also called "causes," because their intrinsic nature consists of afflictions and karma.
For what reason are cause and fruit explained in detail regarding the middle period?
This is because phenomena (*vastu*) are divided into five categories and afflictions (*kleśa*) into two;
in the subsequent limit (*aparānta*), the results are abbreviated because phenomena consist of only two categories;
and in the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), the causes are abbreviated because afflictions consist of only one category.

Since the breadth of the middle period allows one to infer the breadth of the preceding and succeeding periods by analogy, and since this broad meaning has already been established, it is not stated separately; to state it would be redundant.
If the links of dependent origination consisted of only twelve, then by not mentioning the fruit of old age and death, birth and death would have an end;
and by not mentioning the cause of ignorance, birth and death would have a beginning.

Alternatively, one would have to establish further members of dependent origination, and those further members would require yet others, resulting in the fault of infinite regress; thus, no further members should be established.
However, there is no such aforementioned error, for herein the Blessed One has already revealed it through the underlying meaning.
How has this already been explained?
The verse says:
From afflictions arise further afflictions and karma; from karma arises the [resultant] entity.
From phenomena, phenomena and afflictions arise; such is the principle of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*). The treatise says:
