"From afflictions arise afflictions" refers to craving giving rise to grasping (*upādāna*); "from afflictions arise karma" refers to grasping giving rise to becoming (*bhava*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); "from karma arise phenomena" refers to volitional formations giving rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*), and becoming giving rise to birth (*jāti*); "from phenomena arise phenomena" refers to the link of consciousness giving rise to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), continuing up to contact (*sparśa*) giving rise to the link of feeling (*vedanā*), and the link of birth giving rise to aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
The arising of afflictions from the process of existence refers to the craving that arises from sensation; this alone is the principle for establishing the member of "existence" (*bhava*).

Since it has already been shown that old age and death are the causes of the process of existence and afflictions, and that ignorance is the result of the process of existence and afflictions—given that ignorance and old age and death are themselves of the nature of the process of existence and afflictions—why should one need to postulate further members of dependent origination?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In this way, there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.
If it were not so, what would be the purpose of these words?
Another commentator explains:
Other sūtras state that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance in turn gives rise to improper mental attention.
Since improper mental attention is also subsumed under the member of grasping (*upādāna*), it is likewise mentioned in this sūtra.
How is this improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) included within the member of grasping (*upādāna*)?
If you say it is included because it is associated with it, then craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) should also be included therein.
Even if you grant that they are so included, how can it be proven that improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance?

If it were the case that being subsumed under those [aggregates] alone constituted proof of the cause-and-effect relationship, then since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also subsumed under them, they should not be established separately as members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Others further explain:

Other sūtras state that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance, and ignorance in turn gives rise to improper mental attention; since improper mental attention is said to exist at the time of contact (*sparśa*), another sūtra states:
Delusion arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; the defiled attention thus produced necessarily induces ignorance at the stage of feeling.
As another sutra states:
"With feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance as condition, craving arises."
Therefore, at the time of contact, improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra) operates simultaneously with feeling, with ignorance as its condition.
Because of this ignorance, there is no fault of causelessness, nor is it necessary to establish any other members of dependent origination.
Furthermore, there is no fault of infinite regress regarding the members of dependent origination, because irrational mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) arises from delusion (*moha*).
As the Sūtra says:
"With the eye and forms as conditions, delusion arises, which gives rise to defiled and turbid mental attention."
Although such sincere words exist in other sutras, they ought to be stated further in this sutra.
They need not be stated further.
How is this known?
This is known through logical proof.
What is this logic?
It is that feeling (*vedanā*) cannot serve as a condition for craving (*tṛṣṇā*) apart from ignorance (*avidyā*), because feeling does not give rise to craving in Arhats.

Furthermore, non-erroneous contact cannot serve as the condition for defiled feeling, nor can error arise apart from contact associated with ignorance, because the contact of an Arhat is not erroneous.
Based on such reasoning as proof, it is known that if this were the case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For everything that can be established through correct reasoning need not be stated further; therefore, what was said does not constitute a resolution of the objection.

However, as for the objection raised above—that because the Sūtra does not separately state that old age and death have a fruit or that ignorance has a cause, birth and death would consequently possess a beginning and an end—this difficulty is irrational, for the intention of the Sūtra is different.
Nor is it the case that the principle explained therein is incomplete. Why is this?
Because this sutra merely intends to eliminate the ignorance regarding the three periods of time in those to be converted.
Those to be converted give rise to this doubt alone:
"How is it that sentient beings continue through the three periods of time—namely, being born from a previous life into the present life, and the present life being able to produce a future life?"

The Tathāgata merely taught the twelve links as previously explained in order to eliminate their doubts; that is to say, he taught them regarding the past, future, and middle [lives] to dispel the delusions of others.
As the Blessed One told the bhikṣus:
"I shall explain to you the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) and the dharmas arisen through conditions (pratītyasamutpanna)."
What is the difference between these two?
For the time being, according to the root treatise, there is no distinction between them, because both are said to encompass all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
How can future phenomena that have not yet arisen be described as "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) in the same way as those of the past and present?
How can future phenomena, which have not yet performed their function, be designated as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) in the same way as those of the past and present?
This is because they have already been produced by the power of volition (*cetanā*).
If that is so, how can the untainted (*anāsrava*) be conditioned?
That too is because it has already been produced by the power of wholesome volition (*samyak-cetanā*).
If that were so, then one would likewise attain *nirvāṇa*.

In truth, one should say that this is spoken of in terms of its category (*jāti*); just as that which has not yet undergone transformation is still designated by the name "form" (*rūpa*), there is no fault in what is said when the categories are identical.
Now, to correctly explain the intended meaning of the sutra, the verse says:
"The meaning here is correctly stated as: The cause arises; the fruit has already been produced.
The commentary says:
The causal portions of the various members are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), because by means of them as conditions, the effects are able to arise.
The resultant portions of the various members are called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because all of them are produced from conditions.
In this way, both meanings are established, because all the members possess the nature of cause and effect.
If that were the case, their establishment would not be simultaneous.
It is not so, because there is a distinction in what is being observed.

That is to say, if one contemplates this as "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), one does not thereby contemplate it as "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is analogous to the relationship between cause and effect, or father and son.
The Venerable Madhyāntika stated that there are dharmas which are dependent origination but not dependently arisen; thus, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase refers to future dharmas.
The second phrase refers to all past and present dharmas at the stage of the final moment of consciousness of an arhat.
The third phrase refers to other past and present dharmas.
The fourth phrase refers to all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The masters of the Sautrāntika school state:
"Is what is stated here an expression of your own personal opinion, or is it the meaning of the sūtras?"
If this were the meaning of the sūtra, it would not be so. Why is that?
Furthermore, the previously explained dependent origination of states, which identifies the twelve links as the five aggregates at each stage, contradicts the sūtras, for the sūtras state otherwise.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"What is ignorance? It is the lack of knowledge regarding the past," and so forth, as explained at length.
This is a teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and cannot be suppressed or forced into being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Therefore, the previously explained dependent origination of states (*avasthā-pratītyasamutpāda*) contradicts the meaning of the Sūtra.
Not all sūtras are teachings of definitive meaning; there are also those spoken according to what is predominant (*yathāpradhāna*).
As stated in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*:
"What is the internal earth element?
It refers to the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth."
Although it is not that other phenomena such as visible form (*rūpa*) are absent there, the teaching is given in terms of what is predominant.
This case should be understood in the same way.

The cited passage is not a valid proof; for that sutra does not intend to define the hair, body hair, and so forth by means of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) as if it were an incomplete exposition. Rather, in that sutra, the earth element is analyzed by means of the hair, body hair, and so forth, because there is no earth element that transcends the hair, body hair, and so forth. Therefore, that sutra is a complete exposition.
The members such as ignorance (*avidyā*) taught in this sūtra should also be explained in full, exactly as in that [other] case; there is nothing further beyond what has been stated.
Is it not the case that the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) exists in its essence even beyond hair, body hair, mucus, tears, and so forth, yet mucus and the rest are all also mentioned in that sūtra?
As it has been said, there are other things within the body; if there were likewise some other form of ignorance (*avidyā*) similar to those, it should now be demonstrated.
If one were to introduce something of a different category into the midst of ignorance, what benefit would that provide?

Although the five aggregates exist in all stages, a factor may be established as a limb of another factor only when its presence or absence is determined by the presence or absence of that other factor.

For instance, there may be the five aggregates without the formations (saṃskāra) that follow merit, demerit, or immovability, or without consciousness, up to craving (tṛṣṇā), and so forth; therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as stated.
The reasoning of the four alternatives you have stated is also incorrect.
If future phenomena were not "dependently arisen," it would contradict the sūtra.
The sūtra says:
What are dependently originated phenomena?
They are said to be from ignorance through to birth, aging, and death.
Alternatively, one would have to admit that two [factors] exist in the future, which would then destroy the previously established three time periods.
Some say that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), because a sūtra states:
"Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) of dependent origination remains eternally present."
It may be so according to this intended principle, but it is not so according to another intended principle.
What is this intended principle?
And what is the other intended principle?
And it is said that [this] may be so or may not be so.

That is to say, if the intention is to state that whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth always arise conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) and do not arise conditioned by other factors—or alternatively, because they are without conditions—they are said to be permanent.
If this is what is intended by the teaching, then the principle is indeed tenable.

However, if it is claimed that the intended meaning is that there exists a distinct substantial entity called "dependent origination" which is quiescent and eternally abiding, then this alternative interpretation is not logically tenable.
Why is this so? Because both arising and [the entity] itself possess the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
It is not logically tenable that a separate, eternal dharma should serve as the characteristic of impermanence.

Furthermore, that which arises must necessarily be established in dependence upon an ariser; yet what connection or relevance could this permanent dharma have with those [factors] such as ignorance, such that one would say this dharma is established in dependence upon them and is their dependent origination?
Furthermore, to claim that the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) refers to permanence is logically inconsistent with the meaning of its constituent parts.
In this context, what is the meaning of the terms?
*Prati* has the sense of "reaching," and the root *i* has the sense of "going."
Because the meaning of the element (*dhātu*) is transformed by the power of prior assistance, the formations (*saṃskāra*) become conditions through transformation upon reaching [that state].
*Sam* has the meaning of conjunction; *ud* has the meaning of ascending; and the element *pad* has the meaning of existence.

If it is argued that there is a transformation from dependence and conjunction into arising—such that a phenomenon, having reached its conditions, arises through their conjunction—this meaning of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is logically untenable.
Thus, the meaning of this statement cannot be correct.
Why is this so? Because there are two functions belonging to a single agent.
Regarding the prior function, there ought to be the word "already" (kṛta), just as when one person has already bathed and then eats.
There is no dharma of activity that exists prior to its arising; it first reaches the object and only subsequently arises. It is not the case that there can be an operation without an agent.
Therefore, a verse says:
"If it were to arise before reaching the object, It would be irrational for it to exist [then]."
If both were to perish simultaneously, then the former [the cause] should have been mentioned first;
therefore, there is no such fault.
For now, one should instead cross-examine the masters of the science of grammar (śabdavādin):
When does a dharma arise?
Is it in the present, or is it in the future?
If that were so, what fault would there be?
If arising were present, then since arising has not yet occurred, how could it be present?
If the present is that which has already arisen, how could it arise again?
For if that which has already arisen were to arise again, it would lead to an infinite regress.
If arising were in the future, it would not yet exist at that time; how then could it be an agent?
Since the agent is absent, how could there be an activity?
Therefore, at the very moment of arising, it has already reached its conditions.
What is the state of arising?
It refers to the moment when the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the future world are actually arising; it is at this very stage that they are said to "reach" their conditions.
Furthermore, the agent and the action as falsely established by the Grammarians (*Śabdavādins*) do not hold up under rational analysis.
There is an agent who initiates this activity; yet, within this [process], no agent is observed.
Since a distinct activity separate from its initiation cannot be found as a reality, this statement is unerring from the perspective of conventional truth.

This meaning of dependent origination is precisely what was stated as: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. Therefore, one should cite that [teaching] to explain the meaning of dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
Just as that which does not exist arises, So too should it be when conditions are met;
If what has already arisen were to arise again, there would be no end, Or else it would have to exist prior to its arising.
In both cases, once the speech has ceased, the lamp is extinguished when darkness arrives;
likewise, once the mouth has been opened, one falls asleep—if one were to sleep later, the mouth should be closed.
Some maintain this view:
Furthermore, the difficulty is explained through another meaning:
*prati* has the sense of "various" (*nānā*), while the root *i* has the sense of "not abiding" (*aniścala*).
Because it does not abide due to the assistance of "variety," it transforms into the sense of "condition" (*pratyaya*).
*Sam* has the meaning of "gathering," *ud* has the meaning of "ascending," and the root *pad* has the meaning of "to go.
Because *ud* precedes it, "going" (*padyate*) becomes "arising" (*utpāda*).

This explains that once various conditions have converged, they cause the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) to gather and arise; this is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The explanation provided above may be acceptable in this context. However,
when the eye and visible forms each act as conditions to give rise to visual consciousness and so forth,
how could a "various collection" (sāmagrī) be established therein?
For what reason did the Blessed One state the first two phrases—namely, "depending on this, that exists" and "from the arising of this, that arises"?
It was for the sake of knowing with certainty the principle of dependent origination.
As stated elsewhere, conditioned by ignorance, the formations come to be; apart from ignorance, the formations cannot exist.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate the successive arising of the members: conditioned by this member, that member comes to be; because that member arises, the subsequent members arise.

Furthermore, it is to demonstrate the transmission of birth across the three time periods: that is, based on the past limit (*pūrvānta*), the middle limit (*madhyānta*) comes to be; and because the middle limit arises, the future limit (*aparānta*) arises.

Moreover, it is to demonstrate the two conditions of direct and indirect succession: that is, ignorance (*avidyā*) arises immediately prior to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), or else volitional formations arise through the power of successive transmission.
Other masters explain:

these two phrases are intended to refute the two theories of causelessness and an eternal cause; that is to say, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) cannot exist without a cause, nor can they arise from an eternal self-nature (*svabhāva*), a self (*ātman*), or the like, which lack the capacity to serve as a cause for their production.

If that were so, the preceding phrase would become redundant; for the subsequent phrase alone—“because this arises, that arises”—is sufficient to refute both the theory of causelessness and the theory of an eternal cause.

However, there may be those who maintain that the existence of formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth depends upon a self as their basis, and that formations arise because they are produced from causal factors such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, in order to eliminate that attachment, the Blessed One definitively determined that the existence of the fruit arises precisely from its productive cause.
If this arises, that arises; that is, based on the existence of this, that exists. This does not mean that the fruit exists by depending on some other cause.
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise, and so forth, until the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.

The various masters explain these two phrases as demonstrating the non-interruption and the arising of cause and effect: that is to say, dependent upon the non-interruption of ignorance, the formations (saṃskāra) do not cease; and precisely because ignorance arises, the formations are produced.
In this manner, all subsequent cases should be explained in detail.
One interpretation states:

it is to clarify the abiding and arising of cause and effect; that is to say, as long as the continuity of the cause exists, the continuity of the effect also exists, and because the parts of the cause arise, the parts of the various effects likewise arise.
If one intends to discuss arising (*jāti*), for what reason is abiding (*sthiti*) mentioned?
Furthermore, why did the Buddha break the sequential order by first explaining abiding and subsequently explaining arising?
Another explanation states:
"Depending on this, that exists" means that depending on the existence of the fruit, the cessation of the cause occurs.

"Because this arises, that arises" is said because one might suspect that the fruit arises without a cause; therefore, it is further stated that it is only through the arising of the cause that the fruit can emerge, not that it is causeless.
If the meaning of the sūtra were as you suggest, it should have been stated thus: "Depending on this, that ceases and becomes non-existent.

Furthermore, one should first state that "the effect arises because of the cause," and only thereafter say that "depending on the effect, the cause ceases and becomes non-existent. Only through such a sequence can it be called a well-spoken teaching.
If it were otherwise, when one intends to explain dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), upon what sequence could one first speak of the cessation of causes?
Therefore, that interpretation does not accord with the meaning of this sūtra.
Furthermore, how is it that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on, up to birth conditions aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)?
I shall now briefly clarify the meaning in accordance with the sūtras.

That is to say, foolish worldlings, not knowing that dependently arisen phenomena are merely formations (*saṃskāra*), falsely give rise to the view of a self and the grasping of the conceit "I am. For the sake of experiencing pleasure for themselves—rather than suffering or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—they perform the three types of karma of body and so forth: namely, they perform meritorious karma to experience future pleasure for themselves; they perform imperturbable karma to experience future pleasure that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; and they perform non-meritorious karma to experience present pleasure.
This is called "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations.

Driven by the power of projecting karma, the continuum of consciousness flows like a flame, proceeding toward various realms of existence; it relies upon the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to hasten to the place of birth and links with the body of the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). This is called "conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness."
If one provides this interpretation, it accords well with the sūtras which distinguish the *vijñāna*-link as pertaining to all six consciousnesses, because consciousness precedes [name-and-form].

Within this realm of rebirth (*gati*), name-and-form arises; possessing the five aggregates, it continues in a successive stream throughout the entire duration of a single lifetime. This is because such is stated in various sūtras, including the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* and the *Pratītyasamutpādavyākhyā*.

When name-and-form has thus gradually matured, the possession of the faculties such as the eye is termed the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Next, through contact with their respective objects, consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, there occurs contact (*sparśa*) that is conducive to pleasure and so forth.

Based on this, the three feelings, beginning with pleasure, arise; from these three feelings, the three types of craving are induced. That is to say: due to the pressure of suffering, one generates sensual craving (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) toward pleasant feeling; or, one generates form-craving (*rūpatṛṣṇā*) toward pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; or, one generates formless-craving (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*) solely toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
From craving for pleasant feeling arises the grasping of sensual desire and so forth.
Herein, "sensual desire" refers to the five objects of desire (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*).
"Views" refers to the sixty-two views, as explained at length in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
"Precepts" (śīla) refers to the abstention from immoral conduct.
"Vows" (vrata) refers to the vows of dogs, cows, and so forth— namely,

the various types of meaningless ascetic practices undertaken by the Nirgranthas, Brahmins, Pāśupatas, Pāṇḍarabhikṣus, Vālmīkas, and other such heterodox outsiders, such as going naked, plucking out one's hair, wearing the skins of black antelopes, wearing topknots, smearing ashes on the body, carrying triple staves, or shaving off facial hair and head hair.
The "discourse on self" (ātmavāda) refers to speaking of a self based upon the internal body;
other masters state that the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) and the conceit of self (asmimāna) are called the discourse on self.
Why are these two alone called "discourse on self" (*ātmavāda*)?
Because it is by means of these two that one asserts the existence of a self; yet since a self does not exist, they are termed "discourse on self.
As the Sūtra says:

"O bhikṣus, you should know that ignorant ordinary beings who have not heard the Dharma give rise to the grasping of a self in accordance with conventional designations; yet within this, there is in reality neither a self nor anything belonging to a self."
Regarding the first four [nutriments], "clinging" (upādāna) refers to sensual desire (kāmacchanda).
Therefore, in various sūtras, the Blessed One explained: "What is clinging?
It is sensual desire."
With grasping as condition, the accumulation of various karmas that bring about future existence is called "becoming" (*bhava*).
As the Blessed One told Ānanda:
"The karma that brings about future existence is called 'becoming,' because it has becoming as its condition."
The stream of consciousness flows toward a future birth; according to the principle explained previously, the presence of the five aggregates is termed "birth.
With birth as a condition, there is aging and death, the specific characteristics of which are explained at length in the Sūtra.
The phrase "merely this" (iti kevalam) reveals that there are only formations (saṃskāra), devoid of self or what belongs to a self.
The phrase "this great mass of suffering" (ayam mahato duḥkhaskandhasya) reveals the accumulation of suffering without beginning or end.
The word "arising" (samudaya) is used to reveal the production of these various masses of suffering.
The Vaibhāṣika school has already been explained as before.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Nine.
*Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Three: The Analysis of the World, Part Three. What is the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
This means that its essence is not clarity (*vidyā*).
If that were so, then ignorance (*avidyā*) would have to be the eye and other [faculties].
Since this is the case, the meaning of this term must be understood as the absence of clarity.
If that were so, the essence of ignorance would not exist.
To demonstrate that it does have an essence and that its meaning does not overlap with other categories, the verse says:
Ignorance is that which is opposed to knowledge, Just as "non-relative," "untruth," and so forth [are opposed to their opposites].
The treatise says:

Just as those who stand in opposition to one's friends and relatives are called "non-friends" because they are contrary to friends, yet they are not something other than friends, nor is there such a thing as the absence of friends.
Truthful speech is called "real"; that which is its opposite, deceptive discourse, is called "unreal. This unreal is neither different from the real, nor is it the mere absence of the real.

The word "etcetera" (ādi) is used to indicate that what is not the Dharma, not the meaning, or not the fact, is likewise neither different from nor non-existent in relation to their respective natures.
Thus, ignorance possesses a distinct substantial entity; it is that which is counteracted by knowledge, being neither different from it nor non-existent.
How is this known? Because it is taught as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there is corroborating evidence.
The verse says:
Because it is described as a fetter (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, And because it is not [simply] a view of wrong wisdom (*dauṣprajña*).
Because it is associated with views, and because it is said to defile wisdom.
The treatise states:

The Sūtra explains ignorance (*avidyā*) as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), an outflow (*āsrava*), a yoke (*yoga*), a flood (*ogha*), and so forth. It is not the case that other factors such as the eye, or the total absence of a substance, can be described as having the nature of a fetter and so on; therefore, there exists a distinct dharma designated by the name "ignorance."
Just as a wicked wife or son is called "no wife" or "no son," so too should faulty wisdom (*kuprajñā*) be called ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, that [faulty wisdom] is not ignorance, because it possesses views (*dṛṣṭi*). All defiled wisdom is termed faulty wisdom; since views exist within it, it is not ignorance.
If that were so, one would have to admit that non-seeing wisdom (*ajñāna*) is ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is not the case, because ignorance is associated with seeing (*dṛṣṭi*).
If ignorance were wisdom, it would have to be dissociated from seeing, for two entities of wisdom cannot be associated together.
Furthermore, it is said that ignorance can defile wisdom, as a sutra states:
"Greed defiles the mind, preventing liberation; ignorance defiles wisdom, preventing purity. It is not the case, however, that wisdom itself can defile its own essential nature.
Just as craving, being of a different category [from wisdom], can defile the mind, so too should ignorance be able to defile it despite being different from wisdom; why is this not admitted?

Defiled wisdom is said to be "defiling" because it intermingles with wholesome wisdom and prevents it from becoming pure, just as craving defiles the mind and prevents liberation. Why must it necessarily be manifest and associated with the mind to be called "defiling"?

However, because the power of craving afflicts and binds the mind, it prevents liberation; later, when those latencies (*vāsanā*) of craving are transformed and extinguished, the mind becomes liberated.
Likewise, ignorance defiles wisdom (*prajñā*), rendering it impure; it does not associate with wisdom, but merely corrupts and turbidizes wisdom through its influence.
If one analyzes it in this way, what logical contradiction is there? Furthermore, who could possibly obstruct that which is discriminated by oneself?
However, it is well said that ignorance exists as a distinct category of wisdom, just as craving is distinct from the mind.
There are those who maintain that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are simply ignorance (*avidyā*); this too should be refuted by the same reasoning as before.

If all afflictions were ignorance, they should not be mentioned separately among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, nor should they be associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) and the like, because a view cannot be associated with itself.

Alternatively, one should also state that ignorance defiles the mind. If it is argued that this is spoken of in terms of specific distinctions, then one should not employ a general term for the defiled wisdom.
Since it is admitted that ignorance has a distinct dharma as its essence, one should explain what the characteristics of this essence are.
This refers to not understanding the reality of the fruits of karma.
What kind of characteristic constitutes "not understanding"? Is it something distinct from understanding, or is it simply the absence of understanding?
Both [positions] entail faults, as was explained regarding ignorance (*avidyā*).
This refers to understanding that there is a distinct dharma which is the object of counteraction.
Furthermore, this is difficult to fathom: what is its characteristic?
This category of phenomena should be explained in this manner,
as it is stated elsewhere:
"What is the eye?"
That is to say, it is pure matter (*rūpa*) that serves as the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise; its function alone can be discerned.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta states that this ignorance is the nature of the "I-conceit" (*asmimāna*) relied upon by all sentient beings, which is distinct from the pride of "I-am-ness" (*māna*).
What is the nature of this "category" (*jāti*)?
The Sūtra states:

"Now that I have thus known and thus seen, all craving, all views, all categories of being (*jātitva*), all clinging to 'I' and 'mine,' all clinging to the conceit of 'I am,' and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), having been abandoned and fully understood, are extinguished without shadow; therefore, it is known that the nature of the category is distinct from the conceit of 'I am.'"
How can it be known that the nature of this category is precisely ignorance?
It cannot be said to be other afflictions;
yet, could it not be said to be other [afflictions] such as pride?
If one were to investigate this further in great detail, the discourse would become overly prolix; therefore, let it suffice for now.
What is the meaning of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)?
As for "form" (*rūpa*), it has already been explained; here we shall explain only "name" (*nāman*).
The verse says:
They are called the four formless aggregates.
The commentary says:
Why are the four formless aggregates called "name" (*nāma*)?
They are called "name" because they undergo transformation toward their respective objects through the power of the names established for them and the power of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
How do they transform according to the power of names?
This refers to how various conventional names established by worldly consensus shift and express their respective referents, such as the names "ox," "horse," "color," or "taste.
For what reason, furthermore, is this designated by the term "name" (*nāman*)?
It transforms and takes as its object various respective domains.
Furthermore, it resembles names because it manifests in accordance with names.
Other masters say:
The four formless aggregates, having abandoned this body, transition to another birth; because they transform according to their "name" (*nāman*), they are designated by that term.
What is the meaning of "contact" (*sparśa*)?
The verse says:
Contact arises from the conjunction of the six [bases].
The treatise says:
There are six kinds of contact, namely, visual contact up to mental contact.

What, then, is this? It is that which arises from the conjunction of the three; that is to say, because of the coming together of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness—a distinct contact arises.
Furthermore, the arising of the five types of contact can indeed result from the conjunction of the three, as it is admitted that the sense faculty, object, and consciousness arise simultaneously.
The mental faculty (*manas*) is past, the phenomena (*dharma*) may be future, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present; how, then, can they be in conjunction?
This very state is what is called "conjunction," meaning that the principle of cause and effect is established.
Alternatively, they are called "conjoined" (*sāmagrī*) because they share a single result; that is to say, the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness equally conduces to the arising of contact.
Regarding this, the various masters differ in their understanding. Some say:
The coming together of the three is called contact (*sparśa*).
He cites a sūtra as proof,
as it is said in the sutra:
The gathering and conjunction of these three factors is called contact (*sparśa*).
Some say: contact is a distinct factor associated with the mind, produced by the coming together of the three.
He cites a sūtra as proof, stating:
"What are the six? The sūtra says: "What are the six?"
Six categories of phenomena:
first, the six internal sense bases;
second, the six external sense bases.
3. The six groups of consciousness;
4. The six groups of contact;
5. The six groups of feeling;
6. The six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya).
Since in this sūtra contact (sparśa) is mentioned separately from the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, contact exists as a distinct entity.

As for the statement that the mere conjunction of these three is called "contact," this is an explanation of the passage from the *Ṣaṭ-ṣaṭ-sūtra* cited later; it does not mean that because [contact] is mentioned separately, it must possess a separate substantial essence.

There is no such error regarding feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), as they are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that are not associated with them; for apart from craving and feeling, there exists the distinct substance of the sphere of mental objects.

In your own school, apart from contact (*sparśa*), there are no three [factors] existing separately, yet you speak of the distinction between "that which is contacted" and the "three. Although there may be sense faculties and objects that do not produce consciousness, there is no consciousness that does not rely upon a faculty and an object.
Therefore, since the three [causes] have already been explained, to explain contact separately would be redundant.
Others offer this defense:
"Not all eye-objects are causes for all eye-consciousnesses, nor are all eye-consciousnesses effects of all eye-objects."
Those that are neither cause nor effect are separately explained as three; those subsumed under cause and effect are collectively established as contact (*sparśa*).
To say that there is a distinct contact apart from the three conditions is to explain that the aforementioned gathering and conjunction of these three factors is what is termed "contact."

The Sūtra states that the scriptural passages recited by our school differ from this; alternatively, the name of the effect may be metaphorically applied to the cause, as when it is said, "the appearance of the Buddhas is bliss," and so forth.
Such back-and-forth refutations and explanations would involve excessive discourse, and therefore we shall desist for now.
However, the Abhidharmikas maintain that there is a distinct contact; thus, the aforementioned six types of contact are further combined into two.
The verse says:
Five are associated with resistance; The sixth is accompanied by the "designation" (adhivacana).
The treatise states:
The five contacts, beginning with that of the eye, are called "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*), because they have resistant sense faculties as their bases.
The sixth, the contact of the mind, is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).

The reason for this is that "designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to a name (*nāman*). Since a name is the extended object (*prabhūta-viṣaya*) of the mental contact (*mano-saṃsparśa*), it is specifically in reference to this that it is called "designation-contact.

As it is said: visual consciousness can only apprehend blue, but cannot apprehend "it is blue"; whereas mental consciousness apprehends blue and also apprehends "it is blue," and is therefore called "extended."

Therefore, the designation "contact with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) is established according to its support (*āśraya*), while the designation "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is established with respect to its object (*ālambana*).

Some say: "The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) proceeds toward its object only when speech (*vacana*) serves as its designation; the five [sensory] consciousnesses are not so. Therefore, the mental consciousness alone is called 'designation,' and that which is associated with it is called 'designation-contact.'"

Therefore, the designation "contact with resistance" (pratigha-sparśa) is established according to its basis, while the designation "designation-contact" (adhivacana-sparśa) is established in terms of its association.
Thus, the aforementioned six types of contact further constitute eight kinds according to their specific associations.
The verse says:
Knowledge, ignorance, and that which is neither; the untainted, the defiled, and the remainder;
associated with the two—craving and aversion; and corresponding to the three feelings such as pleasure.
The treatise says:

Contact associated with clarity (*vidyā*), non-clarity (*avidyā*), and so forth, constitutes three types: first, contact associated with clarity; second, contact associated with non-clarity; and third, contact associated with neither clarity nor non-clarity.
These three, respectively, should be understood as contact associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the remaining [neutral] states.

"Others" refers to those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as the remaining defiled (*kliṣṭa*) ones; that is, the tainted wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Among these, a portion of "contact associated with ignorance" (*avidyā-sparśa*) arises frequently; based upon that, two further types of contact—namely, "contact associated with craving" (*rāga-sparśa*) and "contact associated with aversion" (*dveṣa-sparśa*)—are established, because they are respectively associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving and aversion.
Taken together, all [contacts] further constitute three types of contact:
first, contact conducive to pleasant feeling; second, contact conducive to painful feeling; and third, contact conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

These three are called "conducive to feeling" (*vedanīya*) because they can induce feelings such as pleasure, or because they are experienced by feelings such as pleasure, or because they serve as the basis for the activity of feeling.
How is it that contact is experienced by feeling?
Because its mode of activity (ākāra) is extremely similar to that of contact, as it arises in dependence upon contact.
Thus, these combine to form sixteen types of contact.
What is the meaning of "feeling" (vedanā)?
The verse says:
From this arise six types of feeling; five belong to the body, the remainder to the mind.
The treatise says:
From the six types of contact, six types of sensation arise—namely, sensation produced by eye-contact through to sensation produced by mind-contact.
Among these six, the first five are called bodily sensations (*kāyikī-vedanā*), because they depend upon the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*).
That which arises from mental contact is called mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*), because it depends solely upon the mind.
Regarding whether the arising of feeling occurs subsequent to contact or simultaneously with it,
the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that they arise at the same time, because contact and feeling are mutually simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.
How can it be that two dharmas arise simultaneously,
such that the relationship between producer and produced can be established?
Why would it not be so established?
Because they lack functional capacity, subsequent dharmas have no power over those that have already arisen.
This is no different in meaning from the thesis being established; for instance, it is said that when two dharmas arise simultaneously, the relationship of producer and produced is not established.
Since the meaning of "subsequent dharmas having no power over those already arisen" is identical to the previous point, what is the use of stating it again?
If that were so, there would be the fault of mutual causation.
Since this is accepted, it is not a fault;
for our school accepts that these two are simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) and are also mutually the effects of one another.
Although you may grant this, the sūtras do not allow for these two to be mutual causes and effects.
The sūtra merely states:
"With eye-contact as condition, there arises feeling produced by eye-contact."
Nowhere in the Sūtras is it stated that contact produced by visual sensation arises with visual sensation as its condition.
Furthermore, this interpretation is illogical, for it violates the principle of the producing factor.
If a phenomenon is established as being able to produce another phenomenon, it is established that these two phenomena are distinct in time.

Just as the seed precedes the sprout, milk precedes curd, striking precedes sound, and the mental faculty precedes consciousness, it is universally established that the cause comes first and the effect follows.

There are also cases where cause and effect are universally established as being simultaneous, such as visual consciousness and its concomitants, the eye and visible form, etc., or the primary elements (mahābhūta) and the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) that coexist with them;
in these instances, it is likewise admitted that the preceding sense organ and object conditions can give rise to the subsequent consciousness.
What principle can prevent prior primary elements from producing subsequent derived matter?
Like a shadow and its body, they are surely co-existent. Some say:

Feeling arises only after contact; with the sense faculty and the object preceding it, consciousness subsequently arises. The conjunction of these three is termed "contact," and in the third moment, feeling arises conditioned by that contact.
If that were so, it would follow that not all consciousnesses possess feeling (*vedanā*), and that not all consciousnesses are contact (*sparśa*).
There is no such fault.

Because feeling arises in the subsequent stage of contact due to the contact of the preceding stage, there is feeling at every moment of contact; and there is no instance of the essence of consciousness that is not contact.
This is not reasonable.
What logic contradicts it?
It would mean that at times the two contacts have different objects, such that contact in the prior state of sensation gives rise to sensation in the subsequent state of contact.
How could a feeling arising from an object different from that of the contact arise?
Or one must admit that this feeling is associated with this mind, yet does not share the same single object as that mind.
If this were so, then if you admit that contact exists, there would be consciousness and contact, but no feeling.
In this preceding stage, there is consciousness and feeling, yet their substance is not contact; this is so because of a discrepancy in conditions.
What fault is there in this?
If that were the case, it would subvert the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), which must invariably coexist in every category of mind.
Upon what teaching are those concentrations established as being always concomitant?
They are established based on this treatise (*śāstra*).
We take only the sūtras as authoritative; since this treatise is not authoritative, what fault is there in rejecting it?
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"One should rely on the authority of the sūtras.
Alternatively, the meaning of "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma) does not necessarily require that they pervade all states of consciousness.
If that is so, what is the meaning of "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika-dharma)?
There are three levels:
first, the level with vitarka and vicāra; second, the level without vitarka and with only vicāra; and third, the level without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, there are three grounds:
first, the wholesome ground; second, the unwholesome ground; third, the indeterminate ground.
Furthermore, there are three grounds:
First, the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi); second, the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa-bhūmi); third, the stage of neither-training-nor-beyond-training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-bhūmi).
Those factors that exist in all these aforementioned stages are called the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma).
If a dharma exists only within all wholesome stages, it is called a great wholesome ground dharma (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
If a dharma exists only within all defiled stages, it is called a great affliction ground dharma (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
These and other such factors arise in alternation according to their respective conditions, rather than arising all at once.

Other explanations regarding these great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) have been introduced here through recitation; they are additions made for the present context and were not part of the original recension.
If feeling were to arise only after contact, how would one explain the Sūtra?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact, and together with it arise feeling, perception, and volition."

If it merely states that they "arise together" (*sahotpanna*) without specifying that they arise "together with contact" (*sparśa-saha*), how does this contradict our own school’s tenets? This must be explained.
Furthermore, the term "together" (*saha*) is also used in the sense of immediate succession (*anantara*), as stated in a sutra:
"One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness in conjunction with loving-kindness."
Therefore, that is not a proof.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"This feeling, this perception, this volition, and this consciousness—these dharmas are intermingled and inseparable; thus, there is no consciousness apart from feeling and the others"?
Now one should reflect carefully: in what sense are they "intermingled"?
This sutra further states:
"Whatever is felt is also what is thought; whatever is thought is also what is perceived; whatever is perceived is also what is cognized."
Not yet having understood this, one might ask: Is this statement made with reference to the object of cognition (*ālambana*), or is it made with reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*)?

Since there are also such statements regarding the co-arising of life-force (*āyus*) and heat (*uṣman*) that speak of their mutual intermingling, we know by analogy that this present teaching must certainly refer to a single moment.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that contact is the conjunction of the three. How could there be consciousness that is not a conjunction of the three?
Or how could there be a conjunction of the three that is not termed "contact"?

Therefore, one must certainly admit that all consciousnesses are invariably accompanied by contact, and that every instance of contact is necessarily co-arisen with feeling and the other mental factors.
The digression is now concluded; the primary subject should now be analyzed.
The verse says:
"These further become eighteen, due to the differences among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*)."
The Treatise says:

Within the aforementioned brief explanation of the single mind-experience (*citta-vedanā*), it is further divided into eighteen types due to the differences among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
One should understand that the word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) here indicates that the subsequent arises based upon the preceding.
What are these eighteen mental applications (*manopavicāra*)?
They are the six applications of joy, the six of sorrow, and the six of equanimity.
For what reason are they established as eighteen?

If categorized by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there should be only three, because the three—inclination (*saumanasya*), dejection (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—differ in their intrinsic natures.
If categorized by way of association (*samprayoga*), there should be only one, because all are associated with the mental faculty (*manas*).
If classified by way of their objects (*ālambana*), there would be only six, because the six objects—form and so forth—are their objects.
These become eighteen when fully categorized by way of the three [factors].
Among them, the fifteen "approaches" (*upavicāra*) to form and so forth are called "unmixed objects" (*asaṃsṛṣṭālambana*), because their respective objects are distinct.
The three types of mental application (*manopavicāra*) all pertain to both kinds [of objects].
What is the meaning of the term "mental application"?
It is traditionally explained that because the mind, with joy and the others as its immediate conditions, repeatedly ranges over various objects, it is called "mental application."
Some say that joy (*prīti*) and the other [mental factors] act as proximate conditions because they cause the mind to range repeatedly over its objects.
How then are bodily sensations (*kāyikī vedanā*) not "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*)?
They are not called "applications" simply because they do not rely solely on the mind; furthermore, because they lack conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*), they are also not "rangings."
Why is the faculty of pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmi*) of the third dhyāna not included among the mental applications (*manopavicāra*)?

It is traditionally taught that this is because the mental consciousness associated with the first realm lacks the faculty of pleasure, and furthermore, because there is no corresponding mental application subsumed under the faculty of suffering.
If these belong exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), why does the Sūtra state:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one gives rise to a mental application (*upavicāra*) of joy toward a form that is conducive to joy," and so forth, as explained at length in the Sūtra?
This statement is made because it refers to the mental applications of joy and so forth on the mental level, which are induced by the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
Just as one induces the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) based on visual consciousness, yet this contemplation of impurity is comprised solely within the mental stage (*manobhūmi*).
Furthermore, since that sutra states, "Having seen forms with the eye," and so forth at length, one should not raise such an objection.
Even if they are not [actual] views, up to and including having touched [an object], if joy, sorrow, or equanimity arise, these are also mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
If it were otherwise, there would be no mental applications in the desire realm that take the forms and so forth of the form realm as their objects.
Furthermore, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there should be no mental applications (manopavicāra) that take the odors, tastes, or tangible objects of the desire realm as their objects.

The mention of "seeing forms" and so forth is stated according to what is most prominent; having seen forms and so forth, one also gives rise to joy, sorrow, or equanimity toward sounds and other objects, which likewise constitute mental applications. This statement is made because there is no confusion [in their respective domains], for within them, the faculties and their objects are established as fixed.
Can that which possesses form, etc., give rise to only one type of mental application (*manopavicāra*) in accordance with joy and the other two?
This is determined by way of the continuity of the stream (*saṃtāna*), not by way of the object (*ālambana*).
Among all these mental applications, how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
How many objects of focus do the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) of the desire realm have?
The same question applies to those of the form and formless realms.
The verse says:
Conditioned by desire, eighteen [factors] pertain to desire; twelve pertain to form, and three to the higher realms.
Twelve are conditioned by both [desire and form]; eight pertain to themselves, and two to the formless.
The latter two are conditioned by desire, six pertain to themselves, and one pertains to the higher realm.
The preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms take the four [lower] form-realm states as their objects and one from their own level;
the four fundamental [formless absorptions] (*maula*) and three of the bordering stages (*sīmānta*) likewise do so; only one takes its own object alone.
The treatise says:
Those bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) number eighteen, and those that take the objects of the desire realm as their domain are likewise eighteen in number.
Those that take the objects of the form realm (rūpadhātu) as their domain number only twelve, excluding the six [consciousnesses] of smell and taste, because those [objects] do not exist there.
Taking formless objects as their domain, there can be only three [types of acquisition], because those [formless realms] lack the five types of objects such as form and so forth.
Having explained those bound to the desire realm, we shall now explain those bound to the form realm.
In the first and second dhyānas, there are only twelve [mental applications], namely, excluding the six associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*).

When taking the objects of the desire realm as their domain, there are likewise twelve; excluding the four associated with odor and taste, the remaining eight take their own realm as objects, while two take the formless realm as objects—namely, the mental application to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*).
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only six [mental applications]. That is to say, equanimity takes the desire realm as its object, and thus its objects also amount to six.

Excluding the two [objects] of odor and taste, the remaining four take their own [level] as objects; one takes the formless realm as its object, namely, the mental application to dharmas (*dharmopavicāra*).
Having explained those bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), one should now explain those bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

In the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there are only four types [of mental applications], namely: equanimity (*upekṣā*) which takes as its objects only visible forms (*rūpa*), sounds (*śabda*), tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*), and phenomena (*dharma*).
Taking the fourth dhyāna as an object also possesses four types; this is said from the perspective of those who maintain that there are distinct objects.
If one holds that that stage takes only the lower stages collectively as its object, then there would be only the mental application of dharmas with mixed objects.

Regarding the objects of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only one: namely, the mental object base (*dharmāyatana*) among the four bases. In its own level and the three higher levels, it has only one object: namely, the mental object base. This is because the fundamental stage of the formless realm does not take lower realms as its objects, and the three higher stages do not take the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their objects.
That they do not take lower objects as their conditions will be explained later.
Do these mental applications (manopavicāra) also pertain to the untainted (anāsrava)?
The verse says:
"Eighteen are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The treatise says:
Since there are no mental applications (*manopavicāra*) that are without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is stated that eighteen are exclusively with outflows."
Who accomplishes how many mental applications (*manopavicāra*)?
It is said: one born in the desire realm who has not yet attained wholesome consciousness of the form realm accomplishes all those of the desire realm;
[one who has attained it] accomplishes eight in the first and second dhyānas, and four in the third and fourth dhyānas.
In the formless realm, there is one [type].
Those belonging to the higher realms that have been acquired do not take lower realms as objects, because they are exclusively defiled.
If one has already acquired a wholesome mind of the form realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire, one accomplishes everything pertaining to the realm of desire.
In the first dhyāna there are ten; the rest are as explained previously.
Within the first dhyāna, only four types of joy (*prīti*) are established, because defiled [joy] does not take lower odors or tastes as its objects.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) fully establishes six, because in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), a wholesome mind can take odors and tastes as its objects.
The remaining cases should be understood accordingly according to this principle.

If one is born in the form realm (rūpadhātu), one accomplishes only a single mental application of equanimity (upekṣā-manopavicāra) belonging to the desire realm, namely that which is associated with the mind of supernormal fruition (abhijñā-phala-citta).
Some say that these various mental applications (*manopavicāra*) were established by the Vaibhāṣika masters according to their specific meanings.
However, in my view, the meaning of the sūtra differs. Why is this so?

Since one cannot give rise to mental applications (*manopavicāra*) directed toward an object belonging to a stage from which one has already attained detachment, the three—joy, sorrow, and equanimity—that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are not all subsumed under the category of mental applications.
Only those that are defiled, which are associated with the mind and frequently range over their objects, are "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*).
How are they associated with the mind and frequently range [over objects]?
Either through attachment, or through aversion, or through equanimity lacking discernment.

To counteract those [afflictions], the six constant abidings (ṣaḍ-āveṇika-vihāra) are taught: having seen a form, one is neither glad nor sad, but the mind constantly abides in equanimity, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension; this is explained in detail up to: the same applies to the cognition of mental phenomena.
It is not that non-Arhat sages lack worldly joy based on wholesome dharmas; rather, this statement was made merely to exclude the near-approaches (*upavicāra*) associated with defilement.
Furthermore, these very states of joy and so forth constitute the thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*), distinguished according to whether they pertain to attachment or to renunciation.
These distinctions between the phrases were taught by the Great Teacher.
That which is based on attachment refers to all defiled feelings;
that which is based on renunciation refers to all wholesome feelings.
The feeling (vedanā) thus described should be understood as occurring within the link of existence (bhava-aṅga).
Although there are immeasurable distinctions in its categories and meanings, for what reason are the remaining links of existence not explained here?
The verse says:
The remainder has been explained or will be explained.
The treatise says:
As for the remaining members of existence (*bhavāṅga*), some have already been discussed and some will be discussed; therefore, they are not treated here.

Among these, the constituent of consciousness (*vijñāna*) has already been explained previously; "consciousness" refers to the individual discernment of objects, which is precisely what is called the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and so forth.

The constituent of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) has also already been explained previously; those supports of consciousness consisting of translucent matter are called the five faculties, such as the eye, and so forth.
The two links of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) will be explained in the Chapter on Karma (*Karmavarga*).
The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) will be explained in the Chapter on Latent Dispositions (*Anuśayavarga*).
These factors of dependent origination are briefly established as three categories: namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and the phenomena that are the results of maturation (*vipākaphala-vastu*).
One should employ external metaphors to clarify their distinct functions.
The verse says:
"Herein, the afflictions are said to be like seeds and also like dragons."
Like the roots of grass and the trunks of trees, and like rice enveloped in husks;
karma is like the rice with its husk, like medicinal herbs and like flowers;
the various matters of ripened results (*vipāka*) are like cooked food and drink.
The treatise says:
How are these three types similar? They are like the production of sprouts, leaves, and so forth from a seed;
likewise, afflictions give rise to further afflictions, karma, and its objects, just as the water in a pond guarded by a nāga never runs dry.
Afflictions suppress karma, causing the continuity of rebirth to be endless, just as when the roots of a plant have not been pulled out, the sprouts grow back again and again despite being cut.
As long as the root of affliction has not been uprooted, one passes from death to death and arises once more, just as branches, flowers, and fruits repeatedly emerge from the trunk of a tree.

From among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), the occurrence of delusion, karma, and their effects is like rice grains enveloped in husks being able to produce sprouts and so forth; they cannot produce them alone.
Or, it is like karma being enveloped [by afflictions] that can bring about a future birth; it cannot bring it about alone.
Delusion should be understood as being like a seed and so forth.
Just as rice with its husk can produce sprouts and the like, karma accompanied by afflictions can summon maturation (*vipāka*).
Just as various medicinal herbs have the ripening of their fruit as their final limit, once karmic fruit has matured, it no longer summons further maturation.
Just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of fruit, so too karma is the proximate cause capable of producing maturation (*vipāka*).
One should understand that karma is like rice and the like;
just as cooked food is merely to be consumed and cannot be transformed back into other food, so it is with the result of maturation.
Once the matter of the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) has already matured, it cannot further project the ripening of another birth.
If various ripenings were to again induce further births, and those in turn induced yet others, there would be no liberation.
The matter is like food and drink; it should be understood in this way.
Thus, the phenomena of afflictions and karma arising through dependent origination continue from life to life without exceeding the four states of existence (*bhava*):
the intermediate state (*antarā-bhava*), the birth state (*upapatti-bhava*), the fundamental state (*pūrva-kāla-bhava*), and the death state (*maraṇa-bhava*), as previously explained.
The meaning of being defiled or undefiled, and their presence or absence within the three realms, shall now be briefly explained.
The verse says:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively defiled.
"By means of the afflictions of its own stage, [it arises]; the other three [existences] and the three formless [existences] likewise.
The commentary states:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively defiled.
By which afflictions?
By the various delusions of its own level.
That is to say, when one is born on a particular level, all the afflictions of that level defile the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) of that level.
Therefore, the Abhidharmikas all say:
among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), there is not a single one that lacks the capacity to moisten at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*).

However, this linking of rebirth occurs solely through the power of the afflictions, and does not arise through the independent power of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) or secondary defilements (*upakleśa*).
Although in this state both mind and body are dull and weak, afflictions nevertheless manifest due to the power of being frequently aroused or triggered by recent mental activity.
One should know that the very first moment of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is necessarily defiled, just like the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).

However, among the remaining three modes of existence (*bhava*), each one corresponds to all three—namely, the fundamental, death, and intermediate existences—which are respectively wholesome, defiled, and neutral.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the intermediate existence is excluded from these three; for in that realm there is no spatial separation of locations, and thus an intermediate existence could only be established if one were traveling to another location.
Since the verse does not mention the desire and form realms, we know that it is accepted that all four types of existence (*bhava*) are present therein.
Having already analyzed in detail the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of sentient beings, by what do these sentient beings subsist?
The verse says:
Sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment; In the realm of desire, the substance of edible food consists of only three [aggregates].
Matter cannot provide benefit, Because it is its own sense organ and because of liberation.
The three nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness, being with outflows, pertain to all three realms;
they arise for those born by mental transformation, those seeking birth, and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who subsist on fragrance.
Of these, the first two benefit this life: the former supports the basis, and the latter supports that which depends upon it.
The latter two [karmas] lead to future existence; they function as the projecting and the arising [causes], respectively.
The Treatise says:
The Sūtra states:

The Blessed One, having personally realized a single Dharma, has attained perfect enlightenment and correctly proclaimed it: that all sentient beings, without exception, subsist by means of nutriment.
What are these nutriments?
There are four kinds of nutriment:
There are four kinds: first, morsel food; second, contact; third, volition; and fourth, consciousness.
Morsel food is of two types: subtle and coarse.
Subtle refers to the food of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), for it has fragrance as its sustenance.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa, when gods first ate food, it did not undergo transformation or become foul, because it was absorbed into their limbs like oil poured onto sand.
Alternatively, the food of minute impure insects, infants, and the like is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*); the opposite of this is termed "gross" (*audārika*).
Thus, edible food exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because those who are free from craving for edible food are born in the higher realms;
it is therefore exclusively bound to the desire realm.

The three [objects] of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility are all the very substance of edible food, as they can be formed into distinct morsels and consumed—that is, received part by part through the mouth and nose.
How can light, shadow, heat, and cold constitute food?
This statement is traditionally explained as being made from a general perspective.

Furthermore, although they are not consumed by drinking or eating, they are capable of sustaining the body and are thus subsumed under "subtle food" (*sūkṣmāhāra*), just like ointments, bathing, and so forth.
Visible form can also be taken as morsels and consumed; for what reason, then, is it not considered nutriment?
It is because it cannot benefit its own corresponding sense organ or those who have attained liberation.
Indeed, that which is called nutriment must first provide sustenance to one's own sense organs and primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and only thereafter extend to others.
When consuming visible forms, they do not even benefit their own primary elements, much less others, because those sense faculties and their objects are distinct.
When joy and pleasure arise from seeing a form at times, this is produced by contact conditioned by the form; thus, it is contact that is the nutriment, not the form itself.
Furthermore, because non-returners and arhats are liberated from craving for food, even though they see various kinds of exquisite food and drink, it provides them no benefit.

"Contact" refers to all contacts produced by the conjunction of the three; "volition" refers to mental karma; and "consciousness" refers to the aggregate of consciousness. These three are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*) and exist throughout all three realms.
How is it that the substance of nutriment does not extend to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)?
The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this explanation:

"That which can sustain the various realms of existence (*bhava*) is the meaning of 'nutriment' (*āhāra'); the cultivation of the outflow-free is for the purpose of extinguishing all realms of existence."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There are four kinds of nutriment that enable *bhūta* sentient beings to abide and provide sustenance for those seeking birth.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is not so; therefore, it is not the essence of nutriment."
The term "bhūta" (being) signifies the sense of having already been born; all those who have arisen within the various realms of existence are said to be "already born.
Furthermore, for what does the expression "seeking birth" (upapatty-arthika) stand?
It refers to the intermediate state (antarābhava), because the Blessed One has described the intermediate state by means of five names.
What are the five?
First is the mind-made body (*manomaya*), because it arises from the mind and is not produced by the conjunction of external conditions such as semen and blood.
Second is the seeker of birth (*upapadya-pariṣeṣin*), because it constantly delights in searching for and examining its future place of rebirth.
Third is the "fragrance-eater" (*gandharva*), because it sustains its body with fragrant food while proceeding toward its place of rebirth.
Fourth is the "intermediate state" (*antarābhava*), because it consists of the aggregates (*skandhas*) existing between two destinies.
Fifth is the "arising by name" (*nāman-udbhava*), because it arises for a brief duration facing toward its future birth.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There is the arising of that which destroys its own self-nature; there is the birth of that which destroys the world.
Here, "arising" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"There is a person who has already severed the fetters of arising (*utpatti-saṃyojana*), but has not yet severed the fetters of birth (*jāti-saṃyojana*.
In this sutra, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained in detail:

Those who have abandoned craving for the two realms and are "those who go upstream" constitute the first category; those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state constitute the second category; all Arhats constitute the third category; and excluding the aforementioned characteristics constitutes the fourth category.
Furthermore, "bhūta" refers to an arhat, while those who still possess craving are called "those seeking birth.
How many types of nutriment enable a bhūta to abide?
And how many types of nutriment sustain a sentient being who seeks birth?
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that all four [nutriments] are present.

Even for those who possess craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) serves as a condition that provides nourishment and leads to the invitation of future existence (*punarbhava*). This is because the Blessed One stated that all four nutriments are the root of sickness, abscesses, and arrows, and the condition for old age and death.
It is also seen that the food of thought and reflection sustains the present body.
There is a traditional saying:
Once there was a father who, encountering a famine, wished to travel to another region.

He himself was already emaciated from hunger, and his two children were still infants; though he wished to take them with him, his strength was insufficient for the task. He therefore filled a bag with ashes and hung it on the wall, consoling the two children by telling them it was a bag of roasted flour.

Two sons hoped that their lives might be prolonged for a long time; later, someone arrived and opened the bag for them, and when the sons saw it was only ashes, their hopes were severed and they died.

Furthermore, there were merchants at sea who encountered a disaster and had their ship wrecked, losing both food and drink. From afar, they gazed upon a mass of foam and suspected it was a shore; hoping to reach it quickly, they managed to prolong their lives for a while, but when they reached it and realized it was not, their hopes were severed and they died.
The *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda* states:

In the great ocean there are large beings who come ashore, lay their eggs and bury them in the sand, and then return to the sea. If the mother constantly thinks of the eggs, they do not perish; if she loses mindfulness of them, the eggs are destroyed.
This cannot be so, for it contradicts the meaning of "food.
How could the food intended by another sustain one's own body?
In truth, one should say that an egg constantly thinks of its mother and thus does not rot; if it forgets her, it dies.
The thought-moment of craving arises at the stage of contact; all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) cause existence (*bhava*) to flourish.
How then did the Blessed One say that there are only four nutriments?
Although this is so, there is no fault in speaking of four based on their predominance.

This means that the first two kinds of nutriment benefit this body, which consists of the basis and that which depends upon it; the latter two kinds of nutriment induce future existence and give rise to future existence.
What is called the "basis" refers to the body endowed with sense faculties (*sendriya-kāya*); edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) provides nourishment and benefit to it.
Regarding the term "that which is supported," this refers to the mind and mental factors; the nutriment of contact is able to provide them with sustenance and benefit.
Thus, these two nutriments possess the most preeminent capacity for sustaining and benefiting existence that has already arisen.
That which is called "that which shall be" refers to future birth; therein, the food of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*) is able to project that which is to be born.
Once projected by the food of volition, subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) arises through the power of the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) perfumed by karma.
Thus, these two types of nutriment possess the most preeminent power for inducing the arising of existence (*bhava*);
therefore, although all outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava*) nourish existence, it is only with respect to their predominant capacity that the four nutriments are taught.
The first two are like foster mothers, for they nourish what has already been born;
