the latter two are like birth mothers, for they give birth to what is yet unborn.
Are all things that constitute edible portions considered "food"?
There are instances of edible food that are not considered nutriment;

these should be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first permutation refers to that which is consumed as a condition for the impairment of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The second permutation refers to the other three types of nutriment.
The third phrase refers to that which is consumed as a condition to benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
The fourth phrase excludes the aforementioned characteristics.
In this manner, one should understand that for each factor, such as contact (*sparśa*), there are likewise four phrases according to their respective applications.
Is there any contact (*sparśa*) or other [condition] that serves as a condition to benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), yet is not nutriment (*āhāra*)?
Yes; this refers to contact and so forth that belong to a different level (*bhūmi*) or are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, even when one has finished eating, that which was previously consumed continues to be called "nutriment" because it initially provided sustenance.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
Food performs the function of food at two times, and is thus designated as "food" in both instances:
first, at the time of initial consumption, it can eliminate hunger and thirst; [and second, it sustains the body thereafter].
2. Once digested, they sustain the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Which destinies (*gati*) and modes of birth (*yoni*) possess how many types of nutriment?
All five destinies and four modes of birth possess all four types of nutriment.
How can there be edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the hells?
Are not iron balls and molten copper not edible food?
If that which can cause harm is also considered food, then it contradicts the four propositions previously stated.
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇapāda* states:
"What is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?
It is that which can nourish and benefit the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); the same applies at length up to consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*)."
That explanation is based on defining "nutriment" (*āhāra*) as that which provides benefit and sustenance; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Nevertheless, although hot iron balls and the like in the hells cause harm once consumed, they can temporarily alleviate hunger and thirst; because they possess the characteristics of nutriment, they are also called "nutriments."
Furthermore, since beings in the isolated hells (pratyeka-naraka) consume solid food just like humans,
all five destinies (gati) possess the four types of nutriment.
As the Blessed One has taught:

If someone were able to give food to a hundred non-Buddhist ascetics who have abandoned desire, and if another were able to give food to a single ordinary person within the Jambū Grove, the fruit of the latter gift would surpass that of the former.
What is meant by "ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the Jambū forest"?
Some offer this explanation:
it refers to all those with bellies who dwell in Jambudvīpa.
That explanation by the Śākya is unreasonable because it speaks of only a single word.

Furthermore, in this context, there was the giving of food to immeasurable ordinary beings; since this is logically superior to giving food to a few non-Buddhist seers who are free from desire, how can it be considered a cause for wonder, comparison, or praise as being superior?
Some say: "He is a Bodhisattva close to Buddhahood.
This reasoning is also incorrect, for the merit obtained from giving to him surpasses that of giving to ten million (*koṭi*) Arhats.
The Vaibhāṣikas state:
"This ordinary person has already attained the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

This name and its meaning are inconsistent; for there is no sūtra or treatise that ever states that one who has attained the aids to penetration dwells within the Jambū forest. One should know that this is merely their own fabrication.
It is reasonable to say that a Bodhisattva in his final birth dwelling in the Jambūvana forest is called an "ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) at that time;

for he is then equal to a rishi who has abandoned desire, and thus [the sūtra] praises him as superior when comparing him to those rishis. Although the merit of giving to such a Bodhisattva is infinitely superior.
Based on the preceding comparison, it was stated that [the stream-enterer] is superior by a factor of one hundred; this must logically be so.

For subsequently, the Blessed One excluded those ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and compared the heterodox practitioners (*tīrthika*) with those who have entered the path of the stream-winner (*srotāpanna-pratipannaka*) to determine their relative superiority or inferiority.
If it were not so, the Blessed One would have compared that ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) with one who has entered the stream (*srotāpanna*).
Having already explained the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the abiding of sentient beings,
as previously stated regarding death through the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyus-kṣaya*) and so forth, we shall now correctly analyze this.
Which consciousness manifests and which feeling is associated with death, birth, and so forth?
The verse says:
The severing of the roots of virtue and their reconnection, Detachment from passion, falling away [from it], and death and birth.
It is permitted that death and birth occur only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and that these states consist only of the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
They do not occur during meditative absorption or in the mindless states; rather, they occur in the two types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) and in *nirvāṇa*.
For those who die gradually, the final cessation of the mental consciousness occurs at the feet, the navel, or the heart.
In the lower realms, among humans, and in the heavens, [the vital points] do not cease; the *marmaccheda* (severance of the vital points) occurs through water and so forth.
The treatise says:

Regarding the severance of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), the reconnection of roots of goodness, the detachment from the defilements of a realm or stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*), the falling away from such detachment, death, and rebirth—in these six states, it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is admitted, and no other.
It should be understood that the term "birth" (*jāti*) as it is spoken of here also includes the initial linking of existence (*pratisaṃdhi*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Death and birth are held to be associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*); because a mind associated with equanimity is not sharp or clear, while other sensations are sharp and clear and thus do not accord with death and birth.

Furthermore, these two occasions are exclusively states of distraction (*vikṣipta*) and not states of meditative concentration (*samāhita*); they must necessarily be states possessing mind (*sacittaka*) and cannot be states without mind (*acittaka*).

There is no possibility of death or birth while the mind is in a state of concentration, because [such a mind] belongs to a different realm and stage (*dhātu-bhūmi*), because it is produced through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and because it is capable of providing benefit and support.
Nor is there the principle of death and rebirth in the absence of mind, because in the state of no-mind, life-force is necessarily not impaired.
If the body that serves as the basis is about to perish, it must necessarily give rise again to a mind that belongs to that basis before one passes away; there is no other possibility.
Furthermore, one who is without mind cannot undergo rebirth because there would be no cause; for apart from the arising of afflictions, there is no undergoing of rebirth.
Although it is said that the death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*) may involve minds of the three natures, entry into nirvana occurs only through the two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds.

If it is asserted that there is neutral maturation (*vipāka*) of equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the desire realm, then they assert that the mind entering *nirvāṇa* in the desire realm also possesses both deportment-neutral (*airyāpathika*) and maturation-neutral states.

If it is asserted that there is no maturation-neutral state of equanimity in the desire realm, then they assert that the mind entering *nirvāṇa* in the desire realm possesses only deportment-neutral states and lacks maturation-neutral states.
Why is it that only neutral (*avyākṛta*) consciousness attains entry into nirvāṇa?
Because the power of the neutral is subtle and accords with the cessation of the mind.
At the moment of death, in which part of the body does consciousness finally cease?
In those who die instantaneously, the mental consciousness and the body-faculty (kāyendriya) cease all at once.

As for those who die gradually—whether they are destined for the lower realms, the human realm, or the heavenly realms—the consciousness ceases sequentially at the feet, the navel, and the heart, respectively. That is to say, those falling into the evil destinies are said to "go downward"; their final consciousness ceases at the feet.
If one is going to the human realm, the consciousness ceases at the navel; if one is being reborn in the heavens, the consciousness ceases at the heart.
The Arhats are called "unborn" (ajāta), and their final consciousness also ceases at the heart-base (*cittāśraya*).
Other masters say:

its cessation occurs at the crown of the head; at the moment of actual death, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) ceases in places such as the feet, and consequently the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also ceases.
At the time of death, the body-faculty gradually ceases; reaching the feet and other parts, it suddenly and completely vanishes.
It is like placing a small amount of water on a heated stone: it diminishes and evaporates bit by bit until it is entirely exhausted in one spot.
Furthermore, regarding those who die gradually: at the time of death, they are mostly oppressed by the painful sensations of the *marmaccheda* (the severing of the vital points).

There is no separate entity called a "vital point" (*marman*); rather, when certain specific joints or members of the body are touched, it causes immediate death—this is what is termed a "vital point."

If any one of the elements—water, fire, or wind—becomes excessively aggravated, it is as if a sharp blade were to strike their vital points (*marmans*); consequently, an intense sensation of suffering arises, and before long, they meet their end.
It is not as when one speaks of "cutting" as in the felling of firewood; rather, it receives the name "cutting" because, like that [felled wood], it is devoid of sensation.
For what reason does the earth element lack this function of cutting?
Because it lacks the fourth internal calamity.
The three internal calamities refer to the increase of wind, heat, and water, which arise respectively according to their correspondence with wind, fire,
and water. Some say that these resemble the three external calamities of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
This [state] does not exist among the gods of the Heaven of the Subduers of Māra; however, when those sons of gods are about to die, five kinds of minor signs of decay first appear:
first, their clothing and ornaments emit unpleasant sounds;
second, the radiance of their own bodies suddenly becomes dim and inferior.
Third, while in the state of bathing, drops of water cling to his body;
fourth, his nature, formerly restless and racing about, now remains fixed upon a single object;
fifth, his eyes, formerly still and serene, now blink repeatedly.
The manifestation of these five signs does not necessarily mean that death is imminent.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of signs of great decline that manifest:
first, one's clothing becomes stained with dust and grime;
Second, his flower garlands wither;
third, sweat breaks out from both armpits;
fourth, a foul odor enters his body.
Fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat.
When these five signs appear, death is certain.
Regarding this world of sentient beings—its birth, abiding, and passing away—the World-Honored One establishes three groups.
What are the three groups?
The verse says:
The group of the rightly fixed, the wrongly fixed, and the indeterminate; the noble ones, those who commit the immediate transgressions, and the rest.
The treatise says:
First, the group of those fixed in the right nature; second, the group of those fixed in the wrong nature; third, the group of those of indeterminate nature.
What is meant by "the right nature"?
As the Sūtra says:
"Greed is abandoned without remainder; hatred is abandoned without remainder; delusion is abandoned without remainder.
When all afflictions are abandoned without remainder, this is called the 'Right State' (samyaktva)."

One who is concentrated is called a noble one (*ārya*). A noble one is so called because the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) has already arisen within them; they are named "noble" because they have distanced themselves from all unwholesome dharmas and have attained the acquisition of ultimate dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
Because it definitively exhausts the afflictions, it is called "right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*).
Since those who have already attained the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) will also certainly attain *nirvāṇa*, why would their state not be "right concentration"?
Because they may subsequently fall into the group of those fixed in error,
and because the time of their attainment of nirvāṇa is not yet certain— unlike stream-enterers who have at most seven more births—
and because they have not yet abandoned their false nature, they are not called "fixed in the right."
What is called "wrong nature" (*mithyātva*)?
It refers to the various hells, animals, and hungry ghosts; these are called wrong nature. "Fixed" (*niyata*) refers to the immediate (*ānantarya*);
those who commit an immediate offense will necessarily fall into hell, and for this reason it is called "wrongly fixed" (*mithyā-niyata*).
Those that remain beyond the determinate states of the right and the wrong are called the indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*),
because they can become either depending on two conditions.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Ten.

Chapter Three: Analysis of the World, Part Four. Thus has the world of sentient beings been explained.
The receptacle world shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
In establishing the receptacle world, the wind-circle dwells at the very bottom;
its extent is immeasurable in width, and its thickness is sixteen lakṣas.
Above that is the water-circle, eleven hundred million and twenty thousand [yojanas] deep.
Eight hundred thousand *lakṣas* of water remain below; the remainder solidifies to form the golden wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*).
This wheel of water and gold is twelve hundred thousand *lakṣas* in diameter—specifically twelve hundred and thirty-four thousand five hundred—and its circumference is three times this amount.
The treatise says:
It is accepted that this trichiliocosm is established in such a manner with various dimensions and forms.

That is to say, through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, first, based upon space at the very bottom, a wind-wheel arises; its breadth is incalculable, and its thickness is sixteen hundred million yojanas.

The substance of such a wind-circle is so firm and dense that even if a great Nārāyaṇa were to brandish a vajra-wheel and strike it with all his might, the vajra would shatter while the wind-circle would remain unharmed.

Furthermore, through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, great clouds and rains arise and pour upon the wind-circle; the drops, as large as axle-trees, accumulate to form the water-circle.
Thus, while this water-circle has not yet solidified, it is eleven billion and twenty thousand *yojanas* deep.
How is it that the water wheel does not flow away or disperse?
Other masters say:
It is sustained by the karmic power of all sentient beings, which prevents it from flowing away or dispersing.
Just as when food and drink have not yet been digested and transformed, they never flow down and fall into the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*).
Other schools say:
it is held by the winds so that it does not flow or scatter, just as grain is held within a granary.

Through the karmic power of sentient beings, a distinct wind arises and strikes this water, causing it to solidify into gold. Just as when boiled milk cools, a film forms on the surface, so too the water-mandala diminishes until its thickness is only eight hundred thousand *lakṣas*, while the remainder transforms into gold, three hundred and twenty million *yojanas* thick.
The dimensions of its two wheels are equal in measure; that is, the diameter is twelve billion, three hundred and four and a half *yojanas*.
The circumference of its perimeter is three times that amount, meaning the total circumference measures thirty-six billion, one thousand, three hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
The verse says:
Sumeru stands in the center; next are Yugandhara, Īṣādhara Mountain, and Khadiraka Mountain.
Sudarśana, Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka Mountain, and Nimindhara Mountain;
outside of the great continents and so forth, there is the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountain.
The first seven mountains are composed of gold; Sumeru is made of the four jewels.
They all enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas], and the height of Mount Meru above the water is likewise.
The remaining eight decrease by half and half respectively; their widths are all equal to their heights.
The treatise states:
Upon the Golden Wheel there are nine great mountains; Sumeru, the King of Mountains, abides in the center, while the other eight surround Sumeru on all sides.
Among the eight mountain ranges, the first seven are called the "inner" mountains; outside the seventh mountain lie the great continents and other features.
Beyond these is the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountain, which encircles the entire world-system like a wheel.
The seven mountain ranges, beginning with Yugandhara, are composed solely of gold.
The king of mountains, Sumeru, has four precious substances as its substance; that is to say, its four faces—north, east, south, and west—consist respectively of gold, silver, vaidūrya, and crystal.
Because the colors manifesting in space follow the majestic power of the jewels, the sky over Jambudvīpa appears to have the color of vaidūrya.
From what do such jewels arise? They likewise arise through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.

Again, great clouds arise and rain upon the golden wheel in drops as thick as axle-trees; the accumulated waters surge into waves, and these waters immediately become a treasury containing the seeds of various jewels.
Through the piercing impact of winds possessing diverse powers and majesty, they are transformed and produced as various classes of jewels.

In this way, when water transforms into jewels and so forth, the cause ceases as the effect arises; their substances do not coexist, unlike that which is produced through *pariṇāma* (transformation) as asserted by the Sāṃkhya school.
How does the Sāṃkhya school maintain the meaning of transformation?
This refers to the adherence to the view that while the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a phenomenon exists eternally, other phenomena arise and other phenomena perish.
How could such a transformation be logically consistent?
It is because it is absolutely impossible for a phenomenon to be permanent while one maintains that distinct phenomena undergo cessation and arising.
Who says that there is a "property-bearer" (dharmin) existing apart from the property (dharma)?
It is simply this very property, at the time of its transformation, which serves as the basis for a different characteristic and is thus called the "property-bearer.
This too is irrational.
What is illogical?
It is to say that this very thing is not as it appears; such a meaning of words has never been heard before.

Once gold, jewels, and so forth have thus transformed and arisen, further winds are induced by the power of karma, which distinguish the jewels and other substances, gathering them together to form mountains and continents, and separating the waters into sweet and salt to establish the inner and outer oceans respectively.

Thus, these nine mountains rest upon the Golden Wheel (kāñcanamaṇḍala), and their immersion in the waters is equal at eighty thousand yojanas; the same applies to Mount Sumeru’s emergence above the water.

For the remaining eight mountains, the height above the water decreases by half for each successive one: that is, Yugandhara emerges at forty thousand yojanas, down to the final Cakravāḍa mountain, which emerges at three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas.
Thus, the width of each of these nine mountains is equal to the height of the water it emerges from.
The verse says:
Between the mountains there are eight seas; the first seven are called "inner."
At its beginning, it is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide; each of its four sides is three times that.
The remaining six are half as wide as the preceding one, respectively.
The eighth is called the outer [ocean], measuring three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas.
The treatise states:
With Mount Sumeru as the first and the Cakravāḍa mountains as the last, there are eight seas in between; the first seven are called the inner seas.
Within these seven, all possess water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities:
First, sweet; second, cool; third, soft; fourth, light; fifth, pure; sixth, odorless; seventh, it does not harm the throat when drinking; eighth, it does not injure the stomach after drinking.

Thus, the first of these seven seas is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide; measured by the circumference of its inner edge along the Yugandhara Mountains, it is three times that amount on each of its four sides, totaling twenty-four million four hundred thousand yojanas for each.

The remaining six oceans decrease by half and half respectively; that is, the extent of the second ocean is forty thousand [yojanas], and so on, until the extent of the seventh is one thousand two hundred and fifty.
The circumference of these is not stated because it would be too cumbersome;
the eighth is called the Outer [Ocean], filled with salt water, measuring three hundred and twenty-two thousand [yojanas] in breadth.
The verse says:
Regarding the characteristics of the great continents: Jambudvīpa in the south is shaped like a chariot;
its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], while its southern side is three and a half.
The continent of Pūrvavideha is shaped like a half-moon;
its three sides are like those of Jambudvīpa, while its eastern side measures three hundred and fifty [yojanas].
The continent of Aparagoyānī is circular and without deficiency.
The diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and its circumference is three times this;
Uttarakuru is square, with each side being equal at two thousand [yojanas].
There are eight intermediate continents, two situated at each side of the four great continents.
The treatise says:
Within the great outer ocean there are four continents, situated on the four sides facing Mount Sumeru.
Jambudvīpa in the south is broad in the north and narrow in the south; its three sides are equal in measure, and its shape is like a chariot.
Its southern side is only three and a half yojanas wide, while each of its other three sides is two thousand yojanas long.

Only on this continent is there a Vajrāsana (Diamond Throne), which reaches from the surface of the earth down to the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanacakra*). All Bodhisattvas who are about to attain perfect enlightenment sit upon this throne to give rise to the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), because no other place possesses the firm power capable of supporting it, including the state of Nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
The continent of Pūrvavideha is narrow in the east and broad in the west; its three sides are equal in measure, and its shape is like a half-moon.
It is three hundred and fifty [yojanas] in width at the eastern edge, and each of its three other sides is two thousand [yojanas].
The continent of Aparagodānīya is circular like the full moon; its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and its circumference is seven thousand five hundred.
The continent of Uttarakuru is shaped like a square seat; its four sides are equal in measure, each being two thousand [yojanas].
The word "etc. (ādi) is used to clarify that there is not the slightest increase or decrease [in this enumeration].
Just as the shape of each continent is, so too is the face of its inhabitants.

Furthermore, there are eight intermediate continents (*antaradvīpa*), which are the satellites of the great continents; that is, there are two intermediate continents situated on each side of the four great continents.
The two intermediate continents bordering Jambudvīpa are: first, Cāmara Island; second, Avara-cāmara Island.
The two intermediate continents bordering Videha are: first, Deha Island; second, Videha Island.
The two intermediate continents bordering Godānīya are: first, Śāṭhā; second, Uttaramantriṇa.
The two intermediate continents bordering Kuru are: first, Kurava; second, Kaurava.
All these continents are inhabited by humans;
however, some say that they are inhabited solely by rākṣasas.
The verse says:
To the north of this [lake] are nine Black Mountains; within the Snowy Mountains and the Fragrant Mountain lies the Anavatapta Lake, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
The treatise states:
From the center of this Jambudvīpa toward the north, there are three locations, each having three layers of Black Mountains (*kṛṣṇaparvata*).
To the north of these Black Mountains lies the Great Snowy Mountain (*himavat*); to the north of the Great Snowy Mountain lies the Fragrant Intoxication Mountain (*gandhamādana*).
To the north of the Snow Mountains and to the south of Fragrant Mountain lies a great lake called Anavatapta (The Heatless), from which four great rivers flow:
first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Sindhu; third, the Sītā; and fourth, the Vakṣu.

The Lake Anavatapta is equal in length and breadth, measuring fifty yojanas on each side; it is filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities, and none who have not attained supernatural powers can reach it.

Beside this lake is a Jambū forest; the trees are tall and large, and their fruit is sweet and delicious. It is named Jambudvīpa after this forest, or the name of the continent was established based on this fruit.
Furthermore, where are the *naraka*s and the *mahānaraka*s situated?
What are their dimensions and how many are there?
The verse says:
Twenty thousand leagues below this, The Avīci Hell is equal in depth and breadth;
Above it are the seven *naraka*s, And eight secondary hells, each with sixteen.
These are known as the Pit of Hot Ashes, the Pit of Corpses and Excrement, The Pit of Razor Blades, and the Pit of the Fierce River.
Each resides in those four directions, along with the other eight cold hells.
The treatise says:
Twenty thousand yojanas beneath this Jambudvīpa lies the great hell of Avīci.
Its depth and breadth are the same as previously stated, meaning each is twenty thousand [yojanas].
Its bottom lies forty thousand *yojanas* below this place.
Because suffering is experienced there without interruption—unlike in the other seven great *naraka*s where suffering is not constant—it is therefore called "Uninterrupted" (*Avīci*).

For instance, in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) hell, although the bodies of sentient beings there are subjected to various forms of cutting, piercing, grinding, and pounding, they are restored to their original state as soon as they encounter a cool breeze; for this reason, it is given the name Saṃjīva.
In the Avīci hell, such things do not exist.
Other masters say:

it is called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) because there is no interval of pleasure amidst the suffering; in other hells, although there is no [pleasure] that is a result of maturation (vipākaja), there is pleasure that arises as a result of uniform outflow (naiṣyandika).
The seven *naraka*s are situated one above the other, stacked in succession, directly above the Avīci hell.
What are these seven? First, the Extremely Hot; second, the Intensely Hot; third, the Great Wailing; fourth, the Wailing; fifth, the Crushing; sixth, the Black Rope; and seventh, the Reviving.
Some say: These seven are situated alongside the Avīci hell.
There are sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*) for each of the eight *naraka*s; therefore, the Bhagavat spoke this verse:
These eight *naraka*s, I declare, are exceedingly difficult to cross;
their ground is made of glowing iron, surrounded by iron walls,
with four gates on each side, closed with iron doors.
The dimensions are skillfully arranged, each having sixteen secondary hells;
spanning many hundreds of *yojanas, those who have committed evil fill them completely,
where blazing flames interlace everywhere and fierce fires burn perpetually.
Regarding the sixteen *utsada* (supplementary hells): outside each of the four gates of the eight *naraka*s, there are four locations.

First is the *Kukūla-utsada* (the Pit of Hot Ashes), wherein hot ashes reach up to the knees; when sentient beings wander there, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and blood are all scorched and fall away, yet when they lift their feet, these are restored to their original state.

Second is the Kṛmibhakṣa (Corpse-Feces) Increase; that is to say, within this increase, the ground is filled with the mud of corpses and excrement. Within it there are many *nirguṇḍī* worms, whose snouts are as sharp as needles, their bodies white and their heads black. When sentient beings wander therein, they are all bored through by these worms, which pierce their skin and break their bones to devour their marrow.
Third is the Increase of Razor Blades (*kṣuradhāra-vardhana*). Within this increase, there are further three types:

first, the Road of Razor Blades (*kṣuradhāra-patha*), which refers to a great road spread out with razor blades facing upward; when sentient beings wander upon it, as soon as they set foot down, their skin, flesh, and blood are all sliced and shattered, yet when they lift their feet, they are restored to their original state.

Second is the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana). This forest has blades of sharp, keen swords for its leaves. When sentient beings wander there, the wind blows the leaves down, hacking and piercing their limbs until their flesh and bones fall apart; then vultures, spotted dogs, and other beasts tear them apart and devour them.

The third is the Forest of Iron Thorns; this forest has sharp iron thorns sixteen finger-widths long. When sentient beings are driven to climb up and down the trees, these thorns pierce them with their keen points as they move upward and downward. There are also iron-beaked birds that peck at the sentient beings, vying with one another to devour their eyes, hearts, and livers.

Although the three types of paths, such as the Path of Sword-Blades, differ from one another, they are subsumed under a single "Augmented Hell" (*utsada*) because the iron clubs used therein are identical.

Fourth is the Augmented Hell of the Fierce River (*vaitaraṇī*); this augmentation is vast in extent and filled with hot, salty water. Sentient beings enter it, sometimes floating and sometimes sinking, sometimes moving upstream, downstream, sideways, or spinning around, being steamed and boiled until their flesh and bones are reduced to a pulp.

It is like a large cauldron filled with lye into which hemp, rice, and other grains are placed; as a fierce fire blazes beneath it, the hemp and other materials swirl up and down within, their entire bodies becoming completely decomposed and rotted. Sentient beings are just the same.
Should one wish to flee, there are various hell-wardens on both banks who, grasping swords and spears, block and repel them, making it impossible to escape.
This river is like a moat; the three preceding [features] resemble gardens; with four *catur-mukha* towers at each of the four sides, they are thus said to total sixteen.

This is a place where one undergoes additional tortures; thus it is called "Additional" (*utsada*), because after having already been subjected to the primary punishments within the main hells, one suffers further harm there.
Some say: sentient beings emerge from the main hells and encounter these sufferings once more, and for this reason they are called "Additional."
Now, within this context, let us pursue a further inquiry arising from the discussion:
Are the hell-wardens sentient beings? Some say:
[They are] insentient. How can they move?
It is by the karmic power of sentient beings, like the wind at the beginning of the eon of formation (vivartakalpa).
If that is so, how does one reconcile this with what the Venerable Dharmasubhūti said?
As his verse states:
"The mind constantly harbors the poison of anger, And delights in accumulating all manner of evil karma."
Rejoicing at the sight of others' suffering, one becomes a henchman of Yama after death.
Those messengers of King Yama who cast sentient beings into the hells are called the henchmen of Yama.
These are not actually sentient beings who harm other sentient beings within the hells; therefore, the hell-wardens are not actual sentient beings.
Some say: they are sentient beings.
If that is so, where is the retribution for this evil karma experienced?
It is within the hells themselves; since even the hells can accommodate the retribution induced by the *ānantarya* [immediate] offenses, what logic could possibly preclude this?
If that is so, for what reason does fire not burn them?
This is because they are obstructed by the power of karma, or because they are produced from distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and thus are not burned.
It has already been explained that there are eight hot *naraka*s.
Furthermore, there are eight other cold *naraka*s. What are these eight?
First, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Hahava; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala; seventh, Padma; eighth, Mahāpadma.
The sentient beings here are oppressed by intense cold; they are named according to the transformations of their bodies and voices.
These eight are situated beneath Jambudvīpa, as previously described alongside the great hells.
This Jambudvīpa is of such small measure; how could it possibly contain the Avīci Hell and the other hells below?
The continent is like a heap of grain—narrow at the top and broad at the bottom—which is why the great ocean gradually narrows and deepens.
The sixteen hells discussed above are induced by the predominant karma (*adhipati-karma*) of all sentient beings.

The remaining isolated hells (*pratyeka-naraka*), however, are summoned by the individual karma of specific beings; they may be inhabited by many, two, or even just one, and their varieties are manifold with no fixed location. They may be situated near rivers, mountains, or wildernesses, or beneath the earth, in the air, or in other places.
The vessels of the various hells are arranged in this manner: their primary locations are below, while their branches are not fixed.
As for the dwelling places of animals (*tiryag-yoni*), they are said to be water, land, and air; their primary location is the great ocean, from which they later spread to other regions.

The original abode of all these ghosts is the realm of King Yama; five hundred yojanas beneath this Jambudvīpa lies the realm of King Yama, which is equal in its longitudinal and transverse dimensions, from which they subsequently disperse to dwell in other places.

Some are handsome and endowed with great majesty, experiencing all manner of wealth and pleasure with sovereignty like the gods; others are emaciated by hunger and have ugly countenances—such categories as these are explained at length in the sūtra.
Regarding the dimensions and significance of the abodes of the sun and moon, the verse says:
The sun and moon are halfway up Mount Meru; [Their radii are] fifty-one and fifty [yojanas].
At midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise, They are respectively at the four continents.
During the second month of the rainy season, the nights gradually increase for the final nine nights;
it is the same for the fourth month of winter. When the nights decrease, the days increase accordingly.
During the periods of traveling north and south, the day and night increase by one lava at a time.
"Recently, as its shadow fell upon it, / The lunar disk was thus seen to be incomplete.
The treatise asks:
Upon what do the sun, the moon, and the various stars depend for their abiding?
It abides by means of wind;

that is to say, through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, winds are collectively induced to arise, circling around Mount Sumeru in the air and supporting the sun and other celestial bodies so that they do not fall.
How many yojanas is the place where they dwell from here?
The summit of Yugandhara is level with the midpoint of Sumeru.
What is the diameter of the sun and moon in yojanas?
The sun is fifty-one [yojanas] in diameter, while the moon is only fifty.
The smallest star is one krośa, and the largest is sixteen yojanas.
The lower surface of the solar disk is composed of *sphatika* jewels that are fire-essence gems; they are capable of heating and illuminating.
The lower surface of the lunar disk is composed of *sphatika* jewels that are water-essence gems; they are capable of cooling and illuminating.

Arising through the predominant influence of the karma of sentient beings, it is able to benefit or harm objects such as eyes, bodies, fruits, flowers, crops, and medicinal herbs, according to what is appropriate for each.
The single sun and moon perform their respective functions throughout the four continents; do they perform the function of one day simultaneously for all four continents?
No. Why is this so?
When it is midnight in the northern continent, the sun sets in the eastern continent, it is midday in the southern continent, and the sun rises in the western continent.
These four times are equal; other instances should be understood by analogy.
Because the sun’s path across this continent varies, days and nights undergo decrease and increase.

From the ninth day of the second half of the second month of the rainy season, the nights gradually increase; from the ninth day of the second half of the fourth month of the cold season, the nights gradually decrease. The periods of increase and decrease for the days are the reverse of this.
When the night gradually increases, the day gradually decreases; when the night gradually decreases, the day gradually increases.
When the day and night increase, by how much does one day and night increase?
It increases by one lava.
The decrease of night and day is likewise.
As the sun moves toward the south or the north of this continent, respectively, the nights increase and the days increase.
For what reason is the lunar disc seen as incomplete at the end of the dark fortnight and at the beginning of the bright fortnight?
In the *Lokaprajñapti*, it is explained as follows:

"Because the lunar palace moves close to the solar orb, the moon is eclipsed by the light of the solar orb; a shadow is cast from the opposite side that covers the lunar disk itself, causing it to appear incomplete at that time."
The former masters explained:
"The appearance of fullness and deficiency is due to the differing orbital paths traversed by the disks of the sun and moon.
In what sentient beings do the palaces of the sun and other celestial bodies dwell?
Regarding the celestial hosts under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings:
do these celestial hosts dwell only here?

If one considers the space-dwelling devas, they dwell only in such palaces as those of the sun and so forth; if one considers the earth-dwelling devas, they dwell on the various terraces of Mount Sumeru and other such places.
How many tiers are there?
What are their dimensions?
And which devas dwell upon which tiers?
The verse says:
Sudarśana has four tiers, Each separated by ten thousand [yojanas];
They extend outward sixteen thousand, Eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively.
The Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādharas, and the Mahārājikas dwell respectively on the four tiers; they also reside on the other seven mountains.
The treatise says:

Mount Sumeru has four terraces; from the water’s edge to the first terrace, the distance is ten thousand yojanas, and likewise, from the third terrace to the end of the fourth, the distance is also ten thousand yojanas.

These four tiers extend outward from the side of Mount Meru, encircling it for its lower half; the first tier extends sixteen thousand [yojanas], while the second, third, and fourth tiers extend eight, four, and two thousand respectively.

There is a yakṣa deity named Dṛḍhapāṇi who dwells on the first tier; one named Mālādhāra dwells on the second tier; and one named Sadāmatta dwells on the third tier. These three are all celestial hosts belonging to the Four Great Kings. Because the fourth tier is the common abode of the Four Great Kings and their retinues, the sūtra refers to them as the Cāturmahārājika devas.

Just as the Four Great Kings and their retinues dwell upon the four outer terraces of Mount Sumeru, so too do devas dwell upon the seven golden mountains, such as Yugandhara and Īṣādhara; these are the fiefdoms under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings, and are known as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings who Dwell on the Ground.
Among the gods of the desire realm, this heaven is the most extensive.
Where do the Gods of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) dwell?
The verse says:
The summit of Sumeru is eighty thousand [yojanas] high; there dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
At its four corners are four peaks where Vajrapāṇi resides.
The central palace is named Sudarśana, measuring ten thousand yojanas in circumference.
Its height is half that of the golden city wall; the ground is adorned with various ornaments and is soft and supple.
In its center is the Palace of Supreme Excellence, measuring one thousand yojanas in circumference.
It is adorned outside by four gardens: Saṃtāna, Cūta, Miśra, and Nandana.
The wondrous ponds are situated at the four cardinal directions, each separated from the others by twenty [yojanas].
To the northeast is the Pārijāta tree; to the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall.
The commentary states:

The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) dwells upon the summit of Mount Meru; each of its four sides measures eighty thousand [yojanas], and its dimensions are no different from those of the four sides below.
Other masters say:
it is eighty thousand [yojanas] in circumference, though when the four sides are mentioned individually, each is only twenty thousand.
At each of the four corners of the mountain peak there is a summit, each measuring five hundred [yojanas] in height and breadth.
There dwells the yakṣa deity Vajrapāṇi, who resides therein to protect the devas.

In the center of the mountain peak is a palace named Sudarśana, measuring two thousand five hundred yojanas on each side and ten thousand yojanas in circumference. Its golden walls are one and a half yojanas high; the ground is level and composed of pure gold, adorned with one hundred and one varieties of precious gems. The surface is as soft to the touch as *tūla* cotton, rising and falling according to the pressure of the feet as one walks upon it. This is the great capital city where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides.

Within that city is the Palace of Excellence (Vaijayanta), fully adorned with various exquisite jewels; it is named "Excellence" because it outshines all other celestial palaces. It measures two hundred and fifty yojanas on each side, totaling one thousand yojanas in circumference.
These are called the various delightful things within the city.
Outside the city on its four sides are four parks, adorned and serving as the common places of recreation for those devas:

first, the Saṃtarpaka (Many-Cart) Park; second, the Pāruṣyaka (Rough-and-Harsh) Park; third, the Miśravana (Mixed Forest) Park; and fourth, the Nandanavana (Joyful Forest) Park. These constitute the external ornaments adorning the great city.

At the four sides of the four groves, there are four exquisite ponds, each situated twenty yojanas from the center of its respective grove; these are the supreme places for the gods' recreation, where the gods compete in excellence and enjoy themselves.
To the northeast outside the city is the Pārijāta tree, the supreme place where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven enjoy sensual pleasures.

Its coiled roots extend fifty yojanas in depth and breadth; its trunk rises upward while its branches spread out to the sides, reaching a height and width of one hundred yojanas. Its leaves stand erect and its flowers bloom with a wondrous fragrance that, when carried by the wind, perfumes the air for one hundred yojanas, and even against the wind, it still pervades fifty yojanas.
It is possible for fragrance to travel with the wind; how then can it be said to "pervade against the wind"?
Other masters say:
fragrance has no inherent capacity to pervade against the wind, but it is said to do so because it does not exceed the boundaries of the tree from which it originates.
In reality, the Pārijāta tree possesses such a quality that the fragrance it emits can permeate even against the wind;

though obstructed by celestial winds and natural gales, it continues to flow toward other directions, gradually becoming weaker and fainter until it ceases in its vicinity, rather than reaching as far as it does when carried with the wind.

Regarding this fragrance of flowers: does it depend on its own substrate and proceed in a continuous stream to another location by means of the wind, or does it merely perfume the wind so that a distinct fragrance is produced?
There is no fixed conclusion on this matter; the various masters of the Vinaya accept both of these positions without fault.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One say:
"The fragrance of flowers cannot waft against the wind, Nor can the scent of roots, stalks, and the like;
But the fragrant perfume of the virtues of the noble ones Flows beautifully against the wind, pervading all directions."
This statement is made based on the fragrances found among humans; for it is commonly understood in the world that no such power exists [among them].
The *Mahīśāsaka* Sūtra states that this fragrance, when with the wind, pervades a hundred *yojana*s, and when there is no wind, it pervades only fifty.

In the outer southwest corner is the Sudharmā Hall, where the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three assemble from time to time to discuss in detail matters concerning what is in accordance with the Dharma and what is not.

Having thus explained the external receptacle world inhabited by the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, one may ask: what is the receptacle world inhabited by the other classes of gods belonging to the realm of form?
The verse says:
Above this are the gods with form, who dwell in palaces supported by space.
The commentary says:
Regarding the aforementioned gods with form who dwell in the heavens of the Thirty-three, they reside in palaces suspended in space.
What are the gods with form who dwell above?
They are the Yāma devas, the Tuṣita devas, the Nirmāṇarati devas, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.

Including the sixteen abodes previously mentioned, such as the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya), there are twenty-two heavens in total, all of which depend upon the external receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
Among these aforementioned celestial hosts, the verse says:
Six enjoy desire through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.
The treatise says:
Only the six heavens of the desire realm experience exquisite objects of desire. Among them, the first two are earth-dwelling devas; their sexual union is no different from that of humans.
However, as soon as the wind-like energy is released, the heat and affliction are immediately dispelled; it is not like in the human realm where there is residual impurity.

Among the hosts of the Yāma Heaven, sexual union is accomplished merely by embracing; in Tuṣita Heaven, it is achieved simply by holding hands; in Nirmāṇarati Heaven, it is achieved by smiling at one another; and in Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it is accomplished by looking into each other's eyes.
The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this explanation:
all six classes of gods engage in sexual intercourse through physical union.
The descriptions in the *Lokaprajñapti* regarding mutual embracing and so forth are intended merely to clarify the differences in the duration of those acts.
This is because the sensory objects of these various devas become increasingly exquisite and their minds of craving become increasingly swift; thus it is so.
Upon the knees of those devas, male and female, boys and girls suddenly manifest through transformation, and they are then said to be the sons and daughters born of those devas.
What is the body size of the newly born devas?
The verse says:
At first they are like [humans] from five to ten [years old]; In the Form Realm, they are complete in form and possess clothing.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, when the various devas of the six desire realms are first born, they are respectively like humans of five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten years of age; once born, their physical forms quickly reach full maturity.
When the celestial hosts of the Form Realm first take birth, their bodies are fully developed in size and they are endowed with exquisite garments.
All these celestial beings speak the noble language; that is to say, their speech is identical to that of Central India.
How should one understand the distinctions among those born through desire and those born through pleasure?
The verse says:
Those born through desire are threefold: humans and devas; Those born through pleasure are threefold: nine abodes.
The treatise says:

Regarding the three types of birth in the desire realm, there are sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various excellent objects of desire present before them; they exercise mastery over such present objects of desire, namely those in the entire human realm and the four lower heavens.

There are sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various exquisite objects of desire emanated by themselves; they exercise mastery over these self-emanated objects of exquisite desire, namely, the gods of the fifth realm, the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).

There are sentient beings who delight in experiencing the various exquisite objects of desire provided by others; they exercise sovereign control over these exquisite objects of desire provided by others, namely, the sixth [heaven], the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

Based on experiencing desire-objects as they arise before one, based on experiencing desire-objects created by oneself as being pleasurable, and based on experiencing desire-objects created by others as being pleasurable, three distinct types of birth in the realm of desire are differentiated.

Regarding the "arising of pleasure" (*sukhopapatti*), within the three dhyānas there arise three kinds of pleasure in nine locations. That is to say, they dwell in the joy and pleasure born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*), the joy and pleasure born of concentration (*samādhija-prītisukha*), and the pleasure born of the fading away of joy (*prītivirāga-sukha*). Because they dwell for a long time, remain free from suffering for a long time, and experience pleasure for a long time, it is called the "arising of pleasure."
One should consider that in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is no joy (*prīti*) or bliss (*sukha*) at all; why, then, is it also called a "heaven of blissful birth" (*sukhopapatti*)?
Regarding the twenty-two abodes of the gods that have been mentioned, what is the distance between them from top to bottom?
The verse says:
As the distance from the bottom is, so too is the number [of yojanas] to the top.
The commentary says:

The distance in *yojanas* between each successive level is not easily calculable; however, one may state the total distance from each level down to the ocean, and the distance to the levels above follows the same principle.
Whichever heaven one follows, the distance from that heaven down to the ocean is equal to the distance from that heaven up to the level immediately above it.

That is to say, from the fourth terrace of Mount Sumeru down to the great ocean is forty thousand yojanas; this is the primary abode of the Four Great Kings. From there up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three is likewise equal to the distance from that heaven down to the great ocean.
Just as the distance from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven down to the great ocean is the same as the distance from it up to the Yāma Heaven;

and so on, until the distance from the Sudarśana Heaven down to the great ocean in yojanas is equal to the distance from that heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, which is likewise equal to the distance from that heaven down to the ocean.
Above this, there is no further place of residence; this location is the highest and is named Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form).
Other masters say that it is called the Heaven of the Ultimate Obstruction (Āvaraṇakaniṣṭha).
He says that the term "obstruction" (*pratigha*) refers to the accumulation of matter; when that obstruction reaches its limit, it receives the name "ultimate.
Can one born in a lower realm ascend to see those in a higher realm?
The verse says:
"Except by means of supernormal power or depending on another, one cannot ascend from a lower level to see those above.
The treatise says:
By means of their own supernormal power, the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens can ascend from their own abode to the Yāma Heaven.
Alternatively, it may depend on others; that is, those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) or celestial beings (*deva*) may escort them to the Yāma heaven.
The same applies by analogy to all other heavens ascending above: whether they come or go, those below see those above.
However, the eyes of a lower realm cannot perceive the higher realms or higher stages, as these are not their objective domain.

Just as one does not perceive the tactile sensations of another, when descending from a higher stage to a lower stage, one does not come with one's own body, but must manifest a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) belonging to the lower stage.
Other schools state:
The gods of those lower realms can also see the forms of the higher realms by their own will, just as those born in this world look down upon the heavens above.
What are the dimensions of the abodes of the celestial palaces of the Yāma and other heavens?
Other masters say:
"The dimensions of the abodes of these four heavens above are equal to those of the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Still other masters say:
Each higher level increases twofold.
Other masters say:

the palaces and their bases in the first dhyāna stage are equal in extent to one four-continent world system; those in the second dhyāna are equal to a small thousandfold world system; those in the third dhyāna are equal to a medium thousandfold world system; and those in the fourth dhyāna are equal to a great thousandfold world system.
Other masters say:
"The three lower dhyānas are respectively equal in extent to the small, medium, and great chiliocosms; the fourth dhyāna is of infinite extent.
To what extent do these small, medium, and great chiliocosms refer?
The verse says:
Four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm,
and the Brahma worlds— each set of one thousand is called a small chiliocosm.
A thousand of these small thousands is called one medium chiliocosm;
a thousand times this is a great trichiliocosm, all of which undergo formation and destruction simultaneously.
The treatise says:

One thousand sets of the four great continents up to the Brahma world are collectively termed a small chiliocosm; one thousand times a small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm; and one thousand medium chiliocosms are collectively termed a great trichiliocosm. Such a great trichiliocosm undergoes formation and destruction simultaneously.
The characteristics of their formation and destruction will be discussed extensively later.
Just as there are differences in the dimensions of the external receptacle world, are there also differences in the dimensions of the bodies [of beings]?
Indeed, there are.
How so? The verse says:
The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits.
The inhabitants of the eastern, western, and northern continents increase successively by double.
For the gods of the desire realm, one *krośa* increases by one-quarter at each stage;
for the gods of the form realm, the first four [levels] increase by half a *yojana* at each.
Above this, they double successively, except that in the Anabhraka heaven, three [yojanas] are subtracted.
The commentary states:
The bodies of humans in Jambudvīpa are mostly three and a half cubits in height; among them, a small portion are four cubits tall.
The inhabitants of Pūrvavideha are eight cubits (*hasta*) in height; those of Aparagodānīya are sixteen cubits; and those of Uttarakuru are thirty-two cubits.

Among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the height of the lowest [heaven] is one-quarter of a *krośa*; thus, increasing by one-quarter of a *krośa* for each successive level, the height reaches one and a half *krośas* at the sixth heaven.

Regarding the body size of the gods of the Form Realm: the first, the Brahmakāyika heaven, is half a yojana; the Brahmapurohita is one full yojana; the Mahābrahmā is one and a half; the Parīttābha is two full yojanas. From these upwards, the remaining heavens all increase twofold at each stage, with the exception of the Anabhraka, which decreases by three yojanas—meaning that while the Apramāṇābha doubles from two to four, this continues up until the Akaniṣṭha, where the increase reaches a full sixteen thousand yojanas.
Since their physical dimensions differ, do their lifespans also differ?
They do indeed differ. How so?
The verse says:
In the Northern Continent, the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years; in the Western and Eastern continents, it is reduced by half and half again respectively.
In this continent (Jambudvīpa), the lifespan is indefinite: ten years at the end, and immeasurable at the beginning.
The fifty years of humans are one day and night in the lowest heaven;
based on this lifespan, they live for five hundred years. In the heavens above, the lifespan increases fivefold at each stage.
In the Form Realm, there is no distinction between day and night; the number of kalpas is equal to the measure of their bodies.
In the formless realm, the first two [levels] are twenty thousand [kalpas]; each subsequent level increases by two thousand.
For the gods from the Parīttābha (Limited Light) upward, a full or half kalpa constitutes their lifespan.
The Treatise says:

The inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years; those of Aparagoyānī live for five hundred years; those of Pūrvavideha live for two hundred and fifty years; and the lifespan of the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa is not fixed.

At the end of the kalpa of decrease, the maximum lifespan is ten years; at the beginning of the kalpa, human lifespan is immeasurable, such that it cannot be calculated by numbers in the hundreds of thousands or more.
Thus has been explained the length and brevity of human lifespans.
One must first establish the days and nights of the heavens before one can calculate the length of celestial lifespans.
How are the days and nights established in the heavens?

Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the lowest of the six classes of gods. Thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve months make a year; their lifespan is five hundred such years.

In the five heavens of the desire realm, [the lifespan] gradually doubles at each level. Specifically, one hundred human years constitute one day and night in the second heaven; based on these days and nights, months and years are calculated, and their lifespan is one thousand years.

In the four heavens beginning with Yāma, the day and night follow the human model in sequence: two, four, eight, and sixteen hundred years constitute one day and night. Based on these days and nights, months and years are calculated; consequently, their lifespans are twenty million, forty million, eighty million, and one hundred and sixty million years respectively.
Above the Yugaṃdhara mountains, neither the sun nor the moon exists; how, then, do those gods establish day and night, and what provides their illumination?
Day and night are established according to the opening and closing of flowers, such as the kumuda and the padma.

Furthermore, depending on the distinctions between the silence and the chirping of various birds, or depending on the differences between the waking and sleeping states of the celestial hosts, they accomplish the phenomenon of external light through the radiance of their own bodies.
Thus has been explained the length of the lifespan of the gods in the desire realm.
In the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no distinction between day and night; rather, the length of their lifespan is known only by means of *kalpas*.
The duration of those *kalpas* corresponds to the measurement of their bodies: that is to say, if the body measures half a *yojana*, the lifespan is half a *kalpa*;
if the body measures one *yojana*, the lifespan is one *kalpa*.
Up to a body size of sixteen thousand [yojanas], the lifespan is likewise sixteen thousand kalpas.
Having thus explained the short and long lifespans of the gods in the Form Realm,
the lifespans of the four heavens of the Formless Realm are, in order from the bottom up, twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty thousand kalpas.
Regarding the kalpas described above, what is their measure?
Are they kalpas of destruction, or of formation,
or intermediate, or great?
From the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha) upward, a full great kalpa constitutes an eon; from the heavens below that, a half great kalpa constitutes an eon.
It is for this reason that it is said that the lifespan of the Great Brahmā King exceeds one and a half kalpas compared to that of the Gods of Brahma’s Retinue (Brahmapurohita).

That is to say, since each of the periods of formation, abiding, and destruction lasts twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa), sixty intermediate kalpas constitute one and a half kalpas; therefore, forty intermediate kalpas—the greater portion of that period—are established as the lifespan for the deities of the lower three heavens.
The lifespan in the happy realms has already been explained, both its brevity and its length.
What of the miserable realms?
The verse says:
In the six hells beginning with Saṃjīva, a day and night is respectively equal to the lifespan of the gods of the Desire Realm;
their own lifespans are likewise equal to those [gods' lifespans].
In Pratāpana, it is half an intermediate kalpa; in Avīci, it is a full intermediate kalpa.
The maximum lifespan of animals is one intermediate kalpa; for hungry ghosts, it is five hundred years by their own reckoning of months and days.
The lifespan in the Arbuda hell is like a *vāha* measure of sesame seeds:
if one seed were removed every hundred years until the supply was exhausted, that would be the duration of one Arbuda; each subsequent hell increases by twentyfold.
The treatise states:

The lifespans of the six heavens of the desire realm, beginning with the Four Great Kings, constitute respectively one day and night for each of the six *naraka*s, starting with Saṃjīva; their lifespans are likewise equal to those of the corresponding heavens.

The lifespan of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years; this constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell. Calculating months and years based on these days and nights, their lifespan there is five hundred such years.

Up to sixteen thousand years in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell; by this reckoning of days and nights, forming months and years, their lifespan there is likewise sixteen thousand years.
The lifespan in the Extremely Hot Hell is half an intermediate kalpa; the lifespan in the Avīci Hell is one intermediate kalpa.
The lifespan of animals is for the most part indefinite; even when it is extremely long, it is at most one intermediate kalpa, such as in the case of the great nāga kings like Nanda and others.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are eight great nāgas, each capable of remaining for an eon to support the great earth.
For the pretas, one human month constitutes a single day; by this reckoning, their months and years form a lifespan of five hundred years.
What is the lifespan in the Cold Hells?
The Blessed One illustrated their lifespan through a simile, saying:

"Suppose there were twenty *khārī* of human sesame seeds, equal to one *vāha* of Magadha; and suppose these were filled to the brim with mustard seeds, and someone were to remove a single seed every hundred years."
In this way, it would be easier to exhaust a great quantity of mustard seeds than to exhaust the lifespan of one born in Arbuda.
Twenty times that amount constitutes the lifespan of the second [hell]; in this manner, each subsequent one increases twentyfold, and these are called the lifespans of the eight cold hells.
Is there premature death among these various lifespans?
The verse says:
In all places there is premature death, except for the continent of Uttarakuru.
The treatise states:
In all locations, there is premature death within the lifespan; only in Uttarakuru is the lifespan fixed at one thousand years.
This is stated with respect to the location as a whole, not to every individual sentient being, for there are certain sentient beings who do not die prematurely.

This refers to Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth who dwell in Tuṣita Heaven, as well as those in their final existence, those for whom a Buddha has given a prophecy, those sent by a Buddha, Bodhisattvas practicing according to faith or according to Dharma, and Universal Monarchs; when their mothers carry these two types of beings in the womb, they all, as appropriate, do not suffer premature death.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Eleven. 5.
Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Fascicle Twelve.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three: The Analysis of the World, Part Five. Thus, having already distinguished the differences in the dimensions of the physical bodies of the receptacle world by means of *yojana*s and other units of measurement.
The distinctions in lifespan have been explained in terms of years and so forth; however, the differences between these two measures have not yet been discussed and must now be addressed.

Since the establishment of these two does not occur without relying on names, and since the former two and their names have not yet been fully detailed regarding their minimum limits, one should first explain the three minimum measures.
The verse says:
The atom, the syllable, and the instant—these are the minimum units of form, name, and time.
The commentary says:
By analyzing all forms down to a single atom (paramāṇu), a single atom is the minimum unit of form.
Likewise, by analyzing all names and time down to a single syllable and a single moment (kṣaṇa), these are the minimum units of name and time.
Regarding the name "a single syllable," it is as when one speaks of the name "Gau.
What is the measure of a single *kṣaṇa*?

It is the duration required for a phenomenon produced by the conjunction of various conditions to acquire its own essence; or, in the case of a moving phenomenon, the time it takes to traverse a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
The masters of Abhidharma say:
"Sixty-five *kṣaṇas* in the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers once is called the measure of one *kṣaṇa*.
Having already understood the three minimum units, what are the measures of the two preceding ones?
Now, let us first analyze the aforementioned *yojana* and other units.
The verse says:
The infinitesimal (*paramāṇu*), the minute (*aṇu*), gold-dust, water-dust, rabbit-hair dust, sheep-hair dust, cow-hair dust, and mote-dust in a sunbeam;
A nit, a louse, a barley grain, and a finger-joint—each subsequent unit increases sevenfold.
Twenty-four finger-joints make one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits constitute the measure of a bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred *krośas* make this eight *yojanas*.
The treatise says: Beginning with the atom (*paramāṇu*) and ending with the finger-joint (*aṅguliparvan*), one should know that each subsequent unit increases sevenfold.

That is to say: seven atoms constitute one minute particle (*aṇu*); seven accumulated minute particles constitute one golden dust mote (*loharaja*); seven accumulated golden dust motes constitute the measure of a water-dust mote (*ab-raja*); seven accumulated water-dust motes constitute one rabbit-hair dust mote (*śaśaraja*); seven accumulated rabbit-hair dust motes constitute the measure of a sheep-hair dust mote (*aurabhra-raja*); seven accumulated sheep-hair dust motes constitute one ox-hair dust mote (*gokṣura-raja*); seven accumulated ox-hair dust motes constitute the measure of a mote moving in a sunbeam (*vātāyana-raja*); seven mote-motes constitute a nit (*likṣā*); seven nits constitute one louse (*yūka*); seven lice constitute a grain of wild barley (*yava*); seven grains of barley constitute one finger-joint; and three joints constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
This is universally established in the world; therefore, it is not separately analyzed in the verse.

Twenty-four finger-breadths laid side-by-side constitute one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits stacked vertically constitute one bow-length, which is called a *vyāma*; five hundred bow-lengths stacked vertically constitute one *krośa*. One *krośa* is accepted as the distance between a village and a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
It is said that eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*.
Having thus explained the *yojana* and other such measures,
we shall now distinguish the subsequent measurements of time, such as the year.
The verse says:
One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute the measure of one tatkṣaṇa;
sixty of these [tatkṣaṇas] make one lava; thirty of these [lavas] make one muhūrta.
These thirty days and nights constitute one month;
twelve months constitute a year, during which half of the nights are subtracted.
The commentary says:
One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa; sixty tatkṣaṇas constitute one lava; thirty lavas constitute one muhūrta; and thirty muhūrtas constitute one day and night.
These days and nights sometimes increase, sometimes decrease, and sometimes are equal.
Thirty days and nights constitute one month; twelve months in total constitute one year.
The year is divided into three seasons—namely, winter, summer, and the rainy season—each consisting of four months.
Among the twelve months, six months have reduced nights, as the total number of nights is diminished by six within the year.
How is this so? Thus, there is a verse that says:
"When half a month has already passed within the periods of cold, heat, and rain,"
During the remaining half-month, the wise know that the nights decrease.
Thus has been explained [the duration] from a *kṣaṇa* up to a year.
As for the different measures of *kalpas*, they shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One should know that there are four kalpas, namely: the kalpa of destruction, formation, intermediate, and great.
The kalpa of destruction begins from the non-arising of beings in the hells and continues until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted.
The eon of formation begins from the rising of the wind until the first birth in hell;
the intermediate eon begins from an immeasurable lifespan, decreasing until life lasts only ten years,
followed by eighteen cycles of increase and decrease, and finally increasing again until it reaches eighty thousand years.
When thus completed, it remains; this is called a medium twenty kalpas.
The periods of formation, destruction, and the void after destruction are all equal to the kalpa of abiding.
Eighty such medium kalpas constitute one great kalpa; three incalculable numbers of great kalpas [constitute the time of a Buddha’s practice].
The treatise says:

Regarding the term "aeon of destruction" (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), it refers to the period from when sentient beings no longer arise in the hells until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted.
There are two kinds of destruction:
First is the destruction of a single realm, and second is the destruction of the world-system.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the destruction of sentient beings, and second, the destruction of the external vessel-world.
That is to say, when this world has completed twenty intermediate kalpas of abiding, there follow another twenty intermediate kalpas of equal duration during which the kalpa of destruction arrives.
When sentient beings in the hells die and no more are newly born, that marks the beginning of the kalpa of destruction.
When not a single sentient being remains in the hells, at that time it is said that the hells have been destroyed.

Those with karma fixed for the hells are drawn by the power of their karma and placed in the hells of other directions; by this principle, one should infer the same for the animal and hungry ghost realms.
However, those who first perish in their respective abodes—those who dwell interspersed among humans and devas—are destroyed together with the humans and devas.

At that time, when a single person in this continent of the human realm, without a teacher, spontaneously attains the first dhyāna through the natural course of the Dharma, they arise from that meditative absorption and proclaim these words:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion are most pleasant and most tranquil."
Upon hearing this, all other people entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and at the end of their lives, they were all reborn in the Brahma world.
When the sentient beings of this continent had thus completely perished, it is said that the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa have been destroyed.
The two continents of the East and West should be explained by analogy with this.
Those in the Northern Continent, when their life ends, are reborn among the gods of the desire realm, because they lack the capacity to enter meditative absorption and become free from desire.
When not even a single sentient being remains in the human realm, at that time it is said that the human realm has been destroyed.

When, among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings in the celestial realm, any one of them spontaneously attains the first dhyāna, and so on until they all attain rebirth in the Brahma-world, at that time the sentient beings of those heavens are entirely exhausted;
this is called the destruction of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The same applies by analogy to the other five classes of desire-realm devas.
When not even a single sentient being remains in the desire realm, it is said that the desire realm has been destroyed as far as sentient beings are concerned.

At that time, when a certain sentient being in the Brahma-world, without a teacher, spontaneously attains the second dhyāna through the natural law (*dharmatā*), and upon arising from that meditative absorption, utters these words:
The joy and bliss born of meditative concentration are exceedingly pleasant and profoundly tranquil.
Upon hearing this, the other devas all entered that dhyāna; when their lives ended, they were all reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When sentient beings have completely perished throughout the Brahma-world, this is called the destruction of the world of sentient beings.
Only the vessel-world remains, vast and empty.

When the karma that caused all sentient beings in the other ten directions to experience this trichiliocosm is exhausted, seven suns gradually appear here. All the oceans dry up and the various mountains burst into flame; the continents and the three wheels are simultaneously consumed by fire. Driven by fierce winds, the flames burn upward through the celestial palaces until even the Brahma-palaces are reduced to nothing but ashes.

The flames of one's own level burn the palaces of that same level; a calamity of another level cannot destroy what belongs to another level. This statement is made because they arise through mutual causal conditions.

The fire from below, driven by the wind, burns the higher levels; that is to say, the fierce flames of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) rise upward, acting as the condition that draws forth the flames of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
The other calamities are likewise to be understood as appropriate.
Thus, from the gradual reduction of beings in hell until the destruction of the receptacle world, this entire period is collectively termed the kalpa of dissolution (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).
What is called the kalpa of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*) refers to the period from the arising of the wind up until the first sentient being is born in hell.

That is to say, once this world has been destroyed by the calamities and remains as mere empty space for twenty intermediate kalpas, after this long duration has passed, there must again follow twenty intermediate kalpas of the "period of abiding," and thus the kalpa of formation arrives.
Through the predominant power of the karma of all sentient beings, subtle winds gradually arise in space; this is the preliminary sign that the receptacle world is about to be formed.

As the winds gradually increase in strength, they establish the wind-circle, water-circle, and gold-circle as previously described; however, first established are the palaces of Mahābrahmā up to those of the Yāma heaven.
Subsequently, the wind-circle and other elements arise; this is called the establishment of the external receptacle world.
First, a single sentient being passes away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and is born in the Great Brahmā realm as the Great Brahmā King.

Thereafter, other sentient beings also passed away from that realm; some were born in the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers, some in the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue, and some in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Gradually descending in birth, they reached the human realms of Kuru, Godānīya, Videha, and Jambudvīpa, and subsequently were born among hungry ghosts, animals, and in the hells.
