It is the natural law that what is destroyed last must necessarily be formed first.

One should know that when the first sentient being is born in the Avīci Hell, twenty intermediate *kalpas* of the formation period (*vivartakalpa*) have already been completed. Following this, there are another twenty intermediate *kalpas* called the "period of abiding after formation" (*vivṛttasthāyikalpa*), which arise in succession; that is, from the arising of the wind that constructs the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) until, at a later time, sentient beings gradually come to inhabit it.
The lifespan of the people on this continent remains immeasurable for a vast period until the beginning of the kalpa of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*), when it begins to gradually decrease.

The period from this immeasurable duration down to a minimum of ten years is called the first intermediate kalpa (*antara-kalpa*) within the kalpa of abiding. Following this, eighteen intermediate kalpas consist of alternating periods of increase and decrease; that is, from ten years increasing up to eighty thousand years, and then from eighty thousand years decreasing back to ten years—this constitutes the second intermediate kalpa.
The subsequent seventeen examples are all like this.
Following the eighteenth, the period from when the lifespan increases from ten years up to its maximum of eighty thousand years is called the twentieth kalpa.
In all kalpas of increase, the duration does not exceed eighty thousand years; in all kalpas of decrease, it reaches a minimum of ten years.

Within eighteen kalpas, each cycle of one increase and one decrease is equal in temporal measure; because the first decrease and the final increase are equal, the temporal measures of all twenty kalpas are identical.
This is collectively termed the kalpa of abiding after formation (*vivartanī-saṃsthita-kalpa*).

As for the remaining kalpas of formation (*vivartanī*), destruction (*saṃvartanī*), and the void after destruction (*saṃvarta-śūnya*), they lack the twentyfold distinctions of decrease and increase; however, because their duration is equal to that of the kalpa of abiding, each is established as consisting of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*) by analogy with the kalpa of abiding.
During the first kalpa of the formation period, the receptacle world arises; during the subsequent nineteen kalpas, sentient beings gradually come to inhabit it.
During the final kalpa of the destruction period, the receptacle world is diminished; during the preceding nineteen kalpas, sentient beings gradually abandon it.

As thus described, the periods of formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness each consist of twenty intermediate kalpas, totaling eighty; these eighty together constitute the measure of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
What is the nature of this kalpa?
It refers solely to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The Sūtras state that one attains Buddhahood only after practicing with diligence for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Among the four types of kalpas previously mentioned, which kalpas are accumulated to constitute these three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas?
Multiplying the preceding great kalpas by ten, a hundred, and a thousand, they accumulate until three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are formed.
Since they are called "innumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*), why further mention "three"?
It is not that the term "innumerable" fails to indicate their incalculability; rather, it is used to manifest that they cannot be counted.
The *Vimokṣa-sūtra* states that among the sixty numerical units, asaṃkhyeya is one such unit.
What are these sixty?
As that sūtra says:

There is a single unit, which is the beginning of counting; ten ones make ten; ten tens make a hundred; ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand; one hundred thousand is a *lakṣa*; ten *lakṣas* are a *vilakṣa*; ten *vilakṣas* are a *koṭi*; ten *koṭis* are a *madhya*; ten *madhyas*... [ten *madhyas* are a *ayuta*]... ten *ayutas* are a *nayuta*... ten *nayutas* are a *prabeda*... ten *prabedas* are a *kamkara*... ten *kamkaras* are a *vigaga*... ten *vigagas* are a *vibhūta*... ten *vibhūtas* are a *balāgra*... ten *balāgras* are a *samāpta*... ten *samāptas* are a *gomati*... ten *gomatis* are a *padma*... ten *padmas* are a *śanku*... ten *śankus* are a *mahāpadma*... ten *mahāpadmas* are a *samudra*... ten *samudras* are a *madhya*... ten *madhyas* are a *nikharva*... ten *nikharvas* are a *mahānikharva*... ten *mahānikharvas* are a *tīrtha*... ten *tīrthas* are a *mahātīrtha*... ten *mahātīrthas* are a *hetu*... ten *hetus* are a *mahāhetu*... ten *mahāhetus* are a *karabha*... ten *karabhas* are a *mahākarabha*... ten *mahākarabhas* are a *bṛnda*... ten *bṛndas* are a *mahābṛnda*... ten *mahābṛndas* are a *kharva*... ten *kharvas* are a *mahākharva*... ten *mahākharvas* are a *nigoda*... ten *nigodas* are a *mahānigoda*... ten *mahānigodas* are a *mudrā*... ten *mudrās* are a *mahāmudrā*... ten *mahāmudrās* are a *bala*... ten *balas* are a *mahābala*... ten *mahābalas* are a *sāgara*... ten *sāgaras* are a *mahāsāgara*...

ten *mahāsāgaras* are a *nisthā*... ten *nisthās* are a *mahānisthā*... ten *mahānisthās* are a *visvara*... ten *visvaras* are a *mahāvisvara*... ten *mahāvisvaras* are a *bahu*... ten *bahus* are a *mahābahu*... ten *mahābahus* are a *samāptalambha*... ten *samāptalambhas* are a *gati*... ten *gatīs* are a *mahāgati*... ten *mahāgatīs* are a *nimbarajas*... ten *nimbarajas* are a *mahānimbarajas*... ten *mahānimbarajas* are a *maha*... ten *mahas* are a *mahāmaha*... ten *mahāmahas* are a *padma*... ten *padmas* are a *mahāpadma*... ten *mahāpadmas* are a *śankha*... ten *śankhas* are a *mahāśankha*... ten *mahāśankhas* are a *samāptah*... ten *samāptas* are a *mahāsamāpta*... ten *mahāsamāptas* are a *galaga*... ten *galagas* are a *mahāgalaga*... ten *mahāgalagas* are a *tathā*... ten *tathās* are a *mahātathā*... ten *mahātathās* are a *hetu*... ten *hetus* are a *mahāhetu*... ten *mahāhetus* are a *karabhājana*... ten *karabhājanas* are a *mahākarabhājana*... ten *mahākarabhājanas* are a *bṛhat*... ten *bṛhats* are a *mahābṛhat*... ten *mahābṛhats* are a *kharva*... ten *kharvas* are a *mahākharva*... ten *mahākharvas* are a *nigoda*... ten *nigodas* are a *mahānigoda*... ten *mahānigodas* are a *mudrā*... ten *mudrās* are a *mahāmudrā*... ten *mahāmudrās* are a *bala*... ten *balas* are a *mahābala*... ten *mahābalas* are a *sāgara*... ten *sāgaras* are a *mahāsāgara*... ten *mahāsāgaras* are a *nisthā*... ten *nisthās* are a *mahānisthā*... ten *mahānisthās* are a *visvara*... ten *visvaras* are a *mahāvisvara*... ten *mahāvisvaras* are a *bahu*... ten *bahus* are a *mahābahu*... ten *mahābahus* are a *samāptalambha*... ten *samāptalambhas* are a *gati*... ten *gatīs* are a *mahāgati*... ten *mahāgatīs* are a *nimbarajas*... ten *nimbarajas* are a *mahānimbarajas*... ten *mahānimbarajas* are a *maha*...

ten *mahas* are a *mahāmaha*... ten *mahāmahas* are a *padma*... ten *padmas* are a *mahāpadma*... ten *mahāpadmas* are a *śankha*... ten *śankhas* are a *mahāśankha*... ten *mahāśankhas* are a *samāptah*... ten *samāptas* are a *mahāsamāpta*... ten *mahāsamāptas* are a *galaga*... ten *galagas* are a *mahāgalaga*... ten *mahāgalagas* are a *tathā*... ten *tathās* are a *mahātathā*... ten *mahātathās* are a *hetu*... ten *hetus* are a *mahāhetu*... ten *mahāhetus* are a *karabhājana*... ten *karabhājanas* are a *mahākarabhājana*... ten *mahākarabhājanas* are a *bṛhat*... ten *bṛhats* are a *mahābṛhat*... ten *mahābṛhats* are a *kharva*... ten *kharvas* are a *mahākharva*... ten *mahākharvas* are a *nigoda*... ten *nigodas* are a *mahānigoda*... ten *mahānigodas* are a *mudrā*... ten *mudrās* are a *mahāmudrā*... ten *mahāmudrās* are a *bala*... ten *balas* are a *mahābala*... ten *mahābalas* are a *sāgara*... ten *sāgaras* are a *mahāsāgara*... ten *mahāsāgaras* are a *nisthā*... ten *nisthās* are a *mahānisthā*... ten *mahānisthās* are a *visvara*... ten *visvaras* are a *mahāvisvara*... ten *mahāvisvaras* are a *bahu*... ten *bahus* are a *mahābahu*... ten *mahābahus* are a *samāptalambha*... ten *samāptalambhas* are a *gati*... ten *gatīs* are a *mahāgati*... ten *mahāgatīs* are a *nimbarajas*... ten *nimbarajas* are a *mahānimbarajas*... ten *mahānimbarajas* are a *maha*... ten *mahas* are a
Ten *uta* make one *ayuta*; ten *ayuta* make one *mahāyuta*;
ten *mahāyuta* make one *nayuta*; ten *nayuta* make one *mahānayuta*;
ten *mahānayuta* make one *prayuta*; ten *prayuta* make one *mahāprayuta*; ten...
Ten *prayuta* make one *kaṅkara*; ten *kaṅkara* make one *mahā-kaṅkara*;
ten *mahā-kaṅkara* make one *bimbara*; ten *bimbara* make one *mahā-bimbara*;
ten *mahā-bimbara* make one *akṣobhya*; ten *akṣobhya* make one *mahā-akṣobhya*.
Ten *akṣobhya* make one *vibhava*; ten *vibhava* make one great *vibhava*;
ten great *vibhava* make one *utsaṅga*; ten *utsaṅga* make one great *utsaṅga*;
ten great *utsaṅga* make one *vahana*; ten *vahana* make one great *vahana*.
Ten *pahaṇa* make one *dhiṭi*, ten *dhiṭi* make one *mahādhiṭi*,
ten *mahādhiṭi* make one *hetu*, ten *hetu* make one *mahāhetu*, ten *mahāhetu* make one *kālāpa*,
ten *kālāpa* make one *mahākālāpa*, and ten *mahākālāpa* make one... [mahākālāpa].
Ten *bha* make one *indra*; ten *indra* make one *mahendra*;
ten *mahendra* make one *samāpta*; thirteen *samāpta* make one *mahāsamāpta*;
ten *mahāsamāpta* make one *gati*; ten *gati* make one *mahāgati*; ten *mahāgati*... [make one *mahāmahāgati*].
Ten *nirvartana* make one great *nirvartana*; ten great *nirvartana* make one *mudrā*;
ten *mudrā* make one great *mudrā*; ten great *mudrā* make one *balakṣa*;
ten *balakṣa* make one great *balakṣa*; ten great *balakṣa*... [make one] *mahābalakṣa*.
Ten *śaṇa* make one *mahā-śaṇa*; ten *mahā-śaṇa* make one *vibhūta*;
ten *vibhūta* make one *mahā-vibhūta*; ten *mahā-vibhūta* make one *balākṣa*;
ten *balākṣa* make one *mahā-balākṣa*; ten *mahā-balākṣa* make one *asaṃkhyeya*.
*Ki-ye*. Within this enumeration, having forgotten the remaining eight, when the calculation of great *kalpas* reaches this number, it is called an *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
When these *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are further accumulated to three, they are described in the sūtras as "three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*."
It is not that they cannot be calculated by means of ordinary reckoning; rather, it is because they cannot be counted that they are described as "three incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
For what reason does a bodhisattva resolve to practice with diligence for such a long duration before finally attaining the fruit of Buddhahood?
Why not allow for the vow to practice over a long duration?
Unsurpassed enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain; it cannot be accomplished without extensive vows and practices.

A bodhisattva must undergo three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to cultivate the great accumulations of merit and wisdom—the six *pāramitās*—and only after hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices can they realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, one must certainly generate the vow for a long duration.
If other skillful means could also lead to nirvāṇa, why would one undertake the long cultivation of many ascetic practices for the sake of awakening?
It is because of the desire to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings that one seeks awakening and makes a long-term vow:
"How may I become fully capable of rescuing all conscious beings from the torrential flood of suffering? For this reason, one renounces the path to nirvāṇa and seeks unsurpassed awakening.
What benefit is there for oneself in saving other sentient beings?
Because a bodhisattva saves all things in order to fulfill their own compassionate heart, saving others is itself the benefit for themselves.
Who would believe that a bodhisattva performs such a thing?
For those who harbor thoughts of benefiting themselves but lack great compassion, it is truly difficult to believe that such sentient beings [could act otherwise].
For those who have no thought of benefiting themselves yet possess great compassion, it is not difficult to believe that such sentient beings [could act otherwise].
It is commonly known in the world that there are those who have long practiced a lack of compassion; though it brings them no personal benefit, they delight in harming others.
How then can one not believe that a Bodhisattva, having long practiced loving-kindness and compassion, delights in benefiting others even though it brings them no personal gain?

Furthermore, as is well known to all wise people, sentient beings, through the power of habitual practice, fail to understand that conditioned phenomena are devoid of a self; they grasp at them as a self and give rise to attachment, thereby willingly undergoing manifold sufferings on account of this cause.

In this way, through the power of repeated practice, the bodhisattva abandons self-love and increases their affection for others; since they willingly take upon themselves all manner of suffering on account of this, how could one not believe it?

Furthermore, due to the difference in their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), this aspiration arises: they regard the suffering of others as their own suffering and the happiness of others as their own happiness; they do not regard their own suffering or happiness as their own matter of suffering or happiness, nor do they perceive any benefit to themselves that is distinct from benefiting others.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
The inferior person exerts effort in skillful means, Constantly seeking their own personal pleasure;
The middling person seeks the cessation of suffering, For pleasure is not so, being the basis of suffering.
The superior person constantly and diligently seeks to end their own suffering and bring peace and happiness to others,
as well as the eternal extinction of others' suffering, because they regard others as themselves.
Thus has the differentiation of the measures of kalpas been explained.
When do the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world—is it during the period of increase or the period of decrease?
The verse says:
From eighty thousand down to one hundred, The Buddhas appear in the world.
Regarding the increase and decrease [of lifespan] for the Pratyekabuddhas, those who are like a rhinoceros horn [attain their goal] after a hundred kalpas.
The treatise says:
From the time when the lifespan of humans on this continent gradually decreases from eighty thousand years down to a minimum of one hundred years, during this interval, the Buddhas appear.
For what reason do Buddhas not appear during the period of increase?
Because sentient beings delight in increase, it is difficult to teach them disillusionment.
For what reason do Buddhas not appear when the lifespan decreases below one hundred years?
Because the five corruptions have increased to such an extreme that they are difficult to transform, they are called the "five corruptions":
first, the corruption of lifespan; second, the corruption of the eon; third, the corruption of afflictions; fourth, the corruption of views; and fifth, the corruption of sentient beings.
At the end of the kalpa’s period of decline, because lifespans and so forth become as base and inferior as dregs and filth, they are called "corruptions" (kaṣāya).
Due to the first two corruptions, lifespan and material resources are, respectively, extremely diminished.

By the next two corruptions, wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*) decline, because of indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification, or because of the impairment of the wholesome qualities of both householders and renunciants.
By the final corruption, one's own person declines; that is to say, it destroys one's own physical stature, complexion, strength, mindfulness, wisdom, diligence, valor, and freedom from disease.
The appearance of Pratyekabuddhas occurs throughout the periods of both increase and decrease of the kalpa.
Furthermore, there are two distinct types of Pratyekabuddhas:
first, those who travel in groups (vargacārin), and second, those who are like the rhinoceros horn (khadgaviṣāṇakalpa).
The *gaṇapratyekabuddha* was formerly a *śrāvaka*; when he attained the superior fruit, his name was changed to *pratyekajina*.

Others say that he was formerly an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who had previously cultivated the *nirvedhabhāgīya* stages of a *śrāvaka*, and having now personally realized the path, he received the name *pratyekajina*.
As it is told in the *Itivṛttaka*:
In a certain mountain region there were five hundred non-Buddhist ascetics practicing austerities.

A monkey who had previously lived in close proximity to a pratyekabuddha observed his dignified demeanor; subsequently traveling from place to place, he arrived at the abode of the non-Buddhist ascetics and displayed the very same demeanor he had previously seen in the pratyekabuddha.
When the various sages beheld him, they all conceived feelings of reverence and admiration; in a brief moment, they all realized the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
If he had previously been a noble being (ārya), he would not have needed to practice such asceticism; those who are likened to a rhinoceros horn must necessarily dwell in solitude.

Among the two types of pratyekabuddhas, those who are like the rhinoceros horn must cultivate the provisions for enlightenment for one hundred great kalpas before they finally become a rhinoceros-horn pratyekabuddha.

They are called "pratyekabuddhas" because, in their present lives, they realize the path through their own awakening without receiving the ultimate teachings from others; thus, they are able to discipline themselves but do not discipline others.
For what reason is it said that Pratyekabuddhas do not discipline others?

It is not because they lack the ability to expound the True Dharma, for they too have attained the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) and are able to recollect the principles of the holy teachings proclaimed by all Buddhas that they heard in the past.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that they lack compassion, for they manifest supernatural powers (ṛddhi) in order to gather sentient beings.

Nor can it be said that there is no capacity among sentient beings to receive the Dharma, because at that time, sentient beings also possess the ability to give rise to the mundane path of antidotes that brings about detachment from desire.
Although this principle exists, it is because sentient beings lack the joy, superior understanding, and aspiration for the teaching due to their past habitual tendencies;
furthermore, one knows that sentient beings find it difficult to receive the profound Dharma, as they have long followed the stream of existence and are thus difficult to lead against that current.
Furthermore, because he wishes to avoid gathering a following, he does not proclaim the True Dharma for others, fearing the clamor and confusion of crowds.
At what time does a Wheel-Turning King appear in the world?
Of how many kinds are they, how many appear together, and what are their majesties and characteristics?
The verse says:
Universal Monarchs appear when the lifespan is above eighty thousand years; they possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron;
they rule over one, two, three, or four continents respectively; like the Buddha, each is unique.
He comes to meet [the Buddha], bows down of his own accord, and is victorious in the battle of debate without causing harm;
yet, because his physical marks are not perfectly complete or luminous, he is not equal to the Buddha.
The commentary says:
From the time when the lifespan of the people of this continent is immeasurable down to eighty thousand years, there arise Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin kings).

When the lifespan decreases below eighty thousand years, the wealth, happiness, and longevity of sentient beings decline, and as various evils gradually increase, they become unfit vessels for Great Beings; therefore, no Universal Monarch appears.
This king, by means of the revolving wheel, guides and subdues all through his majestic power; thus he is called a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning King).
The *Prajñaptipāda* states that there are four types, distinguished by the respective wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron.

According to their respective order—superior, excellent, middling, and inferior—they can respectively rule as kings over one, two, three, or four continents. That is to say, an iron-wheel-turning king rules over one continent; a copper-wheel-turning king, over two; a silver-wheel-turning king, over three; and a gold-wheel-turning king, over the four continents.
The *sūtra* speaks only of the golden wheel (*cakraratna*) from the perspective of its preeminence; thus the *sūtra* says:

"If a king is born into the Kṣatriya caste and has received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), on the fifteenth day when he observes the fast and precepts, having bathed his head and body and undertaken the superior fast and precepts, he ascends a high terrace while his ministers attend him, and suddenly a precious golden wheel appears in the eastern direction."

Its wheel is complete with a thousand spokes, a hub, and a rim; its various features are perfectly pure, as if fashioned by a master craftsman. Emitting wondrous radiance, it has come to the place where the king resides.
This king must surely be a Wheel-Turning King of Gold.
It should be understood that the same applies to other wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).
Like the Buddha, two wheel-turning kings do not appear simultaneously; therefore, the Sūtra states:
"There is no place and no occasion where two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world, neither before nor after one another; there is only one Tathāgata at any given place and time."
As it has been said regarding the Tathāgata, so it is with the Wheel-turning King (cakravartin).
One should carefully examine and discern whether this singular statement refers to a single trichiliocosm or is intended to encompass all world-systems.
Some say: "In other realms, Buddhas certainly do not appear. Why is this so?"
It is not that the power of the Bhagavān is obstructed, for the sole World-Honored One is able to teach and transform beings throughout all ten directions.
If there were even a single location where one Buddha lacked the capacity to teach and transform, it would follow that the same would be true for all others.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said to Śāriputra:
"Suppose someone were to come to you and ask:
'Is there any brahmin or śramaṇa who, at this very time, is exactly equal to the Gautama clan in attaining unsurpassed enlightenment?'"
"If you were asked that question, how would you answer?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"If I were asked that question, I would answer thus:"
At present, there is no brahmin or śramaṇa who has attained unsurpassed enlightenment equal to my World-Honored One. Why is this so?

I have heard and received directly from the World-Honored One that there is no place, no occasion, neither before nor after, where two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world; rather, at any given time and in any given place, there is only one Tathāgata.
If that is so, for what reason does the *Brahmā-sūtra* state:
"I now exercise sovereign power over these worlds of the trichiliocosm"?
That statement possesses an underlying intention (*saṃdhi*).
What is the underlying intention?
It is this: if the Blessed One does not exert deliberate effort (*prayoga*), he can perceive only this trichiliocosm;
however, when the Blessed One exerts deliberate effort, boundless worlds all become the range of his Buddha-eye.
The supernormal power of the divine ear and so forth should be understood by analogy with this.
Other masters of the schools maintain that Buddhas also appear in other worlds within the world-system.

Why is this so? There are many bodhisattvas currently practicing together the accumulations for enlightenment. While there may not be multiple Buddhas in a single world-system at one time, what logic could prevent there being multiple Buddhas in multiple world-systems?
Therefore, within boundless realms, boundless Buddhas appear.

If there were only a single Buddha, even if he were to remain for an entire eon, he would still not be able to perform the Buddha-work throughout a single world-system; how much less could he benefit boundless beings within the span of a human lifespan?

However, sentient beings dwell within boundless realms, and the distinctions of their time, place, faculties, and dispositions are infinite; thus, the Buddha must universally observe these classes of beings.

When they ought to see the World-Honored One at such times and places, the Buddha manifests supernormal powers and preaches the Dharma according to their capacities, so that their faults that have not yet arisen do not arise, those already arisen are brought to cessation, their virtues that have not yet arisen are caused to arise, and those already arisen are brought to full perfection.
How could this matter be accomplished instantaneously by a single Buddha?
Therefore, it is certain that there are multiple Buddhas at the same time.
As for the scriptural passage they cite—stating that "there is no place or occasion where two Tathāgatas appear in the world simultaneously, neither before nor after"—[it refers to a specific sense].
This should be examined together: does this statement refer to a single world-system (*dhātu*) or multiple world-systems?

If it refers to multiple world-systems, then a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) would likewise not exist in other world-systems, because the text states that he is precluded from being born simultaneously [with a Buddha].
If you grant that there are other Cakravartin kings in other realms, why do you not likewise grant that there are Buddhas in other realms?
Since the appearance of a Buddha in the world is endowed with auspicious merit, what fault is there in having many Buddhas in many realms that would warrant such a prohibition?

This means that when many Buddhas appear simultaneously within multiple world systems, they are able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, enabling them to attain higher rebirths (*abhyudaya*) and the path to definitive excellence (*niḥśreyasa*).
If this is so, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not appear simultaneously within a single world system?
Because they are not needed;
that is to say, within a single world-system, one Buddha is sufficient to benefit all beings.
Furthermore, it is due to the power of their vows; that is to say, when the Tathāgatas were bodhisattvas, they first made this vow:

May I attain perfect enlightenment within this realm of blindness and darkness, where there is no rescue and no refuge, to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, acting as their savior, their refuge, their eye, and their guide.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of inspiring reverence; that is to say, because there is only one Tathāgata within a single world-system, beings will hold him in deep veneration.

Moreover, it is for the sake of inciting swift practice; that is to say, it causes them to know that the Honored One of All-Knowledge is extremely difficult to encounter, and that they should swiftly practice the teachings he has established, lest he enter parinirvāṇa or depart to another place, leaving us without protection or refuge.
Therefore, two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously within a single world-system (*dhātu*).
Regarding these four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) thus described, there are also differences in how they establish authority over the various directions.
Specifically, as for the one with the golden wheel, the minor kings each come forward to welcome him and make this request:
"Our lands are vast and abundant, peaceful, prosperous, and filled with many people.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will personally bestow his instructions upon us; we are all your followers and attendants."
If a silver-wheel-turning monarch goes to that land in person, they submit upon his majestic approach.
If a copper-wheel-turning monarch arrives in that country, they acknowledge his superiority after he has proclaimed his majesty and vied with them in virtue.
If an Iron Wheel-turning King arrives in that country as well, he displays his majesty and arranges his battle lines; once he has achieved victory, he stops.

None of the Wheel-turning Kings inflict any harm; having subdued them and secured victory, they allow each person to remain peacefully in their own dwelling, exhorting and transforming them to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action. Therefore, when a Wheel-turning King dies, he is certain to be reborn in heaven.
The Sūtras state that when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, seven treasures appear in the world.
What are these seven? First is the wheel treasure;

second is the elephant treasure; third is the horse treasure; fourth is the jewel treasure; fifth is the woman treasure; sixth is the minister-treasure of the treasury; and seventh is the minister-treasure of the military.
The five treasures, such as the elephant and so forth, are comprised within the category of sentient beings; how then can the karma of one being produce another being?

It is not that the other being arises from the karma of the first. Rather, it is because they previously performed karma that bound them to one another; thus, when one among them takes birth according to his own karma, the others likewise arise simultaneously, each riding upon their own respective karma.

Regarding these aforementioned wheel-turning kings (cakravartin), they differ from other kings not only by possessing the seven jewels, but also by having the thirty-two marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa).
If that is so, how do the wheel-turning kings differ from the Buddhas?
The marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) on a Buddha are upright, distinct, bright, and complete; those of a king are not so, and thus there is a distinction between them.
Regarding the people at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), did they have kings or not?
The verse says:
At the beginning of the eon, they were like the gods of the Form Realm; later, they gradually increased their craving for flavors.
Due to falling into hoarding and the arising of theft, they hired guards to protect the fields.
The Treatise says:
At the beginning of the kalpa, all human beings were like those in the Form Realm; thus the Sūtra says:

"At the beginning of the kalpa, humans were material and mind-made, with limbs fully developed and sense faculties complete, their forms upright and majestic, their bodies radiant with light, moving freely through the air, subsisting on joy and delight, and dwelling for a long time."
In this manner, a kind of earth-essence gradually arose, sweet in taste and rich in fragrance.

At that time, there was a man whose nature was to crave flavors; upon smelling its scent, he conceived a desire for it, took some to taste, and then ate it. Others followed his example, vying with one another to take and eat it.
At that time, it was first called the consumption of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

Because they were sustained by solid food, their bodies gradually became firm and heavy; their radiance vanished and darkness arose, whereupon the sun, moon, and various stars appeared from that point on.
Due to their gradual attachment to its flavor, the *rasa* (earth-essence) disappeared; from this, there subsequently arose the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-crust cakes).
As they vied with one another in eating them, the earth-crust cakes also disappeared. At that time, *vanalatā* (forest-vines) appeared.

Because they became excessively addicted to eating, the forest creepers (*vanalatā*) disappeared once more. Then, non-cultivated fragrant rice grew spontaneously; the multitude gathered it together to serve as their food.
Because this food was coarse, waste and impurities remained in their bodies. To eliminate these, two orifices naturally formed, and from this, male and female sexual organs subsequently arose.

Due to the difference between the two sexes, their physical forms also differ; by the power of past habitual tendencies, they gaze upon one another, whereby unwholesome mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) arises. The demon of sensual craving then deludes and disturbs body and mind, causing them to lose their composure and, in a state of frantic madness, engage in unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*).
At this time, the demon of desire first arose among human beings.

At that time, people would gather fragrant rice as needed according to the timing of their meals, without storing anything away. Later, there was a person whose nature was indolent who took a large quantity of fragrant rice at once to store for future consumption; others followed his example, and those who set aside stores gradually increased.

Consequently, they conceived the notion of "mine" regarding the rice; each, following their greedy impulses, harvested as much as possible without satiety. Thus, wherever it was harvested, it would no longer grow back. Thereupon, they divided the fields among themselves, fearing that the supply might eventually be exhausted.

Regarding their own plots of land, they developed a sense of stinginess and attachment, while harboring thoughts of encroachment and seizure toward the fields of others; thus, the transgression of robbery and theft first arose at this time.

Desiring to prevent such acts, they gathered together to deliberate and, having selected a person of virtue from among the multitude, each hired him with one-sixth of their harvest to provide protection and appointed him as the lord of the fields. For this reason, the name *Kṣatriya* was established.
The great assembly reverently received his grace, which flowed throughout the land; thus he was again named King Mahāsamata, and among all subsequent kings, this king was the first.
At that time, some people became weary of domestic life and took pleasure in dwelling in seclusion to diligently cultivate their moral conduct; for this reason, they acquired the name "Brahmins."
Later, there was a king who was greedy and stingy with wealth; he was unable to distribute it equitably among the people of his realm, and thus many impoverished individuals engaged in acts of theft.
To prohibit such behavior, the king imposed light and heavy punishments, and it was at this time that the karma of killing first began.
At that time, there were those with guilty minds who, fearing punishment, concealed their transgressions and spoke with deceptive intent; the arising of false speech began from this point.
During the period of the kalpa’s decline, there are the three minor calamities.
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
As the paths of unwholesome action increase, the lifespan decreases until it reaches thirteen years, at which point the calamities appear.
Sword, plague, and famine occur respectively, lasting for seven days, seven months, and seven years.
The commentary states:

From the time sentient beings began uttering false speech, the various paths of unwholesome karma increased successively; consequently, the lifespan of the people of this continent gradually decreased until it reached a minimum of ten years, at which point the three minor calamities manifest.
Therefore, all calamities and afflictions have two factors as their root:
first, indulgence in fine food; second, a nature of indolence.
These arise at the end of a *kalpa* during the minor three calamities.
The three calamities are: first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.

This refers to the period at the end of an intermediate kalpa when the human lifespan is ten years. At that time, people’s mental continuums are defiled by unrighteous greed; their minds are obscured by unbalanced craving; they are entangled by false teachings, and the poison of hatred increases to such an extent that as soon as they see one another, they give rise to fierce and harmful intentions.
Now, when hunters see wild birds and beasts, whatever they grasp in their hands becomes a sharp blade, and each displays their ferocity and madness to slaughter one another.

Furthermore, at the end of the intermediate kalpa, during the time of humans with a ten-year lifespan, because they possess all the aforementioned faults, non-humans emit poison and epidemics spread; those who encounter them perish immediately, and it is difficult to provide medical treatment or salvation.

Furthermore, at the end of the intermediate kalpa when the human lifespan is ten years, because people likewise possess all the aforementioned faults, the devas and nāgas reprove them in anger and do not send down sweet rain. Consequently, the world suffers from famine for a long time; as there is no means of relief, the majority of beings perish.
Therefore it is said that due to famine there arise the "accumulation," the "white bones," and the "counting of sticks.
There are two causes by which they are called "accumulations":
first, the accumulation of persons, meaning that at that time people, being extremely emaciated by hunger, gather together and die.
There are two kinds of accumulation: namely, at that time, people, for the benefit of future generations, set aside a portion of their food in small baskets to serve as seed;
therefore, the period of famine is called "having accumulation."
The statement that there are white bones is also due to two causes:
first, at that time, the human body becomes withered and dry, so that not long after death, the white bones appear;
second, at that time, people are driven by famine and collect white bones, boiling them for a broth to drink.

There is also the practice of "counting sticks" (*śalākā*), which likewise has two causes. First, due to a scarcity of grain, they count sticks to determine their meals; that is, within a household, from the eldest to the youngest, each receives a small amount of coarse food on the day corresponding to their assigned stick.

The second refers to those who, using a tally-stick to poke into heaps of grain in old granaries, obtain a few grains which they boil with a large amount of water and share among themselves to sustain their remaining lives.

However, there is a supreme teaching that explains the remedy for this situation: it says that if one can observe the precept against killing for even a single day and night, one will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the calamity of weapons in a future birth.
If one can offer even a single harītakī fruit to the Saṃgha with a fervent and pure mind, one will certainly not encounter the outbreak of epidemics in future lives.
If there is anyone who, with a heart of profound purity, can offer even a single morsel of food as a gift to the Saṃgha, they will certainly not encounter the calamity of famine in future lives.
How long does each of these three calamities last?

The calamity of weapons lasts for at most seven days; the calamity of pestilence lasts for seven months and seven days; and the calamity of famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days, after which it ceases.

As the human lifespan gradually increases, calamities similar to those [of the previous eon] arise in the two continents of the East and West—namely, the intensification of malice, the weakening of physical strength, and the frequent occurrence of hunger and thirst—whereas none of these exist at all in the Northern Continent.
It was previously stated that the world is incinerated by the calamity of fire; the other calamities are likewise to be understood as appropriate. What are these others?
They shall now be fully explained.
The verse says:
The three calamities are fire, water, and wind; the three higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas) serve as their limits.
This is because they correspond respectively to internal calamities and so forth; in the fourth [dhyāna], there is no movement.
However, those receptacles are not eternal, for they arise and perish simultaneously with sentient beings;
thus, there must be seven fires and one water, followed by wind after seven cycles of fire and water.
The Treatise says:
These three great calamities oppress sentient beings, causing them to abandon the lower realms and gather in the higher heavens.

First, the calamity of fire arises due to the appearance of seven suns; next, the calamity of water arises due to incessant torrential rains; finally, the calamity of wind arises due to the mutual clashing of winds.
By the power of these three calamities, the receptacle world is destroyed until not even a single atom remains.
A certain class of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintains that atoms are eternal; they claim that at that time, residual atoms still exist.
For what reason do they maintain that residual atoms still exist?
It is so that gross phenomena may arise later without being devoid of seeds.
Was it not previously stated that the winds produced by the karma of sentient beings serve as the seeds?
Alternatively, this [wind] takes the wind at the peak of the previous calamity as its condition and the generative wind as its seed.
Furthermore, a sūtra of the Mahīśāsaka school states:
"Wind blows seeds from other regions and brings them here."
Even so, it is not admitted that when the sprout and so forth arise, they are directly produced by causes such as the seed.
If this is the case, from what do the sprout and so forth arise?
They arise from their own parts (*svabhāga*).
In this way, each part arises from its own parts, continuing in succession until even the subtlest composite arises from atoms.
Within the process of the arising of sprouts and the like, what power do seeds and such possess?
Apart from the atoms that are drawn together and assembled to form the sprout and so forth, the seed and such have no further power to produce the sprout.
For what reason do you insist on such a position?
That production arises from a different category [of substance] is certainly not logical.
Why is it not so? Because there would be no certainty.
Since the capacity is determinate, there is no fault of indeterminacy.
Just as sound, maturation, transformation, and so forth arise deterministically from different categories,
while qualitative attributes (guṇadharma) possess distinctions, substantial entities (dravyadharma) do not.
We observe that substantial entities arise only from their own kind, such as a vine producing branches or threads producing cloth.
This is not reasonable. Why is it unreasonable?
Because that which is cited as a proof is not universally established (*aprasiddha*).
Why, then, is what is cited here not universally established?
This is because we do not admit that the rattan branches and the threads of the garment are distinct entities.
Rather, it is the combination of the rattan and the threads, arranged in a particular way, that receives the name "branches" or "garment," just as in the case of an ant trail and so forth.
How is this known?
Within a single thread, one never obtains a garment, because one obtains only the thread.
What obstacle could there be that prevents the obtaining of the garment?
If a complete garment does not manifest within a single thread, then it follows that there is only a portion of the garment upon that thread, and no garment itself.
One must admit that the entire garment is merely a collection of its parts, and that there is no further distinct "whole" (avayavin) called a "garment.
Furthermore, how is it known that the parts of the garment are distinct from the threads?
If you claim that a garment requires the conjunction of many substrates [i.e., threads], then one should also obtain a garment when only many warp-threads are joined together.
Alternatively, there would be no principle for ever obtaining a garment, because the middle and other parts do not face the sense organs.

If it is argued that they can all successively face the sense organs, then the eye and body would only perceive the individual parts; thus, one should not say that they perceive the garment as a whole possessing parts. Rather, it is by means of the successive discernment of the various parts that a general cognition of the whole arises, just like the perception of a whirling firebrand.
This means that if one were to exclude the distinct color, category, and activity of the threads, the three [factors] of the robe’s color and so forth could not be apprehended.

If the color and other qualities of the variegated cloth belonged to the cloth itself, then one would have to admit that they arise from distinct categories, for the color and other qualities of each individual thread do not possess such various differences.
Alternatively, on a portion where there is no distinct color and so forth, one should not perceive the cloth, because it is by means of those [distinct colors] that the cloth is manifested.
Or else, on that very same portion, one should perceive distinct colors and so forth, since a cloth must necessarily possess the characteristics of distinct colors and so forth.
They assert that the substance of the parts is only one, yet there are various distinctions in color, category, and function; to have such [a thing] would indeed be most marvelous.

Furthermore, within a single realm of fire and light, because distance and proximity differ, there would be differences in burning and illuminating, and thus the distinction between tactile and visual qualities could not be established.

Although individual atoms transcend the range of the sense faculties, when they aggregate together, they can be perceived by the senses; this is like how, according to their own tenets, a combination can produce an effect, or like how the eyes and other organs combine to give rise to consciousness.

Furthermore, it is like a person with cataracts looking at scattered strands of hair: when many are situated close together, they can see them, but if each strand were situated far apart, there would be no capacity for vision.
The principle regarding atoms in relation to the sense faculties should be understood in the same way.
Furthermore, since the designation "atom" (paramāṇu) is established precisely with respect to form and so forth, when form and so forth perish, the atom must also perish.

Since the atom is subsumed under [the category of] substance (dravya) and form and so forth are subsumed under [the category of] qualities (guṇa), it would be illogical for these distinct entities to necessarily perish simultaneously.
That these two have distinct natures is logically impossible.
When one examines them closely, there are no earth-elements and so forth that exist apart from visible form and the rest; therefore, they do not have distinct natures.
Furthermore, since your own school admits that earth and the others are apprehended by the eye and the body, how could they be anything other than visible form and tangibility?

Furthermore, when wool, cotton, safflower, and so forth are burned, the cognition of them ceases; therefore, the cognition of wool and the like arises merely by taking the specific differences of color and so forth as its objects, because when transformation through heating occurs, it is due to the shape, magnitude, and other such factors.
It is just as when one recognizes a jar or a basin by its arrangement; if one does not observe its form, one cannot recognize it.
Who would then collect the deluded ravings of such a fool?
Therefore, extensive debate against that school should cease.
Where do the upper limits of these three calamities lie?
The second dhyāna is the limit of the calamity of fire, because everything below it is consumed by flames.
The third dhyāna is the limit of the calamity of water, because everything below it is soaked and rotted by water.
The fourth dhyāna is the limit of the calamity of wind, because everything below it is dispersed by wind.
Whatever calamity occurs above a certain level, that level is called the "limit" (kūṭa) of that calamity.
For what reason do the three lower dhyānas encounter the calamities of fire, water, and wind?
In the first, second, and third dhyānas, internal calamities are equivalent to those [external ones].
That is to say, in the first *dhyāna*, vitarka and vicāra serve as internal calamities; because they can burn and afflict the mind, they are equivalent to external fire calamities.

In the second dhyāna, the feeling of joy (*prīti*) serves as the internal calamity; because it moistens the body along with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), the body becomes like water. Consequently, all physical heaviness (*dausthulya*) throughout the body is eliminated, and thus the Sūtra states that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) ceases in the second dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation constitute the internal calamity; since these breaths are also wind, they are equivalent to the external wind disaster.
If one enters this dhyāna, such internal calamities exist; and when one is born in this dhyāna, one encounters this external disaster that brings about its destruction.
For what reason is the earth itself not established as a calamity?
Because the receptacle world is the earth itself; thus, while fire and so forth may be contrary to the earth, it cannot be said that the earth is contrary to the earth.
What constitutes the external calamities of the fourth dhyāna?
It has no external calamities, because it is free from internal calamities.
For this reason, the Buddha called it "immovable" (*āneñja*), as it is beyond the reach of the three types of calamities, both internal and external.
Some say: Because that stage contains the Śuddhāvāsa deities, it is not destroyed by any of the calamities.
Furthermore, since they cannot be reborn in the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), nor should they go elsewhere.
If that were so, the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*) of those realms would have to be eternal.
It is not so, because it arises and perishes simultaneously with sentient beings.
That is to say, there is no single, collective terrain for those celestial abodes; rather, they exist like the individual dwellings of the various stars.
When sentient beings are born or die there, the celestial palaces they inhabit arise and perish along with them; therefore, the substance of those receptacle worlds is also impermanent.
What is the sequence of the three aforementioned calamities?
First, seven calamities of fire must arise in immediate succession; following that, one calamity of water must necessarily arise.

After this, another seven calamities of fire arise in immediate succession, and after those seven fires, there is again one calamity of water. In this manner, it continues until seven calamities of water have been completed.
Furthermore, after seven calamities of fire, a calamity of wind arises. Thus, there are eight cycles of seven calamities of fire, one cycle of seven calamities of water, and one calamity of wind.
For what reason is it so?

Because the causes of meditative concentration cultivated by those sentient beings become progressively superior in the higher realms, the dimensions of their bodies and lifespans are correspondingly longer; consequently, the duration of their residence also increases accordingly.
By this, the passage from the *Prakaraṇapāda* stating that the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas is sixty-four kalpas is well explained.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 12; *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle 13.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four: Analysis of Karma (Karmavibhāga), Part One. As previously stated, there are many distinctions within both the sentient world (*sattvaloka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). From what do such distinctions arise?
The verse says:
The differentiation of the world arises from karma; it consists of volition and what is produced by volition.
Volition itself is mental action; that which is produced refers to bodily and vocal actions.
The treatise says:
It does not arise from the prior awakening of a single creator; rather, it arises solely from the differentiation of the karma of sentient beings.
If this is so, why is it that both [the world and its inhabitants] arise from karma?
Saffron, sandalwood, and the like are exceedingly delightful, yet the internal physical form is the opposite of them.
Because the karmic types of sentient beings are such as these, when one creates mixed karma that induces an internal physical form, impurities constantly flow from the nine orifices.
To counteract that, the external requisites produced are extremely pleasant and delightful in their color, fragrance, taste, and texture.
Because the various classes of devas have performed purely wholesome karma, both of these matters they attract are exquisite.
What is the nature of this karma that serves as its basis?
It consists of volition (*cetanā*) and what is produced by volition (*cetayitvā*).
Thus, the Sūtra says:
There are two kinds of karma: first, the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*); second, the karma after having willed (*cetayitvā-karma*), which refers to what is performed by volition.
These two types of karma are further divided into three, namely: the bodily, vocal, and mental karma of sentient beings.
How are these three types of karma established?
Is it by way of their basis (*āśraya*), by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or by way of their motivation (*samutthāna*)?
Even if that were so, what contradiction would there be?
If categorized according to their basis (*āśraya*), there should be only one type of karma, because all karmas depend upon the body.
If categorized according to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), only speech should be considered karma, because among the three types [of action], only speech is itself karma.
If one considers them from the perspective of their motivation (*samutthāna*), there should also be only a single type of karma, because all karma is motivated by the mind.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state that the three types of karma are established according to the sequence of the three aforementioned causes.

However, that which the mind intends is itself mental action (*manas-karman*); the actions performed through such intention are divided into the two types of bodily and vocal action, because they are originated by that very intention.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two types of bodily and vocal action?
The verse says:
These two types of karma—of body and speech—are both of the nature of informative and non-informative action.
The commentary says:
It should be understood that among the various types of karma thus described, both bodily and vocal karma possess the nature of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).
Now, what are the characteristics of bodily and vocal informative action?
The verse says:
Body-informative action is admitted to be a distinct shape;
it does not have motion as its essence, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish moment by moment.
Furthermore, [if it were motion,] there would be no cause for its cessation, and the cause of its arising would have to be capable of bringing about its destruction.
Form (*rūpa*) is also not substantially existent, because it would have to be apprehended by two sense-faculties, and because there are no distinct atoms (*paramāṇu*).
It is admitted that vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is the sound of speech.
The treatise says:
Due to the power of volition (*cetanā*), a specific bodily form arises in such and such a manner; this is called bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*).
Other schools state:
"Movement is called bodily informative action, because when the body moves, it is moved by [the force of] karma."
To refute this, it is said that there is no movement, because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
What is meant by "momentary"?
That which, upon acquiring its own essence, perishes immediately thereafter—such a phenomenon is called "momentary," just as a person who possesses a staff is called "one who has a staff."
All conditioned phenomena, as soon as they acquire their own essence, necessarily perish and return to non-existence immediately thereafter.

If they arise in a certain place, they perish in that very same place; there is no possibility for them to move from here to another location. Therefore, it cannot be said that motion constitutes the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
If all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess momentariness, the principle that they do not travel to other locations can be established.

It is universally accepted as a logical certainty that all conditioned phenomena are momentary because they must eventually perish; that is to say, the cessation of conditioned phenomena does not depend on a cause.
Why is this so? That which depends on causes is called an effect; cessation that is non-existent does not depend on causes, and therefore it is not an effect.
Since cessation does not depend on causes, it ceases immediately upon arising.
If it does not cease initially, it should likewise not cease later, because the later [moment] possesses the same nature as the initial one.
Since the later [moment] undergoes cessation, we know that the prior [moment] has ceased.
If it were only when there is a difference in the later [moment] that cessation could occur, then this very [later moment] should not be called "different."
That these characteristics are distinct is logically impossible.
Is it not evident in the world that fuel and other such things reach extinction through contact with fire?
Since there is certainly no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) superior to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not the case that the destruction of phenomena does not depend upon causes.
How is it known that fuel and the like perish due to contact with fire?
Because fuel and the like are no longer seen after they have come into contact with fire.
One should reflect together on this: is it because fuel and the like perish due to contact with fire that they are no longer seen?

Is it because the preceding fuel and so forth, having arisen, perish of their own accord, and do not arise again later due to their absence, and thus are not perceived—just as the flame of a lamp or the sound of a bell [are no longer perceived] when met by wind or the hand?
Therefore, this point is established through inference (*anumāna*).
What is inference (*anumāna*)?
It is as previously stated: because cessation is non-existent, it does not depend on a cause.

Furthermore, if cessation were to depend on causes such as fuel and so forth for its occurrence, then every instance of cessation would likewise not depend on a cause; just as arising depends on causes and there is nothing that arises without a cause, so too would it be here.

However, as we observe in the world that cognitions, flames, and sounds perish spontaneously in each moment without depending on other causes, it follows that the extinction of fuel and the like also does not depend on a cause.
Some maintain that cognitions and sounds perish later than their preceding causes.
That too is unreasonable, because the two do not coexist.
It is logically impossible for doubt and knowledge, suffering and pleasure, or greed and hatred, etc., to coexist, as their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are mutually contradictory.
Furthermore, if at some point an indistinct cognition were to arise immediately after a distinct sound, how could a homogeneous indistinct phenomenon destroy a homogeneous distinct phenomenon?
By what, furthermore, is the sound of the final cognition extinguished?
Some maintain that the extinction of a lamp’s flame is caused by the absence of its subsistence.
Others maintain that at the time of the flame's extinction, it is due to the power of *dharma* and *adharma*.
Both [positions] are irrational, because there is no such thing as a non-cause.
Neither dharma nor adharma can serve as the cause for arising and ceasing, because at every moment they are characterized by mutually opposing conditions of conformity and opposition.
Alternatively, one might argue that within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), the sense of having such a cause can be conceptually imputed.
If that were so, the original dispute would necessarily cease, for it would be admitted that all things possess momentariness without depending on any further cause.

Furthermore, if the destruction of fuel and so forth were caused by contact with fire, then since there are inferior, middling, and superior degrees within the process of transformation through heating (*pākaja*), the very entity that serves as the cause of production would necessarily become the cause of destruction.

Why is this so? It is because through conjunction with fire, one can cause wood and other substances to undergo transformation through heating (*pākaja*). As the middle and superior degrees of heating arise, the lower and middle degrees of heating cease.

If that which is either identical to or similar to the cause for the arising of the upper and middle degrees were itself the cause for the cessation of the lower and middle degrees, then the very essence of the cause of arising would be the cause of cessation.

Alternatively, the causes for cessation and arising would have no distinction in their characteristics; it would not be the case that "by means of this very thing, or something similar to it, that exists," while "by means of that very thing, or something similar to it, that does not exist."
Granted that one might conceive of a difference between the causes of arising and ceasing within the case of the distinct production of flames;

but how can one conceive of a difference between the causes of arising and ceasing in the case where wood and other substances undergo transformation through contact with ash, snow, vinegar, the sun, water, or earth?
If that is so, when we observe water boiling away until it is completely exhausted, what function does contact with fire perform therein?

Through contact with fire, the power of the fire element increases; by the increase of the fire element, the mass of water is produced in progressively subtler states in its successive moments, until it reaches its ultimate subtlety and no longer continues. This is what is meant by the function of contact with fire within the water.
Therefore, there is no cause that brings about the cessation of phenomena; phenomena cease of their own accord because they possess the nature of disintegration.
Because they cease spontaneously, they perish as soon as they arise.
Since they perish as soon as they arise, the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*) is established.

Since there are no [entities] that persist for even a single moment, there is certainly no movement; however, because [a thing] arises in successive locations without interval, one conceives the overweening pride of movement, just as in the case of a flame burning through grass.
Since, by this reasoning, movement is certainly non-existent, the principle that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is shape (*saṃsthāna*) is established.
However, the Sautrāntikas say: "Shape is not substantially real.

That is to say, when many [atoms] of visible color (*varṇa*) arise on one side of an aggregate, 'long' color is conventionally designated therein; relative to this long color, when there are few [atoms] on one side of another aggregate of color, 'short' color is conventionally designated; when they arise equally on all four sides, 'square' color is conventionally designated; and when they arise pervasively in all directions, 'round' color is conventionally designated. The remaining shapes should be understood accordingly."

Just as when one sees a torch being moved rapidly and continuously in one direction, it is perceived as "long," and when one sees it moving in a circle, it is perceived as a "round" color; therefore, shape has no real, distinct substantial entity as a type of matter.

If it were claimed that there exists a distinct category of shape as a real entity, then a single color-form would be apprehended by two sense-faculties; that is, regarding the distinctions such as length within a collection of matter, both the eye seeing it and the body touching it could cognize it, whereby the fault of being apprehended by two faculties would necessarily follow.
In principle, there is no form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that is apprehended by two sense-faculties (*indriya*).

However, just as one apprehends characteristics such as length based on the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), so too can one apprehend shape (*saṃsthāna*) based on the manifest color (*varṇa*). Is it not the case that the tangible and the shape coexist within a single aggregate?
Therefore, one is able to recollect shape by means of grasping touch, rather than directly grasping color-and-shape within the sensation of touch itself.

This is like seeing the color of fire and thereby recollecting its heat, or smelling the fragrance of a flower and being able to remember its color; in these cases, the two dharmas are invariably inseparable, and thus by grasping one, the other can be recollected.
Since tangibility and shape are invariably inseparable, how can one apprehend tangibility and yet definitely recollect the shape?

If tangibility and shape were not invariably co-located, yet one could still recollect the shape by apprehending the tangibility, then visible color should likewise be recollected with certainty through tangibility; or else, if shape were as indeterminate as visible color, then at the moment of apprehending tangibility, one should not perceive the shape.
But this is not actually the case; therefore, one should not say that one recollects shape by taking it as a cause through contact.
Alternatively, because many shapes are seen within a piece of brocade or the like, there would consequently have to be many real shapes in a single location.
This is logically untenable, just as in the case of various manifest colors; therefore, shape-color (saṃsthāna-rūpa) does not possess a real substantial entity.
Furthermore, whatever resistant, real matter exists must necessarily consist of real, distinct types of atoms (paramāṇu).
However, there are no atoms that are designated as "long" and so forth; rather, "length" and the like are conventionally established within the specific arrangement of many such entities.
If it is argued that the atoms of shape themselves, arranged in such a manner, are what constitute "length" and so forth, this is merely a partisan claim, for it is not universally established.

That is to say, if the individual self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of distinct atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) were established as real, it would be possible for them to aggregate and be so arranged as to constitute length and so forth.

However, since the individual self-characteristics of atoms of shape are not established as real in the same way that those of color (*varṇa-rūpa*) are, how could there be such aggregation and arrangement?
Is it not evident that among various objects such as earthenware vessels, there are cases where their manifest color-qualities (*varṇa*) are identical while their shapes (*saṃsthāna*) differ?

Has it not already been argued that "length" and so forth are merely conventionally designated based on the specific arrangement of multiple substances; just as in the case of a swarm of ants, their individual appearances do not differ, yet they possess distinct shapes due to their particular arrangement in a moving circle?
The principle that shape depends on color and so forth should likewise apply here.

Is it not the case that in the dark or at a distance, when one perceives objects such as a tree stump, one cognizes the shape but not the color? How, then, could it be that the arrangement of color and so forth constitutes shape? For in the darkness or from afar, one does not clearly perceive the color; therefore, one merely gives rise to conceptual distinctions such as "long" and so on.

It is just as when a person observing a grove of trees from a distance in the dark perceives only a moving army and does not know their individual characteristics; this must necessarily be so, for there are times when one does not perceive the manifest form but knows only the general aggregate.
Since movement and shape have already been refuted, what do you of the Sautrāntika school posit as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)?
You posit shape as bodily intimation, but it is merely conventional and not real.
Since you maintain that only the conventional designation is used for bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), what further dharma do you establish as bodily action (*kāyakarma*)?

If action is established as bodily action because it depends upon the body—that is, the volition (*cetanā*) capable of moving the body in various ways—it is called bodily action because it proceeds through the gateway of the body.
It should be understood that the establishment of distinct names for vocal and mental karma according to their respective applications is likewise so.
If that is the case, why does the Sūtra state that there are two kinds of karma:
first, the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*), and second, the karma after having willed (*cetayitvā-karma*)?
What is the difference between these two?

It is said that during the preceding preparatory stage, one gives rise to volition and reflection, thinking, "I shall perform such and such an action that ought to be done"; this is called the karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*).

Having already reflected, one gives rise to the volition of performing an action; according to what was previously reflected upon, one performs the action to be done, moving the body and initiating speech—this is called the "action subsequent to reflection.
If this were so, then manifest action (vijñapti-karman) would necessarily be non-existent.
If manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) does not exist, then unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*) in the desire realm would likewise not exist, which would lead to a great error.

This great error can be refuted by reason: namely, from the two types of manifest karma previously described, a specific mental state (*cetanā-viśeṣa*) arises due to a preeminent volition; this is what is called unmanifest karma.
What fault is there in this?

One might argue that this should be called "action that follows the mind" (*anuvartaka-karma*), because it arises simultaneously with the mind, just like the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of meditative concentration.
There is no such fault, because it is produced by what is induced by both the decisive volition (*niścaya-cetanā*) and the impelling volition (*samutthāna-cetanā*).
Even if one grants the existence of informative action (*vijñapti*), it too depends upon the power of volition (*cetanā*) as previously described, because its nature is dull.
The Vaibhāṣikas say:

since shape is a real entity, bodily informative karma has shape as its essence; vocal informative karma has the sound of speech as its essence; and the characteristics of non-informative karma (*avijñapti*) have already been explained above.
The Sautrāntikas also say:
"This [unmanifest action] is not substantially existent, because it exists merely by virtue of a prior vow and restraint against performing [an act].

Furthermore, that [vow] is designated based upon past primary elements (*mahābhūta*), yet the substance of past primary elements does not exist; moreover, all unmanifest actions lack the characteristic of form."
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"This also exists substantially.
How is this known to be so?"
The verse says:
It is taught that there are three types of untainted matter (*anāsrava-rūpa*), because they increase and are not produced through effort, and so forth.
The commentary says:
According to the Sūtras, there are three kinds of form (*rūpa*), and these three bases encompass all forms:
first, form that is visible and resistant; second, form that is invisible and resistant; and third, form that is invisible and non-resistant.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras that there is untainted (anāsrava) form. As the sūtra says:
"What are the untainted phenomena?
They are all forms—past, future, and present—toward which neither craving nor aversion arises; this applies likewise up to consciousness."
These are called untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
Excluding non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), what phenomena are designated as "invisible and non-obstructive" (*anidarśana-apratigha*) and "untainted matter"?
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of the increase of merit, as the Sūtra says:

Any person of pure faith, whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family, who accomplishes the seven bases of meritorious action with a physical basis—whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking—will find that their meritorious actions constantly increase and continue to arise in a continuous stream at all times; the same is true for those without a physical basis.
Excluding non-informative action (*avijñapti-karma*), when one gives rise to another state of mind or is without mind, on what basis can it be said that meritorious action increases?
Furthermore, if one does not act oneself but merely dispatches another to do so, the course of action (*karmapatha*) would not be established in the absence of non-informative action.

The informative act of commanding another is not included within that course of action (*karmapatha*), because this [informative act] has not yet performed what was to be done; and once the commanded person has performed what was to be done, the nature of this [informative act] remains no different [from its prior state].
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that 'dharmas' refers to the external sense-sphere (bāhyāyatana).
These are dharmas not subsumed within the other eleven bases; they are invisible and non-obstructive, but it does not say they are formless."
If one does not consider the unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana), this statement would be deficient and thus rendered useless.
Furthermore, if the unmanifest did not exist, there would be no eight branches of the path (aṣṭāṅgamārga), because speech and the other factors are absent during meditative concentration.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
"Knowing thus and seeing thus, one cultivates right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration until they all reach fulfillment"?

Right speech, action, and livelihood were already attained as pure and bright at an earlier time; this is explained in reference to having previously attained the mundane path of freedom from defilement, and thus there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, if one were to deny the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), then there would likewise be no distinct Pratimokṣa restraint; for it would not be the case that after receiving the precepts, the continuity of the precept persists such that one is still designated a Bhikṣu and so forth even when a mind directed toward other objects arises.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"The precepts of abstaining from killing and so forth are called 'dike-precepts' (*setu-śīla*), because they can continuously dam and restrain the transgressions of violating the precepts over a long period of time.
It is not the case that something lacking a substantial entity (*dravya*) could be termed a "dike."
From these proofs, it is known that non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) truly exists.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
although these proofs are numerous and variously marvelous, they are not reasonable.
Why is this so? Regarding the scriptural citations provided, the first sūtra mentions that there are three kinds of form (*rūpa*). The Yogācāra masters explain:

when one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the forms that arise from the power of that concentration as objects of the meditative state are not the domain of the visual faculty; therefore, they are called "invisible" (*anidarśana*). Because they do not obstruct space, they are called "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*).
If it is argued: "Since that is so, how can the explanation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) be the same as that of non-informative matter (avijñapti)?
Furthermore, regarding what the Sūtra calls "untainted matter" (anāsrava-rūpa), the Yogācāras say:
among the types of matter produced by the power of meditative concentration, that which relies upon untainted concentration is itself designated as untainted.
Other masters say:

"The bodily form and all external forms of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are all untainted (anāsrava), for they do not serve as a basis for the outflows (āsrava); thus they receive the name 'untainted.
Why, then, does the Sūtra state that 'tainted phenomena' include everything from the eye up to [the other sense bases], and so forth?"
This is not called "with outflows" (sāsrava) because it is an antidote to the outflows; rather, it would follow that this [state] must be described as both with outflows and without outflows.
If that were so, what fault would there be?
There would be the error of confusion.
If it is on this basis that they are said to be "with outflows" (sāsrava), it has never been on this basis that they are said to be "without outflows" (anāsrava).
The same applies to those without outflows; how could there be any confusion?
If the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) and so forth were exclusively with outflows, for what reason would this sutra speak of them with such distinctions?
As it has been said regarding the fact that contaminated and grasped forms are the basis for the mind’s growth and obscuration, the same applies to sounds and so forth.
Furthermore, concerning the scriptural statement that merit increases, the former masters have explained it thus:
merit and karma increase by the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*), just as the material goods offered by a donor [increase].

In this way, as the recipients enjoy the gifts, because there are distinctions in the merit and benefit derived from those recipients' enjoyment of the donated objects, even if the donor’s mind subsequently shifts to other objects of focus, the subtle continuity of the mental impression (*vāsanā*) perfumed by the prior volition (*cetanā*) directed toward giving gradually undergoes transformation and differentiation. Through this, it will be able to produce abundant fruit in the future.
Therefore, it was taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*) that meritorious actions increase gradually and continue to arise in constant succession.
If one asks: how can a transformation occur in the mind of another continuum, even when it is directed toward a different object, by means of the specific excellence of virtue in one continuum?
This doubt and difficulty are the same as those regarding the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, how could it be that through the specific excellence of virtues in one continuum, another continuum would give rise to a distinct, truly existent dharma called the unmanifest?
