If there are no foundational meritorious actions, how does the continuity of merit increase? It is also due to the repeated cultivation of volitions directed toward those objects, which continue to follow along even within dreams.

For those who maintain the theory of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), since there is no informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) in merit that is independent of a physical basis, how could there be non-informative action? Some say:

even for various meritorious actions based on a physical basis, because the volition (*cetanā*) directed toward those objects is repeatedly practiced, it is said that they increase and continue in a constant succession at all times.
If that is so, the Sūtra states:

"There are bhikṣus who, possessing pure śīla and having perfected the qualities of discipline, after receiving various foods and drinks offered by others, enter the concentration of immeasurable mind (*apramāṇacitta-samādhi*), personally realize it with the body, and dwell in its fulfillment."
From these causes and conditions, one should know that the donor’s continuum is moistened by immeasurable merit and virtue, and immeasurable peace and happiness flow into their body.
At that time, the donor’s merit constantly increases; how could it be that they must always possess a superior volition directed toward that [recipient]?
Therefore, it is certainly reasonable to say that what is called "the subtle continuity perfumed by volition" arises through gradual transformation and differentiation.
Furthermore, as for how a course of action (*karmapatha*) can reach completion when one does not act oneself but merely dispatches another, it should be explained as follows:

through the original preparatory effort (*prayoga*), at the time the task is completed according to the instructions, it is by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that it causes a subtle transformation and differentiation to arise within the continuum of the instigator; by means of this, many fruits will be experienced in the future.
It should be understood that when any action performed by oneself reaches completion, it is likewise by this same principle.

One should know that this very subtle transformation and differentiation within the continuum is called the "path of action" (*karmapatha*); this is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect, because it is the result induced by bodily and vocal actions.

Just as one who maintains that there exists a distinct entity called non-informative action (*avijñapti*) asserts that, according to the tenets of our own school, non-informative action is also termed a path of bodily or vocal karma;
so too does the Venerable [Vasumitra] say:

"Within the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), one is touched by the sin of killing through the arising of volition (*cetanā*) at three moments—namely, 'I shall kill,' 'I am killing,' and 'I have killed.'"

The completion of this course of action does not occur merely by this [thought], lest one should incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) karma simply by thinking one has killed when in fact one’s mother or others have not actually been harmed.
Nevertheless, if one engages in the act of killing oneself without error and gives rise to such a thought, one incurs the sin of killing.

If this explanation is not unreasonable, why do you harbor such particular animosity toward the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) as to flatly deny its existence, while simultaneously accepting that there is a subtle, continuous transformation of the perfumed (*bhāvita*) stream of consciousness?

However, both this [position] and that [previous one] are difficult to comprehend; yet, in this matter, I harbor no animosity or envy. Nevertheless, the doctrine that the paths of action (*karmapatha*) are of the nature of mind, and that when an action is completed through physical exertion, a distinct unmanifest phenomenon (*avijñapti*) arises within the body of the instructor—separate from the mind and body—is not something that inspires joy in me.

If, when an action is brought to completion by means of an impulse that has induced its preliminary application, it arises from a specific transformation within the continuum of that very [impulse], then such a tenet may be found pleasing.
It is solely because of the specific transformation within the continuity of the mind and its associates that they are able to produce future fruits.
Furthermore, this has already been explained previously.
What was explained previously?
That is to say, since manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) does not exist, how could there be non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) and so forth?

Furthermore, it is stated that the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) does not include formless things, because it contains the forms subsumed under the sphere of phenomena—such as the objects of meditative concentration previously described—which are invisible and non-obstructive.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that there should not be eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*): one must first explain how, at the very moment one is on the path, right speech, right action, and right livelihood can exist.
Is it the case that in this state one utters right words, performs right deeds, or seeks clothing and so forth?

It is not so. How is it that by obtaining such a type of untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative action (*avijñapti*), one is able—after emerging from meditative absorption—to give rise to the three right [actions] and not the three wrong ones through the force of that prior [attainment]? Because the name of the effect is established within the cause, the name "verbal action" is applied to the non-informative action.
If that is so, why do you not accept this principle?

Although there is no *avijñapti*, while one is on the Path, one acquires such an intention (*āśaya*) and its basis; therefore, after emerging from meditative absorption, by the force of that prior [intention], one is able to give rise to the three right [actions] and not the three wrong ones.
Because the name of the effect is established within the cause, it is possible to fully establish the eight branches of the Noble Path.
Other masters say:

"It is only by speaking of the non-performance of wrong speech and so forth that they are considered path-branches; that is to say, when one is in meditative concentration, through the power of the Noble Path, one is able to attain the certainty of non-performance."

This meditative concentration is not produced [as a conditioned entity]; rather, it is established by relying on the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) and is therefore called "untainted. It is not the case that in every instance a name or category must be established based on a distinct, substantially existent dharma-body (dharma-svabhāva).

Just as with the eight worldly dharmas—namely, gain and loss, defamation and fame, praise and blame, suffering and pleasure—it is not the case that there exists a separate substantial entity for these things such as the acquisition of food and clothing; this [case] should be understood in the same way.

The prātimokṣa restraint should also be understood accordingly: by the power of volition and aspiration, one first establishes a formal commitment that is capable of definitively preventing and warding off the unwholesome karma of body and speech; it is for this reason that the prātimokṣa restraint is established.

If it were argued that restraint would be absent when a mind directed toward other objects arises, this objection is unreasonable; for by the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), when one intends to commit a transgression, one remembers [the vow] and stops.

The meaning of the precepts as a "dike" (*setu*) should also be understood accordingly: first, one makes a formal vow to refrain from evil; subsequently, through frequent recollection, shame and dread (*hrī-apatrāpya*) manifest, enabling one to maintain self-restraint and avoid violating the precepts.

Therefore, the principle of the embankment and pond is maintained through the mind; if it were the unmanifest (avijñapti) that could prevent the transgression of precepts, there would be no one who breaks the precepts due to loss of mindfulness.
Let us cease these numerous disputes for now.
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that there exists a real entity called unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), which is my own school’s position.
As for what was previously stated—that unmanifest form is derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)—is it created by the same primary elements as manifest form, or is it different?
The verse says:
These primary elements that constitute [unmanifest action] are distinct from those upon which the manifest [action] relies.
The commentary says:
The unmanifest (avijñapti) arises from a different set of primary elements (mahābhūta) than the manifest (vijñapti). Why is this?
Because it is illogical for a subtle and a coarse fruit to arise from a single causal complex (sāmagrī).
Just as the [informative] table and the great elements necessarily arise simultaneously, so too is it with the non-informative; yet there is a distinction.
For the most part, all derived matter arises at the same time as the great elements; however, there are also some instances in the present and future that depend upon those of the past.
What is the partial [case]?
The verse says:
The non-informative [matter] of the last moment of desire arises based on past primary elements.
The treatise says:

Only after the first moment of that which is bound to the desire realm, all subsequent non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises from past great elements; these serve as the basis upon which the non-informative matter is produced.

The manifest great elements can only serve as a basis; they act as the primary cause and the conforming cause respectively, just as when a wheel rolls upon the ground, the hand and the earth serve as its supports.
In which stages do bodily and vocal actions exist?
By which elements of the stages are they produced?
The verse says:
"Defiled [actions] depend on the great elements of their own level; undefiled [actions] follow the place of their arising.
The treatise says:
The two types of action—bodily and vocal—bound to the desire realm are produced solely by the great elements bound to the desire realm.
In this manner, up to the fourth dhyāna, the two types of action—bodily and vocal—are produced solely by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that respective stage.

If bodily or vocal action is untainted (*anāsrava*), it arises and manifests according to the stage where one is born; thus, it is produced by the primary elements of that very stage. This is because untainted phenomena do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*); because there are no primary elements that are themselves untainted; and because the untainted arises through the power of its support (*āśraya*).
What is the nature of these informative and non-informative [forms]?
Furthermore, by what kind of primary elements (mahābhūta) are they produced?
The verse says:
Non-informative matter (avijñapti) is non-appropriated (anupātta), and it is also of the nature of outflow (naiṣyandika) among sentient categories.
That which arises from a state of distraction (vikṣipta) depends on outflow-natured great elements (mahābhūta) that are appropriated and distinct;
that which arises from meditative concentration (samāhita) depends on nurtured (aupacayika) great elements that are non-appropriated and non-distinct.
The [unmanifest] is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), and it belongs to the body as something appropriated (*upātta*).
The commentary states:
In this verse, it is first established that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is not appropriated, because it lacks the characteristic of transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇā*).
It is also of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*); the word "also" indicates that there are some which are momentary, namely the first untainted [state].
All others are of the nature of outflow, meaning they are produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
This exists only in sentient beings, because it arises in dependence upon the internal [body].

Among these, all unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm is a result of outflow (*naiṣyandika*), is associated with feeling (*sāvedanā*), and is produced from distinct primary elements (*bhūta*).

The phrase "produced from distinct primary elements" indicates that each of the seven types of bodily and vocal [unmanifest form] is individually created by its own set of primary elements. Regarding unmanifest form born of meditative concentration (*dhyānaja*), there are two distinctions.
This refers to the dhyāna-restraints and the untainted (anāsrava) restraints;
both of these are nourished by meditative concentration (samādhi),
and are produced from great elements that are neither felt nor differentiated.
The phrase "no difference" indicates that these seven branches of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are produced from the same set of four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Why is this so?
Because the great elements that serve as their basis are, like the mind, singular and without distinction.
One should know that informative action (*vijñapti*) is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*). If this pertains to the body, it is appropriated (*upātta*);

otherwise, its other characteristics are all the same as those of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) in the state of non-concentration. When an informative action arises, does it necessarily destroy the original dimensions of the body, or not?
If that were so, what would be the fault?
If it were destroyed, the resultant matter (*vipākavarṇa*) would be severed and then able to continue again, which would contradict the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*.
If it were not destroyed, how could two distinct physical dimensions (*mātra*) be established within the location of a single body?
There are distinct newly produced *mahābhūtas* of equal outflow (*naiṣyandika*) that constitute manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) without destroying the original body.

If this were so, whichever part of the body one relies upon to initiate manifest action would necessarily become larger than before, because the newly produced *mahābhūtas* would pervasively augment it.
If [the atoms] were not augmented on all sides, how could they produce a pervasive manifest action (*vijñapti*)?
Since the body possesses interstices, they are able to accommodate one another.
Thus has been explained the distinction between the two, three, and five types within the category of karma.
What are the distinctions regarding their nature, realm, and stage?
The verse says:
The unmanifest has three [types]; the others have three. The unwholesome exists only in the desire realm.
Non-informative [matter] (avijñapti) pervades both the desire and form realms; informative [matter] (vijñapti) exists only in the two [realms] where there is sustained thought (savicāra).
In the desire realm, there is no obscured (nivṛta) informative matter, because it lacks a motivating cause (samutthāna).
The treatise says:
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) pertains exclusively to the nature of the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it does not exist as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Why is this so? Because the power of an indeterminate mind is weak and inferior, and thus cannot induce a potent karma to arise such that its fruit would continue to arise even after the cause has ceased.
What is referred to as "the rest" consists of informative action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*).
These three—informative action, non-informative action, and volition—are all common to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.

Among these, the unwholesome exists only in the desire realm and not elsewhere, because the unwholesome roots, along with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), have been severed there.
Wholesome and neutral [unmanifest actions] exist in all stages, as they are not specifically excluded in the verse.
Both the desire and form realms possess unmanifest action, because the great elements do not exist in the formless realm.
Wherever there is the activity of body or speech, it is only in that place that there is restraint of body and speech.

If this were so, then when a person born in the Desire or Form Realms enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they should possess restraint, just as one who gives rise to an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) possesses untainted non-informative matter (*anāsrava-avijñapti*).
This is not so, because it does not fall within the realms (*dhātu*).
If there were unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would have to be an unmanifest form that is not produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
It cannot be said that a contaminated (*sāsrava*) unmanifest form takes the primary elements of a different realm or level as its support.

Furthermore, because one turns away from all forms and enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), no form can arise within those attainments, as those attainments involve the suppression of the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters state:
"Śīla (ethical discipline) arises as an antidote to immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*)."
Only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) do unwholesome precepts exist; the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is distant from the desire realm in four ways:

first, distance of basis (*āśraya*); second, distance of aspect (*ākāra*); third, distance of object (*ālambana*); and fourth, distance of antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Therefore, there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) within the formless realm.
Manifest form exists only in the two levels where there is investigation (savicāra), namely, throughout the desire realm and the first dhyāna; it cannot be said to exist in the higher levels.
As for obscured-unspecified manifest form, it is certainly absent in the desire realm and can only be said to exist within the Brahma-world (Brahmaloka).

It has been heard that even the Great Brahmā has uttered words of deception and flattery—namely, that within his own assembly, in order to avoid being questioned by Aśvajit, he falsely praised himself and so forth.
Since there is no speech in the higher realms, how could there be the sense-sphere of sound?
There is sound produced with external primary elements as its cause.
Other masters say:
"In the upper three dhyānas, there is also unobstructed-neutral manifest karma (vijñapti-karma), which is neither wholesome nor defiled."

Why is this so? One born in a higher realm cannot give rise to a wholesome or defiled mind of a lower realm to produce bodily or vocal intimation, because such minds are inferior and have been abandoned.
What was stated previously is correct.
Furthermore, for what reason is there no manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) at all from the second dhyāna upward?
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma, because there is no motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) that initiates such action.
A mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra is capable of producing manifest karma; such a mind is entirely absent in the two higher dhyānas and above.

Furthermore, the mind that produces manifest karma is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) operate only within the internal [mental] door.

Since there are definitely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are consequently no manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*) at all in the three higher stages.

Within the desire realm, there is no obscured-unspecified manifest action. Is it then solely by virtue of the motivating cause (*samutthāna*) that various phenomena come to possess natures such as wholesome or unwholesome?
It is not so. Why? Because the nature of being wholesome and so forth is established by four kinds of causes:
First, by way of ultimate reality; second, by way of intrinsic nature; third, by way of association; and fourth, by way of origination.
By what cause is which phenomenon established as having which nature?
The verse says:
Ultimate goodness is liberation; intrinsic goodness consists of the roots of shame and dread.
That which is associated with them, that which is conjoined with them, and the material karma arising from them are also good.
The opposite of these is called unwholesome. Ultimate non-definedness refers to the two [unconditioned] eternalities.
The treatise states:
Ultimate goodness refers to true liberation, because within nirvana there is the most extreme peace and security, and all suffering is eternally stilled, just as one is free from illness.

That which is wholesome by intrinsic nature refers to the faculties of shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*). Among conditioned phenomena, only shame, dread, and the three roots of goodness—namely, non-attachment and so forth—are wholesome by their very essence, independent of association or other originating factors, just like efficacious medicine.

Regarding "wholesome by association" (*saṃprayukta-kuśala*): this refers to that which is associated [with wholesome factors]. This is because the mind and mental factors must be associated with the wholesome roots of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) to constitute a wholesome nature; if they are not associated with those factors such as shame, their wholesome nature is not established, just like water mixed with medicinal herbs.

Wholesome by origination refers to bodily and vocal actions as well as formations dissociated from mind, because they are originated by that which is wholesome by nature and by association, just like milk produced by the infusion of medicinal juices.
If acquisitions (*prāpti*) and so forth are produced by minds of a different category, how can they be established as wholesome?
This point should be considered; for as it is said that there are four types of distinctions regarding the nature of wholesomeness, the four types of unwholesomeness are the opposite of these.
How are they contradictory?
Ultimate unwholesomeness refers to the phenomena of saṃsāra.
This is because all phenomena within saṃsāra have suffering as their intrinsic nature; they are utterly unstable, like a chronic illness.

Intrinsic unwholesomeness refers to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the three unwholesome roots. Among the outflowing states (*sāsrava*), it is specifically shamelessness, lack of dread, and the three unwholesome roots—greed, hatred, and so forth—that are unwholesome by their very nature, independent of association (*samprayoga*) or other co-arising factors (*samutthāna*), just like a poisonous drug.

"Associated with the unwholesome" means that which is associated with them; for it is only when mental states and mental factors are associated with shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), and the unwholesome roots that they constitute an unwholesome nature, whereas otherwise this is not the case, just as water mixed with poison.

Unwholesome by origination refers to bodily and vocal actions and the formations dissociated from mind, because they are originated by that which is unwholesome by intrinsic nature and by association, like milk produced by the infusion of a poisonous medicinal juice.
If that were so, there would be no single contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon that is either neutral (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*), because all such phenomena would be subsumed within saṃsāra.
While it is indeed as you say from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), here the explanation is given in terms of maturation (*vipāka*).

Among all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), those that cannot be designated as having a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) are established under the name "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). Within this category, those that can be designated as having a desirable ripened fruit are called "wholesome" (*kuśala*); therefore, there is no fault.

Ultimate indeterminacy refers to the two unconditioned phenomena; for both infinite space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are exclusively of an indeterminate nature and have no other categories.
This point should be considered.

If it were the power of the motivating impulse (*samutthāna*) that renders bodily and vocal actions wholesome or unwholesome, then by extension the same would apply to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
However, this does not constitute a valid analogy, because it is the agent’s mind that originally intends to initiate action, not the four primary elements. Thus, the case is not analogous.

If that is so, the non-informative matter (avijñapti) that follows a concentrated mind is neither produced by the attention (manasikāra) of one currently in meditative absorption, nor is it induced by the preparatory effort of a distracted mind, because they belong to different categories.
How could they become wholesome?
Otherwise, the divine eye and ear would also have to be of a wholesome nature; one should apply diligent effort toward such a point.
As stated above, because the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) operate internally (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), they cannot manifest as physical or vocal action.
If that is so, for what reason does the Sūtra state:
"By means of wrong view, one gives rise to wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, and so forth"?
This is not contradictory.
Why is this? The verse says:
There are two kinds of motivation: that which is causal and that which is simultaneous.
As it should be understood in sequence: the primary [consciousness] is called "turning" (pravṛtti), and the secondary is called "conforming" (anuvartaka).
The consciousnesses abandoned through seeing are exclusively turning; the five sensory consciousnesses are exclusively conforming.
The mental consciousness abandoned through cultivation pertains to both; those that are untainted (anāsrava) or resultant (vipāka) are neither.
