The motivating factors for manifest and non-manifest karma are twofold: namely, the causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*) and the momentary motivation (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*), because the former acts as the cause and the latter exists at that very moment.
Respectively, the first is called "origination" (*pravartaka*) and the second is called "concomitant origination" (*anuvartaka*).
This means that when the motivating cause (*hetu-samutthāna*) is about to perform its action, it is called "origination" because it is capable of initiating [the action].
Because it does not dissociate from the primary action at the moment it arises and performs its function, it is called "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).
What is the efficacy of this concomitance regarding the action?
Although there is a prior cause capable of initiating it, if there were no concomitant factor, the action would be like a dead one and would not exist.
If that is so, how can one produce the precepts when in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*)?
For those with a mind, the arising of karma is distinct; therefore, the *anuvartaka-citta* (concomitant mind) has utility regarding karma.

Regarding the manifestation of action, consciousness abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya-vijñāna*) can only act as the *pravartaka* (initiating factor); it does not act as the *anuvartaka* because it serves only as a provision for the arising of vitarka and vicāra which initiate the manifestation. This is because such [seeing-abandoned] consciousness does not exist at the time when an outward-directed mind is actually engaged in the production of karma.
Furthermore, if the manifest form produced by that which is abandoned by insight were itself abandoned by insight, then this form would have to be abandoned by insight.
If one were to concede that it is abandoned by insight, what fault would there be?
It would contradict the Abhidharma, and moreover, it would imply that clarity and ignorance are not mutually exclusive.
The principle that contaminated material form (*rūpa*) is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) should be further established.
If that were so, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) would also have to be abandoned by insight, because they are likewise produced by the power of a mind that is abandoned by insight.
There is no such fault, as in the case of what is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
Or, even if one were to grant that [it is so], there would be no logical contradiction.

However, one should not grant it; for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are certainly neither abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor abandoned at all (*aprahātavya*), because in every respect non-defiled phenomena are not incompatible with either clarity (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).
That sutra makes this statement solely on the basis of the preceding motivating cause (*samutthāna*), and therefore there is no contradiction.

As for the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), they function only as concomitants (*anuvartaka*), because they are devoid of conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*) and arise directed toward external objects (*bahir-mukha*).
The consciousnesses to be abandoned through cultivation are of two types: because they involve conceptual discrimination and because they arise directed toward external objects.

All untainted minds and those born of maturation are neither primary nor secondary [transformative] consciousnesses, because they exist only within meditative concentration and proceed spontaneously without depending on preparatory effort.
Thus, four distinct categories are established:
there is that which is a primary mover (*pravartaka*) but not a concomitant mover (*anuvartaka*), namely the mind abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*);
and there is that which is a concomitant mover but not a primary mover, namely the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness.
There are those that are both the primary mover and the concomitant mover, namely the mental consciousness of the three natures abandoned through cultivation.
There are those that are neither the primary mover nor the concomitant mover, namely all untainted minds and those born of maturation.
Are the primary mind (*mūlacitta*) and its concomitant minds (*anuvartaka-citta*) necessarily of the same nature? This is not determined.
What is the reason for this?

That is to say, if the preceding impelling mind (*pravartaka-citta*) is of a wholesome nature, the subsequent concomitant consciousness (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) may be of any of the three natures—wholesome and so forth; the same applies when the impelling mind is unwholesome or indeterminate.
Only in the case of the Muni (the Buddha), the impelling and concomitant consciousnesses are for the most part of the same nature, with only slight differences.

That is to say, if the primary mind (*pravartaka*) is wholesome, the concomitant mind (*anuvartaka*) is also wholesome; if the primary mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the concomitant mind is likewise so.
However, while there are times when a wholesome mind follows an indeterminate one, there has never been an instance where an indeterminate mind follows a wholesome one as its concomitant.
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, experiences no decline or exhaustion in his mind when teaching the Dharma and so forth.
Other schools maintain that because the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, are always in meditative concentration, their minds are exclusively wholesome and possess no neutral (avyākṛta) states.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Nāga walks in meditative concentration; the Nāga stands in meditative concentration;
the Nāga sits in meditative concentration; the Nāga lies down in meditative concentration."
The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this explanation:

This reveals that if the Buddha’s mind does not delight in distraction, he is able to remain constantly in meditative absorption throughout the four postures; however, it is not the case that in other states there is no arising of minds associated with the postures, or those born of maturation, or those resulting from supernormal powers.

Regarding the fact that informative actions (*vijñapti-karma*) establish themselves as being wholesome and so forth, do they follow the nature of the primary motivating mind (*pravartaka-citta*), or do they follow the nature of the subsequent conforming mind (*anuvartaka-citta*)?
If this were the case, what would be the fault?

If they followed the primary mind, then within the desire realm there would have to be obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are capable of acting as the primary motivators.

Alternatively, one should make a distinction: not all minds abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are capable of acting as the primary mover (*pravartaka*). If it were otherwise, then the informative action (*vijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa vows, when accompanied by an evil or neutral mind that acts as a conformer (*anuvartaka*), would not possess the nature of virtue.

Regarding this objection, one should apply diligent effort; it should be stated that [the nature] is established as wholesome and so forth just as the manifest action (*vijñapti*) of a transformed mind is, yet it is not like that [manifest action] because it is interrupted by a transformed mind that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), rather than one abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
If manifest karma were not established as virtuous and so forth by the power of the concomitant mind, then one should not say:

"That sutra refers only to the antecedent motivation (*pūrvahetusaṃutthāna*) and not to the momentary [motivation], and therefore there is certainly no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma within the desire realm."
One should simply say this:

that sūtra speaks solely with reference to the motivation (*samutthāna*) as interrupted by other mental factors; therefore, although a mind to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) can indeed act as a motivating cause, there is absolutely no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*) in the realm of desire.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Thirteen (Fascicle Fourteen) Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four, Part Two: The Analysis of Karma. Having concluded the ancillary discussion, one should now further distinguish the characteristics of the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
The verse says:
Non-informative [action] consists of the three types of restraint, non-restraint, and that which is neither.
The commentary says:
In this context, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is briefly said to be of three kinds:
first, restraint (*saṃvara*); second, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); and third, that which is neither, namely, neither restraint nor non-restraint.
It is called *saṃvara* (restraint) because it is able to obstruct and extinguish the continuity of unwholesome discipline.
How many distinctions of such restraint are there?
The verse says:
"Restraint is of the types of prātimokṣa, dhyāna, and that born of the Path.
The commentary says:
"Briefly stated, there are three distinctions of restraint:"
First, the prātimokṣa restraint, which refers to the precepts bound to the desire realm;
second, the restraint born of meditative concentration, which refers to the precepts bound to the form realm;
and third, the restraint born of the path, which refers to the untainted (anāsrava) precepts.
What are the distinctions regarding the characteristics of the initial vows?
The verse says:
The initial vows are of eight kinds, but in terms of their actual substance, there are only four.
Because their forms differ and their names vary, they are each distinct and do not contradict one another.
The treatise says:
There are eight distinctions in the characteristics of the Prātimokṣa vows.

1. The discipline of a bhikṣu; 2. the discipline of a bhikṣuṇī; 3. the discipline of a śikṣamāṇā; 4. the discipline of a śrāmaṇera; 5. the discipline of a śrāmaṇerī; 6. the discipline of an upāsaka; 7. the discipline of an upāsikā; 8. the discipline of an upavāsastha.
These eight distinct varieties of the characteristics of restraint are collectively termed the first, the *prātimokṣa* restraint.
Although there are eight names, the actual entities are only four:
first, the bhikṣu restraint; second, the śrāmaṇera restraint; third, the upāsaka restraint; and fourth, the upavāsa restraint.
Only these four types of prātimokṣa discipline possess substantial reality, as their characteristics are distinct from one another.
Why is this so? Because apart from the bhikṣu discipline, there is no separate bhikṣuṇī discipline; [the latter is not distinct from the former].
Apart from the śrāmaṇera vows, there are no separate śikṣamāṇā or śrāmaṇerī vows;
apart from the upāsaka vows, there are no separate upāsikā vows.
How is this known to be so?
Because when the form undergoes transformation, although the substance itself is neither abandoned nor acquired, its designation changes.
"Form" refers to the physical appearance, namely the male and female sexual organs.

Due to these two faculties, there is a distinction between male and female forms; it is solely through the transformation of form that various vows are designated as those of a *bhikṣu*, a *bhikṣuṇī*, and so forth. That is to say, at the stage of the transformation of the faculties, the original *bhikṣu* vow is termed a *bhikṣuṇī* vow, or the *bhikṣuṇī* vow is termed a *bhikṣu* vow;
the original *śrāmaṇera* vow is termed a *śrāmaṇerī* vow, or the *śrāmaṇerī* vow and the *śikṣamāṇā* vow are termed a *śrāmaṇera* vow;
and the original *upāsaka* vow is termed an *upāsikā* vow, or the *upāsikā* vow is termed an *upāsaka* vow.

Because there is no cause or condition for abandoning what was previously obtained or obtaining what was previously unobtained at the stage of changing one's faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), the four types of restraint do not differ in essence from the three.

If one receives the *śrāmaṇera* restraint from the *upāsaka* restraint, and subsequently receives the *bhikṣu* restraint from the *śrāmaṇera* restraint, these three restraints are established with distinct names based on the increase and fulfillment of the means of abstention (*virati-upāya*).
Just as a single pair of gold coins, or fifty and twenty [coins], arise simultaneously with their respective substances complete and distinct,
so too the three types of vows arise simultaneously with their respective characteristics complete and distinct, their substances not being intermingled.

Within the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), there are three forms of abstaining from killing, up to and including three forms of abstaining from drinking intoxicants; the remaining numbers vary according to what is appropriate.
Since this is so, and they are mutually of the same category, what is their distinction?
Due to the distinction of causes and conditions, there are differences when they are compared to one another.
What is the matter?

Just as one seeks to receive various types of training rules (*śikṣāpada*), so too, when one is able to avoid various bases for negligence and pride, one simultaneously avoids numerous causal origins such as killing and the like.
Since all forms of abstention arise based on causes and conditions, there are distinctions among them according to those causes and conditions.
If this were not the case, then upon relinquishing the bhikṣu vows, one would have to relinquish all three sets of vows at that time, because the first two would be subsumed within the latter one.
Since this is not permitted, the three types of vows are distinct.

Nevertheless, these three kinds do not contradict one another; they function simultaneously within a single body. It is not the case that one abandons a preceding vow by receiving a subsequent one, lest one who relinquishes the bhikṣu precepts would thereby cease to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth.
How are the four types of restraint—those of the lay follower (*upāsaka*), the one observing the fast-day vows (*upavāsa*), the novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and the monk (*bhikṣu*)—established?
The verse says:
"By undertaking the abstention from five, eight, ten, and all things that ought to be avoided," [the four restraints are established].
The lay follower (*upāsaka*), the one observing the fast (*upavāsastha*), the novice (*śrāmaṇera*), and the monk (*bhikṣu*).
The treatise says:
It should be understood that herein, according to their respective order, four types of discipline (*saṃvara*) are established based on the four kinds of abstinence (*virati*).
This refers to establishing the first lay vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) by undertaking the abstention from five things that ought to be avoided.
What are these five things to be avoided?
First, taking life; second, taking what is not given; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, drinking various intoxicants.
If one undertakes the renunciation of the eight things to be avoided, the second discipline, the *upavāsa* (near-abiding), is established.
What are the eight things to be avoided? First, taking life; second, taking what is not given;

third, unchaste conduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, drinking various intoxicants; sixth, anointing with perfumes, wearing garlands, and attending performances of dance and song; seventh, sleeping or sitting on high, broad, and luxurious beds or seats; and eighth, eating at improper times.
If one undertakes the renunciation of the ten things to be avoided, the third *śrāmaṇera* vow is established.
What are these ten things to be avoided? They are as follows:

the first eight [prohibitions] are divided into two categories by adding "applying perfumes and wearing garlands" and "watching and listening to dancing and singing"; furthermore, the acceptance and possession of gold, silver, and other precious objects are added as the tenth.
If one undertakes the abandonment of all bodily and vocal actions that ought to be abandoned, the fourth bhikṣu restraint is established.
Regarding the distinctions in the names of the Pratimokṣa restraints, the verse says:
They are all called *śīla*, Excellent conduct, action, and restraint.
Only the initial manifest and unmanifest [karma] are called "distinct liberation" and "paths of action.
The treatise says:
It is named *śīla* because it can level out treacherous karma.
Regarding the etymological interpretation: it is because it is cool.
As a verse says:
"The joy of upholding the precepts brings no heat or affliction to the body; therefore, it is called śīla."
It is called "sublime conduct" (sucarita) because it is praised by the wise;
it is called "action" (karman) because it is the very essence of what has been performed. One might object:
"Does not non-manifest [form] (avijñapti) also consist in 'not doing'? How then can it now be said to be the essence of what has been performed?"
Those who possess a sense of shame and modesty receive the power of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) and do not commit various evils; therefore, it is called "non-doing.
That which is produced by informative action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*) receives the name "doing.
Others explain, saying:
Because it is the cause of action and because it is the fruit of action, it is called "action" without error.
Because it can restrain body and speech, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

One should understand it thus: the Prātimokṣa vows bear this name without distinction throughout both the initial and subsequent stages; however, only the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) [karma] of the first moment receive the names "Prātimokṣa" and "path of action" (*karmapatha*).
This refers to the initial manifest and unmanifest [karma] at the time of receiving the precepts, because one separately abandons various evils.
Based on the meaning of this initial, individual abandonment, the name "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) is established.

At that very moment, the action is brought to completion; because it is established as a "path of action" (karmapatha) in the sense that the karma is fully manifested, the first moment is called *prātimokṣa*, and it may also be termed *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* and the "fundamental path of action."
From the second moment until it is relinquished, it is not called *prātimokṣa*, but is called the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*;
it is not called a path of action (*karmapatha*), but is termed a subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*).
Who accomplishes which restraint?
The verse says:
Eight accomplish the prātimokṣa; those who have attained dhyāna and the noble ones [accomplish the other two].
Those born of the dhyāna-path and the latter two [types of restraint] follow the mind.
The Commentary says:
All eight classes achieve the prātimokṣa-saṃvara, namely from the bhikṣu down to the upavāsastha.
Do non-Buddhists not possess any received precepts?
Although they do, these are not called *prātimokṣa* vows.
This is because that which they have received lacks the capacity for the permanent liberation from all evils, as it is based upon attachment to existence.
Regarding that which arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja*): this discipline arises from meditative concentration or is based upon meditative concentration.
If one attains meditative concentration, one will certainly accomplish this discipline.
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the various dhyānas are also called "dhyāna," just as those near a village or town receive the name of that village or town.
As some say, "In this village there are rice fields," so it should be understood here as well.
The noble ones achieve the restraint of the path (*mārga-saṃvara*), which is further divided into two types:
that of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Among the previously analyzed co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), it was stated that the two types of restraint follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*); within these three [types of restraint], which two are they?
This refers to the two types arising from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and arising from the Path (*mārga*), but not to that of the Prātimokṣa.
Why is this so? Because it continues to function constantly even when the mind is different or when there is no mind (*acittaka*).
The two types of restraint—those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)—are also called the restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*).
Based on what stage are they established?
The verse says:
"Prior to the nine uninterrupted paths, both are called 'abandonment'.
The treatise says:

Within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) that arise simultaneously with the nine uninterrupted paths are called "restraints of abandonment," because they can permanently sever the evil conduct of the desire realm and the afflictions that give rise to it.
Based on this, there may be cases where the dhyāna restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) is not the restraint of abandonment (prahāṇa-saṃvara); thus, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).

The first permutation consists of the remaining contaminated (sāsrava) dhyāna restraints, excluding the contaminated restraints associated with the nine paths of immediate succession (anantarya-mārga) of the threshold concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna).
The second phrase refers to the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) based on the nine paths of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) of the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna).
The third phrase refers to the tainted restraint (sāsrava-saṃvara) based on the nine paths of immediate succession of the preparatory concentration.

Regarding the fourth phrase: it refers to all remaining untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), excluding the untainted restraints of the nine uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*).

Thus, there may be untainted restraint that is not a restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*); one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), understanding them as appropriate according to the previous four permutations.
If that is so, then regarding the brief precepts spoken by the Blessed One:
"Excellent is restraint of the body; excellent is restraint of speech;
excellent is restraint of the mind; excellent is universal restraint."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"One should well guard and well abide in the restraint of the eye faculty.
What is the intrinsic nature of this restraint of the mind faculty?
These two natures are not unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). If so, what are they?
The verse says:
The conjunction of correct awareness and correct mindfulness is called the restraint of the mental faculty (*manaindriya-saṃvara*).
The commentary states:

To show that these two types of restraint both have correct awareness and correct mindfulness as their essence, the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is stated after listing the names. That is to say, the restraint of the mind has wisdom and mindfulness as its essence; thus, the combination of these two constitutes the restraint of the faculties.
Therefore, the terms "separation" and "conjunction" should not be understood as corresponding respectively [to the preceding categories].
Now, one should investigate: who accomplishes which—informative (vijñapti) or non-informative (avijñapti) karma—and for how long a duration?
Furthermore, to explain the accomplishment of non-informative restraint (*avijñapti-saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*),
the verse says:
Abiding in the non-informative of the Pratimokṣa, One always accomplishes the present [non-informative] as long as it has not been relinquished.
After the first moment, they become past; the same applies to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
One who attains the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*) always possesses both the past and the future;
the Noble One (*ārya*), at the very beginning, excludes the past, while one abiding in the meditative absorption or the Path possesses the present.
The treatise says:
For a person abiding in the prātimokṣa, as long as they have not relinquished it, they always possess the present non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of this prātimokṣa restraint.

After the first moment, it also becomes past; the phrase "not yet abandoned" applies universally to subsequent moments as well. There is no non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) that exists in the future, because its physical force is weak and it does not follow the mind.

As it has been stated regarding abiding in the prātimokṣa vows, one should know that the same applies to abiding in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*): namely, until the time one abandons the evil precepts, one constantly possesses them in the present; furthermore, after the first moment, one also possesses the past non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the evil precepts.

For those who have attained the dhyāna-restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara), they constantly possess it in both the past and the future as long as they have not relinquished it; this is because one necessarily reacquires that past dhyāna-restraint which was lost in a previous life at the very first moment of its present attainment.

All noble ones (*ārya*) constantly possess the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) of both the past and the future; however, there is a distinction: at the first moment, one necessarily possesses the future [restraint] but not the past, because this category of noble path (*āryamārga*) has not yet previously arisen.

If one currently abides in meditative absorption (dhyāna) or its path, one accordingly establishes the present restraint of meditative absorption and the path; however, when emerging from contemplation, there is no establishment of the present [restraint].
Having already explained those who abide in wholesome or unwholesome restraints, how is it for one who abides in the intermediate state?
The verse says:
Abiding in the intermediate state, one possesses non-informative action; at the first moment, one accomplishes the middle [type], and thereafter both [the middle and the last].
The commentary says:

Regarding those who abide in the intermediate state—meaning those who possess neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)—the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma produced by them does not necessarily exist in all cases.
If such unmanifest karma does exist, it is subsumed under the category of either virtuous discipline (*śīla*) or unvirtuous discipline; in its initial moment, it exists only as a present phenomenon.
However, since the present exists within the past and the future, one establishes the present by means of establishing the middle.
From the moment after the first instant until it is relinquished, one constantly establishes the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of both the past and present time periods.
If there are those who abide in either restraint or non-restraint, do they also possess unmanifest (avijñapti) karma of evil or merit?
And if they do possess it, for how long does it endure?
The verse says:
Abiding in restraint or non-restraint, one gives rise to defiled or pure non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
At the initial moment, both are established; thereafter, two persist until the force of the defilement or purity comes to an end.
The commentary says:

If one abides in restraint but commits various unwholesome deeds such as killing or binding due to predominant afflictions, one thereby gives rise to unwholesome non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) and abides in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
Through pure faith, one performs various superior wholesome deeds such as prostrating to the Buddha; by means of these, various wholesome non-informative (avijñapti) factors are also produced.

As long as these two minds have not been severed, the non-informative factors they produce continue in a constant succession. However, in its initial moment, it exists only in the present; from that point onward, it exists in both the past and the present.
Having already explained the non-informative (*avijñapti*), how is the informative (*vijñapti*) established?
The verse says:
The informative is established as present while it is being performed; it is subsequently established as past, not as future.
The obscured and the unobscured [informative actions] are accomplished only in the present.
The commentary states:

For those who abide in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state, as long as they are currently performing various manifest actions (*vijñapti-karman*), they constantly accomplish the manifest action of the present.

From the moment after the first *kṣaṇa* until it is relinquished, one always possesses [the action] as past; there is never the case of possessing a future manifest (*vijñapti*), as explained in the section on the non-manifest (*avijñapti*).

Regarding both obscured and unobscured neutral manifest actions, there is certainly no capacity to possess them as past or future; since the power of the dharma itself is weak, the power of its acquisition (*prāpti*) is likewise slight. Therefore, there is no capacity to retroactively achieve possession of them.
By whose power is the strength of this dharma weakened?
It is by the power of the mind.
If that were so, then obscured-unspecified minds (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) and the like would not attain the status of past or future.
This criticism is unreasonable, because manifest action (*vijñapti*) is dull and obtuse and is dependently originated;

the mind and its associates are not so. Since neutral manifest karma arises from an inferior state of mind, its power is twice as weak as the mind that gives rise to it; therefore, there is a distinction between manifest action and the mind.
Regarding the aforementioned abiding in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), the distinctions in the nomenclature for this non-restraint are stated in verse:
"Evil conduct (*duścarita*), evil discipline (*duḥśīla*), action (*karman*), paths of action (*karmapatha*), and non-restraint."
The treatise states:

These five distinct names, beginning with "misconduct" (*duścarita*), are synonyms for the term "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*). They are designated as "misconduct" because they are censured and loathed by the wise and because their results are undesirable.
It is called "bad discipline" because it obstructs pure ethical conduct (*śīla*); it is called "action" (*karman*) because it is produced by body and speech;
it is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*) because it is subsumed under the fundamental [acts];
and it is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) because it does not restrain body and speech.

However, the name "path of action" (karmapatha) refers exclusively to the first moment; the other four names are established by applying them to both the initial and subsequent stages. Alternatively, one should formulate four permutations regarding cases where there is manifest action (vijñapti-karma) but no non-manifest action (avijñapti), and so forth.
What is the nature of this matter?
The verse says:
One accomplishes informative action, not non-informative action, when performing it with weak volition while abiding in the intermediate state.
The Noble Ones who have abandoned [non-informative action] before it has arisen possess non-informative action, not informative action.
The treatise says:

Those who possess only informative action and not non-informative action are those who dwell in a state that is neither discipline nor non-discipline, and who perform good or evil deeds with weak volition; they produce only informative karma and do not even possess non-informative karma, let alone the informative karma produced by neutral volition—except for meritorious action based on material things (*aupadhika-puṇya*) and the completion of a course of action (*karmapatha*).

Those who possess only non-informative action (*avijñapti*) and not informative action (*vijñapti*) are those noble persons (*ārya-pudgala*) who have been reborn [in a state where such actions are absent], or for whom informative action has not yet arisen, or has arisen and been relinquished. One should understand that the case of possessing neither is to be treated accordingly.

Having explained that those abiding in restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and so forth, possess both manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma, by what means are these various restraints obtained?
The verse says:
Those born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-ja*) are obtained through the stages of concentration; The noble ones obtain those born of the Path (*mārga-ja*).
The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained through the instruction of another and so forth.
The Commentary says:

The dhyāna restraint is obtained at the moment one acquires the mind belonging to the fundamental or preparatory stages of the dhyānas that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); it is obtained simultaneously with that mind, for it is co-existent with the mind.

The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is acquired at the moment one attains the mind of the fundamental or preparatory stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); it is acquired simultaneously with that mind, as it is concomitant with the mind.
The word "that" (*tat*) serves to indicate the aforementioned meditative mind.

Furthermore, the term "noble" (ārya) is used to distinguish and select the untainted (anāsrava). Within the six levels of dhyāna, there exists untainted mind—namely, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental concentrations (mauladhyāna)—but not the three preparatory stages (sāmantaka), as will be explained later.

The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained through the instruction of others and so forth. One who can instruct another is termed "another"; since the precept is generated by the power of such instruction from another, it is said that this precept is obtained through the instruction of another.
This is further divided into two types, based on the distinction between obtaining [the precepts] from the Saṃgha or from an individual (pudgala).
Those obtained from the Saṃgha refer to the precepts of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and śikṣamāṇās.
That which is obtained from a *pudgala* refers to the other five types of precepts.
Since the masters of the Vinaya-vibhāṣā teach that there are ten ways of obtaining the full precepts (*upasampadā*), the word "etc. is used here to include them.
What are the ten?
First, by nature, namely Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Second, by entering into the state of rightness and departure from birth, namely the five bhikṣus.
Third, by the Buddha’s command, "Come, monk," as in the case of Yaśas and others;
fourth, by accepting the Buddha as the Great Master, as in the case of Mahākāśyapa;
fifth, by skillfully answering questions, as in the case of Sudāyin.
Sixth, by respectfully receiving the eight rules of respect, as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī;
seventh, by sending a messenger, as in the case of the nun Dharmadinnā;
eighth, by having a holder of the Vinaya serve as the fifth person, as in the case of border regions.
Ninth, by means of a group of ten, which refers to the Middle Kingdom;
tenth, by means of the threefold recitation of refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, which refers to the sixty virtuous ones gathering together to receive full ordination.
The prātimokṣa restraint thus obtained does not necessarily arise based upon informative action (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, for how long should this aforementioned prātimokṣa restraint be undertaken according to its formal commitment?
The verse says:
The Prātimokṣa restraint lasts for as long as life or for a day and night.
The commentary says:
The prātimokṣa precepts observed by the seven classes of followers should be undertaken with a commitment for as long as life lasts;
the upavāsa precepts observed by those who dwell nearby should be undertaken with a commitment for only one day and night.
At this time, it must necessarily be so. Why is this?
Because there are only two possible limits for the duration of the precepts:
First, the limit of the lifespan; second, the limit of the day and night. The day and night are further specified as half-months and so forth.
What kind of phenomenon is "time"?
It is a designation (*adhivacana*) for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Within the four continents, the states of light and darkness are designated respectively as "day" and "night.

While it is possible for a vow to last for the duration of one's life at the two limits [of existence], after death, even if there is a formal commitment, the Prātimokṣa vows cannot arise; this is because the basis [the body] has changed, and within that different basis, there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) nor any recollection (*smṛti*).
After one day and night, or within five or ten days and nights, etc., one may receive the upavāsa precepts.
What factor acts as an obstacle that prevents those numerous upavāsa restraints from also arising?
There must necessarily be a factor capable of acting as an obstacle, because the Blessed One stated in the sūtras that the *upavāsa* restraint lasts for only one day and night.

Regarding this point, we should investigate together: did the Buddha state in the sūtra that it lasts for one day and night because he correctly perceived that, after one day and night, it is logically impossible for the *upavāsa* restraint to arise?
Is it for the sake of observing those to be converted whose faculties are difficult to discipline that one should, at dawn, bestow the precepts for a single day and night?
On what principle or teaching is such a statement based?
Because there is no contradiction with reason in the arising of these precepts beyond that [period].
The Vaibhāṣikas state as follows:
"No sūtra has ever taught that one can obtain the upavāsa-prātimokṣa-saṃvara apart from the specific duration of a day and night; therefore, our school does not accept this position."
By what limit is non-restraint acquired?
The verse says:
Non-virtuous discipline has no [limit of] day and night, Because it is not received like the virtuous [precepts].
The treatise says:

One obtains non-restraint by making a vow to commit various evil deeds for the duration of one's life, not for a single day and night as is the case with the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts. Why is this so?
This means that it is not like the undertaking of virtuous precepts.

That is to say, there is certainly no such thing as undertaking non-restraint (asamvara) from a teacher by setting a time limit—such as for one day and night—as one does with the one-day precepts (upavāsa), thinking, "I shall definitely undertake non-restraint for this period. This is because such an action is something despised and loathed by the wise.

If that were so, there would likewise be no case of one establishing a limit before a teacher, resolving, "I shall definitely undertake the unwholesome restraint (duḥśīla) until the end of my life," lest one should obtain non-restraint (asaṃvara) for as long as life lasts.

Although there may be no formal commitment before a teacher to perform various evil deeds for the duration of one's life, one obtains non-restraint by generating an intention that is ultimately destructive of the good; it is not the case that one obtains non-restraint from a teacher merely by generating a temporary intention that is destructive of the good. Therefore, non-restraint does not last for a single day and night.

However, regarding the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-saṃvara*), because they are obtained through the power of making a formal commitment in the presence of a teacher, one acquires the restraint even without the intention to abandon evil forever; likewise, if one were to make a formal commitment before a teacher to temporarily undertake non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), one would necessarily acquire it as well.
However, since such a thing has never been observed, we do not establish its existence.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"Just as the virtuous restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*) does not exist as a distinct real entity called 'unmanifest' (*avijñapti*), this non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) likewise should not be a real entity."

The continuous succession of the intention to commit evil and unwholesome acts, which is not relinquished, is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*). Because of this, even if a wholesome mind arises at a later time, one is still said to be "possessed of non-restraint," since that underlying disposition (*āśaya*) has not been abandoned.
Regarding the one-day-and-night *upavāsa* restraint (*samvara*), how should it be received when one wishes to formally undertake it?
The verse says:
The *upavāsa* is observed at dawn; Sitting below the teacher, one receives it from him.
"According to the teaching, it possesses all its branches; it is free from adornments and lasts for a day and night.
The commentary says:
The *upavāsa* restraint is received at dawn; that is to say, one must receive this precept at the time of sunrise, because this precept must last for one full day and night.

Those who have previously made such a formal commitment, saying, "I shall always observe this Upavāsa restraint on the eighth day of the month and other such dates," may receive it even after the fast has ended if there were obstructing circumstances on the morning of that day.

Regarding "taking one's seat": this refers to sitting on a lowly seat before the teacher, either squatting or kneeling with the body bent and palms joined; this applies except in cases of illness, for if one is not respectful, the vow of discipline will not arise.
This must be received from a teacher; it is not permissible to receive it on one's own.
Hereafter, if one encounters conditions for violating the precepts, one will be able to avoid such violations due to a sense of shame before the precept-teacher.

One who receives these precepts should follow the teacher’s instruction by speaking after the teacher; they should neither speak before nor simultaneously with the teacher. Only in this way is the reception of the precepts from the teacher’s instruction perfected; otherwise, both the bestowing and the receiving are incomplete.
One becomes a *upavāsastha* (one who dwells near) only when fully undertaking the eight branches; if any are lacking, the *upavāsa* is not accomplished.
One must necessarily avoid adornments when undertaking this discipline, as they are the basis for arrogance and negligence.
One need not necessarily relinquish one's usual ornaments for the body, because they cannot give rise to excessive pride or negligence as much as new or unusual ones would.
One must receive this discipline for a full day and night, meaning until the first light of dawn when the sun rises.
If one receives [the vows] according to the Dharma in this manner, one merely generates sublime conduct (*sucarita*) but does not attain the formal restraint (*saṃvara*).

Furthermore, if one receives them in this way for the full duration of a day and night, the *upavāsa* restraint—which fully prohibits killing, hunting, sexual misconduct, theft, and harming sentient beings—becomes profoundly effective.
Regarding the term "near-dweller" (*upavāsa*): it means that this discipline dwells near the Arhat, because one trains in accordance with him.
Some say: it dwells near the lifelong precepts (*yāvajjīvika-śīla*).
Such restraint is also called "nurturing" (*āyuṣya*), because it nurtures sentient beings with meager roots of virtue, causing their roots of virtue to gradually increase.
As a verse says:
"By this, one can nurture The virtuous and pure minds of oneself and others."
Therefore, the Bhagavān said that this is called "cultivation.
For what reason must one who undertakes this necessarily possess eight branches?
The verse says:
The factors of the restraint of non-laxity are four, one, and three, respectively,
for the purpose of preventing natural transgressions, loss of mindfulness, and arrogance and negligence.
The commentary says:

Among these eight, the first four are branches of ethical discipline (*śīla*), namely: abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from false speech; for by means of these four, one abandons natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Next, there is one branch of non-negligence (*apramāda*), namely: abstaining from drinking various intoxicants that give rise to negligence.
Although one may have received the śīla, if one drinks various intoxicants, the mind becomes heedless and thus violates the śīla.

Furthermore, there are three types of factors for restraint: abstaining from anointing the body with perfumes and wearing garlands, up to abstaining from eating at improper times; these are because they accord with a mind of renunciation.
For what reason are these three branches fully observed?
If the branches were not complete, one would be unable to avoid the faults of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), forgetfulness, and negligence.

That is to say, the first [branch], from abstaining from killing up to abstaining from false speech, can prevent natural transgressions, because it prevents the various evil karmas such as killing that arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Next, abstaining from drinking alcohol can prevent the loss of mindfulness, because when one drinks alcohol, it causes one to forget what tasks ought to be done and what ought not to be done.

Finally, abstaining from the three types [of sensual pleasures] can prevent arrogance and negligence; for if one indulges in various perfumes, garlands, high and wide beds and seats, or becomes habituated to song and dance, the mind will become puffed up with pride and will soon violate the precepts. By staying far away from these things, the mind remains free from arrogance.

If there is anyone who can observe eating at the proper time, because they are able to restrain constant eating at all times, they will remember their own undertaking of the *upavāsa* vows and will be able to develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward the world.
If one abstains from eating at improper times, both [the fast and its branches] are present; for eating frequently causes the mind to become lax and unrestrained.

Other masters say that abstaining from food at improper times constitutes the essence of the *upavāsa* (fast), while the remaining eight types are called the "branches" (*aṅga*) of the fast, because the acts of anointing with perfumes and wearing garlands, and dancing, singing, and watching performances, are each divided into two.
If one holds such a view, it contradicts the sūtra.
In the sūtra, after stating that one has abstained from eating at improper times, it says:
"This eighth limb, I now follow and train in according to the noble Arhats; I follow their practice and act accordingly."
If that is so, what distinct entity constitutes the essence of the fast (upoṣadha), such that these eight are called "limbs of the fast" (upoṣadhāṅga)?

The term "fast" is designated as a whole, while the individual items are described as its limbs; for it is by means of the particulars that the whole is established, and thus they receive the name of "limbs."
Just as a chariot is [constituted] by its various parts, or an army by its four divisions, or a pentad by its five members, so too should the eight branches of the *upoṣadha* (fasting) be understood.
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain this view:
abstaining from food at improper times is both the *upoṣadha* itself and a branch of the *upoṣadha*; the remaining seven branches are branches of the *upoṣadha* but are not the *upoṣadha* itself.
Just as right view is both the path and a factor of the path, while the remaining seven factors are factors of the path but not the path itself;
so too, the investigation of phenomena (dharma-vicaya) is both awakening and a factor of awakening, while the remaining six factors are factors of awakening but not awakening itself.
The claim that samādhi is both dhyāna and a limb of dhyāna, while the remaining limbs are limbs of dhyāna but not dhyāna itself, is unreasonable;
for it is impossible for right view and so forth to be identical with the limbs of right view and so forth.

If it were claimed that previously arisen right view and so forth serve as the factors for subsequently arisen right view and so forth, then the Noble Path and other states in the first moment would not possess all eight factors and so on.
Is it only a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who can receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*), or can others also receive them?
The verse says:
The one-day precepts may also be received by others; there is no receiving them without having taken the three refuges.
The Treatise says:

For those who have not yet received the lay devotee’s discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), if they take refuge in the Three Jewels for the duration of one day and night and, having recited the three refuges, receive the one-day precepts (*upavāsa-śīla*), they also successfully obtain the discipline of the one-day fast (*upavāsa-saṃvara*).
Apart from this, there is nothing, except for those who do not understand.
As it is said in a sutra:
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

Any layman clad in white who possesses the male organ, takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and with a profound and pure mind utters these sincere words, declaring, "I am an upāsaka; may the Venerable One remember me and protect me with compassion"—to this extent, one is called an upāsaka.
Does one become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) merely by receiving the three refuges?
The masters of foreign lands say that this alone constitutes it.
The masters of the Kaśmīra country say:
"One who is devoid of the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) vows is not a lay practitioner.
If this were so, it would contradict this sūtra.
This is not contradictory, because the precepts have already been undertaken.
At what time are the precepts undertaken?
The verse says:
Regarding the declaration of being a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and the arising of the precepts, it is explained as being like that of the *bhikṣus* and others.
The treatise says:
One gives rise to a profound and pure mind and utters words of sincere truth, declaring: "I am an *upāsaka*; may the Venerable One remember me and protect me with compassion."
At that time, one immediately generates the lay follower (upāsaka) vows;
for by uttering the words "lay follower" and so forth, the vows are generated.
This is because the Sūtra further states:
"From this moment until the end of my life, I renounce taking life"—this is the intent of the sutra's statement.
By omitting "killing" and other specific acts and stating only "renouncing taking life," it indicates that one has already obtained the five precepts at that prior time.

Although he has already obtained the lay devotee's discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), in order to ensure that he understands the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) he ought to observe, [the teacher] further explains the characteristics of the five precepts, such as abstaining from taking life, so that he may recognize and firmly maintain them.

Just as after a bhikṣu has received full ordination, he is instructed in the heavy rules of training so that he may recognize and firmly uphold them, and the same applies to a śrāmaṇera; so it should also be here.
Therefore, a lay follower (upāsaka) must necessarily possess the code of discipline (vinaya).
The verse says:
If all were fully endowed with the restraint, why speak of "one part" and so forth?
This is said in reference to their capacity to maintain it.
The treatise says:
If all lay followers (upāsaka) possess the full restraint (saṃvara), for what reason did the World-Honored One state that there are four types:
first, those who can train in one part; second, those who can train in a small portion; third, those who can train in a large portion; and fourth, those who can train in the complete portion?
This statement is made with reference to the capacity for upholding;
because one is able to uphold what was previously received, the term "one who trains" (*śaikṣa*) is used.
Otherwise, it would have been necessary to say "one who has received a portion," and so forth.
In reality, one is called an upāsaka (lay follower) because they possess the restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to [the prohibitions of] receiving [the precepts] and so forth;
thus, this position you hold contradicts the sūtras.
How does it contradict the sūtras?

This means that no sutra states that the mere utterance of the words "I am a lay follower (*upāsaka*)" and so forth immediately brings about the five precepts; for this sutra does not state the words "from this day forward until the end of my life, I renounce [taking life]."
How does the Sūtra state this?
It is as in the *Mahānāma-sūtra*.
Only in this sūtra is the definition of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) set forth; other sūtras do not do so. Therefore, [your position] contradicts the sūtras.
However, other sūtras state:
"From this time forth until the end of my life, I renounce birth and take refuge in purity. This is a declaration of sincere faith made by taking refuge in the Triple Gem.

Herein it is shown that one who has seen the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya), having attained the purity of realization (avetyaprasāda), pledges their very life as a solemn commitment; this expresses a profound and deep affection for the True Dharma, such that even for the sake of saving their own life, they would never abandon the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.

It is not that those [scriptures] spoke such words as "giving up life" and so forth for the purpose of explaining the characteristics of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); even if they did speak thus, it would not constitute a clear and definitive teaching.
Who could, based on such an obscure text, believe that the five precepts had already been undertaken at a previous time?
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the observance or violation of the precepts, one should not even ask about those who "train in only one part" and so forth, much less provide an answer.

For who, having already understood that the lay devotee's discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) necessarily consists of five branches, would fail to understand that one may observe only one of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) while neglecting the others, up to the point of observing them all, and yet still be called one who trains in "only one part"?
Because they have not yet understood the extent—whether small or great—of the lay practitioner's (upāsaka) vows they receive, one should ask:
"How many kinds of upāsakas are there who are able to train in the precepts?"
He replied:
"There are four types of upāsakas, namely those who train in one part and so forth.
Yet, [the questioner] was still not fully understood.
He asked again: "What is meant by 'being able to train in one part'?

and so forth, at length. [If it were the case that] one could be called a lay follower (*upāsaka*) even if lacking the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*), then it would follow that one could likewise become a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) even if lacking them.
Since that [position] is not established, this case should be understood likewise.
For what reason are the number and measure of the branches of restraint received by those from the upāsaka up to the bhikṣu fixed as they are?
It is because they are so established through the power of the Buddha’s teaching.

If that is so, for what reason do you not accept that it is by the power of the Buddha’s teaching that one is designated as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) despite lacking the vows, rather than being a monk (*bhikṣu*) or the like?
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr do not accept that one can become a lay follower while lacking the vows.
By what means are all these vows, such as those of the lay follower (*upāsaka*), established as inferior, middling, or superior?
The verse says:
"Inferior, middling, and superior follow the mind."
The treatise states:
The prātimokṣa restraints received by the eight classes of practitioners all vary in degree—whether inferior, middling, or superior—in accordance with the state of mind at the time of reception.
By this principle, some arhats may possess only an inferior grade of restraint, whereas some ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) may possess a superior grade.
Is it possible for one to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by merely receiving the lay precepts without receiving the three refuges?
One does not become a lay follower, except in cases where there is ignorance.
For those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, in what exactly do they take refuge?
The verse says:
Taking refuge in that which constitutes the Buddha and the Saṅgha— namely, the two kinds of dharmas of the Aśaikṣas—
and in Nirvāṇa as analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), this is called being fully endowed with the three refuges.
The treatise says:

Taking refuge in the Buddha means taking refuge solely in those dharmas of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣadharma*) that constitute a Buddha. It is because these [dharmas] are preeminent that the body receives the name "Buddha," or because by attaining those dharmas, the Buddha is able to awaken to all things.
What are called the Buddha’s dharmas of one beyond training?
They refer to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, along with their concomitants.
They do not consist of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and so on, because [the latter] are subject to succession, prior and posterior states, and the like.
Is this taking refuge in a single Buddha or in all Buddhas?
In principle, one should say it is taking refuge in all Buddhas, because the characteristics of the path of all Buddhas are without difference.

As for taking refuge in the Saṃgha, this refers to taking refuge generally in all the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute the Saṃgha; it is by attaining these that the Saṃgha is formed as eight types of individuals (*pudgala*), and because it cannot be split.
Does one take refuge in the Saṃgha of a single Buddha or in the Saṃgha of all Buddhas?
In principle, one actually takes refuge in the Saṃgha of all Buddhas, because the characteristics of the path of the Saṃgha are no different across them all.
However, when a sutra states that one should take refuge in the Sangha that will exist in the future, that sutra merely intends to demonstrate the Sangha Jewel as it will be manifest in the future.
As for taking refuge in the Dharma, this refers to taking refuge in Nirvana.

This term "nirvāṇa" reveals only the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the single characteristic of the pacification of afflictions and suffering within the continuums of both oneself and others; therefore, it is universally taken as a refuge.

If the Buddha were merely the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*), how could shedding the blood of the Buddha with a malicious mind constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) by harming only his physical body (*janma-śarīra*)?
The *Vibhāṣā* offers this explanation:
"Because when its basis is destroyed, it is destroyed accordingly.

However, upon examining the original treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), one does not find a statement that the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*) alone are called the Buddha; rather, it simply states that the dharmas of one beyond training are able to constitute a Buddha.
Since this neither excludes the Buddha-body nor includes the physical body, the aforementioned objection cannot apply here.
Were it otherwise, it would follow that when a Buddha or a monk dwells in a conventional state of mind, they would be neither a monk nor a Buddha.
Furthermore, one would have to maintain that the very accomplishment of the bhikṣu-precepts is itself the bhikṣu.
Consequently, anyone wishing to make an offering to a bhikṣu would only be making an offering to the morality (śīla) that constitutes a bhikṣu.
In this way, those who wish to take refuge in the Buddha should likewise take refuge only in the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) that constitute Buddhahood.
Other masters say:
"To take refuge in the Buddha is to take refuge collectively in the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇikadharma) of the Tathāgata."
What dharma constitutes the essence of this taking of refuge?
Its essence is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
What is the meaning of such taking of refuge?
Its meaning is "rescue.
Because by relying upon it, one is able to attain permanent liberation from all suffering.
As the Blessed One said:
Driven by fear, many people take refuge in mountains, parks, groves, solitary trees, and shrines (caityas).
This refuge is not supreme; this refuge is not noble.
One cannot be liberated from all suffering by relying on this refuge alone.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha, and likewise take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
should constantly observe the Four Noble Truths with wisdom.
Knowing suffering, knowing the origin of suffering, knowing the eternal transcendence of all suffering,
and knowing the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the secure state of Nirvana—
this refuge is supreme; this refuge is most venerable.
One must rely upon this refuge to be able to liberate oneself from all sufferings.
Therefore, taking refuge serves as the gateway to all instances where one receives the vows of ethical discipline.
For what reason does the Blessed One establish the abstention from unchaste conduct as the training rule for other types of vows,
yet in the single vow of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) alone, he merely prescribes the abstention from sexual misconduct?
The verse says:
"Wrong conduct is most censurable; it is easy to abandon and to attain non-performance.
The commentary says:

Only sexual misconduct is universally censured by the world because it involves violating the wives of others and so forth, because it leads to rebirth in the miserable realms, and because sexual misconduct is easier to abstain from than non-celibacy.

Because householders are deeply attached to sensual desires, it is difficult for them to maintain abstinence from unchaste conduct; observing that they would be unable to practice such training for a long duration, he did not prohibit them from engaging in unchaste conduct.
Furthermore, all noble ones (ārya) invariably attain the restraint of non-action regarding sexual misconduct, for even those noble ones who have taken rebirth do not engage in it.
This is not the case regarding unchaste conduct; therefore, within the restraint received by a lay follower (upāsaka), only the abstention from sexual misconduct is established as a precept.
A noble one (ārya) who has not yet passed through [further] births does not transgress the lay follower’s (upāsaka) vow.

Regarding the vow of non-action, which means "I shall certainly not do it": for those who first received the lay follower’s vow and subsequently took a wife or concubine—did they obtain the vow with respect to that wife or concubine at the time they originally received the precepts?
In reality, one ought to obtain it;
let it not be that one obtains the Prātimokṣa restraint with respect to only a portion [of the precepts].
If this were so, why would one not be guilty of a transgression of the precepts later on?
The verse says:
The attainment of the discipline is according to one's vow; it is not [attained] universally throughout the continuum.
The commentary says:
One obtains the restraint by means of the original vow one undertakes.
What is this original vow?
It is the abstention from sexual misconduct.

It is not by saying "I shall abstain from unchaste conduct toward all sentient beings" that one obtains the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct toward the mental continuums of all sentient beings; rather, it is through this [general commitment] that one universally obtains the precept of abstaining from sexual misconduct toward the mental continuums of all sentient beings.
Because abstaining from non-celibacy is not a restraint, subsequently taking a wife or concubine does not constitute a violation of the preceding precept.

For what reason is only the abstention from false speech prescribed as the restraint for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), while abstaining from divisive speech and so forth is not? This is also due to the three reasons previously stated.
This is because false speech is the most censurable of all, because it is easy for householders to abstain from, and because all noble ones (ārya) have attained its non-performance.
Furthermore, there is another reason, stated in verse:
"Because by permitting false speech, one would transgress all other precepts."
The treatise says:

When one has transgressed various rules of training and is subjected to interrogation, if one is permitted to speak falsely, one may simply say, "I did not do it. Because of this, there will be many violations of the precepts.
Therefore, the Buddha, wishing to cause them to maintain their vows firmly, prescribed the abstention from false speech within all codes of discipline.
How does this ensure that when they have transgressed a precept, they will immediately confess it themselves and thereby be able to prevent future transgressions?
Furthermore, for what reason is the lay practitioner’s discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) not established by excluding prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
Who says that prohibited offenses are not excluded here?
Which prohibited offenses are excluded?
That is to say, it is the abstention from drinking alcohol.
For what reason, among those various prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), is the abstention from others not prescribed, while only drinking alcohol is forbidden?
The verse says:
Among the prohibitions, one abstains from alcohol alone in order to protect the remaining restraints.
The commentary states:
Those who drink alcohol are for the most part heedless and cannot guard the other restraints; therefore, to protect the remainder, one is made to abstain from drinking alcohol.
How can it be known that drinking alcohol is subsumed under the category of prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
This is because the characteristics of an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are absent herein; for all intrinsic offenses are committed only with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
When one drinks various types of alcohol as a remedy for illness, if one does not do so for the sake of intoxication and confusion, one remains free from a defiled mind.
Is it not the case that one already knows beforehand that alcohol can cause intoxication and confusion, yet deliberately desires to drink? That would indeed be a defiled mind.

However, this is not a defiled mind because one drinks with self-restraint for the purpose of treating an illness; drinking within limits so as not to become intoxicated or confused is therefore not a defiled mind.
The Vinaya-holders state:
"Drinking alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
As that venerable Upāli said:
"How should I provide for the sick?
The World-Honored One replied:
"With the sole exception of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), you may provide whatever is appropriate."
However, there were members of the Śākya clan who were afflicted by illness and required wine; yet the World-Honored One did not permit them to drink it.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Any bhikṣu who declares me to be his teacher must not drink alcohol, not even as little as the amount that might be moistened on the tip of a blade of grass."
Therefore, one should know that drinking alcohol is subsumed under the category of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, because even those who have undergone many births as noble ones (*ārya*) do not commit it— just as they do not kill living beings and so forth—
and because the sūtras state that it is a physical misconduct (*kāya-duścarita*).
The masters of the Abhidharma state that this is not an intrinsic offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); however, they provisionally permit the general prohibitions for the sake of those who are ill.
Furthermore, the prohibition against drinking alcohol at other times is intended to prevent the commission of an intrinsic offense on that account.
Furthermore, because the degree of intoxication is indefinite, the prohibition extends even to drinking as much as might cling to the tip of a blade of grass.
Moreover, all noble ones (ārya) refrain from drinking because the noble ones possess a sense of shame (hrī-apatrāpya), and drinking alcohol causes one to lose right mindfulness (smṛti).
The phrase "not drinking even a small portion" is used because the quantity of alcohol is as undetermined as that of a poisonous drug.
Furthermore, the Sūtra describes it as an evil physical action because alcohol is the basis for all forms of heedlessness.

For this reason, intoxication alone is designated as a "basis for negligence" (*pramāda-sthāna*), whereas the others are not so designated because they are all natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

However, the statement that habitual practice leads to rebirth in the evil destinies (*durgati*) clarifies that drinking alcohol repeatedly enables various unwholesome factors (*akuśala-dharma*) within the body to continue and evolve, can induce karma leading to the evil destinies, or can cause those [unwholesome states] to become increasingly intense.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Surā, maireya, and madya are the bases of negligence.
On what basis is this said?
Fermenting grain to produce wine is called *sura*; fermenting other substances to produce it is called *madirā*.

These two aforementioned liquors, when they are unfermented or already spoiled and cannot cause intoxication, are not termed *madya*; however, when they do cause intoxication, they are termed *madya* liquor.
This name is established again in order to distinguish it from useless states.
However, since betel nut and wild millet can also cause intoxication, one must specify *surā* and *maireya* liquors in order to exclude those.

Although this is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), it causes heedlessness (*pramāda*) and leads to the extensive commission of various evils; therefore, it is taught so that such conduct may be earnestly and strictly prohibited.
Regarding the term "basis of heedlessness," it is because alcohol is the basis upon which heedlessness relies.
