Chapter Four: Analysis of Karma, Part Three. Regarding these three types of restraint—Prātimokṣa, Dhyāna, and Anāsrava—if one obtains one of them, does one also obtain the other two?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
From all [three] and from two manifest [actions], one obtains the restraint of the desire realm;
from the fundamental [path] and at all times, one obtains the dhyāna and the untainted restraints.
The commentary says:
The discipline of the desire realm refers to the prātimokṣa; this is obtained from all fundamental courses of action, as well as from their preliminary applications and subsequent consequences.
"Obtained from two" means it is obtained from two categories: namely, sentient beings and non-sentient things, and natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
"Obtained from the present" means it is obtained from the present aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), not from those of the past or future.
This is because this restraint operates with respect to the locus of sentient beings (sattvādhiṣṭhāna), whereas the past and future are not loci of sentient beings.
If one attains the dhyāna restraint or the untainted (anāsrava) restraint, it should be known that this restraint is acquired solely from the fundamental courses of action (maula-karmapatha).
One does not acquire this restraint even from their preliminary (prayoga) or subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages, much less from prohibited offenses (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya).
Regarding "from all times," this refers to obtaining [the vows] from the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) of the past, present, and future.

Based on these distinctions, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi): there are aggregates, bases, and elements from which one obtains only the Prātimokṣa restraint, and not the other two [types of restraint], and so forth.
The first phrase refers to the preparatory actions (*prayoga*), the subsequent actions (*pṛṣṭha*), and all prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) of the present life.
The second phrase refers to the fundamental paths of action (*mūla-karmapatha*) of the past and future.
The third phrase refers to [the restraint] derived from the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*) of the present.
The fourth phrase refers to [the restraint] derived from the preliminary (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages of the past and future.

Since it is impossible for there to be present paths of unwholesome action at the very moment one attains the wholesome restraint (*śīlasaṃvara*), one should therefore say that it is obtained from the present locus.
It stands to reason that one should speak only of guarding against the future; one certainly should not say that one guards against the past or the present.

Regarding those who have acquired discipline (*saṃvara*) or non-discipline (*asaṃvara*), do they differ in terms of the sentient beings [from whom it is received], the branches [of the precepts], or the causes?
There is indeed a distinction between these concentrations.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Discipline (*saṃvara*) follows from sentient beings; its factors (*aṅga*) and causes (*hetu*) are said to be indeterminate.
Non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) follows from all [sentient beings], but not from their factors or causes.
The commentary says:
Restraint is necessarily obtained from all sentient beings;
there is no principle for it to be obtained from only a few. Regarding the factors and causes, it is said that they are not fixed.
As for the factors being unfixed: some are obtained from all [factors], namely the bhikṣu restraint.

There are those obtained from four factors, namely the remaining types of restraint (*saṃvara*), because only the fundamental paths of action (*mūlakarmapatha*) are designated as "factors of restraint.
Regarding the causes, they are indeterminate: according to some interpretations, they arise from all causes, while according to other interpretations, it is accepted that they arise from only one.
"From all" means arising from non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, because they necessarily arise together.
"Only from one" means arising from a low, middling, or superior state of mind, because these do not arise simultaneously.
Herein, let us first speak in terms of the latter three causes.

There may be a certain class of those abiding in restraint who obtain restraint with respect to all sentient beings, yet not with respect to all branches and not through all causes; that is to say, they receive the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) with a weak, middling, or superior mind.

There may be a certain class of persons abiding in restraint who obtain that restraint with respect to all sentient beings by means of all its branches, but not through all its causes; that is to say, they receive the bhikṣu precepts with a weak, middling, or superior mind.

There is a certain class of persons who abide in restraint and obtain it with respect to all sentient beings, by means of all factors and all causes; that is to say, they receive the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), or a bhikṣu through three mental states.

There is a certain class of persons who abide in restraint and obtain it with respect to all sentient beings; they do so through all causes but not all branches, namely by undertaking the vows of an upāsaka, an upavāsastha, or a śrāmaṇera with three types of motivation.

There is no one who attains restraint without it extending to all sentient beings; for one attains restraint only by abiding in a state of virtuous intentionality toward all sentient beings, otherwise it is not so, because an evil intentionality has not been entirely ceased.
If a person does not establish five kinds of fixed limits, they may then receive the prātimokṣa discipline; namely, the limitations of sentient beings, limbs, places, time, and conditions.
Regarding the restriction of sentient beings, one thinks: "I shall refrain from killing and so forth only toward a certain class of sentient beings.
Regarding the restriction of branches, one thinks: "I shall uphold and not violate only certain branches of the vow."
Regarding "determination by place," it means one reflects: "I shall abide only in a certain type of region and refrain from killing and so forth.
Regarding "determination by time," it means one reflects: "I am able to refrain from killing and so forth only during a period such as one month."
Regarding the "precept with conditions," it means thinking: "I shall abstain from killing and so forth, except under circumstances such as combat.
One who undertakes [the precept] in this way does not obtain the formal restraint (*saṃvara*), but merely obtains a sublime conduct that resembles the restraint.
How can one obtain restraint regarding objects that are beyond one's power?
One obtains restraint by generating a superior intention not to harm the lives of all sentient beings universally.
The Vaibhāṣika masters have made this statement:

"If it were held that the prātimokṣa restraint can only be acquired with respect to objects that are capable [of being harmed], then this restraint would be subject to increase and decrease; for there is the possibility of a shift between the two classes of sentient beings—those who are capable and those who are incapable—and thus the prātimokṣa restraint would incur the fault of being acquired or abandoned independently of the conditions for acquisition and abandonment."
That argument is incorrect.
For example, when grass and the like do not previously exist and then arise, or having arisen they wither away, there is neither increase nor decrease in the restraint (saṃvara) regarding them.
The same principle should apply to the restraint obtained from objects that are either capable or incapable; even when those objects undergo change, it should be understood accordingly.
He says it is not so.
Why is this? Because the nature of sentient beings remains the same before and after, whereas the nature of grass and such things differs before and after.
If that were so, since the nature and category of sentient beings who have already attained parinirvāṇa no longer exist at present, how could there be no decrease in those vows?
Therefore, such an explanation is not logically tenable.
The reason previously stated is logically sound.

If that is so, since a later Buddha does not newly acquire the prātimokṣa discipline with respect to those former Buddhas and the beings they have already liberated who have entered parinirvāṇa, how is it that his śīla does not incur the fault of being diminished compared to theirs?

Because the distinct vows of restraint (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) of all Buddhas are obtained from the presence of all sentient beings, even if those sentient beings were still present at the time of a later Buddha, that later Buddha would likewise obtain the restraint from them; therefore, there is no fault of the later ethical discipline (*śīla*) being diminished compared to the former.
It has already been stated that one obtains these various types of restraint from them;

however, non-restraint is definitely obtained from all sentient beings and from all courses of action, and there is no such thing as non-restraint with respect to a limited number of objects or lacking its constituent parts.
This is certainly not the case, because minds of inferior grade and so forth do not arise simultaneously with all causes.

If a certain class of person were to incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) through an inferior mind, and later, at another time, were to take the life of a sentient being with a superior mind, they would only possess the inferior non-restraint, yet they would also possess the superior manifest action (*vijñapti*) of killing and so forth.
The middle and superior grades should be understood by analogy with this.

In this context, who is called one who lacks restraint (*asaṃvara*)? It refers to those such as sheep-butchers, poultry-butchers, pig-butchers, bird-catchers, fishers, hunters, robbers, executioners, jailers, dragon-binders, dog-cookers, and those who set snares and traps.
The word "etc. indicates those such as kings, judges who administer punishments, and others who investigate and adjudicate crimes, provided they constantly harbor harmful intent.
They are called "those of non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) because that particular class of individuals dwells in a state of non-restraint.

There are those who possess non-restraint (asaṃvara) and are thus called "persons of non-restraint. To speak of a "sheep-slaughterer" means that, for the sake of making a living, they have made a formal commitment to kill sheep throughout their entire life.
It should be understood that the same applies accordingly to others as well.

It is logically consistent that one may obtain all forms of restraint (*saṃvara*) with respect to the entire realm of sentient beings, because such restraint is acquired through a superior intention (*āśaya*) that universally desires to bring about their benefit and happiness. However, how can it be said that those who possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), such as sheep-butchers, acquire non-restraint toward all beings? For such individuals do not harbor any intent to harm even their own closest relatives; indeed, they would not wish to kill them even for the sake of saving their own lives. How, then, could they be said to have acquired non-restraint toward everyone?
If those very kinsmen were to become sheep or the like, one could indeed harbor a harmful intention toward them;
yet, since it is known that these kinsmen are not currently sheep or the like, how could one possibly harbor a harmful intention toward them?
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for a Noble One (ārya) to ever become a sheep or the like; how, then, could he incur non-restraint (asaṃvara) with respect to them?
If one considers the future individuality (ātman) of the sheep and so forth, one incurs non-restraint within one's present continuum with respect to that [future state].
In that case, since sheep and other animals will also have close relatives and their own future selves in a future life, they would certainly harbor no intention to harm them.
Thus, one should regard these future selves; it follows that one does not incur non-restraint with respect to present beings.
Since one possesses the intention to harm when facing the actual bodies of sheep and the like, why does one not incur non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward them?
And since one lacks the intention to harm when facing the actual bodies of one's mother and the like, why does one also incur non-restraint toward them?
In the case of equal matters, one should seek a distinct principle.

Furthermore, how could those who possess non-restraint (asaṃvara), such as sheep-slaughterers, come to possess the full set of branches of non-restraint if they do not take what is not given throughout their entire lives, maintain contentment with their own wives and concubines, and, being mute and unable to speak, are free from the four verbal transgressions?

Because his wholesome *āśaya* (disposition) is universally impaired, although he is mute and does not speak, he expresses through bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) the meaning he intends to say; thus, he fulfills the constituent branches [of the precept].

If this is so, suppose that person had previously received two or three training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and later receives only the [precept against] killing, while not impairing his wholesome *āśaya* regarding the remaining [rules]; how then could he fully give rise to the sevenfold unwholesome discipline (*akuśala-śīla*)?
The Vaibhāṣikas state: "It is absolutely impossible for one who lacks any of the constituent parts, or possesses only a portion of them, to be designated as a person abiding in non-restraint.
The masters of the Sautrāntika school state as follows:
Non-restraint is acquired according to the duration specified, whether the requisites are complete or incomplete, and whether it pertains to the whole or a part;

the same applies to restraint, with the sole exception of the eight precepts. This is because the natures and characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome *śīla* (ethical discipline) are mutually contradictory and thus exclude one another, depending on their respective extent.
It has already been explained how one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) from those [sources].
However, the means by which one acquires non-restraint as well as other types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) have not yet been explained; these shall now be stated.
The verse says:
The various forms of non-restraint are acquired through action and through formal undertaking;
the remaining types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) are acquired through the field, through undertaking, and through intense practice.
The commentary says:
The various forms of non-restraint are acquired through two causes:
first, being born into a family of non-restraint and engaging for the first time in the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of killing and so forth;

second, although born into another family, making an initial vow to undertake acts such as killing—thinking, "I shall perform such work to seek wealth and sustain myself"—at which moment one incurs the evil discipline (*duḥśīla*).
The acquisition of other types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises through three causes.

First, by way of the field (*kṣetra*): that is to say, when one gives a grove or similar gift to such fields of merit, that wholesome non-informative matter arises at the very moment of the initial gift; this is as explained regarding the various meritorious actions based on material things (*upadhi*).
Second, by means of undertaking: that is, making a personal vow such as,
"I shall not eat before prostrating to the Buddha," or establishing a formal restriction.
On fast days, during the fortnight, and throughout the year, one constantly gives food and so forth.
Third, by means of intensive practice, which refers to performing wholesome or unwholesome deeds while giving rise to such earnest mental attention.
From these three causes, other types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arise.
Thus, the acquisition of restraint and so forth has already been explained; however, the relinquishment of restraint and so forth has not yet been discussed and shall now be explained.
First, how is the restraint of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) relinquished?
The verse says:
One relinquishes the restraint of the Pratimokṣa through intentional abandonment, death,
the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs, the severing of the roots of goodness, and the passing of the night.
Some say it is due to committing a grave offense; others say it is due to the disappearance of the Dharma.
The Kashmiris say that committing both is like being burdened by two debts.
The treatise states:
Regarding the term "disciplining" (*vinaya*), it signifies restraint (*saṃvara*), because by means of this, the faculties are brought under control.
With the exception of the one-day fast (*upavāsa*), the remaining seven types of prātimokṣa restraint are abandoned through four conditions:

first, by abandoning the training through the intentional performance of an informative act (*vijñapti-karman*) before a person capable of understanding; second, by discarding the homogeneous life-stream (*nikāya-sabhāga*); third, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*); and fourth, by the severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) that serve as their cause.

The abandonment of the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts occurs through the four aforementioned conditions as well as by the end of the night; therefore, it is said in general that the *prātimokṣa* discipline is abandoned through five conditions.
For what reason are the precepts abandoned by these five conditions?

Because the manifest karma (*vijñapti*) arises in contradiction to the undertaking, because the basis (*āśraya*) is relinquished, because the basis undergoes transformation, because the cause is severed, and because the time limit has expired.
Other schools (*nikāya*) state:
if one commits even one of the four most grave offenses that entail a downfall (*pārājika*), one also relinquishes the vows of a śrāmaṇera or bhikṣu.
Other schools state:

The extinction of the True Dharma also causes one to relinquish the prātimokṣa vows, because at the time of the Dharma’s extinction, all training rules (*śikṣāpada*), boundary demarcations (*sīmābandha*), and ritual acts (*karmavācanā*) come to a halt.
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr state:
"When one commits a root offense, the monastic precepts are not relinquished.

Why is this so? Because it is not the case that the entire code of discipline must be relinquished upon committing a single part [of it], nor is there a severance of *śīla* (ethical conduct) through the commission of other offenses."
Nevertheless, there are two designations: namely, "one who maintains the precepts" and "one who violates the precepts.
This is like a wealthy person who, when owing a debt to another, is called both a "rich man" and a "debtor.

If one confesses and eliminates what has been violated, one is said to possess *śīla* (ethical discipline) and is no longer called a violator of the precepts; this is like having repaid the debt, where one is simply called a rich man.
If that is so, for what reason did the Blessed One say that one who commits the four grave offenses is no longer called a bhikṣu, no longer called a śramaṇa, and is not a son of the Śākyas?
Because he destroys the essence of a bhikṣu, harms the nature of a śramaṇa, and having been ruined and fallen away, he is designated by the name of "defeat" (pārājika).
This was said with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya) regarding the bhikṣu in the ultimate sense (paramārtha).
These words are harsh.
What is meant by "harsh"?

This refers to interpreting the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) spoken by the Blessed One through alternative meanings so as to render them non-definitive (*neyārtha*), thereby providing a basis for those with many afflictions to commit grave offenses.
How can it be known that these words are indeed definitive teachings?
According to the Vinaya’s own explanation, there are four kinds of bhikṣus:
first, the bhikṣu by designation; second, the bhikṣu by self-claim; third, the bhikṣu by begging; and fourth, the bhikṣu by the destruction of delusions.
Regarding the statement "one who is not a bhikṣu" in this context, it refers to one who is not a bhikṣu who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

It is not the case that such a person was previously a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense and later became a non-bhikṣu by committing a grave offense; therefore, it should be understood that this statement is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
However, as for his claim that one need not relinquish the entire code of discipline (*vinaya*) merely by transgressing a single rule, he is effectively challenging the Great Master himself.
For the Great Master has established this analogy: just as a *tāla* tree whose head is severed can never again grow or expand, so it is with the bhikṣus who commit a grave offense (*pārājika*).
What meaning does the Great Master illustrate through this metaphor here?

It intends to show that if one commits even a single fundamental grave offense against the precepts, it will cause the remainder of what has been received to necessarily be unable to grow or expand further.

This means that when one commits various grave offenses, one transgresses the fundamental conduct of a bhikṣu and is associated with extremely intense lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).
Since the roots of their conduct have been severed, it stands to reason that they must universally relinquish all vows of discipline (*saṃvara*).

Furthermore, regarding those who have committed a grave offense (*pārājika*), the Blessed One did not permit them to consume even a single morsel of food from the communal storehouse (*saṃghika-bhoga*) nor to set even one heel upon the grounds of a monastery (*vihāra*); rather, they were expelled from all activities pertaining to the *bhikṣu* community.
The Great Master, relying on that [teaching], spoke these words:

"One should quickly uproot the weeds and tares among the rice; one should quickly cull and discard the rotten beams; one should quickly winnow away the chaff from among the grain; likewise, one should quickly expel from the assembly those who are not truly bhikṣus but merely claim to be bhikṣus."
What is the nature of that bhikṣu, and what are its characteristics? Whatever those characteristics may be, such a nature must necessarily exist.
For the Blessed One has said: "Cunda, you should know that there are four types of śramaṇas; there is no fifth."
Regarding what are called the four types:
first, the śramaṇa who has attained the supreme path; second, the śramaṇa who shows the path; third, the śramaṇa who lives by the path; and fourth, the śramaṇa who defiles the path.
Although this teaching exists, they are called śramaṇas only because they still possess the residual marks of a śramaṇa.
They are like scorched timber, a parrot’s beak made of clay, a dried-up pond, rotten seeds, a fire-wheel, or a dead man.
If one who has committed a grave offense were no longer a bhikṣu, then there would be no such thing as a bhikṣu undergoing the training (śikṣādattaka).
It is not said that all those who commit a grave offense incur a *pārājika* (defeat) offense;
rather, it is definitively stated that only one who incurs a *pārājika* offense is no longer a bhikṣu.

This means that there may be some individuals whose mental continuum is so exceptionally superior that, although they have committed an extremely grave transgression, it does not constitute a *pārājika* offense because they lacked even a single moment of a concealing mind.
The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, has established this rule: if one commits a *pārājika* offense, one is no longer a bhikṣu.
Why not allow such a person to be ordained again and receive the precepts?

It is because their mental continuum has already become possessed by such extreme lack of shame and dread of blame that they lack the power to generate the monastic discipline (*vinaya-saṃvara*), just like a scorched seed.
It is not because one perceives that he possesses the bhikṣu vows that one does not allow him to go forth and receive ordination again.
This is because even if he were to later claim to be a bhikṣu and then abandon what he has learned, it is still not permitted for him to go forth again.
Regarding this lack of purpose, what is the use of seeking relief through suffering?
If such a person still possesses the nature of a bhikṣu, one should personally take refuge in and pay homage to a bhikṣu of such a kind.

At the time when the True Dharma perishes, although all boundary-markings (*sīmā*), ritual acts (*karmavācanā*), and the Vinaya no longer exist, there is no principle for newly acquiring discipline that has not yet been obtained; however, for those who have already acquired it, there is no possibility of its loss.
How are the two types of restraint—the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint—abandoned?
The verse says:
One abandons wholesome dharmas born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja*) Through changing levels (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), falling away (*parihāṇi*), and so forth.
One abandons the noble [states] through attaining a fruit, refining the faculties, or falling away.
The commentary says:
The wholesome dharmas associated with the various dhyāna stages are abandoned due to two conditions:
First, by changing levels (*bhūmi*), which refers to when one is born from a lower level into a higher level, or passes away from a higher level and is reborn into a lower level;
second, by falling back (*parihāṇi*), which refers to when one regresses and loses previously attained qualities of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The word "etc. is used to indicate that one also abandons a portion of the superior roots of goodness when abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); just as all wholesome dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are abandoned through changing planes or through falling away, so it is in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), with the sole exception that there is no formal restraint (*saṃvara*), which differs from the case of the form realm.
Untainted wholesome dharmas are abandoned through three conditions:
first, by the attainment of a fruit, meaning that at the time of attaining a fruit, one abandons the preceding path of application and the path of the fruit;
second, by the refinement of the faculties, meaning that in the stage of refining the faculties, one abandons the dull path by means of attaining a sharp path.
Third, by way of retrogression: that is, at the time of retrogression, one retrogresses from the path of fruition and the superior path of fruition.
Thus has been explained the relinquishing of the various vows.
How, then, are the non-vows relinquished?
The verse says:
One abandons the evil precepts through death, and acquires them through the arising of both sexual organs.
The commentary says:
The various forms of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) are relinquished through three conditions:
first, by death, because the basis [of the body] is relinquished;

second, by the acquisition of restraint—namely, if one receives and attains the *prātimokṣa* restraint, or by obtaining the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), the immoral conduct is then relinquished.

When one attains restraint through the power of causes and conditions, all forms of non-restraint are completely severed; this is because virtuous and non-virtuous precepts are mutually contradictory in nature, and within this context, the force of the virtuous precepts is superior.
Third, it is due to the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs within the continuum, because at that time the basis (the body) has undergone transformation.

For one who abides in non-restraint, even if they occasionally give rise to the volition of non-action and abandon weapons, nets, and so forth, if they do not receive the various virtuous restraints (saṃvara), there is no possibility of discarding their non-restraint (asaṃvara).
For example, although one may avoid the causes and conditions that trigger an illness, if one does not take good medicine, the illness will ultimately be difficult to cure.

When one who lacks restraint (*asaṃvara*) receives the *upavāsa* (near-dwelling) precepts and reaches the end of the night—thereby relinquishing that restraint—is he then considered to have acquired non-restraint, or is he termed one who abides in the intermediate state?
Other masters say:
"One acquires non-restraint because the evil *āśaya* (intent) has not been abandoned forever; it is like when hot iron is set aside: the red color vanishes and the blue color arises.
Other masters say:
If one does not act again, there is no basis for causing that person to obtain non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because non-restraint is acquired based on informative action (*vijñapti*).
How, then, is the intermediate non-informative action (*avijñapti*) abandoned?
The verse says:
The intermediate [non-informative action] is relinquished through the force of undertaking, the completion of the task, or the severance of life and the faculties.
The commentary says:
The intermediate non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is relinquished through six conditions:
first, it is relinquished due to the severance and destruction of the volition of undertaking; that is, one relinquishes what was undertaken, thinking:
"From this time forth, I abandon what I previously undertook."

Second, it is abandoned through the severance of its force; that is to say, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) induced by the force of pure faith or afflictions is abandoned when the limit of those two forces is severed. It is like an arrow that has been shot or a potter’s wheel, which ceases once the force of the bowstring or the hand is exhausted.
Third, it is abandoned through the interruption and destruction of the action performed; that is to say, one no longer performs what was previously undertaken.
Fourth, it is abandoned through the interruption and destruction of the objective basis (*vastu*).
What is this objective basis?
This refers to monasteries, dwellings, bedding and seating, shrines, groves, and such things as nets that one has given away or constructed.
Fifth, there is relinquishment due to the termination and destruction of the life-span, which means that the basis [of the possession] undergoes change.

Sixth, there is relinquishment due to the severance and destruction of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); that is to say, when one initiates the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to sever the roots of goodness, one relinquishes the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) induced by those roots—namely, the non-material wholesome states of the desire realm—as well as all other non-material defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
How is there relinquishment?
The verse says:
The relinquishing of wholesome states of the desire realm that are not of the form realm occurs through the severance of the faculties or by being reborn in a higher realm.
"Through the arising of the path of antidote, one abandons all non-material defilements.
The commentary says:
All non-material wholesome dharmas of the desire realm are abandoned through two conditions.
First, the severance of the roots of goodness; second, rebirth in the higher realms.
All non-material defiled phenomena (*asamrāga-dharma*) of the three realms are abandoned through a single condition: namely, solely by the arising of the path of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
If the path capable of abandoning this category [of afflictions] arises, one shall abandon all the afflictions therein along with their attendants; it cannot be done by any other means.
Regarding the virtuous and non-virtuous restraints (*saṃvara*), which sentient beings possess them?
The verse says:
Regarding unwholesome discipline, humans—excluding those of the North, the two types of eunuchs, and hermaphrodites—are the basis;
Wholesome discipline also exists among the gods; Only humans possess all three types.
Those born in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm possess the dhyāna-restraint;
this includes the untainted restraint, with the exception of the intermediate dhyāna and the state of non-perception.
The commentary says:
Non-restraint exists only among the human realm; however, excluding the northern continent, it exists only in the three continents.
Within those three continents, it further excludes those who are *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, or possess both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
The same applies to restraint (*saṃvara*): excluding those previously excluded among humans, it also exists among the gods; thus, restraint can exist within two realms of rebirth.
Furthermore, by what reason is it known that the mental continuums of *śaṇḍha* and others are not the basis for restraint?
This is because there is authentic evidence within the Sūtras and Vinaya.
As the Sūtra states, the Buddha told Mahānāman:

"Any layman dressed in white who possesses the male organ, having taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, gives rise to a profound and pure mind and utters a sincere and truthful declaration, saying: 'I am an upāsaka; may the World-Honored One remember me and protect me with compassion.'"
This is what is called an upāsaka.
In the Vinaya it is also stated:
"You should exclude persons of this class."
Thus, it is known that restraint does not exist for those types of beings.
Furthermore, by what reasoning do they lack restraint?

It is because the afflictions arising from two bases increase simultaneously within a single continuum; because they lack the capacity for correct discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*); and because they lack an extremely intense sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).
If that is so, why is there no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)?
It is because their minds are not fixed upon evil.
Furthermore, wherever there is virtuous restraint (*saṃvara*), there must also be non-virtuous restraint, for these two are established as being mutually exclusive opposites.
The inhabitants of Uttarakuru lack both meditative absorption and the underlying intention (*āśaya*) to commit evil; therefore, they possess neither virtuous nor non-virtuous precepts.

Furthermore, because intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are absent in the miserable realms (*apāya*), neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exists there either.
Since restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exist only when there is a correspondence with or a contradiction of superior shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*),
and since those such as *śaṇḍha* are like saline wasteland, they cannot produce either virtuous precepts or evil precepts.
In the world, it is commonly observed that saline wasteland cannot produce either fine grain or weeds.

If this is so, why does the Sūtra state that there are egg-born nāgas who, on the eighth day of each half-month, emerge from their palaces to come among humans to seek to receive the eight-limbed upavāsa precepts?
This constitutes the attainment of sublime conduct (*sucarita*), but not the attainment of restraint (*saṃvara*).
Therefore, restraint exists only among humans and devas; however, only humans possess all three types of restraint, namely: the prātimokṣa, the dhyāna, and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints.

If one is born among the gods of the desire realm or in the form realm, it is possible for them to possess the dhyāna restraint; however, this is necessarily absent for those born in the formless realm. The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) also exists in the formless realm.

This means that if one is born among the gods of the desire realm or within the form realm—excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna and the non-conceptual beings (asaṃjñin)—one may possess the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).
For those born in the formless realm, it can only be accomplished as a possession (prāpti), because being formless, it necessarily does not manifest.
Having distinguished the differing natures and characteristics of various karmas, we shall now explain the various karmas designated in the sūtras.
First, the sūtras state that there are three types of karma: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Karma that is peaceful, unpeaceful, or neither Is termed wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The treatise says:

Such are the characteristics of wholesome and other types of karma. That is to say, secure karma is called "wholesome" because it can obtain desirable maturation (*vipāka*) and nirvāṇa, thereby providing relief from all suffering both temporarily and permanently.
Unstable karma is termed "unwholesome" (*akuśala*), because it can bring about an undesirable maturation (*vipāka*) and is thus contrary to the aforementioned nature of stability.
The other two types of karma are not designated as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), because they cannot be defined as either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"There are three kinds of karma: merit, non-merit, and so forth.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable; wholesome karma of the desire realm is called merit, unwholesome is called non-merit, and the wholesome of the upper realms is the imperturbable.
"Because karma and its fruit are immovable within their respective levels.
The treatise states:
"Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called 'merit' (puṇya), because it brings about desirable fruits and benefits sentient beings."
All unwholesome karmas are called "non-meritorious" because they bring about undesirable fruits and harm sentient beings.
The wholesome [karmas] of the two upper realms are called "immovable.
But did not the Blessed One state that the first three meditative concentrations are all "movable"?
The Noble One has taught that this [state] is called "agitated" because it possesses vitarka, vicāra, and so forth.
Since the first three dhyānas possess vitarka, vicāra, and other such afflictions that have not yet subsided, they are designated by the term "agitated.
In the *Āneñja-sūtra*, however, they are called "unshakable" (*āneñja*) based on their capacity to induce unshakable karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
How can a meditative absorption that involves movement result in an immovable maturation?

Although there is movement in the form of calamities within this absorption, the karma does not undergo the same shifting and changing as it does in the desire realm with respect to its fruit; therefore, it is designated by the name "immovable."
This refers to karma within the desire realm that is to be experienced in other destinies or locations; through the power of specific conditions, it is experienced in a different destiny or location.

For instance, there may be karma capable of producing external or internal wealth, status, physical stature, complexion, strength, pleasure, and so forth, which ought to ripen among the gods and other such realms;
however, because it is diverted by the power of specific conditions, this very same karma then ripens among humans and others.

Karma belonging to other levels or locations within the realms of form and formlessness cannot be redirected to produce its results in a different level or location; because the place where the fruit of karma is experienced is fixed, it is designated as "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"There are three kinds of karma: those conducive to pleasant experience, and so forth."
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Those conducive to pleasure, pain, and neither, The wholesome [roots] up to the third dhyāna are conducive to pleasure;
All unwholesome [karma] conforms to suffering; the highest wholesome [karma] conforms to neither [suffering nor pleasure].
It is said that the remaining [wholesome karma] exists even in the lower realms, because it brings about a distinct maturation from the intermediate state.
Furthermore, these three types of karma are so designated because they do not mature sequentially.
There are five types of feeling in total, namely:
by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*), object (*ālambana*), maturation (*vipāka*), and manifestation (*sammukhībhāva*).
The treatise says:
Among all wholesome karmas, those from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna are called "karma conducive to pleasant feeling," because pleasant feelings exist only up to that point.
All unwholesome karmas are called "conducive to painful feeling."
Wholesome karma of the higher stages above the third dhyāna is called "conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling," because above this level there are no longer sensations of pain or pleasure.

It should be understood that these karmas do not produce only the sensation as their fruit, but also produce the requisites for that sensation; here, both the sensation and its requisites are termed "feeling."
Other masters say:

"In the lower stages as well, there exists a third type of karma, that which is neither [wholesome nor unwholesome], because the intermediate meditative state (dhyānāntara) is induced by karma of medium strength.
If it were otherwise, the karma of the intermediate state would lack any maturation (vipāka)."
Alternatively, there would be no karma, because there would be no ripened fruit of suffering or pleasure.
Other masters say:
this karma can induce the ripening of the faculty of pleasure within the fundamental stage.
Some say that this karma does not experience its fruit;
both of these assertions contradict the root treatise.
Therefore, the root treatise asks:
"Is there any karma that produces a mental ripening-feeling (vipāka) but not a bodily one?
It replies:
There is; namely, wholesome karma that is without vitarka.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* asks:
"Is there any case where the three types of karma ripen as maturation neither before nor after one another?"
It is said:

Yes; namely, the matter associated with karma conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya-karma*), the mind and mental factors associated with karma conducive to painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanīya-karma*), and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) associated with karma conducive to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanīya-karma*), and so forth, as explained at length.
From this it is proven that there are also actions conducive to neither [rebirth] in the lower realms; for these three types of action do not ripen simultaneously apart from the desire realm.
Is such action virtuous or non-virtuous?
This [karma] is wholesome but inferior.

If that were so, it would contradict what was previously stated: namely, that karma which is wholesome up to the third dhyāna is "conducive to pleasant feeling," and that which obtains a desirable fruit is called "wholesome karma."
It should be understood that this statement is made on the basis of the majority of cases.
Since the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of this karma and feeling (*vedanā*) are distinct, how can it be said to be "conducive to pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*) and so forth?
Although the essential nature of the karma and that of pleasant feeling are indeed distinct, the karma is able to act as a cause that benefits pleasant feeling.
Alternatively, this karma is experienced as pleasure.
How can that pleasure experience the karma?
For pleasure is the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of this karma.
Alternatively, that pleasure is what is experienced as the result of karma, because by means of it one experiences the maturation (vipāka) of pleasure;
this is just like bath-powder [which produces a pleasant sensation]. It should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, it is called "karma conducive to the experience of pleasure" (sukha-vedanīya-karma).
It should be understood that the same applies to the other two types of karma that accord with experience.
In brief, there are five kinds of karma that accord with experience:
first, karma that accords with experience by its own nature (*svabhāva-vedanīya*), which refers to all feelings (*vedanā*). As stated in the Sūtra:
When experiencing a pleasant feeling, one knows as it truly is that one is experiencing a pleasant feeling; this is explained at length, up to the full exposition.
Second is the "concordant with feeling" (*vedanānukūla*), which refers to all contacts (*sparśa*); as stated in the Sūtra:
"contact conducive to pleasant feeling," and so forth, at length.
Third, the objects of perception that accord with feeling (*ālambana-anukūla-vedanīya*) refers to all objective spheres. As the Sūtra says:
"Having seen a form with the eye, one experiences only the form, not the craving for the form," and so on at length; this is because forms and the other objects are the objects of feeling.
Fourth is experience through maturation (*vipāka-anubhava*), which refers to karma that brings about maturation; as the Sūtra says:
"karma to be experienced in the present life," and so forth, at length.
Fifth is experience through manifestation (*sammukhībhāva-anubhava*), which refers to feeling that is currently active; as the Sūtra states: [and so forth].
"When experiencing a pleasant feeling, the other two feelings cease," and so forth, as explained at length.

It is not that when this pleasant feeling is present there is another feeling capable of experiencing it; rather, it is simply said that one "experiences a pleasant feeling" based on the manifestation of the pleasant feeling itself.
In this context, only the maturation that is concordant with feeling (*vipāka-anubhava-anukūla*) is discussed, because karma is capable of summoning a maturation that is to be felt.
Although karma and feeling differ in their essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is nonetheless designated as "concordant with pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya*) and so forth.
Thus, these three types of karma are either determinate or indeterminate; what are their characteristics?
The verse says:
These are determinate or indeterminate; the determinate are the three [types] such as those to be experienced in the present life.
Some say that karma is of five types; other masters say there are four categories.
The treatise states:

Regarding the "conducive to pleasant experience" and so forth mentioned above, one should know that each has the distinction of being either determinate or indeterminate. Because they are not necessarily experienced, they are designated as "indeterminate."
There are further three types of determinate karma:
first, that to be experienced in the present life; second, that to be experienced in the next birth; and third, that to be experienced in subsequent births.
These three types of determinate karma, together with the aforementioned indeterminate karma, constitute four kinds in total.

Alternatively, there are those who maintain that indeterminate karma (*aniyata-vedanīya-karma*) is further divided into two types—namely, determinate and indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*)—and that when combined with the three types of determinate karma, they constitute five kinds of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), which means that what is performed in this very life ripens in this very life.
Karma to be experienced in the next life refers to that which is created in this life and ripens in the second life.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives refers to that which is created in this life and ripens sequentially from the third life onward.
Other masters say:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life may also ripen in a subsequent birth.
Karma is designated as 'to be experienced in the present life' and so forth based on its initial stage of ripening; this is so that karma of great power does not have a meager result of maturation."
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this point, for there may be cases where the fruit of an action is near rather than superior, or where they are contradictory.
For example, external seeds such as those of the *kāra* plant produce fruit after three or four months, whereas wheat requires six months before it bears fruit.
The Dārṣṭāntikas state that there are four categories of karma:

first, there is karma that is determinate regarding its timing but indeterminate regarding its maturation; this refers to the three types of karma—such as karma to be experienced in the present life—that are not certain to obtain maturation.
Second, there is karma that is determinate regarding its maturation but indeterminate regarding its timing; this refers to indeterminate karma that is certain to obtain maturation.
Third, there is karma that is determinate regarding both; this refers to karma such as that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), which is certain to obtain maturation.
Fourth, there are actions that are indeterminate with respect to both [time and ripening], meaning they are indeterminate actions (*aniyata-karman*) whose ripening is not fixed.

These [masters] state that all actions collectively constitute eight types: namely, those to be experienced in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*) are either determinate or indeterminate, and so on, up to indeterminate actions which likewise have two types.
Regarding these distinctions of karma explained above, the verse says:
Four wholesome [karmas] may be performed simultaneously; Only three can project a homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
In all realms, four types [of karma] are created; In the hells, wholesome [karma] excludes the present.
In the stage of detachment from passion, ordinary beings do not create karma that leads to rebirth;
noble ones do not create karma that leads to rebirth or subsequent existence, nor do they [create such karma] when falling away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence.
The commentary says:
The three types of karma—those to be experienced in the present life and so forth—are categorized as four by adding those that are determinate and indeterminate.

This is explained as being virtuous; herein, only the determinateness or indeterminateness of the timing is revealed, in order to explain the characteristics of the four types of karma taught in the Sūtras.
Is it possible for four types of karma to be performed simultaneously?
It is possible. How so?
Having dispatched the three messengers, one personally engages in sexual misconduct; these are all completed simultaneously.
How many karmas are able to project a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
Only three are able to project it, excluding karma to be experienced in the present life, because the homogeneous class of the present body was already projected by prior karma.

In which realms (*dhātu*) and destinies (*gati*) can how many types of karma be produced? In all realms and destinies—whether wholesome or unwholesome—one may, as appropriate, produce all four types of karma. This is the general rule; however, if one considers specific prohibitions, within the hells, wholesome karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is excluded because it lacks pleasant fruit; all other types of wholesome karma may be produced there. Unwholesome karma may be produced in all realms and destinies. As for neutral karma, since it is not subject to ripening, it is not produced in any realm or destiny. Furthermore, regarding karma that is to be experienced in future lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), it is excluded from the five untainted states (*anāsrava-dhātu*), as well as from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is excluded from the two classes of beings born of transformation (*upapāduka*), namely the gods of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsakāyika*) and the Mahābrahmā gods, because these beings do not die and are reborn again within the same existence. In the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is excluded from the gods of the Pure Abodes and the Mahābrahmā gods, as well as from those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). In the Formless Realm, it is excluded from those who have attained the absorption of cessation. Regarding karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), it is excluded from the aforementioned states where *aparaparyāyavedanīya* is excluded, as well as from those who have entered the path of non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-mārga*). Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life, it is excluded from the aforementioned states where *upapadyavedanīya* is excluded, as well as from those who have entered the path of non-retrogression. Thus, the various realms and destinies are capable of producing these four types of karma according to their respective conditions. As for the specific case of the hells, wholesome karma that is to be experienced in the present life is excluded because they lack the experience of pleasant results; all other types of karma may be produced there. Thus, the various realms and destinies are capable of producing these four types of karma according to their respective conditions. As for the specific case of the hells, wholesome karma that is to be experienced in the present life is excluded because they lack the experience of pleasant results; all other types of karma may be produced there. Unwholesome karma may be produced in all realms and destinies. Neutral karma, being without ripening, is not produced in any realm or destiny. Furthermore, regarding karma to be experienced in future lives, it is excluded from the five untainted states, as well as from the Peak of Existence and the Formless Realm. Within the Desire Realm, it is excluded from the two classes of transformation-born beings—the gods of the Pure Abodes and the Mahābrahmā gods—because these beings do not die and take rebirth again within that same existence. In the Form Realm, it is excluded from the gods of the Pure Abodes, the Mahābrahmā gods, and those who have attained the absorption of cessation. In the Formless Realm, it is excluded from those who have attained the absorption of cessation. Regarding karma to be experienced in the next life, it is excluded from the states where *aparaparyāyavedanīya* is excluded, as well as from those who have entered the path of non-retrogression. Regarding karma to be experienced in the present life, it is excluded from the states where *upapadyavedanīya* is excluded, as well as from those who have entered the path of non-retrogression. Thus, the various realms and destinies are capable of producing these four types of karma according to their respective conditions. As for the specific case of the hells, wholesome karma that is to be experienced in the present life is excluded because they lack the experience of pleasant results; all other types of karma may be produced there. Unwholesome karma may be produced in all realms and destinies. Neutral karma, being without ripening, is not produced in any realm or destiny. Furthermore, regarding karma to be experienced in future lives, it is excluded from the five untainted states, as well as from the Peak of Existence and the Formless Realm. Within the Desire Realm, it is excluded from the two classes of transformation-born beings—the gods of the Pure Abodes and the Mahābrahmā gods—because these beings do not die and take rebirth again within that same existence. In the Form Realm, it is excluded from the gods of the Pure Abodes, the Mahābrahmā gods, and those who have attained the absorption of cessation. In the Formless Realm, it is excluded from those who have attained the absorption of cessation. Regarding karma to be experienced in the next life, it is excluded from the states where *apar
Those of non-retrogressive nature are called "firm" (*sthira*); they reside in the stage free from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*).
If they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they can perform the other three types of karma, excluding that which is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*).
Noble ones (*ārya*) exclude both that which is to be experienced in the next life and that which is to be experienced in subsequent lives, and can thus perform the remaining two types.

Ordinary beings do not fall back; there is no case where one is born in a higher realm and subsequently returns to be born in a lower one. This is because a noble being who has not fallen back can never again be born in any of the lower stages.

In whatever stage one is born, it is possible to create karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*); as for creating indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*), there is no restriction whatsoever in any location.

However, when noble ones have already attained detachment from the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), even though they may experience a fall from that state, they do not create karma conducive to rebirth or subsequent existence; for one who falls from those states necessarily falls from the fruit [of their attainment].
Those who have fallen from a fruit certainly do not die [in that state], as will be explained later.
Does one also create karma while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
One does indeed create it.
How so? The verse says:
In the intermediate state of the desire realm, one can create twenty-two kinds of karma.
All are subsumed under karma to be experienced in the present life, because their type and homogeneous class are one.
The treatise says:
Within the desire realm, while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one may be capable of creating twenty-two types of karma.
This refers to five stages each for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the period within the womb, and the period after birth from the womb.
The five stages within the womb are:
first, the kalala; second, the arbuda; third, the peśī; fourth, the ghana; and fifth, the praśākhā.
The five stages outside the womb are:
first, infancy; second, childhood; third, youth; fourth, middle age; and fifth, old age.
While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is able to create intermediate-state karma as well as determinate or indeterminate karma pertaining to all stages up to old age.

It should be understood that the eleven types of determinate karma (*niyata-karman*) created within this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are all subsumed under "retribution in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no distinction in the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
That is to say, the stage of the intermediate state and the ten stages of its own kind are drawn by a single karma within one single homogeneous class (*eka-sabhāgatā*).

For this reason, karma conducive to existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not mentioned separately, as it is already subsumed under karma conducive to rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and so forth.
What are the characteristics of karma that is definitely experienced (*niyata-vedanīya*)?
The verse says:
Karma committed through intense affliction or a pure mind, that which is performed habitually,
that which arises toward a field of merit, and the karma of harming one’s parents— these are determinate.
The commentary says:
If an action is performed through intense affliction, or with a pure mind, or is habitually practiced, or is directed toward a field of superior merit—
where a "field of superior merit" refers to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, or to an eminent person (pudgala) who has attained superior fruits or superior meditative absorptions.

In this field, even if there is no intense affliction, no pure mind, and it is not a habitual action, any karma produced—whether wholesome or unwholesome—or any act of harm committed toward one's parents according to the degree of their relative importance, all such cases are subsumed under determinate karma; others are not determinately experienced.
What are the characteristics of karma that bears fruit in the present life?
The verse says:
Due to the excellence of the field and the intention, And because it necessarily brings about a specific maturation, [it is karma of the present life].
One attains permanent liberation from the karma of the stage [of rebirth], and it is certain to bring about results in the present life.
The commentary states:
Regarding the excellence of the field, it is heard that there was a bhikṣu who spoke as a woman among the Saṃgha, and he was transformed into a woman in his present life.
There are many such accounts of this kind.
Regarding those with superior intention: it is heard that there was a eunuch who saved various oxen from being castrated; as a result, he transformed into a man in his present life.
There are many such accounts of these traditions.
Or, one who is born in a particular stage and has permanently abandoned the defilements of that stage—

regarding the various wholesome and unwholesome karmas within that stage whose ripening is certain but whose timing is indeterminate— this karma will necessarily bring about a fruit in the present life.

If there is karma to be experienced in other states that is fixed as necessarily to be experienced (*niyatavedanīya*), it is certain that there is no possibility of permanently abandoning defilements; thus, its ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) must necessarily be experienced in those other states.
If, however, even regarding the ripening fruit it is not fixed, then because one has permanently abandoned defilements, the ripening fruit will not be experienced.
In what kind of field does the karma produced necessarily result in immediate retribution?
The verse says:
In the Sangha headed by the Buddha, and in those who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation or the state of non-contention.
"Through loving-kindness, vision, and the path of cultivation, one receives the results of actions that cause harm or benefit immediately.
The commentary states:
Within such fields of merit, wholesome or unwholesome karma performed will certainly result in immediate retribution.
The field of merit refers to the Saṃgha, headed by the Buddha.
In terms of the distinctions among individuals (*pudgala*), there are five types:

first, one who has emerged from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This is because within this absorption the mind attains tranquility, and the stillness of this absorption resembles *nirvāṇa*.
When first emerging from this meditative absorption, it is as if one who has entered nirvana returns once more.

Second is emerging from the "Absorption of Non-contention" (araṇā), which means that within this absorption there is an object consisting of immeasurable sentient beings, accompanied by a superior intention to benefit them.
When emerging from this meditative absorption, the continuity of one's physical existence proceeds as it has been permeated by immeasurable and most excellent meritorious qualities.

Third, one emerges from the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); that is to say, within this absorption, there is a mental orientation toward immeasurable sentient beings as its object, accompanied by a superior intention for their well-being.
When emerging from this meditative absorption, the continuum of the physical body proceeds, permeated by immeasurable and most excellent meritorious qualities.

Fourth, [emerging] from the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): that is to say, within this path, one eternally abandons all afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and attains a superior transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); when emerging from this, a purified bodily continuum arises.

Fifth, emerging from the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): this refers to the attainment of a superior transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) through the permanent abandonment of all afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation within this path; when emerging from this state, a purified continuum of the body arises.
Therefore, these five are called "fields of merit.
If one performs an action—whether harmful or beneficial—toward them, that karma will inevitably bring about its immediate fruit.

When one emerges from other meditative absorptions or other fruits of the path, because the previously cultivated concentration was not particularly sublime and the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have not been completely exhausted, that mental continuum is not a superior field of merit.

Among the fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*), feeling (*vedanā*) is the most preeminent; this should now be investigated: among the various types of karma, is there any that brings about only the maturation of mental feeling, or perhaps brings about bodily feeling but not mental feeling?
There are also [cases where it is]. How so?
The verse says:
It is maintained that wholesome karma devoid of vitarka produces only mental sensation, while unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation;
such is the distinction between these karmas of sensation.
The treatise says:

Wholesome karma devoid of vitarka refers to all wholesome karma from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Among these, it should be understood that only that which brings about the ripening of feeling (*vedanā-vipāka*) results in mental feeling (*citta-vedanā*) and not bodily feeling (*kāya-vedanā*), because bodily feeling necessarily coexists with vitarka and vicāra.

Regarding those unwholesome karmas that can be experienced, it should be understood that they produce only bodily sensation and not mental sensation; for unwholesome causes have painful sensation as their fruit, whereas mental sensation is associated with the mind.
That which is definitively termed "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), as has already been explained above.
Regarding the derangement of the minds of sentient beings, by which consciousness, cause, or object does it arise?
The verse says:
Mental derangement occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), arising from the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, as well as from fear, injury, adverse conditions, and grief;
it exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).
The commentary states:

The derangement of the minds of sentient beings occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); if it were in the five sensory consciousnesses, there would necessarily be no such derangement, because the group of five consciousnesses is devoid of discrimination (*avikalpaka*).
There are five causes by which the minds of sentient beings become deranged: First, it arises from the maturation (*vipāka*) of the karma of sentient beings.

This refers to cases where one uses drugs or incantations to cause others' minds to become deranged; or causes others to drink what they do not desire, such as poison or alcohol; or manifests a terrifying presence to frighten birds, beasts, and the like; or releases fierce fires to burn mountains and marshes; or constructs pits and traps to cause living beings to fall; or performs other activities that cause others to lose mindfulness. Due to these karmic causes, one experiences a distinct ripening in a future life that results in the derangement of the mind.

Second, due to terror: this refers to when non-humans and the like manifest terrifying forms and come to oppress one; upon seeing them, sentient beings consequently become insane. Third, due to injury:
this refers to when, because of one's actions, one vexes non-humans and the like; out of their anger, they injure one's limbs and joints, thereby resulting in insanity.

Fourth, due to disharmony: this refers to mental derangement caused by the mutual conflict of the internal elements of wind, heat, and phlegm, resulting from the imbalance of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Fifth, due to grief: this refers to the mind becoming deranged because it is enveloped by the poison of sorrow following the loss of loved ones and such; as in the case of Vāsava and others.

If mental derangement occurs only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and you further grant that this mental derangement arises as the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, how can it be that mental feeling (*cittavedanā*) is not itself a maturation?
We do not say that mental derangement is the maturation of karma; rather, we say it is produced by the maturation of karma.

This means that due to the cause of unwholesome karma, one experiences the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of an uneven maturation (*vipāka*); based on these great elements, the mind loses mindfulness, and is therefore said to be "deranged" (*unmāda*).

Regarding this mental derangement in relation to mental distraction (*vikṣepa*), one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): namely, there is mental derangement that is not mental distraction, and so forth, as explained at length.
Those who are deranged but not disordered refer to those who are deranged with an undefiled mind.
Those who are disordered but not deranged refer to those who are not deranged with various defiled minds.
Those who are both deranged and disordered refer to those who are deranged with various defiled minds.
"Non-deranged" refers to those who are not insane and whose minds are undefiled.
With the exception of those in Uttarakuru, all other sentient beings within the desire realm may experience mental derangement.

This means that even among the gods of the desire realm there are those whose minds are still deranged; how much more so for humans or those in the miserable destinies who could be free from mental derangement?
In the hells, the mind is constantly deranged because they are oppressed by manifold sufferings.

Specifically, the inhabitants of the various hells are perpetually afflicted by diverse types of instruments of torture that wound their vital points (*marmāṇi*) with such intensity and acuity that they are difficult to endure. Being overwhelmed by such painful sensations, they do not even recognize themselves, let alone discern right from wrong.
Therefore, there are accounts handed down in the world concerning the lamentations of resentment and the frantic, screaming cries within the hells.

Among the noble ones of the desire realm, with the exception of the Buddhas, mental derangement may occur when the primary elements (mahābhūta) are disturbed, though it does not arise from karmic maturation (vipāka).
If there is determinate karma, one must necessarily experience its results first before attaining the state of an Arya.
If it is indeterminate karma, because one has attained the state of an Arya, it can be rendered fruitless and devoid of terror, for one has transcended the five fears.

Furthermore, there is no harm, because for all noble ones (*ārya*) there are no matters of resentment or aversion toward non-human beings (*amanuṣya*), and because they are free from sorrow as they have realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Moreover, it is said in a sutra:
"Karma is of three kinds, namely: crookedness (*vaṅka*), corruption (*doṣa*), and turbidity (*kaṣāya*)."
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The karmas of crookedness, corruption, and turbidity are said to arise from deceit, hatred, and greed.
The treatise says:
Each of the three—body, speech, and mind—has three types, namely, crookedness (*vaṅka*), corruption (*doṣa*), and turbidity (*kaṣāya*).
It should be understood that these arise respectively from deceit (*śāṭhya*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and greed (*lobha*).
That is to say, bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from guile (*śāṭhya*) is called "crooked karma" (*kuṭila-karman*), because it belongs to the category of crookedness.
Bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from hatred (*dveṣa*) is called "corrupt karma" (*daurjanya-karman*), because it belongs to the category of corruption.
If bodily, vocal, and mental karma arise based on greed, they are called turbid karma, because they belong to the category of the turbidity of greed.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Fifteen; *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen.

Chapter Four: Analysis of Karma, Part Four. Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras that there are four kinds of karma: namely, there is karma that is black with black maturation; or again, there is karma that is white with white maturation; or again, there is karma that is black-and-white with black-and-white maturation; or again, there is karma that is neither black nor white, which has no maturation and serves to exhaust all karmas.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Based on the distinctions between the black-and-black and so forth, four types of karma are taught.
Unwholesome [karma], the wholesome of the desire realm, That which can exhaust those [defilements]— the outflow-free (anāsrava)—
Should be known as black, white, both, and neither, respectively. The commentary says:

The Buddha, based on the differences in the nature and categories of karmic results and the distinction between that which is to be remedied and its remedy, taught the four types of karma, such as "black-black" and so forth.
All unwholesome karma is exclusively termed "black" because its nature is defiled; its maturation is also black because it is disagreeable.
Wholesome karma of the form realm is exclusively termed "white" because it is unmixed with evil; its maturation is also white because it is agreeable.
Why is wholesome karma of the formless realm not mentioned?

It is traditionally taught that where there are two types of maturation—namely, existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*) and intermediate existence (*antarābhava*)—and where the three types of karma—namely, those of body, speech, and mind—are present, it is said to be none other than this.
However, in certain places within the Sūtras it is also stated:
"Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called 'black-and-white' because it is interspersed with evil; its maturation is also black-and-white because it is interspersed with undesirable results."
These designations of "black" and "white" are established based on the continuity [of the stream of consciousness], not according to their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why is this so?
Because there is no single karma or single maturation that is both black and white, as these are mutually contradictory.
Is it not the case that because the fruits of unwholesome karma and the fruits of wholesome karma are intermingled, they should also be called "white-black"?

It is not necessarily the case that the fruits of unwholesome karma must be intermingled with the fruits of wholesome karma; however, the fruits of wholesome karma in the desire realm must certainly be intermingled with the fruits of unwholesome karma, because in the desire realm, unwholesomeness outweighs wholesomeness.

All untainted (*anāsrava*) karma that can eternally sever and exhaust the three preceding types of karma is called "non-black," because it is non-defiled; it is also called "non-white," because it cannot produce white karmic fruition (*vipāka*).
This is not a literal statement of "white," but a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*), for in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"All dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are purely wholesome, purely white, and entirely without fault."
This treatise also states:
"What are the white dharmas?

They are all wholesome dharmas and those that are non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) and without maturation (avipāka), because they do not fall within the realms (dhātu) and because their nature is contrary to the phenomena of saṃsāra."
Do all untainted (anāsrava) karmas enable one to exhaust the previous three types of karma? No.
Why is this so?
The verse says:
The four dharmakṣāntis and the detachment from desire, Accompanying the first eight paths of immediate succession,
These twelve untainted volitions Exhaust only the purely black karma.

The ninth thought-moment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-citta*) in the four dhyānas that are free from desire exhausts both the mixed and the purely black [karma], while the four [moments] cause the purely white [karma] to be exhausted.
The commentary says:

Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are twelve volitions (*cetanā*) that arise simultaneously with the four forbearances of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the first eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) during the stage of abandoning the defilements of desire; these exhaust only the purely black karma. Furthermore, the single untainted volition that arises simultaneously with the ninth uninterrupted path during the abandonment of the defilements of the desire realm causes both the black-and-white and the purely black karma to be exhausted; this is because at this time, one completely severs the wholesome karma of the desire realm as well as the ninth category of unwholesome karma.

Regarding the abandonment of the defilements of each level within the four dhyānas, the untainted volition (anāsrava-cetanā) concomitant with the ninth path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) is what exclusively causes pure white karma to be exhausted.
For what reason can only the final path, and no others, sever the tainted wholesome dharmas (sāsrava-kuśala-dharma) of the various levels?
Because wholesome dharmas are not abandoned by their own nature, for once they have been abandoned, there is the possibility of their manifesting again.

Nevertheless, it is said that those wholesome dharmas are abandoned only when the afflictions directed toward them are exhausted; this is because at that time, the wholesome dharmas attain dissociation from those afflictions.

Consequently, as long as even a single grade of those afflictions remains as an object of perception, the meaning of "abandonment" is not established, because at that time wholesome dharmas have not yet been dissociated from their fetters.
The verse says:
Some say that [karma] experienced in hell, and other desire-realm karma, are black and mixed.
Some say that the desire to see [the truth] is extinguished, while other desires and actions are both black.
The commentary says:
Other masters state:
Karma that leads to experience in the hells and karma that leads to other experiences within the desire realm are, respectively, called "purely black" and "mixed" karma.
This means that since the maturation in the hells is induced solely by unwholesome karma, the karma leading to that experience is termed "purely black."

With the exception of the hells, all other maturations (*vipāka*) within the desire realm are produced by both wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore, karma that leads to such experiences is called "black-and-white" karma.
Other masters state:
