Is it not the case that in both of these [cases], there is no actual question, but only a request for an explanation; and likewise, there is no formal answer, but only a counter-interrogation asking, "Which one do you wish to speak of? How, then, can these two constitute a question and an answer?
If someone were to request, "Please teach me the Path," would this not be asking about the Path?
Since one answers such a question by means of a counter-question (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa*), would this not be an answer concerning the Path?
If that is so, both cases should be considered answers by way of counter-questions.
It is not so; for there is a distinction between the directness and the deviousness of the question, and because the recorded responses include both those with differentiation and those without.
As for the response of setting aside (*sthāpanīya*), it is as if someone were to ask:
"Is the world finite, or is it infinite? and so forth.
This should be set aside and not explained.
Now, based on the sūtras, I shall distinguish the characteristics of questions and their responses.
As it is said in a sūtra of the Mahāsāṃghika school:
"Monks, you should know that there are four ways of answering questions.
What are these four? They are:
there are questions that should be answered categorically, and so on, up to questions that should simply be set aside."
What kind of question should be answered categorically?
It refers to a question such as:
"Are all conditioned phenomena impermanent?"
This question is called one that should be answered categorically (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇīya*).
What kind of question should be answered analytically (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*)?
It refers to if someone asks:
When one has intentionally performed an action, what kind of fruit does one experience?
This question is called "to be answered by way of analysis" (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇīya*).
What is a question that should be answered by counter-interrogation (*paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇīya*)?
That is to say, if one should ask:
"Is the conception of a person the same as the self, or is it different?
one should respond by counter-interrogating:
Based on what kind of self (*ātman*) do you ask such a question?
If you say it is based on the coarse self (*audārika-ātman*), then one should answer that [the self] is different from perception (*saṃjñā*).
This question is called one that should be answered by counter-interrogation (*paripṛcchya-vyākaraṇīya*).
What kind of question should be set aside?
It refers to such questions as:
"Is the world eternal, non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal?"
Is the world finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite?
Does the Tathāgata exist after death, does he not exist, does he both exist and not exist, or does he neither exist nor not exist?
"Is the life-principle identical to the body, or is the life-principle different from the body?
This question is termed "one that should be set aside.

The Fifth Chapter on the Analysis of Latent Dispositions (Anuśaya), Part Two: When latent dispositions increase in accordance with a particular object among the classes of sentient beings, it is said that they are "bound" to that object.
It should now be explained: which latent dispositions—past, present, or future—are able to bind which objects?
The verse says: If,
regarding this object, greed, hatred, and pride have not been abandoned,
and have already arisen in the past or present, they will arise in the future as universal mental factors.
Five [types of afflictions] can arise from their own time; those that do not arise are also pervasive.
The remaining ones, whether past or future, are pervasive; those in the present bind when they are currently taking an object.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, there are generally two types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):
first, those with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely greed, hatred, and pride;
second, those with common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), namely views, doubt, and delusion.
Although objects (*vastu*) are manifold, this discourse concerns that which is bound.
As appropriate, that which has not yet been abandoned continues its influence into subsequent categories.
If, within this object, there is greed, hatred, or pride that has already arisen in the past and remains unabandoned, and which has already arisen in the present, it can bind this object.
Because greed, hatred, and pride are afflictions characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*), they do not necessarily arise in all sentient beings at all times.

However, if greed, hatred, and pride associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exist in the future, these three will pervade the three periods of time and remain capable of binding one until they are abandoned.
Regarding future greed and hatred associated with the five consciousnesses: if they have not been abandoned and are capable of arising, they bind only the future life.
If they have not been abandoned but are incapable of arising, they can also bind all three periods of time.
All remaining views, doubt, and ignorance that have not been abandoned bind one throughout the three periods of time—past, present, and future.
This is because these three types are universal afflictions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇakleśa*), as they universally bind all sentient beings alike.
If, in the present time, when correctly taking an object as its condition, [the mind] is able to bind itself to that thing according to what is appropriate,
one must first determine whether past and future things exist substantially or not before one can speak of such binding.
If it were truly existent, then because all conditioned phenomena would exist at all times, they should be described as permanent;
if it were truly non-existent, how could one speak of there being that which binds and that which is bound, as well as liberation from bondage?

The Vaibhāṣika masters definitively establish that [the conditioned factors] exist substantially; yet, they do not designate those conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as permanent, because they are conjoined with the various characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
To further clarify and illuminate this established position, the fundamental tenet should be briefly stated to reveal its underlying principle.
The verse says:

The existence of the three times is established by scripture, By the existence of objects and results, And by the statement that "the three times exist"; Therefore, they are accepted as the Sarvāstivādins.
The treatise says:
The three time periods truly exist. Why is this so?
This is because the Blessed One has stated so in the sūtras.
Specifically, the Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if past form did not exist, the assembly of learned noble disciples would not cultivate the diligent abandonment of past form."
Because past form exists, the learned noble disciples should diligently cultivate disenchantment and relinquishment toward past form.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciples would not need to diligently sever their longing and pursuit for future form.
Because future form exists, the learned noble disciples should diligently abandon longing for future form.
Furthermore, because consciousness arises only when two conditions are present—as stated in the Sūtra:
"Consciousness arises dependent on two conditions."
What are these two?
They are the eye and visible forms;
explained in detail, this extends up to the mind and mental phenomena.
If the past and future were not substantially existent, the consciousness that takes them as objects would lack two of its necessary conditions.

Having already established the existence of the past and future based on the authoritative scriptures, one should now establish their existence through correct reasoning, because whenever consciousness arises, there must necessarily be an object.
This means that consciousness arises only when there is an object; it does not arise in their absence, for this principle is certain.

If the substantial entity of objects in the past and future were truly non-existent, then there would have to be consciousness without an objective referent; since the referent would be absent, the consciousness itself would also necessarily be non-existent.

Furthermore, because past karma possesses its future fruit: if the past entity were truly non-existent, then the future fruits of both wholesome and unwholesome karma would not exist; for at the time the fruit arises, no present cause is present.
Based on this teaching and reasoning, the Vaibhāṣikas definitively establish that the two periods of the past and future exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*).

If one considers oneself a proponent of the Sarvāstivāda school, one must certainly admit that the past and future exist substantially; for since they assert that all three time periods exist determinately as substantial entities, one is recognized as a Sarvāstivādin.
That is to say, if someone asserts that the three time periods truly exist, only then may they be accepted as belonging to the Sarvāstivāda school.

If a person asserts only the existence of the present period and those past actions that have not yet yielded their fruit, while asserting the non-existence of the future period and those past actions that have already yielded their fruit, such a person may be accepted as belonging to the Vibhajyavāda school, and is not included within this school.
Now, how many distinctions are there within this school?
Whose presentation of time is the most excellent and reliable?
The verse says:
Within this, there are four types: [differences] based on category, characteristic, state, and relative dependence;
the third, which establishes the time periods (*adhvan*) by way of activity (*kāritra*), is the most excellent.
The treatise says:
The Venerable Dharmatrāta speaks thus:
"The distinction between the three time periods arises from a difference in mode (*bhāva*), not from a difference in substance (*dravya*).
He maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, they differ due to their distinct modes, but not due to any alteration in their essential nature.
It is like when a golden vessel is broken to be made into another object: although the shape differs, the substance remains unchanged.
Or, it is like when milk transforms into curd: it relinquishes its taste and potency, but does not relinquish its visible color.

When these phenomena proceed through time, moving from the future to the present and from the present into the past, they merely relinquish and acquire their "categories" (jāti), but do not relinquish or acquire their essential substance (svabhāva).
The Venerable Ghosaka stated as follows:
"The distinction between the three time periods arises from the difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

He [Ghosaka] maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, a past phenomenon is currently conjoined with its past characteristic, yet it is not said to be separated from its present and future characteristics."
The future is currently conjoined with the future aspect, yet it is not said to be separated from the aspects of the past and present.
The present is currently conjoined with the present aspect, yet it is not said to be separated from the aspects of the past and future.
Just as when a man is currently attached to one wife, he is not said to be detached from his other concubines;
so too did the Venerable Vasumitra state:
"Due to the difference in states, there is a distinction between the three time periods."

He [the opponent] maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods (*adhvan*), they receive different designations at each successive stage; while there are distinctions between these stages, there is no difference in their essence (*svabhāva*).
It is like moving a single counting-stick: when placed in the units place it is called "one," in the hundreds place it is called "hundred," and in the thousands place it is called "thousand."
The Venerable Buddhadeva speaks thus:
"The distinctions among the three time periods arise from their mutual dependence.

He maintains that when phenomena proceed through the time periods, they are designated with different names based on their mutual relation to what precedes and follows them, just as a single woman is called 'mother' or 'daughter'."
Among these four types of Sarvāstivādins, the first should be placed among the ranks of the Sāṃkhya heretics, because they maintain that dharmas undergo transformation.
As for the second, their established system involves a confusion of the time periods, since they hold that the characteristics of all three time periods exist within each period.
When a person’s greed is currently active toward their spouse, they possess greed only for other objects;
since greed does not arise in the present [toward those others], in what sense are they the same?
The fourth position establishes [the periods] through mutual dependence; thus, within a single dharma of one time-period, there would have to be all three time-periods.
That is to say, the preceding and succeeding moments of the past should be termed "past" and "future," while the middle is the "present.
The same logic should apply to the future and the present.

Therefore, among these four [theories], the third is the most excellent, because it establishes distinctions among the time periods based on the differences in their functional states; it is by virtue of these differing states that the distinctions between the time periods are established.

He [the opponent] maintains that when the activity (*kāritra*) of phenomena has not yet arisen, they are called "future"; when they possess activity, they are called "present"; and when their activity has ceased, they are called "past"—there is no difference in their essential substance (*svabhāva*).
This has already been fully understood.
You should further explain this: if the essence of the past and future also truly exists, they ought to be called "present"; why then are they designated as "past" and "future"?
Is it not the case that you previously stated these are established based on their functional activity?
If that is so, what function do the currently existing faculties, such as the eye, have when they are subsumed under their respective "homogeneous" (sabhāga) categories?
Could it not be that they are capable of both grasping and giving results?
In that case, since past causes of similar kind (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others are already able to give results, they too should possess a functional activity.
If there were a partial activity, the temporal characteristics [of past, present, and future] would become intermingled.
Having briefly subjected this to logical inquiry, we shall now provide a detailed refutation.
The verse says:
What obstructs its function? How could it be?
If there were no difference between [past and] future times, the world would be destroyed; who then would not have already perished?
This nature of phenomena is profoundly deep.
The treatise says:

It should be explained that if a phenomenon exists eternally in its own essence, it ought to be able to perform its function at all times. By what obstructing force could the function performed by this essential nature sometimes exist and sometimes not?
If it is argued that the various conditions are not in conjunction, this defense is irrational, because [the entity] is admitted to be eternal.
Furthermore, how can this activity be said to belong to the past, future, or present?
How could one further establish another activity within an activity?

If this activity is neither past, future, nor present, yet it is still said that activity exists, then because it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it should be eternally non-deficient; therefore, one should not say that activity has already ceased, nor that a phenomenon which does not yet exist is called "past" or "future."

If one were to grant that the activity (kāritra) is distinct from the essence (svabhāva) of the phenomenon, this fault would indeed follow; however, since there is no such distinction, one should not say that this fault exists.

If that were so, the established definition of the time-periods (adhvan) would be undermined; for if the activity were identical to the essence, then since the essence is eternal, the activity would likewise have to be so.
How can there be times designated as "past" or "future"?
Therefore, the definition of the time periods (*adhvan*) established by them is untenable.
Why is it untenable?
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are designated as "future" when they have not yet arisen; as "present" when they have arisen but not yet ceased; and as "past" when they have already ceased.

They should further explain this: if the substantial entity (*dravya*) of a phenomenon exists in the same way in the past and future as it does in the present, then what is it that has "not yet arisen"?
Who, moreover, has already ceased?
Since the essence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exists eternally in reality, how could it be established that they are "not yet arisen" or "already ceased"?
What was previously lacking?
Because that has not yet come into being, it is called "not yet arisen.
What further deficiency exists later?
Because that has already ceased to exist, it is called "already extinguished."

Therefore, if one does not admit that phenomena are non-existent now and come into existence, or that having existed they return to non-existence, then the doctrine of the three times would fail to be established in every respect.
Yet, as for what they [the Sarvāstivādins] have said, it is because [phenomena] are always conjoined with the various characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
To claim that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent is nothing but empty words, for there is no principle by which they could arise and cease.
To assert that their substance (*svabhāva*) exists eternally while claiming their nature (*dharmatā*) is impermanent—such a statement has never before been heard.
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says:
"The substance of phenomena is admitted to be eternally existent, yet their nature is said to be non-constant;
the nature and the substance are not distinct— this is truly the work of Maheśvara."
Furthermore, regarding their claim that the past and future exist substantially because the Blessed One has so stated, we also maintain that the past and future exist.
That is to say, the past existed as it once was, and the future will exist, because there are causes and fruits.
Based on this meaning, it is said that there is going and coming; however, this does not mean that going and coming exist as real entities in the same way as the present.
Who says they exist as they do in the present world?
If not as in the present world, how then do they exist?
That [past and future] possesses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the two periods of time, past and future.
This, moreover, should be questioned:
if both are existent, how can it be said that they exist because they possess the nature of being past and future?
However, based on the two natures of past and future causes and effects, they do not exist as substantial entities.

The World-Honored One, in order to refute the view that denies cause and effect, spoke of the existence of the past and future based on the sense of "having been" and "about to be," because the term "existence" (asti) can apply to both existent and non-existent phenomena.
As it is said in the world: "There was no lamp before; there will be no lamp after.
Furthermore, as another says:
"The lamp has already been extinguished; it is not I who am extinguishing it now."
The meaning of the statement that there is going and coming should likewise be so.
If it were not so, the nature of the past and future would not be established.
If this is the case, for what reason did the Blessed One, in reference to the ascetic Śīlavat, state that although karma is past, exhausted, ceased, and transformed, it nevertheless exists?
Is it that they do not admit that karma has ever possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet now the World-Honored One speaks of its existence?
It is because he speaks of its existence in a hidden sense, based on the capacity to yield a fruit within the manifest continuum (*saṃtati*) that has been induced by that [karma].
If it were not so, then that past karma would possess the nature of existing in the present; how could the past then be established?
This must logically be the case, for the Bhagavān stated in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*:
When the visual faculty arises, it comes from nowhere; when the visual faculty ceases, nothing is accumulated.
It was originally non-existent and now exists; having existed, it returns to non-existence.
If the past and future visual faculties were substantially real, the Sūtra would not have spoken of "originally non-existent" and so forth.
If it is argued that this statement refers to the present life, such a defense is irrational, because the nature of the present is not distinct from the essence of that eye-faculty.

If one admits that the present was originally non-existent and now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence, then the position that the past and future lack an essential substance for the eye-faculty is already established.
Furthermore, regarding their claim that consciousness arises only when two conditions are present, and thus the entities of the past and future exist substantially:

we should together investigate this. When the mind and mental objects serve as conditions to produce mental consciousness, do the mental objects act as productive conditions for the mind in the same way that the mind acts [for its own subsequent states]?
Does a phenomenon merely function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon acts as a generative condition (*janaka-pratyaya*) according to one's will, how could that phenomenon exist a hundred thousand kalpas into the future?
Alternatively, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) could not serve as a productive condition for consciousness at the present time.
Furthermore, since the nature of *nirvāṇa* is contrary to all arising, it would be unreasonable to establish it as a productive cause.

If a phenomenon can merely function as an object of cognition (*ālambana*), I say that even the past and future are objects of cognition; if they did not exist, how could they constitute objects of cognition?
I say that they exist in the same manner as they constitute objects of cognition.
How is it established as an object-condition (*ālambana*)?
It refers to that which has existed and that which will exist.
When one recollects past forms, sensations, and so forth, one does not clearly perceive them as existing in the present; rather, one merely recollects the aspect of their having existed.

Contemplating the future as having existence is likewise so; that is to say, just as one recollects past forms (rūpa) as having existed based on the characteristics of form previously experienced in the present, so too does one contemplate the future as having existence based on the characteristics of form that will be experienced in the present.
If it existed in the manner that it appears, it would follow that it is present.
If its substance were non-existent, then one must admit the existence of a consciousness that takes a non-existent object as its domain; this principle is self-evident.

If it is argued that past and future atoms exist in a disordered state but are not manifest, this reasoning is also incorrect, because when their characteristics are apprehended, they are not disordered.
Furthermore, if that matter were identical to the present, differing only in that its atoms are dispersed, then the substance of those atomic matters would have to be permanent.
Moreover, matter would consist solely of the aggregation and dispersion of atoms, such that there would ultimately be not even the slightest portion that could be called arising or ceasing.
This follows and honors the doctrines of those who lead a wrong livelihood, while abandoning and turning away from the sūtras spoken by the Sugata.
As a sūtra says:
"At the moment the eye-faculty arises, it comes from nowhere," and so on at length; furthermore, it is not a composite formed by the accumulation of atoms such as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest.
How can one speak of distraction regarding the past and future?

Nevertheless, when one recollects or anticipates feelings and so forth, they appear as having the characteristics of being already arisen or yet to be extinguished, even though they do not exist at that time.

If these [mental objects] possessed a real substance (dravya) just as they appear to exist, they would have to be eternal; if their substance were truly non-existent, then one must still admit the existence of consciousness that takes a non-existent object as its domain, which is logically self-evident.

If that which is entirely non-existent could be an object of cognition (*ālambana*), then the thirteenth base (*āyatana*) should also be an object of cognition; yet there are none who realize the existence of a thirteenth base.
What, then, would be the object of the consciousness that cognizes it?
If you claim that the name itself is the object of cognition, then you must deny that the name exists.
Furthermore, if one cognizes a sound that did not previously exist, what would be the object of that cognizing consciousness?
If it is claimed that one takes that very sound as the object [of cognition] when seeking its absence, then one should produce the sound again.
If it is claimed that the absence of sound abides in the future state, how can something that truly exists in the future be said to be non-existent?
If it is claimed that the past and future lack the present, this too is unreasonable, because their substance is one and the same.
If there were even a slight differentiation in their substance, the principle that "what was originally non-existent now exists" would be established as a matter of course.
Therefore, consciousness universally takes as its objects both what exists and what does not exist.

However, when the Bodhisattva states that it is impossible for him to know or see that which does not exist in the world, his intention is to say that while others, out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), perceive signs of existence even in what does not exist, he perceives things as existing only when they actually exist.
If it were otherwise, then all cognitions would have objects of perception; for what reason, then, could there be doubt or differentiation regarding an object?
This must necessarily be so according to principle.
For the Blessed One has stated elsewhere:
"Welcome, monks!

If you can be my disciples—free from guile, free from deceit, possessing faith and diligence—I shall teach you in the morning so that you may attain victory by evening, and I shall teach you in the evening so that you may attain victory by morning."
Thus, one knows that what exists is existent, what does not exist is non-existent, that which has a superior is surpassed, and that which has no superior is unsurpassed.
Consequently, the argument that past and future exist because consciousness has an object is also an unestablished reason.
Furthermore, as for their claim that the past and future exist because karma has results, this reasoning is also incorrect.

The Sautrāntika masters do not assert that past karma itself can produce a future result; rather, it is the continuity (saṃtati) initiated by prior karma, through its transformation and differentiation, that causes the future result to arise.
This shall be demonstrated in detail in the "Chapter on Self and Other.
If one maintains that the past and future exist substantially, then the essence of the fruit would exist at all times; what, then, would be the efficacy of karma regarding that fruit?
If one claims that there is a capacity to produce, then it follows as a matter of course that the produced effect was originally non-existent and now exists.
If all phenomena existed at all times, what would have the functional capacity to produce what?
Furthermore, this would clearly establish the heterodox arguments favored by the Vātsīputrīya outsiders, who assert:
"That which exists must always exist; that which does not exist must always not exist."
That which does not exist necessarily does not arise; that which exists necessarily does not cease.
If you claim that [the cause] can bring the fruit into the present, how does it bring the fruit into the present?
If you claim that it draws the fruit to another location, then the substance of the drawn fruit must be permanent.
Furthermore, how could formless dharmas be drawn forth?
Moreover, that which is so drawn forth must essentially have been non-existent [prior to its arising].
If one claims that it merely causes the essence to undergo differentiation, then the principle that "what was originally non-existent now exists" is established of itself.
Therefore, when the Sarvāstivādins claim that the past and future exist substantially, their explanation is not a sound one within the Noble Teaching.
If one wishes to explain "all exists" correctly, one should do so in accordance with what is taught in the Sūtras.
How does the Sūtra state this?
As it says in the Saṃyukta Āgama:
"Brahmin, you should know that all that exists consists only of the twelve bases (āyatana) or only of the three periods of time (adhvan)."
One speaks of existence according to how things actually exist.
If the past and future do not exist, how could one speak of there being that which binds and that which is bound, as well as liberation from bondage?
Because the latent dispositions (anuśaya), which are the causes for their arising, exist, it is said that there are afflictions capable of binding in the past and future.
Because those afflictive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) exist, it is said that there are things bound by the past and future.
When these latent tendencies are severed, one obtains the designation of "disentanglement" (*visamyoga*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters speak thus.

Just as the past and future exist in reality, those who cherish the Dharma should understand that there are certain points which cannot be explained away; the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep and beyond the scope of discursive thought. How could one simply deny its existence because it cannot be explained?
From one perspective, this arises and this ceases, meaning that the arising of form and so forth is itself the cessation of form and so forth.
From another perspective, one thing arises and another ceases, meaning that what arises in the future ceases in the present world.
From one perspective, the world itself is called "arising," because at the very moment of arising, it is subsumed within the world.
From another perspective, it is said that the world has arising, because the future world consists of many moments (*kṣaṇa*).
The digression is concluded; we should now investigate: when a given entity (*vastu*) has been abandoned, is it necessarily dissociated from its fetters (*visaṃyukta*)?
Or, if an entity is dissociated from its fetters, has it necessarily been abandoned?
If an entity is dissociated from its fetters, it has necessarily been abandoned; however, there are entities that have been abandoned but are not yet dissociated from their fetters.
What is the nature of abandonment that is not dissociation?
The verse says:
Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering, the remaining universal latent dispositions (anuśaya) [are abandoned].
"And although [the objects] of the preceding category have already been abandoned, one is still bound to them by remaining [defilements].
The treatise says:

For instance, during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, the various entities (*vastu*) to be abandoned through the seeing of suffering have already been abandoned; however, if the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the seeing of origin have not yet been permanently severed, those [dispositions] which can take these [abandoned entities] as their object remain bound to them.
Furthermore, regarding the stage of cultivating the path, by whichever path one arises:

among the nine grades of afflictions, once the preceding grade has been abandoned, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the remaining unabandoned grades that are able to take this as their object still bind one to it.
It should be understood that abandonment is not disjunction.
Regarding which objects how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase:

if one were to answer for each individual object, it would require extensive discourse; therefore, a concise *Vibhāṣā* should be composed, by means of which, though requiring only a small amount of effort, one may cross over the great torrent of questions.
Although phenomena are numerous, they are summarized into sixteen types: namely, the three realms, the five categories, and untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
The number and names of the consciousnesses that take these as objects are likewise the same.
One should simply understand which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses, and what matters it is easy to contemplate, and which latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase therein.
Among these, one should first know which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses.
The verse says:

Those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, if they are bound to the desire realm, are the objects of three types of consciousness from their own realm and one type from the form realm; they are also the objects of untainted consciousness.
The [objects] of form, each with three [levels] below it, and the single pure [level] above, are the objects of consciousness;
the formless [realms] pervade all three realms, each being the object of three types of pure consciousness.
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path both increase the activity of their own respective consciousnesses.
"Among the uncontaminated [dharmas] within the three realms, the latter three are the objects of pure consciousness.
The treatise says:

If one considers the dharmas bound to the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and through cultivation, each is the object of five types of consciousness. That is to say, there are three from its own realm as previously explained, plus one from the form realm—namely, that which is abandoned through cultivation—and the fifth is the uncontaminated [consciousness], for all of these are capable of taking them as objects.

If they belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), these aforementioned dharmas of the three categories are each the objects of eight consciousnesses; that is to say, the three [categories] of its own level and the lower levels are all as previously stated, and one from the higher realm—namely, that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—as well as the eighth [consciousness], the untainted (*anāsrava*), may all take them as objects.

If they are bound to the formless realm, then the aforementioned dharmas of the three categories are each the objects of ten consciousnesses; that is to say, the three categories of each of the three realms are as previously explained, and the tenth, the untainted (anāsrava), is included because all are capable of taking them as objects.

Regarding the dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), it should be understood that each increases the objects of its own respective consciousness. How is this so?

It means that those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) abandoned through the vision of cessation serve as objects for six consciousnesses; five are as previously stated, with the addition of those abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) serve as objects for six consciousnesses; five are as previously stated, with the addition of those abandoned by the path of seeing.
Those abandoned by the path of seeing regarding cessation and the path within the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) serve, as appropriate, as objects for ninety-one consciousnesses.

If untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) serve as objects for ten consciousnesses—namely, the three final categories within each of the three realms (i.e., the consciousnesses abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through cultivation), plus the tenth, the untainted consciousness—they are all capable of taking them as objects.
To summarize the preceding meaning, it is further stated in verse:
Those abandoned through seeing suffering and origin, and those abandoned through cultivation, Bound to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, Should be known,
in their respective order, As having five, eight, and ten consciousnesses as their objects.
Those [dharmas] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path each increase by being the objects of their own respective consciousnesses;
it should be known that untainted dharmas can serve as the objects of ten consciousnesses.

Having thus understood that these sixteen kinds of dharmas are the objects of the sixteen consciousnesses, one should now consider which underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in relation to which object.
If I were to provide a detailed commentary on each individual category, the text would become overly voluminous; therefore, I shall here briefly indicate the general principles.
Now, suppose someone asks:
"Within the objects of bondage, how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase in association with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)?"

One should observe that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) comprises seven types in total: namely, one from the desire realm which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), five categories from the form realm, and the seventh, which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
As previously stated, all untainted phenomena are not subject to the increase of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Among these, as appropriate, the six preceding [categories] are increased by the latent dispositions (anuśaya) to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), the universal (sarvatraga) ones, and all those belonging to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
If it is asked:
"How many kinds of latent dispositions increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) as its object?"

One should observe that this consciousness consists of twelve types in total: namely, four from the desire realm (excluding those abandoned through the vision of the cessation of suffering), five categories from the form realm, two from the formless realm—namely, those abandoned through the vision of the truth of the path and those abandoned through cultivation—and the twelfth, which is untainted; all of these are able to take the faculty of pleasure as their object.

These [defilements] increase according to their respective objects: the four categories of the desire realm, the conditioned objects of the form realm, the two categories of the formless realm, and all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, if it is asked:
"How many kinds of latent dispositions (anuśaya) increase in relation to the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object?

One should observe that this consciousness consists of fourteen types in total; to the previous twelve, two more are added, namely those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin within the formless realm.

Thus, these fourteen consciousnesses can take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object; regarding these, as appropriate, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire and form realms increase as described above, while those of the four categories of the formless realm increase accordingly.
Following this principle, the remaining cases should be analyzed in the same manner.
If a mind is said to be "with latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) because of them, do those dispositions necessarily increase in relation to that mind?

This is not certain. There are cases where they are present: namely, when they are associated with the mind and their objects have not been abandoned; however, when they are associated but have already been abandoned, they do not increase.
Based on this thematic framework, it should be stated as follows.
The verse says:
The mind accompanied by latent dispositions (anuśaya) is of two kinds: namely, that which is defiled and that which is undefiled.
Defiled minds pertain to both; undefiled minds are restricted to [those where] the latent tendencies increase.
The Commentary says:
Minds accompanied by latent tendencies (anuśaya) are generally of two kinds, distinguished as defiled and undefiled minds.

Among these, there are those that are defiled or increase through association; that is to say, when the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have not yet been abandoned, they increase through association and through their objects. Once associated [dispositions] have been abandoned, they no longer increase, yet they are still said to be "possessing latent dispositions" because they remain constantly associated.
If there is no defilement, it is restricted solely to "increase" (anuśaya).

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take this as their object must necessarily not yet have been permanently abandoned; for here, the term "possessing latent dispositions" (sānuśaya) is used strictly in the sense of "increasing."
Regarding the sequence in which the ten types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) arise as described above, which precedes and which follows?
The verse says:
Ignorance, doubt, false view, the view of self-identity, Extreme views, adherence to precepts and rituals, and the grasping at views.
Greed, pride, and hatred arise sequentially, with each preceding one inducing the next.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, regarding the sequential arising of the various afflictions, first, due to ignorance, one lacks understanding of the truths and thus has no desire to contemplate suffering up to the truth of the path.

Due to this lack of understanding, doubt is subsequently induced; that is, upon hearing two conflicting paths, one harbors hesitation as to whether [existence] is suffering or not suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.

From this hesitation, false views are induced; that is, through improper hearing and reflection, one produces a false certainty, denying the existence of the Truth of Suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.

From the negation of the truths, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is induced; that is to say, by denying the principle of suffering within the appropriated aggregates, one resolutely clings to them as being "self.
From this view of a self, the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) is induced; that is to say, based on the clinging to a self, one adheres to the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.

From this extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is induced; that is to say, because one adheres to one side regarding the self, one then reckons this adherence to be capable of purification.

From the clinging to rules and observances, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises; that is to say, having reckoned [the aforementioned] as capable of purification, one necessarily clings to it as being superior.
From this adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), greed (*lobha*) is subsequently induced, because there is a deep affection for one's own views.

Following this greed, pride (*māna*) is subsequently induced, because once one has become deeply attached to one's own views, one relies upon them to give rise to haughtiness and to look down upon others.

Following this pride, anger is subsequently induced; that is to say, having developed deep attachment to and reliance upon one's own views, one cannot endure the arising of views in others that contradict one's own, and thus necessarily feels hatred and aversion.
Other masters say:
Because one gives rise to aversion and resentment during the process of accepting or rejecting one's own views;
for when greed and other afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths arise, they take as their object the views within one's own continuum.
Thus far, the explanation has proceeded according to the sequential arising [of afflictions]. As for those that arise out of sequence, there is no fixed order between the preceding and the following.
By how many causes and conditions do the various afflictions arise?
The verse says:
Because the latent dispositions have not been abandoned, because the corresponding objects appear,
and because improper mental attention arises, it is said that the afflictions possess their full causes and conditions.
The treatise says:
The various afflictions arise due to three causes and conditions.

For instance, when the obsession of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*) is about to arise: because the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*) has not yet been abandoned or fully understood; because an object conducive to sensual desire has appeared before one; and because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward that object arises; by the power of these factors, sensual desire then arises.

These three causes and conditions correspond, in their respective order, to the three powers of the cause (*hetu*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the application (*prayoga*); other arisings of afflictions should be understood as being analogous to this.
That is to say, this has been explained here based on the presence of all causes and conditions; however, there are cases where an affliction arises solely by relying on the power of the object.

In the case of Arhats of the "receding" (parihāṇadharman) faculty and others, the aforementioned proclivities (anuśaya) along with the outbursts (paryavasthāna) are described in the Sūtras as outflows (āsrava),
floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), and graspings (upādāna).
The outflows (āsrava) refer to the three outflows:
first, the outflow of desire (kāmāsrava); second, the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava); and third, the outflow of ignorance (avidyāsrava).
As for the floods (ogha), they refer to the four floods:

The first is the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), the second is the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the third is the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the fourth is the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
The yokes (*yoga*) consist of four yokes, as explained in the case of the floods.
"Grasping" refers to the four types of grasping:
first, grasping at sense-pleasures; second, grasping at views; third, grasping at precepts and observances; and fourth, grasping at the doctrine of self.
What is the essential nature of these outflows and so forth?
The verse says:
The afflictions of the desire realm, together with the envelopments, excluding ignorance, are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*);
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) pertains to the two upper realms and consists solely of afflictions, excluding ignorance.
Being equally indeterminate, inward-directed, and belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (samāpatti), they are combined into one;
because ignorance is the root of all existence (bhava), it is established separately as a single outflow (āsrava).
The same applies to the floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga); however, views (dṛṣṭi) are established separately because of their sharpness.
Because views do not abide in accordance [with the truth], they are not established as independent outflows (*āsrava*).
The yokes (*yoga*) of desire and existence, together with delusion (*moha*), have views divided into two and named "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not established separately because it is not a grasper.
The Treatise says:

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), together with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding delusion (*moha*), totaling forty-one entities, are collectively termed the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*). That is to say, the thirty-one root afflictions bound to the desire realm, together with the ten envelopments.

Excluding delusion (*moha*), the fifty-two entities that constitute the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form and formless realms are collectively termed "outflows" (*āsrava*). Specifically, this refers to twenty-six fundamental afflictions in each of the two higher realms.
Is it not the case that those [defilements] include the two types of envelopments, namely torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)?
The *Prakaraṇapāda* also states this:
"What are the outflows (*sāsrava*)?"

That is to say, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), there are the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) associated with the two realms of form and formlessness.
Why, then, are these not mentioned here?
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say:
Because the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) in those two realms are few and lack autonomy,
for what reason are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of these two realms combined and designated as a single "outflow" (*āsrava*)?

They are combined into one because they share three common characteristics: being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), functioning within the internal sphere, and arising from the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
That which was previously described as the cause of craving (*sarāga-hetu*) is precisely what is meant here by the term "outflowing" (*sāsrava*).
Based on this principle, since the meaning of the fifteen types of ignorance within the three realms has already been established as the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*),
for what reason is this alone separately designated by the name "outflow"?
It is because ignorance is able to serve as the root of all existence (*bhava*).

The nature of the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) is the same as that of the outflows (*āsrava*); however, among them, views (*dṛṣṭi*) are established separately. That is to say, the aforementioned outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is itself the flood of desire and the yoke of desire; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is itself the flood of existence and the yoke of existence.

The extraction of various views to constitute the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*) and the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*) is because they are so intense that they cause one to remain [in saṃsāra] and are thus termed "outflows" (*āsrava*), as will be explained later.

Views do not conform to those [other outflows]; because their nature is so intense, they do not establish independent names among the outflows, but can only be established as outflows when combined with others.

Thus, twenty-nine entities have been shown to constitute the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*): namely, five types each of greed, hatred, and pride; four types of doubt; and ten types of entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
Twenty-eight entities constitute the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*): namely, ten types each of greed and pride, and eight types of doubt.
The thirty-six factors are called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*); that is, twelve views for each of the three realms.
The fifteen factors are called the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*); that is, five types of ignorance for each of the three realms.
One should know that the four yokes (yoga) are identical to the floods (ogha). One should know that the four graspings (upādāna) are identical in substance to the four yokes.
However, desire and the discourse on self each include ignorance; furthermore, views are divided into two, which differ from the aforementioned yokes.

The thirty-four entities consisting of the aforementioned yoke of desire (*kāmayoga*) together with the ignorance of desire (*kāma-avidyā*) are collectively termed the "clinging to desire" (*kāma-upādāna*); that is to say, five each of greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance; four types of doubt; and the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

That is to say, the previously mentioned yokes (*yoga*), together with the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the two realms, totaling thirty-eight entities, are collectively termed the grasping to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*); namely, ten each of craving (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance, and eight of doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Within the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*), with the exception of the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the remaining thirty factors are collectively termed the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). The six factors that were excluded are termed the attachment to precepts and observances.
For what reason is the attachment to precepts and observances established separately?
Because it alone acts as the enemy of the noble path and deceives both the lay and monastic communities alike—
meaning that the lay community is deluded by it, reckoning such things as self-starvation to be the way to heaven.
The various classes of renunciants are deluded by this, for they reckon that abandoning desirable objects constitutes the path to purity.
For what reason is ignorance (*avidyā*) not established separately as a "clinging" (*upādāna*)?
It is called "clinging" because it is able to grasp at the various states of existence (*bhava*); however, ignorance is not itself capable of grasping.

That which is defined as ignorance (*avidyā*) is the lack of comprehension regarding the characteristics [of phenomena]; it is not a "grasping" (*upādāna*) because it is not sharp or intense, and thus can only be established as grasping when conjoined with other factors.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra asks:
"What is the yoke of desire (*kāmayoga*)?"

That which consists of desire-attachment, desire-longing, desire-intimacy, desire-love, desire-delight, desire-oppression, desire-addiction, desire-relishing, desire-joy, desire-concealment, desire-pursuit, and desire-clinging toward various sensual pleasures, which bind and weigh down the mind—this is called the yoke of sensual desire.
It should be understood that the yokes of existence (*bhavayoga*) and views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*) are likewise.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"Sensual craving is called grasping (*upādāna*)."
From this it is known that the desire and greed arising toward the four [objects], such as sensual pleasures, are called the "grasping" (upādāna) of sensual pleasures and so forth.

Thus have the latent dispositions (anuśaya) along with the active outbursts (paryavasthāna) been explained as the "outflows" (āsrava), "floods" (ogha), "yokes" (yoga), and "graspings" (upādāna) mentioned in the Sūtras.
What is the meaning of these names, such as "latent disposition" (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
Subtle, and twofold increase; Pursuing, and binding.
"Abiding, flowing, drifting, conjoining, and grasping—these are the meanings of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth.
The treatise says:
When the root afflictions manifest, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are difficult to discern; therefore, they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
The two types of "increase" (*anuśaya*) refer to their ability to increase stagnation both within the object of perception (*ālambana*) and within that which is associated (*saṃprayukta*).

As for "pursuing" (*anubandha*), it means they can give rise to acquisition (*prāpti*) that constantly follows sentient beings, always acting as a source of affliction, arising even without the application of deliberate effort.
Alternatively, although effort is exerted to prevent their arising, they repeatedly manifest; therefore, they are called "concomitant fetters" (*anuśaya*).
By such a definition, they are termed "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).
They detain sentient beings, causing them to dwell long in saṃsāra, or cause them to transmigrate within saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci Hell.

Because that continuum discharges faults inexhaustibly through the six wound-gates, it is called an "outflow" (āsrava); because it violently sweeps away wholesome qualities, it is called a "flood" (ogha); because it binds sentient beings together, it is called a "yoke" (yoga); and because it serves as a basis for grasping, it is called a "clinging" (upādāna).

One who provides a correct explanation should say this: because they flow, continue in succession, and discharge faults without ceasing amidst all objects of perception, they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Venerable one, you should know that it is like pulling a boat upstream; even with great effort, progress remains difficult."

If one were to release this boat so that it drifts with the current, although it would not be difficult to abandon the effortful practice, one should know that the arising of wholesome or defiled minds is likewise.

According to the intent of this sutra, when afflictions are not severed within the midst of objects, they are called "outflows" (āsrava); if their force is predominant, they are called "floods" (ogha).
This means that if sentient beings fall into these states, they can only comply with them and have no power to resist; because they surge, overflow, drift, and lash out, they are difficult to oppose.
When they are active, they are not called "dominant" (adhipati) but are termed "yokes" (yoga), simply because they cause sentient beings to be joined with various kinds of suffering.
Because they frequently manifest, they are called "yokes" (*yoga*);
because they grasp at desire and so forth, they are called "clenches" (*upādāna*).
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 20. *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle 21.

Chapter Five, Part Three: The Analysis of the Latent Defilements (Anuśaya). Thus, having already analyzed the latent defilements along with the outbursts (paryavasthāna), which the Blessed One has described as the outflows (āsrava), the floods (ogha), and so forth.
Is it only that many, or are there further categories?
The verse says:
Through the distinctions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, they are further said to be of five kinds.
The treatise says:

These very afflictions are further explained as being of five kinds based on the distinctions in their meanings: fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Furthermore, what are the fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
The verse says:
The fetters are nine; because of their objects, nature, and so forth, the two fetters of views and grasping are established.
Because these two are exclusively unwholesome and arise spontaneously,
among the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), only envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are established as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Alternatively, it is because they frequently occur, and because they are the causes of low status and poverty.
Because they fully manifest the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and because they disturb both groups.

The treatise says: There are nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*): first, the fetter of craving; second, the fetter of hostility; third, the fetter of pride; fourth, the fetter of ignorance; fifth, the fetter of views; sixth, the fetter of grasping; seventh, the fetter of doubt; eighth, the fetter of envy; and ninth, the fetter of avarice.
Among these, the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) refers to greed within the three realms; the characteristics of the others should be explained as appropriate.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) refers to the three views, and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) refers to the two types of grasping.
Based on this principle, it has been said:

Is there not a case where a phenomenon associated with views is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), yet the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of views does not fail to increase therein?
He said: "There is. How so?"

When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the factors associated with the two types of grasping (*dvividhā-upādāna*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are bound to them by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) as their object, but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), because the universal fetter of views has already been permanently abandoned.
It is not a fetter of pervasive view (*sarvatraga-dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), because both [the conditions of] object (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*) are absent.
Nevertheless, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of view do increase therein, because the latent tendencies of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha-dṛṣṭi*) increase with respect to it.

For what reason are the three views established separately as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while the two graspings (*parāmarśa*) are established separately as the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
Because the three views and the two graspings are equal in terms of their substance and their grasping.
That is to say, those three views consist of eighteen substances, and the two graspings are likewise; therefore, they are called "equal in substance."
The three [categories] are the grasped (grāhya), and the two are the grasper (grāhaka); thus they are called "equal graspings" (upādāna).
Because there is a distinction between the grasped and the grasper, they are established as two fetters (saṃyojana).
Why, among the envelopments (paryavasthāna), are only the two types—envy (īrṣyā) and avarice (mātsarya)—established as fetters, and not the other envelopments?
Second, because these two alone arise independently and are exclusively unwholesome.
That is to say, only these two possess both of these characteristics; the others do not, and therefore only two are established.

This explanation would be acceptable if there were only eight *paryavasthānas*, but it is unreasonable if ten *paryavasthānas* are admitted, for the two types—anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*)—also possess both characteristics.
Based on this, if one admits that all ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are present, one must say that the faults of envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are particularly grave;

for these two types manifest frequently, and furthermore, because they serve as causes for low birth and poverty, because they universally manifest the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of dejection and joy, because they disturb both the monastic and lay communities, or because they disturb the gods (*deva*) and asuras, or because they disturb the two superior destinies of humans and gods, or because they disturb both others and one’s own group.
In other places, the Buddha, relying on the method of classification, spoke of five types using the term "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*); Due to two of them, one does not transcend the desire realm.
Due to three [factors], one returns to the lower realms; because they govern the gates and the faculties, there are three.

Alternatively, those who lack the desire to set out, who are deluded regarding the path, and who doubt the path—since these can obstruct progress toward liberation, only the abandonment of these three is taught.
The Treatise says:
What are these five?
They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), and ill will (*vyāpāda*).
For what reason are these five called "conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*)?
Because these five are conducive to the benefit of the lower realm.
That is to say, only the desire realm receives the name "lower realm," and these five are able to provide benefit to it.

Because of the latter two [fetters], one cannot transcend the desire realm; even if one were able to transcend it, one would return to the lower state due to the former three, like a prison guard or a patrolman.
Other masters say:
the term "lower part" (avarabhāgīya) refers to "lower sentient beings," namely ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and the "lower realm," namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The first three [fetters] can obstruct the transcendence of lower sentient beings, while the latter two can prevent one from transcending the lower realm; therefore, all five are given the name "factors conducive to the lower part" (*avarabhāgīya*).
If one who has attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) has abandoned six afflictions, for what reason is it said that they have only abandoned the three fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
In truth, one should say that six afflictions are abandoned; however, because they subsume the categories, the gates, and the roots, only three are mentioned.

That is to say, among those to be abandoned, there are three types: one type pertains to two [categories], and one pertains to four divisions. Thus, by stating that these three types are abandoned, all three gates are subsumed.

Furthermore, among those [afflictions] to be abandoned, three follow the other three in their operation: namely, the view of extremes operates following the view of a self-identity; the grasping at views operates following the grasping at precepts and observances; and false view operates following doubt.
It is said that by abandoning three things, one subsumes those three faculties; therefore, having spoken of abandoning the three, it is already said that one abandons the six.
Some offer this explanation:
there are three kinds of obstacles for anyone traveling to a different region:
First, the lack of desire to set forth;
second, being deluded regarding the right path because of relying on a false path;
and third, doubting the right path.

Those who aspire toward liberation likewise encounter three similar obstacles: namely, through the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), they fear liberation and lack the desire to set out for it; through the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), they rely upon and adhere to false paths, thereby losing their way on the true path; and through doubt (vicikitsā), they harbor deep hesitation regarding the path.
The Buddha revealed that the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) has permanently severed such obstacles to liberation from the [lower] realms; therefore, he spoke of severing three.
In other sūtras, as with the "factors conducive to the lower realm" (avarabhāgīya), the Buddha also taught five kinds of "factors conducive to the upper realm" (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
The verse says:
The fetters conducive to the higher realms are also five: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, pride, and ignorance;
because they prevent one from transcending the higher realms.
The Treatise says:
When these five types have not yet been abandoned, they cause sentient beings to be unable to transcend the higher realms.
Because they accord with and benefit the higher realms, they are called the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The fetters have already been explained.
What, then, are the bonds?
The verse says:
The three bonds arise from the three feelings.
The treatise says:
There are three kinds of bonds.
First is the bond of greed, which refers to all forms of greed;
second is the bond of hatred, which refers to all forms of hatred;
third is the bond of delusion, which refers to all forms of delusion.
For what reason are only these three explained as bonds?
Because there are three bonds corresponding to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
That is to say, the bond of craving (*rāga*) increases in relation to pleasant sensation, because it increases both through its object (*ālambana*) and through association (*samprayoga*).
It should be understood that this is likewise the case for aversion toward painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) and delusion toward neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Although greed and aversion also exist toward neutral feeling, they do not do so to the same extent as delusion.
This definitive statement is made with respect to one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*), identifying the three feelings—pleasure and the others—as the objects of bondage.
The fetters have already been analyzed.
What are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have been explained previously.
The treatise says:
There are six, or seven, or ten, or ninety-eight latent dispositions, as has already been stated above.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have already been explained.
What, then, are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
The verse says:
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are these others, the defiled mental factors belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The treatise says:
These various afflictions are also called secondary afflictions because they all follow the mind to cause disturbance and turmoil.

Furthermore, there are other distinct afflictions that defile the mind and are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); because they arise as secondary to the primary afflictions, they are also called "secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), but they are not termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*) themselves because they are not fundamental.
The detailed enumeration of their characteristics is as found in the *Saṃyuktavastu*; they shall be discussed briefly later.
Regarding those subsumed under the "envelopers" (*paryavasthāna*) and the "defilements" (*kleśamala*), one should first analyze what the characteristics of the envelopers are.
The verse says:
The eight envelopments are shamelessness and lack of dread, envy and avarice, along with regret, torpor, restlessness, and lethargy;
or ten, when anger and concealment are added.
Lack of shame, stinginess, and restlessness—these all arise from greed;
lack of dread, drowsiness, and lethargy—these arise from ignorance;
envy and anger arise from hatred; regret arises from doubt, while concealment and contention arise from delusion.
The treatise says:
The root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are also called "envelopments" (*paryavasthāna*), because the Sūtras state that the envelopment of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*) serves as a condition.
However, the *Prakaraṇapāda* speaks of eight envelopments, while the Vaibhāṣika school asserts there are ten, namely the aforementioned eight plus anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) have already been explained as before.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) refers to the state of the mind being displeased by the various flourishing successes of others.
Avarice (*mātsarya*) refers to the state of the mind being stingily attached, which is the opposite of skillfully bestowing wealth or the Dharma.
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is precisely *styāna* (evil-doing), as has already been explained above.
Torpor (*middha*) is characterized by causing the mind to become dull and withdrawn, such that it lacks the functional capacity to sustain the body.
Of these two envelopments, remorse and torpor, only those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) are included.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) and lethargy (*styāna*) are also explained as before.
To harbor indignation toward sentient and non-sentient beings by excluding malice (*vyāpāda*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) is called anger (*krodha*).
To conceal one's own transgressions is called hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*).

Among these ten types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) thus described, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of greed; lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), sleep (*middha*), and lethargy (*styāna*) are the outflows of ignorance; envy (*īrṣyā*) and anger (*krodha*) are the outflows of hatred; and regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the outflow of doubt.
Some say that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of greed (*lobha*). Others say:
This is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Some say it is the simultaneous outflow (*sahabhū-niṣyanda*).
There is knowledge and non-knowledge, according to their respective order.
What are the characteristics of the remaining afflictive stains?
The verse says:
The stains of affliction are the six vexations: harm, resentment, flattery, deception, and pride.
Deception and pride arise from greed; harm and resentment arise from hatred;
vexation arises from views and grasping; and flattery arises from all [wrong] views.
The treatise states:
*Pradāsa* (malice) refers to the stubborn adherence to various blameworthy matters; by means of this, one does not accept reasoned admonition.
*Vihiṃsā* (harmfulness) refers to the ability to inflict oppression upon others; by means of this, one is able to carry out acts such as beating and reviling.
*Upanāha* (enmity) refers to the repeated contemplation of and failure to relinquish resentment toward an object that has already been the focus of *krodha* (anger).

*Śāṭhya* (deceit) refers to crookedness of mind; by means of this, one is unable to manifest oneself as one truly is, either by perversely denying reality or by employing expedients to cause others' understanding to be unclear.
Deceit (*māyā*) means deluding others.
Arrogance (*mada*) has already been explained previously.
These six types arise from the afflictions; because their defiled characteristics are coarse, they are called the "affliction-corruptions" (*kleśamala*).

Among these six kinds of afflictive stains (*kleśamala*), deceit (*māyā*) and arrogance (*mada*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of attachment; harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) and resentment (*upanāha*) are the outflows of aversion; vexation (*pradāsa*) is the outflow of the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and guile (*śāṭhya*) is the outflow of all [wrong] views.
As for the question "What is crookedness?

it refers to various wrong views; therefore, guile is certainly the outflow of those views. These stains, along with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*); for this reason, they are all designated as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
By what are these stains (*mala*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) abandoned?
The verse says:

The envelopments of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*), along with sleep (*middha*), are abandoned through both seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"The remaining [factors] and the afflictive stains (*kleśamala*) are abandoned through cultivation alone because they are autonomous.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, among the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), the five beginning with lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) are abandoned by both seeing and cultivation, because they arise in association with the afflictions of both categories.
Whichever [affliction] is associated with what is abandoned by seeing a particular truth is said to be abandoned by seeing that truth.

The remaining afflictions—envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and the outflows (*mala*)—arise independently; therefore, they are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because they are associated only with the other-power ignorance (*paratantra-avidyā*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are called "arising independently" (*svatantra*).
Regarding these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which ones are associated with which natures?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, three [factors]—sleep, torpor, and restlessness—are of two natures; the remaining unwholesome ones are [also there]. In the higher realms, all are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary states:

Among those bound to the desire realm, the three—sleep, torpor, and restlessness—pervade both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) natures; all others are exclusively unwholesome.
Whatever exists in the two upper realms, all of it is comprised solely within the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which ones belong to which realm?
The verse says:
Flattery and deception exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna; the other three [unwholesome roots] exist in all three realms, while the remaining [afflictions] exist in the desire realm.
The commentary states:
Flattery and deception exist only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
How could one know that there is flattery and deception in the Brahma-world?
Because the Great Brahmā King concealed his own true state and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the Bhikṣu Aśvajit.
Although these two points have already been analyzed previously, they are discussed again here for the sake of consistency with the present context.
The three factors of torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and pride (*mada*) all pertain to the three realms; all the remaining ones exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That is to say, among the sixteen [factors], five are as previously explained, while the remaining eleven are bound exclusively to the desire realm.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) have already been explained.
Among these, how many arise exclusively in the mental stage (*manobhūmi*),
and how many arise based on all six stages of consciousness?
The verse says:
The conceit and latent tendencies abandoned through seeing, along with the independent secondary afflictions, arise solely in the mental faculty; the others pertain to all six consciousnesses.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that, in brief, among all the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

those such as pride (*māna*) and torpor (*styāna*) that arise independently all rely upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), for there is no possibility for them to arise in dependence on the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).

All remaining [defilements] depend universally upon the six consciousnesses; that is to say, greed, hatred, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation, along with their associated secondary afflictions—namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and other secondary afflictions subsumed under the "great ground of affliction" (*mahākleśabhūmika*)—are all capable of arising in dependence upon the six groups of consciousness.
