Regarding the five faculties of feeling, such as pleasure and so forth, which were previously analyzed, and the afflictions and secondary afflictions elucidated here: which afflictions and so forth are associated with which faculties?
In this regard, one should first analyze the various afflictions.
The verse says:
The afflictions of the desire realm are associated with greed, joy, and pleasure;
hatred is associated with grief and pain; delusion is universal; and false view is associated with both grief and joy.
Doubt and sorrow are associated with the remaining five [mental factors]; all are associated with equanimity.
In the higher stages, they are each associated as appropriate with all feelings of their own respective consciousnesses.
The commentary says:

Among the various afflictions bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), craving is associated with joy and pleasure, because it functions through a mode of elation and pervades all six consciousnesses.
Hatred is associated with grief and suffering, because it functions through a mode of dejection and pervades all six consciousnesses.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally associated with the first four [mental factors], because it functions through both modes of joy and sorrow across all six consciousnesses.
False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with both sorrow and joy, because it functions through both modes of joy and sorrow exclusively within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
For what reason do wrong views proceed with both joy and grief?
Because one has previously committed sinful or meritorious karma, respectively.
Doubt is associated with sorrow, as it proceeds with a mode of grief and belongs exclusively to the mental level.
Those who harbor hesitation seek a mind of decisive knowledge; because they are afflicted by sorrow, [doubt] is associated with mental distress.
The other four views and pride are associated with joy, because they function through a mode of gladness and belong exclusively to the level of the mental consciousness.
Having already explained the association with feeling (*vedanā*) according to specific characteristics, regarding the explanation of the association with feeling according to general characteristics:

all [latent tendencies] are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because at the stage when the continuity of the latent tendencies is severed, their power having subsided, they necessarily abide in the feeling of equanimity.
If it is thus in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how is it in the higher stages?
In each case, they arise in association with all feelings (*vedanā*) belonging to their own respective stage and their own respective consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), as appropriate.

That is to say, in any stage where four consciousnesses are present, the afflictions (*kleśa*) arising from each of those consciousnesses are respectively associated with all the feelings belonging to that same consciousness.

If, within the various stages (bhūmi), there is only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), then the afflictions (kleśa) arising from that very mental consciousness are universally associated with the feelings (vedanā) of that mental consciousness.
Regarding the quantity of consciousness and feeling in the higher stages, as has already been analyzed previously, they will not be discussed separately here.
Having already explained the association of the primary afflictions with the various feelings, we shall now further explain the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The verse says:
Among the secondary afflictions, envy (*īrṣyā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), and vexation (*pradāśa*)...
Harmfulness and resentment arise together with sorrow; stinginess is associated with joy and the feeling of equanimity.
Deceit, guile, torpor, and concealment all arise together with both sorrow and joy.
Arrogance arises with joy, pleasure, and equanimity; the remaining four are universally associated.
The treatise states:

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the six types beginning with envy (*īrṣyā*) are all associated with the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), because they function through a mode of dejection and belong exclusively to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*).
Avarice is associated with joy, because it functions through a mode of gladness and belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
It functions through a mode of gladness because its characteristic is extremely similar to that of greed (*lobha*).

Deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), torpor (*middha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are associated with both sorrow and joy, because they function through both modes of gladness and dejection and belong exclusively to the mental level.
Regarding those associated with joy and grief: sometimes one practices flattery and the like with a joyful mind, and at other times one practices them with a sorrowful mind.
Arrogance is associated with joy and pleasure, because the practice of joy belongs exclusively to the mental faculty.
In the third dhyāna, they are associated with pleasure (*sukha*); in the lower stages, they are associated with joy (*prīti*).

All the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) mentioned above are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because at the moment the continuity [of the mind] is severed, one abides in equanimity, and because there exists a path of practice that belongs exclusively to the stage of equanimity.
Abandonment (*upekṣā*) is associated with all [five feelings] without exception, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally associated with them.

The remaining four—lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are all universally associated with the five feelings. This is because the first two are subsumed under the "universal unwholesome mental factors" (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*), while the latter two are subsumed under the "universal afflictive mental factors" (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).

Among the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that have been explained, there are those which the Buddha has described as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) according to different perspectives.
These shall now be analyzed.
What are the characteristics of these hindrances?
The verse says:
The five hindrances exist only in the desire realm;
because their nutriment, antidote, and function are the same, two are established as a single hindrance. Because they obstruct the aggregates, there are only five.
The Treatise says:

In the sūtras, the Buddha taught that there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill-will; third, the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt.

Regarding the torpor, restlessness, and doubt mentioned here: are they, like sensual desire, ill-will, sleep, and regret, restricted solely to the desire realm, or do they pertain to all three realms?
It should be understood that these three also exist only in the desire realm, because the Sūtra states that these five types constitute a purely complete aggregate of unwholesomeness.

In the realms of form and formlessness, there is no unwholesome [state]. However, because these five [hindrances] are exclusively unwholesome, they exist only in the desire realm and not in the realms of form or formlessness.
For what reason are the two hindrances of torpor-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret each established as a single entity despite having two distinct natures?
Because their functions as nutriment (*āhāra*), remedy (*pratipakṣa*), and utility (*upabhoga*) are the same, they are combined and established as one.
"Nutriment" refers to that which is consumed, also termed "provision" (*sambhāra*).
"Remedy" refers to that which counteracts, also termed "non-nutriment" (*anāhāra*).
"Function" (yòng) refers to the activity of a thing, also termed "efficacy" (gōngnéng).
It is for this reason that the Sūtra states:
"Although torpor and sleep are two distinct states, they share the same nutriment and non-nutriment."
What are called the nutriment of the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness?
They are five kinds of factors:
first, lethargy; second, lack of joy; third, yawning; fourth, irregularity of diet; and fifth, dullness and inferiority of mind.
What is called the non-nutriment for this hindrance?
It is the perception of light.
These two things function in the same way, namely, that both cause the nature of the mind to become sunken and obscured.
Although restlessness and remorse are two distinct states, their nutriment and non-nutriment are the same.
What are called the nutriments of the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?
They are four kinds of factors:
First, reflection on relatives; second, reflection on the country; third, reflection on immortality; fourth, recollection of various past experiences such as play, laughter, joy, and service.
What is called the "non-nutriment" for this hindrance? It is *śamatha*.
Thus, the functions of these two are also the same, in that both cause the mind to lack tranquility.
Because they are said to be identical in terms of their nutriment, remedy, and function, torpor-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret are combined into two pairs.
Since all afflictions possess the quality of being hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), why did the Tathāgata teach only these five?
Only these [five] are established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) because they are capable of acting as superior obstacles to the five aggregates (*skandha*).

That is to say: the hindrance of sensual desire and ill-will obstructs the aggregate of ethical discipline; torpor and drowsiness obstruct the aggregate of wisdom; restlessness and remorse obstruct the aggregate of concentration. Because concentration and wisdom are absent, there arises doubt regarding the Four Truths. Due to this doubt, everything up to liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation cannot arise. Therefore, only these five are established as hindrances.

If one were to explain the meaning of the sūtra in this manner, restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) should logically have been mentioned before lethargy and sleep (*styāna-middha*); for wisdom (*prajñā*) arises only by depending on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus the hindrance to concentration should likewise precede the hindrance to wisdom.
Based on this principle, other masters state:

"Among these five hindrances, torpor-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret respectively obstruct the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom; it is for this reason that the Sūtra speaks thus."
Those who cultivate meditative concentration fear lethargy and sleep; those who cultivate the discernment of phenomena fear restlessness and remorse.
Others offer a different explanation, asserting that there are only five causes.
What is their explanation?

It is said that while in the stage of active engagement (*caryā-avasthā*), one first grasps the two types of signs—those of the attractive and the repulsive—within various objects such as forms; subsequently, while in the stage of abiding (*sthiti-avasthā*), due to those prior acts serving as causes, the two hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) of sensual desire and ill-will arise.

These two are able to obstruct the mind that is about to enter meditative absorption; consequently, at the time when one is actually entering absorption, one is unable to properly cultivate *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
From this, lethargy-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret arise respectively, obstructing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* so that they cannot emerge.

Consequently, when one emerges from meditative absorption and subsequently engages in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), doubt again acts as an obstacle; therefore, only these five are established as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Now it should be considered: regarding the universal afflictions (*sarvatragakleśa*) of other realms, and those with outflow (*sāsrava*) that take cessation or the path as their object and are abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path—when those [afflictions] are being abandoned, one does not know their objects; yet when one knows their objects, those [afflictions] are not abandoned.
By what cause are these various afflictions abandoned?
It is not necessarily through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of their objects that they are abandoned.
If so, by how many causes in total are the afflictions abandoned?
Due to four kinds of causes. What are these four?
The verse says:
"By thoroughly knowing the object, by abandoning that which takes it as its object,
by abandoning that which is taken as its object, and by the arising of the antidote, [afflictions] are abandoned.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, the abandonment of afflictions abandoned through seeing occurs by means of the first three causes:

first, abandonment due to thorough knowledge of the object; this refers to those abandoned through seeing suffering and origin that take their own realm as an object, as well as those abandoned through seeing cessation and the path that take the untainted as an object.

Second, they are abandoned by abandoning their objects of cognition (*ālambana*). This refers to those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin that take other realms as their objects; because those [defilements] take what belongs to their own realm as their objects of cognition, when the object of cognition is abandoned, they are abandoned accordingly.

Third, they are abandoned by abandoning their objects; that is to say, those [afflictions] associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) or the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) are abandoned because those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) can serve as their objective conditions (*viṣaya*), and when the object is abandoned, they are abandoned accordingly.

If it concerns the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), their abandonment results from the last cause; that is, they are abandoned solely because the fourth counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) arises.
For when the path of counteraction belonging to a particular category arises, all the afflictions within that category are abandoned instantaneously.
Regarding which category of afflictions is countered by which antidote:
all afflictions of the highest-of-the-high degree are countered by the lowest-of-the-low path;
continuing in this manner until all afflictions of the lowest-of-the-low degree are countered by the highest-of-the-high path.
The categories of this meaning shall be analyzed in detail later.
As for the types of remedies (*pratipakṣa*), how many are there in total?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of remedies: namely, abandonment, maintenance, distancing, and aversion.
The commentary states:
In general, there are four types of remedial categories.
1. The antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
2. The antidote of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the paths subsequent to that, because they are able to maintain the attainment of this abandonment.

3. The antidote of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*), which refers to all paths following the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because those paths cause the attainment of the abandoned afflictions to become further removed.
Other masters say:
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is also [an antidote], because like that [path of abandonment], it causes the abandoned afflictions to become further removed.
The fourth is the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to any path that, upon seeing the faults of this realm, gives rise to profound revulsion.
However, if one wishes to explain these remedies correctly, the actual logical sequence should be as follows:
first, the remedy of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) arising in dependence upon suffering and its origin.
Second is the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the arising of all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) taking everything as their object.
Third is the counteractive of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the arising of all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) taking everything as their object.
Fourth is the counteractive of distancing (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the arising of all paths of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) taking everything as their object.
From what is the permanent abandonment of all afflictions definitively established?
The verse says:
One should know that by means of their objects, The various afflictions can be brought to cessation.
The treatise says:

It should be understood that when the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are permanently severed, they cannot be separated from their associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*); rather, one can only cause them to distance themselves from their objects (*ālambana*), so that they no longer arise with respect to those objects.
The principle that future afflictions can be abandoned is indeed plausible, as it is possible to prevent them from arising again with respect to their objects.
But how can past afflictions be said to be abandoned?
If one argues that the verse’s mention of "from the object" (ālambana) intends to show that they are abandoned by means of thoroughly understanding (*parijñā*) the object; [we reply:]...
This too is unreasonable, because it is not determinate.

Therefore, one must explain from what the abandonment of afflictions and so forth is determined: the abandonment of afflictions within one's own continuum occurs through the acquisition of abandonment (*prāpti*).

The abandonment of all afflictions and other non-defiled phenomena within the mental continuums of others, as well as all material forms, occurs because the various afflictions existing within one's own continuum that take those as objects have been ultimately abandoned.
Regarding what was called "remoteness," how many types of remoteness are there?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of remoteness, Namely: difference in nature, opposition, location, and time.
As with the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*), [the same applies to] different directions and the two time periods, etc.
The treatise says:
It is traditionally taught that remoteness (*dūratā*) is of four kinds in total:

First is remoteness by way of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-viprakarṣa*): for example, the four great elements, which, although they arise together within a single aggregate, are also said to be remote because their characteristics are different.

Second is remoteness by way of opposition (*pratipakṣa-viprakarṣa*): for example, the observance and violation of precepts, which, although they both operate within a single body, are also said to be remote because they are mutually opposed in nature.

Third is remoteness of location (*deśa-viprakarṣa*): for example, the eastern and western oceans; although both are situated within a single world-system, they are also called "distant" because their locations are separated.

Fourth is remoteness of time (*kāla-viprakarṣa*): for example, the past and future worlds; although both are established based upon the same phenomena, they are also called "distant" because their temporal intervals are separated.
In what sense is it said to be distant?
It is in relation to the present world.
Since that which has ceased immediately prior and that which is currently arising are adjacent to the present, how can they be called distant?
The designation "distant" is obtained due to the distinct nature of the time periods; it is not only that which was long past or will be long future that receives the name "distant.
If that were so, then the present should also receive the name "distant," because its nature is likewise distinct when viewed in relation to the past and future.

If you claim that past and future phenomena are distant because they lack functional activity (*kāritra*), and are thus called "distant" due to the absence of such activity, then since it is taught that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) lack functional activity, how could they be called "near"?

If you claim that it is called "proximate" because one currently and universally attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then by the same logic, this should also apply to the two periods of the past and future.
Furthermore, how could space, which is unconditioned, be called "proximate"?
If it is argued that the past and future are called "distant" because they are separated from each other by the present,

whereas the present is extremely proximate to both time periods and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is entirely without separation and thus "near," then it would follow that the past and future, being adjacent to the present world yet separated from each other, should possess both names [near and distant], rather than being described exclusively as "distant."

According to correct reasoning, one should say that the past and future are called "distant" because they are devoid of the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon; for the future has not yet acquired the intrinsic characteristic of the phenomenon, while the past has already relinquished it.

The word "etc. is used to clarify that the examples cited are not exhaustive. It was previously stated that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the arising of the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*); when the path advances to a higher stage, are those afflictions already abandoned abandoned yet again?
Is there a "re-acquisition" (*punar-lābha*) of the disconnection (*visamyoga*) that has been attained?
The verse says:
No delusion is severed twice; Disconnection may be re-acquired.
That is to say: during the six occasions of attaining the fruits [of the path] through the practice for their removal, and during the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The treatise says:

If an affliction encounters the path capable of severing it, that affliction is severed instantaneously by that very path; there is absolutely no principle of severing that same affliction again at a later time.

Although there is no principle for the gradual advancement of the disjunction (visamyoga) obtained [from defilements] in accordance with the path, it is possible that when the path progresses, there may be the sense of its superior acquisition (prāpti) arising again.
How many times in total does this "re-acquisition" occur?
In total there are six occasions.
What are these six? They are:
the arising of the path of counteraction, the attainment of the fruit, and the refinement of the faculties.
The time when the path of cultivation arises refers to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The time of attaining the fruits refers to attaining the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship (*arhattva*).
The time of refining the faculties refers to the time of transforming the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

Among these six times, for all disconnections from the afflictions (*kleśa-visaṃyoga*), a superior attainment (*viśeṣa-prāpti*) arises repeatedly as one progresses through the superior stages of the path.
However, regarding these disconnections, it should be understood according to the circumstances that some arise with a superior attainment during all six times, while others do so during only two.

That is to say, all dissociations from the defilements of the desire realm abandoned through the vision of the four truths, as well as those of the form and formless realms abandoned through the vision of the [first] three truths, are attained at six moments;

whereas all dissociations from the defilements of the form and formless realms abandoned through the vision of the path-truth are attained at only five moments, because the fruit is obtained at the very moment the antidote arises.

One should not divide this into two periods; rather, the acquisition of the five grades of dissociation from the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm also occurs in five periods, with the exception of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

The sixth grade of dissociation is acquired in only four periods—namely, those same five periods minus one—because there is no difference between the time of attaining the fruit and the time when the antidote arises.
The seventh and eighth categories are also attained at four times, because among the four times for attaining the fruits, the first two are excluded.
The ninth disconnection is attained at only three times; that is, from the aforementioned four, one time is further excluded, because the fruit is attained at the very moment the antidote arises.

Among those abandonments through cultivation in the form and formless realms, with the exception of the ninth disconnection of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the remaining disconnections are also attained at three times;
this is because, among the four types of fruit-attainment, the first three are excluded.

The ninth [attainment] of the Peak of Existence is acquired at only two moments; that is, within the aforementioned three, one moment is further excluded, because it is acquired at the very moment the antidote arises, which is simultaneously the attainment of the fruit.
This has been stated thus as a presentation of what is possible according to the reasoning of the treatise.

For those of sharp faculties, because they have already attained the refinement of their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) within each of the preceding stages, and because those who enter the Noble Path by means of "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*) must accordingly have abandoned [the fetters of] Stream-enterer and so forth, the term "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) applies to each respective stage of disconnection (*visamyoga*).
There are two kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*):
first, thorough knowledge by way of wisdom (*jñāna-parijñā*); second, thorough knowledge by way of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Thorough knowledge by way of wisdom refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Regarding "full knowledge through abandonment" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): this refers to the various abandonments themselves, because the name of the cause is applied here to the result.
Is a single full knowledge established for all abandonments? No.
How so? The verse says:
There are nine complete knowledges of abandonment; for the first two abandonments in the desire realm, there is one.
Two [factors] each have one [result], totaling three; the three of the upper realm are likewise.
The remaining five are the fetters conducive to the lower realm; for the form realm, there are three for the total abandonment of all.
The treatise says:

All abandonments are collectively established as nine kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*): namely, six thorough knowledges are established for the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the three realms that are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), and three thorough knowledges are established for the abandonment of the remaining afflictions and so forth belonging to the three realms that are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, how is it that the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth associated with the three realms and abandoned through the vision of the truths is established as six?

It is said that the abandonment of the first two categories associated with the desire realm is established as one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); the phrase "first two categories" specifically indicates those abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin.

Next, a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is established for each of the two classes [of afflictions] abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path; the phrase "the next two classes" indicates those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.
Thus, three thorough knowledges are established for the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth in the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths.

As it is with the three [categories] of the desire realm, so it is with the two higher realms; that is to say, those bound to the form and formless realms also consist of three: the first two being abandoned by the abandonment of the first [truth], and the latter one being abandoned by the second, each having one, totaling three. This establishes the meaning of the three categories for the abandonment of dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, and the vision of cessation and the path.

Thus, these are called the six types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) within the three realms.

How is it that three [types of universal knowledge] are established for the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth belonging to the other three realms that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

That is to say, the abandonment of the afflictions and so forth belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is established as one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); it should be understood that this is precisely the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*), because it is established together with the preceding [thorough knowledges].

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is established as one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*); it should be understood that this is precisely the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūpatṛṣṇākṣaya-parijñā*).

The abandonment of the afflictions and so forth associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of cultivation is established as one thorough knowledge; this is the thorough knowledge of the permanent exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna-parijñā*).
Since this is also combined with the preceding [categories] to establish a single [knowledge],
these are called the three types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) regarding the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the three realms.

For what reason are the abandonments of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and other factors to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms established as distinct universal knowledges, whereas those to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are not?
Because the antidotes for what is abandoned through cultivation differ,
one should analyze among these nine types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) how many constitute the fruits of the paths.
The verse says:
Among these, six are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*); the remaining three are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*).
All are the fruits of the *anāgamya* stage; five or eight are the fruits of the fundamental [dhyānas];
one is the fruit of the preparatory stage of the formless realm (*ārūpya-sāmantaka*); and the same applies to the three fundamental [formless attainments].
The worldly fruits are two; the noble ones are nine. Dharma-knowledge has three; subsequent knowledge has two.
The fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge are six; the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge are five.
The Treatise says:
Among these nine, one should first explain the distinctions regarding their results as the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and the path (*mārga*).
There are six results of patience, namely, the six kinds of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) consisting of the abandonment of the dharmas to be abandoned by seeing that are bound to the three realms.

There are three fruits of wisdom, namely: the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the fetters conducive to the lower realm, the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm, and the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters. Since these three thorough knowledges are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), how can the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*) be said to be thorough knowledges?
Since all patiences (kṣānti) are attendants of wisdom (jñāna), they are metaphorically designated by the name "king," just as the attendants of a king are so called.
Alternatively, it is because patience and wisdom share the same fruit.
Next, one should now distinguish the differences between the fruits of the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and the fundamental stages (maula) of the dhyānas.

The fruit of the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*) possesses nine [results], because by relying upon it, one is able to abandon the afflictions of the three realms that are to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation.
The fruit of the fundamental dhyānas consists of either five or eight [results].

Regarding the statement that there are five [results], the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the fundamental dhyāna stages can only permanently sever the afflictions and so forth subsumed under the form and formless realms; this is because they assert that the severance of the afflictions bound to the desire realm is exclusively the result of the *anāgamya* (unattained) stage.

Regarding what is called "the eight," the Venerable Ghosaka states that the fundamental dhyāna stages (*maulabhūmi*) also serve as the antidote for abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) in relation to the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

For those who have previously detached from the defilements of the desire realm, when they enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) by relying on the fundamental dhyāna stages, it is accepted that a distinct path (*mārga*) induces the acquisition of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state regarding the abandonment of the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*). Therefore, this [abandonment] is also the fruit of that path of vision.

Excluding the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*), because that is exclusively the fruit of the *anāgamya* [preliminary concentration], and there is no possibility of cultivating its antidote for abandonment therein.
The intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is explained as being like the fundamental dhyānas.
Now, one must distinguish the differences in the results produced by the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental states (*maula*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the results of the preparatory stages of the formless realm, there is only one: namely, that by relying on the path of the preparatory stage of the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*), one attains the result of the "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya-parijñā*).

The first three fundamental fruits are also unique; that is to say, by relying on the first three fundamental [dhyānas] of the formless realm, one attains the fruit of the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) regarding all [defilements].
Next, we shall now distinguish the differences between these as fruits of the mundane path and the various noble paths.

There are two types of results of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*): namely, because by the power of the mundane path one can only obtain the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the exhaustion of attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*).
There are nine types of results of the noble path (*āryamārga*): namely, because by the power of the noble path one is able to eternally sever all phenomena of the three realms.
Now, one should distinguish the differences regarding the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

There are three fruits of the knowledge of phenomena; that is, because the power of the knowledge of phenomena is able to abandon what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the three realms, it attains the latter three fruits.

The result of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) consists of two fruits; that is, because the power of subsequent knowledge can only permanently sever those defilements to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the form and formless realms, it attains the latter two fruits.
Next, one should now distinguish the differences in the results produced by various paths that belong to the same category as the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge.
The fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) are six; that is, the six fruits obtained by the aforementioned dharma-knowledges and dharma-patiences.
The fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna-pakṣa) are five; that is, the five fruits obtained by the aforementioned subsequent knowledges and subsequent patiences.
Since the term "category" (*pakṣa*) comprehensively includes both knowledge (*jñāna*) and receptivity (*kṣānti*),
why are the individual abandonments not each established as a separate thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), but rather established only according to the nine aforementioned stages?
The verse says:
Because one attains the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows (*anāsrava-prahāṇa-lābha*), and because of the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*),
the extinction of both causes, and the transcendence of realms, therefore nine universal knowledges (*parijñā*) are established.
The Treatise says:

Although the abandonment of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) involves many entities and stages, nine types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*) are established based on four conditions. Furthermore, six results of the patiences (*kṣānti-phala*) are established by way of three conditions: namely, because one attains the untainted acquisition of dissociation (*anāsravavisamyogaprāpti*), because one lacks [the afflictions] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and because one eliminates both causes [of future suffering].
The designation "universal knowledge" (parijñā) is established for the abandonment of defilements only when these three conditions are present; if they are lacking, it is not so.

For example, in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), although one may extinguish both causes [of rebirth] and lack the acquisition of the untainted abandonment (anāsrava-prahāṇa-prāpti), because the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) has not yet been eliminated, even though one has attained abandonment, it is not called universal knowledge.

Within the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), from the entry into the vision of the truths until the manifestation of the "subsequent patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*), although one has already attained the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*) of abandonment, the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) has not yet been eliminated and the two causes have not yet been destroyed. Upon reaching the stage of the "subsequent knowledge regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*) and the "dharma-patience regarding origin" (*samudaye dharma-kṣānti*), although the peak of existence has indeed been eliminated, the two causes still have not been destroyed, because the universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin have not yet been destroyed.

Regarding the abandonments attained during the subsequent stages of dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), because the three conditions are fulfilled, "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) is established for each respective stage. The establishment of the fruits of the three knowledges is based on four conditions; that is, to the aforementioned three, the condition of "transcending a realm" (*dhātusamatikrama*) is added.
Regarding the term "transcending the realm" (*dhātusamatikrama*), it refers to the complete separation from all phenomena such as afflictions within that particular realm.
Since some maintain that the separation from both types of fetters (*ubhayasaṃyojana*) also constitutes a condition, there are established five kinds of conditions for full knowledge (*parijñā*).

Regarding "separation from both fetters" (*ubhaya-bandhana-vigama*): although this [defilement] has been abandoned, full knowledge (*parijñā*) has not yet been established; it can only be established once one is separated from other [defilements] that take this same object as their basis.

Because this separation from both fetters is functionally indistinguishable from the cessation of the dual causes and the transcending of the object-basis (*ālambana*), they are not mentioned separately despite having different meanings.

Although the causes of both [fetters] are extinguished in all instances of transcending a realm, the time of extinguishing the causes of both does not necessarily coincide with transcending a realm; therefore, the condition of transcending a realm is established separately from the extinction of the causes of both. This is because the knowledge of universal comprehension (*parijñā*) has not yet been established when the causes of both are extinguished across three stages.
Who accomplishes how many types of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
In the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), there are none; Or one may accomplish from one up to five.
The practitioner accomplishes six, one, or two; the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) accomplishes only one.
The commentary states:
It is certain that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) lack the principle of accomplishing full knowledge (parijñā).

If noble ones abide in the stage of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), from the beginning up until the moment of the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudayadharmakṣānti*), they have not yet accomplished any of the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).

Upon reaching the moment of the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudayadharmajñāna*) and the subsequent patience regarding the category of origination (*samudayānvayakṣānti*), they accomplish only one.
Upon reaching the knowledge of the collection (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-kṣānti*), one accomplishes two.
Upon reaching the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the subsequent [knowledge] of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-kṣānti*), one accomplishes three.
Upon reaching the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*), one accomplishes four.
At the moment of the dharma-knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) and the subsequent patience regarding the path (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti), one accomplishes five [knowledges].

Abiding in the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), beginning from the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) up until one has not yet attained complete detachment from the defilements of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or has regressed from such detachment, one accomplishes six [knowledges].

Upon reaching the stage where one is completely detached from desire but has not yet exhausted craving for the form realm—or alternatively, for one previously detached from desire, prior to the arising of the path of knowledge of subsequent classes (mārgānvaya-jñāna) and before the path of superior fruit that exhausts the form realm—one possesses only a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely, the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kṣaya*).

Falling away from the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) and from the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) due to the arising of a fetter of the form realm is also exactly as described before.

For one who still possesses craving for the form realm, there is the attainment of the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kṣaya*) and the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*) once craving for the form realm is permanently exhausted; for one who has previously abandoned the form realm, this occurs from the moment the path that exhausts the form realm arises until the point before craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*) is entirely abandoned.

When one falls from the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) and gives rise to the fetters of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), two complete knowledges (parijñā) are established; their names are as previously explained.
One who abides in the state of no-more-learning accomplishes only one, namely, the complete knowledge of the eternal exhaustion of all fetters (sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā).
For what reason are the abandonments of the Non-returner and the Arhat fruit collectively established as a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
Because of transcending a realm and attaining a fruit, Thorough knowledges are collected in two places.
The treatise states:
Because two conditions are fulfilled, all abandonments are collectively established as a single "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*):
first, the transcendence of a realm; second, the attainment of a fruit.
Only those two [categories of persons] possess both conditions; therefore, their thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are combined into one.
Who abandons which thorough knowledge, and how many kinds of thorough knowledge does each obtain?
The verse says:
One abandons one, two, five, or six; acquisition is likewise, except for five.
The commentary says:

"Abandoning one" refers to falling away from the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), or from the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*), or from complete detachment from desire (*vairāgya*).

Regarding the statement "abandoning two": this refers to when non-returners (anāgāmin) fall back from the exhaustion of desire for the form realm (*rūparāga*) due to the arising of desire-ties (*kāma-bandhana*), as well as when they attain the state of arhatship.

Regarding the statement "abandoning five": this refers to when one who has previously been free from desire enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the stage of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); because they attain the exhaustion of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), they abandon the previous five.
Regarding the statement "abandoning six," this refers to when noble beings who have not yet abandoned desire attain the abandonment of desire.
Regarding "attainment is likewise," this means that there are cases of attaining one, two, or six; only the attainment of five is excluded.

To say "one is attained" means that one attains what was not previously attained, as well as when one falls away from the state of *aśaikṣa* due to the arising of the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) of the form realm.
To say "two are attained" means when one falls away from the state of *aśaikṣa* due to the arising of the various fetters of the formless realm.
Regarding the statement "attaining six," this refers to one who falls back from the state of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Having thus explained the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and completed the analysis of their abandonment,
ends the twenty-first fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-two.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

6. Chapter on the Analysis of the Noble Ones (Ārya-vibhaṅga), Part One. Thus has been explained how the abandonment of afflictions and so forth is termed "thorough knowledge" (parijñā) upon attaining the nine superior stages.
However, since abandonment must be attained through the power of the Path, what are the characteristics of this Path by which it is achieved?
The verse says:
It has already been stated that the abandonment of afflictions Is due to the Path of Seeing Truths and the Path of Cultivation.
The path of seeing is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertains to both types.
The treatise says:
It has already been explained at length that the abandonment of all afflictions occurs through the path of seeing the truths (*satyadarśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation.
Is the Path exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), or is it also contaminated (*sāsrava*)?
One should know that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is exclusively uncontaminated, while the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertains to both. Why is this so?
Because the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is able to counteract the three realms swiftly,

and because it abandons the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya) all at once— capacities that the mundane path (laukikamārga) does not possess— the path within the stage of seeing is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because there are differences in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it pertains to both types, as was previously stated regarding the realization of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
What are the characteristics of these realized truths?
The verse says:
The four truths have already been explained— namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—
and their intrinsic natures are likewise so, following the order of their realization (*abhisamaya*).
The treatise says:
The four truths have already been mentioned by name.
Where were they explained?
They were explained in the first chapter, in the section distinguishing between contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
How does he explain this?
It is said in that verse:
"The untainted refers to the Noble Path"; this explains the Truth of the Path.
Cessation through deliberation refers to disjunction; this explains the Truth of Cessation.
Furthermore, "suffering, origin, and the world" explain the Truths of Suffering and Origin.
Is the sequence of the Four Noble Truths as it has been stated there?
It is not so. Why? It is as follows in the list provided:
First, suffering; second, origination; third, cessation; fourth, the path.
Is there also a difference in the intrinsic nature of these Four Noble Truths? No.
How so? As previously analyzed, the word "likewise" (tathā) is spoken to show that its essence is identical to that [of the preceding].
For what reason do the Four Noble Truths follow this specific order?

This is explained according to the sequence of the stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); that is to say, among the objects of clear realization, those realized first are explained first. Were it otherwise, one would have to explain the cause first and the result only afterwards.
However, some dharmas are taught according to the order of their arising, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth;
others are taught according to convenience, such as the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

This means that there is no fixed principle here that dictates one must first abandon what has already arisen and subsequently prevent what has not yet arisen out of a specific desire [to follow that sequence]; rather, it is merely according to the convenience of expression.
The Four Truths are now explained according to the sequential order of their realization during the stage of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) for a practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*).
For what reason is the sequence of this clear observation necessarily fixed?
It is because one observes them in such a manner during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
For what reason must one observe in this way during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*)?

It is because if there is a phenomenon that is an object of attachment and capable of causing affliction, and one seeks the cause for liberation from it, it is logically necessary to observe that phenomenon first. Therefore, at the beginning of the stage of preparatory application, the practitioner observes suffering (*duḥkha*), which is precisely the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Next, one further contemplates suffering: by what is it caused?
One then contemplates the cause of suffering; this cause is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Next, one further contemplates suffering: by what is it extinguished?
He then contemplates the cessation of suffering; this cessation is the Truth of Cessation.
Subsequently, contemplating the path by which suffering ceases, he contemplates the path to cessation; this path is the Truth of the Path.
Just as, having seen an illness, one next seeks its cause, then contemplates its cure, and finally seeks an excellent medicine;
so too the Sūtra speaks of a simile for the sequence of the Truths.
Which Sūtra states this?
This refers to the *Bhaisajyavastu-sūtra*.
As that sūtra states:
"A king of physicians is one who possesses four qualities and is able to extract poisoned arrows."

First, one is skilled in knowing the symptoms of illness; second, one is skilled in knowing the cause of illness; third, one is skilled in knowing the cure of illness; and fourth, one is skilled in knowing the excellent medicine. The Tathāgata is likewise;
as a great king of physicians, he knows, according to reality, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Therefore, one contemplates in this sequence during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga), and the sequence is likewise the same during the stage of clear realization (abhisamaya); for it is induced by the power of the preparatory application, just as a horse gallops freely once the ground has already been inspected.
To what meaning does this term "clear realization" (abhisamaya) refer?
It should be understood that it refers to the meaning of "manifestly perfect awakening.
For what reason is it said to be exclusively untainted (anāsrava)?
Because it is directed toward the state of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) that is nirvāṇa, and because this awakening is truly pure, it receives the name "correct" (samyak).

One should understand that herein, the appropriated aggregates (upādāna-skandha) in their nature as fruit are called the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), while the appropriated aggregates in their nature as cause are called the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), for they are that which accumulates [suffering].
Because of this distinction between cause and effect within the truths of suffering and its origin, although their names differ, the entities themselves are not distinct.
However, as for the two truths of cessation and the path, the entities themselves are indeed distinct; in what sense, then, does the Sūtra refer to them as "Noble Truths"?
Because these are the truths of the noble ones, they receive the name "noble";
how could they possibly be false for those who are not noble?
They are truths for everyone, because their nature is non-erroneous.
However, only the noble ones perceive reality as it truly is, not others; therefore, they are called "Noble Truths" (āryasatya) in the sūtras.
They are not "non-noble truths," because [others] possess inverted views. As a verse says:
What the noble ones describe as pleasure, the non-noble describe as suffering;
what the noble ones describe as suffering, the non-noble describe as pleasure.
Other masters say:
Two [of the truths] are exclusively noble truths (*āryasatya*), while the remaining two are both noble and non-noble truths.
Only one portion of sensation (*vedanā*) constitutes the essential nature of suffering (*duḥkha-svabhāva*); the rest is not.
How, then, can it be said that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are the truth of suffering?
The verse says:
Suffering arises from the conjunction with the three types of suffering;
all things, as appropriate—whether agreeable, disagreeable, or otherwise—are impure conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Treatise says:

There are three natures of suffering: first, the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); second, the nature of suffering as conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); and third, the nature of suffering as change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

Because all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are, as appropriate, conjoined with these three natures of suffering, it is without error to say that they are all the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Among these, agreeable conditioned phenomena that are subject to outflows are called suffering because they are associated with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*).
All disagreeable conditioned phenomena that are subject to outflows are called suffering because they are associated with the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*).
Aside from these, all other contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called suffering because they are associated with the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
What are those that are agreeable, disagreeable, and the remainder?

They refer to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), such as pleasure and so forth, respectively; by virtue of the power of these three sensations, all contaminated conditioned phenomena that accord with pleasant sensation and so on receive the designations of "agreeable" and so forth.
Why is this so? Because if all pleasant sensations (sukha-vedanā) become of the nature of suffering through their own transformation,
as stated in the Sūtra:
All pleasant feelings are pleasant when they arise and pleasant while they endure, but painful when they perish; whereas all painful feelings are, by their very nature, of the character of suffering.
As the Sūtra says:
"Painful feelings are painful when they arise and painful while they endure."
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is of the nature of suffering by virtue of its conditioned arising, because it is produced by a multitude of causes.
As the Sūtra says:
"That which is impermanent is itself suffering."
Just as feeling and its corresponding feelings are so, so too are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Other masters explain it thus:

suffering itself, being the nature of suffering, is called the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); likewise, up to and including, conditioned phenomena themselves, being the nature of suffering, are called the "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

It should be understood that among these, the agreeable and the disagreeable are taught as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) respectively because they are unique [to those categories].

In reality, however, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); this can be perceived only by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Thus, there is a verse that says:
"Just as when a single eyelash Is placed upon the palm, one does not perceive it;
But if placed upon the eye, It causes injury and distress."
The fool is like the palm of the hand, failing to perceive the eyelash of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
the wise are like the eye, feeling extreme revulsion and dread toward it.

This is because the mind of fools feels terror at the mass of intense suffering experienced in the Avīci hell no more than the minds of the noble ones feel toward the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) should also be subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), because it is conditioned by nature.
Yet the Truth of the Path is not suffering; for the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned existence is that which is contrary to the noble mind (*āryacitta*).
The arising of the Noble Path is not contrary to the noble mind, because it leads to the exhaustion of all sufferings.

If one contemplates all conditioned phenomena as being quiescent in nirvāṇa, it is because one first perceives those phenomena as suffering and subsequently views their cessation as quiescence; therefore, the term "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) here indicates only that which is tainted (sāsrava).
If it is admitted that there is also pleasure among all phenomena, for what reason is only suffering declared to be a Noble Truth?
One class of commentators explains:
because pleasure is so slight.
It is like placing green beans into a heap of black beans; because the few follow the many, it is called a "heap of black beans.
What wise person, when draining water from an abscess and experiencing a slight sensation of pleasure, would calculate that abscess to be happiness?
Others have explained this in verse:
"Because it is the cause of suffering, because it accumulates manifold sufferings,
and because one desires it due to the presence of suffering— therefore, even pleasure is said to be suffering."

In truth, one should say that the Noble Ones perceive the essence of all existence (*bhava*) and pleasure as being entirely suffering (*duḥkha*), because they share the same single flavor as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). For this reason, suffering is established as a Truth (*satya*), and not pleasure.
How is it that one also contemplates pleasant feeling as suffering?
It is because its nature is impermanent and contrary to the noble mind.
This is just as when one contemplates form and so forth through the characteristic of suffering; their characteristic of suffering is not identical to that of a painful feeling.
Some claim that because pleasant feeling is a cause of suffering, the Noble Ones also regard it as suffering;
however, this explanation is irrational, for the aspect of "origin" (*samudaya*) consists in being a cause of suffering—how could it pertain to suffering itself?
Furthermore, when noble ones (*ārya*) are born in the form and formless realms, how could the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*) arise with respect to those [realms]?
For the aggregates (*skandha*) there do not serve as the cause for painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*).
Moreover, what would be the purpose of the teaching on "suffering inherent in conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) in the Sūtras?
If one contemplates pleasure as suffering by way of its impermanence, what is the distinction between the aspect of contemplating impermanence and the aspect of contemplating suffering?
One contemplates it as impermanent because it is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing; one contemplates it as suffering because it is contrary to the noble mind.
One perceives only impermanence and thereby knows that it contradicts the Noble One’s mind; thus, the aspect of impermanence can induce the aspect of suffering.
Other masters of the school maintain this position:
there is certainly no real pleasure, and feeling is exclusively suffering.
How is this known?
It is by means of scripture and reasoning.
How is it known by means of scripture?
As the Blessed One said:
"Whatever sensations there are, none are not suffering.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
You should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"To perceive what is suffering as pleasure is called a perversion."
How is this established by reasoning?
It is because all causes of pleasure are indeterminate.

That is to say, regarding all things such as clothing, food and drink, cold and warmth, which sentient beings accept as causes of pleasure: if these are used at an improper time or in excessive measure, they produce suffering; thus, they become causes of suffering rather than causes of pleasure.
Whether in a state of intensification or even when they are in equilibrium, clothing and other such things become causes of suffering and produce suffering simply due to being untimely.
Thus, one should know that clothing and so forth are fundamentally causes of suffering; it is only when suffering intensifies that their true nature becomes manifest.
The same principle should apply to the ease with which postures are abandoned.
Furthermore, the perception of pleasure arises precisely when suffering is being alleviated, and only when suffering has been relieved does the perception of pleasure emerge.
That is to say, if one is not oppressed by sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fatigue, or desire, one does not give rise to the perception of pleasure toward the causes of pleasure.

Therefore, regarding the causes that counteract intense suffering, the foolish falsely imagine that these can produce happiness; in reality, there is no definitive cause capable of producing happiness.
Within the context of easily shifting suffering, the foolish call it happiness, just as when one momentarily shifts a heavy burden from one shoulder to the other.
Therefore, sensation is exclusively suffering; there is certainly no real pleasure.
The masters of the Abhidharma claim that pleasure truly exists, and this statement is logical.
How is this known to be so?
Furthermore, one should counter-argue by questioning those who deny the existence of pleasure: what is it that you call suffering?
If you claim it is because of oppression, then since there is also that which is gratifying, the existence of pleasure must be established.
If you claim it is because of harm, then since there is also that which is beneficial, the existence of pleasure must be established.
If it is argued that because there is what is unloved, there must also exist what is lovable, and thus pleasure must exist;

or if it is argued that the essence of what is lovable is not truly established, because for the noble ones (*ārya*) at the time they become free from passion, what was once lovable becomes again unlovable.
Not so. For when a noble one becomes detached from an agreeable [feeling], they regard it as disagreeable by way of a different perspective.
That is to say, if a feeling possesses its own characteristic of being agreeable, that feeling never becomes disagreeable.

However, when the noble ones become free from defilement, they cultivate a sense of revulsion toward this feeling through other mental aspects; that is, they contemplate this feeling as a basis for heedlessness, seeing that it is produced by vast effort and is subject to transformation and impermanence, and is therefore not desirable. It is not that its own intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is an undesirable phenomenon.
If that intrinsic nature were unattractive, one should not give rise to craving for it;

if no craving arose, then at the time of detachment from passion, the noble one (ārya) would not observe pleasant feeling with other mental aspects and develop a profound sense of revulsion toward it. Therefore, by its own characteristic, there exists a real pleasant feeling.
However, as for the Blessed One’s statement that "all sensations whatsoever are nothing but suffering," the Buddha himself provided an explanation to clarify it.
As a sutra says,
the Buddha told Ānanda:
Based on the fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are subject to decay, I have spoken this in secret:
"Whatever is felt is none other than suffering. Therefore, one should know that this sutra does not speak in this way based on the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
If it is by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that all feelings are said to be suffering, for what reason did Ānanda ask this question:
"In another sutra, the Buddha stated that there are three feelings, namely: pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure"?
Based on what underlying intention does this sutra further state that "whatever is felt is none other than suffering"?
Ānanda should instead have asked:
"Based on what underlying intention is it said that there are three types of feeling?"
The Blessed One should likewise have answered only this:
"It is based on this intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that I say there are three feelings.
Since such a question and answer do not exist in the sūtras, it follows that by their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the three feelings truly exist.

Since the Blessed One has stated that he spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) when saying that all sensations whatsoever are nothing but suffering, he has thereby demonstrated that this sūtra was spoken with a specific underlying intention and is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, a sutra states: "You should contemplate pleasant feeling as suffering. One should understand that the intention of this sutra reveals two natures within pleasant feeling:
first, it has the nature of pleasure, meaning that this pleasant feeling is desirable when considered by way of its own characteristic;
second, it has the nature of suffering, meaning that when considered by way of another aspect, it is likewise a phenomenon that is impermanent and subject to change and decay.
However, when observing pleasure, it can act as a bond, for those who crave existence consume its flavor.
When observing suffering, it can bring about liberation, for one who observes in this way attains freedom from craving.
Because the Buddha taught that contemplating suffering can lead to liberation, he exhorted sentient beings to contemplate pleasure as suffering.
How is it known that this intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed pleasure? As a verse says:

The Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and that all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) are subject to decay; therefore, they teach that all feeling (*vedanā*) is suffering.

Furthermore, when the Sūtras state that to perceive pleasure within suffering is a perversion (*viparyāsa*), this is said with a specific intention: because worldly beings unilaterally reckon as "pleasure" pleasant feelings, exquisite sensual desires, and a portion of the pleasure found within the realms of existence (*bhava*), they thus constitute a perversion.

This means that although pleasant feelings (sukha-vedanā), when analyzed from another perspective, also possess the nature of suffering, worldly beings perceive them solely as pleasure; thus, they fall into error.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of exquisite sensual desires, there is little pleasure and much suffering; yet, because beings perceive them solely as pleasure, they fall into error.
The same applies to all conditioned phenomena; therefore, this [argument] cannot establish the proof that the nature of pleasant feeling is unreal.
If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of feeling were truly nothing but suffering, what would be the purpose of the Buddha’s teaching of the three types of feeling?
If it is claimed that the Blessed One spoke in accordance with worldly convention, this is not consistent with correct reasoning.
For the Blessed One stated, "I have spoken cryptically that feeling is not non-suffering," and because he spoke words of suchness when contemplating the five types of feeling.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Whatever faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and whatever faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), both of these should be known as pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā)," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it says:
"If one observes these five faculties with right wisdom as they truly are, the three fetters are forever severed," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, how does the Buddha, regarding a single sensation of suffering, conform to worldly convention and distinguish it into three?

If it is argued that worldly people give rise to the three perceptions—of pleasure and so forth—in relation to low, high, and middling suffering respectively, and that the Buddha taught the three [feelings] of pleasure and so forth in accordance with them, this reasoning is also incorrect.

This is because pleasure itself is also threefold; consequently, one would have to give rise to a perception of only superior pleasure in relation to the three types of suffering, such as the low and so forth.

Furthermore, when experiencing the pleasure produced by superior odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth, what inferior suffering could there be such that the world would perceive it as a pleasant sensation?

If one were to admit that such inferior suffering exists at that time, then since this inferior suffering has already ceased and not yet arisen, the world should experience an awareness of extreme bliss at that moment, because all forms of suffering are entirely absent in this state.
The same applies to the inquiry regarding the experience of sensual pleasure.

Furthermore, when a weak degree of feeling (*mṛduvedanā*) manifests, you admit that the feeling is distinct, intense, and perceivable; yet you admit that when a medium degree of feeling (*madhyavedanā*) manifests, it is the opposite of this. How can this be consistent with reason?
Furthermore, since the three lower dhyānas are said to possess pleasure, they should also possess lower-grade suffering;
and since the higher stages are said to possess equanimity, they should possess middling-grade suffering.
If meditative absorption increases while suffering intensifies, how could this possibly accord with correct principle?
Therefore, one should not establish the three feelings—pleasure and so forth—by following the three types of suffering, such as the inferior and so on, respectively.
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"If form were exclusively suffering and not pleasure, and were not accompanied by pleasure," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, it is known that there must certainly exist a small portion of actual pleasure.

Thus, having briefly analyzed the scriptural citations they have adduced, it is shown that their proof—that there is no actual pleasure—is unestablished; the logical arguments they have put forward likewise fail to serve as proof.
Furthermore, as for the claim that "the causes of pleasure are all indeterminate," this is not correct reasoning, for it confuses the meaning of the term "cause.

That is to say, one must observe the specific distinctions of the state of the basis [the body] for external objects to become causes of pleasure or causes of suffering; it is not the case that external objects alone are such causes.

If this external object, upon reaching such a state of its support, can serve as a cause for pleasure, and has never reached it without serving as a cause for pleasure, then the cause of pleasure is not indeterminate.

Just as with worldly fire, one observes that depending on the specific state of what is being boiled or roasted, it serves as the cause for delicious ripening or as a contrary cause; it is not the case that the fire alone is [the cause].

If this fire reaches such a state of the object being boiled or roasted, it becomes the cause for delicious ripening, and it has never reached a state where it is not a cause for delicious ripening. Therefore, the cause for delicious ripening is not indeterminate.
The same reasoning definitively establishes that the cause of pleasure is likewise so.
Furthermore, how could the cause of pleasure within the three dhyānas not be determinate?
For its cause is never capable of producing suffering.
Furthermore, as for their claim that the perception of pleasure arises only when suffering is being remedied, this has already been refuted above.

That is to say, when one experiences the pleasure produced by superior odors, tastes, tangibles, and so forth, what suffering is being remedied such that the world would give rise to the perception of pleasure therein?

If it is granted that at that time one is treating coarse suffering, then since this suffering being treated has already ceased and has not yet arisen, at that time there ought rather to arise a perception of extreme bliss.
Furthermore, what kind of suffering is being treated by the bliss of dhyāna such that it arises?
Such refutations as these should be explained according to the preceding [arguments].

Furthermore, regarding their claim that the perception of pleasure arises within suffering when it is easily removed—just as when one shifts a burden onto another shoulder—the specific state of the body can indeed produce pleasure; as long as such a state of the body has not ceased, pleasure must necessarily arise, but once it ceases, this is no longer the case.
If it were otherwise, pleasure would increase further in this state over time as suffering gradually diminishes.
One should know that the same applies to the ease of emerging from the four postures of the body and the arising of pleasure through the relief of fatigue.
If pleasure were not preceded by suffering, why would the perception of suffering suddenly arise at the final stage?

Because of the distinct states resulting from the transformation of the body—just as sweet or sour tastes emerge later from wine and the like—the logical existence of the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) is established.

From this, it is known with certainty that all contaminated formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are designated as "suffering" (*duḥkha*) according to their respective correspondence because they are conjoined with the three types of suffering.

Thus, the very substance of these formations of suffering would also be called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). This assertion certainly contradicts the Sūtras, for the Sūtras state only that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the origination.
The Sūtra speaks of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the origin (*samudaya*) because it is the most prominent [cause]; however, in reality, the remaining factors are also the truth of the origin.
By what reasoning is this principle known?
It is known because other sūtras also mention these remaining factors [as the origin].
As the Blessed One stated in a gāthā:
"Karma, craving, and ignorance act as causes to summon future formations;
causing all modes of existence to continue in succession, they are termed 'pudgala' (person)."
Furthermore, the sūtra speaks of five kinds of seeds; this is a distinct designation for the consciousness with appropriation (*sopādāna-vijñāna*).
Moreover, that same sūtra speaks of placing them within the element of earth; this is a distinct designation for the four stations of consciousness (*catasro vijñānasthitayaḥ*).
Therefore, what is taught in the Sūtras is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-vacana*), whereas the Abhidharma explains according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
However, when the Sūtra states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the origin (*samudaya*), it speaks specifically of the cause of arising.
Regarding the statement in the *gāthā* that karma, craving, and ignorance are all causes: this fully explains both the arising [of existence] and its causal conditions.
How is this known?
Because it is stated in the Sūtras that karma is the cause of birth and craving is the cause of origination.
