Furthermore, because that sutra sequentially demonstrates that future karma has causes, conditions, and continuities, it establishes the seed and the field as distinct entities by teaching the appropriating consciousness (*upādāna-vijñāna*) and the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*). Therefore, craving alone does not constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
What dharma is called "birth" (*jāti*)?
What dharma is called "arising" (*utpāda*)?
The manifestation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) through the various categories of distinctions—such as realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and modes of birth (*yoni*)—is termed "birth."
If there is a continuity of subsequent existence without differentiation, this is called "arising.

Karma and craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) serve as the two causes for these respectively; one should understand that karma and craving for existence function as the causes for production and arising, just as, for example, seeds are the productive causes for sprouts of specific species such as rice or barley, while water is the cause for the arising of all undifferentiated sprouts.
What reasoning serves as proof that craving is the cause?
It is because subsequent existence does not arise in the absence of craving.

That is to say, when two individuals—one possessing craving and one free from craving—both reach the end of their lives, we observe only the one possessing craving for whom subsequent existence arises again.
By this reasoning, craving is proven to be the originating cause, because the arising or non-arising of existence (bhava) is invariably contingent upon craving.
Furthermore, it is due to craving that the continuum proceeds toward a future state; for we observe that wherever there is craving, the mental continuum repeatedly tends toward that object.
From this inference, it is known that because craving exists, it causes the continuum to rush toward future existence (*punarbhava*).

Furthermore, there is no other phenomenon that grasps at a future body with such firm attachment as craving; it is like powdered *bīṭuka* beans mixed with water and applied to the body during bathing, which, once dry, adheres so firmly to the skin that nothing else can surpass its tenacity.

Thus, there is no other phenomenon that serves as a cause for grasping at a future existence as one does out of craving for a self; by this reasoning, it is proven that craving is the originating cause.
In this way, the Blessed One taught that there are four truths.
Another sutra further states:
"There are two kinds of truths: first, conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); second, ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
What are the characteristics of these two truths?"
The verse says:
When that cognition ceases upon breaking [the object], and likewise when wisdom analyzes it further, such as a jar or water, these are conventional; otherwise, they are called ultimate.
The treatise says:
If the cognition of an object ceases when that object is broken, that object should be known as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
For example, when a jar is broken into shards, the cognition of "jar" no longer exists; the same applies to garments and other such things.

Furthermore, if there is an object such that when it is analyzed by wisdom into its remaining parts, the cognition of that object no longer occurs, it is also conventional; for example, when water is analyzed by wisdom into its constituent elements such as color and so forth, the cognition of "water" ceases, and the same applies to fire and other things.

That is to say, while those objects have not yet been broken down or analyzed, they are designated by worldly conventions and names; because they are established through such designation, they are called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).
Based on the principle of convention, it is said that things such as vases exist as real and not false; this is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
If a thing is otherwise than this, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

That is to say, when that thing is broken, the cognition of it does not cease; and when other factors are analytically excluded by wisdom, that cognition still persists—one should know that such a thing is named the ultimate truth.

Just as when objects such as form are broken down to their ultimate atoms, or when taste and other qualities are analytically excluded by superior wisdom, the cognition of them persists; the same applies to feeling and so forth. Because these exist truly, they are called "ultimate" (paramārtha).
According to the ultimate principle, that which possesses form and so forth is said to be real and not false; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The former masters have stated as follows:

"Those phenomena apprehended by supramundane cognition and by the correct mundane cognition obtained subsequent to it are called the ultimate truth; likewise, those phenomena gathered by other types of cognition are called conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)."
The truths have already been explained; it should now be stated how one should diligently practice the means for entering the path that leads to the vision of the truths.
The verse says:
When about to enter the path for the vision of the truths, One should abide in ethical discipline and diligently practice.
Those produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation have as their objects names, both names and referents, and referents alone.
The treatise says:
All who resolve to proceed toward the vision of the truths should first abide in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), and thereafter diligently cultivate that which is produced by hearing and so forth.

This means that one first acquires the teachings conducive to the vision of the truths; having heard them, one diligently seeks the meaning of the Dharma as it was heard; having heard the meaning of the Dharma, one reflects upon it without error; and only after such reflection is one able to practice based on meditative concentration.

The practitioner thus abides in the precepts and practices diligently; relying on the wisdom derived from hearing, they give rise to the wisdom derived from reflection; relying on the wisdom derived from reflection, they give rise to the wisdom derived from cultivation.
What is the distinction between the characteristics of these three types of wisdom?

The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the characteristics of these three wisdoms differ according to whether they take names (*nāman*), both names and meanings (*artha*), or meanings alone as their objects, respectively:
the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) takes only names as its object, because it is not yet able to set aside the literal text to contemplate the meaning.

The wisdom derived from reflection takes both names and meanings as its objects; sometimes it draws out meaning from the phrasing, and sometimes it draws out the phrasing from the meaning, because it has not yet completely set aside the phrasing to contemplate the meaning alone.
The wisdom produced by cultivation takes only the meaning as its object, for it has already been able to abandon the words and contemplates only the meaning.

It is like a person swimming in deep, swift water: one who has never learned does not let go of their support; one who has learned but not yet mastered it may either let go or cling to it; whereas one who has learned well crosses by their own power without depending on a support.
The three types of wisdom are also like this. Some say:
"If that were so, then the wisdom of reflection would not be established."

That is to say, since these [three types of wisdom] take both names and meanings as their objects, they should respectively be considered as consisting of hearing (*śruta-mayī*), reflection (*cintā-mayī*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī*).

Now, upon careful examination, there is no fault in this distinction: the superior wisdom arising from relying on the teachings of the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) is called that consisting of hearing; the superior wisdom arising from relying on correct reasoning (*yukti*) is called that consisting of reflection; and the superior wisdom arising from relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is called that consisting of cultivation.

The use of the term "that which is accomplished" (sādhya) indicates that the three superior wisdoms are accomplished by means of the three causes, namely hearing, reflection, and so forth; this is just as in the world, where life, cattle, and so on are respectively said to be "accomplished by eating grass."
For those who wish to apply themselves with diligence to cultivation, how can they purify the vessel of the body so that cultivation may be swiftly accomplished?
The verse says:
Possessing physical and mental seclusion, Free from lack and great desire,
That which has been obtained and that which has not yet been obtained— The desire for much is what they lack.
They counteract the three realms of discordant factors; Their nature is untainted non-attachment.
The four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are likewise; The first three consist solely of contentment.
The three existences possess subsequent karma, Acting as the remedy for the arising of the four types of craving;
Because they temporarily pacify and permanently eliminate Desire for "mine," for the self, and for objects of the self.
The Commentary says:
The purification of the physical vessel is briefly due to three causes.
What are these three causes?
First, physical and mental seclusion; second, contentment and fewness of desires; and third, abiding in the four noble lineages.
Physical seclusion means dwelling apart from social entanglement;
mental seclusion means being free from unwholesome thoughts.
These two are easily accomplished through contentment and fewness of desires.
Regarding "contentment" (saṃtuṣṭi), there is no lack of contentment; regarding "fewness of desires" (alpecchatā), there is no great desire.
What is the distinction between these two?
The masters of Abhidharma all say this:

Seeking more than what one has already obtained, such as exquisite robes and so forth, is called "lack of contentment" (*asantuṣṭi*); seeking excessively for exquisite robes and so forth that one has not yet obtained is called "great desire" (*mahecchatā*).
Would it not be the case that seeking more also takes as its object what has not yet been obtained, and thus the distinction between these two would fail to be established?
Therefore, it should be stated here as follows:

being dissatisfied and lacking joy regarding what has already been obtained—whether it be excellent or not, or whether it be much or little—is called "lack of contentment" (asantuṣṭi); whereas seeking excellence and seeking abundance regarding things such as clothing that have not yet been obtained is called "great desire" (mahecchatā).
Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) are able to counteract these [faults]; therefore, one should understand their distinctions as being the opposite of those faults.
Contentment and fewness of desires pertain to all three realms and are untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas the two types of faults they counteract are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and having few desires (*alpecchatā*) are, in their essential nature, non-attachment (*alobha*); that which they counteract consists of two kinds of desire and greed (*rāga*).
They are called "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*) because they can give rise to the various noble ones.

The essence of the four noble lineages is also non-attachment; among these four, the first three are exclusively contentment. That is to say, one gives rise to contentment with whatever clothing, food, and bedding one obtains. As for the fourth noble lineage, which is the delight in abandonment and cultivation (*prahāṇabhāvanārati*), how is it also characterized by non-attachment as its essence?
Because they are able to relinquish desire and greed for existence,
for what purpose are the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) established?
It is to demonstrate that the disciples, having abandoned worldly requisites and worldly occupations, go forth from home to follow the Buddha in order to seek liberation.
The World-Honored One, Lord of Dharma, out of compassion for them, established two matters that assist the path:
first, the equipment for birth; second, the activity of practice.
The former three are precisely the equipment for birth that assists the path, while the last one is precisely the activity of practice that assists the path.
If you can perform subsequent tasks by relying on the equipment provided in previous lives, liberation will not be long in coming.
For what reason are these two matters established?
It is because they serve as antidotes to the four types of craving; thus, the Sūtra says:
“Bhikṣus, listen attentively!
Craving arises when it should arise, abides when it should abide, and clings when it should cling, on account of clothing.
It is the same for food, drink, bedding, and for both existence and non-existence; all are explained in this way.”
To remedy these four, the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are taught.

Based on this very meaning, they are further explained through another formulation: that is, the Buddha taught the four noble lineages because he wished to temporarily pacify and permanently eliminate the desire for "mine" (*mama-kāra*) and the "self-entity" (*ātma-vastu*).
"Things belonging to 'mine'" refers to clothing and so forth; "the self" refers to one's own body. Craving that takes these as its object is called *kāma* (desire).

The first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are taught for the sake of temporarily ceasing the aforementioned three types of craving, while the fourth noble lineage is taught for the sake of permanently eradicating all four types of craving.
Thus has been explained the vessel that serves as the basis for cultivation.
By means of which gateways can one correctly enter into cultivation?
The verse says:
There are two essential gateways for entering cultivation: the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing.
Those in whom greed and discursive thought predominate should practice these in their respective order.
The treatise says:
There are two essential gateways for entering into cultivation: first, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); second, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
As for who can correctly enter cultivation through which gateway, one should understand this according to the sequence [as follows].

Regarding those for whom craving and discursive thought increase: this refers to those whose craving is intense and frequently manifests before them; such sentient beings are called "craving-practitioners," and they are able to correctly enter into cultivation by contemplating impurity.
One whose mind is frequently distracted is called a "seeker" (vitarkacarita); such a person is able to enter correct cultivation by relying on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Other masters say:

because this mindfulness of breathing has few objects, it can suppress distracting discursive thoughts (*vitarka*); whereas the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā*) has many objects—manifesting various distinctions of form and shape—and thus induces many discursive thoughts, making it incapable of counteracting them.
Others further say:

At this time, because mindfulness of breathing operates within the internal door, it is able to suppress distracted discursive thoughts; however, since the meditation on impurity mostly operates through the external door, it is like visual consciousness, which lacks the power to remedy those [distractions].
Among these, one should first explain the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
What are the characteristics of such contemplation?
The verse says:
To treat the four types of craving universally, one first contemplates a skeleton;
expanding this to the ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of "beginning practice.
From removing the feet up to the midpoint of the head is called "mature cultivation."
Binding the mind between the eyebrows is called the stage of transcending mental application (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).
The treatise says:
The cultivation of the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is primarily intended to counteract greed; however, there are briefly four types of greed:
There are four types of craving: first, craving for color; second, craving for shape; third, craving for exquisite touch; and fourth, craving for service and honor.

One counteracts the first craving by practicing the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) focused on the livid corpse and so forth; one counteracts the second craving by practicing the meditation on impurity focused on the corpse being devoured by scavengers and so forth; one counteracts the third craving by practicing the meditation on impurity focused on the corpse infested with maggots and so forth; and one counteracts the fourth craving by practicing the meditation on impurity focused on the motionless corpse.

If one cultivates the contemplation of impurity by taking a skeleton as the object, it is universally capable of counteracting these four types of craving; since the four objects of craving do not exist within the skeleton, one should first explain the cultivation of the skeleton contemplation.

Because this is comprised solely of attention through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*) and because its object is only partial, it does not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), but can only suppress them so that they do not manifest.
Furthermore, there are generally three stages in which a practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) cultivates the meditation on the skeleton (*asthi-saṃkalikā*):
first, the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika*); second, the stage of mature cultivation (*kṛtaparicaya*); and third, the stage of transcending mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).

This means that when a practitioner wishes to cultivate such a meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), they should first fix the mind upon a part of their own body—whether it be the toes, the forehead, or another location—and once the mind has become settled in whichever place is preferred, they should, by the power of resolute conviction (adhimukti), engage in imaginative contemplation of that bodily part, visualizing the skin and flesh rotting and falling away until the bone is purified, eventually contemplating the entire skeleton of the body in its completeness.

Having seen one set, one further contemplates a second; in this manner, one gradually expands the scope until it encompasses a single room, a single monastery, a single grove, a single village, and a single country, eventually pervading the entire earth bounded by the oceans, filled throughout with skeletons, so that one's resolute understanding may increase.

One gradually contracts the observation from the extensive object until one observes only a single set of skeletal bones; when the meditation on impurity has been perfected through this gradual contraction, it is called the stage of the beginner practitioner (*ādikarmika*).

In order to increase the power of resolve through this abbreviated contemplation, one first removes the bones of the feet from within a single set and dwells with the mind focused on the remaining bones; gradually, one proceeds until the bones of half the head are removed and dwells with the mind focused on that remaining half-bone. Up to this point, the abbreviated contemplation of impurity is perfected, and the practitioner is said to have reached the stage of "mastery in cultivation."

To bring mastery over the resolve of concise contemplation, one removes half of the skull-bone and fixes the mind between the eyebrows, dwelling in a state of profound stillness by focusing single-mindedly on this one object; when this extreme conciseness of the contemplation of impurity is accomplished, it is called the stage of the yoga practitioner who has transcended mental attention (*manasikāra*).

There are cases of the contemplation on the impure (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) that are small in terms of their object (*ālambana*) but not small in terms of mastery (*vaśitā*); one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). This is due to the distinction between whether the mental application (*manasikāra*) is matured or immature, and whether the object extends from one's own body to the ocean.
What is the nature of this contemplation of impurity?
To how many stages does it belong?
What is its object?
In what place does it arise?
What is its mode of activity?
To what time period does it take as its object?
Is it with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*);
is it acquired through detachment from passion (*vairāgya-lābhika*) or acquired through application (*prāyogika*)?
The verse says:
The nature of non-attachment consists of ten stages; it arises taking the desire and form realms as its object, and is produced by humans.
It takes the impure as its object within its own realm, is associated with outflows, and is acquired through both types of attainment.
The commentary says:
To answer the questions previously asked in their proper sequence:

this contemplation has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature and is based upon ten stages—namely, the four dhyānas, the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm—and takes as its object only the visible forms perceived within the desire realm.
What is it that is seen?
It refers to manifest color and shape.
This is already established by the fact that they take objects as their cognitive domain.
It arises only among human beings, excluding those of the Northern Continent; it does not arise in other realms of existence, much less in other world-systems.
Since it is designated by the name "impure," its characteristic aspect is exclusively that of impurity.
Whichever world it may belong to, it takes as its object the realm of that same world; however, if it is a dharma that does not arise, it universally takes the three times as its object.
Since it is associated exclusively with *adhimokṣa-manasikāra* (attention consisting of resolute conviction), this contemplation should logically be only *sāsrava* (with outflows).

It is acquired both through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-pratilambhika*) and through preparatory effort (*prayoga-pratilambhika*), because there is that which has been previously acquired and that which has not.
Having explained the distinctions regarding the characteristics of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one should next analyze mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
What are the characteristics of these distinctions?
The verse says:
Mindfulness of breathing is wisdom belonging to five stages; it takes wind as its object and relies upon a body in the desire realm.
The second [type] consists of those that exist externally but lack reality; there are six, namely number and so forth.
The Treatise says:
"Mindfulness of breathing" (ānāpānasmṛti) refers to what is described in the Sūtras as mindfulness of *āna* and *apāna*.
"Āna" refers to the inhalation of breath; it means drawing external air into the body.
"Apāna" refers to the exhalation of breath; it means drawing internal air out of the body.
Wisdom observes this as its object by means of the power of mindfulness; therefore, it is called *ānāpānasmṛti*.

Although its intrinsic nature is wisdom, it is described as "mindfulness" because the power of mindfulness sustains it, enabling the task to be accomplished with clarity regarding the object, just as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

It pervades five stages: namely, the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) of the first, second, and third dhyānas, the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This mindfulness is associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*);
that is to say, because painful and pleasant sensations tend to induce discursive thought (*vitarka*), and this mindfulness counteracts discursive thought, it does not arise simultaneously with them.
The two feelings of joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*) are able to obstruct one-pointed concentration;
since this mindfulness is accomplished through one-pointed concentration upon its object, they do not arise simultaneously due to this contradiction. Some say:
The fundamental lower three dhyānas also possess the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It is said that this [attainment] relies upon eight stages, because in the higher meditative absorptions, the cessation of [breathing] does not exist.
This concentration takes wind as its object and arises based on a body in the desire realm.
It exists only in the realms of humans and devas, excluding those of Uttarakuru;

it is obtained both through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-lābha*) and through preparatory effort (*prayoga-lābha*), and is associated exclusively with authentic mental attention (*bhūta-manasikāra*).

Only sentient beings within the True Dharma are able to cultivate it; non-Buddhists do not possess it, because they lack a teacher who can explain it and because they cannot personally realize the subtle dharmas on their own.
This perfection of the signs is achieved through six causes:
first, counting; second, following; third, settling; fourth, observing; fifth, transforming; and sixth, purifying.

Counting means binding the mind to the object of the inhalation and exhalation without applying effort, relaxing both body and mind while merely recollecting and maintaining the count of the breaths from one to ten, neither decreasing nor increasing [the number], for fear that the mind might become excessively agitated or distracted in the present moment.
However, within this context, three types of error may occur:
first, the error of omission, which is to say one for two;
second, the error of addition, which is to say two for one.
The third is the fault of confusion, wherein one mistakes inhalation for exhalation or exhalation for inhalation.
If one is free from these three faults, it is called correct counting (*samyaksaṃkhyā*).

If the mind becomes distracted during the interval between [counts] up to ten, one should again count sequentially from one, starting over from the beginning until meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained.

"Following" means binding the mind to the object of inhalation and exhalation, proceeding with the breath without applying deliberate effort (*prayoga*). One contemplates how far the breath extends during its entry and exit:
when contemplating the inhalation, one considers whether it pervades the entire body or moves through only a portion of it.
Following that breath as it enters, one’s mindfulness constantly follows it as it travels through the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, calves, and down to the toes.
If one is mindful of the breath as it goes out, leaving the body, one’s mindfulness constantly follows it as far as a span or a fathom, according to the distance it reaches.
Other masters claim that the exhalation of the breath extends as far as the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) or even to the Vairambha winds; however,
this is not reasonable, because this mindfulness is conjoined with attention directed toward reality (tattva-manasikāra).

"Stopping" (śamatha) means binding the mindfulness so that it dwells solely at the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even as far as the toes; one settles the mind in whichever place is preferred.
One contemplates the breath abiding in the body like a thread through a pearl, observing whether it is cold or warm, and whether it is detrimental or beneficial.

"Contemplation" means that after having observed this wind of breath, one simultaneously observes the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) produced by the primary elements (mahābhūta) coexisting with the breath, as well as the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) that abide supported by that matter; thus, one takes all five aggregates (pañca-skandha) as the object of observation.

"Transformation" (*parivṛtti*) refers to the shifting of the awareness of the wind of the breath into increasingly superior and wholesome roots, up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
"Purification" (*viśuddhi*) refers to the ascending entry into the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.
Other masters say:

that which begins with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and ends with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is called "transformation" (*parivarta*); only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth are called "purity" (*viśuddhi*). To encompass these six characteristics, a verse is spoken:
"One should know that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) Has six distinct characteristics."
That is to say, it refers to the distinctions of counting, following, stopping, contemplating, and transforming into purity.
How should the distinctions of the characteristic of calming be understood?
The verse says:
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body; they proceed based on two distinctions.
They are of the nature of sentient beings, non-appropriated, of the nature of outflow, and do not take a lower level as their object.
The commentary says:
The breath belongs to the same level as the body in which it arises, because the breath is comprised as a part of that very body.

This inhalation and exhalation proceed based on the distinction between body and mind; for they do not proceed at all in those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), nor in the *kalala* stage of embryonic development, nor during the attainment of the mindless state (*acittaka-samāpatti*) or the fourth dhyāna.

This means that inhalation and exhalation occur only when there are cavities within the body, when the mental state belonging to the level of inhalation and exhalation is present, and when the breath is able to circulate at that time.

At the moment of emerging from the fourth dhyāna and other such states, or at the time of initial birth, the breath first enters. At the moment of entering the fourth dhyāna and other such states, or at the time of death, the breath finally exits.
Breath is included within the category of sentient beings because it is a constituent part of a sentient being.
It is not appropriated (*anupātta*) because it is separated from the sense faculties.
It is of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*) because it is produced by a cause of similar kind (*sabhāga-hetu*).
It is not produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*), because it diminishes when the body grows.
It is not produced as maturation (*vipākaja*), because it continues its succession even after being severed, whereas other matter born of maturation does not possess such a quality.
It is exclusively the object of mind belonging to its own level or a higher level;
it is not the object of the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the mind of supernormal fruition (*nairmāṇika*) belonging to a lower level.

Chapter Six: The Analysis of the Noble Ones, Part Two. Thus has been explained the entry into the two doors of cultivation; through these two doors, the mind attains concentration.
Having attained concentration, what should one cultivate next?
The verse says:
Relying on the already cultivated and perfected *śamatha*, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness for the sake of *vipaśyanā*.
By means of their specific and general characteristics, one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
The intrinsic natures are the wisdoms of hearing and so forth; the others are the mixed objects of focus.
Their sequence is taught according to their arising, and they are only four because they remedy the [four] inversions.
The treatise states:
Based on the already cultivated and perfected excellence of śamatha, one cultivates the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) for the sake of vipaśyanā.
How does one cultivate the four applications of mindfulness?
This refers to observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The individual intrinsic natures of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena are called specific characteristics.

The fact that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, that all contaminated phenomena are of the nature of suffering, and that all phenomena are empty and non-self, are called general characteristics.
The intrinsic nature of the body consists of the primary elements and derived matter.
The intrinsic natures of sensation and mind are evident from their respective names.
The intrinsic nature of phenomena consists of those factors remaining after excluding the [other] three.

It is said that when one contemplates the body by observing each individual atom and moment within meditative concentration, the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) is perfected; the criteria for the perfection of the other three should be understood accordingly.
What is the essential nature (svabhāva) of these four applications of mindfulness?

Each of these four foundations of mindfulness has three distinct types, based on the differences between their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their association (*saṃsarga*), and their objects (*ālambana*).

The foundation of mindfulness in its intrinsic nature has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence; this wisdom is of three kinds—namely, that which is derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī*), and so forth—and these are also called the three types of foundation of mindfulness.
The application of mindfulness as associated with characteristics (saṃsṛṣṭa-smṛtyupasthāna) has wisdom and its concomitant factors as its essence;
the application of mindfulness as the object (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna) has all dharmas that are the objects of wisdom as its essence.
How is it known that its intrinsic nature is wisdom and nothing else?
The Sūtra states:
"Abiding in the contemplation of the body with respect to the body is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
the same applies to the other three."
The term "applications of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) refers exclusively to the essence of wisdom (prajñā), for without wisdom, there would be no function of application.
For what reason is the name "application of mindfulness" established for wisdom?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
In this chapter, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is predominant;
thus, it is by the power of mindfulness that wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to function, just as an axe cuts wood by being supported by the force of a wedge.

In truth, however, one should say that wisdom causes mindfulness to abide; therefore, the name "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established for wisdom, because it clearly remembers according to what wisdom contemplates. For this reason, Aniruddha spoke as follows:
"If there is one who can abide in the contemplation of the body regarding the body, mindfulness established by taking the body as its object will remain," and so forth, as explained at length.
The Blessed One also said:
"If there is one who abides in the contemplation of the body regarding the body, mindfulness will remain steady and unerring."
However, there is a sūtra that says:
"By what cause do these four foundations of mindfulness arise?
By what cause do they cease?"
Because of the accumulation of nutriment, contact, name-and-form, and attention, there is, respectively, the accumulation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Because of the cessation of nutriment, contact, name-and-form, and attention, there is, respectively, the cessation of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
It should be understood that this refers to the application of mindfulness with respect to its objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), because mindfulness abides therein.
Furthermore, the specific names of the applications of mindfulness differ according to the objects, based on the distinctions between one's own continuum, another's continuum, or both.
Each foundation of mindfulness has three types; these four foundations of mindfulness are taught in the order in which they arise.
For what reason do they arise?
Their sequence is as follows.

Because one should first contemplate that which is coarse according to its objects, or because sensual desire operates primarily with respect to the body, the contemplation of the body is placed first among the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

However, craving for the body arises through delighting in feeling; delighting in feeling arises from the lack of tranquility in the mind; and the lack of tranquility in the mind arises because afflictions have not been abandoned. Therefore, the contemplation of feeling and the others follows this sequential order.
These four foundations of mindfulness counteract, respectively, the four types of perversions—purity, pleasure, permanence, and self; therefore, there are exactly four, neither more nor less.
Among these four, three have exclusively non-mixed objects, while the object of the fourth applies to both mixed and non-mixed objects.

If one contemplates only phenomena (*dharma*), it is called "non-mixed object" (*asaṃbhinnālambana*); if one observes two, three, or all four [objects] such as the body and so forth collectively, it is called "mixed object" (*saṃbhinnālambana*).
Having thus thoroughly cultivated the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) with mixed objects such as the body and so forth, what further should be cultivated?
The verse says:
Abiding in that dharma-smṛtyupasthāna, one contemplates the four objects of focus collectively,
cultivating the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The Treatise says:

That practitioner, abiding in the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena as a composite of all objects, contemplates the four objects—body and so forth—in their totality, cultivating the four aspects of contemplation, namely: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
What roots of goodness arise after practicing this contemplation?
The verse says:
From this arises the stage of Heat (uṣmagata), fully contemplating the Four Noble Truths.
One cultivates the sixteen aspects; the subsequent arising of the *mūrdhan* (Summits) is likewise.
These two roots of goodness both consist of the first [moment] as the dharma-attention and the subsequent four [moments].
Next, the *kṣānti* (Patience) consists solely of dharma-attention; its lower and middle grades are the same as the *mūrdhan*.
The highest [level] contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm; it consists of a single application and a single moment.
The World-First Dharma is likewise. All are wisdom, excluding acquisition (*prāpti*).
The treatise says:
By cultivating the mindfulness of dharmas that takes general characteristics as its object, it gradually matures through the stages up to the highest of the high degrees.
Following this mindfulness, there arises the first root of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), which is called the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma.

This dharma is established by the name "Heat" (ūṣmagata) because it is like heat; it is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path that can burn the fuel of the afflictions, and thus, being like the precursor to fire, it is called "Heat.
Because this stage of the wholesome root of Heat is long-lasting, it is able to fully observe the objects of the Four Noble Truths and fully cultivate the sixteen aspects (ākāra).
One contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering by cultivating four aspects:
first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self.
One contemplates the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering] by cultivating four aspects:
First, cause; second, accumulation; third, arising; fourth, condition.
One contemplates the Noble Truth of Cessation through four aspects:
first, cessation; second, tranquility; third, excellence; fourth, renunciation.
One contemplates the Noble Truth of the Path through four aspects:
first, the path; second, the correct method; third, practice; and fourth, renunciation.
The distinctions between these aspects will be explained later.

When these roots of goodness of heat (*uṣmagata*) gradually increase through their lower, middle, and upper stages until they reach full maturity, another root of goodness arises which is called the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*); because this is even more excellent, it is established as a distinct name.
Among the moving roots of goodness, this dharma is the most supreme; because it is like the crown of a person's head, it is called the "Summit Dharma" (*mūrdhan*).
Alternatively, because it marks the boundary between advancing and retreating, like the peak of a mountain, it is said to be named the "Summit."
This is also like the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), which fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths and is capable of fully cultivating the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
Thus, at the moment these two roots of goodness—Heat and Peak (*mūrdhan*)—are first established, they consist solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
In what sense is it called "the first placing of the foot"?

It means that whichever root of goodness [is employed], by means of the sixteen aspects, one initially traverses the path of the Four Noble Truths; subsequently, when progressing further, one becomes endowed with the four foundations of mindfulness.
Those roots of goodness previously attained do not manifest later, because one no longer gives rise to a sense of reverence toward them.

These roots of goodness of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) increase gradually through the stages of inferior, medium, and superior; when they reach the point of full maturity, a root of goodness arises called the "Dharma of Patience" (*kṣānti*), for among those capable of patient acceptance regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths, this is the most excellent.
Furthermore, because this stage of patience (kṣānti) is free from falling back, it is called the "Dharma of Patience" (kṣāntidharma).
These roots of goodness of patience—whether established or further advanced—are all the mindfulness of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna), which distinguishes them from what preceded.

However, this dharma of patience (kṣānti) has three grades—lower, middle, and upper. The lower and middle grades are identical to the stage of the summits (mūrdhan), meaning they involve the full investigation of the objects of the Four Noble Truths and the complete cultivation of the sixteen aspects (ākāra).
The upper grade differs: it contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm, as it is immediately contiguous with the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma).

Based on this principle, it is established that the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) are all capable of fully taking the suffering and other truths of the three realms as their objects, as there is no distinction made [in the texts].

This means that as the practitioner of yoga gradually reduces and condenses the aspects and objects of each Noble Truth—such as the paths of antidote for the form and formless realms—until they are contemplating the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm with only two moments of mental attention, the stage prior to this point is called the "Middle Patience" (*madhyamā kṣānti*).

Immediately following this stage, the arising of a superior root of goodness for a single moment and a single mental application is called "superior patience" (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), because these roots of goodness arise without continuity.
Immediately after superior patience, the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is produced.

As with the aforementioned "patience of the highest degree," which takes the truth of suffering in the desire realm as its object and cultivates a single aspect for only a single moment, this too is called "mundane" because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), and it is called "foremost" because it is the most excellent.
These contaminated phenomena are the most excellent within the mundane world; therefore, they are called the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Because they possess human effort (*puruṣakāra*), they transcend their homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) and induce the arising of the Noble Path; thus, they are named "most excellent."

These four types of wholesome roots, such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence because they are of the nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). If accompanied by their associated factors (*sahabhū*), they consist of all five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
However, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of these is excluded, lest the wholesome roots of Heat and so forth should manifest again in those who are already Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Among these, when the stage of Heat (uṣmagata) is first established, with respect to the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna taking the three truths as its object, one cultivates the four [smṛtyupasthānas] in the future; with respect to each individual aspect (ākāra), one cultivates the four in the future while it is present.

When the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna is cultivated in the present with the truth of cessation as its object, one [smṛtyupasthāna] is cultivated in the future; regarding one aspect, four aspects are cultivated in the future.
This is because this lineage has not been previously attained, and only those of the same category can be cultivated.

When subsequently progressing, one takes the three truths as objects; according to each momentary abiding (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one cultivates the four present and the four future; according to each mode of activity (*ākāra*), one cultivates the sixteen present and the sixteen future.

When the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna is cultivated in the present with the truth of cessation as its object, four are cultivated in the future; for one aspect is cultivated in the present and sixteen are cultivated in the future, because those of this lineage have already previously attained them, and even those of a different category can cultivate them.

When first placing the foot upon the crown of the head, one practices the present mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) based on the four truths, which brings about the future four; according to each individual aspect (ākāra), one practices the present [aspect], which brings about the future sixteen.

Later, at the time of further progress, when taking the three truths as objects, one cultivates four future [applications of mindfulness] in accordance with whichever single application of mindfulness is present, and cultivates sixteen future [aspects] in accordance with whichever single aspect is present.

Taking the Dharma pertaining to the Truth of Cessation as an object, one cultivates the present foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the four future ones; according to each respective aspect (ākāra), one cultivates the present and the sixteen future ones.

Regarding the initial establishment and subsequent progress of Patience (kṣānti), taking the Dharmas pertaining to the Four Truths as objects, one cultivates the present foundations of mindfulness and the four future ones; according to each respective aspect, one cultivates the present and the sixteen future ones.

However, when the objects of focus are abbreviated during the stage of intensification, one follows that abbreviation of the objects and does not cultivate those specific mental aspects (*ākāra*). Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*):

when taking the suffering truth of the desire realm as an object, one cultivates the present application of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the four future ones; for each single mental aspect, one cultivates the present one and the four future ones. This is because there is no differentiation [of aspects] and because they resemble the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Having already explained the characteristics and essence of the roots of goodness that arise, we shall now explain their specific distinctions.
The verse says:
These factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are all produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
The sixth stage has two, or the seventh; based on a body of the desire realm, there are nine.
Three types of individuals—female, male, and neutral—attain two; the same applies to the female in the fourth stage.
The noble ones relinquish them by losing their stage, while ordinary beings do so by the end of their life.

The first two are also abandoned through falling away; based on the fundamental [attainment], one must see the truths. Having abandoned them, what is acquired was not previously so. The nature of these two abandonments is non-possession (*aprāpti*). The treatise says: The first two [paths of seeing] are also abandoned through falling away. Based on the fundamental [attainment], one must necessarily see the truths. Once abandoned, what is acquired was not previously so. The nature of these two abandonments is non-possession. The commentary states: The first two paths of seeing are also abandoned through falling away. When based on the fundamental attainment, one must necessarily see the truths. Having abandoned them, what is subsequently acquired was not previously so. The nature of these two types of abandonment is non-possession. The treatise says:
These four distinguished roots of goodness—heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas—are called the "aids to penetration" (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Based on what meaning is the name "aids to penetration" established?
"Decisive" (*niścaya*) means decisive resolution; "discernment" (*pravicaya*) means analytical discernment.

Decisive resolution and analytical discernment refer to the noble paths (*āryamārga*), because the noble paths are able to sever doubt and are able to differentiate the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths.

"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to a portion; this term intends to show that what is conformed to is only one part of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), specifically the portion of "thorough discernment" (*nirvedha*), and thus it receives the name "portion conducive to thorough discernment" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

These four serve as conditions to draw forth the portion of thorough discernment; because they are beneficial and conform to it, they receive the name "conducive to that. Therefore, these are called the "factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

These four types are all accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), not through hearing or reflection (*śruta-maya* or *cintā-maya*), because they belong exclusively to the stage of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
Among these four, the first two are comprised within the inferior grade, as both are subject to fluctuation and can still be lost.

The stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is comprised of the middle grade, because it is superior to the preceding two stages and because the "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) serves as its upper limit.
The supreme worldly dharma alone constitutes the upper grade.
These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) all rely upon six stages, namely: the four *dhyānas*, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
It does not exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it lacks the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
It also does not exist in the other higher realms, because [the path of seeing] is an associate of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, because the mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) does not take the desire realm as its object, and because the objects of the desire realm must first be fully known and abandoned.

These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) serve as the cause for the full maturation (*vipāka*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), but they cannot project [a new existence], because they are characterized by aversion toward and turning away from existence (*bhava*).
The word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate that there are two differing views regarding the first two, namely, *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit).
The Venerable Ghosaka says:

These four roots of goodness depend upon the six stages [of the form realm] and the seventh stage, which is the desire realm. They arise within the bodies of the desire realm; among humans and devas, they arise in nine locations, excluding Uttarakuru. The first three roots of goodness initially arise in the three continents, and subsequently continue to manifest even when one is born in the celestial realms.
The fourth root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) also arises in the celestial realms (*devasthāna*), for it lacks beginning or end and lasts for but a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

These four roots of goodness depend exclusively upon those who are male or female: while the first three are obtained by both males and females alike, the fourth is also obtained by two types within the female body.
A male, relying on this stage, acquires only the roots of goodness of the male body, because he has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body.

When a noble one attains these roots of goodness while relying on this stage, they are abandoned only when that stage is lost; the phrase "losing the stage" indicates the transition to birth in a higher stage.
Whether ordinary beings lose or do not lose a particular stage (*bhūmi*), they necessarily abandon these roots of goodness if they lose their homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

The first two roots of goodness are also abandoned through falling away (*parihāṇi*); abandonment through death and falling away applies only to ordinary beings and not to noble ones (*ārya*), while abandonment through losing the stage applies only to noble ones and not to ordinary beings.
Regarding patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), even ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not regress.

When one gives rise to the roots of goodness such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) based on the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), they will certainly attain the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) in this very life, because their mind of revulsion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is extremely intense.
If one reacquires [a discipline] after having previously relinquished it, that which is acquired is necessarily not the same as what was previously relinquished.

This is like the case of reacquiring the prātimokṣa restraint after it has been relinquished; because it was never previously cultivated through habitual practice, it must be accomplished through great effort.

If one has previously attained the wholesome roots such as *ūṣmagata* and loses them due to passing through a rebirth, one will produce the *mūrdhan* and subsequent stages upon encountering a teacher who skillfully explains the various phases of realization; if one does not encounter such a teacher, one must cultivate from the beginning again.

The two types of abandonment—loss (*hāni*) and falling away (*parihāṇi*)—have non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) as their nature. Falling away necessarily involves the arising of faults, whereas loss does not necessarily do so.
What are the benefits of attaining these roots of virtue?
The verse says:
Those with *ūṣmagata* will certainly attain *nirvāṇa*; those at the stage of *mūrdhan* never sever the roots of goodness;
those with *kṣānti* do not fall into the evil destinies; and those at the first stage enter the state beyond birth (*niyāma*).
The commentary says:

Among the four roots of goodness, if one attains the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), although there may be regression, the severing of the roots of goodness, the commission of deeds of immediate retribution, or falling into the evil destinies, one will not wander for long, as one is certain to reach nirvāṇa.
If that is so, how does this differ from the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*)?
If there are no obstacles, one is close to seeing the truth (*darśana*), for this is identical in its mode of operation to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
If one attains the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), although there may be regression and so forth, one increases the capacity for ultimate non-interruption of the roots of virtue.

When one attains *kṣānti*, although at the end of life one relinquishes it and remains in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one increases [in merit] without regression, does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), and does not fall into the evil destinies.

However, since the verse mentions only the phrase "not falling into the evil destinies," it is understood by implication that one does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution; for those who commit the deeds of immediate retribution necessarily fall into the evil destinies.
That there is no falling back from the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) has already been explained above.
One does not fall into the various evil destinies at this stage because one has already distanced oneself from the karma and afflictions that lead to them.
If one reaches the stage of patience, one attains the quality of non-arising (*anutpatti-dharma*) regarding rebirth in certain destinies, births, places, bodies, and among the delusions.
"Destinies" refers to the various evil destinies.
"Births" refers to birth from eggs and moisture.
"Abodes" refers to the station of non-perception, Uttarakuru, and the station of Mahābrahmā.
"Body" refers to the bodies of *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*).
"Existence" refers to the eighth existence and so forth.
"Afflictions" refers to the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).

These are attained according to their respective levels, whether lower or higher; that is to say, the non-arising of rebirth in the evil destinies is attained at the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), while the non-arising of the remaining [rebirths] is attained only upon reaching "supreme patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).

One who has attained the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), although still abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is able to enter the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Although the verse does not explicitly state that it is abandoned at the end of life, since one enters the state of rightness and departure from birth immediately thereafter, it follows by implication that there is no abandonment at the end of life.
For what reason can only these [roots] enter the state of being free from birth?

Because one has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and because they can abandon the nature of an ordinary person just as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) does.
These four roots of goodness each have three grades, due to the differences in the lineages (*gotra*) of the śrāvakas and others.
Once roots of goodness have arisen within any given spiritual lineage (*gotra*), can they be shifted and turned toward another vehicle?
The verse states:
The lineage of the Śrāvaka may be transformed: two become Buddhas; three become others.
The Pratyekabuddha who is like a rhinoceros horn has no turning back, because he attains awakening while seated in a single session.
The Commentary says:

Those of the Śrāvaka lineage for whom the stages of *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summit) have already arisen may still turn toward and achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; however, if they attain the stage of *kṣānti* (patience), there is no principle by which they could become a Buddha, because they have already transcended the evil destinies.

Bodhisattvas take the benefit of sentient beings as their primary concern; in order to transform them, they must inevitably go to the evil realms. Since their lineage of patience is irreversible, it is certain that there is no possibility of their attaining Buddhahood.

The three stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* within the *śrāvaka* lineage can all be transformed into the state of a *pratyekabuddha*; because they lie outside the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*), they are referred to as "the others.
The terms "rhinoceros-like" and "Buddha" clarify the rhinoceros-like *pratyekabuddha* and the Unsurpassed Enlightenment (*anuttarabodhi*), respectively.

The roots of goodness, such as "Heat" (uṣmagata) and the others, have no sense of being transferred or redirected toward other vehicles; they all take the fourth dhyāna as their basis, because one achieves the awakening of one's own vehicle in a single sitting.
Because the fourth dhyāna is an unshakable and most intensely lucid samādhi, it is capable of serving as the basis for the supreme awakening of the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha].
Here, the term "awakening" (bodhi) indicates the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, which will be explained later, as this is the very nature of bodhi.
Regarding the phrase "sitting on one seat": from the root of goodness known as *ūṣmagata* until the attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*), he does not rise from his seat.
Other masters say:
from the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) until the attainment of enlightenment, he does not rise from his seat.

There are other Pratyekabuddhas, distinct from those who resemble a rhinoceros horn, who give rise to the first two roots of goodness belonging to that lineage and then turn toward another vehicle; this is logically unobstructed.
Is it possible that one who initiates this practice for the first time in this very life can, in that same life, bring forth the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
It is not so. Why? The verse says:
The preceding stage of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) leads to liberation within at most three lifetimes;
it is accomplished through hearing and reflection, constitutes the three types of karma, and is planted by humans in the three continents.
The commentary states:
Those who give rise to the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in this life must have previously given rise to the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
For those who first plant the seeds of the aids to liberation, it takes at most three lifetimes before they attain liberation.

This means that in the first birth one gives rise to the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); in the second birth one gives rise to the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); and in the third birth one enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*) and even attains liberation.
This is analogous to three distinct stages: sowing the seed, the growth of the sprout, and the ripening of the fruit.
The three stages of entering the dharma-nature, maturation, and liberation are likewise so.

It is traditionally taught that these factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) consist solely of what is produced by hearing and reflection, and have the three types of action as their essence.

Although, in the ultimate sense, this consists solely of mental action (*manas-karman*), the volition and aspiration that encompass bodily and vocal actions are also designated as "factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).

When one who deeply desires liberation offers a single meal or observes a single precept, and these acts are sustained by the power of such an aspiration, they are termed the "planting of factors conducive to liberation."

The cultivation of the roots of merit conducive to liberation occurs only among humans in the three continents, because in other realms there is a lack of the necessary factors—namely, world-weariness, renunciation, and wisdom—as appropriate. One cultivates these roots of goodness upon encountering the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Other masters say:
"One may also encounter a Pratyekabuddha.

Having already discussed the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) as an incidental point, the actual subject under discussion is now the sequence of entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

Among these, the various paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) have already been explained, with the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) as their final stage. It should now be stated what path arises immediately thereafter.
The verse says:
Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, One takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object.
One gives rise to the patience regarding the dharma of the outflow-free; following patience, one gives rise to the dharma-knowledge.
Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as its object, one gives rise to the subsequent patience and subsequent knowledge.
Taking the truths of origin, cessation, and the path as objects, four [knowledges and patiences] arise for each in the same manner.
These sixteen moments of mind are called the "clear realization of the noble truths" (*āryasatyābhisamaya*).
This is comprised of three types, namely: [the distinction between] seeing, the object, and the particulars.
The treatise says:

Immediately following the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) root of goodness, there arises the "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), which takes the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering within the desire realm and is comprised within the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. To demonstrate that this receptivity is outflow-free, the subsequent concordant result (*niṣyanda*) is cited as its defining characteristic.

This is capable of producing the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); as it is the cause of the knowledge of phenomena, it receives the name "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), just as a tree is named after its flowers or fruit.

This very state is called "entering into the state of correctness and departure from birth" (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*), and it is also called "entering into the state of correctness and certainty" (*samyaktvaniyama*).
Because this is the initial entry into the state of correctness and freedom from outflows (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and also the initial entry into the state of certainty (*niyāma*).
The Sūtra speaks of "correctness" (*samyaktva*), which refers to Nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, the term "right nature" (samyaktva) refers to the various noble paths (*āryamārga*).
"Birth" (*jāti*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), or to the faculties not yet being mature.

Because the noble path is able to transcend these, it is called "leaving birth" (*niyāma*). It is so named because it is able to definitively lead toward *nirvāṇa*, or because it definitively realizes the characteristics of the truths (*satya-lakṣaṇa*).
The various noble paths receive the designation "definitive," and reaching this stage is called "entry.
Once this patience (*kṣānti*) has arisen, one obtains the name of a noble one (*ārya*); while it exists in the future, it abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

This means that it is accepted that this patience (*kṣānti*) possesses this function when it arises in the future, and no other [dharma] does, just like a lamp or the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).
Other masters say:

"The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). This interpretation is not correct, because both are equally termed mundane dharmas and their natures are mutually contradictory.
Nor is there any fault [in this], just as one might strike off an enemy's life by leaning upon the enemy's shoulder.
Other masters say:
these two abandon [the object] together, because they are like the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object; this is called "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*).
It should be understood that this knowledge is also included within the category of the untainted (*anāsrava*), because the preceding term "untainted" applies universally to what follows.

Just as when taking the noble truth of suffering in the desire realm as its object, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arise;

likewise, immediately following that knowledge of the dharma, there arises a patience regarding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) which takes the noble truth of suffering in the remaining realms collectively as its object, and this is called the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) taking this same object as its focus; it is called "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).

Because it is the first to realize the true reality of all phenomena, it is termed "dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*); because the subsequent object and knowledge resemble those of the former, it receives the name "subsequent" (*anvaya*), as it realizes the object by following after the former.

Just as there arise the four—namely, the receptivities to the dharma and subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñāna-kṣānti* and *anvayajñāna-kṣānti*, and the corresponding knowledges)—taking the Truth of Suffering in the Desire Realm and elsewhere as their object, so it is for each of the remaining three Truths.

That is to say, following the aforementioned subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*), there subsequently arises a receptivity to dharma-knowledge taking the Noble Truth of the Origin (*samudaya-āryasatya*) in the Desire Realm as its object; this is called the receptivity to dharma-knowledge of the origin (*samudayadharmajñānakṣānti*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that takes as its object the phenomena belonging to the origin of suffering in the desire realm; this is called the "dharma-knowledge of origin" (*samudayadharmajñāna*).

Next, there arises a subsequent-knowledge-patience (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) that takes as its object the noble truth of the origin of suffering in the remaining realms; this is called the "subsequent-knowledge-patience of origin" (*samudayanvayajñānakṣānti*).
Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) taking this same object; it is called the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*).

Next, there arises a dharma-knowledge patience (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) taking the noble truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the desire realm as its object; it is called the dharma-knowledge patience of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that takes as its object the cessation of phenomena belonging to the desire realm; this is called the "dharma-knowledge of cessation" (*nirodhadharmajñāna*).

Subsequently, there arises a subsequent-knowledge patience (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) that takes as its object the noble truth of cessation pertaining to the remaining realms; this is called the "subsequent-knowledge patience of cessation" (*nirodhānvayajñānakṣānti*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) taking this same object; it is called the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*).

Next, there arises a patience regarding the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) taking the noble truth of the path (*mārga-āryasatya*) of the desire realm as its object; it is called the patience of the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) taking the path of the desire realm as its object; this is called the "dharma-knowledge of the path" (*mārga-dharmajñāna*).

Next, there arises a subsequent-knowledge-patience (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) taking the noble truth of the path in the remaining realms as its object; this is called the "subsequent-knowledge-patience of the path" (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).

Immediately following this patience (*kṣānti*), there arises a subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) taking this same object as its domain; this is called the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).
In this manner, there are sixteen moments of mind in succession, which collectively are termed the "clear realization of the noble truths" (*āryasatya-abhisamaya*).
Regarding this, other schools (nikāyas) maintain that within the truths,
there is only a simultaneous realization (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*).
However, their underlying intention should be further investigated, for their use of the term "realization" is made without distinction.
In detail, there are three types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), distinguished by way of vision, object, and activity.

Only untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that clearly perceives the objects of the truths is called "clear realization as vision" (*darśana-abhisamaya*). This untainted wisdom, together with its associated factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) sharing the same object, is called "clear realization as object" (*ālambana-abhisamaya*). These various cognitive subjects, together with their concomitant non-associated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) such as morality (*śīla*) and birth (*jāti*), which share the same activity, are called "clear realization as activity" (*kārya-abhisamaya*).

When one perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one possesses the three types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering; regarding the other three truths, there is only the clear realization of the object (*vastv-abhisamaya*), namely, abandonment (*prahāṇa*), realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

If it were said that clear realization is simultaneous (*sakṛd-abhisamaya*) with respect to the perception of the truths, this would necessarily be illogical, because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ among the various truths.

If one were to say that all truths are perceived collectively through the single aspect of selflessness, then one would not need to perceive the Truth of Suffering and the others through their respective aspects such as suffering; this would thus contradict the sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"The noble disciples contemplate suffering through the aspect of suffering, they contemplate origination through the aspect of origination, they contemplate cessation through the aspect of cessation, and they contemplate the path through the aspect of the path; this is the discernment of phenomena associated with untainted mental attention."

If it is argued that this sutra describes the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this is also not the case, because it is like [the description of] the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Furthermore, if they were to claim that when one truth is seen, one attains mastery over the remaining truths and thus speaks of simultaneous realization (*ekakṣaṇābhisamaya*), there is no logical fault in this either.
However, within such a process of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one must separately investigate whether [the realization] arises or does not arise.

If they further claim that at the time of seeing suffering (*duḥkha*), one is simultaneously able to abandon the origin (*samudaya*), realize cessation (*nirodha*), and cultivate the path (*mārga*)—that is, that there is a simultaneous clear realization—there is no logical fault in this, because it has already been stated previously that at the time of seeing the truth of suffering, there is a clear realization of the objective fact (*vastv-abhisamaya*) regarding the other three truths.
Regarding the clear realization through vision (*darśana-abhisamaya*), there is an explicit scriptural passage in the sūtras that speaks of gradual clear realization.
As a sūtra states,
the Buddha addressed a householder:
"One does not realize the Four Noble Truths instantaneously, but must realize them progressively," and so forth, as explained at length.
There are three such sūtras, each containing a distinct analogy.
If it is argued that there is a sūtra stating: "One has neither doubt nor uncertainty regarding the Truth of Suffering alone, and likewise none regarding the Buddha;
therefore, there is sudden realization (abhisamaya)," this too is not proof, for it refers to a state where [doubt] does not function due to meditative concentration (samādhi).
Or it must necessarily be abandoned, because it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Having already analyzed that the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) consists of sixteen moments of mind, upon which basis do these sixteen moments of mind rely?
The verse says:
All [the moments of mind] share with the Supreme Mundane Dharma the same basis on a single stage.
The Commentary says:
One should know that whichever stages serve as the basis for the Supreme Mundane Dharma are likewise the bases for these sixteen moments of mind.
Those [stages] rely upon six grounds, as previously explained.
For what reason must such forbearance (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) necessarily arise in an alternating sequence of prior and posterior?
The verse says:
"Patience and knowledge follow their respective order as the path of uninterrupted realization and the path of liberation.
The commentary states:

Among the sixteen moments of mind, patience (*kṣānti*) constitutes the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), because with respect to the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions, it is incapable of being obstructed or hindered.
Wisdom is the path of liberation, because once one has attained liberation from the afflictions, it arises simultaneously with the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
This principle must necessarily be so according to the two successive stages, just as in the world one drives out thieves and then closes the door.

If it is claimed that in the second case the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises simultaneously with the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), then in that state, one would necessarily fail to give rise to the knowledge that has already severed doubt regarding those respective objects.

If it is claimed that in the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) only the receptivities (*kṣānti*) sever the afflictions, then this contradicts the *Śāstra*’s exposition on the nine clusters of fetters (*saṃyojana-kāya*).
This objection is not valid, because all forms of patience (*kṣānti*) are attendants of wisdom (*jñāna*); thus, the deeds performed by a king’s attendants are called the deeds of the king.
Since all these sixteen moments of mind perceive the principle of the truths (*satyadarśana*), can it be said that they are all subsumed within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
