Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
The first fifteen moments constitute the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what has not been seen before.
The treatise says:

Beginning with the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and ending with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), there are a total of fifteen moments within this interval; all are subsumed under the Path of Seeing, as they involve seeing the Truths (*satya*) not previously seen.

Upon reaching the sixteenth moment, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there is not a single principle of truth that was previously unseen and is now seen; rather, it is like practicing what has already been seen. Therefore, it is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

One might object: "At that time, does one not observe the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) as a principle of the truth of the path that was previously unseen and is now seen?"
In this context, the reference is to the truths (*satya*) and not to moments (*kṣaṇa*).

It is not the case that one could say "one now sees what was previously unseen" regarding a single moment; for it is impossible to say that a field of rice has not been harvested simply because one stalk remains, as if the entire field were still unharvested.

Furthermore, because the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is subsumed under the category of fruition, because it involves the simultaneous cultivation of eight knowledges and sixteen aspects, because it abandons the preceding path, and because it arises in a continuous succession—just like other paths of cultivation—it is not subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

However, as for the fact that the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is necessarily non-retrogressive, this is because it maintains the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). For this very reason, it should be subsumed under the path of seeing.
This objection is not valid, for it entails the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For what reason are the seven knowledges also subsumed under the Path of Seeing?

Because the realization of the principles of the Truths has not yet been finalized; that is to say, because they arise during the interim before the realization of the principles of the Truths has been fully completed, they are also subsumed under the Path of Seeing.

Having already explained the differences in the arising of the two paths—seeing and cultivation—one should now establish the various noble *pudgalas* based on the distinctions in the stages of these paths.
First, regarding the establishment of the distinctions among noble beings based on the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing, the verse says:
They are named "Followers by Faith" and "Followers by Dharma," Due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties.
One who possesses the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and has abandoned from one up to five [categories] is a candidate for the first fruit;
having abandoned the next three, one is a candidate for the second; and having abandoned those up to the eighth category, one is a candidate for the third.
The Commentary says:

Within the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two types of noble ones (*ārya*): first, those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), and second, those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*). These two names are established based on the distinction between dull and sharp faculties; those with dull faculties are called followers by faith, while those with sharp faculties are called followers by dharma.

One who practices in accordance with faith is called a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārī*). Because such a person possesses this practice of following faith, they are termed a "follower by faith"; alternatively, because they have cultivated this practice of following faith until it becomes their very nature, they are called a "follower by faith," since they previously followed the meaning [of the teachings] based on the faith of others.

Based on this, one should explain the "follower of the Dharma" (*dharmānusārī*): because in a previous time they followed the meaning of the teachings by personally studying the *sūtras* and other such dharmas.

These two types of noble ones (*ārya*) are established as three "paths of approach" (*pratipannaka*) due to differences in their complete abandonment of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). That is to say, if these two noble ones, at a prior time, have not yet abandoned the afflictions of cultivation through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they are called "fully bound" (*sakalabandhana*). Alternatively, if they have previously abandoned from one up to five categories (*prakāra*) of the desire realm, upon reaching this stage they are called "approaching the first fruit" (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*), because they are proceeding toward the first fruit.

Regarding the "first fruit," this refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), because it is necessarily the first fruit attained among all the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya-phala*).

If one has previously abandoned six, seven, or eight categories of afflictions of the desire realm, upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the second fruit (*dvitīya-phala-pratipannaka*), because one is proceeding toward the second fruit.
The second fruit refers to the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), as it is the second among all fruits attained.

If one has previously abandoned the nine grades of desire-realm attachment, or has previously severed even a single grade of the first dhyāna, up to having completely abandoned the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), then upon reaching this stage, one is called a candidate for the third fruit (*tṛtīyaphalapratipannaka*), because one is proceeding toward the third fruit.
The third fruit refers to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*); its enumeration follows the previous explanation.

Next, regarding the establishment of distinctions among the noble ones (*ārya*) at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the verse says:
Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, One abides in a fruit according to one of the three directions.
They are named *śraddhādhimukta* and *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, distinguished by the difference between dull and sharp faculties.
The treatise says:

Those previously described as followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind—the knowledge of the path-category (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*)—are said to be "abiding in the fruit" and are no longer called "strivers."

Following the three previous paths of approach, one now abides in the three fruits: that is, the previous candidate for the fruit of stream-entry now abides in the fruit of stream-entry; the previous candidate for the fruit of once-returning now abides in the fruit of once-returning; and the previous candidate for the fruit of non-returning now abides in the fruit of non-returning.

The fruit of Arhatship can never be attained for the first time [at this stage], because the Path of Seeing cannot eliminate the afflictions of the realm of cultivation, and the mundane path cannot bring about detachment from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Upon reaching the stage of abiding in the fruit, one abandons two names and acquires two others: namely, one no longer bears the names of "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) or "follower by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*), but instead acquires the two names of "one resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). This distinction likewise arises from the difference between dull and sharp faculties.

Those of dull faculties who were previously termed "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin) are now termed "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta); those of sharp faculties who were previously termed "followers by dharma" (dharmānusārin) are now termed "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

Because these two types of noble ones possess a predominance of either faith or wisdom respectively, they are distinguished by the specific names "resolved through faith" and "attained through vision."

For what reason, when one has previously abandoned from one to five levels of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, is it only at the sixteenth moment—the path-knowledge of subsequent types—that one is said to have attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth, rather than being designated as one "progressing toward" a later fruit?
The verse says:
Among those who have attained the stages of fruition, because they have not yet attained the path to a superior fruition,
and thus have not yet given rise to that superior path, they are called "abiders in fruition" rather than "candidates."
The Commentary states:

At the time of attaining any fruit, one has necessarily not yet attained the path of the superior fruit; therefore, as long as one who abides in a fruit has not yet given rise to the path of the superior fruit, they are called merely "abiding in the fruit" and not "oriented toward the subsequent [fruit]."

However, for those who have previously abandoned from one to five levels of the afflictions to be abandoned through meditation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, at the time they attain the fruit, it is certain that in this very life they will give rise to the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Consequently, those who have previously become detached from the defilements of the three dhyānas and subsequently entered the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) based on a lower stage, once they have attained the fruit, will necessarily be able to induce the subsequent path of superior fruit within their present life.
If it were otherwise, one born as a noble being in a higher stage could not be said to necessarily possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

Having thus established the distinctions among the noble beings based on those who enter the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) while already possessing, partially free from, or entirely free from desire, we shall now explain the distinctions in the stages of the gradual arising of the antidotal paths (*pratipakṣamārga*) with respect to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The verse says:
In each stage, there are nine faults and virtues; three each for the inferior, middling, and superior.
The commentary says:
"Loss" refers to faults, which are the obstacles to be remedied;
"virtue" refers to meritorious qualities, which are the path that serves as the remedy.

As was previously explained regarding the nine grades of distinctions for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, the same principle should be applied by analogy to the higher stages up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Just as the obstacles to be abandoned in each stage (bhūmi) are each divided into nine grades, so too are the remedial paths—the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga)—each divided into nine grades.
How is it that these faults are each divided into nine grades?

This means that within the fundamental categories there are inferior, middling, and superior levels; each of these three is further divided into inferior, middling, and superior distinctions. Consequently, the faults and virtues are each divided into nine grades: namely, the inferior-inferior, inferior-middling, and inferior-superior; the middling-inferior, middling-middling, and middling-superior; and the superior-inferior, superior-middling, and superior-superior.

It should be understood that herein, the power of the lowest-of-the-low path is able to sever the highest-of-the-high obstructions, and so on, up until the power of the highest-of-the-high path is able to sever the lowest-of-the-low obstructions.

Because the various remedial qualities, such as the highest-of-the-high grade (*adhimātrādhimātra*), are initially absent, and because these qualities eventually cause the faults of the highest-of-the-high grade and so forth to cease to exist;
it is like the stage of washing clothes, where coarse stains are removed first, and subsequently, finer stains are gradually eliminated.
Furthermore, just as coarse darkness can be dispelled by a small light, but only a great light can dispel subtle darkness,
the same principle applies to the relationship between faults and virtues.

Since the power of the white dharma is strong while the power of the black dharma is weak, when the inferior path manifests for even a single moment, it can cause the superior afflictions— which have been successively reinforced since beginningless time— to be severed instantaneously.
Just as various ailments accumulated over a long period can be cured all at once by taking a small amount of excellent medicine,
or as great darkness accumulated over a long time can be extinguished in a single instant by a small lamp.
Having already distinguished the nine grades of the faults and defects, we shall next establish the distinctions among the noble ones based upon them.

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for those in training (*śaikṣa*), they are collectively termed "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Furthermore, there are many specific subdivisions according to their respective stages; first, we shall establish the case of those who have not yet abandoned any [defilements].
The verse says:
Having not yet abandoned the faults to be abandoned by cultivation, one who abides in the fruit [of Stream-enterer] returns at most seven times.
The commentary says:

Those who abide in the fruit [of stream-entry] and have not yet abandoned any of the faults to be eliminated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in any stage are called "stream-enterers" (*srotāpanna*).
Regarding the expression "at most seven returns," the term "seven returns" indicates seven cycles of returning; this signifies the meaning of seven births each among gods and humans.
The use of the term "maximum" is intended to show that the number of rebirths is greatest, for not all stream-enterers undergo exactly seven returns.
When the Sūtra speaks of "at most seven returns," it means that seven returns is the maximum number of births they may experience.
All untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are collectively termed "flows" (*srotas*), because one proceeds toward nirvāṇa by means of them as the cause.
The term "entering" (*prati*) is used to indicate the initial attainment; because one has entered those [flows], one is called a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*).
What is the meaning of the term "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna)?
If the first attainment of the path is what constitutes a stream-enterer, then the name "stream-enterer" should apply to the eighth person (aṣṭamaka).

If the first attainment of the fruit is what constitutes a stream-enterer, then those who have either partially or fully abandoned desire would have to be called stream-enterers upon reaching the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna).
This designation "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) refers to the first fruit attained; however, it is established based on the first fruit obtained by one who will eventually attain all the fruits.

Since the fruits of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and non-returner (anāgāmin) are not necessarily attained first, whereas this [fruit] is definitely attained first, it is therefore called "stream-entry."
For what reason is this name not applied to the eighth [moment]?

Because it is only upon reaching the time of attaining *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* that one fully acquires both the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*), as well as the untainted paths of both seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

One is called a "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) because they have attained the universal flow of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); the eighth [candidate] is not so, therefore the name "Stream-enterer" does not refer to the eighth.

From that point onward, among humans, they undergo at most seven intermediate existences (*antarābhava*) and seven existences of birth (*upapattibhava*); the same applies to the heavenly realms, totaling twenty-eight. Since all these are in groups of seven, it is said they are "at most seven times reborn" (*sapta-kṛtvah-parama*), just as with the "skillful in seven places" (*saptasthānakauśalya*) or the "seven-leaf tree" (*saptaparṇa*).
Such is the explanation given by the Vaibhāṣika masters.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state that it is impossible and there is no occasion for one who is perfected to undergo an eighth existence?
The intention of this sutra refers to a single destination (*ekāyana*). If one were to adhere to the literal meaning, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist.
If that were so, then for those who "flow upwards" to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there would likewise be no eighth birth within that single destination.
There is no such fault because this is spoken in reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
What serves as the proof for this?
Is it scripture (*āgama*) or reasoning (*yukti*)?
By what means is it proven that one undergoes seven births separately among humans and devas, rather than receiving seven births collectively?
It is because the sūtra speaks of "seven [births] among devas and humans.

The Kāśyapīya school’s sūtra clearly distinguishes that one undergoes seven births in each of the human and deva realms; therefore, one should not dogmatically insist on the former interpretation here.
If one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) within the human realm, they attain parinirvāṇa by returning to the human realm;
if attained within the celestial realm, they do so by returning to the celestial realm.
For what reason does such a person not undergo an eighth existence?
Because the continuity [of their existence] must necessarily reach maturity by this point, such is the natural law regarding the categories of the Noble Path.
It is like a seven-step snake or a quartan malaria fever.

Furthermore, because they still possess seven remaining fetters—namely, the two lower fetters and the five higher fetters—even though the Noble Path may manifest in the interim, they do not realize parinirvāṇa due to the sustaining power of their residual karma.
Upon reaching his seventh existence, when he encounters a time when the Buddha-dharma has disappeared, he attains the fruit of Arhatship while still living as a householder.
Having attained this fruit, he will certainly not remain in the household life; by the very nature of things, he spontaneously assumes the physical appearance of a bhikṣu.
Some say:
"He has gone forth as a renunciant in another path.
How, then, can he be said to possess the quality of non-retrogression?"

Because they do not produce karma leading to decline; because they oppose the production of such karma and its fruits; because powerful roots of goodness suppress their bodies; and because both their applied effort and their underlying intention are pure.
Even those who possess the karma that would certainly cause them to fall into the evil destinies do not yet give rise to patience, let alone attain the stage of Stream-enterer.
Thus, a verse says:
"The fool, though his transgression be small, falls into the evil destinies; The wise, though their transgression be great, are liberated from suffering."
Just as a lump of iron sinks even if it is small, yet a bowl made of iron floats even if it is large;
so too, the Sūtra states that the Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) makes an end to suffering. Based on what meaning is the term "end of suffering" established?
Based on this [attainment], suffering will not arise again hereafter; this is the meaning of ensuring that subsequent suffering does not continue.
Alternatively, the limit of suffering is what is called nirvāṇa. How could nirvāṇa be something produced?
Because those [other states] have their obstacles removed, the word "making" (kṛtvā) is used.
It is like saying "making empty," which refers to the demolition of a palace or pavilion.
Although other stages also involve at most seven more births, they are not certain; therefore, they are not mentioned.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-three [continued] / Fascicle Twenty-four,
composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree.

Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Noble Ones, Part Three. It has already been explained that one who abides in the fruit [of stream-entry] without having yet abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation is called a "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna), who is reborn at most seven times.
Now, one should distinguish the noble ones according to their stages of abandonment; first, one should establish the candidates for and fruits of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The verse says:
Having abandoned the third or fourth category of desire, One is a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner, having three or two more births.
"Having abandoned up to five [categories of afflictions], one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six, one attains the fruit of once-returner.
The commentary states:

"That is to say, when a stream-enterer further abandons the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, if three conditions are met, they are designated as a 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula) practitioner."
First, by the abandonment of afflictions, because one abandons three or four categories of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Second, by the attainment of faculties, because one acquires the untainted faculties that serve as antidotes to those afflictions.
Third, by the taking of birth, because one takes further birth for three or two existences within the desire realm.

In the verse, only the first and last conditions are mentioned; this is because it is stated that after the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), one proceeds to abandon the afflictions, thereby establishing the various untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that serve as their antidotes.
Since this meaning is established by implication, they are not mentioned in full detail.

Furthermore, it should be explained that there are those who attain liberation in three or two births because there is further progress; for regarding the births they have received, they may have fewer, or none at all, or more than this.
For what reason is it that these [noble ones] do not abandon five categories [of afflictions]?

Because upon abandoning the fifth [grade of defilement], one necessarily abandons the sixth; for a single grade of delusion cannot obstruct the attainment of the fruit, as it is like being separated by only one interval before transcending the realm.
One should know that there are generally two types of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family):

first, the *devakulaṃkula*, which refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born into three or two families among the celestial realms of the desire world—either in one celestial abode, or two, or three.

The "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner refers to one who, having been born into two or three families within the human realm, realizes parinirvāṇa—either in one continent, or in two, or in three.

That is to say, when a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) further abandons from one grade up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, it should be known that they are designated as one progressing toward the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphalapratipannaka). If they abandon the sixth grade, they achieve the fruit of once-returner; having gone once to the heavens and returning once to the human world, they attain parinirvāṇa, which is called the fruit of once-returner, because there will be no further rebirth beyond this.
This stage is also called "one whose greed, hatred, and delusion are thinned," because only the lowest grade of greed, hatred, and delusion remains.
Having already distinguished the stages of the candidate for and the fruit of Once-returner, one should next establish the stages of the candidate for and the fruit of Non-returner.
The verse says:
Having abandoned seven or eight grades, one who has one birth remaining is called an *ekavīcika*;
this is the third stage of advancement; having abandoned nine, one attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The Commentary says:
That same Once-returner, by further severing remaining afflictions, transforms into what is called a "Single-interval" (Ekavīcika) when three conditions are met:
first, by the severance of afflictions, because they have severed seven or eight categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm.
Second, by the attainment of faculties, because one acquires the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) that serve as their antidote.
Third, by the taking of birth, because one undergoes one further birth within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
In the verse, only the first and last of these two conditions are mentioned, while the attainment of faculties is not; the meaning is as explained previously.
How can one attain the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) while still possessing a single category of afflictive obstruction?
This is because, were that [obstruction] severed, one would thereby transcend the realm (dhātu).

It was previously stated that karma of the three times constitutes an extreme obstruction; it should be understood that afflictions are likewise identical to karma in this regard, for they cause one to transcend the stage of their own outflow and maturation (niṣyanda-vipāka-bhūmi).
"Interval" (antara) means separation; because one is separated by the remainder of one more birth, one does not realize parinirvāṇa.
Alternatively, because one is separated by the remaining grade of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), one cannot attain the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

One who has one interval remaining is called a "one-interval" (ekavīcika); that is, one who has abandoned seven or eight categories of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation should be known as being on the path toward the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka).

Those who previously entered the vision of the truths after having abandoned three, four, seven, or eight categories of afflictions are not yet designated as "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) or "one-interval" at the time they attain the fruit, so long as they have not yet cultivated the superior path of the subsequent fruit, because they have not yet perfected the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) that counteract those [afflictions].
If one abandons the ninth [affliction], one achieves the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), because one will certainly not return to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This affliction is called the "abandonment of the five lower fetters" (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-prahāṇa*); although two or three must necessarily have been abandoned previously, they are all abandoned collectively at this time.
Based on the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), various distinctions are established through diverse approaches in the sūtras; we shall now explain the characteristics of those distinctions.
The verse says:
Among these, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain it without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*).
If those of the upward-stream class practice the mixed cultivation, they can go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
by leaping over, half-leaping, or passing away entirely, others can go to the Peak of Existence.
There are four types of practitioners of the formless realm; some attain parinirvāṇa while remaining here.
The treatise says: These non-returners (anāgāmin) are generally said to be of seven types; specifically, there are five distinctions regarding those who proceed to the form realm (rūpadhātu):

first, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); second, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin); third, one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin); fourth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin); and fifth, one who flows upward (ūrdhvasrotas).
Because this one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, it is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).

In the same way, it should be understood that because this one attains parinirvāṇa after being born, or because this one does so with exertion or without exertion, they are respectively called "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin), and so forth.
Because they proceed upward, they are called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) are those who, having gone to the form realm, attain parinirvāṇa while still in the intermediate state (antarābhava).

Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) are those who, having gone to the form realm and been born there, attain parinirvāṇa before long, because they possess the path of swift progress through diligent cultivation.
The parinirvāṇa spoken of here refers to that with a remainder of the substratum (sopadhiśeṣa).
Other masters say it also refers to that without a remainder of the substratum (nirupadhiśeṣa).
This is not reasonable, because such a person lacks mastery over the relinquishing of life.

One who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) is one who, having been born in the realm of form, does not cease their preparatory practice for a long time, and only attains parinirvāṇa through great effort; this is because they possess only diligent cultivation and lack the path of rapid progress.

One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) refers to one who, having been born in the form realm for a long time, has their preparatory application slackened and attains parinirvāṇa with little effort because they lack the diligent cultivation of the path of swift progress.

Some say that there is a distinction between these two because one attains nirvāṇa through the noble path conditioned by the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), respectively.
This explanation is irrational, as it entails an excessive logical fault.

However, regarding the fact that the sūtras first speak of parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāra*) and subsequently speak of parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisamskāra*), this sequence accords with reason.
Because there are paths of swift progress and paths lacking swift progress, one achieves completion through either exertion or without effort.

Because it is attained through effort, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) has attained the most rapid and supreme path; since their underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are extremely weak, they attain parinirvāṇa shortly after being born.
The term "Upstream-bound" (ūrdhvasrotas) carries the meaning of "moving upward," for the meanings of "flow" (*srotas*) and "movement" (*gati*) are identical.

This refers to one who, passing away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet does not realize parinirvāṇa immediately therein; rather, they must move upward through successive births before attaining parinirvāṇa.
There are two distinctions among these *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), due to differences in cause and fruit.
Regarding the difference in cause: this is because there is either mixed or unmixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-aviyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) of the dhyānas.
Regarding the distinction of the result: because Akaniṣṭha Heaven and the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) are the ultimate limits.
That is to say, if one has practiced the meditative cultivation of the dhyānas with intermingling, one can go to Akaniṣṭha and there attain parinirvāṇa.
This, moreover, has three further distinctions based on the differences between "full-leaping," "half-leaping," and "passing away everywhere. Regarding "full-leaping":

this refers to one who, while in the desire realm, has already fully practiced the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas, but due to encountering certain conditions, falls away from the upper three dhyānas; taking the relish for the first dhyāna as a condition, at the end of life, they are reborn in the Brahmakāyika heaven.

Due to the force of habitual practice from previous lives, one is further able to practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; passing away from that state, one is born in Akaniṣṭha. Passing away from the first station and being born in the final heaven, skipping all intermediate stations at once—this is the meaning of "complete transcendence" (sakalābhisambheda).

Regarding the term "half-leaper" (ardhapluta): starting from that state, one gradually takes birth in the lower Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), and even in the interim, is able to leap over one location to take birth in Akaniṣṭha; because the leap is not complete, it is called a "half-leaper."
A noble one (*ārya*) will certainly not be reborn in the realm of Mahābrahmā, because it is a place of biased views and there is but a single teacher there.

Regarding the term "universal death" (*sarvacyuta*): having died there, they gradually undergo rebirth in all places until finally they are able to be born in Akaniṣṭha; because they die in every location, it is called "universal death."

There are no non-returners who undergo a second birth in a place where they have already been born, because such a person may seek further progress within that birth, rather than remaining equal to or inferior to it.
It is precisely for this reason that the meaning of "non-returner" is fulfilled: one will certainly not return to a place where one has previously been born.
Since they do not even take birth in their own original place, how much less could they be born in a lower one?

It should be understood that this refers to those among the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* who, due to the cause of having practiced the meditative absorptions with intermingling (*vyavakīrṇa*), attain parinirvāṇa in Akaniṣṭha; whereas others, who have not practiced the meditative absorptions with intermingling, are able to go only as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) before attaining parinirvāṇa. That is to say, because they previously lacked the practice of intermingled meditative absorptions and took relish (*āsvāda*) for the various concentrations as a condition, after passing away here they are reborn throughout all the places of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet they alone are unable to go to the Five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Having passed away from the realm of form and been born successively in the three formless realms, one subsequently attains parinirvāṇa in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Between these two types of "upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the former is a practitioner of insight (*vipaśyanā*) and the latter is a practitioner of tranquility (*śamatha*), due to their respective preferences for wisdom and meditative concentration.

Regarding the two types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards), it is not unreasonable to see that they may attain parinirvāṇa within the lower stages; however, it is said that their ultimate destination is the Akaniṣṭha heaven or the Bhavāgra heaven because, having passed beyond those [lower realms], there is no further place to go, just as for a *srotaāpanna*, seven births at most are the limit.
These five are called those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

There are four distinctions among those who proceed to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): namely, those who, while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), become detached from craving for the form realm, and upon passing away from there, are reborn in the formless realm.

Within this category, there are only four distinctions based on the differences in attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*); these, together with the five previously mentioned, constitute six types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, there are those who do not proceed to the realms of form or formlessness, but instead attain parinirvāṇa while remaining right here; they are called those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*), and together with the previous six, they form seven.
Regarding those who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as non-returners (*anāgāmin*), there is another classification that reveals their distinctions.
The verse says:
There are nine who proceed to the form realm, Namely, three types each divided into three.
Because there are distinctions in karma, afflictions, faculties, and existence, they are established as three and nine types respectively.
The Treatise says:
That is to say, the five kinds of non-returners in the form realm are collectively established as three; since each of these is further divided into three types, they constitute nine kinds.
What are these three?

They are distinguished by the differences among those who are reborn in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who ascend to the higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
How is each of these three types further divided into three?

Furthermore, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are divided into three types—those who attain parinirvāṇa quickly, those who do not do so quickly, and those who attain it after a long duration—as illustrated by the analogy of the three sparks of fire.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth are also divided into three types, because they attain parinirvāṇa after being born, with effort, and so forth.
Since all of them attain parinirvāṇa after having been born, they should all be designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin).
Within the "Upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas) category, there are also three types, distinguished by the differences between the "Leaper" (pluta), the "Half-Leaper" (ardhapluta), and so forth.

Nevertheless, since all three types attain parinirvāṇa—whether quickly, not quickly, or after a long duration—they do not lose their distinct identities when compared to one another, as they remain unmixed.

Thus, these three types and nine types of non-returners differ in terms of speed, lack of speed, and duration due to distinctions in their karma, afflictions, and faculties; furthermore, they are collectively categorized as three based on the distinctions between the karma that is performed, accumulated, conducive to arising, or conducive to future existence.

Because there are distinctions in the manifestation of afflictions according to their sequence—namely, inferior, medium, and superior—and because there are distinctions among the faculties—superior, medium, and inferior—each of these three corresponds respectively to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, because there are distinctions in karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*), each of these categories has three subdivisions, resulting in nine types in total.
Specifically, the first two groups of three are each formed by the distinction of afflictions and faculties, rather than by differences in karma;

the latter three are likewise divided into three types due to differences in karma that is to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*). Thus, it is said that these non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are distinguished as nine through the variations in their karma, afflictions, and faculties.
If that is so, for what reason do the various sūtras state that the Buddha taught only seven destinies for noble beings?
The verse says:
The establishment of the seven destinies of noble beings Is due to the lack of distinction among those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Because of practicing or not practicing good and evil deeds, there is going forth but no returning.
The commentary states:

There are three types each for the intermediate (*antara*) and those born at the peak (*upapadya*), and one for the upward-streamer (*ūrdhvasrotas*); based on this, the Sūtra establishes the seven destinies of the noble person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Because there is a dharma characterized by "upward streaming," it is called "upward-streaming"; for this reason, despite their similarities, they are established as one.
Why is it that the "destination of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati) is established based on this alone, and not based on the other śaikṣa āryas?
"Destiny" (gati) has the meaning of "going" (gamana).

Since all other trainees (śaikṣa) perform wholesome karma without distinction, it is only these seven types who exclusively perform wholesome karma and do not perform unwholesome karma; others are not so.
Furthermore, only those who practice the seven types of conduct proceed to the higher realms and do not return; others do not.
Therefore, it is based solely on these that the "destinies of the noble person" (satpuruṣagati) are established. If this is so, why does the Sūtra state:
What is a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*)?
It refers to one who has attained the right view of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), and so forth, as explained at length.

As for other trainees, if considered from another perspective, they may also be said to possess the nature of a virtuous person; for all trainees have obtained the restraint of absolute non-performance regarding the five kinds of evil, and because most of their unwholesome afflictions have been abandoned.

One establishes the destiny of a virtuous person (*satpuruṣagati*) and does not resort to other categories, because one practices only what is wholesome and does not perform evil, and because one relies solely on superior causes to ascend to the higher realms.
Do those who abide in the state of a noble one (*ārya*) and have already undergone rebirth also possess these same distinctive characteristics?
Not so. Why is this? The verse says:
A noble one who has taken birth in the desire realm does not go to take birth in another realm;
whether they are born here or ascend to a higher realm, there is no refinement of faculties nor any falling away.
The Commentary says:

If one who is in the stage of a noble being undergoes rebirth in the desire realm, they will certainly not be reborn in the form or formless realms; for having realized the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), they will necessarily attain parinirvāṇa in that very same body.

If a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) were to be reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it would be possible, as in the case of one who proceeds to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) within the form realm.
However, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke thus:
"I have heard that there is a heaven named Akaniṣṭha; when I eventually fall from my current state, I shall be born there."
The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this explanation:
Because those [beings] do not understand the characteristics of the Abhidharma, and in order to gladden them, the Buddha did not prohibit it.

Furthermore, for those noble ones who have already undergone birth in the desire realm, as well as those who have already been born from here into the higher realms, there is absolutely no further training of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) nor any falling back (parihāṇi).
For what reason do you not allow that noble ones who have been born in the desire realm or in the higher realms undergo the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) or experience a fall?
Because such things necessarily do not occur. For what reason do they necessarily not occur?
Because their faculties, cultivated over successive births, have reached ultimate maturity, and because they have attained a particularly excellent basis for existence.
For what reason is it that those in training who have not yet abandoned sensual desire do not attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
Because that noble path has not yet reached full maturity, because it cannot easily be brought into manifestation, and because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not extremely weak.
The Vaibhāṣikas explain it thus:

Because the phenomena of the desire realm are extremely difficult to transcend, and because there is still much further to be done—namely, one must proceed to abandon the two types of afflictions, the unwholesome and the neutral; one must proceed to attain either two or three fruits of śrāmaṇya; and one must completely transcend the phenomena of all three realms—one who abides in the state of intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) lacks such capacity.

It was previously stated that the upward-streamer (ūrdhvasrotas), by taking the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas as a cause, is able to go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. First, which dhyāna should one mix-cultivate?
And by what stage is it known that the mixed cultivation has been accomplished?
Furthermore, for what reason does one practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna?
The verse says:
First, one mixes the fourth [dhyāna]; its accomplishment arises from a single moment of mixing.
"For the sake of taking birth, manifesting pleasure, and preventing regression through afflictions.
The treatise says:

Those who practice the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas must first practice the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, because that meditative concentration is most capable and it is the most excellent among all practices leading to bliss.

One who thus practices the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas is either an arhat or a non-returner (anāgāmin). Such a person must first enter the fourth dhyāna, wherein a succession of many moments of untainted (anāsrava) states manifests before them. From this, they induce many moments of tainted (sāsrava) states; subsequently, many more moments of untainted states manifest again. In this manner, they alternate, with each successive stage gradually decreasing, until finally two moments of untainted states are followed by the manifestation of two moments of tainted states, immediately succeeded by the arising of two moments of untainted states. This is called the completion of the preparatory application for the mixed cultivation of concentration.

Thereafter, from a single moment of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind, one moment of contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind is induced to manifest; immediately following this, another moment of uncontaminated mind arises. Because the intermediate moment of contamination is thus interspersed before and after the moments of uncontaminated mind, it is called the fundamental perfection of the meditative concentration of mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā-samādhi*).
The first two moments resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the third moment resembles the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Having thus practiced the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, one is able—by the force of this power—to likewise practice the mixed cultivation of the three lower meditative absorptions as appropriate.

Having previously practiced such mixed cultivation of the dhyānas within the three continents of the human realm in the desire realm, one may later, even if falling away from those attainments and being reborn in the form realm, still be able to practice the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas as before.
The intermittent cultivation of dhyāna serves three purposes: first, for the sake of rebirth;
second, for the sake of happiness in the present life; and third, for the sake of preventing the arising of afflictions that lead to regression.
This refers to those of sharp faculties among the non-returners (anāgāmin), who cultivate it for the sake of happiness in the present life and for rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Those of dull faculties also practice this for the sake of preventing regression, as they fear falling back;
likewise, such mixed cultivation distances them from the meditative attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādanasamprayukta-samādhi*).

As for the Arhats, those of sharp faculties do so for the sake of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*), while those of dull faculties do so to prevent the arising of afflictions that lead to regression; furthermore, they cultivate the dhyānas in a mixed manner to be reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
For what reason are there only five Pure Abodes?
The verse says:
Because of the five grades of mixed cultivation, there are five births in the Pure Abodes.
The treatise says:
Because the fourth dhyāna is cultivated through a mixture [of the wholesome and the defiled] in five grades, there are only five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
What are these five grades?
This refers to the distinctions between the inferior, the intermediate, the superior, the more superior, and the supreme categories.

Among these, for the first category, fulfillment is attained as soon as three moments of mind manifest: namely, the first is untainted (*anāsrava*), followed by the arising of a tainted (*sāsrava*) moment, and finally the arising of another untainted moment.
The second stage has six, the third stage nine, the fourth stage twelve, and the fifth stage fifteen.
By thus practicing the mixed cultivation of dhyāna in these five stages, one attains the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) in their respective order.
It should be understood that herein, the power of the untainted (*anāsrava*) perfumes the tainted (*sāsrava*), causing it to bring about rebirth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
Other masters say:
"The five Pure Abodes are brought about by the successive predominance of the five faculties, beginning with faith."
The Sūtra states that among those who are Non-returners (anāgāmin), there is one called "Body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
Based on what superior quality is the name "Body-witness" established?
The verse says:
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is further designated as "one realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*).
The treatise states:

One who possesses the attainment of the absorption of cessation is called "one who has attained the absorption of cessation"; that is, if such a non-returner possesses the attainment of the absorption of cessation within their own body, they are further designated as "one realized through the body."
It is said that the non-returner is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) because they have personally realized through the body a state resembling nirvāṇa.
How is it that they are described as being merely a "body-witness"?
It is because the mind is absent [at that time] and [the realization] arises in dependence upon the body.
In truth, it should be said that when one emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation, having attained what was previously unattained—the tranquility of the conscious body—one reflects:
"This attainment of cessation is the most tranquil and most closely resembles nirvāṇa."
Having thus realized the tranquility of the body, one is called "one who has realized through the body" (kāyasākṣin).
Because this tranquility of the body is realized through the manifestation of attainment and knowledge, the Sūtra speaks of eighteen types of those in training (śaikṣa).
For what reason is bodily realization (kāyasākṣin) not mentioned therein?
Because the basis and cause do not exist.
What are meant by "basis" and "cause"?
This refers to the various untainted (anāsrava) three trainings (*śikṣā*) and their fruits, because it is based on their distinctions that the category of "one in training" (*śaikṣa*) is established.
Since the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is neither training nor the fruit of training, the distinctions of those in training are not explained in reference to its accomplishment.
The coarse characteristics of the distinctions among non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are thus; yet, if analyzed in detail, they number in the thousands.
What is the meaning of this?

For instance, if the state of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) is established according to their faculties (*indriya*), it constitutes three types, because there are distinctions among inferior, middling, and superior faculties.
When established according to the stages (*bhūmi*), they constitute four types, because there are distinctions such as those who have gone to the first dhyāna and so forth.

When established according to the spiritual lineages (*gotra*), they constitute six types, because there are distinctions such as the lineage of those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth.
Established by way of location, there are sixteen types, due to the distinctions between locations such as the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya) and others.

Established by way of detachment from the defilements of the stages, there are thirty-six types, because this includes those who are fully bound in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) up to those who have already abandoned eight categories of defilement in the fourth dhyāna.
When established by way of location (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), freedom from passion (*vairāgya*), and faculties (*indriya*), the total number becomes two thousand five hundred and ninety-two.

How is this so? First, within a single location there are six lineages; each lineage is differentiated by nine stages according to the door of freedom from passion—namely, beginning with one who is bound by all fetters in any given stage and ending with one who has abandoned eight categories [of afflictions]. Thus, six times nine equals fifty-four. Multiplying the sixteen locations by fifty-four yields eight hundred and sixty-four. When this is further multiplied by the faculties, it becomes threefold, resulting in a total of two thousand five hundred and ninety-two.

Those who have abandoned the nine grades of defilement of a lower stage are said to be "fully bound" (sakalabandhana) regarding the higher stage; this is for the purpose of establishing the equal number of stages of abandonment of defilement for each stage.
This applies likewise up to the highest stream-enterer (ūrdhvasrotas).
In total there are five types; when their numbers are accumulated, they comprise twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty.
Having already analyzed the distinctions between the third stage of application (*pratipannaka*) and its fruit (*phala*), one should next establish the fourth stage of application and its fruit.
The verse says:

Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, from the abandonment of the first grade of the first dhyāna up to the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence, one is in every case a candidate for Arhatship.
The ninth path of immediate succession is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*);
together with the attainment of exhaustion, it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), whereby one becomes an adept (*aśaikṣa*) who has attained the fruit of arhatship.
The commentary says:

The Non-returner who proceeds to further sever the afflictions abandoned through cultivation within the form realm and the formless realm—beginning from the severance of the first dhyāna’s first grade and ending with the severance of the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)—should be known as having changed his designation to that of an Arhat-approacher (arhattva-pratipannaka).

Within this very context of the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*), the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is also called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropamasamādhi*), because it is capable of destroying all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and because those [other tendencies] have already been destroyed previously.
It does not destroy all that is substantially existent, yet it can destroy all functional capacities.
Among all paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that sever the afflictions, this [concentration] is the most excellent because it is associated with this [attainment].

The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is said to be of many kinds. It arises as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the ninth grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Because it can rely upon all nine stages, this concentration is said to differ in its wisdom, activity, and object. Included within the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) are fifty-two varieties: 1. The subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) each have four aspects (*ākāra*) regarding the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence; these correspond to eight varieties. 2. The dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) each have four aspects; these correspond to eight varieties. 3. The subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) takes the cessations of the eight stages as its objects; for each, there are four aspects, totaling thirty-two varieties. 4. The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) takes the paths of the eight stages as its objects; collectively, there are four aspects, corresponding to four varieties. This is because the paths belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge that counteract the eight stages act as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and must necessarily take them collectively as their objects.
Just as there are fifty-two [types of knowledge] included in the *anāgamya* stage, it should be known that the same applies to the four intermediate dhyānas.

In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there are twenty-eight; in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), twenty-four; and in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), twenty. This is because, in the formless realms, there is no *dharmajñāna*, nor is there *nirodhānvayajñāna* taking the cessation of a lower realm as its object.
However, as for taking the remedial path of a lower stage as an object, it is because paths of the same category serve as mutual causes for one another.
Some say: "In this meditative absorption, the wisdom, the mental application, and the objects are distinct."

There are eighty types included within the stage of the Unattained (*anāgamya*), namely, the path of subsequent knowledge (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) taking the eight stages of the path as its object, each associated with four distinct aspects (*ākāra*). Consequently, twenty-eight are added to the previous total.
Just as there are eighty types included in the *anāgamya* (preliminary stage), it should be known that the same applies to the four intermediate dhyānas.

There are forty in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty-two in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has distinct objects for its wisdom and activity; thus, when subsumed under the stage of the Not-yet-attained (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), there are one hundred and sixty-four types in total. This is because the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) takes the cessations of the eight stages as its object, with both specific and general aspects, each associated with four modes of activity (*ākāra*). Consequently, this adds one hundred and twelve [types] to the initial count.
Just as there are one hundred and sixty-four [factors] subsumed under the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived), it should be known that the same applies to the four intermediate dhyānas.

There are fifty-two in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty-six in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
If one were to differentiate this according to lineage (*gotra*), faculties (*indriya*), and so forth, it would further constitute many types; these should be reflected upon according to reason.

Since this meditative absorption can sever the ninth category of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it can induce the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that occurs simultaneously with the attainment of the total destruction of those afflictions.

The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) arises as the final uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) among those that sever the afflictions; the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) among those that sever the afflictions. Because this path of liberation arises simultaneously with the initial acquisition of the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-prāpti*), it is named the knowledge of exhaustion.

Thus, when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen, one becomes an Arhat of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), because one has already attained the dharmas of the fruit of the Worthy One of no-more-learning.
Since there are no further trainings to be practiced for the sake of attaining another distinct fruit, one receives the name "of no-more-learning."
Because he should perform only the welfare of others and because he is worthy of offerings from all those who are subject to defilement, the name "Arhat" is established based on this meaning;
the implication of the term is thereby established.
The four stages of approach and the three fruits previously discussed are all termed "those in training" (śaikṣa). For what reason do the first seven [stages] receive the name "those in training"?
It is because they constantly delight in training for the sake of attaining the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
There are three essentials of training:
first, higher ethical discipline; second, higher mental concentration; and third, higher wisdom.
These take ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom as their three essential natures.
If that were so, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would have to be called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).

This is not the case; for they have not yet seen and known the principles of the Truths (*satya*) as they truly are, and it is possible that they might later lose their correct training. It is for this reason that the Sugata spoke the word "training" once again.
As stated in a sūtra, the Buddha told Dharmadinnā:
"One who trains in what should be trained, one who trains in what should be trained—I speak of such a person alone as a 'trainee' (śaikṣa).
In order to make it known that one who trains in the correct training without falling away is called a trainee, the Blessed One repeated the word "training" (śikṣā).
How can an Ārya who abides in their fundamental nature be called one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
Because the intention to train has not yet been fulfilled.
It is like a traveler taking a temporary rest; or because the attainment of the dharmas of training constantly follows them.
What are the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa)?
They are the untainted (anāsrava) conditioned dharmas of one in training.
What are the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
This refers to the untainted conditioned dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Why is nirvāṇa not called "training" (*śaikṣa*)?
Because it is also accomplished by those beyond training and by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For what reason, then, are these not called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
Because they are also accomplished by those still in training (śaikṣa) and by ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Thus, the śaikṣas and aśaikṣas together constitute eight noble persons (āryapudgala), as there are four each who are either proceeding toward the fruits or abiding in them.

This refers to the stages from the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship that has been realized; although there are eight designations, there are only five actual entities. These consist of one who abides in the four fruits and the candidate for the first fruit, because the candidates for the latter three fruits are not distinct from their preceding fruits.
This is explained in reference to those who attain the fruits through gradual progression.

If one who has partially abandoned desire (*vītarāga*) or one who has completely abandoned desire (*atyantavītarāga*) abides within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are designated as a candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*) or Non-returner (*anāgāmipratipannaka*); they are not included within the preceding fruits. This is because, as previously stated, there is a distinction between the two types of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*): the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
By which path is defilement abandoned in which stage?
The verse says:
The Peak of Existence is abandoned by the untainted [path]; the others are abandoned by both.
The treatise says:
Only the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) abandons the defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), not the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*). Why is this so?

This is because there is no mundane path (*laukikamārga*) higher than this; because that which belongs to its own level cannot counteract its own level; and because it is increased by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of its own level.
If those afflictions increase with respect to this [level], then this [path] must necessarily be unable to counteract those afflictions.

If this power can act as an antidote to that [defilement], then that defilement will certainly not increase in relation to it; therefore, the path of its own stage does not serve as an antidote to its own stage.
The separation from the other eight stages occurs through both types of paths, because both the mundane and supramundane paths are capable of effecting such separation.

Since both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation] involve the abandonment of the defilements of the eight stages, how many acquisitions of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) are there for each?
The verse says:
The Noble One abandons the two through the two paths; In abandoning the eight stages of cultivation, There are respectively two acquisitions of disjunction for each.
The treatise states:

When noble beings on the path of training (*śaikṣa*) employ the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) to abandon the defilements of the lower eight stages through cultivation, they are able to fully bring about the acquisition of two types of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
It is likewise when they employ the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to abandon those [defilements], because both types of paths perform the same function.
Another master explains:

When one becomes free from those defilements by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), for what reason is it known that one also produces the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) which is tainted (*sāsrava*)? Because when the untainted acquisition is relinquished, the afflictions do not re-arise.

That is to say, when a noble one in training (śaikṣa) becomes detached from those defilements by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), if they were not to produce a contaminated acquisition of disjunction (saṃyojana-visaṃyoga-prāpti) that shares the same antidote, then even though they have completely abandoned the [defilements] of the eight stages by means of the noble path, later, when they attain the transformation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) based on dhyāna, they would suddenly discard all the previously held dull noble paths and obtain only the sharp fruit-noble paths of dhyāna. Consequently, the disjunction from the higher-level afflictions would fail to be established, and thus those afflictions would once again become manifest.
This proof is irrational. Why is this so?

Because even if those noble ones did not possess the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*), they would still not be possessed of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages.

This is because, for example, when one who has already separated from the defilements of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) undergoes a transformation of the faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), or when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is reborn in a higher realm, they do not remain possessed of those afflictions.

That is to say, just as when one who has separated from the defilements of the stage of the Peak of Existence subsequently attains a transformation of the faculties based on the dhyānas, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the cessation through the outflow-free path (*anāsrava*) is immediately relinquished; since there is no longer any acquisition of the outflow-free state regarding the dissociation from that stage, the afflictions of that stage are likewise no longer possessed.

Furthermore, just as ordinary beings who have attained the second dhyāna or higher levels, although they relinquish the acquisitions of the abandonment of afflictions belonging to the desire realm and so forth, do not remain possessed of those afflictions of the desire realm and so forth, this case should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, this does not constitute a valid proof.

Since it has been stated that for noble ones (*ārya*), both types of detachment (*vairāgya*)—those attained through the two paths and those through the eight stages of cultivation—each can induce the acquisition of two kinds of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*), it follows by implication that for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the use of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) can only induce the acquisition of disconnection from the contaminated [defilements], while for noble ones, the use of the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) to abandon the defilements abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) as well as those of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can only induce the acquisition of uncontaminated disconnection.
By means of which path and stage is one detached from the defilements of which stage?
The verse says:
The untainted path of the *anāgamya* stage is able to effect detachment from all stages.
The other eight abandon their own and higher levels; the contaminated abandon the level immediately below.
The Treatise says:
If the various uncontaminated paths are subsumed under the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) stage, they can abandon [the afflictions] from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
The intermediate dhyāna and the four dhyānas, together with the three formless attainments, each enable the abandonment of the defilements of their own level and of higher levels as appropriate.
They do not abandon lower levels, because those have already been abandoned.

All contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) are capable only of abandoning the afflictions of the immediately lower stage, and not those of their own stage or higher stages; this is because the afflictions of one's own stage increase in accordance with them, because these paths are weak in power, and because [the afflictions of one's own stage] have already been abandoned.
Regarding those [attainments] that rely on the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) to separate from the defilements of the lower levels:

while all uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) are subsumed under the preparatory stages, are all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) likewise subsumed under the preparatory stages? No, they are not.
How so? The verse says:
"In the case of the 'near-separation' [attainments], one is freed from the defilements of the lower realms; this occurs at the first, third, and final liberations."
The fundamental or the preparatory [attainments], while for the higher stages there is only the fundamental.
The commentary states:
There are eight preparatory attainments that serve as the basis for the various paths, namely, the lower limits of the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
There are nine stages of detachment, namely the desire realm and the eight dhyānas.

In the first three near-attainments (*sāmantaka*), one separates from the defilements of the three lower realms; when the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) manifests, one either enters the fundamental dhyāna (*maula*) or remains in the near-attainment itself.

Each of the five upper preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) is free from the defilements of the lower realm; however, when the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) manifests, one necessarily enters the fundamental stage (*maula*) rather than remaining in the preparatory stage. This is because the preparatory and fundamental stages are equal in terms of their faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), whereas the faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*) differ between the preparatory and fundamental stages of the first three dhyānas.

There are cases where one cannot enter [the fundamental dhyāna], because one enters instead into a different type of feeling which involves some slight difficulty, and because when one is free from the defilements of a lower stage, one necessarily rejoices in the higher stage.
If there were no difference in feeling, one would necessarily enter the fundamental [dhyāna].

The paths of transcendence (*lokottara-mārga*), including their uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) stages, have already been explained; by extension, it is established that they take the four noble truths as their objects and possess the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
But what do the mundane paths (*laukika-mārga*) take as their objects, and what aspects do they employ?
The verse says:
The worldly paths of immediate succession and liberation take the lower and upper realms as their objects respectively;
they practice the contemplations of coarseness, suffering, and obstruction, as well as the three contemplations of tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
The treatise states:

The mundane paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation respectively take the lower and higher stages as their objects, perceiving them as coarse, painful, and obstructive, and as calm, sublime, and detached.

This means that all paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) take as their objects the contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) of their own level or the immediately lower level, and employ one of the three aspects (ākāra)—coarseness, suffering, and so forth.

All paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), however, take as their objects the contaminated phenomena of the immediately higher level and employ one of the three aspects—tranquility, excellence, and so forth.
Because it is not tranquil, it is called "coarse" (*audārika*); because it can only be transcended through great exertion and because it is not exquisite, it is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*);
and because it is characterized by much heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that causes harm and because it is not an escape, [it is so designated].
It is called an "obstruction" because it can hinder one from transcending its own level, just as thick prison walls obstruct escape.
The three qualities of tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) should be explained as the opposites of this.
The digression is concluded; one should now analyze the primary subject.
What knowledge arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The verse says:
After the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) of one who is immovable, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) necessarily arises;
for others, either the knowledge of exhaustion or right view [arises]. These are all present in the fruit of arhatship.
The treatise says:

For Arhats of the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*); it is not the case that further instances of the knowledge of exhaustion or the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*) arise.

For Arhats other than those of the immovable dharma, the knowledge of exhaustion arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion; or rather, it induces the right view of one beyond training, but not the knowledge of non-arising, because they are subject to falling back later.
Is it that right view does not arise for those of the previously established immovable lineage?
It does indeed arise; however, it is not mentioned because all who have attained the fruit of arhatship possess it.

That is to say, for one of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*), after the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), either further knowledge of non-arising arises or the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) arises.
Regarding the four fruits previously mentioned, whose fruits are they?
These four should be understood as the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
What is meant by the nature of a śramaṇa?
What is the essence of this fruit?
How many distinct types of fruit-attainments are there in total?
The verse says:
The nature of a śramaṇa is the pure path; its fruits are both conditioned and unconditioned.
These consist of eighty-nine [moments]: the paths of liberation and cessations.
The treatise states:

All untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) constitute the nature of a śramaṇa; one who harbors these paths is called a śramaṇa, because they are able to exert themselves diligently to extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Because one can diligently exert effort to eliminate various evil and unwholesome dharmas—and as explained at length up to—therefore one is called a śramaṇa.
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot reach the ultimate nirvāṇa without distinction, they are not true śramaṇas.
The conditioned and the unconditioned are the fruits of śramaṇaship.

Although the sūtras state that there are four distinctions among them, in reality, according to their positions, there are eighty-nine, all of which have the nature of the path of liberation and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

That is to say, there are eight paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation for the permanent abandonment of afflictions abandoned through seeing, as well as eighty-one paths of uninterrupted transition and eighty-one paths of liberation for the permanent abandonment of afflictions abandoned through cultivation.

All paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) are exclusively the nature of a śramaṇa; all paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are also the conditioned fruit of a śramaṇa, because they are its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
