Each individual analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is exclusively the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) of the śramaṇa, because it is their fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Thus, they collectively constitute eighty-nine types.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One not explain them in full?
Although there are many fruits, he did not mention them all. The verse says:
Four fruits are established by five causes; One abandons what was previously attained and acquires a superior path.
"Attaining the eight knowledges through the abandonment of the aggregates, one suddenly cultivates the sixteen aspects.
The treatise says:
If the stage of the path of abandonment possesses five causes, the Buddha establishes it as a fruit within the sūtras.
Regarding the five causes: first, the relinquishing of the former path, meaning the relinquishing of the previously attained paths of fruition and application;
second, the attainment of a superior path, meaning the attainment of the distinguished paths subsumed within the fruition.
Third, the collective abandonment of defilements, meaning that one attains all abandonments through a single attainment.
Fourth, the acquisition of the eight knowledges, meaning that one acquires the four dharma-knowledges and the four subsequent knowledges.
Fifth, the ability to simultaneously cultivate the sixteen aspects, meaning that one can simultaneously cultivate the aspects of impermanence and so forth.
The five causes are present in all four fruits; they are not so in other stages, and therefore the Buddha did not mention them.
If only the pure path constitutes the nature of a śramaṇa, how can the two fruits obtained through the power of the contaminated path also be subsumed under the fruits of a śramaṇa?
The verse says:
That which is abandoned through the mundane path is also called a fruit of śrāmaṇya, because it is mixed with that obtained by the noble ones,
and because it is maintained by untainted acquisition.
The treatise says:

When one attains the two fruits by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), these fruits do not have as their nature of abandonment (*prahāṇaphala*) solely the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) obtained by the mundane path; rather, they are formed by the integration of the cessation through deliberation obtained by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). This is because both are attained by a single fruit-path (*ekaphalamārga*).
Accordingly, this sutra states:
"What is the fruit of once-returning?
It is the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion."
What is the fruit of non-returning?
It refers to the abandonment of the five lower fetters.

Furthermore, because the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained through the mundane path is sustained by the acquisition of abandonment (prāpti) that is untainted (anāsrava), and because one does not die while subject to falling away from what is sustained by this power, it may also be designated as the essence of the fruit of śramaṇaship.
Does this nature of a śramaṇa have alternative names? It does. What are they?
The verse says:
That which is described as the nature of a śramaṇa is also called a brāhmaṇa,
and is also called the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the true Brahmā.
Among these, only the Path of Seeing is called the Wheel of Dharma;
it is so named because its speed and other qualities resemble a wheel, or because it possesses spokes and other such parts.
The treatise says:
That which was previously described as the true nature of a śramaṇa is also called the nature of a brāhmaṇa in the sūtras, because it is able to eliminate all afflictions.
This very same thing is also called the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the power of the true Brahmā-king.
The Buddha is endowed with unsurpassed Brahma-virtue; therefore, the World-Honored One alone deserves to be named "Brahma.
As stated in the sūtras, the Buddha is also called "Brahma," also called "Tranquil," and also called "Cool."
In this context, the Blessed One has in certain instances designated the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) alone as the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Just as a worldly wheel possesses characteristics such as speed and so forth, the path of vision resembles it; therefore, it is called the Wheel of Dharma.
In what way is the path of seeing (darśanamārga) similar to that [wheel]?
It is because it resembles a wheel through its rapid movement and other such qualities.

That is to say, the path of seeing the truths (satyadarśanamārga) possesses these five similarities to a worldly wheel: because it proceeds with great speed; because it involves discarding and taking up; because it subdues what has not yet been subdued; because it suppresses what has already been subdued; and because it revolves upward and downward.
The Venerable Ghosaka spoke thus:
"Just as a worldly wheel possesses characteristics such as spokes and so forth, the Noble Eightfold Path is called a 'wheel' because it resembles that [worldly wheel].

That is to say, right view, right intention, right effort, and right mindfulness resemble the spokes of a worldly wheel; right speech, right action, and right livelihood resemble the hub; and right concentration resembles the rim. For this reason, it is called the Wheel of Dharma."
How do you know that the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is exclusively the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Because when the Path of Seeing arose for Kauṇḍinya and the others, it was said that the True Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion.
What are the three turnings and twelve aspects (*trivartanā-dvādaśākāra*)?
"This is the noble truth of suffering; this should be fully known; this has been fully known"—this is called the three turnings.
At each of these individual turnings, there arises respectively the eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; these are called the twelve aspects.

In this way, each of the Truths possesses these three turnings and twelve aspects; however, because their number is equal, they are simply described as "three turnings and twelve aspects," just as one speaks of the "two dharmas" or "skillfulness in the seven bases."
By these three turnings, the three paths—the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)—are respectively revealed;
such is the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters.

If this is so, since the three turnings and twelve aspects do not pertain solely to the path of seeing, how can it be said that the name "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*) is established exclusively for the path of seeing?
Therefore, it is only logical that the Dharma-discourse consisting of these very three turnings and twelve aspects should be called the Wheel of Dharma.
How, then, are there three turnings?
Because it revolves three times.
How does it possess twelve aspects?
Because it proceeds through the four noble truths in three cycles.

That is to say: "This is suffering; this is its origin; this is its cessation; this is the path. "This should be fully understood; this should be permanently abandoned; this should be realized; this should be cultivated. "This has been fully understood; this has been permanently abandoned; this has been realized; this has been cultivated."
What is meant by "turning"?
It is because, through this Dharma-gate, one proceeds to the mental continuums of others to cause them to understand the meaning.
Alternatively, all noble paths are the Wheel of Dharma, for they turn within the bodies of those beings being converted.
When the Path of Seeing arises within the mental continuum of another, it is called "already transformed" (*vivartita*) because it has already reached the initial stage of transformation.
Which fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) is attained in which realm?
The verse says:
The three [supernormal knowledges] rely on the desire realm; the latter three [rely on all three realms].

Because there is no Path of Seeing above [the desire realm], because there is no hearing [of the Dharma] there, because they do not take the lower [realms] as objects, because there is no weariness [with suffering] there, and because of the Sūtra.
The Treatise says:
The first three fruits are attained based solely on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the attainment of arhatship is based on bodies belonging to all three realms.

While it is logically plausible that the first two fruits are not attained based on higher [realms] because one has not yet abandoned desire for them, why is the third fruit likewise not attained based on a higher realm?
This is due to both reasoning and scripture.
First, what is the reasoning?

Because there is no path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) based upon a body belonging to the higher realms, it is impossible for one who has already become free from desire (*vītarāga*) apart from the path of seeing to attain the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) by means of a leap-over realization (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*).
For what reason is there necessarily no Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) in the higher realms?
First, because in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) there is no correct hearing [of the Dharma].

Furthermore, because in that realm one does not take the lower realms as an object, and because ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the form realm (rūpadhātu) are attached to the bliss of superior meditative concentration (samādhi).
Furthermore, because there is no aversion when there is no feeling of suffering, one cannot attain the Path of Seeing without such aversion.
How, then, is this taught?
It is by virtue of what is stated in the Sūtra.
The Sūtra states:

"There are five types of persons who attain penetration here and reach finality there—namely, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) up to those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas).
This term "penetration" refers exclusively to the path of seeing (darśanamārga), for it is the initial preparatory application for realizing parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, it is definitively absent from the path of vision and the form realm.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 24. *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, Fascicle 25.
