Chapter Six: Analysis of the Noble Ones, Part Four. As previously stated, following the initial *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion), the Arhat of unshakable nature gives rise to *anutpādajñāna* (knowledge of non-arising).
Are there distinctions among the various arhats, such as those between stream-enterers and the others?
There are indeed. What are they?
The verse says:
There are six types of Arhats, ranging from the "receding" to the "immovable.
The first five arise from the stage of faith-understanding; collectively they are termed "liberated by time."
"Subsequently, those not liberated at any time arise from the previously mentioned 'attained through vision' (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
The commentary states:

In the sūtras, it is taught that there are six types of arhats due to differences in their spiritual lineages (gotra): first, the one liable to fall away (parihāṇadharman); second, the one intent on reflection (cetayitadharman); third, the one intent on guarding (anurakṣaṇādharman); fourth, the one established in stability (sthitākampyadharman); fifth, the one capable of penetration (prativedhanādharman); and sixth, the one immovable (akopyadharman).

Among these six, the first five arise from the nature of liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukti*) during the previous stage of training; they are collectively termed "liberation through love at times" (*sāmāyikī kāntā cetovimuktiḥ*), because they are protected at all times and involve the liberation of the mind.
They are also called "those liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) because they must wait for the right time and because they are liberated.
This is a case of omitting the first word, as in the term "butter-jar.

Thus, they are able to enter meditative absorption only when waiting for the proper time; that is, they enter absorption only when favorable conditions—such as the necessary requisites, freedom from illness, and a suitable location—converge.

The immovable nature of phenomena (*akopya-dharmatā*) is called "the latter"; it is precisely this that is termed the "immovable liberation of the mind" (*akopya-cetovimukti*), because it is free from retrogression and because it is a liberation of the mind.
It is also termed "liberation not dependent on time" (*asamayavimukti*), because it does not depend upon time and is [perpetually] liberated.
This means that samādhi manifests according to one's wish, as it does not depend upon the convergence of superior conditions.

Alternatively, the designations "liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*) and "not liberated by time" (*asamayavimukta*) are established based on temporary or ultimate liberation, because there may be occasions for falling away or no occasions for falling away. These arise from the nature of the "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
Regarding the lineages (gotra) of the six types of arhats thus elucidated: do they exist from the outset, or are they acquired only later?
It is not fixed.
Why is this so?
The verse says:
Some possess this from their original lineage; some acquire it later through the refinement of their faculties.
The commentary says:

The lineage of the "one liable to fall back" (*parihāṇadharman*) must necessarily exist from the outset; however, the five [lineages] beginning with the "one who reflects" (*cetana-dharman*) may also be acquired later.

That is to say, there are those who have been of the nature of the "one who reflects" from the beginning, and there are those who were originally of the nature of the "one liable to fall back" but later perfected their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) to become the "one who reflects," and so on, up to the "immovable one" (*akopyadharman*), as should be explained according to the circumstances.

One who is said to be "of the nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman) is one who falls away from what has been attained upon encountering even slight conditions, but not one who is "of the nature of reflecting" (cetanādharman) and so forth.
One who is said to be "of the nature of reflecting" is one who, fearing loss and fall, constantly contemplates self-harm.
Regarding "guarding the Dharma," this refers to taking joy in what has been attained and protecting it oneself.

Regarding "abiding in the Dharma," although one does not guard it oneself, because one is free from conditions for decline, one is able to avoid falling back; yet, because one is free from superior application, one does not further advance.

Regarding those capable of reaching the state of *dharmākara*, their nature is such that they are capable of and delight in practicing the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), thereby swiftly attaining the immovable state (*akopyadharman*).
As for those of the immovable nature, they are necessarily free from regression.
Among these six types of lineage, the first two during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) lack constant and intensive application; they differ due to the distinctions in their faculties.

The third possesses only constant application; the fourth possesses only respectful application; the fifth possesses both but has dull faculties; and the sixth has sharp faculties and possesses both types of application.

The lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) does not necessarily fall away, and so on up to those capable of reaching [the highest goal] (*prativedhanādharman*), who do not necessarily reach it; these names are established merely in terms of what is possible. Therefore, all six types of arhats exist throughout all three realms.

If one maintains that those who are subject to regression (parihāṇadharman) must necessarily regress, and so on up to those who are capable of reaching [the goal] (prativedhanādharman) must necessarily reach it, then according to that position, the desire realm possesses all six types; whereas in the form and formless realms there are only the "abiding" (sthitākampya) and the "immovable" (akopyadharman), because they lack regression, self-harm, self-protection, and the cultivation of the faculties (indriya-saṃcāra), and thus possess only two.
Among these six types of arhats, who falls away from what?
Is it from their nature (*prakṛti*) or from their fruit (*phala*)?
The verse says:
Fourth, there is falling away from the lineage; fifth, there is no falling away from a fruit that was not previously attained.
The treatise says:
For one of immovable lineage, there is necessarily no possibility of falling away.

Of the five aforementioned types, all possess the possibility of falling away (*parihāṇi*). Among them, the latter four may fall away from their [respective] natures (*gotra*); however, for the single type known as "one liable to fall away" (*parihāṇadharman*), there is no principle of falling away from its nature, because this lineage occupies the very lowest position.
All five types possess the possibility of falling away from their fruits; yet although all may fall away, none do so from their original state.

This means that for those Arhats who, while in the stage of training (śaikṣa), abided in a particular lineage (gotra), there is no possibility of them falling away from that lineage, because it was firmly established by both the paths of training and non-training (aśaikṣa).

If those in training (śaikṣa) previously resided in a certain lineage during their stage as ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), there is likewise no possibility of falling away from that lineage, because it has been rendered firm by the mundane and supramundane paths.
If, after abiding in this stage, one cultivates the faculties and attains the four types of lineage such as the *cetana* (thought) lineage, there is the possibility of falling away from that lineage.

However, for those who previously abided in the *cetana* lineage or other lineages during the prior stages, there is necessarily no falling away from the fruit attained therein; only those of the former *parihāṇadharman* (subject to falling away) have the sense of falling away from the fruit.

Furthermore, there is no falling away from a fruit already attained; however, it is possible for one to fall away from a fruit yet to be attained. Therefore, it is certain that there is no falling away from the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Consequently, there are three types of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) among the Arhats:

first, those who advance their faculties (*indriyottāpana*); second, those who fall back and remain at the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*); and third, those who enter parinirvāṇa while remaining in their own station.

There are four types of those who contemplate the Dharma (*cintāmayī*): three are as previously described, with the addition of one more—the type that dwells in the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
The remaining three, in their respective order, possess five, six, and seven [qualities], for it should be understood that each subsequent category increases by one.
When those such as the *cetanādharmas* (those liable to regression) fall back and abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), they abide in regression and not otherwise.
If it were otherwise, because they would have attained a superior lineage, this would be progress rather than regression.
For what reason is it certain that there is no falling away from a previously attained fruit?
It is because those afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) rely upon non-existent objects (*avastuka*).

That is to say, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) functions by relying on the locus of a self; since the afflictions abandoned through seeing have this view as their root, and the substance of a self does not exist, they are said to rely upon non-existent objects. Because they rely upon non-existent objects, there is necessarily no principle of falling away.
If that were so, one should say that this affliction takes non-existence as its object; it does not take non-existence as its object, because its objective sphere is the Truths (*satya*).
Yet, among all the afflictions, which one does not take its objective sphere, the Truths, in a manner that is not in accordance with reality?

Although all are thus, there is a distinction, because the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation each have their own specific objects—namely, the agreeable and the disagreeable—and these characteristics are not absent within the objective spheres of perception.

The afflictions abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) involve the conceptualization of a self and so forth; however, the objects of the [Four] Truths do not possess the characteristics of a self and so forth, because such things do not exist. Thus, they differ from those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

That is to say, within the objective spheres such as form (*rūpa*), the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) falsely superimposes an agent, an experiencer, or one who acts with autonomy; it is not a real nature of a self.
The views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth arise in accordance with these; therefore, they are all said to be afflictions based on non-existent objects (*avastuka-kleśa*).

As for the greed, hatred, pride, and ignorance abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they function respectively as attachment, aversion, arrogance, and lack of comprehension toward objects such as form (*rūpa*); therefore, they are all said to be afflictions based on existent objects (*savastuka-kleśa*).

Furthermore, the afflictions abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) consist of the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, as well as views of eternalism and nihilism, within the context of the principles of the Truths; yet there is not even the slightest entity such as a "self" within those Truths.
Since the greed and other afflictions abandoned through seeing arise by taking these [erroneous conceptions] as their objects, they are all termed "afflictions based on non-existent entities."

The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation consist of conceptualizing beauty and ugliness within form and other objects; however, since the objects such as form do possess some degree of distinction between beauty and ugliness, these afflictions may be termed "afflictions based on existent things."

Furthermore, the afflictions abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) arise from delusion regarding the principles of the truths and are thus called "based on non-existent entities" (avastuka); the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) arise from delusion regarding coarse objects and are thus called "based on existent entities" (savastuka).
The principles of the truths are real and true, providing a fixed standard upon which one can rely.

Since noble wisdom has already been realized, there is no possibility of regression; however, because the characteristics of phenomena are superficial and deceptive, lacking any fixed basis for reliance, one may lose mindfulness and regress by severing the delusions regarding them.
Alternatively, the afflictions abandoned through cultivation do not arise from careful deliberation, as their nature is dull and obscured.
The afflictions abandoned through seeing arise from deliberation, because they possess the nature of conceptual investigation.

Such lapses do not occur for the Noble Ones when they fail to deliberate regarding coarse objects; rather, such lapses may occur through a loss of mindfulness. Deliberation is not like this, just as one might suddenly mistake a rope for a snake.

Therefore, while noble ones may fall back and give rise to afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they cannot give rise to afflictions abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) merely by chance.
If a noble one engages in careful deliberation, they immediately perceive the principles of the truths; thus, there is certainly no possibility of falling back from what is abandoned through vision.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"There is also no possibility of falling away from the state of an Arhat.
This explanation is logical.
How is this known? It is known through scripture and reasoning.
How is it known through scripture?
The Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus!
To sever the afflictions through noble wisdom is called true severance."
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"I say that those in training (śaikṣa) should be heedful, but not the Arhats.
Although there is a sutra that says this:
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I have said that gains and honors, and so forth, are also obstacles for an arhat; however, I do not say that they cause one to fall back from the fruit of arhatship, but only that they cause one to fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life."
The Sūtra states:
"I definitively declare that there is no cause or condition for falling back from the immovable liberation of mind (akopya-cetovimukti) once it has been realized through bodily witness.
If you claim there is such falling back, I likewise accept this, as the Sūtra also speaks of occasional liberation through love (sāmayikī-kāntā-vimukti).
One should simply examine whether that which has regressed is of the nature of the fruit (*phala*), or rather of the dhyānas and so forth.
However, because their fundamental dhyānas and meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) manifest only when conditions are met, they are called "those liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*).
Because one repeatedly desires its manifestation for the sake of attaining a pleasant dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Some say:

This meditative absorption is the "taste" (*āsvāda*) that is craved; however, because the liberation inherent in the fruit of Arhatship is constantly pursued, it should not be called "occasional" (*sāmayika*); and because there is no further longing or seeking for it, it is not called "craving."

If it were possible for one in the state of Arhatship to fall away, why did the Blessed One state only that there is the possibility of falling away from the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra) that has been realized?
From this, it is proven that the liberation of the nature of the fruit of Arhatship must necessarily be unshakable (akopya).
However, due to the faults of being disturbed by gain and so forth, those of dull faculties may lose their mastery over the attained dwelling in happiness in the present life;
those of sharp faculties, however, do not suffer such decline.

Therefore, regarding the attainment of the pleasant dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), there is either falling away from it or no falling away; thus they are called those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and those not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*).
One should reflect in this same manner upon the [other types], such as those characterized by reflection (*cintāmayadharman*) and so forth, according to reason.
What is the distinction between those who are non-falling (*aparihāṇa*), those who are stable (*sthita-akampya*), and those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*)?
One does not attain the name "non-retrogressive" by means of refining the faculties; rather, what is obtained through the refinement of the faculties is called "immovable.
These two types of superior meditative attainments (samāpatti) that arise cannot possibly undergo retrogression, even if they encounter conditions for retrogression.

One who abides in the state of stability (sthitākampya) is merely able to avoid falling away from the superior qualities already attained, but cannot further induce the arising of other superior qualities; even if they were to induce such arising, one could still fall away from them.
These are the three distinctions, beginning with the non-retrogressive (avaivartika).

However, in the past, while still in the stage of training (śaikṣa), Gautika excessively relished the state of occasional liberation (samayavimukti); furthermore, because he possessed dull faculties (mṛdvindriya), he repeatedly fell away from it. Deeply loathing and reproaching himself, he took up a blade and committed suicide.
Because he had no attachment to his body or life, he attained arhatship at the moment of death and entered parinirvāṇa; therefore, Gautika did not fall away from the fruit of arhatship.
Furthermore, the *Daśottara-sūtra* states as follows:
"One dharma should be cultivated, namely, the liberation through love at the proper time (*sāmayikī-kānta-vimukti*).
One dharma should be realized, namely, the unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā-ceto-vimukti*)."

If the nature of the fruit of arhatship were designated as "liberation through love and time" (*samayikī kāntā vimuktiḥ*), why would the fruit of arhatship be mentioned twice in this *Daśottara-sūtra*?
Furthermore, nowhere has it been stated that the fruit of arhatship is called "to be brought forth" (*utpādayitavya*); rather, it is said to be "to be realized" (*sākṣātkartavya*).

Furthermore, when it is said that the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-phala) belonging to those of dull faculties is called "to be brought forth" (utpādayitavya), what meaning is intended to be revealed?
If it were to reveal that they are capable of bringing it forth into manifestation, then those of sharp faculties would most certainly be even more capable of doing so.
If it were for the purpose of manifesting that [attainment] which ought to arise, then other [types of] those with sharp faculties would also be most capable of causing it to arise.
Therefore, the "one liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*) is not, by nature, one who has attained the fruit of arhatship.
If this is so, why is it said that the one liberated by time is an arhat?
This means that there are those who, being Arhats with dull faculties, require time and depend upon specific conditions for their concentration to manifest.
Those who are the opposite of this are called "those liberated at any time" (asamayavimukta).
The Abhidharma also states: "The latent tendency of sensual desire arises from three conditions:

first, because the latent tendency of sensual desire has not been abandoned or fully understood; second, because the teachings concordant with it are correctly present before one; and third, because improper mental attention directed toward them is currently arising."
If it is argued that he [the Master] spoke based on the production of things possessing their causes, then what phenomenon could possibly arise without its causes being complete?
This is what is meant by "based on scripture.
How is it established by reasoning?
If an Arhat possesses the path of antidote that ensures afflictions will never arise again, then he should not fall back and give rise to afflictions.

Conversely, if this path has not yet arisen in an Arhat, then because he has not yet permanently uprooted the seeds of the afflictions, he would not be one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*).
If one has not exhausted the outflows, how can one be said to be "worthy" (arhat)?
This is what is meant by "by way of reasoning.
If that is so, then the Charcoal Simile Sūtra should be explained accordingly.
As it is said:
"When a well-learned noble disciple is walking or standing, there may be occasions and times when, due to a lapse in mindfulness, unwholesome and evil thoughts arise.
This sutra speaks solely of the fruit of arhatship, as evidenced by these words from the sutra:
That noble disciple’s mind has, for a long night, conformed to seclusion, as explained at length up until the point of entering parinirvāṇa.
In other sūtras, this very conformity to seclusion and so forth is designated as the power of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva*).
Furthermore, this sutra states:
"He has already been able to permanently eject all that is conducive to the outflows (āsrava) and has already attained coolness.
From this, it is known with certainty that he is an Arhat.
What was stated previously refers to an Arhat; however, it is possible that such a thing might occur so long as one has not yet fully mastered oneself even during the times of walking or standing.

That is to say, for a learner (*śaikṣa*), afflictions may arise during the times of walking or standing due to a lapse of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*); but once one has become a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), there is no possibility for them to arise.
Since the preceding was based on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), there is no fault in saying so.
The Vaibhāṣika masters definitively maintain this position:
that even the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) is subject to falling away (*parihāṇi*).
If only the lineage of the Arhat is sixfold, do others also possess six lineages?
And if they do, are all of them capable of cultivating and refining their faculties?
The verse says:
The Śaikṣas and ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) also have six [lineages]; the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) does not occur during the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
The treatise says:
The lineages of the Śaikṣas and ordinary beings are likewise six, because these six types of Arhat-fruits (arhattva-phala) take them as their antecedents.

However, there is certainly no refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because it is impossible for preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to arise at this stage.

Only within the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is a follower by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) can one cultivate the refinement of the faculties, as is done in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
As stated in the Sūtra:

"I say that regarding any one of the four dwellings in happiness in this present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) realized through these [attainments], there may be falling away; however, concerning the unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*) which has been personally realized, I definitively declare that there is no cause or condition for falling away from it."
How can one who possesses the quality of being unshakable (akopyadharman) fall away from the blissful abiding in the present life?
The verse says:
It should be known that there are three kinds of falling away: From what has been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
The Buddha possesses only the last; for those of sharp faculties, the middle and the last; and for those of dull faculties, all three.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that there are, in total, three kinds of retrogression.
First is the loss of what has already been attained (*prāpti-hāni*), which refers to falling away from superior qualities already acquired.
Second is the loss of what has not yet been attained (*aprāpti-hāni*), which refers to being unable to attain superior qualities.
Third is the loss of enjoyment (*upabhoga-hāni*), which refers to superior qualities already acquired no longer manifesting before one.
Among these three types, the Blessed One possesses only the "retrogression from enjoyment" (*parihāṇi-bhoga*), because although he is endowed with all virtues, they cannot manifest simultaneously.

The others who possess immovability (*akopya-dharman*) possess both "retrogression from enjoyment" and "retrogression from non-attainment" (*aprāpti-parihāṇi*), as they have not yet attained the particularly sublime qualities that surpass their own.
The other five types of lineage may possess all three [kinds of retrogression], as they are also susceptible to losing qualities already attained.

With respect to retrogression from enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*), it is said that those of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) can retrogress from the bliss of the present life; thus, there is no contradiction.
The proponents of the theory of non-retrogression state as follows:
All untainted liberations (*anāsrava-vimukti*) are termed "unshakable" (*akopya*).

However, regarding the separate establishment of the sixth type, the "one of unshakable nature" (*akopyadharman*), it should not be considered a difficulty, as it has already been explained and resolved above.
Since it is admitted that Arhats may fall away from their fruit, are they born again?
Do they perform at the time of falling away those actions which they did not perform while abiding in the fruit? No, they do not.
For what reason?
The verse says:
All who fall back from a fruit will certainly attain it again before they die.
That which one who abides in the fruit does not do, he does not do because his sense of shame (*hrī*) has increased.
The commentary says:
There is no falling away from the fruit and dying in the interim; for once fallen, one will necessarily regain it in an instant.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that when such well-learned noble disciples lose right mindfulness, they are able to quickly recover and cause what has been lost to be exhausted, extinguished, and abandoned."
If one were to say otherwise, the fruit of practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) would not be a state of security that can be relied upon.

Furthermore, one who abides in the stage of fruition should not engage in actions contrary to that fruition; because their sense of shame (*hrī*) has increased, they will certainly not commit such acts even during a temporary lapse, just as a strong man may stumble but does not fall.

As stated above, there are those who attain the state of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning) or *śaikṣa* (in-training) through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*). At the time of such refinement, how many paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and how many paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there for each case?
To what nature (*svabhāva*) do they belong?
What is its basis?
The verse says:

In the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) consists of nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Because of long-term cultivation, the learner (śaikṣa) relies on one; the outflow-free (anāsrava) relies on three persons.
The non-learner (aśaikṣa) relies on nine stages, while the learner relies only on six.
This is because [the non-learner] abandons the path of the fruit and the path of superior fruits, retaining only the path of the fruit itself.
The Treatise says:

For one who seeks a superior spiritual lineage and cultivates the faculties (*indriya*), within the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for each transformation of a single lineage, just as in the attainment of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattva-phala*).

Why is this? Because that dull faculty has been habituated for a long time; it cannot be transformed by a small amount of effort, as it is made firm by what is accomplished through the paths of training and beyond-training.

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), when transitioning through each of the [nine] dispositions (*gotra*), there is respectively one path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as in the attainment of the first fruit; this is because they are contrary to those above.
In each of the stages of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), there is likewise one of each.
Thus, both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are comprised exclusively of the untainted (*anāsrava*) nature.
It is logically impossible for a noble one (*ārya*) to transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) by means of a tainted path, as such a path lacks the necessary predominance (*ādhipatya*).
"Support" refers to the body and the stage (*bhūmi*). This supporting body exists only among humans in the three continents, as there is no falling away [from the state of arhatship] elsewhere.

As for this supporting stage, the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is common to nine: namely, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
Those in training (śaikṣa) possess only six [faculties], namely, excluding the latter three.

Why is this? For one who undergoes the transformation of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra), it is possible to abandon both the fruit and the path superior to the fruit; however, that which is obtained is only the fruit, not the path of approach (mārga-pratipannaka).
Since there is no fruit of training (*śaikṣaphala*) included within the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), those who train their faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) rely solely upon the six stages.
How many types of individuals (*pudgala*) belonging to the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) are there in total?
By what distinction?
The verse says:
Seven śrāvakas and two buddhas Are distinguished by nine faculties.
The Commentary states:
There are nine noble ones who abide in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*): namely, seven śrāvakas and two types of awakened ones (*buddha*).

The five beginning with those subject to retrogression (*parihāṇadharman*) and the immovable one (*akopyadharman*)—which is divided into two based on the distinction between the latter and the former—are called the "seven śrāvakas."
The Pratyekabuddha and the Mahābuddha are called the two types of Awakened Ones (*buddha*).

Due to the differences among the nine grades of faculties—ranging from the lowest of the low and so forth—the noble ones who have attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are established as nine distinct categories.
There are seven types of noble beings within the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training; all noble beings are subsumed within these.

First, the follower by faith; second, the follower by Dharma; third, the one resolved through faith; fourth, the one attained through vision; fifth, the bodily witness; sixth, the one liberated through wisdom; seventh, the one doubly liberated.
On what basis are the seven established?
How many distinct entities are there?
The verse says:
The preparatory stages, the faculties, the cessation attainment, and the liberations constitute seven;
yet as distinct entities, there are only six, because each of the three paths has two.
The treatise says:

The first two types are established based on differences in their preparatory application (*prayoga*); that is, because they previously applied themselves to the objects of their pursuit by following others or the Dharma, they are designated with the names "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and "follower by Dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).

The next two types are established based on differences in their faculties (*indriya*): that is, based on the predominance of either dull or sharp faculties, and faith or wisdom, they are respectively named "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

The name "bodily witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) is established based on the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because one has bodily realized the attainment of cessation.

The latter two types are established based on differences in liberation: that is, one who is liberated from the hindrance of afflictions through wisdom alone is established as "liberated by wisdom," while one who additionally attains meditative concentration and is liberated from the hindrance to liberation is established as "doubly liberated."

Although these are designated by seven names, there are actually only six distinct entities. That is to say, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are two types of noble beings: first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*). Upon reaching the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these are given two distinct names: first, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); second, the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), they are again given two names: namely, the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*).
It should be understood that herein, the one who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin) becomes threefold by way of faculties—namely, inferior, medium, and superior;
fivefold by way of nature—namely, those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) and so forth;
and fifteenfold by way of the path—namely, the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the seven knowledges (jñāna).
There are seventy-three types based on the abandonment of defilements, meaning one who is bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana) and those who have abandoned the defilements of the eight stages.
There are nine types based on the physical basis (āśraya), namely the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm.

When these factors—faculties (indriya), spiritual lineage (gotra), path (mārga), abandonment of defilements, and physical basis—are multiplied together, they total one hundred and four million seven thousand eight hundred and twenty-five varieties.
The [categories of] those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmanusārin) and so forth should be considered according to reason.
What are those called "liberated by both" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and "liberated through wisdom" (prajñāvimukta)?
The verse says:
"Those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation are called 'liberated in both ways'; the others are called 'liberated by wisdom alone.
The Commentary says:

Those Arhats who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation are called "liberated in both ways," because through the power of both wisdom and concentration, they are liberated from both the afflictions and the hindrance to liberation.

Those who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta), because they have attained liberation from the hindrance of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) solely through the power of wisdom.
As the Blessed One said:
"One who has abandoned the five afflictions but is still susceptible to being led astray is not yet called a 'complete learner' (paripūrṇa-śaikṣa)."
By how many causes are those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) and those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) each uniquely designated as "perfected" (paripūrṇa) within their respective stages?
The verse says:
One in training is called "perfected" By virtue of three factors: faculties, fruit, and meditative concentration.
The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) receives the name "perfected" solely by virtue of two factors: faculties and meditative absorption.
The treatise says:
In the stage of training (śaikṣa), one alone receives the name "perfected" due to three causes, namely: faculties, fruition, and meditative absorption.

There are those in training who receive the designation "complete" solely by virtue of their faculties; this refers to those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) but have not yet abandoned the defilements of desire.

There are also those in training who receive the designation "complete" solely by virtue of their fruit; this refers to those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and non-returners (anāgāmin) who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

There are those among the learners (*śaikṣa*) who receive the designation "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) by virtue of both their faculties and their fruit; that is, those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

There are also those among the learners who receive the designation "complete" by virtue of their fruit and their meditative absorption; that is, those of the faith-follower type (*śraddhādhimukta*) who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation.

There are those in training who alone receive the designation "complete" by virtue of three factors: namely, those who have attained the state of "vision-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
There are no others among those in training who receive the designation "complete" solely by virtue of meditative absorption, nor even by virtue of both faculties and absorption.

Among those in the stage of no-more-learning, the designation "perfected" is attained solely through two factors—faculties and meditative concentration—within that stage of no-more-learning. Since there is nothing within the stage of no-more-learning that is not already perfected as a fruit, the designation "perfected" is not established on the basis of the fruit.

There are those who are called "complete" solely by virtue of their faculties, namely, those who are liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) but have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

There are those who are called "complete" solely by virtue of their meditative absorption, namely, those who are liberated by time (samayavimukta) and have attained the meditative absorption of cessation.

There are those who are called "complete" by virtue of two factors alone: namely, those liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) who have already attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
The distinctions among the various paths are immeasurable when explained in detail, such as the mundane and supramundane paths, the path of seeing, and the path of cultivation.
Briefly stated, how many paths can encompass them all?
The verse says:
One should know that all paths, when briefly stated, are only four.
That is to say: the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path, the path of liberation, and the path of excellence.
The Commentary states:
The path of preparation refers to that from which the uninterrupted path subsequently arises.
The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to that which is able to sever the obstructions that ought to be severed.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) refers to that which first arises once one has already been liberated from the obstructions that ought to be severed.
The path of superior progress refers to the three remaining paths.
What is the meaning of "path"?
It means the road to nirvāṇa, for by mounting it one is able to proceed to the city of nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, "path" (*mārga*) refers to that which is sought as a basis, for it is by relying upon this that one seeks the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
How can liberation (*vimukti*) and superior progress (*viśeṣa-gati*) be called a path?

Because they are of the same category as the path, as they transition to a higher grade; or because the power of each preceding stage reaches each succeeding stage; or because they are capable of leading one to enter the state of no-remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The Path is designated by the name "effective progress" (*pratipad*) in other contexts because it is able to lead one toward Nirvāṇa.
How many kinds of this are there?
Upon what basis are they established?
The verse says:
There are four types of practice: those based on the fundamental dhyānas are pleasant, while those based on the remaining stages are painful;
they are slow or swift according to whether one possesses dull or sharp faculties.
The treatise states:
The sūtras teach that there are four types of practice leading to penetration (*pratipad*):

first, the painful practice with slow progress; second, the painful practice with quick progress; third, the pleasant practice with slow progress; and fourth, the pleasant practice with quick progress.

The path that arises based on the four fundamental dhyānas is called the "path of ease" (*sukha-pratipad*), because it is supported by the factors [of dhyāna] and proceeds spontaneously through the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

The path that relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is called the "path of difficulty" (*duḥkha-pratipad*), because it lacks the supporting factors and proceeds with hardship due to the inequality of calm abiding and insight.

This means that in the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), insight (*vipaśyanā*) decreases while tranquility (*śamatha*) increases; in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), insight increases while tranquility decreases.
Within these two paths of practice—pleasurable and painful—that which involves dull faculties is called "slow," while that which involves sharp faculties is called "swift."
Because the two types of practice take a long time to penetrate their objects, they are called "slow penetration" (*mandābhijñā*); the opposite of this is called "swift.
Alternatively, the path of practice initiated by those who are dull-witted is called "the path of slow practice," while the swift is its opposite.
The Path is also called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
How many kinds are there,
and what are their names and meanings?
The verse says:
There are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, namely the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth;
"enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, and because they accord with this, they are called "factors."
The treatise states:

The sūtras explain that there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are designated as "awakening" (*bodhi*).
According to the distinctions among those who attain awakening, three types of awakening are established:
first, the awakening of the śrāvaka; second, the awakening of the pratyekabuddha; and third, the unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*).
Because ignorance and sleep have been forever severed, and because one knows as it truly is that what was to be done has been done and need not be done again—these two are called "awakening.
Since the thirty-seven factors accord with and lead toward enlightenment (*bodhi*), they are all termed "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Are the entities of these thirty-seven [factors] distinct from one another? No.
Why is this so?
The verse says:
In substance, these consist of only ten: namely, wisdom, diligence, concentration, faith, mindfulness, joy, equanimity, pliancy, as well as ethical discipline and investigation.
The treatise states:
Although these factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are thirty-seven in name, in actual substance there are only ten, namely: wisdom (prajñā), diligence (vīrya), and so forth.

That is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena, and right view all have wisdom as their essence.
The four right endeavors, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, the factor of enlightenment of energy, and right effort have diligence as their essence.
The four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration have concentration as their essence.
The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) have faith as their essence.

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) have mindfulness as their essence. The factor of enlightenment of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*) has joy as its essence; the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*) has equanimity of formation (*saṃskāropekṣā*) as its essence; the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*) has pliancy as its essence; right speech (*samyagvāk*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyagājīva*) have ethical discipline (*śīla*) as their essence; and right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) has applied thought (*vitarka*) as its essence.

Thus, the actual entities of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are only ten; that is, they consist of the five faculties and powers beginning with faith, plus joy, equanimity, pliancy, morality, and applied thought.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say there are eleven; because bodily action and vocal action are not intermingled, the precepts are divided into two, while the remaining nine are the same as before.

Since the three names—mindfulness foundations (*smṛtyupasthāna*), etc.—have no distinct individual referents, how can they be said to consist solely of wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*)?
The verse says:

The four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power are said to be, in order of their predominance, wisdom, diligence, and concentration; in reality, they are all wholesome states of application.
The treatise states:

The three categories of wholesome dharmas, beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness, substantially encompass all preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*). Nevertheless, they are designated respectively as wisdom, diligence, and meditative concentration, according to their predominant wholesome roots within each respective category.
For what reason is the name "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna) established for wisdom?
The Vaibhāṣika masters explain it thus:
because wisdom is maintained and made to abide by the power of mindfulness.

In reality, it is through wisdom that mindfulness causes the mind to abide upon its object; for one who sees things as they truly are is able to remember them clearly, as has already been extensively established in the section on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Why, then, is diligence called "right abandonment" (*samyakprahāṇa*)?
In the stage of correctly practicing abandonment and cultivation, this diligence is called "right effort" (*samyakprahāṇa*) because it is capable of abandoning laziness;
alternatively, it is called "right exertion" (*samyagvyāyāma*) because it is the most excellent among the correct application of body, speech, and mind.
For what reason is the name "basis of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda) established for meditative concentration?
Because it is the basis upon which all sublime and wondrous qualities depend.
Other masters say:
The "divine" (*divya*) is concentration (*samādhi*), while "feet" (*pāda*) refers to desire and the others.
According to that [position], there would be thirteen factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), because desire and mind have been added.
Furthermore, this contradicts the sūtra; as the sūtra says:

I shall now explain for you the *ṛddhi-pāda*s (bases of supernormal power). "Supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the enjoyment of various miraculous feats, such as dividing one into many, and so forth, as explained at length.

"Bases" (*pāda*) refer to the four *samādhi*s beginning with desire. Herein, the Buddha states that the fruit of meditative concentration is called "supernormal power," while the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) produced by desire and the others are called "bases."
For what reason are faith and the others first called "faculties" (indriya) and later termed "powers" (bala)?

It is because these five factors are distinguished as preceding or succeeding based on their lower or superior grades, and because they are respectively susceptible to being overcome or incapable of being overcome.
For what reason do faith and the others follow this specific sequence?

It is because one first gives rise to faith regarding cause and effect; having done so, one cultivates the causes for the sake of the fruit. Next, one gives rise to diligence. By means of diligence, mindfulness abides upon its object. Sustained by the power of mindfulness, the mind attains concentration. Because the mind has attained concentration, one is able to know things as they truly are. Therefore, faith and the others follow this sequence.
At which stage should it be said that which factor of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) predominates?
The verse says:
In the stages of the beginner, the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), And the paths of cultivation and seeing.
The seven categories, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood as increasing in sequence.
The Commentary states:

In the stage of a beginner (*ādikarmika*), one is able to discern and clearly perceive the four objects, such as the body; because the function of wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant at this time, it is said that the foundations of mindfulness increase.

In the stage of the Heat-dharma (*uṣmagata*), because the application of diligence is predominant as one is able to realize superior qualities of a different category, the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) are said to increase.

In the stage of the Summit-dharma (*mūrdhan*), because the application of concentration is predominant as one is able to maintain superior wholesome states and proceed toward non-retrogression, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are said to increase.

Within the stage of the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*), one necessarily does not fall back, for because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are firm and attain the sense of superiority, they are said to be "increased faculties" (*indriya-vardhana*).
Within the first stage [the stage of heat], one cannot be subdued by afflictions or worldly dharmas; because one attains the sense of being unsubdued, it is said that the "powers" (*bala*) increase.

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one is close to the state of enlightenment; because they assist awakening preeminently, the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) are said to increase.
In the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one proceeds with rapidity; because the practice is preeminent, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are said to increase.
However, in the sūtras, the numbers are stated in ascending order—first seven and then eight—but this does not represent the actual sequence of cultivation.
Among these eight, right view is both the path and a factor of the path; the remaining seven are factors of the path but are not the path itself.
Among the seven [limbs], the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is both awakening (*bodhi*) and a limb of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*);
the others are limbs of awakening but not awakening itself. Such is the teaching of the Vaibhāṣikas.

Others, without contradicting the sequence taught in the sūtras, establish the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth as follows: when a practitioner is about to engage in cultivation, their mind is distracted among many objects; therefore, they first cultivate the foundations of mindfulness to subdue that mind. Thus, the sūtra says:
These four foundations of mindfulness are able to bind the mind to its objects and correctly eliminate mindfulness that relies on sensual indulgence;
therefore, the foundations of mindfulness are taught first.

Through this power, diligence subsequently increases; in order to accomplish four tasks, the mind is correctly exerted and sustained. For this reason, the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) are taught as the second [foundation].

Because of diligence, there is no state of regret or remorse, and one thus possesses the capacity to cultivate and refine superior concentration (*samādhi*). For this reason, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught as the third.

With the supreme meditative concentration as their basis, they cause faith and the other faculties to serve as dominant conditions for supramundane dharmas; for this reason, these five faculties are designated as the fourth [set].

Once the meaning of "faculty" (indriya) is established, they are able to correctly suppress and eliminate the active manifestations of their opposites and draw forth the noble dharmas; for this reason, these five powers (bala) are designated as the fifth [set].
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are established at the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one realizes the four noble truths as they truly are.
The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established throughout both stages, because both are equally conducive to proceeding directly toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"One who has cultivated the eight factors of the path to perfection has also cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness up to the seven factors of enlightenment to perfection.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that speaking words of suchness is a metaphor for teaching the Four Noble Truths;
causing one to travel swiftly out by way of the original path is a metaphor for causing one to cultivate the eight branches of the Noble Path."
Thus we know that the eight factors of the path are taught as applying to both stages.
Since the sequence has been explained according to the stage of predominance, one should now state the actual principle:
among these thirty-seven factors, how many pertain to the outflowing (sāsrava) and how many to the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
The verse says:
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eight path factors are exclusively untainted;
the three, four, five faculties, and powers all pertain to both types.
The Commentary states:

Among these, the seven factors of enlightenment and the eight branches of the noble path are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are established only within the stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
There are also factors such as right view in the mundane world, yet they do not receive the designation of "limbs of the noble path.
All the remaining factors are common to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding these thirty-seven [factors], how many are present in which stage (*bhūmi*)?
The verse says:
In the first dhyāna, all [factors] are present; in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the faculty of joy is excluded;
in the second dhyāna, vitarka is excluded; in the third, fourth, and intermediate [dhyānas], both [vitarka and vicāra] are excluded.
In the first three formless stages, the two preceding types [of factors] excluding the precepts are absent;
in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, the factors of enlightenment and the path members are excluded.
The commentary says:

In the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors are present. In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) is excluded because, being a threshold stage, one must exert effort and because there is still doubt regarding the factors of the lower stages.
In the second dhyāna, right thought (samyak-saṃkalpa) is excluded, because vitarka is already absent in that dhyāna.
Thus, these two stages each have thirty-six [factors].
In the third and fourth dhyānas, as well as in the intermediate dhyāna, both joy (prīti) and vitarka are excluded, leaving thirty-five in each.
In the first three formless realms, thirty-two factors are present, excluding the three branches of morality as well as joy and applied thought;

in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), twenty-two factors are present, excluding the factors of enlightenment and the path factors respectively, because they lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) states. When the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are active, one necessarily attains the verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).
How many types of this are there?
In what state is it attained?
What dharma is its substantial entity?
Are they with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
There are four kinds of verified purity (*avetyaprasāda*), namely: those regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts.
Upon seeing the three [truths], one acquires the dharma-precept; upon seeing the path, one also acquires the Buddha- and Sangha-precepts.
"Dharma" refers here to the complete three truths and the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas.
These two—faith and precept—are their essence; all four are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
The Commentary states:
The Sūtra teaches that there are four kinds of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*):

first, verified clarity regarding the Buddha; second, verified clarity regarding the Dharma; third, verified clarity regarding the Saṃgha; and fourth, verified clarity regarding noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*).

Furthermore, when one perceives the three truths during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), in each instance one attains only the verified confidence in the Dharma and the precepts (*dharma-śīla-prasāda*).

At the stage of perceiving the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*), one additionally attains verified confidence in the Buddha and the Sangha; that is to say, at that time, one simultaneously attains verified confidence in the various dharmas of the Aśaikṣas who have become Buddhas, as well as in the Śaikṣa and Aśaikṣa dharmas that constitute the Sangha of Śrāvakas.
The inclusion of the word "also" (兼) is intended to show that at the time of seeing the Truth of the Path, one also attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma and the precepts.
Furthermore, the Dharma that is the object of faith is briefly of two kinds: first, the specific; second, the general.
In general, this pertains to all four truths; specifically, however, it refers only to three truths.
Since it encompasses the entire path of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas, one attains the verified clarity regarding the Dharma upon seeing each of the four truths.
Because the morality cherished by the Noble Ones arises simultaneously with clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there is no time when it is not likewise attained.

Because the objects of faith differ, there are four names; however, one should know that in terms of actual entities, there are only two kinds. That is to say, the three types of verified clarity regarding the Buddha and so forth have faith as their essence, while the verified clarity of noble ethical discipline has ethical discipline as its essence; therefore, there are only two.
These four types are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena are not "clear realization" (*avetyaprasāda*).
Based on what meaning is the name "clear realization" established?
It is called "realization" (*pratyakṣa*) because one realizes the principle of the Four Noble Truths exactly as they are.
The Three Jewels in which one has faith and the sublime ethical discipline (śīla) are both termed "pure," because they are free from the stains of lack of faith and the stains of impaired morality.
Because these are established through the realization of purity, they are designated by the name "realization of purity" (avetyaprasāda).
Just as there is a sequence of manifestation when emerging from meditative absorption, it is said that the sequence within the absorption is likewise.
What is the sequence of manifestation at the time of emergence?

It is as follows: at the stage of emerging from absorption, one first places faith in the Blessed One as the Perfectly Awakened One; next, one places faith in the True Dharma and the Vinaya as being well-expounded; and finally, one places faith in the Noble Ones as those who practice excellently.
Because right faith in the Three Jewels is like a skilled physician, like excellent medicine, and like a caregiver for the sick;
because pure ethical discipline (śīla) arises from the purity of the mind, ethical discipline is therefore taught as the fourth.
Pure faith must be present for this [realization] to manifest, just as an illness is only cured when three conditions are met.
Alternatively, these four are like a guide, the road, traveling companions, and the vehicle one rides.
The Sūtra states:
"Those in the stage of training (śaikṣa) accomplish eight factors; those in the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa) fully accomplish ten.
For what reason does it not say that those in the stage of training possess right liberation (samyag-vimukti) and right knowledge (samyag-jñāna)?
What is the essential nature of right liberation and right knowledge?
The verse says:
Because those in training still possess remaining fetters, they do not have the factor of right knowledge of liberation.
Liberation is both conditioned and unconditioned; it is said that the superior liberation consists in the destruction of the fetters.
The conditioned factors of the adept (aśaikṣa) are precisely the two aggregates of liberation.
Right knowledge is as explained in the case of enlightenment: it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
The treatise says:
Within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), because there are still remaining fetters not yet liberated, there is no factor of liberation (*vimokṣāṅga*).
One cannot be called "liberated" while separated from even a few fetters; nor can the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*) be established in the absence of the essence of liberation.

The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) has already been liberated from the bonds of all afflictions and can further give rise to two types of clear knowledge regarding liberation; because these two are manifest, two factors may be established.
This is not the case for the one still in training (śaikṣa), and therefore only eight [factors] are established.
The essence of liberation is twofold: namely, conditioned and unconditioned.
Conditioned liberation refers to the resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); unconditioned liberation refers to the extinction of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Conditioned liberation is called a limb of one beyond training (*aśaikṣāṅga*), because the designation "limb" is established based on what is conditioned.
Furthermore, there are two types of liberation included among these limbs, namely those spoken of in other sūtras as mental liberation (*ceto-vimukti*) and wisdom liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*).
One should know that these two are precisely the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*).
If this is so, it would contradict the Sūtra which asks:
"What is the most excellent purity of liberation?"
This refers to the mind being liberated from the defilement of greed, and liberated from the defilements of hatred and delusion.

Because one cultivates desire, effort, and so forth to fulfill the aggregate of liberation that is not yet fulfilled, or to maintain that which is already fulfilled, the aggregate of liberation is not merely resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*).
If that is so, what is it? Other masters say:
when greed, hatred, and delusion are dispelled by the power of true knowledge, the mind itself, being free from defilement, is called the aggregate of liberation.
Thus, the essence of right liberation has been explained.

As for the essence of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it is as previously stated regarding awakening—that is, the aforementioned knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
At which time does the mind truly attain liberation that it is called "the liberation of the mind of one beyond training" (*aśaikṣacittavimukti*)?
The verse says:
When the mind of one beyond training arises, it is precisely then that it is liberated from its obstructions.
The commentary says:
As stated in the treatise, when the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is about to arise in the future, it is liberated from an obstacle.
What is this obstacle? It refers to the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because that [diamond-like concentration] is able to obstruct the arising of this mind, it is completely severed at the moment of its actual cessation; meanwhile, the first mind of one beyond training attains liberation at the moment of its actual arising.

In the state where the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has already ceased, those [defilements] have been abandoned; thus, the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), in its state of having already arisen, is called "already liberated.
At that same time, the unarisen minds of one beyond training as well as worldly minds (*laukika-citta*) are also termed "liberated."
However, for now, we shall speak of those who are certain to be born, because at that time they still engage in the body and the world.
From what are these conventional minds liberated?
They are liberated from those very obstacles that hinder the arising of the mind.
Is it not the case that this [consciousness] does not arise during the state prior to liberation?
Although it has already arisen, it is not like what it is now.
To what, then, is it similar?
It arises simultaneously with the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*). Thereafter, if it were to arise, there would be no simultaneous acquisition of the afflictions.
At what stage does the Path cause the obstruction to arising to be severed?
The verse says:
Only at the stage of the Path’s present cessation can it cause those obstacles to be severed.
The commentary says:
The term "the stage of being in the process of ceasing" indicates that [the path] resides in the present;
the term "the process of arising" indicates the future life.
This is because the Path can sever hindrances only at the moment it is in the process of ceasing, as it certainly lacks the function of severing hindrances in other stages.

This is not like liberation, which extends to those who have not yet been born [in a particular realm], because there is no distinction between those already born and those not yet born in terms of being free from hindrances.
When the Sūtra speaks of the three realms as "cessation through abandonment," "separation," and "extinction," what constitutes their essential nature?
What is the distinction?
The verse says:
The unconditioned is said to be the three realms; the realm of detachment is exclusively the detachment from greed.
The realm of abandonment abandons the remaining fetters; the realm of cessation ceases those phenomena.
The commentary states:
These three realms—abandonment and so forth—are simply divisions of the previously explained unconditioned liberation, which they take as their own essence.
Regarding the "element of detachment" (*virāga-dhātu*), it refers to being detached from craving alone.
Regarding the "element of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-dhātu*), it refers to abandoning the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding the "element of cessation" (*nirodha-dhātu*), it refers to the cessation of those remaining objects (*vastu*) that are augmented by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as craving.
The Sūtra states that the three realms are themselves unconditioned liberation.
If a phenomenon can induce weariness, must it necessarily lead to detachment? Not so.
How so? The verse says:
The wisdom that takes suffering and its origin as its object is "disgust"; The wisdom that takes the four truths as its object is "detachment" and can sever [the fetters].
Relative to one another, they vary in breadth and narrowness; thus, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
The treatise says:

Only the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) arising from taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as their objects are designated as "aversion" (*nirveda*); the others are not so.

The patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) that arise regarding the objects of the Four Truths and are capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) all receive the designation "detachment" (*vairāgya*); however, because there are differences in their breadth and narrowness, they form four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*).

There is that which is aversion (*vidūṣaṇā*) but not detachment: this refers to all patience and knowledge that take suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as their objects but do not cause the afflictions to be severed, because they take objects of aversion as their domain and are not yet detached from defilement.

There is detachment that is not aversion, namely, all forms of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) that take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their object and are capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they take a joyful object as their focus and are able to bring about freedom from defilement.

There is both aversion and detachment, namely, all forms of patience and knowledge that take suffering (*duḥkha*) or origination (*samudaya*) as their object and are capable of severing the afflictions.

There is that which is not "disgust" (*vidūṣaṇā*), namely, those forms of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) that take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their object and do not cause the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).

It should be understood that among the various patiences and knowledges belonging to one who has first abandoned the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*) and subsequently realizes the truths (*satyadarśana*), those included within the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) do not cause the abandonment of afflictions; for the afflictions have already been abandoned, and these [paths] are not antidotes for abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*).
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-five.

Chapter Seven: Analysis of Knowledge (Vijñāna-vibhaṅga). Part One of Seven. At the beginning of the preceding chapter, the various patiences (kṣānti) and knowledges (jñāna) were explained; subsequently, right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi) and right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) were further discussed.
Is there that which is patience but not knowledge?
Is there that which is knowledge but not vision?
The verse says:
Noble patience (*ārya-kṣānti*) is not knowledge (*jñāna*); the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are not views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The remaining two types of outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) are both knowledge; six have the nature of view.
The commentary says:
Wisdom is of two kinds: with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*). Only wisdom without outflows is designated by the name "noble" (*ārya*).
Within this noble wisdom, the eight forbearances (*kṣānti*) do not possess the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), because the doubts to be abandoned by them have not yet been severed.
The nature of seeing (*darśana*) is comprised within [the first two knowledges], because it is of the nature of inferential deliberation (*tarka*).

The two knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣaya*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*) are not of the nature of seeing, because the mind of seeking has already ceased and they do not engage in inferential deliberation.
All remaining [knowledges] are common to both the natures of knowledge (*jñāna*) and seeing, because self-doubt has been severed and they are of the nature of inferential deliberation.

All contaminated wisdoms are subsumed under the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*); among these, only six are also of the nature of vision (*dṛṣṭi*), namely: the five defiled views and worldly right view as the sixth.
The noble and impure wisdoms thus described are all subsumed under the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), as they all consist in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
How many kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*) are there,
and what are their distinct characteristics?
The verse says:
Wisdom is tenfold in total, divided into the contaminated and the uncontaminated;
the contaminated is called conventional, while the uncontaminated is named dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.
The conventional [knowledge] takes all as its object;
the dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge take, respectively, the truths of suffering and so forth in the desire realm and the higher realms as their objects.
The treatise says:
Wisdom is of ten kinds, encompassing all forms of knowledge:

first, conventional wisdom; second, dharma-wisdom; third, subsequent wisdom; fourth, wisdom of suffering; fifth, wisdom of origination; sixth, wisdom of cessation; seventh, wisdom of the path; eighth, wisdom of others' minds; ninth, wisdom of exhaustion; and tenth, wisdom of non-arising.
Thus, these ten knowledges are in total only two kinds, distinguished by their nature as being either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
These two knowledges are further differentiated into three types: namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
The former, contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*), is collectively termed conventional (*saṃvṛti*), because it predominantly takes conventional objects such as jars and the like as its domain.
The latter, uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), is divided into the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of categories (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Among these three types of knowledge, the conventional is all-pervasive, taking all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as its cognitive objects.
The two types of knowledge—dharma-knowledge and subsequent-knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—take as their respective objects the Four Truths of the desire realm and the higher realms.
Regarding these two types of knowledge, the verse says:
"Dharma and subsequent [knowledges] are established by the distinction of their objects; They are designated by the four names of suffering and so forth."
All are fully penetrating and lead to the unborn; initially, they consist only of the categories of suffering and its origin.
The Commentary states:
Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are divided into four knowledges—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—based on the distinctions of their objects.

Thus, if these six knowledges are comprised within the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and are not of the nature of vision (*darśana*), they are termed the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

When these two first arise, they consist only of the inferential knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin; this is because they take the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object by means of the six modes of activity (*ākāra*) that observe suffering and its origin.
Is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) the same as this?
It depends on whether it takes suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as its object, or cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
Among the nine types of knowledge previously mentioned, the verse says:
The knowledge of others' minds is established through the Dharma-knowledge, Subsequent-knowledge, Path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge;
it does not know [the objects] of superior stages, faculties, or states, nor those of the past or future.
Furthermore, Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge do not know one another. This applies to Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas.
"Respectively, one knows the path of seeing through two or three moments and all [moments].
The commentary says:
There are dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge that constitute the knowledge of others' minds; the others do not.
This knowledge possesses a determinate aspect regarding its object, namely that it does not know a superior mind or minds of the past and future.
There are three kinds of superior minds: those distinguished by stage (*bhūmi*), faculty (*indriya*), and state (*avasthā*).
Regarding "levels" (*bhūmi*): the knowledge of a lower level does not know the mind of a higher level.

Regarding "faculties" (*indriya*): the knowledge of those with the faculty of faith-resolve (*śraddhādhimukta*) or the faculty of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) does not know the mind of those with the faculty of vision-attainment (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or the faculty of non-occasional liberation (*asamayavimukta*).
"Stages" refers to the fruit of non-returning for śrāvakas, the fruit of arhatship, pratyekabuddhas, and great awakening.

The cognition of each preceding stage does not know the mind of a subsequent, superior stage; this cognition does not know past or future minds because it takes as its object only the minds and mental factors capable of cognition within the present mental continuum of another.

Furthermore, the categories of Dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and Subsequent-knowledge (anvayajñāna) do not mutually cognize one another; that is to say, the various forms of knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) subsumed under Dharma-knowledge do not know the category of Subsequent-knowledge, and the various forms of knowledge of others' minds subsumed under Subsequent-knowledge do not know the category of Dharma-knowledge. This is because Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge take as their objects of cognition, respectively, the complete antidotes for the Desire Realm and the higher realms.
