first, equanimity; second, right mindfulness; third, right discernment; fourth, the experience of bliss; and fifth, meditative concentration.
The fourth dhyāna possesses only four factors:
First, the purity of equanimity; second, the purity of mindfulness; third, the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant;
and fourth, meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since there are eighteen names for these factors of dhyāna, how many distinct entities are there in total among them?
The verse says:
These are eleven real entities; the first two are bliss and pliancy;
inner serenity is the faculty of faith; and joy is the feeling of gladness.
The Commentary states:
These factors (aṅga) consist of only eleven actual entities (dravya). That is to say, the first five factors are five actual entities.
The three factors of the second dhyāna are as previously described; with the addition of the factor of internal serenity (adhyātmasaṃprasāda), they total six.
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the third dhyāna is as previously described; with the addition of the other four factors, it totals ten.
The three factors of the fourth dhyāna are as previously described; with the addition of the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*), they total eleven.
For this reason, it is said that there may be that which is the first factor but not the second factor; one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation refers to vitarka and vicāra.
The second permutation refers to internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
The third phrase refers to joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The fourth phrase refers to all other phenomena (*dharma*) excluding those previously mentioned.
The remaining factors should be considered in relation to one another according to reason.
Why is it that the third [dhyāna] is said to have an increase in pleasant feeling?
Because the pleasant feelings of the first two [dhyānas] are comprised within pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
What reasoning serves as proof that this is *praśrabdhi* (pliancy)?
Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) does not exist within the first and second dhyānas.

It is not the case that there is pleasure of the body (*kāyika-sukha*) in the first and second dhyānas, because when one is actually in meditative absorption, the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are absent.
Furthermore, there is no mental experience of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because it is said that there is joy (*prīti*).
Joy is itself the feeling of joy (*prīti-vedanā*); since two feelings do not coexist within a single moment of mind, there is no feeling of pleasure.
It is not that the [feelings of] non-delight and delight manifest alternately, for they are said to possess five factors and four factors respectively. Some say:

there is no mental faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); those instances of the factor of pleasure mentioned within the three dhyānas are all instances of the pleasure faculty subsumed under bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*).
If that is so, why does a sūtra state:
"What is the faculty of pleasure?
It refers to the pleasant bodily and mental sensations produced by the power of contact conducive to pleasure"?
Others add the word "mental" (*caitasika*) here, arguing that the various schools' sūtras speak only of it as being "bodily" (*kāyika*).
Furthermore, they claim that the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*) established in the third dhyāna is explicitly stated by the sūtra itself to be "bliss experienced by the body."
If it is claimed that "body" (*kāya*) refers to the mind (*manas*) in this context, what benefit is there in using the term "body"?
Furthermore, since pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) increases manifold in the fourth dhyāna, yet it is not said that this stage possesses the factor of pleasure (*sukha*).

If it is argued that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) must be called "pleasure" only when it accords with a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), then the pliancy of the third dhyāna, which accords with pleasure, should also be a factor of pleasure (*sukha-aṅga*).
If it is further argued that the pliancy there is impaired by equanimity (*upekṣā*), [then the same would apply elsewhere].
It is not so, because the cultivation of equanimity increases pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Furthermore, that pliancy is superior to the previous two.
Moreover, a sutra states:

If, at that time, the noble disciples personally realize the joy born of seclusion with their bodies and dwell in its fulfillment, they have at that time already abandoned five qualities and fully cultivated five qualities. To speak extensively, what are the five qualities that are to be cultivated?
First, joy; second, gladness; third, pliancy; fourth, bliss; fifth, samādhi.
Since this sutra explains pliancy and bliss separately, the first two types of bliss are not identical to pliancy.
If one asks, "How can there be body-consciousness within meditative absorption?

there is no fault in saying that there is; for it is admitted that within absorption there exists the wind of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-vāyu*), which arises from superior concentration and, being conducive to the production of pleasant feeling, pervades the entire body.

If it is argued that concentration must be lost due to external distraction, such a fault does not apply; for this wind of pliancy arises from superior concentration and, by inducing internal physical bliss, is itself conducive to the further arising of samādhi.
If it is argued that one should be said to have emerged from meditative absorption when the body-consciousness arises, this objection is not valid for the reasons stated previously.

If it is argued that a tactile consciousness of the form realm cannot arise based on the body-faculty of the desire realm, there is no fault in admitting its arising when it takes pliancy as its object.

If that were so, then contact (*sparśa*) and body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) occurring while one is actually in an untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*) would themselves have to be untainted.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of contradicting reason, whereby the factors (*aṅga*) established [as constituents of the absorption] would be partly tainted (*sāsrava*) and partly untainted.
There is no fault of contradicting reason.
Why is this? Because it is admitted that the physical pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) spoken of is included within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

If it is argued that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are so called because they are conducive to them, then one must likewise admit that the untainted (anāsrava) states are also spoken of in this way.
If it is argued that admitting such a statement contradicts the sūtra, as the sūtra says:
"Whatever eyes there are," and so forth, as explained at length.

Since this sūtra states that all fifteen elements are entirely with outflows (*sāsrava*), it does not contradict the sūtras; for this was spoken with the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) of referring to other types of contact and other body-consciousnesses.
How can an untainted (*anāsrava*) dhyāna manifest with some factors being tainted (*sāsrava*) and others untainted?
Since these do not arise simultaneously, what fault is there in this?
If it is argued that because joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) do not arise together, there would be no logical basis for the five factors or the four factors [of the dhyānas], [we reply: ...

This is also without fault, for it is spoken of in terms of what is possible; thus, the factors of joy and bliss are said to exist [in that state], just as applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are said to exist.

If you argue that since applied and sustained thought are also admitted to arise simultaneously, they cannot serve as an analogy for something that does not arise simultaneously, [we reply: this is not so.
This is not unestablished; because the coarseness and subtlety of the mind are mutually contradictory, they should not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, no fault can be found in their non-simultaneous arising.

From this it can be said that, based on the first five factors, by reducing two, three, or four, the second [dhyāna] and so forth are established. It is precisely by this principle that the five factors are first mentioned, intended as a gradual departure from the former and the establishment of the latter.
Because there is no gradual reduction [of factors], perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth are not mentioned.
Alternatively, one might ask: for what reason are only five factors established in the first [dhyāna]?
If it is argued that these five are established as factors because they are superior in supporting the first dhyāna, [then the same logic would apply to other factors].
This is not reasonable, because mindfulness and wisdom can support superior vitarka and vicāra.
Although some may speak thus, it is not a position established by the ancient masters in common; therefore, it should be carefully examined and deliberated.

One should explain that what is called "inner serenity" (adhyātmasaṃprasāda) refers to this meditative concentration which, being far removed from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), proceeds with a continuous purity; thus it is named inner serenity.
If there is agitation caused by vitarka and vicāra, the continuum proceeds in an impure manner, like a river with waves.
If this were so, these [mental factors] would have no distinct substance; how then could one allow for eleven real entities?
Therefore, it should be said that this is precisely the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

That is to say, when one realizes the second dhyāna, there arises a profound faith capable of being free from [the hindrances] even within the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*); this is called internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
Faith is the characteristic of purity; therefore, it is designated by the name "purity.
Because it is free from external influences and flows evenly, it is called "internal equanimity.
Being pure and internally equanimous, it is thus designated by the name "internal equanimous purity."
Other masters say:
"In this case, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have no distinct entities.
If they have no distinct entities, mental factors (*caitta*) would not be established; however, even though they are merely specific states of mind, they may still be designated as 'mental factors'."
Although this principle exists, it is not our tenet.
As stated above, joy (*prīti*) is simply the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*).
What serves as proof that this is definitively so?
How could you say that joy (*prīti*) is not the feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*), as other schools permit? I also permit it to be so.
How do the other schools permit it to be not the feeling of joy?

They claim that there is a distinct joy which is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), and that the bliss (*sukha*) in the three dhyānas is entirely the feeling of joy; therefore, joy and the feeling of joy are different in their essential natures.
The bliss of the third dhyāna cannot be designated as the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), for this is clearly established by two Āgamas.
As stated in the *Viparyāsa-vibhaṅga-sūtra*:

"The five faculties, beginning with sorrow (*daurmanasya*), are gradually and completely extinguished; in the third dhyāna, joy is completely extinguished; and in the fourth dhyāna, bliss is completely extinguished."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"In the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (sukha) is abandoned, pain (duḥkha) is abandoned, and previously joy (prīti) and sorrow (daurmanasya) have subsided.
Therefore, the third dhyāna must certainly lack the faculty of joy (prīti-indriya); for this reason, the feeling of joy is *prīti*, not *sukha*.
Regarding these aforementioned factors of dhyāna, are they all present within the defiled dhyānas? No.
Why is this so?
The verse says:
The defiled [dhyānas] follow in order from the first;
they lack joy, bliss, internal purity, right mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and mindfulness. Others say they also lack tranquility and equanimity.
The treatise says:
Regarding the factors of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*) as described above, they are not all present within defiled absorptions.
Furthermore, there is a certain class [of teachers] who speak according to the characteristics [of each factor]:
In the first defiled [dhyāna], there is no joy and happiness born of seclusion, because it does not arise apart from afflictions.
In the second defiled [dhyāna], there is no internal clarity, because it is disturbed and turbid by afflictions.
In the third dhyāna with outflows, there is no right mindfulness or wisdom, because it is deluded by the pleasure of defilement.
In the fourth dhyāna with outflows, there is no equanimity, mindfulness, or purity, because it is defiled by afflictions.
Other masters say:

"In the first two defiled [meditative attainments], there is simply no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); in the latter two defiled ones, there is simply no equanimity of formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), because these are subsumed under the great wholesome states.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The first three concentrations are subject to movement, while the fourth is immovable.
Based on what meaning is this said?
The verse states:
The fourth is called "unshakable" (āniñjya), because it is free from the eight calamities.
These eight are: vitarka and vicāra, and the four [types of] inhalation and exhalation associated with the four feelings (*vedanā*).
The commentary says:
The lower three dhyānas are called "subject to movement" because they possess afflictions;
the fourth dhyāna is called "unmoving" because it is free from afflictions.
There are eight such afflictions; what are these eight?

Vitarka, vicāra, the four types of feeling, inhalation, and exhalation—these eight afflictions are entirely absent in the fourth [dhyāna]; therefore, the Blessed One described it as "unshakable" (āneñja).
However, a sūtra states:
"The fourth dhyāna is not moved by vitarka, vicāra, prīti, or sukha.
Other masters say:
The fourth dhyāna is like a lamp in a sealed room, shining without flickering.
Is it the case that all feelings produced in the meditative dhyānas are likewise? No, they are not.
How so? The verse says:
In the first dhyāna and those arising from it, there are the feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity.
And joy, equanimity, and the pleasure of equanimity; these are exclusively feelings of equanimity, respectively.
The treatise says:
Within the dhyānas, there are initially three feelings:
First, the sensation of joy (*saumanasya-vedanā*), which is associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*);
second, the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), which is associated with the first three consciousnesses;
and third, the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), which is associated with the four consciousnesses.

The second [dhyāna] has two [mental factors], namely joy (*prīti*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*); it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and lacks the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), because there is no other consciousness present and because mental gladness (*cittaudvilya*) is coarse.
The third [dhyāna] has two, namely pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which are associated with the mental consciousness.
The fourth [dhyāna] has only one [type of feeling], namely, exclusively equanimity associated with the mental consciousness.
This is what is meant by the distinction in the feelings produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Since the upper three dhyānas lack the three groups of sensory consciousnesses and are devoid of vitarka and vicāra, how can one born there see, hear, touch, or produce manifest action (*vijñapti-karma*)?
It is not that those born in that stage lack eye-consciousness and the rest;
rather, it is simply that they are not bound to that stage.
Why is this? The verse says:
When one is born in the three higher dhyānas and gives rise to the minds of the three consciousnesses that manifest intimation,
these are all subsumed under the first dhyāna and are exclusively non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
The treatise says:

When one is born in the three higher stages, the arising of the three groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and the mind that initiates manifest action (*vijñapti-citta*) are all bound to the first dhyāna.

Just as when one born in a higher stage gives rise to a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), so too can they see, hear, touch, and initiate manifest action; these four are exclusively non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
One does not give rise to defiled states of a lower level because one has already abandoned defilement;
one does not give rise to wholesome states of a lower level because they are inferior.
Having thus explained the matter of dhyāna individually, [the text continues:]
Regarding the initial attainment of the pure [dhyānas] and so forth, how does it occur?
The verse says:
One attains them entirely without having previously possessed them; The pure ones arise through the abandonment of defilements.
The untainted [attainments] arise from detachment; the tainted [attainments] arise from birth and from falling away.
The Commentary says:

Regarding the eight fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*), as appropriate to each case, if one acquires them when they were previously entirely unestablished, the pure (*śuddhaka*) ones arise through detachment and through taking birth. That is to say, they arise when one detaches from the defilements of a lower stage while in a lower stage, and when one is born into one's own stage from a higher stage.
The same applies to all seven lower levels.
This is not the case for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because there is no way to be born there except through the abandonment of attachment (*vairāgya*).
For what purpose is the term "entirely unaccomplished" (*sarveṇa-asamanvāgata*) stated? It serves to exclude [the possibility that it might be accomplished] by any other means.

To preclude the notion that what has already been attained can be acquired again in part— such as the attainment of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) through application, or the attainment of the concentration conducive to decline (*parihāṇabhāgīya-samādhi*) through falling away—
one asks, based on this very point:
"Is there any pure concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*) that is obtained through the removal of passion (*vairāgya-lābhika*)?"
The same applies to the question regarding [the abandonment of] detachment through the loss of that detachment, through falling away, or through rebirth.
It is said:
There is; namely, the stage conducive to decline (*parihāṇabhāgīya*).

Furthermore, the first dhyāna categorized as conducive to retrogression is acquired when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm and is abandoned when one becomes free from the defilements of its own level; it is acquired when one retrogresses from freedom from the defilements of its own level and is abandoned when one retrogresses from freedom from the defilements of the desire realm.
One acquires [the dharmas] of a higher stage through self-attainment, and one relinquishes those of a lower stage through self-relinquishment.
Those subsumed under other stages should be considered according to reason.

The untainted (anāsrava) is acquired solely through the abandonment of defilement; that is to say, when a noble one abandons the defilements of a lower stage, they acquire the untainted [dharmas] of a higher stage.

This also refers only to those who have not yet attained it at all; if one has already attained it previously, it may also be acquired at other times—namely, the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga) is attained at the stage of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), and both the paths of learning (śaikṣa) and no-more-learning are attained at the time of refining the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra).
The remaining preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and retrogressions should all be considered according to reason.

Is it not the case that by entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one is also said to have attained the first untainted meditative attainment (*anāsrava-samāpatti*)?
This is not a fixed rule.
For one who follows the sequential path, at that time they have not yet attained the fundamental dhyāna.
Here, we are discussing only those who definitely attain it; as for the defiled [attainment], it is acquired through rebirth and through falling away.

That is to say, when one dies in a higher stage and is reborn in a lower stage, one acquires the defilements of that lower stage; likewise, when one falls away from detachment regarding a particular stage, one acquires the defilements of that stage.
Regarding which attainments (*samāpatti*) arise after which [attainments], and how many such attainments arise?
The verse says:
An untainted [state] is followed by the arising of the wholesome, Extending upward and downward to the third level;
The same applies to the arising after a pure [state], Which also gives rise to the defiled states of its own level.
Defiled [states] arise from their own pure and defiled [states], as well as from the pure states of the immediately lower stage.
At death, the pure state gives rise to all [states]. Defiled [states] arise from their own and lower defiled [states].
The Commentary says:

The untainted [state] gives rise in succession to its own level and to the wholesome states of the levels above and below; the term "wholesome" here fully includes both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
However, it reaches only as far as the third level in either direction; because they are too distant, it lacks the capacity to skip over and arise in the fourth.

Therefore, among the seven uncontaminated attainments (*anāsrava-samāpatti*), six arise immediately after the first dhyāna: namely, the pure and uncontaminated [attainments] of its own level, the second, and the third.
Seven arise immediately after the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*): namely, the six of its own level and the lower levels, and the pure [attainment] of the higher level.
From the second dhyāna, eight [minds] arise in immediate succession: namely, the six belonging to its own level and the higher levels, plus two from the lower level.

From the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), nine [minds] arise in immediate succession: namely, the six belonging to its own level and the lower levels, plus three from the higher levels.
From the third and fourth formless attainments (*ārūpya*), ten [minds] arise immediately thereafter: namely, the eight from the upper and lower realms, plus the two of its own level.
Subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) can immediately give rise to the formless realm;
conventional knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) cannot, because it relies upon and takes as its object the lower realms.
The same applies to that which arises from the pure *samāpatti*: each also simultaneously gives rise to its own level’s defiled states.

From the pure state of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), six states arise immediately thereafter: namely, its own level’s pure and defiled states, as well as the pure and untainted states of the lower levels.
From the first dhyāna, seven [attainments] arise immediately;
from the sphere of nothingness, eight; from the second dhyāna, nine; from the sphere of infinite consciousness, ten; and from the remaining [spheres], eleven.
From a defiled meditative attainment, one arises in its own pure or defiled state, as well as in the pure concentration of the stage immediately below it.

This means that when one is oppressed by the afflictions of one's own level, one also develops a sense of respect for the pure concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*) of a lower level; thus, there is a case where from a defiled state one arises into the pure state of the next lower level.
If one can correctly understand both the defiled and the pure, it is possible to transition from the defiled to the lower pure state;
however, since defiled states themselves lack the capacity for correct understanding, how could they produce the pure state?
This is due to the power of prior vows;
that is to say, one previously made this vow:
"I would rather obtain the purity of the lower realm than require the defilement of the upper realm."
Because the force of a prior vow continues to operate throughout the mental continuum, a subsequent pure meditative absorption arises from within a state of defilement.
This is like first making a resolution before falling asleep, whereby one is able to awaken at the appointed time.

The untainted (*anāsrava*) and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) necessarily do not produce one another; because the pure (*śuddha*) produces both [the pure and the defiled], there is a distinction between the three.
What has been stated regarding the pure producing the defiled refers only to the pure within meditative concentration (*samāhita-śuddha*) and the defiled.

If [the mind] arises as either pure or defiled, its arising as defiled is not so; that is to say, at the time of death, from a pure mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), each and every moment of interruption gives rise to all defiled minds.

If it arises from a defiled mind acquired at birth, each and every moment of interruption can give rise to all defiled minds of its own level and those of lower levels, but it does not give rise to those of higher levels because it has not yet abandoned the lower ones.
Regarding the statement that "the untainted arises from the pure," does it arise in all its aspects? It is not so. How then?
The verse says:
Pure concentration is of four kinds, namely:
that which is conducive to decline, that which is conducive to maintenance, that which is conducive to progress, and that which is subsumed under the stage conducive to penetration.
In order, they accord with the afflictions;
from their own and higher stages, the untainted [states] mutually produce two, three, one, and one respectively.
The commentary says:
There are, in total, four types of pure meditative attainments (*śuddha-samāpatti*):

first, those comprised within the category of retrogression (*hāna-bhāgīya*); second, those comprised within the category of maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*); third, those comprised within the category of progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*); and fourth, those comprised within the category of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).

Each level has four [categories], while the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has only three; this is because there is no higher level to be reached from it, and thus that level lacks the category of "factors conducive to progress" (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
Among these four, only the fourth part can produce the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Why is this so? Because these four types possess such characteristics: the part conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*) conduces to the afflictions; the part conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) conduces to its own level; the part conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) conduces to a higher level; and the part conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*) conduces to the untainted. Therefore, all untainted states arise solely from this last one.

Regarding the mutual production of these four in relation to one another: the first can produce two, namely the *anuloma-avasthāna* (conducive to decline) and the *anuloma-sthiti* (conducive to maintenance).
The second produces three, excluding the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (conducive to penetration).
The third produces three, excluding the *parihāṇabhāgīya* (conducive to decline).
The fourth produces one, namely itself and nothing else.
As stated above, both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) attainments can all leap upward or downward as far as the third.
How does the practitioner cultivate these leap-attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*)?
The verse says:
The two types of meditative concentration proceed both in direct and reverse order; They involve equal intervals, immediate succession, and skipping;
When skipping reaches its limit, it is perfected; This occurs among those of sharp faculties in the three continents who are beyond training.
The treatise states:
The fundamental wholesome attainments (*samāpatti*) are divided into two categories:
first, those with outflows (*sāsrava*), and second, those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Moving upward is called "ascending" (anuloma); returning downward is called "descending" (pratiloma).
Being of the same category is called "even" (sama); being of a different category is called "interrupted" (vyavakīrṇa).
Being adjacent is called "sequential" (krama); skipping one [stage] is called "leaping" (ullaṅghana).

This means that when a practitioner cultivates the leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*), they first repeatedly practice the eight contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) in both forward and reverse order; next, they repeatedly practice the seven uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative attainments in both forward and reverse order; next, they repeatedly practice the contaminated and uncontaminated attainments in alternating forward and reverse order; next, they repeatedly practice the contaminated attainments by leaping over them in both forward and reverse order; and finally, they repeatedly practice the uncontaminated attainments by leaping over them in both forward and reverse order. This is called the completion of the preparatory application for cultivating the leap-concentration.

Subsequently, when one practices the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—in both forward and reverse order, alternating and skipping stages, this is called the accomplishment of the "leap-over concentration" (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*).
Within this, one can only skip over one stage; because it is too distant, there is no capacity to leap over and enter the fourth stage.

The cultivation of the leap-attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) occurs only among humans of the three continents who are Arhats liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*). This is because they possess mastery over meditative concentration and are free from afflictions (*kleśa*).

Those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*), though free from afflictions, lack mastery over concentration; those liberated through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), though possessing mastery over concentration, still have remaining afflictions. Therefore, neither of these groups can cultivate the leap-attainment.
Upon what kind of body do these meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) arise?
The verse says:
The various concentrations depend on their own level or a lower one; not upon a higher level, because it would be useless.
Only a noble one born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can give rise to [a meditative attainment] of a lower stage to exhaust the remaining afflictions.
The treatise says:
All meditative attainments arise based on their own level or a lower level.

Based on a body belonging to a higher stage, it is impossible to give rise to [a mind] of a lower stage, because there is no purpose in giving rise to a lower stage while in a higher stage, because one possesses superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of one's own, because the power of the lower stage is inferior, because it has already been relinquished, and because it is to be despised and rejected.

Although this is the general rule, if one explains it in detail: when a noble being is born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they must necessarily give rise to the untainted state of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). This is because they must exhaust the remaining afflictions of their own level; because they lack a noble path on that level and thus take delight in its arising; and because the Sphere of Nothingness is the most proximate to it. Thus, they cause that [untainted state] to manifest before them and exhaust the remaining afflictions.
What objects do these meditative attainments take as their conditions?
The verse says:
The attainment of relishing takes its own bound [realm] as its object; the pure and the untainted take all realms as their objects.
The fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not take the contaminated states of lower levels as their objects.
The Commentary says:

Attainments through relishing take only the contaminated states of their own level as objects; they never take those of lower levels as objects, because [the practitioner] has already become detached from them.
Nor does it take the higher stages as its object, because the stages of craving are distinct.
It does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, for that would entail it being wholesome (*kuśala*).

Both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted are able to universally take as their objects all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena of their own stage, the lower stages, and the higher stages, as these are all their objects.
Regarding the distinctions: neutral (*avyākṛta*) unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are not objects of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) included within the fundamental stages do not take tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena of lower stages as their objects; however, there are no phenomena of their own or higher stages that they cannot take as objects.

Although it can also take the uncontaminated [states] of lower stages as its object, it takes the category of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as its path, but does not take the category of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*); furthermore, it cannot take the cessation of dharmas of lower stages as its object.

The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realm also take lower levels as their objects, because their uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) necessarily take lower levels as their objects.
Among the three types of meditative attainments—tasting (*āsvādana*), pure (*śuddha*), and untainted (*anāsrava*)—which has the power to sever the various afflictions?
The verse says:
"The untainted [attainments] can sever the afflictions, as can the various pure near-attainments.
The commentary says:
All untainted meditative attainments (*anāsrava-samādhi*) are capable of severing afflictions; even the fundamental purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) lacks such power, let alone the defiled states.
They cannot sever lower [levels of existence], because one has already become free from attachment to them.
One cannot abandon [defilements] of one's own level because one is bound by them;
nor can one abandon those of higher levels because they are superior to oneself.
However, if the pure preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are involved, they can also abandon defilements, because they are all capable of abandoning the defilements of the level immediately below.
The intermediate absorption (*dhyānāntara*) also cannot abandon [the defilements];
how many preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are there;
and with what feelings (*vedanā*) are they associated?
Regarding the three [factors] beginning with taste, are they all present?
The verse says:
The eight preparatory stages possess equanimity and the pure; The first also possesses the noble, and the afflictions are of three kinds.
The treatise states:
There are likewise eight kinds of preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*), as they serve as the gateways to the eight fundamental dhyānas.

All of them are associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because they proceed through the application of effort and because fear of the lower stages has not yet been abandoned.

These eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are all comprised within the pure concentrations (*śuddhaka-samādhi*); however, only the first preparatory stage also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
None of them possess attachment (*āsvādana*), because they are paths for the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya-mārga*).

Although the minds of these preparatory stages may involve the defilement of rebirth (*pratisandhi-kleśa*), this statement is made because they exclude the defilement associated with meditative absorption (*dhyāna-kleśa*).
Some say that the *anāgamya* concentration is also associated with attachment (*sāsvāda*), because even before the fundamental [dhyāna] has arisen, one still craves it.
For this reason, the *anāgamya* possesses all three types; the same applies to the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the [four] main dhyānas, and the various preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Is there no difference in meaning, or is there also a distinction?

There is indeed a distinction in meaning: it is said that all preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) serve as the primary cause for entering [the fundamental dhyāna] by becoming detached from the defilements of the lower stage, whereas this is not the case for the intermediate dhyānas (*dhyānāntara*).
Furthermore, there is another meaning, stated in verse:
In the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka; It possesses all three [dhyāna factors] and consists solely of the feeling of equanimity.
The commentary says:

The initial fundamental dhyāna is associated with vitarka and vicāra, while among the seven higher meditative absorptions (dhyānas), both vitarka and vicāra are entirely absent; only the intermediate dhyāna possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka. Therefore, it excels the first dhyāna yet does not reach the level of the second; based on this principle, it is designated by the name "intermediate."
Because there are no intermediate dhyānas above this level, such fluctuations between stages do not occur.
This concentration possesses all three types, including that which is "savored" (āsvādya), because it possesses superior qualities that are desirable to savor.
All these preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are associated exclusively with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and not with joy (*prīti*), because they proceed through effortful application (*abhisamskāra*).
For this reason, they are said to be subsumed under the "difficult path of practice" (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
This concentration can bring about the fruit of the Great Brahma realm (*mahābrahmā-loka*); those who cultivate it extensively become Great Brahmas.
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) have already been explained.
What, then, are the concentrations (*samādhi*)?
The Sūtras state that there are, in total, three kinds of concentration:
First, with vitarka and vicāra; second, without vitarka and with vicāra only; third, without vitarka and without vicāra.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
The first [dhyāna] possesses vitarka and vicāra; the middle possesses only vicāra; the upper has neither.
The treatise says:
"Samādhi with vitarka and vicāra" refers to meditative concentration (samādhi) associated with vitarka and vicāra; this is comprised within the first dhyāna and the preparatory stage (anāgamya).
Samādhi with no vitarka and only vicāra refers to meditative concentration associated exclusively with vicāra; this is subsumed under the intermediate dhyāna stage.

Samādhi with neither vitarka nor vicāra refers to meditative concentration not associated with either vitarka or vicāra; this extends from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The sūtras further speak of three kinds of samādhi:
first, emptiness; second, wishlessness; and third, signlessness.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Emptiness refers to emptiness and non-self; signlessness refers to the cessation of the four [signs];
wishlessness refers to the remaining ten. These are associated with the aspects of the truths.
This [concentration] is both pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); the untainted is the three doors of liberation.
The treatise says:
"The concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) associated with the two aspects (*ākāra*) of emptiness and non-self."
The signless samādhi refers to meditative concentration associated with the four aspects of the Truth of Cessation.
Because nirvāṇa is free from the ten signs, it is called "signless"; the samādhi that takes that as its object receives the name "signless."
What are the ten aspects?
They are the five [aspects] beginning with form, the two types—male and female—and the three conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

The wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) refers to the meditative absorption (*samāhita*) associated with the ten modes of activity (*ākāra*) that take the remaining truths as their object. This is because [the truths of] suffering and its cause are to be loathed, and the path is like a raft that must necessarily be abandoned.
The meditative attainments that take these as their objects can receive the name "wishless" (apraṇihita) because they all serve to transcend what is currently confronted.
The characteristics of emptiness and non-self are not to be rejected or abandoned, for they resemble the characteristics of nirvāṇa.
Each of these three is of two kinds—namely, pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*)—due to the distinction between mundane and supramundane meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Those included within the mundane pertain to all eleven stages, while those included within the supramundane pertain only to nine stages.
Among these, those that are untainted (anāsrava) are called the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), for they serve as the entryways to nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the sūtras speak of three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
first, the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*); second, the wishlessness of wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita*); and third, the signlessness of signlessness (*animittā-animitta*).
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
The two types of [contemplation on] the heavy [objects] take the Unlearned as their object, and grasp the characteristics of emptiness and impermanence.
Subsequently, taking the concentration on the signless as its object, it regards non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as tranquility.
It is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), belongs to humans, and is not occasional (*akālika*). It is free from the seven lower preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The treatise says:

These three types of meditative concentration (samādhi) take the previously mentioned emptiness and so forth as their objects and apprehend the characteristics of emptiness and so forth; therefore, they are designated by names such as "emptiness-of-emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

The concentration on the emptiness-of-emptiness takes the previously mentioned non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) emptiness-trance (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) as its object and apprehends its characteristic of emptiness; this is because the characteristic of emptiness is more conducive to revulsion than the characteristic of non-self (*anātman*).

The wishless concentration of the wishless takes as its object the wishless concentration of the Aśaikṣas mentioned previously, grasping it through the aspect of impermanence; it does not grasp it through the aspects of suffering or cause and so forth, because those are not the aspects of the untainted (anāsrava), nor does it grasp it through the aspects of the Path and so forth, for the purpose of wearying and relinquishing.

The signless-within-the-signless takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the signless concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is because untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) have no analytical cessation. It apprehends only the aspect of tranquility (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), and not the aspects of cessation, excellence, or detachment (*niḥsaraṇa*), because [otherwise] it would be confused with impermanence-cessation, because [non-analytical cessation] is ethically indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and because it is not a fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
These three types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), because they involve a distaste for the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is not so. Only those from the three continents who are "not occasionally liberated" (*asamayavimukta*) are able to give rise to such profound meditative concentration.

Based on the eleven stages—excluding the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), namely the desire realm, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the eight fundamental dhyānas, and the intermediate concentration—the sūtras further describe four types of meditative cultivation (*samādhi-bhāvanā*):

first, for dwelling in happiness in the present life; second, for attaining superior knowledge and vision; third, for attaining analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, for the perpetual exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
To attain happiness in the present life, one cultivates the various wholesome dhyānas.
To attain superior knowledge and vision, one cultivates the supernormal power of the pure divine eye;
To attain discerning wisdom, one cultivates various preparatory virtues;
To attain the exhaustion of all outflows, one cultivates the diamond-like concentration.
The treatise says:
As stated in the Sūtra:
"There is the cultivation of samādhi; if one practices it, cultivates it, or makes much of it, one attains abiding in happiness in the present life," and so forth, as explained at length.
The term "wholesome" (kuśala) comprehensively includes both the pure (śuddha) and the untainted (anāsrava).

While one attains the happiness of the present life by cultivating all wholesome dhyānas, the Sūtra mentions only the first dhyāna; this is because citing the first illustrates the subsequent ones, though in principle it applies to all.

It is not said that one "dwells" in the happiness of future lives because that happiness is not a fixed state; for one might either fall back, be reborn in a higher realm, or enter parinirvāṇa, and thus no longer abide therein.
If one cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye based on the various meditative concentrations, one will be able to obtain superior knowledge and vision.
If one cultivates the various conditioned wholesome states and untainted wholesome states of the three realms, one will attain analytical wisdom.
If one cultivates the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), one attains the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).

In reality, the cultivation of this concentration relies upon all stages (*bhūmi*); however, that the Sūtra mentions only the fourth dhyāna is because it is traditionally said that the Blessed One was speaking with reference to his own state.

Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-Nine.
Composed by the Venerable Vasubandhu.

Chapter Eight, Part Two: Analysis of Concentration. Having thus explained the concentration that serves as the basis, one should now analyze the merits that arise based upon that concentration.
Among all the virtues, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are explained first.
The verse says:
There are four kinds of immeasurables; they serve as antidotes to hatred and the like.
Compassion has non-hatred as its nature; joy is non-attachment, and equanimity is the relinquishing of both.
These aspects follow their respective order: bestowing happiness, removing suffering, sympathetic joy, and impartiality toward sentient beings.
They take sentient beings of the desire realm as their object.
The first two dhyānas are accompanied by joy; the remaining six are either accompanied by five or ten [mental factors].
They cannot sever the various afflictions; when arising in the human realm, they constitute three types of meditative absorption.
The Commentary says:
There are four immeasurables: first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; and fourth, equanimity.
They are called "immeasurable" because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their object, they induce immeasurable merit, and they result in immeasurable fruits.
For what reason are there only these four?
Because they serve as antidotes to the four types of predominant obstacles.
What are these four obstacles?
That is to say, malice, ill-will, lack of appreciation, sensual desire, and hatred are [the afflictions];
in order to counteract these respectively, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others are established.
If both the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) counteract sensual desire, what is the difference between them?
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"There are two types of sensual desire: first, desire for form; second, sexual desire. Impurity (*aśubha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) serve as their respective remedies.
In reality, however, it is impurity that serves as the remedy for sexual desire, while equanimity serves as the remedy for desire for other relatives and friends.

Among these four, the essence of the first two is non-hatred; in reality, it should be said that compassion (karuṇā) is non-harming (avihiṃsā), sympathetic joy (muditā) is the feeling of joy (saumanasya), and equanimity (upekṣā) is non-attachment (alobha). If their retinues are included, they have the five aggregates as their essence.
If equanimity has non-attachment as its nature, how can it counteract hatred?
Since the hatred to be countered is induced by attachment, it follows logically that [equanimity] should actually have both factors as its essence.
Regarding the specific aspects (*ākāra*) of these four immeasurables: how might one cause all classes of sentient beings to obtain such happiness?
Thinking thus, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of loving-kindness.
"How might I cause all sentient beings to be free from such suffering?
Thinking thus, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of compassion (*karuṇā*).
"How wonderful it would be if all sentient beings were to obtain happiness and be free from suffering!"
Reflecting in this way, one enters the meditative attainment of joy (*muditā-samāpatti*).
Reflecting that all classes of sentient beings are equal and without distinction between friend and enemy,
one enters the meditative attainment of equanimity (*upekṣā-samāpatti*).
Since these four immeasurables cannot actually cause others to obtain happiness and so forth, are they not erroneous?

No, because one wishes for them to obtain happiness and so forth, and because the underlying intention (*āśaya*) is non-erroneous, arising in association with the perception of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-saṃjñā*).
If this were a perversion, what further fault would there be?
If it were to be considered non-virtuous, that would not be logical, because it arises in association with the roots of virtue.
If it were to be considered a cause for drawing forth evil, that too would not be logical, because its power is able to counteract hatred and other such afflictions.
This [immeasurable] takes all sentient beings of the desire realm as its object, because it can counteract obstacles such as hatred directed toward them.
Nevertheless, the Sūtra states:
"One cultivates loving-kindness and the others by contemplating one direction and then the entire world."
This sutra mentions the vessel to reveal what is within it.
The third [type] relies solely on the first two dhyānas, because it is subsumed under the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*); it does not exist in other meditative stages.
The remaining three types rely universally upon six stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).

Some maintain that these depend solely on five stages—excluding the *anāgamya* (threshold) stage—on the grounds that this is a quality of composure (*praśrabdhi*) that can only be generated by those who have already abandoned desire.

Others maintain that these four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), as appropriate, depend on all ten stages: namely, the four fundamental dhyānas, their four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). This latter view intends to include both the fundamental and preparatory stages, as well as both the concentrated (*samāhita*) and non-concentrated (*asamāhita*) levels, within the category of the immeasurables.

Although it was previously stated that this [meditative state] can counteract the four obstacles, it cannot bring about the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because it is comprised within the fundamental dhyānas of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) realm, because it arises in association with attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), and because it takes all sentient beings as its universal object.

In this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one subdues anger and other afflictions; alternatively, it is because this [stage] can cause what has already been abandoned to become even more remote.

It was previously stated that this serves as the antidote to the four obstacles; that is to say, even in the desire realm and the threshold state (*anāgamya*), there exist loving-kindness and the others, which resemble the fundamental immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) accomplished through cultivation.

Having thereby subdued obstacles such as hatred, one brings about the arising of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), which is capable of severing all afflictions (*kleśa*). Once the afflictions have been severed, it is only within the state of freedom from defilement (*vairāgyāvasthā*) that one attains the four fundamental immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
In this subsequent stage, even when encountering powerful conditions, one is not obscured or overwhelmed by anger and the like.
How does one cultivate loving-kindness during the stage of initial practice?

It means first reflecting upon the happiness one has personally experienced, or hearing descriptions of the happiness experienced by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, and then forming this thought:
May all sentient beings equally experience such happiness.

If their afflictions are naturally so intense that they are unable to direct their minds with such equanimity, they should categorize sentient beings into three classes: namely, friends and kin, neutral persons, and enemies.
Friends are further divided into three categories—superior, middling, and inferior;
those of the middling category are singular;
and enemies are likewise divided into three—inferior, middling, and superior—thus forming seven categories in total.
Having thus distinguished the categories, one first generates a sincere resolve for the supreme happiness of one's closest relatives.
Once this aspiration is accomplished, one gradually cultivates such a resolve for those of middling and lower intimacy as well.

Having attained equanimity toward the three grades of friends, one next gradually cultivates such resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) toward those who are neutral, and toward enemies—whether middling, inferior, or superior. Through the power of repeated practice, one becomes able to give rise to the wish to bestow happiness upon a superior enemy, equal to that which one feels toward a superior friend.

Once this resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) has been cultivated to the point of being irreversible, one next gradually expands it with respect to the object of focus. That is to say, one progressively extends the mental visualization to contemplate a single village, a single country, a single region, and finally all worlds, such that the aspect of bestowing happiness pervades them all without exception; this constitutes the completion of the cultivation of the immeasurable state of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).

One who seeks out the virtues of sentient beings is able to cultivate the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and bring it to swift accomplishment, whereas one who seeks out their faults cannot. This is because even those who have severed the roots of goodness possess virtues that may be recorded, and even rhinoceros-like solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*) possess faults that may be noted, as the fruits of their prior merit and demerit are visible in the present.
The cultivation of the methods of compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) should be understood according to this principle.

That is to say, one contemplates sentient beings submerged in the ocean of manifold sufferings and forms the wish that they all attain liberation; furthermore, one imagines sentient beings obtaining happiness and being free from suffering, and then feels profound gratification, thinking, "How truly joyful it is!"

The cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) first arises from neutral persons, and proceeds gradually until one is able to give rise to a mind of impartiality toward superior relatives, making them equal to neutral persons.
These four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) arise only in human beings and not in others; whenever one attains even one of them, the other three are necessarily accomplished as well.
Because those born in the third dhyāna and above do not possess joy (*prīti*).
Having already explained the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), next the liberations (*vimokṣa*) will be explained.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of liberation: the first three have non-attachment as their nature;
they are each fixed to two, two, and one dhyāna respectively; the four formless absorptions are wholesome;
and the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception arises immediately after the "subtle-subtle" mind.
From the pure mind of its own stage, and from the outflow-free [minds] of the lower stages, there are three objects:
the desire realm and the visible; four objects:
the category of the Path and the Suffering, Origin, and Cessation of one's own and higher stages; as well as non-analytical cessation and space.
The treatise states: There are eight liberations:

first, the liberation consisting of perceiving external forms while having internal perception of form; second, the liberation consisting of perceiving external forms while lacking internal perception of form; third, the pure liberation, which is realized through bodily witness and dwelt in fully; fourth through seventh, the four formless attainments as the next four liberations; and eighth, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling as the eighth liberation.
Among these eight, the first three have non-attachment as their essential nature, because they directly counteract attachment.
However, when the Sūtras speak of "perception" (saṃjñā) and "contemplation" (vipaśyanā), it is because perception and contemplation are predominant therein.
Of these three, the first two proceed by way of the aspect of impurity, as they produce various mental images such as the bluish discoloration of a corpse.
The third liberation functions as the transformation of the aspect of purity, because it functions by producing the aspect of pure, radiant clarity.
All three, together with their attendants, are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

As for the first two liberations, each relies upon both the first and second *dhyānas*, because they are able to counteract the craving for visible forms within the desire realm and the first *dhyāna*.
The third liberation relies upon the final dhyāna because the mind is pure and clear, being free from the eight calamities.
Although similar liberations exist in other stages, they are not established [as formal liberations] because they are not predominant.
The next four liberations, in their respective order, have the wholesome states of the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) as their intrinsic nature.
They are neither neutral nor defiled, because these are not liberations;
nor are they mundane wholesome states, because their nature is weak and inferior.
Regarding those wholesome states of distraction, they are like the mind at the moment of death.
Some say that there are also wholesome states of distraction at other times.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the proximate stage also receives the name "liberation," whereas the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) does not,
because it takes a lower stage as its object.
That [path] must turn its back upon the lower stage before it can be called "liberation."

However, in other places, it is mostly stated that only those fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) are called "liberations" (*vimokṣa*), because they are not fully present within the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The eighth liberation is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth have already been explained previously.

Because this [attainment] arises from turning away from feeling and perception, or because it turns away from all objects of cognition in general, this attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) receives the name "liberation.
Some say: "By means of this, one is liberated from the hindrances to meditative concentration; following the 'subtle-subtle' mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), this attainment manifests."
The preceding state of perception and mind was already termed "subtle"; because this is even more subtle than that, it is called "ultra-subtle" (sūkṣma-sūkṣma).

Next, with such a mind, one enters the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Emerging from the attainment of cessation, one either gives rise to a pure meditative mind of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) or is able to give rise to an untainted (anāsrava) mind of the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Thus, the mind that enters [the attainment] is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the mind that emerges from it may be either contaminated or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Among these eight [attainments], the first three take only the form base (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as their object.
Regarding their distinctions: two objects are loathsome while one object is desirable.

Furthermore, each of the subsequent four liberations takes as its objective support the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation of its own level and those above it, the category of path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna) belonging to all levels, the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of those [truths], and empty space.
Why is there no liberation in the third dhyāna?
Because within the third dhyāna there is no craving for the formless, and because it is disturbed by the exquisite pleasure of its own stage.
For what reason does the practitioner cultivate the pure liberation?
This is for the purpose of causing the mind to experience a momentary state of joy.
Previously, the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) caused the mind to become dejected; now, by practicing the meditation on purity (śubha-bhāvanā), one stimulates and inspires it toward joy.
Alternatively, it is for the sake of definitively knowing one's own capability: namely, whether the previously cultivated liberation through impurity has been accomplished or not.
If one contemplates the aspect of purity (*śubha-nimitta*), afflictions do not arise, for that [contemplation] is what brings about their cessation.
Due to two conditions, practitioners of yoga cultivate liberation and so forth: first, to ensure that already-abandoned afflictions are further distanced;

second, to attain superior mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Consequently, they are able to give rise to qualities such as the "absence of strife" (*araṇā*) and the noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), through which they can transform various phenomena and perform diverse functions such as prolonging or relinquishing life.
For what reason does the Sūtra state that bodily realization (*kāyena sākṣātkriyā*) is mentioned for the third and eighth [liberations] alone, and not for the other six?
It is because these two are superior among the eight, and because each occupies an extreme position within its respective pair of realms.
Having already explained the liberations (*vimokṣa*), next the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are explained.
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of spheres of mastery; Two are like the first liberation.
The next two are like the second [base], and the final four are like the third.
The treatise says:
There are eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

First, perceiving external forms while having internal perception of form, observing them as few; second, perceiving external forms while having internal perception of form, observing them as many; third, being without internal perception of form, perceiving external forms as few; fourth, being without internal perception of form, perceiving external forms as many. Adding to these four the four consisting of being without internal perception of form while perceiving external forms as blue, yellow, red, and white, they total eight.
Among the eight, the first two are like the first liberation; the next two are like the second liberation; and the latter four are like the third liberation.
If this is so, how do the eight bases of mastery differ from the three liberations?

The cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*) previously discussed can only involve turning away [from objects], whereas the subsequent cultivation of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) can control the focal object (*ālambana*); thus, according to whatever one contemplates with pleasure, afflictions will ultimately not arise.
Having explained the spheres of mastery, next the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) will be explained.
The verse says:
There are ten kinds of totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*); eight are like the pure liberations (*śubhavimokṣa*);
the latter two are the pure formless attainments (*śuddhārūpyasamāpatti*); they take the four aggregates of their own level as their object.
The treatise states:
There are ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), namely: observing earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, as well as the two boundless spheres of space and consciousness.
Because they observe all places universally and without interval, they are called "totalities" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Among the ten, the first eight are like the pure liberations (*śuddhavimokṣa*); that is, their eight intrinsic natures are all non-attachment (*alobha*).
If their associated factors (*sāhāya*) are included, they have the five aggregates as their nature; they rely on the fourth dhyāna and take the visible forms of the desire realm as their object.
Other masters say:

Only the *vāyu-kṛtsnāyatana* takes the wind element among the tangible objects as its object; the latter two *kṛtsnāyatanas* have, respectively, the two pure formless states of space and consciousness as their intrinsic nature, each taking the four aggregates of its own level as its object.

It should be understood that herein, the practitioner of meditation enters the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) from the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and enters the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) from the spheres of mastery; this is because each subsequent stage arises as superior to each preceding one.
By what means are the merits of these three gateways—liberation and so forth—attained?
Upon what body do they arise?
The verse says:
The attainment of cessation has been explained as before; all others are obtained through both types [of acquisition].
Those in the formless realms depend on the three realms; the rest arise only in the human destiny.
The treatise says:
The eighth liberation has already been explained previously, as it is identical to the aforementioned attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The remaining liberations and so forth are obtained through both means—that is, through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*) and through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)—because there are those that have been practiced before and those that have not.

The four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*) and the two formless totalities (*ārūpya-kṛtsnāyatana*) each arise based on bodies belonging to any of the three realms; the remaining ones arise only among humans.
By the power of the teaching, both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) are able to manifest them.
By what specific conditions do those born in the form and formless realms give rise to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
The verse says:
In the two realms, by means of causes and karma, One is able to give rise to the formless concentrations.
The arising of dhyāna in the form realm is also due to the power of *dharmatā*.
The treatise says:
Birth in the two higher realms is generally brought about by three conditions, which enable one to further induce the production of the form and formless absorptions (*dhyāna*).
First, by the power of the cause (*hetu-bala*): this refers to having previously cultivated [the concentration] both recently and repeatedly, thereby serving as the causal condition.

Second, by the power of karma (*karma-bala*): this refers to having previously created karma that brings about rebirth in a higher realm and is to be experienced in a subsequent life; when the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma is about to arise and manifest, its force is able to cause one to further give rise to that meditative absorption.
Because if one has not yet abandoned the afflictions of a lower stage, there is absolutely no possibility of being born in a higher stage.

Third is the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that is to say, when the vessel-world is about to be destroyed, sentient beings of the lower stages naturally (*dharmataḥ*) are able to give rise to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher stages.
Because all wholesome dharmas present in this state increase and flourish through the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).

Those born in the two higher realms who give rise to formless attainments do so through the power of causes and karma, not through the power of the nature of things; thus, the Anabhraka and other heavens are not destroyed by the three calamities.

When one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) gives rise to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it occurs through the two aforementioned conditions as well as the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
When one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gives rise to a higher meditative concentration, it should be understood that each instance occurs solely through the power of instruction (*śāsana*).
The various Dharma-gates previously analyzed were all for the purpose of propagating and upholding the True Dharma of the World-Honored One.
What is meant by the "True Dharma," and for how long shall it remain?
The verse says:
The Buddha’s True Dharma is twofold, Having as its essence the teaching and the realization;
As long as there are those who uphold, explain, and practice it, It shall abide in the world.
The treatise states:
The essence of the World-Honored One’s True Dharma is twofold: first, the teaching; second, the realization.
"Teaching" refers to the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma; "realization" refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of the three vehicles.
If there are those who can receive, uphold, and correctly expound [the teachings], the Buddha’s true teaching of the Dharma will abide in the world.
If there are those who can rely on the teaching and practice it correctly, the Buddha’s true realization of the Dharma will abide in the world.
Therefore, one should know that the duration for which the True Dharma (saddharma) remains corresponds to the lifespan of these three individuals while they abide in the world.

Although the holy teachings generally state that it remains for only a thousand years, some explain that the Dharma of realization (adhigamadharma) remains for only a thousand years, while the Dharma of instruction (śāsanadharma) remains for a period exceeding this.
This treatise relies upon the Abhidharma; by what principle does it explain the *Abhidharma*?
The verse says:
The system established by the scholars of Kaśmīra— I have for the most part relied upon that to explain the *Abhidharma*.
"Where there is little depreciation [of their views], that is my fault; the determination of the correct principles of the Dharma rests with the Muni.
The treatise says:

The masters of the *Vibhāṣā* in the kingdom of Kaśmīra have well-established the principles of the Abhidharma; I have for the most part relied upon them to explain the tenets of the Abhidharma, and where there is little depreciation [of their views], that is my own error.
The discernment of the correct principles of the Dharma belongs solely to the World-Honored One and the great holy disciples of the Tathāgatas.
Since the Great Teacher, the Eye of the World, has long since closed his eyes, and those capable of serving as witnesses have for the most part perished,
those who do not perceive the True Reality and lack self-restraint will, through their base speculations, bring disorder to the Holy Teaching.
Having personally realized the supreme peace, those who upheld his teachings have mostly passed away;
the world is now without a protector, its manifold virtues lost, and the afflictions roam at will, unrestrained by the hook of discipline.
Knowing that the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is gradually perishing as if it had reached one's throat,
and that this is a time when the power of all afflictions increases, one should seek liberation and not be negligent.
Chapter Nine: Refuting the Attachment to a Self, Part One. If one transcends this [basis] and relies upon something else, could there not be liberation?
In principle, there certainly would not.
Why is this so? Because they are deluded by false grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

This means that these various selves grasped at by those outside the Dharma do not consist of a truly existent self separate from the aggregates (*skandha*), for they falsely grasp at such a self as being established upon the continuity of the aggregates.
The afflictions arise through the power of self-grasping, such that liberation from the saṃsāra of the three realms of existence is impossible.
What serves as proof?
One knows that the various names for "self" merely designate the continuity of the aggregates; they do not refer to a separate, substantial self-entity.
Within that postulated self which is distinct from the aggregates, there exists no true realization or valid inference;
for if the essence of the self were a separate, substantial entity, it would be like any other existing phenomenon.

If there were no obstructing conditions, it should be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as in the case of the six objects and the mind; or it should be apprehended through inference (*anumāna*), as in the case of the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*).

Regarding the statement that the five material sense-faculties are apprehended through inference: it is as seen in the world, where although various conditions are present, the result does not arise due to the absence of a specific condition, yet it arises when that is not absent—just as a seed produces a sprout.

Likewise, it is observed that even when conditions such as present objects and mental attention are present, consciousness arises or does not arise in those who are blind or deaf versus those who are not; from this, one certainly knows that there must be a deficiency or non-deficiency of some other specific condition.
These distinct conditions are the sense faculties, such as the eye; this is what is called inference based on the physical sense faculties (*rūpīndriya-anumāna*).
Since neither of these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies to a self that is separate from the aggregates, it is thereby established that there is no real essence of a self.
However, the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the *pudgala* exists, its substance being neither identical to nor different from the aggregates (*skandha*).
This must be investigated: is it real or is it merely conventional?
What is the distinction between the characteristics of substantial existence (*dravyasat*) and nominal existence (*prajñaptisat*)?
The characteristic of substantial existence is that there is a distinct entity, such as form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth.
The characteristic of nominal existence is that there is merely an aggregation, such as milk, curd, and so forth.
What faults are there in asserting it as real or asserting it as conventional?
If its substance were real, it would have to be distinct from the aggregates, because it would possess a separate nature, like the individual aggregates.
Furthermore, any real entity must necessarily have a cause, or else it would have to be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, it would be useless to insist that it exists substantially;
if its essence were merely conventional, it would be identical to my own position.
Is the *pudgala* I establish not like what you have questioned—neither substantially nor conventionally existent?
To say merely that "the person (pudgala) is established based on the appropriated aggregates belonging to the internal present" does not clarify the meaning of this erroneous statement;
I still do not understand in what sense it is called "based."

If "appropriating the aggregates" means "being the basis for this," then since the *pudgala* is formed by appropriating the aggregates, the *pudgala* must be a conventional existence (*prajñaptisat*), just as milk, curd, and so forth are formed by appropriating color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects].

If the meaning of "basis" were that it is dependent upon the aggregates, then since the *pudgala* is established in dependence upon the aggregates, the *pudgala* would likewise incur this same fault; therefore, it is not established in such a manner.
How is this established?
It is like the conventional establishment of fire based upon fuel. How can it be said that fire is established based upon fuel?
It means that while fire cannot be established as existing apart from fuel, fuel and fire are neither different nor identical.
If fire were different from fuel, the fuel would not be hot.
If fire and fuel were one, that which is burned would be the burner itself.
In this same way, the person (pudgala) is not established as distinct from the aggregates (skandhas).

However, the person (pudgala) is neither different from nor identical to the aggregates (skandhas). If it were of a different substance from the aggregates, it would be eternal; if it were of one substance with the aggregates, it would result in annihilationism.
You should now provide a definitive statement on this: what is fire?
What constitutes the fuel?
May you cause me to understand the meaning of fire depending upon fuel.
What should be explained?
If it is said that what is burned is the fuel and what burns is the fire, one must further explain:
which is the burned and which is the burner that are designated as "fuel" and "fire"?
